chapters.title: Introductory Chapter
paragraphs: Among the new things that drew my attention during my stay in the United States, none struck me more forcefully than the general equality of conditions. I soon saw the enormous influence this basic fact has on the whole course of society. It gives a certain direction to public opinion and a certain tone to the laws. It gives new maxims to those who govern and distinctive habits to those who are governed. I quickly realized that the influence of this fact reaches far beyond the country’s politics and laws. It has just as much power over civil society as over the government: it creates opinions, gives rise to feelings, suggests the ordinary practices of life, and changes whatever it does not itself produce. The further I went in studying American society, the more I saw that equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to follow, and the central point to which all my observations kept returning.

I then turned my thoughts to our own hemisphere, where I thought I could see something similar to the spectacle the New World had shown me. I observed that equality of conditions is advancing every day toward the extreme limits it seems to have reached in the United States, and that the democracy that governs the American communities is rising rapidly to power in Europe. That is how I came to conceive the book now before the reader.

Everyone can see that a great democratic revolution is under way among us, but people hold two opinions about its nature and consequences. Some regard it as a recent accident that can still be stopped. Others think it irresistible, because it is the most uniform, the most ancient, and the most lasting tendency in all of history. Consider the situation of France seven hundred years ago. The land was divided among a small number of families, who owned the soil and ruled the people living on it. The right to govern passed down with the family inheritance from generation to generation. Force was the only way one person could act on another, and landed property was the only source of power. Soon, however, the political power of the clergy arose and began to assert itself. The clergy opened its ranks to all classes, poor and rich, serf and lord. Equality entered the government through the Church, and a man who as a serf would have lived out his life in perpetual bondage took his place as a priest among nobles, often above the heads of kings.

As society gradually became more stable and more civilized, the relations among men grew more complicated and more numerous. People began to feel the need for civil laws, and the order of legal officials soon rose from the obscurity of the courts and their dusty chambers to appear at the monarch’s court, beside the feudal barons in their ermine and their mail. While kings were ruining themselves with their great enterprises and nobles were exhausting their resources in private wars, the lower orders were growing rich through commerce. The influence of money began to be felt in affairs of state. Business opened a new road to power, and the financier rose to a position of political influence in which he was both flattered and despised. Gradually, as learning spread and the taste for literature and art grew, talent gained chances of success. Science became a means of government, intelligence led to social power, and the man of letters took part in the affairs of state. The value placed on the privileges of birth fell in exact proportion as new paths to advancement opened. In the eleventh century nobility was beyond all price. In the thirteenth it could be bought. It was conferred for the first time in 1270, and so equality was introduced into the government by the aristocracy itself.

In the course of these seven hundred years, the nobles sometimes granted the people a share of political rights, either to resist the authority of the Crown or to weaken their rivals. More often, the king allowed the lower orders some measure of power in order to hold the aristocracy in check. In France the kings have always been the most active and the most constant levelers. When they were strong and ambitious, they spared no effort to raise the people to the level of the nobles. When they were moderate or weak, they let the people rise above themselves. Some helped democracy by their talents, others by their vices. Louis XI and Louis XIV reduced every rank beneath the throne to the same subjection. Louis XV, with his whole court, sank into the dust.

As soon as land came to be held on terms other than feudal tenure, and personal property in its turn began to confer influence and power, every improvement in commerce or manufacturing became a fresh element of the equality of conditions. From then on, every new discovery, every new want it created, and every new desire demanding satisfaction was a step toward a universal level. The taste for luxury, the love of war, the sway of fashion, and the most superficial as well as the deepest passions of the human heart all worked together to enrich the poor and impoverish the rich.

From the time when exercising the intellect became a source of strength and wealth, every addition to science, every fresh truth, and every new idea had to be seen as a seed of power placed within the people’s reach. Poetry, eloquence, memory, the grace of wit, the glow of imagination, the depth of thought, and all the gifts that Providence hands out with an equal hand turned to the advantage of democracy. Even when its adversaries possessed these gifts, they still served its cause by bringing out the natural greatness of man. Its conquests therefore spread along with those of civilization and knowledge, and literature became an arsenal where the poorest and the weakest could always find weapons ready to hand.

If we read through our history, we will hardly find a single great event in the past seven hundred years that has not turned to the advantage of equality. The Crusades and the English wars thinned out the nobles and divided their estates. The founding of communes introduced an element of democratic liberty into the heart of the feudal monarchy. The invention of firearms made the serf and the noble equal on the battlefield. Printing offered the same resources to the minds of all classes. The post was organized to bring the same information to the door of the poor man’s cottage and to the gate of the palace. Protestantism declared that all men are equally able to find the road to heaven. The discovery of America opened a thousand new paths to fortune and put riches and power within reach of the adventurous and the obscure. If we look at what has happened in France at intervals of fifty years, beginning with the eleventh century, we will invariably see a twofold revolution in the state of society. The noble has gone down the social ladder, and the commoner has gone up. One descends as the other rises. Every half century brings them closer together, and very soon they will meet.

Nor is this phenomenon at all peculiar to France. Wherever we turn our eyes, we see the same continual revolution throughout the whole of Christendom. In every country, the various events of national life have turned to the advantage of democracy. All men have helped it with their efforts: those who deliberately worked for its cause and those who served it without knowing it, those who fought for it and those who declared themselves its opponents. All have been driven along the same track and have worked toward the same end, some in ignorance and some unwillingly. All have been blind instruments in the hands of God.

The gradual development of the equality of conditions is therefore a providential fact, and it has all the characteristics of a divine decree. It is universal, it is lasting, it constantly escapes all human interference, and all events as well as all men contribute to its progress. Would it then be wise to imagine that a social movement dating from so far back can be stopped by the efforts of one generation? Is it believable that the democracy that has destroyed the feudal system and defeated kings will respect the citizen and the capitalist? Will it stop now that it has grown so strong and its adversaries so weak? No one can say where we are going, for we have nothing to compare with. Equality of conditions is more complete in the Christian countries of today than it has ever been at any time or in any part of the world. The extent of what already exists therefore prevents us from foreseeing what may still come.

This whole book has been written under the influence of a kind of religious dread, which the author felt as he contemplated a revolution so irresistible. It has advanced for centuries in spite of astonishing obstacles, and it is still going on in the midst of the ruins it has made. God does not need to speak himself for us to see the unmistakable signs of his will. We can discern them in the ordinary course of nature and in the constant tendency of events. I know, without any special revelation, that the planets move in the orbits traced by the Creator’s finger. Suppose the men of our time were led by careful observation and honest reflection to recognize that the gradual, progressive development of social equality is both the past and the future of their history. That single truth would give the change the sacred character of a divine decree. To try to stop democracy would then be to resist the will of God, and nations would have no choice but to make the best of the social lot Providence has assigned them.

The Christian nations of our age seem to me to present a most alarming spectacle. The movement carrying them along is so strong that it cannot be stopped, but it is not yet so fast that it cannot be guided. Their fate is in their own hands, though in a little while it may no longer be. The first duty of those who direct our affairs at this time is to educate the democracy: to warm its faith, if that is possible; to purify its morals; to direct its energies; to replace its inexperience with a knowledge of practical affairs, and its blind impulses with an understanding of its true interests; to adapt its government to time and place; and to change it to suit the events and the people of the age. A new science of politics is needed for a new world. Yet this is what we think about least. Launched into the middle of a rapid stream, we stubbornly fix our eyes on the ruins still visible on the shore we have left, while the current sweeps us along and drives us backward toward the abyss.

In no country in Europe has the great social revolution I have been describing advanced as rapidly as in France, but there it has always been carried forward by chance. The heads of the state never planned for its demands, and its victories were won without their consent or without their knowledge. The most powerful, the most intelligent, and the most moral classes of the nation never tried to ally themselves with it in order to guide it. The people were therefore left to their wild impulses, and they grew up like those outcasts who are educated in the public streets and know nothing of society but its vices and its misery. The existence of a democracy seemed to be unknown, until it suddenly took possession of supreme power. Then everything was submitted to its whims, and it was worshipped as the idol of strength. At last, weakened by its own excesses, it was met by lawmakers who rashly conceived the plan of destroying its power instead of instructing it and correcting its vices. No one tried to prepare it to govern. Everyone set about shutting it out of the government.

The result has been that the democratic revolution has taken place only in the material parts of society, without the accompanying change in laws, ideas, customs, and mores that was needed to make such a revolution beneficial. We have gotten a democracy, but without the conditions that would reduce its vices and bring out its natural advantages. And although we already see the evils it brings, we do not know the benefits it may offer.

While the power of the Crown, supported by the aristocracy, governed the nations of Europe in peace, society had, amid its misery, several advantages that are now hard to appreciate or even imagine. The power of one part of his subjects was an insurmountable barrier to the prince’s tyranny. The monarch felt that the multitude saw him as almost divine, and the respect he inspired gave him a reason to use his power justly. However high they stood above the people, the nobles could not help taking the calm and kindly interest in its fate that a shepherd takes in his flock. Without acknowledging the poor as their equals, they watched over the destiny of those whose welfare Providence had entrusted to their care. The people had never conceived of a social condition different from their own, and they did not expect ever to rank with their chiefs. They accepted benefits from their superiors without questioning their rights. They grew attached to them when they were merciful and just, and they submitted to their exactions without resistance or servility, as to the unavoidable visitations of the arm of God. Custom and the habits of the time had also created a kind of law amid the violence and set certain limits to oppression. The noble never suspected that anyone would try to deprive him of the privileges he believed to be legitimate, and the serf regarded his own inferiority as a consequence of the unchangeable order of nature. It is therefore easy to imagine that a mutual exchange of goodwill took place between two classes so differently endowed by fate. Inequality and misery existed in society then, but the souls of neither class were degraded. Men are not corrupted by exercising power or debased by the habit of obeying. They are corrupted by exercising a power they believe to be illegitimate, and by obeying a rule they consider usurped and oppressive. On one side were wealth, strength, and leisure, along with the refinements of luxury, the elegance of taste, the pleasures of wit, and the religion of art. On the other were labor and a crude ignorance. Yet among this coarse and ignorant multitude it was not uncommon to find energetic passions, generous feelings, deep religious convictions, and independent virtues. A body politic organized in this way could boast of its stability, its power, and above all its glory.

But the scene has now changed. Gradually the two ranks are mingling. The divisions that once separated mankind are being lowered, property is being divided, power is shared, the light of intelligence is spreading, and the abilities of all classes are being cultivated equally. The state becomes democratic, and the empire of democracy is slowly and peacefully introduced into the institutions and customs of the nation. I can imagine a society in which all men would profess an equal attachment and respect for the laws, of which they are the common authors. The authority of the state would be respected as necessary, though not as divine, and the subject’s loyalty to the chief magistrate would be not a passion but a calm and rational conviction. Every individual would possess rights he is sure to keep, and a kind of manly confidence and mutual courtesy would arise among all classes, equally far from pride and from baseness. The people, well aware of their true interests, would accept that to enjoy the advantages of society they must meet its demands. In such a state of things, the voluntary association of citizens could take the place of the individual efforts of the nobles, and the community would be protected equally from anarchy and from oppression.

I admit that in a democratic state so constituted, society will not stand still. But the impulses of the social body can be regulated and directed forward. If there is less splendor than in the halls of an aristocracy, the contrast of misery will also be less frequent. The pleasures of enjoyment may be less extreme, but those of comfort will be more widely shared. The sciences may be less perfectly cultivated, but ignorance will be less common. The violence of feeling will be restrained, and the habits of the nation softened. There will be more vices and fewer crimes. Without enthusiasm or ardent faith, great sacrifices may be obtained from the members of a commonwealth by appealing to their understanding and their experience. Each individual will feel the same need to unite with his fellow citizens to protect his own weakness. Knowing that if they are to help him he must cooperate with them, he will readily see that his personal interest is the same as the interest of the community. The nation as a whole will be less brilliant, less glorious, and perhaps less strong. But the majority of citizens will enjoy greater prosperity, and the people will remain quiet, not because they despair of improvement but because they are aware of the advantages of their condition. Not all the consequences of this state of things would be good or useful, but society would at least have taken for itself all those that are. And having renounced the social advantages of aristocracy once and for all, mankind would enter into possession of all the benefits democracy can offer.

But here we may ask what we have adopted in place of the institutions, ideas, and customs of our forefathers that we have abandoned. The spell of royalty is broken, but it has not been replaced by the majesty of the laws. The people have learned to despise all authority, yet fear now extracts a larger tribute of obedience than reverence and love once did.

I see that we have destroyed the independent individuals who were able to face tyranny single-handed. But it is the government that has inherited the privileges taken from families, corporations, and individuals. The weakness of the whole community has therefore replaced the influence of a small body of citizens, which, if it was sometimes oppressive, was often conservative. The division of property has narrowed the distance between rich and poor. But it seems that the closer they come to each other, the greater their mutual hatred, and the more violent the envy and fear with which they resist each other’s claims to power. The notion of Right means nothing to either class, and Force gives both of them the only argument for the present and the only guarantee for the future. The poor man keeps the prejudices of his forefathers without their faith, and their ignorance without their virtues. He has adopted the doctrine of self-interest as the rule of his actions without understanding the science that governs it, and his egotism is no less blind than his devotion once was. If society is calm, it is not because it relies on its strength and well-being, but because it knows its weakness and its frailty. A single effort may cost it its life. Everyone feels the evil, but no one has the courage or energy to seek the cure. The desires, regrets, sorrows, and joys of the time produce nothing visible or lasting, like the passions of old men, which end in impotence.

We have, then, given up whatever advantages the old state of things offered, without receiving any compensation from our present condition. We have destroyed an aristocracy, and we seem inclined to look at its ruins with complacency and to make our home in the midst of them.

The state of the intellectual world is no less deplorable. The democracy of France, checked in its course or abandoned to its lawless passions, has overthrown whatever stood in its path and has shaken everything it has not destroyed. Its empire over society has not been introduced gradually or established peacefully. It has advanced constantly amid disorder and the turmoil of conflict. In the heat of the struggle, each partisan is carried beyond the limits of his own opinions by the opinions and excesses of his opponents. In the end he loses sight of the goal of his efforts and uses language that disguises his real feelings or secret instincts. Hence the strange confusion we are witnessing. I cannot recall a passage in history more worthy of sorrow and pity than the scenes taking place before our eyes. It is as if the natural bond that joins a man’s opinions to his tastes and his actions to his principles had now been broken. The sympathy that has always been recognized between human feelings and ideas seems to have dissolved, and all the laws of moral analogy seem to have been abolished.

There are zealous Christians among us whose minds are nourished by the love and knowledge of a future life, and who readily take up the cause of human liberty as the source of all moral greatness. Christianity, which has declared all men equal in the sight of God, will not refuse to acknowledge that all citizens are equal in the eyes of the law. But by an odd concurrence of events, religion has become entangled in those institutions that democracy attacks. It is not infrequently driven to reject the equality it loves, and to curse as an enemy the cause of liberty, which it might hallow by its alliance.

Beside these religious men I see others whose eyes are turned more toward the earth than toward Heaven. They support liberty not only as the source of the noblest virtues but especially as the root of all solid advantages, and they sincerely want to extend its sway and bring its blessings to mankind. It would be natural for them to hurry to call on religion for help, for they must know that liberty cannot be established without morality, nor morality without faith. But they have seen religion in the ranks of their adversaries, and they inquire no further. Some of them attack it openly, and the rest are afraid to defend it.

In earlier ages, slavery was defended by the venal and the servile-minded, while the independent and the warm-hearted struggled without hope to save the liberties of mankind. But today we meet men of high and generous character whose opinions contradict their inclinations, and who praise a servility they have never known themselves. Others, on the contrary, speak in the name of liberty as if they could feel its sanctity and its majesty, and loudly claim for humanity rights that they have always denied. There are virtuous and peaceable people whose pure morality, quiet habits, affluence, and talents fit them to be the leaders of those around them. Their love of country is sincere, and they are ready to make the greatest sacrifices for its welfare. But they confuse the abuses of civilization with its benefits, and in their minds the idea of evil cannot be separated from that of novelty.

Not far from this class is another party, whose aim is to make mankind materialistic: to find what is expedient without regard for what is just, to gain knowledge without faith, and prosperity apart from virtue. They take the title of champions of modern civilization and put themselves in a position that they insolently usurp and from which their own unworthiness drives them. Where are we, then? The religious are the enemies of liberty, and the friends of liberty attack religion. The high-minded and noble advocate subjection, and the meanest and most servile minds preach independence. Honest and educated citizens oppose all progress, while men without patriotism or principles are the apostles of civilization and intelligence. Has this been the fate of the centuries before ours? Has man always lived in a world like the present one, where nothing is linked together, where virtue lacks genius and genius lacks honor, where the love of order is confused with a taste for oppression and the sacred rites of freedom with contempt for law? Is it a world where the light conscience casts on human actions is dim, and where nothing seems any longer forbidden or allowed, honorable or shameful, false or true? I cannot believe, however, that the Creator made man in order to leave him in an endless struggle with the intellectual miseries that surround us. God has a calmer and more certain future in store for the communities of Europe. I do not know his designs, but I will not stop believing in them because I cannot fathom them. I would rather doubt my own understanding than his justice.

There is one country in the world where the great revolution I am speaking of seems to have nearly reached its natural limits. It has been carried out there with ease and simplicity. Or rather, that country has arrived at the consequences of the democratic revolution we are going through without having experienced the revolution itself. The emigrants who settled on the shores of America at the beginning of the seventeenth century separated the democratic principle from all the principles that held it back in the old communities of Europe, and they transplanted it, unmixed, to the New World. There it has been allowed to grow in perfect freedom and to bring out its consequences in the laws by shaping the customs of the country.

It seems to me beyond doubt that sooner or later we will arrive, like the Americans, at an almost complete equality of conditions. But I do not conclude from this that we will necessarily be led to draw the same political consequences that the Americans have drawn from a similar social organization. I am far from supposing that they have chosen the only form of government a democracy can adopt. But the fact that the same underlying cause shapes laws and customs in both countries is enough to explain why we have such an immense interest in knowing its effects in each of them.

It is not, then, merely to satisfy a legitimate curiosity that I have examined America. I wanted to find lessons from which we can ourselves profit. Anyone who imagines that I meant to write a panegyric will see that this was not my purpose. Nor have I tried to argue for any particular form of government, for I believe that absolute excellence is rarely to be found in any legislation. I have not even pretended to discuss whether the social revolution, which I believe to be irresistible, is good or bad for mankind. I have accepted this revolution as a fact already accomplished or on the eve of being accomplished. Among the nations that have undergone it, I chose the one in which its development has been the most peaceful and the most complete, so that I could discern its natural consequences and, if possible, identify the means by which it can be made profitable. I confess that in America I saw more than America. I looked for the image of democracy itself, with its inclinations, its character, its prejudices, and its passions, in order to learn what we have to fear or hope from its progress.

In the first part of this work I have tried to show the tendency that the democracy of America gives to the laws. That democracy is left almost without restraint to its instinctive impulses. I have also tried to show the course it prescribes for the government and the influence it has on public affairs. I have sought to discover the evils and the advantages it produces. I have examined the precautions the Americans take to direct it, and those they have not taken, and I have undertaken to point out the causes that enable it to govern society. I do not know whether I have succeeded in making known what I saw in America. But I am certain that this has been my sincere desire, and that I have never knowingly bent facts to fit ideas instead of ideas to fit facts.

Whenever a point could be established from written documents, I went to the original text and to the most authentic and respected works. I have cited my authorities in the notes, and anyone may consult them. Whenever the question concerned an opinion, a political custom, or a remark about the customs of the country, I tried to consult the best-informed men I met. If the point was important or doubtful, I was not satisfied with one witness, but formed my opinion from the testimony of several. Here the reader must necessarily take my word. I could often have named people he knows, or who deserve to be known, as proof of what I say, but I have carefully avoided doing so. A stranger often hears important truths at his host’s fireside that the host would perhaps hide from the ear of a friend. The host consoles himself with his guest for the silence he is otherwise bound to keep, and the shortness of the traveler’s stay removes any fear that he will be indiscreet. I carefully noted down every conversation of this kind as soon as it happened, but these notes will never leave my writing case. I would rather weaken the force of my statements than add my name to the list of strangers who repay generous hospitality with later vexation and annoyance.

I know that, in spite of my care, nothing will be easier than to criticize this book, if anyone ever chooses to. Readers who examine it closely will discover the fundamental idea that connects its several parts. But the subjects I have had to treat are extremely diverse, and it will not be difficult to set an isolated fact against the body of facts I cite, or an isolated idea against the body of ideas I put forward. I hope to be read in the spirit that has guided my work, and I hope my book will be judged by the general impression it leaves, just as I formed my own judgment not on any single reason but on the mass of evidence. We must not forget that an author who wants to be understood is obliged to push all his ideas to their furthest theoretical consequences, often to the verge of what is false or impractical. In active life we sometimes have to depart from the rules of logic, but this is not so in discourse, and a man finds that nearly as many difficulties come from inconsistency of language as usually come from inconsistency of conduct.

I conclude by pointing out myself what many readers will consider the main defect of the work. This book is written to favor no particular views, and in composing it I have had no intention of serving or attacking any party. I have tried not to see differently from them but to look further than they do. While they are busy with tomorrow, I have turned my thoughts to the Future.

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Exterior Form Of North America
paragraphs: North America has certain general features in its outward form that are easy to pick out at first glance. A kind of methodical order seems to have governed the division of land and water, mountains and valleys. Amid the confusion of objects and the enormous variety of scenery, one can make out a simple but grand design. The continent is divided almost equally into two vast regions. The first is bounded on the north by the Arctic Pole, and on the east and west by the two great oceans. It stretches southward in the shape of a triangle, whose irregular sides finally meet below the great lakes of Canada. The second region begins where the first ends and takes in the rest of the continent. The first slopes gently toward the Pole, the second toward the Equator.

The land in the first region descends toward the north with a slope so gradual that it can almost be called a level plain. Within this immense stretch of country there are no high mountains and no deep valleys. Streams wander through it without any fixed course. Great rivers mingle their currents, part and meet again, scatter into vast marshes, and lose every trace of their channels in the maze of waters they have created themselves. After countless windings they finally reach the Polar Seas. The great lakes that border this first region are not walled in between hills and rocks, as most lakes in the Old World are. Their banks are flat and rise only a few feet above the water, so that each lake forms a vast bowl filled to the brim. The slightest change in the structure of the globe would send their waters rushing either toward the Pole or toward the tropical sea.

The second region has a more varied surface and is better suited to human habitation. Two long chains of mountains divide it from one end to the other. The Alleghany ridge follows the shape of the Atlantic coast, and the other chain runs parallel to the Pacific. The space between these two chains covers 1,341,649 square miles. *a Its area is therefore about six times that of France. Yet this vast territory forms a single valley. One side descends gradually from the rounded summits of the Alleghanies, while the other rises in an unbroken slope toward the tops of the Rocky Mountains. At the bottom of the valley flows an immense river, which receives the streams coming down from the mountains on every side. In memory of their homeland, the French once called this river the St. Louis. The Native Americans, in their pompous language, named it the Father of Waters, the Mississippi.
a [ Darby’s “View of the United States.”]

The Mississippi rises above the boundary between the two great regions I have described, not far from the highest point of the plateau where they meet. Another river rises near the same spot, *b and it empties into the Polar seas. The Mississippi’s early course is uncertain. Several times it winds back toward the north, where it began. Finally, after being held up in lakes and marshes, it flows slowly south. Sometimes it glides quietly along the clay bed that nature has given it, and sometimes it is swollen by storms. In all, the Mississippi waters 2,500 miles of country in its course. *c At a distance of 1,364 miles from its mouth, the river reaches an average depth of fifteen feet, and vessels of 300 tons burden can sail it for nearly 500 miles. Fifty-seven large navigable rivers add to its waters. Among them are the Missouri, which runs for 2,500 miles; the Arkansas, 1,300 miles; the Red River, 1,000 miles; and four others of 800 to 1,000 miles each, namely the Illinois, the St. Peter’s, the St. Francis, and the Moingona. Besides these there is a countless multitude of smaller streams, which bring their tributary waters from every direction.
c [ Warden’s “Description of the United States.”]

The valley watered by the Mississippi seems to have been shaped to be the bed of this mighty river, which, like a god of antiquity, dispenses both good and evil along its course. On the banks of the stream, nature shows an inexhaustible fertility. As you move away from the banks, the power of growth weakens, the soil becomes poor, and the plants that survive grow sickly. Nowhere have the great upheavals of the globe left clearer traces than in the valley of the Mississippi. The whole look of the country shows the powerful effects of water, in its fertility as well as in its barrenness. The waters of the primeval ocean piled up enormous beds of rich soil in the valley, and leveled them as they drew back. On the right bank of the river, one sees immense plains as smooth as if a farmer had gone over them with a roller. As you approach the mountains, the ground becomes steadily more uneven and barren. In a thousand places it is pierced by primitive rocks, which look like the bones of a skeleton whose flesh has partly wasted away. The surface of the earth is covered with granite sand and huge, irregular masses of stone. A few plants force their way up among them, and the whole looks like a green field strewn with the ruins of a vast building. On examination, these stones and this sand prove to be perfectly analogous to those that make up the dry, broken summits of the Rocky Mountains. The flood that washed the soil down to the bottom of the valley later carried off pieces of the rocks themselves. These were dashed and battered against the neighboring cliffs, and were left scattered like wrecks at their feet. *d On the whole, the valley of the Mississippi is the most magnificent dwelling place that God has prepared for man; and yet at present it can be called only a mighty desert.
d [ See Appendix, A.]

On the eastern side of the Alleghanies, between the foot of these mountains and the Atlantic Ocean, lies a long ridge of rocks and sand that the sea seems to have left behind when it withdrew. This strip of land averages no more than one hundred miles in breadth, but it is about nine hundred miles long. The soil of this part of the American continent offers every obstacle to the farmer, and its vegetation is sparse and monotonous.

It was on this inhospitable coast that human industry first made a united effort. That tongue of barren land was the cradle of the English colonies that were destined one day to become the United States of America. The center of power still lies here. Meanwhile, in the backwoods, the true elements of the great people to whom the future control of the continent belongs are gathering almost in secret.

When the Europeans first landed on the shores of the West Indies, and later on the coast of South America, they thought they had been carried into those fabled regions that poets had sung about. The sea sparkled with phosphorescent light, and the extraordinary clearness of its waters showed the navigator everything that had until then been hidden in the deep. *e Here and there small islands appeared, perfumed with fragrant plants and looking like baskets of flowers floating on the calm surface of the ocean. Everything the eye met in this enchanting region seemed prepared to meet man’s needs or add to his pleasures. Almost all the trees were loaded with nourishing fruits, and those that were useless as food delighted the eye with the brilliance and variety of their colors. In groves of fragrant lemon trees, wild figs, flowering myrtles, acacias, and oleanders, hung with garlands of climbing plants in bloom, a multitude of birds unknown in Europe displayed their bright plumage, glittering with purple and azure. Their warbling mingled with the harmony of a world teeming with life and motion. *f Beneath this brilliant surface death lay concealed. But the air of these climates had such an enervating influence that man, absorbed in present enjoyment, became careless of the future.

e [ Malte Brun tells us (vol. v. p. 726) that the water of the Caribbean Sea is so transparent that corals and fish can be seen at a depth of sixty fathoms. The ship seemed to float in air. The navigator grew dizzy as his eye looked down through the crystal flood and saw underwater gardens, or beds of shells, or gilded fishes gliding among tufts and thickets of seaweed.]
f [ See Appendix, B.]

North America appeared in a very different light. There everything was grave, serious, and solemn. It seemed to have been created to be the domain of the intellect, as the South was the domain of sensual delight. A turbulent and foggy ocean washed its shores. It was ringed by a belt of granite rocks or by wide stretches of sand. The foliage of its woods was dark and gloomy, for they consisted of firs, larches, evergreen oaks, wild olive trees, and laurels. Beyond this outer belt lay the thick shade of the central forest, where the largest trees produced in the two hemispheres grow side by side. The plane, the catalpa, the sugar maple, and the Virginian poplar mingled their branches with those of the oak, the beech, and the lime. In these forests, as in those of the Old World, destruction went on without pause. The remains of dead vegetation were heaped on one another, but no laboring hand was there to clear them away, and they did not rot fast enough to make room for the constant work of new growth. Climbing plants, grasses, and other herbs forced their way up through the mass of dying trees. They crept along the bending trunks, found nourishment in their dusty hollows, and made a path beneath the lifeless bark. In this way decay helped life, and the products of the two were mingled together. The depths of these forests were gloomy and dark, and a thousand small streams, whose course no human industry directed, kept them constantly damp. It was rare to find flowers, wild fruits, or birds in their shade. The fall of a tree overthrown by age, the roar of a waterfall, the lowing of the buffalo, and the howling of the wind were the only sounds that broke the silence of nature.

East of the great river, the woods almost disappeared, and prairies of immense extent took their place. Did Nature, in her infinite variety, deny the seeds of trees to these fertile plains? Or were they once covered with forests that human hands later destroyed? Neither tradition nor scientific research has been able to settle the question.

These immense deserts were not, however, without human inhabitants. Some wandering tribes had lived for ages scattered among the forest shades or the green pastures of the prairie. From the mouth of the St. Lawrence to the delta of the Mississippi, and from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean, these savages shared certain resemblances that bore witness to a common origin. At the same time they differed from all other known races of men. *g They were neither white like the Europeans, nor yellow like most Asians, nor black, as Black people are. Their skin was reddish brown, their hair long and shining, their lips thin, and their cheekbones very prominent. The languages of the North American tribes differed in their words, but they followed the same grammatical rules. In several respects these rules differed from the ones that had been observed to govern the origin of language elsewhere. The speech of the Native Americans seemed to be the product of new combinations, and it showed an effort of the understanding of which the Native Americans of our own day would be incapable. *h

g [ As discovery has advanced, some resemblance has been found between the physical build, the language, and the habits of the Native Americans of North America and those of the Tongous, Mantchous, Mongols, Tartars, and other wandering tribes of Asia. The land those tribes occupy is not very far from Behring’s Strait, which makes it possible to suppose that at a remote period they supplied inhabitants to the empty continent of America. But science has not yet made this point clear. See Malte Brun, vol. v.; the works of Humboldt; Fischer, “Conjecture sur l’Origine des Americains”; Adair, “History of the American Indians.”]
h [ See Appendix, C.]

The social state of these tribes also differed in many respects from anything seen in the Old World. They seemed to have multiplied freely in the midst of their deserts, without coming into contact with other races more civilized than themselves. Accordingly, they showed none of those vague and confused notions of right and wrong, and none of that deep corruption of customs, which usually go together with ignorance and crudeness in nations that have advanced to civilization and then fallen back into barbarism. The Native American owed nothing to anyone but himself. His virtues, his vices, and his prejudices were his own work. He had grown up in the wild independence of his nature.

If the lowest classes in polished countries are rude and uncivil, it is not merely because they are poor and ignorant. It is because, being poor and ignorant, they are in daily contact with rich and educated men. The sight of their own hard lot and of their weakness, which is contrasted every day with the happiness and power of some of their fellow creatures, stirs up anger and fear in their hearts at the same time. Their awareness of their inferiority and dependence irritates them even as it humiliates them. This state of mind shows itself in their manners and language, and they are at once insolent and servile. Observation easily proves this. The common people are ruder in aristocratic countries than elsewhere, and ruder in wealthy cities than in the countryside. Where the rich and powerful are gathered together, the weak and the poor feel oppressed by their inferior condition. They cannot see a single chance of regaining equality, so they give way to despair and let themselves sink below the dignity of human nature.

This unfortunate effect of the disparity of conditions is not seen in savage life. The Native Americans, though ignorant and poor, are equal and free. When Europeans first came among them, the natives of North America did not know the value of riches, and they were indifferent to the pleasures that civilized man obtains for himself by means of them. Yet there was nothing coarse in their behavior. They kept a habitual reserve and a kind of aristocratic politeness. In peace they were mild and hospitable, though in war they were merciless beyond any known degree of human ferocity. A Native American would risk dying of hunger to help a stranger who asked for shelter at the door of his hut by night; yet he could tear apart with his bare hands the still-quivering limbs of his prisoner. The famous republics of antiquity never gave examples of steadier courage, prouder spirits, or a more unyielding love of independence than those that once lay hidden in the wild forests of the New World. *i The Europeans made no great impression when they landed on the shores of North America. Their presence aroused neither envy nor fear. What influence could they have over men such as I have described? The Native American could live without wants, suffer without complaint, and sing his death song at the stake. *j Like all other members of the great human family, these savages believed in a better world, and under various names they worshiped God, the creator of the universe. Their ideas on the great intellectual truths were in general simple and philosophical. *k

i [ We learn from President Jefferson’s “Notes upon Virginia,” p. 148, that among the Iroquois, when a superior force attacked them, aged men refused to flee or to outlive the destruction of their country. They faced death as the ancient Romans did when the Gauls sacked their capital. Further on, p. 150, he tells us that there is no example of a Native American who, having fallen into the hands of his enemies, begged for his life. On the contrary, the captive tried to win death from his conquerors by insulting and provoking them.]

j [ See “Histoire de la Louisiane,” by Lepage Dupratz; Charlevoix, “Histoire de la Nouvelle France”; “Lettres du Rev. G. Hecwelder;” “Transactions of the American Philosophical Society,” v. I; Jefferson’s “Notes on Virginia,” pp. 135-190. What Jefferson says carries special weight, because of the personal merit of the writer, his particular position, and the matter-of-fact age in which he lived.]
k [ See Appendix, D.]
Although we have here traced the character of a primitive people, there can be no doubt that another people, more civilized and more advanced in every respect, had come before it in the same regions.

An obscure tradition among the Native Americans north of the Atlantic tells us that these same tribes once lived on the west side of the Mississippi. Along the banks of the Ohio, and throughout the central valley, mounds raised by human hands are still found today. When these heaps of earth are dug into toward their center, one commonly meets human bones, strange instruments, and weapons and utensils of every kind, made of metal or meant for purposes unknown to the present race. The Native Americans of our time can give no information about the history of this unknown people. Nor did those who lived three hundred years ago, when America was first discovered, leave any account from which even a hypothesis could be formed. Tradition, that perishable yet ever renewed monument of the primitive world, throws no light on the subject. It is nevertheless beyond doubt that thousands of our fellow beings once lived in this part of the globe. When they came here, what their origin, their destiny, and their history were, and how they perished, no one can tell. How strange it seems that nations should exist and then vanish so completely from the earth that the memory of their very names is erased, their languages are lost, and their glory is gone like a sound without an echo. And yet perhaps there is not one of them that has not left behind some tomb in memory of its passage. The most lasting monument of human labor is the one that recalls the wretchedness and nothingness of man.

Although many native tribes lived in the vast country we have been describing, it may justly be said that at the time Europeans discovered it, it formed one great desert. The Native Americans occupied the land without possessing it. Man takes possession of the soil by agricultural labor, and the early inhabitants of North America lived on the produce of the hunt. Their implacable prejudices, their uncontrolled passions, their vices, and perhaps still more their savage virtues, condemned them to certain destruction. The ruin of these nations began the day the Europeans landed on their shores. It has continued ever since, and we are now watching it reach its end. They seem to have been placed by Providence amid the riches of the New World to enjoy them for a season and then give them up. Those coasts, so well suited to commerce and industry; those wide and deep rivers; that inexhaustible valley of the Mississippi; in short, the whole continent seemed prepared to be the home of a great nation that was not yet born.

In that land civilized man was to make the great experiment of trying to build society on a new foundation. There, for the first time, theories that had been unknown until then, or thought impracticable, were to present a spectacle for which the history of the past had not prepared the world.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Origin Of The Anglo-Americans
paragraphs: Origin of the Anglo-Americans, and Its Importance in Relation to Their Future Condition.

After a human being is born, the early years pass obscurely in the labors or pleasures of childhood. As he grows up, the world receives him when manhood begins, and he comes into contact with other people. Only then is he studied for the first time, and people imagine that the seeds of the vices and virtues of his mature years are formed at that point. This, if I am not mistaken, is a great error. We must begin earlier. We must watch the infant in its mother’s arms; we must see the first images that the outside world casts upon the dark mirror of his mind and the first events he witnesses; we must hear the first words that awaken the sleeping powers of thought, and stand by his earliest efforts, if we want to understand the prejudices, habits, and passions that will rule his life. The whole man, so to speak, can be seen in the cradle of the child.

The growth of nations is something like this. They all bear some marks of their origin, and the circumstances that accompanied their birth and helped them rise affect their whole existence. If we could go back to the beginnings of states and examine the oldest records of their history, I do not doubt that we would find the first cause of their prejudices, habits, and ruling passions, in short, of everything that makes up what is called the national character. We would then find the explanation of certain customs that now seem at odds with the prevailing mores, of laws that conflict with established principles, and of the incoherent opinions found here and there in society, like those fragments of broken chains that we sometimes see hanging from the vault of a building and supporting nothing. This might explain the destinies of certain nations, which seem carried along by an unknown force toward ends of which they themselves are ignorant. But until now, facts have been lacking for research of this kind. The spirit of inquiry has come upon societies only in their later days, and when they finally looked back at their origin, time had already obscured it, or ignorance and pride had dressed it up in fables that hide the truth.

America is the only country where it has been possible to watch the natural and peaceful growth of a society, and where the influence of a state’s origin on its future condition can be clearly seen. When the peoples of Europe landed in the New World, their national characters were already fully formed. Each had a distinct face of its own. And since they had already reached the stage of civilization at which people come to study themselves, they have handed down to us a faithful picture of their opinions, their customs, and their laws. The men of the sixteenth century are almost as well known to us as our contemporaries. America therefore shows in broad daylight what the ignorance or rudeness of earlier ages hides from our research. We live near enough to the founding of the American states to know their elements accurately, and far enough from it to judge some of their results. So the men of our day seem destined to see further into the sequence of human events than their predecessors. Providence has given us a torch that our forefathers did not have, and has allowed us to discern fundamental causes in the history of the world that the obscurity of the past hid from them. If we carefully examine the social and political state of America after studying its history, we will be fully convinced that there is not an opinion, a custom, or a law, and I may even say not an event, on record that the origin of that people will not explain. Readers of this book will find the seed of everything that follows in this chapter, and the key to almost the whole work.

The emigrants who came at different times to settle the territory now covered by the American Union differed from each other in many respects. Their aims were not the same, and they governed themselves on different principles. Yet these men had certain features in common, and they were all in a similar situation. The tie of language is perhaps the strongest and most lasting that can unite human beings. All the emigrants spoke the same tongue, and all were offshoots of the same people. They were born in a country that had been shaken for centuries by the struggles of faction, in which every party had been obliged in its turn to place itself under the protection of the laws. Their political education had been completed in this rough school, and they were more familiar with the ideas of right and the principles of true freedom than most of their European contemporaries. At the time of their first emigrations, the parish system, that fruitful seed of free institutions, was deeply rooted in the habits of the English, and with it the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people had been brought into the heart of the monarchy of the House of Tudor.

The religious quarrels that have agitated the Christian world were then at their height. England had plunged into the new order of things with headlong force. The character of its people, which had always been sedate and thoughtful, became argumentative and austere. Intellectual debate had increased general knowledge, and the mind had received deeper cultivation. While religion was the topic of discussion, the morals of the people were reformed. All these national features can be recognized, more or less, in the character of those adventurers who came to seek a new home on the opposite shores of the Atlantic.

Another remark, to which we will return later, applies not only to the English but to the French, the Spaniards, and all the Europeans who successively settled in the New World. All these European colonies contained the elements, if not the full development, of a complete democracy. Two causes led to this result. It may safely be said that when the emigrants left the mother country, they generally had no idea of superiority over one another. The happy and the powerful do not go into exile, and there are no surer guarantees of equality among men than poverty and misfortune. On several occasions, however, persons of rank were driven to America by political and religious quarrels. Laws were made to set up a gradation of ranks, but it was soon found that the soil of America was opposed to a territorial aristocracy. To bring that stubborn land into cultivation, the constant effort of the owner himself, working for his own interest, was necessary. And once the ground was prepared, its produce proved insufficient to enrich a master and a farmer at the same time. The land was therefore naturally broken up into small portions, which the owner cultivated for himself. Land is the basis of an aristocracy, which clings to the soil that supports it. For an aristocracy is constituted not by privileges alone, nor by birth, but by landed property handed down from generation to generation. A nation may have immense fortunes and extreme wretchedness, but unless those fortunes are in land there is no aristocracy, only the class of the rich and the class of the poor.

At the time of their settlement, then, all the British colonies were very much alike. From their first beginnings, all of them seemed destined to see the growth, not of the aristocratic liberty of their mother country, but of the freedom of the middle and lower orders, of which the history of the world had so far furnished no complete example.

Within this general uniformity, however, several striking differences could be seen, and they need to be pointed out. Two branches can be distinguished in the Anglo-American family. Until now they have grown up without entirely mingling: one in the South, the other in the North.

Virginia received the first English colony; the emigrants took possession of it in 1607. The idea that mines of gold and silver are the sources of national wealth was at that time remarkably widespread in Europe. It was a fatal delusion, which has done more to impoverish the nations that adopted it, and has cost more lives in America, than war and bad laws combined. The men sent to Virginia *a were seekers of gold, adventurers without resources and without character, whose turbulent and restless spirit endangered the infant colony *b and made its progress uncertain. The artisans and farmers arrived afterward. Although they were a more moral and orderly sort of people, they were in no way above the level of the lower classes in England. *c No lofty conceptions, no intellectual system, guided the founding of these new settlements. The colony was scarcely established when slavery was introduced, *d and this was the main circumstance that has had such an enormous influence on the character, the laws, and all the future prospects of the South. Slavery, as we will show later, dishonors labor. It brings idleness into society, and with idleness come ignorance and pride, luxury and distress. It weakens the powers of the mind and numbs human activity. The influence of slavery, combined with the English character, explains the customs and social condition of the Southern States.

a [ The charter granted by the Crown of England in 1609 stipulated, among other conditions, that the adventurers should pay to the Crown a fifth of the produce of all gold and silver mines. See Marshall’s “Life of Washington,” vol. i. pp. 18-66.] [Footnote b: Stith (“History of Virginia”) says that a large portion of the adventurers were unprincipled young men from good families, whom their parents were glad to send away, along with dismissed servants, fraudulent bankrupts, and debauchees. Other men of the same kind, more inclined to plunder and destroy than to help the settlement, became the seditious leaders, and they easily drew this band into every sort of extravagance and excess. For the history of Virginia, see the following works:—
“History of Virginia, from the First Settlements in the year 1624,” by Smith.
“History of Virginia,” by William Stith.
“History of Virginia, from the Earliest Period,” by Beverley.]
c [ It was not until some time later that a certain number of rich English capitalists came to settle in the colony.]
d [ Slavery was introduced about the year 1620 by a Dutch ship that landed twenty Black people on the banks of the James River. See Chalmer.]

In the North, the same English foundation took on very different shades of character, and here I hope I may be allowed to go into some detail. The two or three central ideas on which the social theory of the United States rests first came together in the English colonies of the North, which are usually called the States of New England. *e At first the principles of New England reached only the neighboring states. They then moved on, one after another, to the more distant ones, and in the end they permeated the whole Confederation. Today their influence reaches beyond its borders, across the whole American world. The civilization of New England has been like a beacon lit on a hill: it first spreads its warmth all around, and then its glow colors the far horizon.
e [ The States of New England are the ones lying east of the Hudson. There are six of them today: 1, Connecticut; 2, Rhode Island; 3, Massachusetts; 4, Vermont; 5, New Hampshire; 6, Maine.]

The founding of New England was a new kind of spectacle, and all the circumstances attending it were unusual and original. The large majority of colonies were first settled either by men without education and without resources, driven from the land of their birth by poverty and misconduct, or by speculators and adventurers greedy for gain. Some settlements cannot even claim so honorable an origin. St. Domingo was founded by buccaneers, and the criminal courts of England originally supplied the population of Australia.

The settlers who established themselves on the shores of New England all belonged to the more independent classes of their native country. When they came together on American soil, they at once presented the unusual phenomenon of a society containing neither lords nor common people, neither rich nor poor. In proportion to their number, these men possessed a greater mass of intelligence than is found in any European nation of our own time. All of them, without a single exception, had received a good education, and many were known in Europe for their talents and their accomplishments. The other colonies had been founded by adventurers without families. The emigrants of New England brought with them the best elements of order and morality, and they landed in the wilderness accompanied by their wives and children. But what most especially distinguished them was the aim of their undertaking. Necessity had not forced them to leave their country; the social position they gave up was one to be regretted, and their means of living were secure. Nor did they cross the Atlantic to improve their situation or increase their wealth. The call that summoned them from the comforts of their homes was purely intellectual, and in facing the unavoidable sufferings of exile, their object was the triumph of an idea.

The emigrants, who rightly called themselves the Pilgrims, belonged to the English sect that had earned the name of Puritans through the austerity of its principles. Puritanism was more than a religious doctrine. On many points it coincided with the most absolute democratic and republican theories, and it was this tendency that had stirred up its most dangerous enemies. The government of the mother country persecuted the Puritans, and the habits of a society that rejected the rigor of their principles disgusted them. So they went off in search of some rude and unvisited corner of the world where they could live by their own opinions and worship God in freedom.

A few quotations will throw more light on the spirit of these pious adventurers than anything we could say about them. Nathaniel Morton, *f the historian of the first years of the settlement, opens his subject this way:
f [ “New England’s Memorial,” p. 13; Boston, 1826. See also “Hutchinson’s History,” vol. ii. p. 440.]

“Gentle Reader,—I have for some length of time looked upon it as a duty incumbent, especially on the immediate successors of those that have had so large experience of those many memorable and signal demonstrations of God’s goodness, viz., the first beginners of this Plantation in New England, to commit to writing his gracious dispensations on that behalf; having so many inducements thereunto, not onely otherwise but so plentifully in the Sacred Scriptures: that so, what we have seen, and what our fathers have told us (Psalm lxxviii. 3, 4), we may not hide from our children, showing to the generations to come the praises of the Lord; that especially the seed of Abraham his servant, and the children of Jacob his chosen (Psalm cv. 5, 6), may remember his marvelous works in the beginning and progress of the planting of New England, his wonders and the judgments of his mouth; how that God brought a vine into this wilderness; that he cast out the heathen, and planted it; that he made room for it and caused it to take deep root; and it filled the land (Psalm lxxx. 8, 9). And not onely so, but also that he hath guided his people by his strength to his holy habitation and planted them in the mountain of his inheritance in respect of precious Gospel enjoyments: and that as especially God may have the glory of all unto whom it is most due; so also some rays of glory may reach the names of those blessed Saints that were the main instruments and the beginning of this happy enterprise.”

It is impossible to read this opening paragraph without an involuntary feeling of religious awe. It breathes the very savor of the Gospel age. The author’s sincerity heightens the power of his language. The band that in his eyes was a mere party of adventurers gone out to seek their fortune overseas appears to the reader as the seed of a great nation, carried by Providence to a predestined shore.
The author then continues his account of the departure of the first pilgrims:—

“So they left that goodly and pleasant city of Leyden, *g which had been their resting-place for above eleven years; but they knew that they were pilgrims and strangers here below, and looked not much on these things, but lifted up their eyes to Heaven, their dearest country, where God hath prepared for them a city (Heb. xi. 16), and therein quieted their spirits. When they came to Delfs-Haven they found the ship and all things ready; and such of their friends as could not come with them followed after them, and sundry came from Amsterdam to see them shipt, and to take their leaves of them. One night was spent with little sleep with the most, but with friendly entertainment and Christian discourse, and other real expressions of true Christian love. The next day they went on board, and their friends with them, where truly doleful was the sight of that sad and mournful parting, to hear what sighs and sobs and prayers did sound among them; what tears did gush from every eye, and pithy speeches pierced each other’s heart, that sundry of the Dutch strangers that stood on the Key as spectators could not refrain from tears. But the tide (which stays for no man) calling them away, that were thus loth to depart, their Reverend Pastor falling down on his knees, and they all with him, with watery cheeks commended them with most fervent prayers unto the Lord and his blessing; and then, with mutual embraces and many tears they took their leaves one of another, which proved to be the last leave to many of them.”

g [ Most of the emigrants were devout Christians from the North of England. They had left their native country because they were “studious of reformation, and entered into covenant to walk with one another according to the primitive pattern of the Word of God.” They went to Holland and settled in the city of Leyden in 1610, where they lived for many years and were warmly respected by the Dutch. They left in 1620 for several reasons. The last was a fear that within a few generations their descendants would become Dutch and so lose their stake in the English nation. They preferred to extend His Majesty’s dominions and to live under their natural prince.—Translator’s Note.]

The emigrants numbered about 150, including the women and children. Their object was to plant a colony on the shores of the Hudson. But after being driven about for some time in the Atlantic Ocean, they were forced to land on that arid coast of New England which is now the site of the town of Plymouth. The rock on which the pilgrims disembarked is still shown. *h

h [ This rock has become an object of veneration in the United States. I have seen bits of it carefully preserved in several towns of the Union. Does this not show clearly enough how entirely all human power and greatness is in the soul of man? Here is a stone that the feet of a few outcasts pressed for an instant, and this stone becomes famous. A great nation treasures it, and its very dust is shared as a relic. And what has become of the gateways of a thousand palaces?]

“But before we pass on,” continues our historian, “let the reader with me make a pause and seriously consider this poor people’s present condition, the more to be raised up to admiration of God’s goodness towards them in their preservation: for being now passed the vast ocean, and a sea of troubles before them in expectation, they had now no friends to welcome them, no inns to entertain or refresh them, no houses, or much less towns to repair unto to seek for succor: and for the season it was winter, and they that know the winters of the country know them to be sharp and violent, subject to cruel and fierce storms, dangerous to travel to known places, much more to search unknown coasts. Besides, what could they see but a hideous and desolate wilderness, full of wilde beasts, and wilde men? and what multitudes of them there were, they then knew not: for which way soever they turned their eyes (save upward to Heaven) they could have but little solace or content in respect of any outward object; for summer being ended, all things stand in appearance with a weather-beaten face, and the whole country full of woods and thickets, represented a wild and savage hew; if they looked behind them, there was the mighty ocean which they had passed, and was now as a main bar or gulph to separate them from all the civil parts of the world.”

One should not suppose that Puritan piety was purely a matter of theory, or that it paid no attention to the course of worldly affairs. As I have already said, Puritanism was almost as much a political doctrine as a religious one. The emigrants had barely set foot on the barren coast that Nathaniel Morton describes when their first concern was to found a society. They did so by passing the following Act:

“In the name of God. Amen. We, whose names are underwritten, the loyal subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James, etc., etc., Having undertaken for the glory of God, and advancement of the Christian Faith, and the honor of our King and country, a voyage to plant the first colony in the northern parts of Virginia; Do by these presents solemnly and mutually, in the presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politick, for our better ordering and preservation, and furtherance of the ends aforesaid: and by virtue hereof do enact, constitute and frame such just and equal laws, ordinances, acts, constitutions, and officers, from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the Colony: unto which we promise all due submission and obedience,” etc. *i

i [ The emigrants who founded the State of Rhode Island in 1638, those who landed at New Haven in 1637, the first settlers of Connecticut in 1639, and the founders of Providence in 1640 all started in the same way: they drew up a social contract, which every party concerned accepted. See “Pitkin’s History,” pp. 42 and 47.]

This happened in 1620, and from then on the emigration continued. The religious and political passions that ravaged the British Empire during the whole reign of Charles I drove fresh crowds of sectarians to the shores of America every year. In England the stronghold of Puritanism was in the middle classes, and the majority of the emigrants came from the middle classes. The population of New England grew rapidly. While the hierarchy of rank despotically classified the inhabitants of the mother country, the colony continued to present the new spectacle of a community uniform in all its parts. A democracy more perfect than any that antiquity had dreamed of sprang up, full-grown and fully armed, from the midst of an ancient feudal society.

The English government was not displeased with an emigration that removed the seeds of fresh discord and further revolutions. On the contrary, everything was done to encourage it, and great efforts were made to ease the hardships of those who sought shelter on American soil from the rigor of their own country’s laws. It seemed as if New England was a region given over to the dreams of fancy and the unrestrained experiments of innovators.

The English colonies have always had more freedom in their internal affairs, and more political independence, than the colonies of other nations, and this is one of the main causes of their prosperity. Yet the principle of liberty was nowhere carried further than in the States of New England.

It was generally accepted at that time that the territories of the New World belonged to whichever European nation first discovered them. Nearly the whole coast of North America thus became a British possession toward the end of the sixteenth century. The English government used several means to populate these new domains. Sometimes the King appointed a governor of his own choice, who ruled a portion of the New World in the name of the Crown and under its direct orders; *j this is the colonial system adopted by other countries of Europe. Sometimes the Crown granted certain tracts to an individual or to a company, *k in which case all civil and political power fell into the hands of one or more persons, who sold the lands and governed the inhabitants under the Crown’s inspection and control. Finally, a third system consisted in allowing a certain number of emigrants to form a political society under the protection of the mother country, and to govern themselves in everything not contrary to her laws. This mode of colonization, so remarkably favorable to liberty, was adopted only in New England. *l
j [ This was the case in the State of New York.]
k [ Maryland, the Carolinas, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey were in this situation. See “Pitkin’s History,” vol. i. pp. 11-31.]

l [ See the work entitled “Historical Collection of State Papers and other authentic Documents intended as materials for a History of the United States of America, by Ebenezer Hasard. Philadelphia, 1792,” for a large number of documents on the beginnings of the colonies, which are valuable both for what they say and for their authenticity. They include the various charters granted by the King of England and the first acts of the local governments.

See also the analysis of all these charters by Mr. Story, Judge of the Supreme Court of the United States, in the Introduction to his “Commentary on the Constitution of the United States.” It follows from these documents that the principles of representative government and the outward forms of political liberty were brought into all the colonies at their founding. The North put these principles into practice more fully than the South, but they were present everywhere.]

In 1628 *m Charles I gave a charter of this kind to the emigrants who set out to form the colony of Massachusetts. In general, though, the colonies of New England received charters only after they were already established. Plymouth, Providence, New Haven, the State of Connecticut, and the State of Rhode Island *n were founded without any help from the mother country and almost without her knowledge. The new settlers did not get their legal existence from the seat of the empire, although they did not deny its supremacy. They formed a society on their own initiative. Only thirty or forty years later, under Charles II, did a royal charter give their existence legal recognition.
m [ See “Pitkin’s History,” p, 35. See the “History of the Colony of Massachusetts Bay,” by Hutchinson, vol. i. p. 9.] [Footnote n: See “Pitkin’s History,” pp. 42, 47.]

This often makes it difficult, in studying the earliest historical and legislative records of New England, to detect the link that connected the emigrants with the land of their forefathers. They exercised the rights of sovereignty. They named their magistrates, made peace or declared war, issued police regulations, and enacted laws as if their allegiance were owed only to God. *o Nothing could be more curious, and at the same time more instructive, than the legislation of that period. It is there that the solution of the great social problem the United States now presents to the world is to be found.

o [ The people of Massachusetts had broken away from the forms kept in English criminal and civil procedure. As late as 1650, judicial decrees were still not issued under the royal title. See Hutchinson, vol. i. p. 452.]

Among these documents, one that stands out as especially characteristic is the code of laws that the little State of Connecticut issued in 1650. *p Its legislators *q start with the penal laws, and, strangely, they take their provisions straight from the text of Holy Scripture. “Whosoever shall worship any other God than the Lord,” says the preamble of the Code, “shall surely be put to death.” Ten or twelve provisions of the same kind follow, copied word for word from the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy. Blasphemy, sorcery, adultery, *r and rape carried the death penalty, and a son who outraged his parents was to pay for it in the same way. The legislation of a rude and half-civilized people was being applied to an educated and moral community. As a result, the death penalty was written into the statute book more often than ever before, yet it was enforced against the guilty more rarely than ever.
p [ Code of 1650, p. 28; Hartford, 1830.]

q [ See also “Hutchinson’s History,” vol. i. pp. 435, 456, for the analysis of the penal code that the Colony of Massachusetts adopted in 1648. It is built on the same principles as the code of Connecticut.]

r [ Massachusetts law also made adultery punishable by death, and Hutchinson, vol. i. p. 441, says that several people were in fact executed for it. He tells a curious story from the year 1663. A married woman had had an adulterous relationship with a young man. Her husband died, and she married her lover. Several years went by before people began to suspect the couple’s earlier adulterous relationship. They were thrown into prison and brought to trial, and they very narrowly escaped the death penalty.]

In this body of penal laws, the legislators cared above all about keeping the community orderly and moral. They invaded the realm of conscience again and again, and there was hardly a sin that the magistrates could not censure. The reader has seen how rigorously these laws punished rape and adultery. Sex between unmarried people was also harshly suppressed. The judge had the power to impose a fine, a whipping, or marriage *s on offenders, and if the records of the old courts of New Haven can be believed, such prosecutions were not uncommon. One sentence, dated the first of May, 1660, fines and reprimands a young woman who was accused of using improper language and letting herself be kissed. *t The Code of 1650 is full of preventive measures. It deals severely with idleness and drunkenness. *u Innkeepers may not serve any customer more than a fixed amount of liquor, and plain lying, whenever it may do harm, *v is checked with a fine or a flogging. Elsewhere the legislator completely forgets the great principles of religious toleration that he himself had defended in Europe.
