He makes attendance at divine service compulsory, *w and he even goes so far as to inflict severe punishment, ** and even death, on Christians who chose to worship God according to a ritual different from his own. *x At times the zeal of his enactments leads him down to the pettiest details; the same Code, for instance, contains a law that forbids the use of tobacco. *y We must not forget that these fantastical and vexatious laws were not imposed from above. All the people concerned voted for them freely, and the customs of the community were even more austere and puritanical than the laws. In 1649 a solemn association was formed in Boston to put a stop to the worldly luxury of long hair. *z

s [ Code of 1650, p. 48. Judges seem sometimes to have combined these punishments, as in a sentence pronounced in 1643 (p. 114, “New Haven Antiquities”), in which Margaret Bedford, convicted of loose conduct, was sentenced to be whipped and then to marry her accomplice, Nicholas Jemmings.]
t [ “New Haven Antiquities,” p. 104. See also “Hutchinson’s History” for several equally extraordinary cases.]

* [ This was not peculiar to Connecticut. See, for instance, the law which, on September 13, 1644, banished the Anabaptists from the State of Massachusetts. (“Historical Collection of State Papers,” vol. i. p. 538.) See also the law against the Quakers, passed on October 14, 1656: “Whereas,” says the preamble, “an accursed race of heretics called Quakers has sprung up,” etc. The statute imposes a heavy fine on any ship captain who brings Quakers into the country. Quakers found in the colony are to be whipped and put to hard labor in prison. Members of the sect who defend their opinions are to be fined first, then imprisoned, and finally driven out of the province.—“Historical Collection of State Papers,” vol. i. p. 630.]
x [ Under the penal law of Massachusetts, a Catholic priest who had once been driven out of the colony and then set foot in it again could be put to death.]
y [ Code of 1650, p. 96.]
z [ “New England’s Memorial,” p. 316. See Appendix, E.]

These errors are no doubt discreditable to human reason. They attest the inferiority of our nature, which is incapable of taking firm hold of what is true and just, and is often reduced to a choice between two excesses. Closely connected with this penal legislation, which bears such striking marks of a narrow sectarian spirit and of religious passions warmed by persecution and still fermenting among the people, there is a body of political laws that, though written two hundred years ago, is still ahead of the liberties of our age. The general principles that are the groundwork of modern constitutions were imperfectly known in Europe in the seventeenth century, and not completely triumphant even in Great Britain. Yet the laws of New England recognized and established all of them: the intervention of the people in public affairs, the free voting of taxes, the responsibility of authorities, personal liberty, and trial by jury were all positively established without debate. From these fruitful principles, consequences have been drawn and applications made such as no nation in Europe has yet ventured to attempt.

In Connecticut the electoral body consisted, from its origin, of all the citizens. This is readily understood *a when we recall that this people enjoyed an almost perfect equality of fortune and a still greater uniformity of opinions. *b In Connecticut at this period all the executive officials were elected, including the Governor of the State. *c Citizens above the age of sixteen were obliged to bear arms. They formed a national militia, which appointed its own officers and was to hold itself ready at all times to march to the defense of the country. *d
a [ Constitution of 1638, p. 17.]

b [ In 1641 the General Assembly of Rhode Island declared unanimously that the government of the State was a democracy, and that power rested with the body of free citizens, who alone had the right to make the laws and to oversee their execution.—Code of 1650, p. 70.]
c [ “Pitkin’s History,” p. 47.]
d [ Constitution of 1638, p. 12.]

In the laws of Connecticut, as in all the laws of New England, we find the seed, and the gradual growth, of the independence of the township, which today is the life and mainspring of American liberty. Most European nations began their political life in the upper ranks of society, and it was passed down slowly and imperfectly to the other members of the social body. In America it was the other way around. One may say that the township was organized before the county, the county before the State, and the State before the Union. In New England, townships were fully and definitively established as early as 1650. Local interests, passions, rights, and duties gathered and clung around the independence of the township as around a nucleus. It made room for a truly political life, thoroughly democratic and republican. The colonies still acknowledged the supremacy of the mother country, and monarchy was still the law of the State, yet the republic was already alive in every township. The townships appointed their own magistrates of every kind, taxed themselves, and collected their own taxes. *e In the New England parish the principle of representation was not adopted. Instead, as at Athens, the affairs of the community were debated in the marketplace by a general assembly of the citizens.
e [ Code of 1650, p. 80.]

Anyone who studies the laws issued in this first era of the American republics cannot help being struck by how much they show of the science of government and how advanced their theory of legislation was. The ideas they express about the duties of society toward its members are clearly much loftier and broader than those of European lawmakers of the time. They imposed obligations that were neglected elsewhere. In the States of New England, the condition of the poor was provided for from the start. *f Strict measures were taken to maintain the roads, and surveyors were appointed to look after them. *g Registers were set up in every parish, in which the results of public deliberations and the births, deaths, and marriages of the citizens were recorded. *h Clerks were ordered to keep these registers. *i Officers were put in charge of administering unclaimed inheritances and of settling disputes over boundary marks. Many other officers were created whose chief task was to maintain public order in the community. *j The law takes up a thousand useful provisions for social needs that are, at present, very poorly felt in France. [Footnote f: Ibid., p. 78.]
h [ See “Hutchinson’s History,” vol. i. p. 455.]
i [ Code of 1650, p. 86.]

But it is in the attention it gives to public education that the original character of American civilization shows most clearly. “It being,” says the law, “one chief project of Satan to keep men from the knowledge of the Scripture by persuading from the use of tongues, to the end that learning may not be buried in the graves of our forefathers, in church and commonwealth, the Lord assisting our endeavors. . . .” *k What follows are clauses that establish schools in every township and require the inhabitants, under heavy fines, to support them. Schools of a higher kind were founded in the same way in the more populous districts. The municipal authorities had to see that parents sent their children to school. They were empowered to fine anyone who refused, and if the refusal continued, society took the parent’s place, took possession of the child, and deprived the father of the natural rights he was using so badly. The reader will surely have noticed the preamble of these enactments: in America, religion is the road to knowledge, and observing the divine laws leads a person to civil freedom.

Suppose we glance quickly at the state of American society in 1650 and then turn to the condition of Europe at the same time, especially the Continent. We cannot help being astonished. On the Continent at the beginning of the seventeenth century, absolute monarchy had triumphed everywhere over the ruins of the oligarchical and feudal liberties of the Middle Ages. Ideas of right were never more thoroughly confused than amid the splendor and literature of Europe. The people had never been less active in politics, and the principles of true freedom had never been less widely known. Yet at that very moment, those principles, scorned or unknown by the nations of Europe, were being proclaimed in the wilderness of the New World and accepted as the future creed of a great people. The boldest theories of human reason were being put into practice by a community so humble that not a single statesman bothered to notice it. A legislation without precedent was produced on the spot by the imagination of the citizens. In the heart of this obscure democracy, which had so far produced no generals, no philosophers, and no authors, a man could stand up before a free people and give the following fine definition of liberty. *l

l [ Mather’s “Magnalia Christi Americana,” vol. ii. p. 13. This speech was made by Winthrop. He had been accused of arbitrary actions during his time as magistrate, but after he made the speech of which the above is a fragment, he was acquitted by acclamation, and from then on he was always re-elected governor of the State. See Marshal, vol. i. p. 166.]

“Nor would I have you to mistake in the point of your own liberty. There is a liberty of a corrupt nature which is effected both by men and beasts to do what they list, and this liberty is inconsistent with authority, impatient of all restraint; by this liberty ‘sumus omnes deteriores’: ’tis the grand enemy of truth and peace, and all the ordinances of God are bent against it. But there is a civil, a moral, a federal liberty which is the proper end and object of authority; it is a liberty for that only which is just and good: for this liberty you are to stand with the hazard of your very lives and whatsoever crosses it is not authority, but a distemper thereof. This liberty is maintained in a way of subjection to authority; and the authority set over you will, in all administrations for your good, be quietly submitted unto by all but such as have a disposition to shake off the yoke and lose their true liberty, by their murmuring at the honor and power of authority.”

What I have said is enough to show Anglo-American civilization in its true light. It is the product of two distinct elements (and this should be kept constantly in mind). In other places these have often been in conflict, but in America they have been admirably joined and blended. I mean the spirit of Religion and the spirit of Liberty.

The settlers of New England were at once ardent sectarians and daring innovators. Some of their religious opinions were very narrow, but they were entirely free of political prejudices. Two tendencies followed from this. They were distinct but not opposed, and they can be constantly seen in the customs as well as in the laws of the country.

One might imagine that men who gave up their friends, their families, and their native land for a religious conviction would be wholly absorbed in the pursuit of the intellectual benefits they had paid for so dearly. Yet they strove just as energetically to gain wealth, moral enjoyment, and the comforts as well as the liberties of this world. That energy is hardly less than the energy with which they devoted themselves to Heaven.

Political principles and all human laws and institutions were shaped and changed at their pleasure. The barriers of the society they were born in fell before them, and the old principles that had governed the world for ages were gone. A path with no turning and a field with no horizon opened up to the eager, exploring curiosity of man. But at the boundary of the political world he stops his inquiries. He prudently sets aside the use of his most formidable faculties. He no longer agrees to doubt or to innovate. He carefully avoids lifting the curtain of the sanctuary, and he yields with submissive respect to truths that he will not discuss. So in the moral world everything is classified, adjusted, decided, and foreseen, while in the political world everything is stirred up, uncertain, and disputed. In the one there is a passive, though voluntary, obedience. In the other there is an independence that scorns experience and is jealous of authority.

These two tendencies seem very different, yet they are far from conflicting. They advance together and support each other. Religion sees that civil liberty gives the faculties of man a noble field of exercise, and that the political world is a field the Creator prepared for the efforts of the intelligence. Religion is content with the freedom and power it enjoys in its own sphere and with the place it holds. Its empire is never more securely established than when it reigns in the hearts of men with no support beyond its own native strength. Religion is no less the companion of liberty in all its battles and triumphs, the cradle of its infancy, and the divine source of its claims. Religion is the safeguard of morality, and morality is the best security of law and the surest pledge of freedom. *m
m [ See Appendix, F.]
Reasons of Certain Anomalies Which the Laws and Customs of the Anglo-Americans Present
Remains of aristocratic institutions in the midst of a complete democracy — Why? — Distinction to be carefully drawn between what is of Puritan origin and what is of English origin.

The reader is cautioned not to draw too general or too absolute a conclusion from what has been said. The social condition, the religion, and the customs of the first emigrants undoubtedly had an immense influence on the destiny of their new country. Nevertheless, they were not in a position to found a state of things that depended on them alone. No one can entirely shake off the influence of the past. The settlers, whether they meant to or not, mixed habits and ideas that came from their education and from the traditions of their country with the habits and ideas that were purely their own. To judge the Anglo-Americans of the present day, it is therefore necessary to distinguish what is of Puritan origin from what is of English origin.

Laws and customs are often found in the United States that contrast sharply with everything around them. These laws seem to have been drawn up in a spirit contrary to the general tenor of American legislation, and these customs are just as opposed to the tone of society. If the English colonies had been founded in an age of darkness, or if their origin had already been lost in the passage of years, the problem would be unsolvable.

I shall give a single example to illustrate my point. American civil and criminal procedure has only two means of action, committal and bail. The magistrate’s first step is to require security from the defendant, or to put him in prison if he refuses. Only then are the grounds of the accusation and the seriousness of the charges against him discussed. It is evident that legislation of this kind is hostile to the poor man and favors only the rich. The poor man cannot always produce security, even in a civil case, and if he has to wait for justice in prison, he is soon reduced to distress. The wealthy man, on the other hand, always escapes imprisonment in civil cases. More than that, he can easily avoid the punishment that awaits him for a crime by forfeiting his bail. So for him all the penalties of the law come down to fines. *n Nothing could be more aristocratic than this system of legislation. Yet in America it is the poor who make the law, and they usually keep the greatest social advantages for themselves. The explanation of this phenomenon is to be found in England. The laws I am speaking of are English, *o and the Americans have kept them, however repugnant they may be to the tenor of their legislation and to the mass of their ideas. After its habits, the thing a nation is least likely to change is its civil legislation. Civil laws are familiarly known only to lawyers, whose direct interest is to keep them as they are, good or bad, simply because they themselves are well versed in them. The body of the nation hardly knows them. It sees their action only in particular cases, has some difficulty grasping their tendency, and obeys them without thinking. I have given one instance where it would have been easy to cite a great many others. The surface of American society is, if I may put it this way, covered with a layer of democracy, and from underneath it the old aristocratic colors sometimes show through.
n [ Crimes no doubt exist for which bail is inadmissible, but they are few in number.]
o [ See Blackstone; and Delolme, book I chap. x.]

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Social Conditions Of The Anglo-Americans
paragraphs: A social condition is usually the result of circumstances, sometimes of laws, and more often of the two together. But wherever it exists, it can rightly be seen as the source of almost all the laws, practices, and ideas that govern the conduct of nations. Whatever it does not produce, it modifies. Anyone who wants to understand the legislation and the customs of a nation must therefore begin by studying its social condition.
The Striking Characteristic of the Social Condition of the Anglo-Americans in Its Essential Democracy.

The first emigrants of New England — Their equality — Aristocratic laws introduced in the South — The period of the Revolution — Change in the law of descent — Effects of this change — Democracy carried to its utmost limits in the new States of the West — Equality of education.

Many important observations arise about the social condition of the Anglo-Americans, but one comes before all the others. The social condition of the Americans is eminently democratic. This was its character when the Colonies were founded, and it is more strongly marked today. I stated in the preceding chapter that there was great equality among the emigrants who settled on the shores of New England. The seed of aristocracy was never planted in that part of the Union. The only influence that held there was the influence of intellect. The people were used to revering certain names as emblems of knowledge and virtue. Some of their fellow citizens gained a power over the rest that could truly have been called aristocratic, if it could have been passed down from father to son.

That was the state of things east of the Hudson. Southwest of that river, in the direction of the Floridas, the case was different. In most of the States southwest of the Hudson, some great English proprietors had settled. They brought with them aristocratic principles and the English law of descent. I have explained why it was never possible to establish a powerful aristocracy in America, and those reasons applied with less force southwest of the Hudson. In the South, one man with the help of slaves could cultivate a vast stretch of land, so it was common to find rich landed proprietors. But their influence was not wholly aristocratic as Europeans understand that term, because they had no privileges. And since slaves worked their estates, they had no tenants who depended on them, and so no patronage. Still, the great proprietors south of the Hudson formed a superior class, with ideas and tastes of its own, and it became the center of political action. This kind of aristocracy sympathized with the body of the people and easily took up its passions and interests. But it was too weak and too short-lived to arouse either love or hatred toward itself. This was the class that led the insurrection in the South and supplied the best leaders of the American Revolution.

At the period we are now speaking of, society was shaken to its center. The people, in whose name the struggle had been fought, conceived a desire to exercise the authority they had won. Their democratic tendencies were awakened, and having thrown off the yoke of the mother country, they aspired to independence of every kind. The influence of individuals gradually faded, and custom and law joined together to produce the same result.

But the law of descent was the last step toward equality. I am surprised that ancient and modern jurists have not recognized a greater influence of this law on human affairs. *a It is true that these laws belong to civil affairs. Nevertheless, they ought to be placed at the head of all political institutions, for political laws are only the symbol of a nation’s condition, whereas these laws exercise an incredible influence on its social state. They also operate on society in a sure and uniform way, reaching, as it were, generations not yet born.

a [ By the law of descent I mean all those laws whose principal object is to regulate the distribution of property after its owner’s death. The law of entail is one of these. It certainly prevents the owner from disposing of his possessions before his death, but only so as to keep them whole for the heir. The principal object of the law of entail is therefore to regulate the descent of property after its owner’s death, and its other provisions are only means to that end.]

Through these laws, man gains a kind of superhuman power over the future lot of his fellow creatures. Once the legislator has settled the law of inheritance, he can rest from his labor. The machine, once set in motion, will run for ages and advance toward a given point as if guided by itself. When this law is framed in one way, it unites property and power, draws them together, and vests them in a few hands. Its tendency is clearly aristocratic. On opposite principles, it works still faster, dividing, distributing, and scattering both property and power. Those who despair of stopping its motion are alarmed by the speed of its progress, and they try to obstruct it with difficulties and impediments. They try in vain to counteract its effect by opposing efforts. But the law gradually wears down or destroys every obstacle. By its ceaseless activity, the bulwarks of the influence of wealth are ground down to the fine, shifting sand that is the basis of democracy. When the law of inheritance permits, and still more when it commands, the equal division of a father’s property among all his children, its effects are of two kinds. It is important to distinguish them from each other, although they tend toward the same end.

Under the law of partible inheritance, the death of every proprietor brings about a kind of revolution in property. His possessions pass into other hands, and their very nature also changes, since they are divided into shares that grow smaller with each division. This is the direct and, so to speak, physical effect of the law. It follows that in countries where equal inheritance is established by law, property, and especially landed property, must tend to shrink continually. Yet the effects of such legislation would be noticeable only after some time, if the law were left to work by itself. Suppose a family has two children (and in a country as populous as France the average is no more than three). Sharing the fortune of both parents between them, these children would be no poorer than their father or mother.

But the law of equal division exerts its influence not only on the property itself. It also affects the minds of the heirs and brings their passions into play. These indirect consequences strongly tend to destroy large fortunes, and especially large domains. Among nations whose law of descent rests on the right of primogeniture, landed estates often pass from generation to generation without being divided. As a result, family feeling becomes to some degree bound up with the estate. The family stands for the estate, and the estate for the family. The family’s name, with its origin, glory, power, and virtues, is thus preserved in an imperishable memorial of the past and a sure pledge of the future.

When equal partition of property is established by law, the close connection between family feeling and the preservation of the paternal estate is broken. The property no longer represents the family. Since it must inevitably be divided after one or two generations, it clearly tends to shrink constantly and must in the end be completely scattered. The sons of a great landed proprietor, if there are few of them or if fortune favors them, may indeed hope to be as wealthy as their father, but not to own the same property he did. Their wealth must necessarily be made up of different elements from his.

Now, once you take away the landowner’s interest in preserving his estate, which comes from association, tradition, and family pride, you can be sure that sooner or later he will sell it. There is a strong financial incentive to sell, since money in circulation earns a higher return than real property and is more readily available to satisfy the passions of the moment.

Great landed estates, once divided, never come together again. The small proprietor draws a better return from his land, in proportion to its size, than the large owner does from his, and so of course he sells it at a higher price. *b The calculations of gain that persuade the rich man to sell his domain will therefore work even more strongly to keep him from buying small estates in order to join them into a large one.
b [ I do not mean that the small proprietor cultivates his land better, but he cultivates it with more eagerness and care, so that he makes up for his lack of skill by his labor.]

What is called family pride often rests on an illusion of self-love. A man wishes to perpetuate and immortalize himself, so to speak, in his great-grandchildren. Where the esprit de famille ceases to act, individual selfishness comes into play. When the idea of family becomes vague, indefinite, and uncertain, a man thinks of his present convenience. He provides for the establishment of the next generation, and no more. Either he gives up the idea of perpetuating his family, or at any rate he tries to achieve it by means other than a landed estate. In this way, the law of partible inheritance not only makes it hard for families to keep their ancestral domains whole, but also takes away their inclination to try, and in some measure forces them to cooperate with the law in their own extinction.

The law of equal distribution works in two ways. By acting on things, it acts on persons, and by influencing persons, it affects things. By these means the law succeeds in striking at the root of landed property and quickly scattering both families and fortunes. *c

c [ Land being the most stable kind of property, we find from time to time rich individuals who are willing to make great sacrifices to obtain it, and who gladly give up a considerable part of their income to make sure of the rest. But these are accidental cases. The preference for landed property is no longer found habitually in any class except the poor. The small landowner, who has less information, less imagination, and fewer passions than the great one, is generally occupied with the desire of increasing his estate, and it often happens that through inheritance, marriage, or the chances of trade he is gradually given the means. Thus, to balance the tendency that leads men to divide their estates, there exists another that urges them to add to them. This tendency is enough to prevent estates from being divided ad infinitum, but it is not strong enough to create great territorial possessions, and certainly not to keep them up in the same family.]

We Frenchmen of the nineteenth century, who see every day the political and social changes that the law of partition is bringing about, are certainly in no position to doubt its influence. It is constantly visible in our country, pulling down the walls of our houses and removing the landmarks of our fields. But although it has had great effects in France, much remains for it to do. Our memories, opinions, and habits put powerful obstacles in the way of its progress.

In the United States it has almost finished its work of destruction, and there we can best study its results. The English laws on the transmission of property were abolished in almost all the States at the time of the Revolution. The law of entail was changed so that it no longer interrupts the free circulation of property. *d After the first generation passed away, estates began to be divided into parcels, and as time went on the change became faster and faster. Today, a little more than sixty years later, the face of society has been completely altered. The families of the great landed proprietors have almost all merged into the general mass. In the State of New York, which once had many of them, only two still keep their heads above the stream, and they must soon disappear. The sons of these wealthy citizens have become merchants, lawyers, or physicians. Most of them have sunk into obscurity. The last trace of hereditary ranks and distinctions has been destroyed. The law of partition has brought everyone to one level. [Footnote d: See Appendix, G.]

I do not mean that the United States lacks wealthy individuals. Indeed, I know of no country where the love of money has taken a stronger hold on the hearts of men, or where deeper contempt is expressed for the theory of permanent equality of property. But wealth circulates with inconceivable speed, and experience shows that it is rare to find two successive generations in full enjoyment of it.

This picture, which may perhaps seem exaggerated, still gives a very imperfect idea of what is happening in the new States of the West and Southwest. At the end of the last century, a few bold adventurers began to push into the valleys of the Mississippi, and the mass of the population soon began to move in that direction. Communities never heard of before were seen to rise from the wilderness. States whose names had not existed a few years earlier took their place in the American Union. In the Western settlements we can see democracy at its utmost extreme. These States were founded on the spur of the moment and, so to speak, by chance, and their inhabitants are people of yesterday. They hardly know one another, and even the nearest neighbors do not know each other’s history. In this part of the American continent, therefore, the population has not felt the influence of great names and great wealth, or even that of the natural aristocracy of knowledge and virtue. No one is there to wield the respected power that men willingly give to the memory of a life spent doing good before their eyes. The new States of the West already have inhabitants, but society does not exist among them. *e

e [ This may have been true in 1832, but is not so in 1874, when great cities like Chicago and San Francisco have sprung up in the Western States. But as yet the Western States exert no powerful influence on American society. — Translator’s Note.]

In America it is not only men’s fortunes that are equal. Even their needs share, to some degree, the same uniformity. I do not believe there is any country in the world where, in proportion to the population, there are so few uneducated people and at the same time so few learned ones. Primary instruction is within everyone’s reach, and advanced instruction is hardly within anyone’s. This is not surprising. It is in fact the necessary result of what I have said above. Almost all Americans are comfortably off, and so they can obtain the first elements of human knowledge.

In America, comparatively few people are rich enough to live without a profession. Every profession requires an apprenticeship, which limits the time of instruction to the early years of life. At fifteen they enter upon their calling, and so their education ends at the age when ours begins. Whatever they study afterward is aimed at some specific and profitable goal. They take up a science as a matter of business, and they attend only to the branch of it that has an immediate practical use. In America most of the rich were once poor, and most of those who now enjoy leisure were absorbed in business in their youth. As a result, when they might have had a taste for study, they had no time for it, and when they have time, they no longer have the inclination.

There is therefore no class in America in which a taste for intellectual pleasures is handed down along with hereditary fortune and leisure, and which holds the labors of the intellect in honor. Accordingly, the desire and the capacity to apply oneself to such pursuits are equally lacking.

A middle standard of human knowledge is fixed in America. Everyone comes as near to it as they can, some rising toward it and others sinking toward it. Of course, an immense multitude of people hold the same number of ideas on religion, history, science, political economy, legislation, and government. The gifts of intellect come directly from God, and man cannot prevent their unequal distribution. But because of the state of things I have described here, it happens that although men’s capacities are widely different, as the Creator doubtless intended, they are all subjected to the same method of treatment.

In America, the aristocratic element has been feeble from its birth. If today it is not actually destroyed, it is at any rate so completely disabled that we can hardly assign it any influence on the course of affairs. The democratic principle, on the contrary, has gained so much strength through time, events, and legislation that it has become not only dominant but all-powerful. There is no family or corporate authority, and it is rare to find even the influence of individual character lasting for long.

America, then, shows in her social state a most extraordinary phenomenon. Nowhere else in the world, and in no age of which history has kept the memory, have men been seen on such a level of equality in fortune and intellect, or, in other words, so equal in their strength.
Political Consequences of the Social Condition of the Anglo-Americans

The political consequences of a social condition like this are easy to deduce. It is impossible to believe that equality will not eventually find its way into the political world, as it does everywhere else. It is impossible to imagine men remaining forever unequal on one single point yet equal on all others. In the end they must become equal on all. Now, I know of only two ways of establishing equality in the political world. Either every citizen must be given his rights, or no one must be given any. For nations that have reached the same stage of social existence as the Anglo-Americans, it is therefore very hard to find a middle course between the sovereignty of all and the absolute power of one man. It would be pointless to deny that the social condition I have been describing is equally liable to either of these consequences.

There is, in fact, a manly and lawful passion for equality that makes men wish to see everyone powerful and honored. This passion tends to raise the humble to the rank of the great. But there is also in the human heart a depraved taste for equality, which drives the weak to try to bring the powerful down to their own level and leads men to prefer equality in slavery to inequality in freedom. This is not to say that nations whose social condition is democratic naturally despise liberty. On the contrary, they have an instinctive love of it. But liberty is not the chief and constant object of their desires. Equality is their idol. They make quick, sudden efforts to obtain liberty, and if they miss their aim they resign themselves to the disappointment. But nothing can satisfy them except equality, and rather than lose it they are resolved to perish.

On the other hand, in a State where the citizens are nearly equal, it becomes difficult for them to preserve their independence against the aggressions of power. None of them is strong enough to enter the struggle with any advantage, so nothing but a general combination can protect their liberty. And such a union is not always to be found.
From the same social position, then, nations may arrive at either of two great political results. These results are extremely different from each other, yet both may come from the same cause.

The Anglo-Americans are the first nation that, having been exposed to this formidable alternative, has been fortunate enough to escape the dominion of absolute power. Their circumstances, their origin, their intelligence, and above all their moral feeling have allowed them to establish and maintain the sovereignty of the people.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — The Principle Of The Sovereignty Of The People In America
paragraphs: Whenever we discuss the political laws of the United States, we must start with the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people. This principle lies, to a greater or lesser degree, at the bottom of almost all human institutions, yet it usually stays hidden from view. People obey it without recognizing it, or if it is briefly brought into the light, it is hurriedly thrust back into the darkness of the sanctuary. “The will of the nation” is one of the phrases that the crafty and the despotic of every age have abused most shamelessly. Some have pictured it in the purchased votes of a few servants of power; others in the votes of a timid or self-interested minority; and some have even found it in a people’s silence, on the assumption that the mere fact of submission established the right to command.

In America the principle of the sovereignty of the people is neither barren nor hidden, as it is in some other nations. The customs recognize it and the laws proclaim it. It spreads freely and reaches its most remote consequences without obstruction. If there is any country in the world where the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people can be fairly judged, where it can be studied as it is applied to the affairs of society, and where its dangers and its advantages can be foreseen, that country is certainly America.

I have already observed that, from their origin, the sovereignty of the people was the fundamental principle of most of the British colonies in America. But it was far from having then the influence on the government of society that it has now. Two obstacles, one external and one internal, held back its advance. It could not openly show itself in the laws of colonies that were still required to obey the mother country. It was therefore forced to spread in secret and to gain ground in the provincial assemblies, and especially in the townships.

American society was not yet prepared to adopt it with all its consequences. The intelligence of New England and the wealth of the country south of the Hudson (as I showed in the preceding chapter) long exercised a kind of aristocratic influence, which tended to keep the exercise of social authority in the hands of a few. Public officials were not all elected, and not all citizens were voters. The right to vote was everywhere kept within certain limits and made to depend on a certain qualification, which was extremely low in the North and higher in the South.

Then the American Revolution broke out, and the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people, which had been nurtured in the townships and municipalities, took possession of the state. Every class was enlisted in its cause. Battles were fought and victories won for it, until it became the law of laws.
A change just as rapid took place within society itself, where the law of descent completed the destruction of local influences.

At the very time when this consequence of the laws and of the Revolution was plain to every eye, victory was irrevocably declared for the democratic cause. All power was in fact in its hands, and resistance was no longer possible. The higher orders submitted without a murmur and without a struggle to an evil that was now inevitable. The usual fate of falling powers awaited them. Each of their members followed his own interests, and since it was impossible to wrest power from the hands of a people they did not hate enough to defy, their only aim was to win its good will at any price. The most democratic laws were therefore voted by the very men whose interests they harmed. And so, although the higher classes did not stir up the passions of the people against their own order, they hastened the triumph of the new state of things. By a strange reversal, the democratic impulse proved most irresistible in the very States where the aristocracy had the firmest hold. Maryland, which had been founded by men of rank, was the first State to proclaim universal suffrage and to introduce the most democratic forms into the conduct of its government.

When a nation changes the qualification for voting, it is easy to foresee that sooner or later the qualification will be abolished altogether. There is no more constant rule in the history of society: the further voting rights are extended, the greater the need to extend them. After each concession the strength of the democracy grows, and its demands grow with its strength. The ambition of those who fall below the set level is irritated in exact proportion to the number of those who rise above it. The exception finally becomes the rule, concession follows concession, and there is no stopping point short of universal suffrage.

Today the principle of the sovereignty of the people has reached, in the United States, every practical development the imagination can conceive. It is free of the fictions that have been draped over it in other countries, and it appears in every possible form as the occasion requires. Sometimes the people as a body make the laws, as at Athens. Sometimes its representatives, chosen by universal suffrage, transact business in its name and almost under its direct control.

In some countries there is a power that is, to some extent, foreign to the social body, and that directs it and forces it along a certain path. In others the ruling force is divided, lying partly within and partly outside the ranks of the people. But nothing of the kind is to be seen in the United States. There society governs itself for itself. All power is centered in its own bosom, and you will scarcely meet a single individual who would venture to conceive, much less to express, the idea of seeking power elsewhere. The nation takes part in making its laws by choosing its legislators, and in carrying them out by choosing the agents of the executive government. It may almost be said to govern itself, so feeble and so restricted is the share left to the administration, and so little do the authorities forget their popular origin and the power from which they derive. *a [Footnote a: See Appendix, H.]

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Necessity Of Examining The Condition Of The States Before That Of The Union At Large
paragraphs: In the following chapter I propose to examine the form of government established in America on the principle of the sovereignty of the people: what its resources are, what hinders it, what advantages it has, and what dangers. The first difficulty comes from the complex nature of the Constitution of the United States. It consists of two distinct social structures, joined together and, as it were, encased one within the other. There are two governments, completely separate and almost independent. One fulfills the ordinary duties and answers the daily and unpredictable calls of a community. The other is confined within certain limits and exercises only an exceptional authority over the general interests of the country. In short, there are twenty-four small sovereign nations, and together they make up the body of the Union. To examine the Union before we have studied the States would be to adopt a method full of obstacles. The form of the Federal Government of the United States was the last to be adopted. It is in fact nothing more than a modification or a summary of the republican principles that were already current throughout the community before it existed, and independently of its existence. Moreover, as I have just observed, the Federal Government is the exception, and the government of the States is the rule. An author who tried to present the picture as a whole before he had explained its details would inevitably fall into obscurity and repetition.

The great political principles that govern American society today undoubtedly took their origin and their growth in the State. It is therefore necessary to become acquainted with the State in order to have a clue to everything else. The States that now make up the American Union all present the same features in the outward appearance of their institutions. Their political and administrative life is centered in three focal points, which may fairly be compared to the different nerve centers that carry movement to the human body. The township is the lowest in order, then the county, and last the State. I propose to devote the following chapter to examining these three divisions.
The American System of Townships and Municipal Bodies

Why the author begins the examination of political institutions with the township—Its existence in all nations—Difficulty of establishing and preserving municipal independence—Its importance—Why the author has chosen the township system of New England as the main topic of his discussion.

It is not by accident that I begin this subject with the township. The village or township is the only association so perfectly natural that wherever a number of men are gathered together, it seems to form itself.

The town, or tithing, as the smallest division of a community, must exist in all nations, whatever their laws and customs may be. Whether men make monarchies or establish republics, the first association of mankind seems to have been formed by the hand of God. But although the township is as old as humanity, its liberties are rarely respected and are easily destroyed. A nation can always set up great political assemblies, because it ordinarily contains a certain number of individuals fitted by their talents, if not by their habits, to direct public affairs. The township, by contrast, is made of coarser material, which the legislator shapes less easily. The difficulties in the way of consolidating its independence tend to grow rather than shrink as the people become more educated. A highly civilized community scorns attempts at local independence, is disgusted by its many blunders, and is inclined to despair of success before the experiment is finished. Again, no immunities are so poorly protected against the encroachments of the supreme power as those of municipal bodies in general. They cannot struggle alone against a strong or enterprising government, and they cannot defend their cause successfully unless it is identified with the customs of the nation and supported by public opinion. Thus, until the independence of townships has fused with the mores of a people, it is easily destroyed, and it can fuse with them only after a long existence in the laws. Municipal freedom is not the fruit of human invention. It is rarely created, but it is, as it were, secretly and spontaneously born in the midst of a semi-barbarous state of society. The constant action of the laws and national habits, particular circumstances, and above all time may consolidate it. But there is certainly no nation on the continent of Europe that has experienced its advantages. Nevertheless, local assemblies of citizens are the strength of free nations. Town meetings are to liberty what primary schools are to science: they bring it within the people’s reach and teach them how to use it and enjoy it. A nation may establish a system of free government, but without the spirit of municipal institutions it cannot have the spirit of liberty. The passing passions and interests of an hour, or the chance of circumstances, may have created the outward forms of independence. But the despotic tendency that has been driven back will, sooner or later, inevitably reappear on the surface.

To explain to the reader the general principles on which the political organization of the counties and townships of the United States rests, I have thought it best to choose one of the States of New England as an example, to examine the workings of its constitution, and then to take a general look over the rest of the country. The township and the county are not organized in the same way in every part of the Union. Still, it is easy to see that the same principles guided the formation of both throughout the Union. I am inclined to believe that these principles have been carried further in New England than elsewhere, and that they therefore give a foreigner more opportunity to observe them. The institutions of New England form a complete and orderly whole. Time has sanctioned them, the laws support them, and the mores of the community support them more strongly still, and they exercise an immense influence over that community. They therefore deserve our attention on every count.
Limits of the Township

The township of New England is a division that stands between the commune and the canton of France, and it corresponds in general to the English tithing, or town. Its average population is from two to three thousand. *a So the interests of its inhabitants are unlikely to conflict, and yet men capable of conducting its affairs can always be found among its citizens.
a [ In 1830 there were 305 townships in the State of Massachusetts, and 610,014 inhabitants, which gives an average of about 2,000 inhabitants to each township.]
Authorities of the Township in New England

The people the source of all power here as elsewhere—Manages its own affairs—No corporation—The greater part of the authority vested in the hands of the Selectmen—How the Selectmen act—Town meeting—Enumeration of the public officers of the township—Obligatory and remunerated functions.

In the township, as everywhere else, the people is the only source of power. But at no other stage of government does the body of citizens exercise a more direct influence. In America the people is a master whose demands must be obeyed to the utmost limits of possibility.

In New England the majority acts through representatives in conducting the public business of the State. Such an arrangement may be necessary in general affairs, but in the townships the legislative and administrative action of the government is in closer contact with those it governs, and there the system of representation is not adopted. There is no corporation. Instead, the body of electors, after naming its magistrates, directs them in everything that goes beyond the simple, ordinary executive business of the State. *b

b [ The same rules do not apply to the great towns, which generally have a mayor and a corporation divided into two bodies. This, however, is an exception that requires the sanction of a law.—See the Act of February 22, 1822, for appointing the authorities of the city of Boston. It often happens that small towns as well as cities are subject to a special administration. In 1832, 104 townships in the State of New York were governed in this manner.—Williams’ Register.]
This state of things is so contrary to our ideas, and so different from our customs, that I must give some examples to explain it fully.

The public duties in the township are extremely numerous and minutely divided, as we shall see further on. But the larger share of administrative power is held by a small number of individuals called “the Selectmen.” *c The general laws of the State impose a certain number of obligations on the selectmen. They may fulfill these without authorization from the body they represent, but they can neglect them only at their own risk. The law of the State requires them, for instance, to draw up the list of electors in their townships, and if they omit this part of their duties, they are guilty of a misdemeanor. In all the affairs that the town meeting decides, however, the selectmen are the instruments of the popular mandate, just as in France the mayor carries out the decree of the municipal council. They usually act on their own responsibility and simply put into practice principles the majority has already recognized. But if any change is to be made in the existing state of things, or if they wish to undertake some new enterprise, they must go back to the source of their power. If, for instance, a school is to be established, the selectmen call the whole body of electors together on a certain day at an appointed place. They explain the urgency of the case. They give their opinion on the means of meeting it, on the probable expense, and on the site that seems most favorable. The meeting is consulted on each of these points. It adopts the principle, marks out the site, votes the tax, and entrusts the carrying out of its resolution to the selectmen.

c [ Three selectmen are appointed in the small townships, and nine in the large ones. See “The Town-Officer,” p. 186. See also the principal laws of the State of Massachusetts relative to the selectmen:

Act of February 20, 1786, vol. i. p. 219; February 24, 1796, vol. i. p. 488; March 7, 1801, vol. ii. p. 45; June 16, 1795, vol. i. p. 475; March 12, 1808, vol. ii. p. 186; February 28, 1787, vol. i. p. 302; June 22, 1797, vol. i. p. 539.]

The selectmen alone have the right to call a town meeting, but they may be asked to do so. If ten citizens want to submit a new project to the township for its approval, they may demand a general assembly of the inhabitants. The selectmen are obliged to comply, but they have only the right to preside at the meeting. *d
d [ See Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 150, Act of March 25, 1786.]

The selectmen are elected every year in April or May. At the same time the town meeting chooses a number of other municipal magistrates, who are entrusted with important administrative functions. The assessors set the township’s tax rate, and the collectors receive the tax. A constable is appointed to keep the peace, watch the streets, and help enforce the laws. The town clerk records all the town votes, orders, grants, births, deaths, and marriages. The treasurer keeps the funds. The overseer of the poor takes on the difficult task of supervising the working of the poor laws. Committeemen are appointed to look after the schools and public instruction, and the road surveyors, who take care of the larger and smaller thoroughfares of the township, complete the list of the principal officials. These offices are, however, divided still further. Among the municipal officers are parish commissioners, who audit the expenses of public worship, and different classes of inspectors, some of whom direct the citizens in case of fire. There are also tithing-men, listers, haywards, chimney-viewers, fence-viewers to maintain property boundaries, timber-measurers, and sealers of weights and measures. *e

e [ All these magistrates actually exist; their different functions are all detailed in a book called “The Town-Officer,” by Isaac Goodwin, Worcester, 1827; and in the “Collection of the General Laws of Massachusetts,” 3 vols., Boston, 1823.]

There are nineteen principal officers in a township. Every inhabitant is required, on pain of a fine, to take on these different duties. Almost all of them are paid, however, so that poorer citizens can give up their time without loss. In general the American system does not give its officials a fixed salary. Every service has its price, and they are paid in proportion to what they have done.
Existence of the Township

Everyone the best judge of his own interest—Corollary of the principle of the sovereignty of the people—Application of these doctrines in the townships of America—The township of New England is sovereign in all that concerns itself alone, and subject to the State in all other matters—Bond between the township and the State—In France the Government lends its agent to the commune—In America the reverse occurs.

I have already observed that the principle of the sovereignty of the people governs the whole political system of the Anglo-Americans. Every page of this book will give new instances of the same doctrine. In nations that recognize the sovereignty of the people, every individual holds an equal share of power and takes an equal part in the government of the State. Every individual is therefore assumed to be as well informed, as virtuous, and as strong as any of his fellow citizens. He obeys the government, not because he is inferior to the authorities who run it, or less capable than his neighbor of governing himself, but because he acknowledges the usefulness of an association with his fellow men and knows that no such association can exist without a regulating force. In everything that concerns the mutual relations of citizens he is a subject, but in everything that concerns himself he is free and answerable to God alone. From this comes the maxim that everyone is the best and the only judge of his own private interest, and that society has no right to control a man’s actions unless they harm the common good, or unless the common good requires his cooperation. This doctrine is universally accepted in the United States. I shall examine later the general influence it has on the ordinary actions of life. For now I am speaking of the nature of municipal bodies.

The township, taken as a whole and in relation to the government of the country, may be seen as an individual to whom the theory I have just described is applied. Municipal independence is therefore a natural consequence of the principle of the sovereignty of the people in the United States. All the American republics recognize it to some degree, but circumstances have favored its growth in a particular way in New England.

In this part of the Union political activity began in the townships, and it may almost be said that each of them originally formed an independent nation. When the Kings of England asserted their supremacy, they were content to take over the central power of the State. The townships of New England remained as they had been before. Although they are now subject to the State, at first they were scarcely dependent on it. It is important to remember that they were not granted privileges. On the contrary, they gave up a portion of their independence to the State. The townships are subordinate to the State only in those interests that I shall call social, because they are common to all the citizens. In everything that concerns themselves alone they are independent. Among the inhabitants of New England I believe there is not a man who would admit that the State has any right to interfere in their local interests. The towns of New England buy and sell, sue and are sued, raise or lower their taxes, without the slightest opposition from the administrative authority of the State.

They are bound, however, to comply with the demands of the community. If the State needs money, a town can neither grant nor withhold the funds. If the State plans a road, the township cannot refuse to let it cross its territory. If the State makes a police regulation, the town must enforce it. A uniform system of instruction is organized throughout the country, and every town is obliged to establish the schools the law orders. When I speak of the administration of the United States, I shall have occasion to point out the means by which the townships are compelled to obey in these different cases. Here I merely show that the obligation exists. Strict as it is, the government of the State imposes it only in principle, and in carrying it out the township regains all its independent rights. Thus taxes are voted by the State, but they are levied and collected by the township. The existence of a school is compulsory, but the township builds it, pays for it, and supervises it. In France the State’s tax collector receives the local taxes. In America the town’s collector receives the taxes of the State. Thus the French government lends its agents to the commune, whereas in America the township is the agent of the government. This fact alone shows how great the differences are between the two nations.
Public Spirit of the Townships of New England

How the township of New England wins the affections of its inhabitants—Difficulty of creating local public spirit in Europe—The rights and duties of the American township favorable to it—Characteristics of home in the United States—Manifestations of public spirit in New England—Its happy effects.

In America municipal bodies not only exist, but public spirit keeps them alive and supports them. The township of New England has two advantages that unfailingly secure the attentive interest of mankind, namely independence and authority. Its sphere is indeed small and limited, but within that sphere its action is unrestrained. Its independence gives it a real importance that its size and population might not always ensure.

We should remember that men’s affections generally lie on the side of authority. Patriotism does not last in a conquered nation. The New Englander is attached to his township not only because he was born in it, but because it is a social body of which he is a member, and because its government claims, and deserves, the use of his judgment. In Europe, those in power often regret the absence of local public spirit. Everyone agrees that there is no surer guarantee of order and tranquility, and yet nothing is harder to create. If municipal bodies were made powerful and independent, the authorities of the nation might be divided and the peace of the country endangered. Yet without power and independence, a town may contain good subjects, but it can have no active citizens. Another important fact is that the township of New England is so constituted as to arouse the warmest of human affections without awakening the ambitious passions of the human heart. The officers of the county are not elected, and their authority is very limited. Even the State is only a second-rate community, whose quiet and obscure administration offers no inducement strong enough to draw men away from the circle of their own interests into the turmoil of public affairs. The federal government confers power and honor on the men who run it, but those individuals can never be very numerous. The high office of the Presidency can be reached only late in life, and the other federal officials are generally men who have been favored by fortune or have distinguished themselves in some other career. Such offices cannot be the permanent aim of the ambitious. But the township serves as a center for the desire of public esteem, the need for stimulating interests, and the taste for authority and popularity, all within the ordinary relations of life. The passions that commonly embroil society change their character when they find an outlet so near the domestic hearth and the family circle.

In the American States power has been distributed with admirable skill in order to interest the greatest possible number of persons in the common good. Apart from the electors, who are called into action from time to time, the body politic is divided among innumerable officials and officers. Each, in his own sphere, represents the same powerful whole in whose name he acts. Local administration thus provides an unfailing source of profit and interest to a vast number of individuals.

The American system divides local authority among so many citizens, and it does not hesitate to multiply the functions of the town officers. For in the United States it is believed, and with truth, that patriotism is a kind of devotion that is strengthened by ritual observance. In this way the activity of the township is continually felt. It shows itself daily in the fulfillment of a duty or the exercise of a right, and a constant but gentle motion is thus kept up in society, which stirs it without disturbing it.

The American attaches himself to his home as the mountaineer clings to his hills, because the distinctive features of his country are marked more clearly there than elsewhere. The townships of New England are in general happy. Their government suits their tastes and is chosen by themselves. In the midst of the profound peace and general comfort that reign in America, the upheavals of municipal discord are rare. The conduct of local business is easy. The political education of the people has long been complete. Or rather, it was complete when the people first set foot on the soil. In New England there is no tradition of a distinction of ranks. No part of the community is tempted to oppress the rest, and the abuses that may injure isolated individuals are forgotten in the general contentment that prevails. The government may be defective (and no doubt it would be easy to point out its defects). Still, the fact that it really comes from those it governs, and that it acts, whether badly or well, casts over its faults the protective spell of a parent’s pride. No point of comparison disturbs the citizen’s satisfaction. England once governed the mass of the colonies, but the people was always sovereign in the township, where its rule is not only an ancient state of things but a primitive one.

The native of New England is attached to his township because it is independent and free. His share in its affairs ensures his attachment to its interest. The well-being it gives him secures his affection, and its welfare is the aim of his ambition and of his future efforts. He takes part in every event in the place. He practices the art of government in the small sphere within his reach. He accustoms himself to those forms that alone can ensure the steady progress of liberty, and he absorbs their spirit. He acquires a taste for order, understands the union or the balance of powers, and gathers clear, practical ideas about the nature of his duties and the extent of his rights.
The Counties of New England

The division of the counties in America is very similar to that of the arrondissements of France. The boundaries of the counties are laid down arbitrarily, and the various districts they contain have no necessary connection, no common tradition and no natural sympathy. Their purpose is simply to make the administration of justice easier.

The township was too small to contain a system of judicial institutions. Each county, however, has a court of justice, *f a sheriff to carry out its decrees, and a prison for criminals. There are certain needs that all the townships of a county feel alike, so it is natural that a central authority should meet them. In the State of Massachusetts this authority is held by several magistrates, who are appointed by the Governor of the State with the advice *g of his council. *h The officers of the county have only a limited and occasional authority, which applies to certain predetermined cases. The State and the townships hold all the power needed to conduct public business. The county’s budget is drawn up by its officers and voted by the legislature, but no assembly directly or indirectly represents the county. Properly speaking, therefore, it has no political existence.
f [ See the Act of February 14, 1821, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 551.]
g [ See the Act of February 20, 1819, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. ii. p. 494.]

h [ The council of the Governor is an elective body.] A twofold tendency can be seen in the American constitutions. It drives the legislator to centralize legislative power and to disperse executive power. The township of New England has within itself an indestructible element of independence, and this separate existence could be introduced into the county only artificially, since there its usefulness has not been felt. But all the townships together have only one representation, which is the State, the center of the national authority. Beyond the action of the township and that of the nation, nothing can be said to exist except the influence of individual effort.
Administration in New England

Administration not perceived in America—Why?—Europeans believe that liberty is promoted by depriving the social authority of some of its rights; Americans, by dividing its exercise—Almost all administration confined to the township and divided among the town officers—No trace of an administrative body to be perceived, either in the township or above it—The reason for this—How it happens that the administration of the State is uniform—Who is empowered to enforce the obedience of the township and the county to the law—The introduction of judicial power into the administration—Consequence of extending the elective principle to all officials—The Justice of the Peace in New England—By whom appointed—County officer: ensures the administration of the townships—Court of Sessions—Its action—Right of inspection and indictment distributed like the other administrative functions—Informers encouraged by the division of fines.

Nothing strikes a European traveler in the United States more than the absence of what we call the government, or the administration. Written laws exist in America, and one sees them carried out every day. But although everything is in motion, the hand that sets the social machine going cannot be found anywhere. Nevertheless, all peoples must use certain grammatical forms, which are the foundation of human language, in order to express their thoughts. In the same way, all communities must secure their existence by submitting to a certain amount of authority, without which they fall prey to anarchy. This authority may be distributed in several ways, but it must always exist somewhere.

There are two ways of reducing the force of authority in a nation. The first is to weaken the supreme power at its very root, by forbidding or preventing society from acting in its own defense under certain circumstances. To weaken authority in this way is what is generally called in Europe laying the foundations of freedom. The second way of reducing the influence of authority does not strip society of any of its rights or paralyze its efforts. Instead, it distributes the exercise of its privileges among various hands and multiplies the officials, each of whom is entrusted with the degree of power he needs to do his duty. There may be nations for whom this distribution of social powers might lead to anarchy. But in itself it is not anarchical. The action of authority is indeed made less irresistible and less perilous in this way, but it is not suppressed altogether.

The revolution of the United States was the result of a mature and dignified taste for freedom, not of a vague and ill-defined craving for independence. It made no alliance with the turbulent passions of anarchy. On the contrary, its course was marked by an attachment to whatever was lawful and orderly.

It was never assumed in the United States that the citizen of a free country has the right to do whatever he pleases. On the contrary, more varied social obligations were imposed on him there than anywhere else. No one ever thought of attacking the principles of society or contesting its rights. But the exercise of its authority was divided, so that the office might be powerful and the officeholder insignificant, and so that the community might be at once regulated and free. In no country in the world does the law speak so absolute a language as in America, and in no country is the right to apply it placed in so many hands. The administrative power in the United States is neither central nor hierarchical in its makeup, and this is why it passes unnoticed. The power exists, but its representative cannot be seen.

We have already seen that the independent townships of New England look after their own private interests. The municipal magistrates are the people most often entrusted with carrying out the laws of the State. *i Besides the general laws, the State sometimes passes general police regulations. More commonly, though, the townships and town officers, together with justices of the peace, regulate the minor details of social life according to the needs of the different localities. They issue such rules as concern the health of the community and the peace and morality of the citizens. *j Finally, these municipal magistrates provide, on their own initiative and without any delegated powers, for the unforeseen emergencies that often arise in society. *k

i [ See “The Town-Officer,” especially at the words Selectmen, Assessors, Collectors, Schools, Surveyors of Highways. I take one example in a thousand: the State prohibits traveling on Sunday; the tything-men, who are town officers, are specially charged with keeping watch and enforcing the law. See the Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 410.
The selectmen draw up the lists of electors for the election of the Governor, and send the result of the ballot to the Secretary of the State. See Act of February 24, 1796: Id., vol. i. p. 488.]

j [ Thus, for instance, the selectmen authorize the construction of drains and point out the proper sites for slaughterhouses and other trades that are a nuisance to the neighborhood. See the Act of June 7, 1785: Id., vol. i. p. 193.]
k [ The selectmen take measures for the security of the public in case of contagious diseases, together with the justices of the peace. See Act of June 22, 1797, vol. i. p. 539.]

It follows from what we have said that in the State of Massachusetts the administrative authority is almost entirely restricted to the township, *l but that it is distributed among a great number of individuals. In the French commune there is properly only one official, the mayor. In New England, as we have seen, there are nineteen. These nineteen officials do not in general depend on one another. The law carefully marks out a sphere of action for each of these magistrates, and within that sphere each has a full right to carry out his duties independently of any other authority. Above the township scarcely any trace of a ranked series of officials is to be found. It sometimes happens that the county officers alter a decision of the townships or town magistrates. *m But in general the authorities of the county have no right to interfere with the authorities of the township, *n except in matters that concern the county.

l [ I say almost, because some matters in the life of a township are regulated by a justice of the peace acting alone, or by the justices of the peace assembled in the chief town of the county. Licenses, for example, are granted by the justices. See the Act of February 28, 1787, vol. i. p. 297.]

m [ Thus licenses are granted only to those who can produce a certificate of good conduct from the selectmen. If the selectmen refuse to give the certificate, the applicant may appeal to the justices assembled in the Court of Sessions, who may then grant the license. See Act of March 12, 1808, vol. ii. p. 186.
The townships have the right to make by-laws and to enforce them with fines set by law, but the Court of Sessions must approve these by-laws. See Act of March 23, 1786, vol. i. p. 254.]

n [ In Massachusetts the county magistrates are often called on to investigate the acts of the town magistrates. But it will be shown further on that this investigation results from their judicial power, not their administrative power.]

The magistrates of the township, like those of the county, are bound to report their acts to the central government in a very small number of predetermined cases. *o But the central government is not represented by any individual whose business it is to publish police regulations and ordinances enforcing the execution of the laws, to keep up regular communication with the officers of the township and the county, to inspect their conduct, to direct their actions, or to reprimand their faults. There is no point that serves as a center for the radii of the administration.
o [ The town committees of schools are obliged to make an annual report to the Secretary of the State on the condition of the school. See Act of March 10, 1827, vol. iii. p. 183.]

What, then, is the uniform plan on which the government is conducted, and how is compliance enforced on the counties and their magistrates, or on the townships and their officers? In the States of New England the legislative authority covers more subjects than it does in France. The legislator reaches to the very core of the administration. The law goes down to the smallest details. The same enactment lays down both the principle and the method of applying it, and so imposes a multitude of strict and rigorously defined obligations on the secondary officials of the State. The consequence is that if all the secondary officials of the administration conform to the law, society in all its branches moves with the greatest uniformity. The difficulty that remains is how to compel the secondary officials of the administration to conform to the law. It may be affirmed that, in general, society has only two methods at its disposal for enforcing the execution of the laws. One is to give a superior official discretionary power to direct all the others and to dismiss them if they disobey. The other is to authorize the courts of justice to inflict judicial penalties on the offender. But these two methods are not always available.

The right to direct a civil officer presupposes the right to dismiss him if he does not obey orders, and to reward him by promotion if he does his duty properly. But an elected magistrate can be neither dismissed nor promoted. All elective offices are inalienable until their term has expired. In fact, the elected magistrate has nothing to expect or to fear from his constituents. And when all public offices are filled by ballot, there can be no ranked series of official dignities. The double right of commanding and of enforcing obedience can never be vested in the same individual, and the power to give an order can never be joined to the power to inflict a punishment or give a reward.

Communities in which the secondary officials of the government are elected are therefore forced to make great use of judicial penalties as a means of administration. This is not obvious at first sight. Those in power tend to regard the institution of elective officials as one concession, and the subjection of the elected magistrate to the judges of the land as another. They dislike both these innovations equally. And since they are pressed more urgently to grant the first than the second, they agree to the election of the magistrate and leave him independent of the judicial power. Nevertheless, the second measure is the only thing that can possibly counterbalance the first. It will be found that an elective authority that is not subject to judicial power will, sooner or later, either escape all control or be destroyed. The courts of justice are the only possible intermediary between the central power and the administrative bodies. They alone can compel the elected official to obey without violating the rights of the elector. The extension of judicial power in the political world ought therefore to be in exact proportion to the extension of elective offices. If these two institutions do not go hand in hand, the state must fall into anarchy or into subjection.

People have always noticed that the habits of legal business do not prepare men to exercise administrative authority. The Americans took from the English, their forefathers, an institution that the continent of Europe does not know: the Justices of the Peace. The Justice of the Peace stands halfway between the magistrate and the ordinary man of the world, between the civil officer and the judge.
