He is a well-informed citizen, though not necessarily someone trained in the law. His office simply requires him to enforce the police regulations of society, and for that task good sense and integrity count for more than legal science. The justice brings to the administration a certain taste for established forms and for publicity, which makes him a most unserviceable instrument of despotism. At the same time, he is free of the superstitions that make legal officers poor members of a government. The Americans have adopted the English system of justices of the peace, but they have removed the aristocratic character it has in the mother country. The Governor of Massachusetts *p appoints a certain number of justices of the peace in every county, for terms of seven years. *q He also chooses three of them from the whole body of justices, and in each county these three form what is called the Court of Sessions. The justices take a personal share in public business. Sometimes they receive administrative functions alongside elected officers, *r and sometimes they form a tribunal before which the magistrates summarily prosecute a refractory citizen, or the citizens report abuses by a magistrate. But the Court of Sessions is where they exercise their most important functions. This court meets twice a year in the county town, and in Massachusetts it has the power to enforce the obedience of most *s public officers. *t It should be noted that in Massachusetts the Court of Sessions is at once an administrative body in the proper sense and a political tribunal. Some have claimed that the county is a purely administrative division. The Court of Sessions handles the few affairs that concern several townships, or all the townships of the county in common, and that therefore cannot be left to any one of them. *u In everything that concerns county business, its duties are purely administrative. If in its investigations it sometimes borrows the forms of judicial procedure, it does so only to inform itself, *v or as a guarantee to the community it presides over. But when the administration of a township is brought before it, it always acts as a judicial body, and in a few cases as an official assembly.
p [ We shall learn later what a Governor is. I will content myself here with noting that he represents the executive power of the whole State.]
q [ See the Constitution of Massachusetts, chap. II. sect. 1. Section 9; chap. III. Section 3.]

r [ Thus, for example, a stranger arrives in a township from a country where a contagious disease prevails, and he falls ill. Two justices of the peace can, with the assent of the selectmen, order the sheriff of the county to remove him and look after him.—Act of June 22, 1797, vol. i. p. 540.

In general the justices take part in all the important acts of the administration and give them a semi-judicial character.] [Footnote s: I say most, because certain administrative misdemeanors are brought before ordinary tribunals. If, for instance, a township refuses to make the necessary expenditure for its schools or to name a school committee, it is liable to a heavy fine. But this penalty is pronounced by the Supreme Judicial Court or the Court of Common Pleas. See Act of March 10, 1827, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. iii. p. 190. The same is true when a township neglects to provide the necessary war supplies.—Act of February 21, 1822: Id., vol. ii. p. 570.]

t [ In their individual capacity the justices of the peace take part in the business of the counties and townships.] [Footnote u: These affairs can be grouped under the following heads:—1. The building of prisons and courthouses. 2. The county budget, which is afterward voted by the State. 3. The distribution of the taxes so voted. 4. The granting of certain patents. 5. The laying out and repair of the county roads.]
v [ Thus, when a road is under consideration, almost all difficulties are settled with the help of the jury.]

The first difficulty is getting obedience from an authority as entirely independent of the State’s general laws as the township is. We have said that the town meetings name assessors every year to levy the taxes. Suppose a township tries to avoid paying taxes by failing to name its assessors. The Court of Sessions then sentences it to a heavy penalty. *w The fine falls on each of the inhabitants, and the sheriff of the county, who is the officer of justice, carries out the order. In this way, in the United States, the authority of the government hides mysteriously behind the forms of a judicial sentence, and at the same time it gains strength from the irresistible power that people have given to the formalities of law.
w [ See Act of February 20, 1786, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 217.]

These proceedings are easy to follow and to understand. The demands made on a township are in general plain and exactly defined; they consist of a simple fact without any complication, or of a principle without detailed application. *x But the difficulty grows when what must be enforced is not the obedience of the township but that of the town officers. All the blameworthy actions of which a public official may be guilty can be reduced to the following heads:

x [ There is an indirect method of enforcing the obedience of a township. Suppose that the funds the law requires for the upkeep of the roads have not been voted. The town surveyor is then authorized, ex officio, to raise the money. Since he is personally liable to private individuals for the state of the roads, and can be indicted before the Court of Sessions, he is sure to use the extraordinary right the law gives him against the township. Thus, by threatening the officer, the Court of Sessions extracts compliance from the town. See Act of March 5, 1787, Id., vol. i. p. 305.]
He may carry out the law without energy or zeal;
He may neglect to carry out the law;
He may do what the law forbids him to do.

Only the last two violations of duty can come before a tribunal, because an action at law needs a positive, measurable fact as its foundation. Thus the selectmen may be fined if they fail to follow the legal formalities customary at town elections; *y but when a public officer does his duty badly, or obeys the letter of the law without zeal or energy, he is at least safe from judicial interference. Here even the Court of Sessions, with its full official powers, cannot force him into more satisfactory obedience. Fear of removal is the only check on such quasi-offences, and since the Court of Sessions does not create the town authorities, it cannot remove officials it does not appoint. Besides, proving negligence or lukewarmness would take constant investigation, while the Court of Sessions sits only twice a year and judges only the offences that are brought to its attention. A court of justice cannot impose that active and enlightened obedience on public officers; the only security for it is the possibility of removing them at will. In France this security is sought in the powers of the heads of the administration; in America it is sought in the principle of election.
y [ Laws of Massachusetts, vol. ii. p. 45.]

To sum up in a few words what I have been showing: if a public officer in New England commits a crime in the exercise of his functions, the ordinary courts of justice are always called on to sentence him. If he commits a fault in his official capacity, a purely administrative tribunal has the power to punish him; and if the matter is important or urgent, the judge makes up for what the officer failed to do. *z Finally, if the same man is guilty of one of those intangible offences that human justice does not notice, he must appear every year before a tribunal from which there is no appeal, one that can at once reduce him to insignificance and take away his office. This system undoubtedly has great advantages, but putting it into practice involves a difficulty that deserves to be pointed out.

z [ If, for instance, a township persists in refusing to name its assessors, the Court of Sessions appoints them, and the magistrates so appointed have the same authority as elected officers. See the Act quoted above, February 20, 1787.]

I have already observed that the administrative tribunal called the Court of Sessions has no right to inspect the town officers. It can step in only when the conduct of a magistrate is specifically brought to its attention, and this is the delicate part of the system. The Americans of New England have no public prosecutor in the Court of Sessions, *a and it is easy to see that creating one would have been difficult. Suppose an accusing magistrate had been appointed only in the chief town of each county, with no agents to help him in the townships. He would have known no more about what was going on in the county than the members of the Court of Sessions. But appointing agents in every township would have placed in his hands the most formidable of powers, that of a judicial administration. Besides, laws are the children of habit, and nothing of the kind exists in English legislation. The Americans have therefore divided the functions of inspection and prosecution, as they have divided all the other functions of the administration. The law requires grand jurors to inform the court to which they belong of every misdemeanor committed in their county. *b Certain great offences are prosecuted officially by the States; *c but more often the job of punishing offenders falls to the fiscal officer, whose duty it is to receive the fine. Thus the treasurer of the township is responsible for prosecuting the administrative offences that come to his notice. But American legislation also appeals in a more particular way to the private interest of the citizen; *d and anyone studying the laws of the United States meets this great principle constantly. American legislators are readier to credit men with intelligence than with honesty, and they count heavily on personal greed to get the laws carried out. When someone is really and noticeably harmed by an administrative abuse, it is natural that his own interest should lead him to prosecute. But suppose a legal formality is required that benefits the community yet matters little to individuals. Plaintiffs may then be harder to find, and by a tacit agreement the laws may fall into disuse. Their system has brought the Americans to this extreme, and so they are obliged to encourage informers by giving them a share of the penalty in certain cases, *e and to secure the execution of the laws by the dangerous expedient of degrading the morals of the people. The only administrative authority above the county magistrates is, properly speaking, that of the government.
a [ I say the Court of Sessions, because in common courts there is a magistrate who exercises some of the functions of a public prosecutor.]
b [ The grand-jurors are, for instance, bound to inform the court of the bad state of the roads.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 308.]

c [ If, for instance, the treasurer of the county holds back his accounts.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 406.] [Footnote d: Thus, if a private individual suffers a breakdown or is injured because of the bad state of a road, he can sue the township or the county for damages at the sessions.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 309.]

e [ In cases of invasion or insurrection, if the town officers neglect to furnish the necessary stores and ammunition for the militia, the township may be sentenced to a fine of from $200 to $500. One can easily imagine that in such a case no one might care to prosecute; hence the law adds that any citizen may bring an indictment for offences of this kind, and that half of the fine shall go to the plaintiff. See Act of March 6, 1810, vol. ii. p. 236. The same clause is frequently found in the law of Massachusetts. Private individuals are not only encouraged in this way to prosecute public officers; public officers are likewise encouraged to bring the disobedience of private individuals to justice. If a citizen refuses to do the work assigned to him on a road, the road surveyor may prosecute him, and he receives half the penalty for himself. See the Laws cited above, vol. i. p. 308.]

General Remarks on the Administration of the United States Differences among the States of the Union in their systems of administration—Activity and perfection of the local authorities decrease toward the South—Power of the magistrate increases; that of the elector diminishes—Administration passes from the township to the county—States of New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania—Principles of administration applicable to the whole Union—Election of public officers, and inalienability of their functions—Absence of gradation of ranks—Introduction of judicial resources into the administration.

I said earlier that, after examining the constitution of the township and the county in New England in detail, I would take a general view of the rest of the Union. Every State has townships and local activity, but nowhere in the confederation will we find a township exactly like those of New England. The farther south we go, the less active the business of the township or parish becomes. There are fewer magistrates, functions, and rights; the population has a less direct influence on affairs; town meetings are less frequent and have fewer subjects to debate. The elected magistrate gains power and the elector loses it, while the public spirit of local communities is less awake and less influential. *f We can see these differences to some extent in New York; they are very noticeable in Pennsylvania; and they grow less striking as we move toward the northwest. Most emigrants who settle in the northwestern States are natives of New England, and they bring the habits of their mother country into the one they adopt. A township in Ohio is by no means unlike a township in Massachusetts.
f [ For details see the Revised Statutes of the State of New York, part i. chap. xi. vol. i. pp. 336-364, entitled, “Of the Powers, Duties, and Privileges of Towns.”

See in the Digest of the Laws of Pennsylvania, the words Assessors, Collector, Constables, Overseer of the Poor, Supervisors of Highways; and in the Acts of a general nature of the State of Ohio, the Act of February 25, 1834, relating to townships, p. 412; besides the particular provisions relating to various town officers, such as Township’s Clerk, Trustees, Overseers of the Poor, Fence Viewers, Appraisers of Property, Township’s Treasurer, Constables, Supervisors of Highways.]

We have seen that in Massachusetts the mainspring of public administration is the township, which is the common center of the citizens’ interests and affections. This stops being true as we go down to States where knowledge is less widely spread and where the township therefore offers fewer guarantees of a wise and active administration. As we leave New England, we find the importance of the town passing gradually to the county. The county becomes the center of administration and the intermediate power between the government and the citizen. In Massachusetts a Court of Sessions conducts county business, and it is made up of a quorum named by the Governor and his council; the county has no representative assembly, and the national legislature votes its expenditure. In the great State of New York, by contrast, and in Ohio and Pennsylvania, the inhabitants of each county choose a number of representatives, who form the county assembly. *g This assembly may tax the inhabitants to a certain extent, and in this respect it has the privileges of a real legislative body. It also exercises executive power in the county, often directs the administration of the townships, and keeps their authority within much narrower limits than in Massachusetts.

g [ See the Revised Statutes of the State of New York, part i. chap. xi. vol. i. p. 340. Id. chap. xii. p. 366; also in the Acts of the State of Ohio, an act relating to county commissioners, February 25, 1824, p. 263. See the Digest of the Laws of Pennsylvania, at the words County-rates and Levies, p. 170. In the State of New York each township elects a representative, who takes part in the administration of the county as well as in that of the township.]

Those are the main differences between the systems of county and town administration in the Federal States. If I meant to examine American law in minute detail, I would have to point out still more differences in how the several communities carry out their business. But what I have said is enough to show the general principles on which administration in the United States rests. These principles are applied in different ways, and they produce more or fewer consequences from place to place, but they remain substantially the same. The laws differ and their outward features change; their character does not. The township and the county are not set up the same way everywhere, yet in the United States both always rest on one principle: each person is the best judge of what concerns himself alone, and the best person to meet his own private needs. So the township and the county must look after their own special interests. The State governs, but it does not interfere in how they administer them. We may find exceptions to this rule, but never a contrary principle.

The first consequence of this doctrine is that all the magistrates are chosen either by the citizens or at least from among them. Officers are everywhere elected or appointed for a fixed term, so it was impossible to set up a dependent chain of authorities. There are almost as many independent officials as there are functions, and the executive power is scattered among a multitude of hands. This made it indispensable to bring the administration under the control of the courts of justice, and to use a system of pecuniary penalties to force the secondary bodies and their representatives to obey the laws. This system prevails from one end of the Union to the other. The States have not, however, all given the same judges the power to punish misconduct by public officers, or to act as the executive in urgent cases. The Anglo-Americans took the institution of justices of the peace from a common source, but although it exists in all the States, it is not always put to the same use. Everywhere the justices of the peace take part in administering the townships and the counties, *h either as public officers or as judges of public misdemeanors; but in most of the States the more important classes of public offences go before the ordinary tribunals.
h [ In some of the Southern States the county courts are charged with all the details of the administration. See the Statutes of the State of Tennessee, arts. Judiciary, Taxes, etc.]

Election of public officers, or the inalienability of their functions; the absence of any gradation of powers; judicial control over the secondary branches of the administration: these are the features found everywhere in the American system, from Maine to the Floridas. In some States traces of a centralized administration begin to show, and New York has gone furthest in this direction. In New York the officers of the central government sometimes exercise a kind of inspection or control over the secondary bodies. *i

i [ For instance, the direction of public instruction is centered in the hands of the government. The legislature names the members of the University, who are called Regents; the Governor and Lieutenant-Governor of the State are necessarily among them.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 455. The Regents of the University visit the colleges and academies every year and report to the legislature. Their supervision is not ineffective, for several reasons: colleges, in order to become corporations, need a charter, which is granted only on the recommendation of the Regents; every year funds are distributed by the State to encourage learning, and the Regents distribute this money. See chap. xv. “Instruction,” Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 455.
The school commissioners are required to send an annual report to the Superintendent of the Republic.—Id. p. 488.
A similar report is made every year to the same person on the number and condition of the poor.—Id. p. 631.]

At other times they form a court of appeal for deciding affairs. *j In New York, judicial penalties are used less than elsewhere as a means of administration, and the right to prosecute offences by public officers is placed in fewer hands. *k The same tendency can faintly be seen in some other States; *l but in general the most prominent feature of administration in the United States is its excessive local independence.

j [ If anyone believes himself wronged by the school commissioners (who are town officers), he can appeal to the superintendent of the primary schools, whose decision is final.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 487.

Provisions similar to those cited above are found from time to time in the laws of the State of New York; but in general these attempts at centralization are weak and unproductive. The great authorities of the State have the right to watch and control the subordinate agents, but not to reward or punish them. The same individual is never empowered both to give an order and to punish disobedience; he therefore has the right to command without the means of exacting compliance. In 1830 the Superintendent of Schools complained in his Annual Report to the legislature that several school commissioners had neglected, despite his request, to send him the accounts that were due. He added that if this omission continued, he would be obliged to prosecute them, as the law directs, before the proper tribunals.]
k [ Thus the district attorney is directed to recover all fines below the sum of fifty dollars, unless that right has been specially given to another magistrate.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 383.]

l [ Several traces of centralization can be found in Massachusetts; for instance, the committees of the town schools are directed to make an annual report to the Secretary of State. See Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 367.]

I have described the townships and the administration. It now remains for me to speak of the State and its government. I can cover this ground quickly without fear of being misunderstood, for all I have to say is found in the written forms of the various constitutions, which are easy to obtain. These constitutions rest on a simple and rational theory. All constitutional nations have adopted their forms, and we know them well. So I need give only a short analysis here, and I shall try afterward to pass judgment on what I now describe.
Legislative Power of the State
Division of the Legislative Body into Two Houses—Senate—House of Representatives—Different Functions of These Two Bodies.

The legislative power of the State rests in two assemblies; the first usually carries the name of Senate. The Senate is normally a legislative body, but at times it also acts as an executive and judicial one. How it takes part in government varies with the constitutions of the different States; *m but it most often exercises executive power in nominating public officers. It shares in judicial power when certain political offences are tried, and sometimes when certain civil cases are decided. *n It always has few members. The other branch of the legislature, usually called the House of Representatives, has no share at all in the administration. It takes part in judicial power only by impeaching public officers before the Senate. Almost everywhere the members of the two Houses are subject to the same conditions of election, and are chosen in the same way by the same citizens. The one difference between them is that senators are generally chosen for a longer term than representatives. Representatives seldom stay in office more than a year; senators usually sit two or three years. Because senators may be chosen for several years and are renewed in rotation, the law keeps in the legislative body a nucleus of men who are already used to public business and who can have a salutary influence on the junior members.
m [ In Massachusetts the Senate is not invested with any administrative functions.]
n [ As in the State of New York.]

The Americans clearly did not mean, by dividing the legislative body into two branches, to make one house hereditary and the other elected, one aristocratic and the other democratic. Their purpose was not to make the one a bulwark of power while the other represented the interests and passions of the people. The present constitution of the United States gives only these advantages: the legislative power is divided, which checks political assemblies, and there is a tribunal of appeal for revising the laws.

Time and experience, however, have convinced the Americans that, even if these are its only advantages, dividing the legislative power is still a principle of the greatest necessity. Pennsylvania was the only one of the United States that at first tried to set up a single House of Assembly. Franklin himself was so swept along by the necessary consequences of the principle of the sovereignty of the people that he went along with it. But the Pennsylvanians soon had to change the law and create two Houses. So the principle of dividing the legislative power was finally established, and its necessity can now be regarded as a demonstrated truth. The republics of antiquity hardly knew this theory. It entered the world almost by accident, as so many other great truths have, and several modern nations have misunderstood it. At last it has become an axiom of the political science of our age.
[See Benjamin Franklin]
The Executive Power of the State
Office of Governor in an American State—The place he occupies in relation to the legislature—His rights and his duties—His dependence on the people.

It may truly be said that the Governor represents the executive power of the State, although he holds only a portion of its rights. The supreme magistrate, with the title of Governor, is the official moderator and counselor of the legislature. He has a veto, or suspensive power, with which he can stop its movements or at least delay them as he pleases. He lays the needs of the country before the legislative body and points out the means he thinks could usefully be used to meet them. In every undertaking that concerns the nation at large, he is the natural executor of the legislature’s decrees. *o When the legislature is not in session, the Governor must take every necessary step to protect the State from violent shocks and unforeseen dangers. The whole military power of the State is at his disposal. He commands the militia and heads the armed force. When the authority that people generally agree to give the laws is disregarded, the Governor puts himself at the head of the State’s armed force to put down resistance and restore order. Lastly, the Governor has no share in administering townships and counties, except indirectly through nominating Justices of the Peace, a nomination he cannot cancel. *p The Governor is an elected magistrate, usually chosen for only one or two years, so he always remains strictly dependent on the majority that elected him.

o [ In practice, it is not always the Governor who carries out the plans of the legislature; it often happens that the legislature, in voting a measure, names special agents to oversee its execution.]
p [ In some of the States the justices of the peace are not chosen by the Governor.]
Political Effects of the System of Local Administration in the United States

Necessary distinction between the general centralization of government and the centralization of the local administration—Local administration not centralized in the United States: great general centralization of the government—Some bad consequences resulting to the United States from the local administration—Administrative advantages of this order of things—The power that conducts the government is less regular, less enlightened, less learned, but much greater than in Europe—Political advantages of this order of things—In the United States the interests of the country are everywhere kept in view—Support given to the government by the community—Provincial institutions more necessary as the social condition becomes more democratic—Reason for this.

Centralization has become a word in general, daily use, though no precise meaning is attached to it. Yet there are two distinct kinds of centralization, and we must carefully tell them apart. Some interests are common to all parts of a nation, such as enacting its general laws and conducting its foreign relations. Other interests belong to particular parts of the nation, such as the business of the different townships. When the power that directs the general interests is gathered in one place, or held by the same persons, it forms a central government. In the same way, when the power of directing partial or local interests is brought together in one place, it forms what may be called a central administration.

On some points the two kinds of centralization merge, but if we sort the matters that fall more particularly within the province of each, we can easily tell them apart. Clearly, a central government gains immense power when it is joined to administrative centralization. In that combination it teaches men to set their own will aside habitually and completely, to submit not just once or on one point but in every respect and at all times. So this union of power does more than subdue them by force. It also affects them in the ordinary habits of life, and it influences each individual, first separately and then collectively.

These two kinds of centralization help and draw each other on, but we should not think them inseparable. One cannot imagine a more completely central government than the one France had under Louis XIV. The same man made the laws and interpreted them, and he represented France at home and abroad, so he was justified in claiming that the State was identified with his person. Even so, the administration was much less centralized under Louis XIV than it is today.

In England the centralization of the government is carried to great perfection. The State has the compact vigor of a single man; by an act of its will alone it sets immense machinery in motion and wields or gathers the efforts of its authority. Indeed, I cannot conceive that a nation can have a secure or prosperous existence without a powerful centralization of government. But I think that a central administration saps the strength of the nations in which it exists, because it constantly weakens their public spirit. Such an administration may succeed, at a given moment and at a given point, in gathering all the available resources of a people. Even so, it at least harms the renewal of those resources. It may secure victory in the hour of struggle, but it slowly loosens the sinews of strength. It can do wonders for the passing greatness of one man; it cannot ensure the lasting prosperity of a nation.

If we look carefully, we shall find that whenever people say a State cannot act because it has no central point, what it lacks is centralization of government. People often claim, and we are ready to believe, that the German empire never managed to bring all its powers into action. The reason was that the State could never enforce obedience to its general laws. The several members of that great body always claimed the right, or found the means, to refuse their cooperation to the representatives of the common authority, even in matters that concerned the mass of the people. In other words, there was no centralization of government. The same remark applies to the Middle Ages. All the confusion of feudal society came from this: control over general interests, as well as local ones, was divided among a thousand hands and broken up in a thousand ways. Without a central government, the nations of Europe could not move energetically along any straight course.

We have shown that the United States has no central administration and no dependent chain of public officials. Local authority has been pushed to lengths that no European nation could tolerate without great inconvenience, and that have even had some harmful results in America. But in the United States the centralization of the government is complete, and it would be easy to prove that the national power is more compact than it has ever been in the old nations of Europe. Each State has only one legislative body and only one source of political authority. District assemblies and county courts have generally not been multiplied, for fear that they might be tempted to go beyond their administrative duties and interfere with the government. In America the legislature of each State is supreme. Nothing can impede its authority: not privileges, not local immunities, not personal influence, not even the empire of reason, since the legislature represents the majority, which claims to be the sole organ of reason. Its own decision is therefore the only limit on its action. Beside it, and under its immediate control, stands the representative of the executive power, whose duty is to make the refractory submit by superior force. The only sign of weakness lies in certain details of how the government acts. The American republics have no standing armies to intimidate a discontented minority; but no minority has yet been driven to declare open war, so the need for an army has not been felt. *q The State usually uses the officers of the township or the county to deal with the citizens. Thus, in New England, the assessor sets the rate of taxes, the collector receives them, the town treasurer sends the amount to the public treasury, and any disputes that arise go before the ordinary courts of justice. This way of collecting taxes is slow as well as inconvenient, and it would be a permanent hindrance to a government with large financial demands. In whatever materially affects its existence, the government ought to be served by officers of its own, appointed by itself, removable at will, and used to rapid methods of proceeding. But it will always be easy for the central government, organized as it is in America, to introduce new and more effective ways of acting, suited to its needs. [Footnote q: [The Civil War of 1860-65 cruelly belied this statement, and in the course of the struggle the North alone called two and a half million men to arms; but to the honor of the United States it must be added that, when the contest ended, this army disappeared as rapidly as it had been raised.—Translator’s Note.]]

The absence of a central government will not, then, prove the destruction of the republics of the New World, as has often been claimed. Far from supposing that the American governments are not centralized enough, I shall show later that they are too centralized. The legislative bodies encroach on the authority of the government every day, and their tendency, like that of the French Convention, is to take it entirely for themselves. In these circumstances the social power is constantly changing hands, because it is subordinate to the power of the people, which in its awareness of its own strength is all too ready to forget the maxims of wisdom and foresight. Here lies its danger. Its vigor, and not its weakness, will probably be the cause of its eventual destruction.

The system of local administration produces several different effects in America. The Americans seem to me to have gone beyond the limits of sound policy in isolating the administration of the government, for order, even in secondary matters, is of national importance. *r Because the State has no administrative officials of its own, stationed at various points across its territory, to whom it can give a common direction, it rarely tries to issue any general police regulations. The lack of these regulations is keenly felt, and Europeans frequently notice it. The appearance of disorder on the surface leads a European at first to imagine that society is in a state of anarchy, and he does not see his mistake until he has looked deeper into the subject. Certain undertakings matter to the whole State, but they cannot be carried out, because there is no national administration to direct them. Left to the efforts of the towns or counties, under the care of elected or temporary agents, they lead to no result, or at least to no lasting benefit.

r [ The authority that represents the State ought not, I think, to give up the right of inspecting the local administration, even when it does not intervene more actively. Suppose, for instance, that an agent of the government were stationed at some fixed place in the country to prosecute the misdemeanors of the town and county officers. Would not a more uniform order result, without in any way compromising the independence of the township? Nothing of the kind exists in America, however. There is nothing above the county courts, which have, as it were, only an incidental jurisdiction over the offenses they are meant to repress.]

The partisans of centralization in Europe are accustomed to maintain that the government directs the affairs of each locality better than the citizens could do it for themselves. This may be true when the central power is educated and the local districts are ignorant, when it is as quick as they are slow, and when it is used to acting while they are used to obeying. Indeed, it is plain that this double tendency must grow as centralization increases, and that the readiness of the one and the incapacity of the others must become more and more pronounced. But I deny that this is the case when the people is as well-informed, as alert to its interests, and as accustomed to reflect on them as the Americans are. I am convinced, on the contrary, that in this case the collective strength of the citizens will always serve the public welfare more effectively than the authority of the government. It is hard to say with certainty how to rouse a sleeping population and give it passions and knowledge it does not possess. I am well aware that it is a difficult task to persuade men to busy themselves with their own affairs, and it would often be easier to interest them in the fine points of court etiquette than in the repair of their common dwelling. But whenever a central administration claims to replace the people most concerned, I am inclined to suppose that it is either mistaken or trying to mislead. However enlightened and however skillful a central power may be, it cannot by itself take in all the details of the life of a great nation. Such vigilance is beyond human powers. And when it tries to build and set in motion so many complicated springs, it must accept a very imperfect result or wear itself out in futile efforts.

Centralization does succeed more easily in imposing a certain uniformity on the outward actions of men. This uniformity commands our respect for its own sake, whatever it is applied to, like those devotees who worship the statue and forget the deity it represents. Centralization gives an admirable regularity to the routine of business without difficulty. It attends to the details of public order with skill, represses the smallest disorder and the pettiest misdemeanors, and keeps society in a status quo that is safe alike from improvement and from decline. It perpetuates a drowsy precision in the conduct of affairs, which the heads of the administration welcome as a sign of perfect order and public tranquillity. *s In short, it is better at prevention than at action. Its force deserts it when society needs to be disturbed or hurried along in its course, and as soon as the cooperation of private citizens is necessary to carry out its measures, the secret of its weakness is exposed. Even while it asks for their help, it does so on the condition that they act exactly as much as the government chooses, and exactly in the manner it prescribes. They are to take charge of the details without aspiring to guide the system. They are to work in a dark and subordinate sphere, and to judge the acts they have helped to carry out only by their results. These are not the conditions on which the alliance of the human will can be won. Its bearing must be free and its actions responsible, or else (such is the nature of man) the citizen would rather remain a passive spectator than be a dependent actor in schemes he knows nothing about.

s [ China appears to me to offer the most perfect example of the kind of well-being that a completely centralized administration can provide for the nations under it. Travelers assure us that the Chinese have peace without happiness, industry without improvement, stability without strength, and public order without public morality. The condition of society is always tolerable, never excellent. I am convinced that when China is opened to European observation, it will be found to contain the most perfect model of a central administration that exists in the world.]

It cannot be denied that the United States not infrequently feels the lack of those uniform regulations that govern the conduct of every inhabitant of France. Gross cases of social indifference and neglect are to be found, and from time to time disgraceful blemishes appear in complete contrast with the civilization around them. Useful undertakings that cannot succeed without constant attention and rigorous exactness are very often abandoned in the end, for in America, as in other countries, the people is subject to sudden impulses and short bursts of effort. The European is accustomed to finding an official always at hand to interfere in everything he undertakes, and he has some difficulty getting used to the complex machinery of township administration. In general it may be said that the lesser details of police, which make life easy and comfortable, are neglected in America, but that the essential guarantees of man in society are as strong there as anywhere else. In America the power that conducts the government is far less regular, less enlightened, and less learned than in Europe, but a hundred times more authoritative. In no country in the world do the citizens make such efforts for the common good. I know of no people that has established schools as numerous and as effective, places of public worship better suited to the needs of the inhabitants, or roads kept in better repair. Uniformity and permanence of design, the minute arrangement of details, *t and the perfection of an ingenious administration must not be looked for in the United States. But it is easy to find there the signs of a power that, if somewhat barbarous, is at least robust, and of a life that is full of accidents, but also cheered by animation and effort.

t [ A writer of talent compared the finances of France with those of the United States, and in doing so proved that ingenuity cannot always take the place of a knowledge of facts. He very justly reproaches the Americans for the kind of confusion that exists in the accounts of township expenditure, and after giving the model of a departmental budget in France, he adds:—“We are indebted to centralization, that admirable invention of a great man, for the uniform order and method which prevail alike in all the municipal budgets, from the largest town to the humblest commune.” However much I may admire this result, I see the communes of France, with their excellent system of accounts, sunk in the grossest ignorance of their true interests and abandoned to so incurable an apathy that they seem to vegetate rather than to live. On the other hand, I observe the activity, the information, and the spirit of enterprise that keep society in perpetual labor in those American townships whose budgets are drawn up with little method and still less uniformity. The contrast strikes me, for in my view the purpose of a good government is to ensure the welfare of a people, and not to establish order and regularity in the midst of its misery and distress. I am therefore led to suppose that the prosperity of the American townships and the apparent confusion of their accounts, and the distress of the French communes and the perfection of their budget, may be due to the same cause. At any rate, I am suspicious of a benefit that comes with so many evils, and I do not mind an evil that is made up for by so many benefits.]

Suppose for a moment that the villages and counties of the United States would be governed more usefully by a distant authority they had never seen than by officials drawn from among themselves. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the country would be safer and the resources of society better used if the whole administration were centered in a single hand. Even so, the political advantages the Americans gain from their system would lead me to prefer it to the opposite plan. After all, it does me little good that a vigilant authority protects the tranquillity of my pleasures and constantly keeps every danger from my path, without any care or concern on my part, if this same authority is the absolute master of my liberty and my life. It does me little good if it so monopolizes all the energy of existence that when it languishes everything around it languishes, when it sleeps everything must sleep, and when it dies the state itself must perish.

In certain countries of Europe the natives regard themselves as a kind of settlers, indifferent to the fate of the place where they live. The greatest changes are carried out without their participation and, unless chance happens to inform them, without their knowledge. What is more, the citizen is unconcerned about the condition of his village, the policing of his street, or the repair of the church or the parsonage. He looks on all these things as having nothing to do with himself, and as the property of a powerful stranger whom he calls the government. He has only a life interest in these possessions, and he has no idea of ownership or of improvement. This lack of interest in his own affairs goes so far that if his own safety or that of his children is in danger, he will not try to avert the peril. Instead he will fold his arms and wait for the nation to come to his assistance. This same man, who has so completely given up his own free will, has no natural inclination to obedience. He cowers, it is true, before the pettiest official, but he defies the law with the spirit of a conquered enemy as soon as its superior force is removed. He swings constantly between servitude and license. When a nation has reached this state, it must either change its customs and its laws or perish. The source of public virtue is dry, and though the nation may still contain subjects, the race of citizens is extinct. Such communities are a natural prey to foreign conquest. If they do not disappear from the scene, it is because they are surrounded by other nations similar or inferior to themselves. It is because the instinctive feeling for their country’s claims still lives in their hearts, and because an involuntary pride in its name, or a vague memory of its past glory, is enough to give them the impulse of self-preservation.

Nor can the prodigious efforts that tribes have made in defense of a country that was not their own be cited in favor of such a system. In these cases it will be found that their main motive was religion. The permanence, the glory, or the prosperity of the nation had become part of their faith, and in defending the country they lived in, they defended that Holy City of which they were all citizens. The Turkish tribes never took an active part in the conduct of public affairs, yet they accomplished stupendous enterprises as long as the victories of the Sultan were the triumphs of the Mohammedan faith. In the present age they are in rapid decay, because their religion is departing and only despotism remains. Montesquieu attributed to absolute power an authority peculiar to itself, and in doing so, I think, he gave it an honor it did not deserve, for despotism, taken by itself, can produce no lasting results. On close inspection we shall find that religion, and not fear, has always been the cause of the long-lived prosperity of an absolute government. Whatever efforts may be made, no true power can be founded among men that does not rest on the free union of their inclinations. Patriotism and religion are the only two motives in the world that can permanently direct a whole body politic toward one end.

Laws cannot rekindle the ardor of an extinguished faith, but they can make men take an interest in the fate of their country. Through this influence the vague impulse of patriotism, which never abandons the human heart, may be directed and revived. If it is connected with the thoughts, the passions, and the daily habits of life, it may be consolidated into a lasting and rational feeling.
Do not say that the time for the experiment has already passed. Nations do not grow old the way men do, and each new generation is a fresh people, waiting for the legislator’s care.

It is not the administrative effects but the political effects of the local system that I admire most in America. In the United States the interests of the country are kept in view everywhere. They are an object of concern to the people of the whole Union, and every citizen is as warmly attached to them as if they were his own. He takes pride in the glory of his nation. He boasts of its successes, to which he believes he has contributed, and he rejoices in the general prosperity from which he profits. The feeling he has toward the State is like the one that binds him to his family, and it is through a kind of egotism that he takes an interest in the welfare of his country.

The European generally submits to a public official because the official represents a superior force. To an American, the official represents a right. In America it may be said that no one obeys man, but only justice and the law. If the opinion a citizen holds of himself is exaggerated, it is at least healthy. He confidently trusts in his own powers, which appear to him to be all-sufficient. When a private individual plans an undertaking, however directly it may concern the welfare of society, he never thinks of asking for the cooperation of the government. He publishes his plan, offers to carry it out himself, seeks the help of other individuals, and struggles manfully against all obstacles. No doubt he is often less successful than the State would have been in his place, but in the end the sum of these private undertakings far exceeds anything the government could have done.

Because the administrative authority is within the reach of the citizens, whom it in some degree represents, it arouses neither their jealousy nor their hatred. Because its resources are limited, everyone feels that he must not rely on its assistance alone. Thus, when the administration sees fit to intervene, it is not left to itself as it is in Europe. The duties of private citizens are not supposed to have lapsed because the State helps in carrying them out. On the contrary, everyone is ready to guide and support it. This combination of individual efforts with those of the public authorities often accomplishes what the most energetic central administration would be unable to do. It would be easy to cite several facts in proof of what I say, but I prefer to give only one, with which I am better acquainted. *u In America the means that the authorities have for discovering crimes and arresting criminals are few. There is no State police, and passports are unknown. The criminal police of the United States cannot be compared to that of France. The magistrates and public prosecutors are not numerous, and the examinations of prisoners are quick and oral. Nevertheless, in no country does crime more rarely escape punishment. The reason is that everyone considers himself concerned in providing evidence of the act committed and in stopping the offender. During my stay in the United States I saw committees form spontaneously to pursue and prosecute a man who had committed a great crime in a certain county. In Europe a criminal is an unhappy being struggling for his life against the ministers of justice, while the population merely watches the conflict. In America he is looked on as an enemy of the human race, and the whole of mankind is against him.
u [ See Appendix, I.]

I believe that provincial institutions benefit every nation, but nowhere do they seem to me more necessary than among a democratic people. In an aristocracy, order can always be kept even amid liberty, and since the rulers have a great deal to lose, order is their first concern. In the same way, an aristocracy shields the people from the excesses of despotism, because it always has an organized power ready to resist a despot. A democracy without provincial institutions has no protection against either evil. How can a populace that has never been used to freedom in small matters learn to use it with moderation in great affairs? What resistance can be offered to tyranny in a country where every private individual is powerless and no common tie unites the citizens? Those who dread the license of the mob, and those who fear the rule of absolute power, ought equally to want provincial liberties to grow steadily.

On the other hand, I am convinced that democratic nations are the most exposed to falling under the yoke of a central administration, for several reasons, among them the following. The constant tendency of these nations is to concentrate all the strength of the government in the hands of the only power that directly represents the people, because beyond the people nothing can be seen but a mass of equal individuals merged together. But when that same power already holds all the attributes of government, it can hardly refrain from reaching into the details of administration, and an opportunity to do so is sure to present itself in the end, as happened in France. In the French Revolution there were two impulses in opposite directions, which must never be confused. One favored liberty, the other despotism. Under the ancient monarchy the King was the sole author of the laws, and beneath the sovereign’s power certain half-destroyed vestiges of provincial institutions could still be made out. These provincial institutions were incoherent, loosely constructed, and often absurd. In the hands of the aristocracy they had sometimes been turned into instruments of oppression. The Revolution declared itself the enemy of royalty and of provincial institutions at the same time. It lumped together everything that had come before it, despotic power and the checks on its abuses alike, in indiscriminate hatred, and its tendency was both to overthrow and to centralize. This double character of the French Revolution is a fact that the friends of absolute power have skillfully handled. Can they be accused of working for despotism when they defend that central administration, which was one of the great innovations of the Revolution? *v In this way popularity may be won along with hostility to the rights of the people, and the secret slave of tyranny may be the professed admirer of freedom.
v [ See Appendix K.]

I have visited the two nations where the system of provincial liberty is most fully established, and I listened to what different parties there had to say. In America I met men who secretly hoped to destroy the democratic institutions of the Union. In England I found others who openly attacked the aristocracy. Yet I know of no one in either country who does not regard provincial independence as a great benefit. In both countries I heard a thousand different causes named for the evils of the State, but the local system was never among them. I heard citizens credit the power and prosperity of their country to a multitude of reasons, but all of them put the advantages of local institutions first. Am I to suppose that men who are so divided by nature in religious opinion and political theory are all mistaken when they agree on one point, and one they experience every day? The only nations that deny the usefulness of provincial liberties are those that have the fewest of them. In other words, only those who do not know the institution condemn it.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Judicial Power In The United States
paragraphs: Judicial Power in the United States and Its Influence on Political Society.

I thought it essential to devote a separate chapter to the judicial authorities of the United States. If I mentioned them only in passing, their great political importance might be lessened in the reader’s eyes. Confederations have existed in other countries besides America, and republics have been established on more than the shores of the New World. Several States of Europe have adopted the representative system of government. But I am not aware that any nation in the world has so far organized a judicial power on the principle the Americans now follow. The judicial organization of the United States is the institution a foreigner has the most difficulty understanding. He hears the authority of a judge invoked in the political events of every day, and he naturally concludes that in the United States judges are important political officials. Yet when he examines the nature of the courts, he finds nothing contrary to the usual habits and privileges of such bodies, and the judges seem to him to interfere in public affairs only by chance — but by a chance that recurs every day.

When the Parliament of Paris remonstrated, refused to register an edict, or summoned an official accused of misconduct in office to its bar, its political influence as a judicial body was plainly visible. Nothing of the kind is to be seen in the United States. The Americans have kept all the ordinary characteristics of judicial authority and have carefully confined its action to the ordinary circle of its functions.

The first characteristic of judicial power in all nations is the duty of arbitration. But for a tribunal to intervene, rights must be contested, and a lawsuit must be brought to obtain a judge’s decision. As long as the law is uncontested, therefore, the judicial authority is not called on to discuss it, and it may exist without being noticed. When a judge, in a given case, attacks a law relating to that case, he extends the circle of his customary duties without stepping beyond it, because he is to some extent obliged to rule on the law in order to rule on the case. But if he pronounces on a law without resting on a case, he clearly steps outside his sphere and invades that of the legislative authority.

The second characteristic of judicial power is that it rules on particular cases, not on general principles. Suppose a judge, in deciding a particular point, destroys a general principle. His judgment tends to reject all the inferences from that principle and so to annul it, yet he remains within the ordinary limits of his functions. But if he attacks a general principle directly, without having a particular case in view, he leaves the circle in which all nations have agreed to confine his authority. He assumes a more important, and perhaps more useful, influence than that of a magistrate, but he ceases to represent the judicial power.

The third characteristic of the judicial power is that it cannot act unless it is appealed to, or until it has taken up a matter. This characteristic is less general than the other two. But despite the exceptions, I think it may be regarded as essential. By its nature the judicial power has no action of its own; it must be set in motion to produce a result. When it is called on to repress a crime, it punishes the criminal. When a wrong is to be redressed, it is ready to redress it. When an act requires interpretation, it is prepared to interpret it. But it does not pursue criminals, hunt out wrongs, or examine evidence of its own accord. A judicial official who opened proceedings on his own and usurped the censorship of the laws would to some extent do violence to the passive nature of his authority.

The Americans have kept these three distinguishing characteristics of the judicial power. An American judge can pronounce a decision only when litigation has arisen. He deals only with particular cases. And he cannot act until the case has been duly brought before the court. His position is therefore exactly like that of the magistrate in other nations, and yet he is invested with immense political power. If the sphere of his authority and his means of action are the same as those of other judges, one may ask where he gets a power they do not have. The cause of the difference lies in a simple fact: the Americans have acknowledged the right of judges to base their decisions on the constitution rather than on the laws. In other words, they have left judges free not to apply laws that seem to them unconstitutional.

I am aware that courts in other countries have claimed a similar right, but claimed it in vain. In America, however, all authorities recognize it, and no party, not even a single individual, is found to contest it. This fact can be explained only by the principles of the American constitution. In France the constitution is (or at least is supposed to be) immutable, and the received theory is that no power has the right to change any part of it. In England Parliament has an acknowledged right to modify the constitution. Since the constitution can therefore undergo perpetual changes, it does not in reality exist; Parliament is at once a legislative and a constituent assembly. The political theories of America are simpler and more rational. An American constitution is not supposed to be immutable, as in France, nor can the ordinary powers of society modify it, as in England. It forms a separate whole. Because it represents the determination of the whole people, it is no less binding on the legislator than on the private citizen. But the will of the people may alter it, in predetermined cases, according to established rules. In America, then, the constitution may change, but as long as it exists it is the origin of all authority and the sole vehicle of the predominant force. *a

a [ [The fifth article of the original Constitution of the United States lays down how amendments to the Constitution may be made. Two-thirds of both Houses of Congress must propose an amendment, and the legislatures of three-fourths of the several States must ratify it. Fifteen amendments have been made at different times since 1789. The most important are the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth, which were framed and ratified after the Civil War. The original Constitution of the United States, followed by these fifteen amendments, is printed at the end of this edition. — Translator’s Note, 1874.]]

It is easy to see how these differences must affect the position and the rights of the judicial bodies in the three countries I have cited. Suppose the tribunals in France were authorized to disobey laws on the ground that they conflict with the constitution. The supreme power would in fact be placed in their hands, since they alone would have the right to interpret a constitution whose clauses no authority can modify. They would therefore take the place of the nation and exercise as absolute a sway over society as the inherent weakness of judicial power would allow. Undoubtedly, because French judges are not competent to declare a law unconstitutional, the power to change the constitution is indirectly given to the legislative body, since no legal barrier would oppose the alterations it might prescribe. But it is better to grant the power to change the people’s constitution to men who represent (however imperfectly) the will of the people than to men who represent no one but themselves.

It would be still more unreasonable to give English judges the right to resist the decisions of the legislative body, since the Parliament that makes the laws also makes the constitution. Consequently a law that emanates from the three powers of the State can in no case be unconstitutional. But neither of these remarks applies to America.

In the United States the constitution binds the legislator just as it binds the private citizen. It is the first of laws, so it cannot be modified by a law, and it is only right that the courts should obey the constitution in preference to any law. The power of the judiciary depends on this condition, because every magistrate has a natural right to choose the legal obligation that binds him most strictly.

In France the constitution is also the first of laws, and judges have the same right to take it as the ground of their decisions. But if they exercised this right, they would inevitably encroach on rights more sacred than their own, namely those of society, in whose name they act. In that case the motive of the State clearly prevails over the motives of an individual. In America the nation can always bring its magistrates to obedience by changing its constitution, so no danger of this kind is to be feared. On this point, therefore, the political and the logical reasons agree, and the people as well as the judges keep their privileges.

Whenever a law that the judge holds to be unconstitutional is argued in a court of the United States, he may refuse to accept it as a rule. This power is the only one peculiar to the American magistrate, but it gives rise to immense political influence. Few laws can escape the searching analysis of the judicial power for long, for there are few that do not harm some private interest or other, and none that cannot be brought before a court, whether by the choice of the parties or by the necessity of the case. But from the moment a judge has refused to apply a given law in a case, that law loses some of its moral force. The people whose interests it harms learn that ways exist of evading its authority, and similar suits multiply until the law becomes powerless. One of two alternatives must then be taken: the people must alter the constitution, or the legislature must repeal the law. The political power the Americans have entrusted to their courts is therefore immense. But the evils of this power are considerably reduced by the obligation to attack laws only through the courts. Suppose the judge had been empowered to contest laws on the ground of theoretical generalities, or to open an attack or pass a censure on the legislator. He would then have played a prominent part in the political sphere, and as the champion or the antagonist of a party he would have drawn the hostile passions of the nation into the conflict. But when a judge contests a law applied to some particular case in an obscure proceeding, the importance of his attack is hidden from the public gaze. His decision bears on the interest of an individual, and if the law is slighted, it is only indirectly. Moreover, although the law is censured, it is not abolished. Its moral force may be diminished, but its binding force is by no means suspended, and its final destruction can be accomplished only by the repeated attacks of judicial officials. It is easy to understand that legislation is protected from wanton assailants and from the daily aggressions of party spirit, because the censorship of the laws is tied to the private interests of members of the community and the prosecution of the law is intimately joined to the prosecution of an individual. The errors of the legislator are exposed when their evil consequences are most felt, and the basis of a prosecution is always a positive, appreciable fact.

I am inclined to believe that this practice of the American courts is at once the most favorable to liberty and to public order. If the judge could attack the legislator only openly and directly, he would sometimes be afraid to offer any resistance to the legislator’s will. At other moments party spirit might encourage him to defy it at every turn. The laws would consequently be attacked when the power they come from is weak, and obeyed when it is strong. That is to say, they would be contested when it would be useful to respect them, and respected when it would be easy to turn them into an instrument of oppression. But the American judge is brought into the political arena independently of his own will. He judges the law only because he is obliged to judge a case. The political question he is called on to resolve is connected with the interest of the parties to the suit, and he cannot refuse to decide it without abdicating the duties of his post. He performs his duties as a citizen by fulfilling the precise duties that belong to his profession as a magistrate. It is true that under this system the judicial censorship the courts exercise over legislation cannot extend to all laws indiscriminately. Some laws can never give rise to the exact kind of contest called a lawsuit, and even when such a contest is possible, it may happen that no one cares to bring it before a court. The Americans have often felt this disadvantage, but they have left the remedy incomplete, lest they give it an efficacy that might in some cases prove dangerous. Within these limits, the power of American courts to pronounce a statute unconstitutional forms one of the most powerful barriers ever devised against the tyranny of political assemblies.
Other Powers Granted to American Judges

In the United States all citizens have the right to indict public officials before the ordinary courts — How they use this right — Article 75 of the French Constitution of the Year VIII — The Americans and the English cannot understand the meaning of this clause.

It is perfectly natural that in a free country like America all citizens should have the right to indict public officials before the ordinary courts, and that all judges should have the power to punish public offenses. The right granted to the courts to judge the agents of the executive government when they have violated the laws is so natural that it cannot be seen as an extraordinary privilege. Nor do the springs of government seem to me weakened in the United States by the custom of making all public officers answerable to the judges of the land. On the contrary, the Americans seem by this means to have increased the respect due to the authorities, and at the same time to have made those in power more careful not to offend public opinion. I was struck by the small number of political trials in the United States, but I had no difficulty accounting for it. A lawsuit, of whatever kind, is always a difficult and expensive undertaking. It is easy to attack a public man in a newspaper, but the motives that can warrant an action at law must be serious. A solid ground of complaint must therefore exist before an individual will prosecute a public officer, and public officers take care not to furnish such grounds when they are afraid of being prosecuted.

This does not come from the republican form of American institutions, since the same facts are found in England. Neither nation regards the impeachment of the principal officers of State as enough to guarantee its independence. Both hold that the right to bring minor prosecutions, which the whole community can reach, is a better pledge of freedom than those great judicial actions, which are rarely used until it is too late.

In the Middle Ages offenders were very hard to catch, and judges inflicted the most dreadful tortures on the few who were arrested. This did nothing to reduce the number of crimes. People have since discovered that justice is more effective when it is both more certain and more mild. The English and the Americans hold that tyranny and oppression should be treated like any other crime: lighten the penalty and make conviction easier.

In the Year VIII of the French Republic a constitution was drawn up that included the following clause: “Art. 75. All the agents of the government below the rank of ministers can only be prosecuted for offenses relating to their several functions by virtue of a decree of the Conseil d’Etat; in which case the prosecution takes place before the ordinary tribunals.” This clause outlasted the “Constitution de l’An VIII,” and it is still maintained in spite of the just complaints of the nation. I have always had the utmost difficulty explaining its meaning to Englishmen or Americans. They at once concluded that the Conseil d’Etat in France was a great tribunal, established in the center of the kingdom, exercising a preliminary and somewhat tyrannical jurisdiction in all political cases. But when I told them that the Conseil d’Etat was not a judicial body in the common sense of the term, but an administrative council made up of men dependent on the Crown, so that the king, after ordering one of his servants, called a Prefect, to commit an injustice, has the power to command another of his servants, called a Councillor of State, to prevent the first from being punished; when I showed them that a citizen injured by the sovereign’s order is obliged to ask the sovereign for permission to obtain redress, they refused to believe so flagrant an abuse and were tempted to accuse me of falsehood or ignorance. Before the Revolution it often happened that a Parliament issued a warrant against a public officer who had committed an offense, and sometimes the proceedings were stopped by the authority of the Crown, which enforced compliance with its absolute and despotic will. It is painful to see how much lower we have sunk than our forefathers, since we allow to pass, under the color of justice and the sanction of the law, things that only violence could impose.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Political Jurisdiction In The United States
paragraphs: By political jurisdiction I mean the temporary right to pronounce a legal decision that may be given to a political body.

Under absolute governments, extraordinary forms of procedure would serve no purpose. The prince in whose name an offender is prosecuted is as much the sovereign of the courts as of everything else, and the way people think of his power is security enough. His only fear is that the outward formalities of justice may be neglected, and that his authority may be dishonored from a wish to make it more absolute. But in most free countries, where the majority can never influence the courts as an absolute monarch does, judicial power has sometimes been placed for a time in the representatives of the nation. People have judged it better to confuse the functions of the different authorities for a while than to violate the necessary principle that government is one.

England, France, and the United States have established this political jurisdiction by law, and it is interesting to see how differently these three great nations have applied the principle. In England and in France the House of Lords and the Chambre des Pairs *a form the highest criminal court of their respective nations. Although they do not habitually try all political offenses, they are competent to try them all. Another political body has the right of impeachment before the House of Lords. The only difference between the two countries in this respect is that in England the Commons may impeach whomever they please before the Lords, whereas in France the Deputies can use this mode of prosecution only against the ministers of the Crown.
a [ [As it existed under the constitutional monarchy until 1848.]]
In both countries the upper house may use all the existing penal laws of the nation to punish the offenders.

In the United States, as in Europe, one branch of the legislature has the power to impeach and another to judge. The House of Representatives accuses the offender, and the Senate decides his sentence. But the Senate may try only the people the House of Representatives sends to it, and these must be public officials. The Senate’s jurisdiction is therefore narrower than that of the Peers of France, while the Representatives’ right of impeachment is broader than the Deputies’. The great difference between Europe and America, however, is this. In Europe political tribunals may apply every provision of the penal code. In America, once they have removed the offender from his official rank and declared him unfit to hold any political office in the future, their jurisdiction ends and the ordinary tribunals take over.

Suppose, for instance, that the President of the United States has committed the crime of high treason. The House of Representatives impeaches him and the Senate removes him from office; he must then be tried by a jury, which alone can deprive him of his liberty or his life. This illustrates the subject we are treating exactly. The political jurisdiction established by the laws of Europe is intended to try great offenders, whatever their birth, their rank, or their power in the State, and to this end all the privileges of the courts of justice are temporarily extended to a great political assembly. The legislator is then transformed into a magistrate. He is called on to admit, to distinguish, and to punish the offense, and because he exercises all the authority of a judge, the law binds him to observe all the duties of that high office and all the formalities of justice. When a public official is impeached before an English or a French political tribunal and found guilty, the sentence deprives him ipso facto of his functions, and it may declare him incapable of resuming them or any others in the future. But in this case the political interdict is a consequence of the sentence and not the sentence itself. In Europe the sentence of a political tribunal is to be regarded as a judicial verdict rather than as an administrative measure. In the United States the opposite is true. The decision of the Senate is judicial in form, since the senators must follow the practices and formalities of a court of justice. It is judicial in the motives it rests on, since the Senate is in general obliged to take an offense at common law as the basis of its sentence. Nevertheless the object of the proceeding is purely administrative. Had the American legislator intended to invest a political body with great judicial authority, its action would not have been limited to the circle of public officials, since the most dangerous enemies of the State may hold no office at all. This is especially true in republics, where party influence is the first of authorities and where many a leader’s strength is increased by his holding no legal power.

Suppose the American legislator had meant to give society a way of repressing offenses against the State by exemplary punishment, as ordinary justice does. Then he would have put every resource of the penal code at the disposal of the political tribunals. But the weapon they hold is imperfect. It can never reach the most dangerous offenders, because men who aim at the total overthrow of the laws are not likely to complain of a political interdict.

The main object of the political jurisdiction that exists in the United States is therefore to deprive the ill-disposed citizen of an authority he has misused and to prevent him from ever acquiring it again. This is plainly an administrative measure sanctioned by the formalities of a judicial decision. In this matter the Americans have created a mixed system. They have surrounded the act that removes a public official with the safeguards of a political trial, and they have taken from all political condemnations their severest penalties. Every link of the system can easily be traced from this point.
