Political importance of the judiciary in the United States — Difficulty of treating this subject — Usefulness of judicial power in confederations — What tribunals could be introduced into the Union — Necessity of establishing federal courts of justice — Organization of the national judiciary — The Supreme Court — How it differs from all known tribunals.

I have examined the legislative and executive power of the Union, and the judicial power remains to be studied. But here I cannot hide my fears from the reader. The judicial institutions of the Anglo-Americans have great influence on their condition, and they hold a prominent place among what are properly called political institutions. In this respect they deserve our special attention. But I find it hard to explain the political role of the American tribunals without going into some technical details of their constitution and their forms of procedure. And I do not know how to descend to these minutiae without wearying the reader’s curiosity with the natural dryness of the subject, or without risking obscurity in my effort to be brief. I can hardly hope to escape these various evils. If I seem too long to a man of the world, a lawyer may complain of my brevity. But these are the natural drawbacks of my subject, and especially of the point I am about to discuss.

The great difficulty was not to design a Constitution for the Federal government, but to find a way of enforcing its laws. Governments generally have only two means of overcoming the opposition of the people they govern: the physical force at their own disposal, and the moral force they draw from the decisions of the courts of justice.

A government with no other means of demanding obedience than open war would be very near its ruin, for one of two things would probably happen. If its authority was slight and its character moderate, it would not resort to violence until the last extremity. It would overlook a number of partial acts of insubordination, and the State would gradually fall into anarchy. If it was enterprising and powerful, it would constantly fall back on its physical strength and would quickly degenerate into a military despotism. Its activity would then be no less harmful to the community than its inaction.

The great end of justice is to substitute the idea of right for that of violence, and to place a legal barrier between the power of the government and the use of physical force. The authority that the general opinion of mankind grants to the intervention of a court of justice is so surprisingly great that it clings to the mere formalities of justice and gives physical weight to the shadow of the law. The moral force that courts of justice possess makes the use of physical force exceedingly rare, and very often takes its place. And if physical force proves indispensable, its power is doubled by the association with the idea of law.

A federal government needs the support of judicial institutions more than any other, because it is naturally weak and exposed to formidable opposition. *c If it were always obliged to resort to violence in the first instance, it could not fulfill its task. The Union therefore needed a national judiciary to enforce the citizens’ obedience to the laws and to repel attacks that might be directed against them. The question then was which tribunals should exercise these powers. Should they be entrusted to the courts of justice already organized in every State? Or was it necessary to create federal courts? It is easy to prove that the Union could not adapt the judicial power of the States to its needs. The separation of the judiciary from the administrative power of the State no doubt affects the security of every citizen and the liberty of all. But it is no less important to the life of the nation that these several powers should have the same origin, follow the same principles, and act in the same sphere. In a word, they should be correlative and homogeneous. No one, I presume, ever suggested the advantage of trying offenses committed in France before a foreign court of justice, in order to secure the judges’ impartiality. The Americans form one people in relation to their Federal government. But within this people various political bodies have been allowed to remain in existence. They depend on the national government in a few points and are independent in all the rest. Each has a distinct origin, maxims peculiar to itself, and its own means of carrying on its affairs. To entrust the execution of the laws of the Union to tribunals set up by these political bodies would be to allow foreign judges to preside over the nation. More than that, each State is not only foreign to the Union at large, but in perpetual opposition to the common interests, since whatever authority the Union loses turns to the advantage of the States. Thus to enforce the laws of the Union through the tribunals of the States would be to allow judges who are not only foreign but partial to preside over the nation.

c [ Federal laws are the ones that most need courts of justice, and at the same time the ones for which courts have most rarely been established. The reason is that confederations have usually been formed by independent States that had no real intention of obeying the central government, that very readily ceded the right of command to the federal executive, and that very prudently reserved the right of non-compliance for themselves.]

But the number of the State tribunals, even more than their character, made them unfit to serve the nation. When the Federal Constitution was formed, there were already thirteen courts of justice in the United States deciding cases without appeal. That number has now grown to twenty-four. To suppose that a State can survive when its fundamental laws may be subjected to twenty-four different interpretations at the same time is to advance a proposition contrary to both reason and experience.

The American legislators therefore agreed to create a federal judiciary to apply the laws of the Union and to decide certain questions affecting general interests, which were carefully defined in advance. The entire judicial power of the Union was concentrated in one tribunal, called the Supreme Court of the United States. But to speed the dispatch of business, inferior courts were attached to it. These were empowered to decide cases of small importance without appeal, and cases of greater magnitude with appeal. The members of the Supreme Court are named neither by the people nor by the legislature, but by the President of the United States, acting with the advice of the Senate. To make them independent of the other authorities, their office was made irremovable, and it was decided that once their salary was fixed, the legislature could not alter it. *d It was easy to proclaim the principle of a Federal judiciary, but difficulties multiplied when the extent of its jurisdiction had to be determined.

d [ The Union was divided into districts, and a resident Federal judge was appointed in each; the court over which he presides was called a “District Court.” Each judge of the Supreme Court visits a certain part of the Republic every year to try the most important cases on the spot; the court over which such a judge presides is called a “Circuit Court.” Finally, all the most serious litigation is brought before the Supreme Court, which holds one solemn session a year, attended by all the judges of the Circuit Courts. The jury was introduced into the Federal courts in the same way, and in the same kinds of cases, as in the courts of the States.

It should be noted that the Supreme Court of the United States has nothing in common with the French Cour de Cassation, since the latter hears appeals only on questions of law. The Supreme Court decides the facts of a case on the evidence as well as the law, whereas the Cour de Cassation does not give a decision of its own but sends the case to another tribunal for judgment. See the law of September 24, 1789, “Laws of the United States,” by Story, vol. i. p. 53.]

Means of Determining the Jurisdiction of the Federal Courts The difficulty of defining the jurisdiction of separate courts in confederations — The courts of the Union received the right to fix their own jurisdiction — In what way this rule infringes on the portion of sovereignty reserved to the several States — The sovereignty of these States is limited by the laws and by the interpretation of the laws — Hence the danger to the States is more apparent than real.

The Constitution of the United States recognized two distinct powers confronting each other, represented in the judicial sphere by two distinct classes of courts. Even the greatest care in defining their separate jurisdictions could not have prevented frequent collisions between those tribunals. The question then arose: who should have the right to decide the competence of each court?

In nations that form a single body politic, when two courts dispute their mutual jurisdiction, a third tribunal is generally at hand to settle the difference. This is done without difficulty, because in such nations questions of judicial competence have no bearing on the privileges of national supremacy. But it was impossible to create an arbiter between a superior court of the Union and the superior court of a separate State that would not itself belong to one of those two classes. It was therefore necessary to let one of the courts judge its own cause, and take or keep cognizance of the point in dispute. To grant this privilege to the courts of the States would have destroyed the sovereignty of the Union in fact after establishing it in law; for the interpretation of the Constitution would soon have given back to the States the very portion of independence that the terms of that act took from them. The purpose of creating a Federal tribunal was to stop the courts of the States from deciding, each in its own sphere, questions affecting national interests, and so to form a uniform body of jurisprudence for the interpretation of the laws of the Union. This purpose would not have been achieved if the courts of the several States had been competent to decide, in their separate capacities, cases from which they were obliged to abstain as Federal tribunals. The Supreme Court of the United States was therefore given the right to determine all questions of jurisdiction. *e

e [ To cut down on such suits, many Federal cases were made open to the courts of the States as well as those of the Union, and the party who loses has a right to appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States. The Supreme Court of Virginia denied that the Supreme Court of the United States could hear an appeal from its decisions, but it did not prevail. See “Kent’s Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 300, pp. 370 et seq.; Story’s “Commentaries,” p. 646; and “The Organic Law of the United States,” vol. i. p. 35.]

This was a heavy blow to the independence of the States. They were now bound not only by the laws but by the interpretation of the laws: by one limit that was known and another that was uncertain, by a rule that was fixed and another that was arbitrary. The Constitution did lay down the exact limits of Federal supremacy, yet whenever a State disputes that supremacy, a Federal tribunal rules on the question. Still, the threat this arrangement posed to the independence of the States is less serious than it looks. We shall see later that in America the true strength of the country lies far more in the State governments than in the Federal government. The Federal judges are aware of the relative weakness of the power in whose name they act. They are readier to give up a claim of jurisdiction that is rightfully theirs than to press a privilege they have no legal title to.
Different Cases of Jurisdiction

The matter and the party are the first conditions of Federal jurisdiction — Suits in which ambassadors are involved — Suits of the Union — Of a separate State — By whom tried — Cases arising from the laws of the Union — Why they are judged by the Federal tribunals — Cases concerning the performance of contracts tried by the Federal courts — Consequence of this arrangement.

Having provided the means of fixing the competence of the Federal courts, the legislators of the Union defined the cases that should fall within their jurisdiction. They established, on the one hand, that certain parties must always be brought before the Federal courts, whatever the special nature of the case; and, on the other, that certain kinds of cases must always be brought before those same courts, whatever the standing of the parties to the suit. These distinctions were thus accepted as the basis of Federal jurisdiction.

Ambassadors are the representatives of nations at peace with the Union, and whatever concerns them concerns the whole Union to some degree. When an ambassador is a party to a suit, the suit affects the welfare of the nation, and it is natural that a Federal tribunal should be called on to decide it.

The Union itself may be sued or may bring a suit. In that case, to take the matter to a tribunal of any other sovereignty than its own would go against the usage of every nation and against common sense. So the Federal courts hear these affairs.

Suppose two parties from two different States are at law with each other. It would hardly be fitting to try the case before a court of either State. The safest remedy is a tribunal like that of the Union, which neither party can distrust, and which is the most natural as well as the most reliable choice.

When the parties are not private persons but States, a weighty political concern joins the same motive of fairness. The rank of the parties lends national importance to all their quarrels, and even the pettiest lawsuit between States may be said to touch the peace of the whole Union. *f

f [ The Constitution also says that the Federal courts shall decide “controversies between a State and the citizens of another State.” Here a most important constitutional question arose: whether the jurisdiction given by the Constitution in cases where a State is a party extended to suits brought against a State as well as by it, or was confined exclusively to the latter. The question was examined at great length in the case of Chisholm v. Georgia, and the majority of the Supreme Court decided it in the affirmative. The decision caused general alarm among the States, and an amendment was proposed and ratified that removed the power entirely, as far as suits brought against a State are concerned. See Story’s “Commentaries,” p. 624, or in the large edition Section 1677.]

The nature of the case often determines which court is competent. Thus all questions concerning maritime commerce clearly fall within the cognizance of the Federal tribunals. *g Almost all these questions are connected with the interpretation of the law of nations, and in that respect they essentially concern the Union in its relations with foreign powers. Moreover, since the sea lies within the limits of no particular jurisdiction, the national courts are the only ones that can hear cases arising out of maritime affairs.
g [ For instance, all cases of piracy.]

The Constitution brings almost all the cases that by their nature belong to the Federal courts under a single heading. The rule it states is simple, yet it contains a whole system of ideas and a great multitude of facts. It declares that the judicial power of the Supreme Court extends to all cases in law and equity arising under the laws of the United States.
Two examples will show the intention of the legislator in the clearest light:

The Constitution forbids the States to pass laws on the value and circulation of money. Suppose a State passes such a law anyway, and the people affected refuse to obey it because it violates the Constitution. The case must go before a Federal court, since it arises under the laws of the United States. Or suppose trouble arises over the collection of import duties that Congress has voted. The Federal court must decide that case too, because it depends on the interpretation of a law of the United States.

This rule agrees perfectly with the basic principles of the Federal Constitution. The Union as established in 1789 has, it is true, only a limited supremacy; but within those limits it was meant to form a single people. *h Within them the Union is sovereign. Once that is settled and admitted, the conclusion is easy. If the United States are acknowledged to form one people within the bounds their Constitution sets, then it is impossible to deny them the rights of other nations. And since the beginning of society it has been accepted that every nation may decide, in its own courts, the questions that concern the enforcement of its own laws. The reply is that the Union is in such an odd position that on some matters it is a people, and on all the rest it is nothing. But the conclusion to draw from this is that, in laws on those matters, the Union holds every right of absolute sovereignty. The difficulty lies in knowing what those matters are. Once that is resolved (and we have shown how it was resolved, when we spoke of how the jurisdiction of the Federal courts is determined), no further doubt can arise. As soon as a suit is shown to be Federal, that is, to belong to the share of sovereignty the Constitution reserves to the Union, it follows naturally that it should fall within the jurisdiction of a Federal court.

h [ This principle was restricted to some extent by the admission of the several States into the Senate as independent powers, and by allowing them to vote separately in the House of Representatives when the President is elected by that body. But these are exceptions, and the opposite principle is the rule.]

Whenever the laws of the United States are attacked, or relied on for self-defense, the Federal courts must be turned to. So the jurisdiction of the Union’s tribunals grows or shrinks in exact proportion to the sovereignty of the Union. We have shown that the main aim of the legislators of 1789 was to divide sovereign authority into two parts. In the first they placed the management of all the general interests of the Union; in the second, the management of the particular interests of its member States. Above all they wanted to give the Federal government enough power to resist, within its own sphere, any encroachment by the States. For the States themselves they adopted the principle of independence within certain limits of their own, so that they were kept out of sight of the central government and safe from its control. When I discussed the division of authority, I noted that this second principle had not always been kept sacred, because the States are barred from passing certain laws that seem to belong to their own particular sphere. When a State of the Union passes such a law, citizens who are harmed by its enforcement may appeal to the Federal courts.

So the jurisdiction of the Federal courts covers not only every case under the laws of the Union, but also every case under laws that States have made in defiance of the Constitution. A State may not pass ex post facto laws in criminal matters, and anyone convicted under such a law may appeal to the judicial power of the Union. A State also may not pass laws that tend to impair the obligation of contracts. *i A citizen who thinks such an obligation has been impaired by a law of his own State may refuse to obey it and appeal to the Federal courts. *j

i [ It is perfectly clear, says Mr. Story (“Commentaries,” p. 503, or in the large edition Section 1379), that any law that enlarges, abridges, or in any manner changes the intention of the parties, as it results from the stipulations of the contract, necessarily impairs it. In the same place he gives a very long and careful definition of what Federal jurisprudence understands by a contract. A grant made by the State to a private individual and accepted by him is a contract, and cannot be revoked by any future law. A charter granted by the State to a company is a contract, and binds the State as much as the grantee. The clause of the Constitution referred to here therefore protects the existence of a great part of acquired rights, but not of all. Property may be legally held even though it did not pass into the possessor’s hands by means of a contract; and its possession is an acquired right that the Federal Constitution does not guarantee.]

j [ Mr. Story gives a remarkable instance of this (p. 508, or in the large edition Section 1388): “Dartmouth College in New Hampshire had been founded by a charter granted to certain individuals before the American Revolution, and its trustees formed a corporation under this charter. The college was deemed, like other colleges of private foundation, to be a private eleemosynary institution, endowed by its charter with a capacity to take property unconnected with the Government. Its funds were bestowed upon the faith of the charter, and those funds consisted entirely of private donations. It is true that the uses were in some sense public, that is, for the general benefit, and not for the mere benefit of the corporators; but this did not make the corporation a public corporation. It was a private institution for general charity. And the State itself, if it had bestowed funds upon a charity of the same nature, could not resume those funds.”]

This provision seems to me the most serious attack on the independence of the States. The rights granted to the Federal government for purposes of obvious national importance are definite and easy to understand; but the rights this last clause gives it can be neither clearly appreciated nor accurately defined. For there are vast numbers of political laws that affect the existence of obligations of contracts, and these may easily furnish a pretext for aggression by the central authority.
Procedure of the Federal Courts

Natural weakness of the judicial power in confederations — Legislators ought to strive as far as possible to bring private individuals, not States, before the Federal courts — How the Americans have succeeded in this — Direct prosecution of private individuals in the Federal courts — Indirect prosecution of the States that violate the laws of the Union — The decrees of the Supreme Court weaken but do not destroy the provincial laws.

I have shown what the privileges of the Federal courts are; it is no less important to point out how they are exercised. In countries where sovereignty is undivided, the irresistible authority of justice comes from the fact that the tribunals represent the entire nation in conflict with the individual against whom their decree is directed, so that the idea of power is added to support the idea of right. But this is not always the case in countries where sovereignty is divided. There the judicial power more often confronts a fraction of the nation than an isolated individual, and its moral authority and physical strength are consequently diminished. In federal States the power of the judge is naturally reduced, and that of the parties before the court is increased. In confederate States the legislator’s aim ought therefore to be to make the position of the courts similar to the one they hold in countries where sovereignty is undivided. In other words, his efforts ought constantly to tend to keep the judicial power of the confederation as the representative of the nation, and the party before the court as the representative of an individual interest.

Every government, whatever its constitution, needs the means to compel its subjects to discharge their obligations and to protect its privileges from their attacks. As far as the government’s direct action on the community is concerned, the Constitution of the United States contrived, by a master stroke of policy, that the Federal courts, acting in the name of the laws, should take cognizance only of parties in their individual capacity. For since it had been declared that the Union consisted of one and the same people within the limits laid down by the Constitution, the inference was that the government created by this Constitution, and acting within those limits, was invested with all the privileges of a national government, and one of the principal of these is the right to send its commands directly to the private citizen. When the Union votes a tax, for instance, it does not apply to the States to levy it, but to every American citizen in proportion to his assessment. The Supreme Court, which is empowered to enforce this law of the Union, exerts its influence not on a refractory State but on the private taxpayer; and, like the judicial power of other nations, it is set against the person of an individual. It should be observed that the Union chose its own opponent; and since that opponent is weak, he is naturally defeated.

But the difficulty increases when the proceedings are brought not by the Union but against it. The Constitution recognizes the legislative power of the States, and a law so enacted may impair the privileges of the Union. In that case a collision between the Union and the State that passed the law is unavoidable, and all that remains is to select the least dangerous remedy, which follows very clearly from the general principles I have already established. *k
k [ See Chapter VI. on “Judicial Power in America.”]

It might be thought that, in the case under consideration, the Union could have sued the State before a Federal court, which would have annulled the act; this would have been a natural course of proceeding. But the judicial power would then have been placed in open hostility to the State, and it was desirable to avoid that situation as far as possible. The Americans hold that it is nearly impossible for a new law not to impair the interests of some private individual by its provisions. American legislators take these private interests as the ground for attacking measures that may be prejudicial to the Union, and it is to such cases that the protection of the Supreme Court is extended.

Suppose a State sells a certain portion of its territory to a company, and a year later passes a law disposing of the territory in another way, so that the clause of the Constitution prohibiting laws that impair the obligation of contracts is violated. When the purchaser under the second act appears to take possession, the possessor under the first act brings his action before the tribunals of the Union and has the claimant’s title declared null and void. *l Thus in fact the judicial power of the Union is contesting the claims of a State’s sovereignty; but it acts only indirectly and on a special application in a particular case. It attacks the law in its consequences, not in its principle, and it weakens it rather than destroys it.
l [ See Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 387.]

The last possibility was that each State is a corporation with its own existence and its own civil rights, and so may sue or be sued in court. A State could therefore bring an action against another State. Here the Union was not asked to challenge a provincial law but to try a suit with a State as a party. Such a suit was exactly like any other, except for the standing of the parties; and here the danger noted at the start of this chapter is present, and harder to avoid. It is a built-in drawback of Federal constitutions, rooted in their very nature, that they produce parties within the nation that stand as powerful obstacles to the free course of justice.

High Rank of the Supreme Court Among the Great Powers of State No nation has ever created so great a judicial power as the Americans — Extent of its prerogative — Its political influence — The tranquility and the very existence of the Union depend on the discretion of the seven Federal judges.

When we have examined in turn the organization of the Supreme Court and all the prerogatives it exercises, we shall readily admit that no people has ever created a more imposing judicial power. The Supreme Court stands at the head of all known tribunals, both by the nature of its rights and by the class of parties over which it has jurisdiction.

In all the civilized countries of Europe the government has always shown the greatest reluctance to let cases in which it is itself a party be decided in the ordinary course of justice. This reluctance naturally reaches its height in an absolute government; and, on the other hand, the privileges of the courts widen as the people’s liberties increase. But no European nation has so far held that all judicial controversies, regardless of their origin, can be decided by the judges of common law.

In America this theory has been carried into practice, and the Supreme Court of the United States is the single tribunal of the nation. Its power reaches every case under laws and treaties made by the executive and legislative authorities, every case of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction, and in general every point that touches the law of nations. One can even say that, although the court is judicial in its makeup, its prerogatives are almost wholly political. Its only purpose is to see that the laws of the Union are carried out. The Union governs only the dealings of the government with the citizens and of the nation with foreign powers; the dealings of citizens with one another are governed almost entirely by the sovereignty of the States.

A second and still greater cause of this court’s preponderance can be given. In the nations of Europe the courts are called on to try only the controversies of private individuals; but the Supreme Court of the United States summons sovereign powers to its bar. When the clerk of the court steps forward and says simply, “The State of New York versus the State of Ohio,” one cannot help feeling that the court he addresses is no ordinary body. And when one recalls that one of these parties represents one million men and the other two million, one is struck by the responsibility of the seven judges whose decision is about to satisfy or disappoint so large a number of their fellow citizens.

The peace, the prosperity, and the very existence of the Union rest in the hands of these seven judges. Without their active help the Constitution would be a dead letter. The executive looks to them for aid against the encroachments of the legislature; the legislature seeks their protection against the designs of the executive. They defend the Union against the disobedience of the States, the States against the inflated claims of the Union, the public interest against the interests of private citizens, and the conservative spirit of order against the passing innovations of democracy. Their power is enormous, but it is clothed in the authority of public opinion. They are the all-powerful guardians of a people that respects the law; against popular neglect or popular contempt they would be helpless. Public opinion is the hardest of forces to manage, because its exact limits cannot be defined, and it is just as dangerous to go beyond the boundary it sets as to stay short of it.

The Federal judges must not only be good citizens, and men with the knowledge and integrity indispensable to magistrates; they must also be statesmen. They must be politicians, well read in the signs of the times, unafraid to face obstacles that can be overcome, and not slow to turn aside any encroaching forces that may threaten the supremacy of the Union and the obedience due to the laws.

The President holds only a limited power, and he may make mistakes without doing great harm to the State. Congress may decide badly without destroying the Union, because the voters who send it can make it reverse its decision by changing its members. But if the Supreme Court were ever made up of imprudent men or bad citizens, the Union could be thrown into anarchy or civil war.

The real cause of this danger, however, lies not in the constitution of the tribunal but in the very nature of Federal governments. We have observed that in confederate peoples it is especially necessary to consolidate the judicial authority, because in no other nations are the independent individuals who can cope with the social body so powerful, or so well placed to resist the physical strength of the government. But the more a power needs to be strengthened, the more extensive and independent it must be made, and the dangers its abuse may create grow with its independence and strength. The source of the evil is therefore not in the constitution of the power but in the constitution of the States that make its existence necessary.
In What Respects the Federal Constitution Is Superior to That of the States

In what respects the Constitution of the Union can be compared to those of the States — The superiority of the Constitution of the Union is due to the wisdom of the Federal legislators — The legislature of the Union is less dependent on the people than those of the States — The executive power is more independent in its sphere — The judicial power is less subject to the inclinations of the majority — Practical consequence of these facts — The dangers inherent in a democratic government were avoided by the Federal legislators and increased by the legislators of the States.

The Federal Constitution differs essentially from those of the States in the ends it is meant to achieve, but in the means by which those ends are pursued there is a closer resemblance. The objects of the governments are different, but their forms are the same; and from this particular point of view there is some advantage in comparing them.
I am of the opinion that the Federal Constitution is superior to all the Constitutions of the States, for several reasons.

The present Constitution of the Union was drawn up later than those of most of the States, and it may have benefited from what experience had taught by then. But we shall be led to acknowledge that this is only a secondary cause of its superiority, when we recall that eleven new States *n have joined the American Confederation since the Federal Constitution was promulgated, and that these new republics have always rather exaggerated the defects of the earlier Constitutions than avoided them.
n [ [The number of States has now risen to 46 (1874), besides the District of Columbia.]]

The main reason the Federal Constitution is superior lies in the character of the men who drew it up. At the time, the Confederation was in imminent danger and its ruin looked certain. In this crisis the people chose the men who most deserved the country’s esteem, not the ones who had won its affection. I have already observed that almost all the legislators of the Union were distinguished for their intelligence, but even more for their patriotism. They had all grown up while the spirit of liberty was being hardened by a constant struggle against a powerful and dominant authority. When that contest was over, the excited passions of the populace went on fighting dangers that no longer threatened them. These men stopped short. They looked at their country, now truly their own, with a calmer and more searching eye. They saw that the war of independence was finally over, and that the only dangers America still had to fear were those that could come from abusing the freedom she had won. They had the courage to say what they believed to be true, because they were driven by a warm and sincere love of liberty; and they dared to propose restrictions, because they were firmly set against destruction. *o
o [ At that time Alexander Hamilton, one of the chief founders of the Constitution, dared to state the following views in “The Federalist,” No. 71:

“There are some who would be inclined to regard the servile pliancy of the Executive to a prevailing current, either in the community or in the Legislature, as its best recommendation. But such men entertain very crude notions, as well of the purposes for which government was instituted as of the true means by which the public happiness may be promoted. The Republican principle demands that the deliberative sense of the community should govern the conduct of those to whom they entrust the management of their affairs; but it does not require an unqualified complaisance to every sudden breeze of passion, or to every transient impulse which the people may receive from the arts of men who flatter their prejudices to betray their interests. It is a just observation, that the people commonly intend the public good. This often applies to their very errors. But their good sense would despise the adulator who should pretend that they always reason right about the means of promoting it. They know from experience that they sometimes err; and the wonder is that they so seldom err as they do, beset, as they continually are, by the wiles of parasites and sycophants; by the snares of the ambitious, the avaricious, the desperate; by the artifices of men who possess their confidence more than they deserve it, and of those who seek to possess rather than to deserve it. When occasions present themselves in which the interests of the people are at variance with their inclinations, it is the duty of persons whom they have appointed to be the guardians of those interests to withstand the temporary delusion, in order to give them time and opportunity for more cool and sedate reflection. Instances might be cited in which a conduct of this kind has saved the people from very fatal consequences of their own mistakes, and has procured lasting monuments of their gratitude to the men who had courage and magnanimity enough to serve them at the peril of their displeasure.”]

Most of the Constitutions of the States set the term of the House of Representatives at one year and that of the Senate at two, so that members of the legislative body are constantly and narrowly tied down by the slightest wishes of their constituents. The legislators of the Union held that this excessive dependence of the legislature tended to alter the nature of the main consequences of the representative system, since it placed the source, not only of authority but of government, in the people. They lengthened the term for which representatives are returned, to give them freer scope to exercise their own judgment.

The Federal Constitution, like the Constitutions of the individual States, divided the legislative body into two branches. In the States, however, both branches were made up of the same elements and chosen in the same way. As a result the passions and moods of the populace were voiced as quickly and as forcefully in one chamber as in the other, and laws were made in a violent and hasty manner. Under the Federal Constitution the two houses also come from the choice of the people, but the requirements for eligibility and the method of election were changed, so that if one branch of the legislature represents the same interests as the other, as is the case in certain nations, it may at least represent a higher degree of intelligence and discretion. A mature age was made a requirement for a senator, and the upper house was chosen by an elected assembly with a limited number of members.

The natural tendency of democracies is to gather the whole force of society into the hands of the legislative body. Because that is the power that comes most directly from the people, it shares most fully in the overwhelming authority of the multitude, and it is naturally led to monopolize every kind of influence. This concentration harms good administration and favors the despotism of the majority. The legislators of the States often gave in to these democratic tendencies; the founders of the Union always resisted them, and did so with courage.

In the States the executive power is placed in the hands of a magistrate who seems to stand level with the legislature but is in fact only its blind agent and passive tool. His term, which ends with the year, gives him no influence, and neither do his prerogatives, which hardly exist. The legislature can condemn him to idleness by giving the carrying out of the laws to special committees drawn from its own members, and it can strip away his temporary dignity by cutting off his salary. The Federal Constitution places all the privileges and all the responsibility of the executive power in a single person. The Presidency lasts four years; the holder’s salary cannot be changed during his term; he is supported by a body of official dependents and armed with a suspensive veto. In short, every effort was made to give the executive authority a strong and independent position within the limits set for it.

Under the Constitutions of all the States, the judicial power is the one that stays most independent of the legislative authority. Even so, in every State the legislature has kept for itself the right to set the judges’ pay, which necessarily puts these magistrates under its direct influence. In some States judges are appointed only for a limited time, which strips them of much of their power and freedom. In others the legislative and judicial powers are completely mixed together: the Senate of New York, for example, serves in certain cases as the Superior Court of the State. The Federal Constitution, by contrast, carefully shields judicial authority from every outside influence. It secures the independence of the judges by declaring that their salary cannot be changed and that their office cannot be taken from them.

The practical consequences of these different systems are easy to see. A careful observer will soon notice that the business of the Union is far better conducted than that of any individual State. The Federal government acts more fairly and more moderately than the States do. Its designs show more wisdom, its projects are more lasting and more skillfully combined, and its measures are carried out with more vigor and consistency.

I will sum up the substance of this chapter in a few words. The existence of democracies is threatened by two dangers: the complete subjection of the legislative body to the whims of the electoral body, and the concentration of all the powers of government in the legislative authority. The legislators of the States have encouraged the growth of these evils. The legislators of the Union have resisted them by every means within their control.

Characteristics That Distinguish the Federal Constitution of the United States of America from All Other Federal Constitutions — The American Union seems to resemble all other confederations — Nevertheless its effects are different — The reason for this — How the Union differs from all other confederations — The American government is not a federal government but an imperfect national government.

The United States of America is neither the first nor the only example of confederate States. Several have existed in modern Europe, not to mention those of antiquity. Switzerland, the Germanic Empire, and the Republic of the United Provinces either were or still are confederations. When the student of politics examines the constitutions of these countries, he is surprised to find that the powers they gave the Federal government are nearly identical to those the American Constitution gives the government of the United States. They give the central power the same rights of making peace and war, of raising money and troops, and of providing for the general needs and common interests of the nation. Nevertheless, the Federal government of these other peoples has always been as remarkable for its weakness and inefficiency as that of the Union is for its vigor and enterprise. Again, the first American Confederation perished because its government was too weak, and yet that weak government held rights even more extensive than those of the Federal government today. But the more recent Constitution of the United States contains certain principles that have a most important influence, although they do not strike the observer at once.

This Constitution may at first sight be confused with the federal constitutions that came before it, but it rests on a new theory, which may be considered a great invention in modern political science. In all the confederations formed before the American Constitution of 1789, the allied States agreed to obey the directions of a Federal government, but they kept for themselves the right to order and enforce the execution of the laws of the Union. The American States that joined together in 1789 agreed that the Federal government should not only make the laws but also carry out its own enactments. In both cases the right is the same, but the way it is exercised is different, and this difference produced the most momentous consequences.

In all the confederations formed before the American Union, the Federal government demanded its supplies from the separate governments. If the measure it prescribed was burdensome to any one of those bodies, ways were found to evade its claims. A powerful State resorted to arms; a weak one tolerated the resistance that the law of the Union, its sovereign, met with, and fell back on inaction under the excuse of inability. In these circumstances one of two outcomes has invariably occurred. Either the most dominant of the allied peoples has taken over the privileges of the Federal authority and ruled all the States in its name, *p or the Federal government has been abandoned by its natural supporters, anarchy has arisen among the confederates, and the Union has lost all power to act. *q

p [ This was the case in Greece, when Philip undertook to execute the decree of the Amphictyons; in the Low Countries, where the province of Holland always gave the law; and, in our own time, in the Germanic Confederation, in which Austria and Prussia assume a great degree of influence over the whole country, in the name of the Diet.]
q [ Such has always been the situation of the Swiss Confederation, which would have perished ages ago but for the mutual jealousies of its neighbors.]

In America the subjects of the Union are not States but private citizens. The national government levies a tax not on the State of Massachusetts but on each inhabitant of Massachusetts. All earlier confederate governments presided over communities, but the government of the Union rules individuals. Its force is not borrowed but its own, and it is served by its own civil and military officers, its own army, and its own courts of justice. There is no doubt that the spirit of the nation, the passions of the multitude, and the local prejudices of each State tend strongly to weaken the authority of a Federal power constituted in this way, and to make it easier to resist its commands. But the comparative weakness of a limited sovereignty is an evil inherent in the federal system. In America, each State has fewer opportunities to resist and fewer temptations to refuse compliance. Nor can such a plan be carried out (if it is entertained at all) without an open violation of the laws of the Union, a direct interruption of the ordinary course of justice, and a bold declaration of revolt — in a word, without taking a decisive step that men hesitate to take.

In all earlier confederations, the privileges of the Union furnished more causes of discord than of power, since they multiplied the claims of the nation without increasing the means of enforcing them. Accordingly, we may note that the real weakness of federal governments has almost always been in exact proportion to their nominal power. This is not the case in the American Union, where, as in ordinary governments, the Federal government has the means of enforcing everything it is empowered to demand.

The human mind invents new things more easily than new words, and so we are forced to use a multitude of improper and inadequate expressions. When several nations form a permanent league and establish a supreme authority, which does not have the same influence over the members of the community as a national government but acts on each of the Confederate States as a whole, this government, so essentially different from all others, is called a Federal one. Later another form of society is discovered, in which several peoples are fused into one and the same nation with regard to certain common interests, while they remain distinct, or at least only confederate, with regard to all their other concerns. In this case the central power acts directly on those it governs, rules, and judges, in the same manner as a national government but within a more limited sphere. Here the term Federal government clearly no longer applies to a state of things that must be called an incomplete national government. A form of government has been found that is neither exactly national nor federal. But no further progress has been made, and the new word that will one day name this new invention does not yet exist.

The lack of this new kind of confederation has brought all earlier Unions to civil war, to subjection, or to a stagnant apathy. The peoples that formed these leagues were either too dull to see this great remedy or too timid to apply it. The American Confederation perished from the same defects.

But the Confederate States of America had long been accustomed to forming part of one empire before they won their independence. They had not acquired the habit of governing themselves, and their national prejudices had not taken deep root in their minds. Superior to the rest of the world in political knowledge, and sharing that knowledge equally among themselves, they were little troubled by the passions that generally oppose the extension of federal authority in a nation, and the wisdom of the leading citizens kept those passions in check. The Americans applied the remedy with prudent firmness as soon as they became aware of the evil. They amended their laws, and they saved their country.
Advantages of the Federal System in General, and Its Special Usefulness in America.

Happiness and freedom of small nations — Power of great nations — Great empires favorable to the growth of civilization — Strength is often the first element of national prosperity — The aim of the Federal system is to unite the twofold advantages of a small and a large territory — Advantages the United States has gained from this system — The law adapts itself to the needs of the population; the population does not conform to the needs of the law — Activity, improvement, and love and enjoyment of freedom in the American communities — The public spirit of the Union is the summary of provincial patriotism — Principles and things circulate freely over the territory of the United States — The Union is happy and free like a small nation, and respected like a great empire.

In small nations the scrutiny of society reaches into every part, and the spirit of improvement enters into the smallest details. The ambition of the people is necessarily held in check by its weakness, so all the efforts and resources of the citizens are turned to the internal benefit of the community and are not likely to vanish in the fleeting breath of glory. The desires of every individual are limited, because extraordinary abilities are rarely found. The gifts of an equal fortune make the various conditions of life uniform, and the customs of the inhabitants are orderly and simple. So if we weigh the degrees of popular morality and education, we shall generally find that small nations have more people in easy circumstances, a more numerous population, and a more tranquil society than great empires do.

When tyranny is established in the heart of a small nation, it is more galling than elsewhere. Because it acts within a narrow circle, every point of that circle is subject to its direct influence. It makes up for the great designs it cannot entertain by violent or exasperating interference in a multitude of minute details. It leaves the political world, to which it properly belongs, to meddle with the arrangements of domestic life. Tastes as well as actions are to be regulated at its pleasure, and the families of the citizens as well as the affairs of the State are to be governed by its decisions. This invasion of rights, however, occurs only rarely, and freedom is in truth the natural state of small communities. The temptations that government offers to ambition are too weak, and the resources of private individuals are too slight, for the sovereign power easily to fall into the grasp of a single citizen. And if such a thing did happen, the subjects of the State could without difficulty overthrow the tyrant and his oppression by a simultaneous effort.

Small nations have therefore always been the birthplace of political liberty. Many of them have lost their freedoms by expanding their dominion, and this shows that the freedom they enjoyed owed more to their small size than to the character of their people.

No great nation in the history of the world has kept a republican form of government for a long series of years, *r and this has led people to conclude that such a thing is impracticable. For my part, I cannot help blaming the imprudence of a being who tries to limit the possible and to judge the future. He is deceived every hour by the most obvious realities of life, and he is constantly taken by surprise in the circumstances he knows best. But it may be said with confidence that a great republic will always be exposed to far greater perils than a small one.
r [ I do not speak of a confederation of small republics, but of a great consolidated Republic.]

All the passions most fatal to republican institutions spread as territory grows, while the virtues that maintain their dignity do not grow in the same proportion. The ambition of the citizens increases with the power of the State, and the strength of parties with the importance of the ends they have in view. But devotion to the common good, which is the surest check on destructive passions, is no stronger in a large republic than in a small one. Indeed, it could easily be proved that it is weaker and less sincere. The arrogance of wealth and the dejection of the wretched, capital cities of unusual size, a lax morality, a vulgar selfishness, and a great confusion of interests — these are the dangers that almost invariably arise from the great size of States. But several of these evils are hardly harmful to a monarchy, and some of them help to maintain it. In monarchical States the strength of the government is its own; it may use the community, but it does not depend on it, and the authority of the prince is proportioned to the prosperity of the nation. But the only security a republican government has against these evils lies in the support of the majority. This support is not proportionally greater in a large republic than in a small one. So while the means of attack constantly increase in both number and influence, the power of resistance remains the same, or rather it may be said to diminish, since the inclinations and interests of the people become more varied as the population grows, and the difficulty of forming a solid majority keeps increasing. It has also been observed that the intensity of human passions is heightened not only by the importance of the end they aim at but by the number of individuals who are moved by them at the same time. Everyone has had occasion to notice that his emotions in the midst of a sympathetic crowd are far greater than those he would have felt alone. In great republics the force of political passion is irresistible, not only because it aims at gigantic purposes, but because it is felt and shared by millions of men at the same time.

It may therefore be stated as a general proposition that nothing is more opposed to the well-being and the freedom of man than vast empires. Nevertheless, it is important to acknowledge the particular advantages of great States. The very reason that makes the desire for power more intense in these communities than among ordinary men also makes the love of glory more prominent in the hearts of one class of citizens, who regard the applause of a great people as a reward worthy of their efforts and as an uplifting encouragement. If we want to learn why great nations contribute more powerfully to the spread of human improvement than small States do, we shall find an adequate cause in the rapid and energetic circulation of ideas, and in those great cities that are the intellectual centers where all the rays of human genius are reflected and combined. To this it may be added that most important discoveries require a display of national power that the government of a small State cannot make. In great nations the government entertains a greater number of general ideas, and it is more completely free from the routine of precedent and the selfishness of local prejudice. Its designs are conceived with more talent and carried out with more boldness.

In time of peace the well-being of small nations is undoubtedly more general and more complete. But they tend to suffer more acutely from the calamities of war than great empires do. The distant frontiers of great empires may for ages keep danger away from the mass of the people, who are therefore more often afflicted than ruined by war.

But in this matter, as in many others, the argument from necessity outweighs all others. If only small nations existed, I do not doubt that mankind would be happier and freer, but the existence of great nations is unavoidable.

This consideration introduces physical strength as a condition of national prosperity. It profits a people little to be wealthy and free if it is perpetually exposed to being plundered or conquered. The number of its manufactures and the extent of its commerce are of little advantage if another nation commands the seas and gives the law in all the markets of the globe. Small nations are often poor not because they are small but because they are weak, and great empires prosper less because they are great than because they are strong. Physical strength is therefore one of the first conditions of the happiness, and even of the existence, of nations. Hence it happens that, unless very unusual circumstances intervene, small nations are always joined to large empires in the end, either by force or by their own consent. Yet I know of no more deplorable spectacle than that of a people unable either to defend or to maintain its independence.

The Federal system was created with the intention of combining the different advantages of larger and smaller nations, and a single glance at the United States of America is enough to see the advantages they have drawn from adopting it.

In great centralized nations the legislator is obliged to give the laws a uniform character that does not always suit the variety of customs and districts. Since he takes no notice of particular cases, he can only proceed on general principles. The population is obliged to conform to the demands of the legislation, because the legislation cannot adapt itself to the needs and customs of the population, and this is the cause of endless trouble and misery. This disadvantage does not exist in confederations. Congress regulates the principal measures of the national government, and all the details of administration are left to the provincial legislatures. It is impossible to imagine how much this division of sovereignty contributes to the well-being of each of the States that make up the Union. These small communities are never troubled by the desire for expansion or the cares of self-defense, so all public authority and private energy is employed in internal improvement. The central government of each State, being in immediate contact with the citizens, is informed daily of the needs that arise in society. New projects are proposed every year, discussed either at town meetings or by the legislature of the State, and passed on by the press to stimulate the zeal and excite the interest of the citizens. This spirit of improvement is constantly alive in the American republics without disturbing their tranquillity. The ambition for power gives way to the less refined and less dangerous love of comfort. It is generally believed in America that the existence and permanence of the republican form of government in the New World depend on the existence and permanence of the Federal system. It is not unusual to blame a large share of the misfortunes of the new States of South America on the unwise creation of great republics instead of a divided and confederate sovereignty.

It is beyond dispute that the love and the habits of republican government in the United States were produced in the townships and in the provincial assemblies. In a small State like Connecticut, for instance, cutting a canal or building a road is a weighty political question. The State has no army to pay and no wars to wage, and it cannot bestow much wealth or honor on its leading citizens. In such a State no form of government could be more natural or more suitable than a republic. But it is this same republican spirit, these manners and customs of a free people, produced and nurtured in the different States, that are afterward applied to the country at large. The public spirit of the Union is, so to speak, nothing more than a summary of the patriotic zeal of the provinces. Every citizen of the United States transfers his attachment to his little republic into the common store of American patriotism. In defending the Union he defends the growing prosperity of his own district, the right to conduct its affairs, and the hope of getting improvements adopted that may favor his own interest. These are motives that move men more readily than the general interests of the country and the glory of the nation.

On the other hand, if the temper and the customs of the inhabitants especially fitted them to promote the welfare of a great republic, the Federal system cleared away the obstacles they might have met. The confederation of all the American States has none of the ordinary disadvantages that result from great concentrations of people. The Union is a great republic in size, but the small number of objects its government provides for makes it resemble a small State. Its acts are important, but they are rare. Because the sovereignty of the Union is limited and incomplete, its exercise is not incompatible with liberty, for it does not excite those insatiable desires for fame and power that have proved so fatal to great republics. Because the country has no common center, vast capital cities, colossal wealth, abject poverty, and sudden revolutions are all unknown. Political passion, instead of sweeping over the land like a torrent of desolation, spends its strength against the interests and individual passions of each State.

Nevertheless, all goods and ideas circulate throughout the Union as freely as in a country inhabited by one people. Nothing checks the spirit of enterprise. The government makes use of the help of everyone who has talents or knowledge to serve it. Within the frontiers of the Union the profoundest peace prevails, as in the heart of some great empire. Abroad, the Union ranks with the most powerful nations of the earth. Two thousand miles of coast are open to the commerce of the world, and because it holds the keys of the globe, its flag is respected in the most distant seas. The Union is as happy and as free as a small people, and as glorious and as strong as a great nation.
Why the Federal System Is Not Suited to All Peoples, and How the Anglo-Americans Were Able to Adopt It.

Every Federal system contains defects that baffle the efforts of the legislator — The Federal system is complex — It demands a daily exercise of judgment on the part of the citizens — Practical knowledge of government is common among the Americans — The relative weakness of the government of the Union, another defect inherent in the Federal system — The Americans have reduced it without remedying it — The sovereignty of the separate States appears weaker, but is really stronger, than that of the Union — Why? — Natural causes of union must exist between confederate peoples besides the laws — What these causes are among the Anglo-Americans — Maine and Georgia, separated by a distance of a thousand miles, are more naturally united than Normandy and Brittany — War, the main danger of confederations — This is proved even by the example of the United States — The Union has no great wars to fear — Why? — Dangers to which Europeans would be exposed if they adopted the Federal system of the Americans.

When a legislator succeeds, after persistent efforts, in exerting an indirect influence on the destiny of nations, mankind praises his genius. But in fact the geographical position of the country, which he cannot change, a social condition that arose without his help, customs and opinions whose source he cannot trace, and an origin he does not know all exercise such an irresistible influence over the course of society that he himself is carried away by the current after a futile resistance. Like the navigator, he may steer the vessel that carries him along, but he can neither change its structure, nor raise the winds, nor calm the waters that swell beneath him.

I have shown the advantages the Americans draw from their federal system. It remains for me to point out the circumstances that made that system workable, since not all nations can enjoy its benefits. The incidental defects of the Federal system that come from the laws may be corrected by the skill of the legislator. But there are further evils inherent in the system that the peoples who adopt it cannot counteract. These nations must therefore find the strength needed to bear the natural imperfections of their government.

The most prominent evil of all Federal systems is the very complex nature of the means they employ. Two sovereignties necessarily stand face to face. The legislator may simplify and balance the action of these two sovereignties by limiting each to a carefully defined sphere of authority. But he cannot merge them into one, or prevent them from coming into collision at certain points. The Federal system therefore rests on a theory that is necessarily complicated, and that requires those it governs to exercise a considerable amount of judgment every day.

A proposition must be plain to be accepted by the understanding of a people. A false idea that is clear and precise will always win more followers in the world than a true principle that is obscure or involved. Hence parties, which are like small communities within the nation, invariably adopt some principle or some name as a symbol. This symbol represents very inadequately the end they have in view and the means at their disposal, but without it they could neither act nor survive. Governments founded on a single principle or a single feeling that is easily defined are perhaps not the best, but they are unquestionably the strongest and the most lasting in the world.

On the other hand, when one examines the Constitution of the United States, the most perfect federal constitution that ever existed, one is startled by the variety of knowledge and the excellence of judgment that it presupposes in the people it is meant to govern. The government of the Union depends entirely on legal fictions. The Union is an ideal nation that exists only in the mind, and its limits and extent can be discerned only by the understanding.

Once the general theory is understood, countless difficulties remain to be solved in applying it. The sovereignty of the Union is so entangled with that of the States that it is impossible to see its boundaries at first glance. The whole structure of the government is artificial and conventional. It would be poorly suited to a people that has not long been accustomed to conducting its own affairs, or to one in which the science of politics has not reached the humblest classes of society. I have never been more struck by the good sense and practical judgment of the Americans than in the ingenious devices by which they get around the countless difficulties arising from their Federal Constitution. I have scarcely ever met a plain American citizen who could not distinguish, with surprising ease, the obligations created by the laws of Congress from those created by the laws of his own State, or who, after separating the matters that fall under the authority of the Union from those the local legislature is competent to regulate, could not point out the exact limits of the several jurisdictions of the Federal courts and the tribunals of the State.

The Constitution of the United States is like those exquisite products of human skill that bring wealth and renown to their inventors but are worthless in any other hands. This truth is shown by the condition of Mexico at the present time. The Mexicans wanted to establish a federal system. They took the Federal Constitution of their neighbors, the Anglo-Americans, as their model and copied it with considerable accuracy. *s But although they had borrowed the letter of the law, they were unable to create or introduce the spirit and meaning that give it life. They were caught in ceaseless difficulties between the machinery of their double government. The sovereignty of the States and that of the Union perpetually exceeded their respective privileges and came into collision. To this day Mexico is alternately the victim of anarchy and the slave of military despotism.
s [ See the Mexican Constitution of 1824.]

The second and most fatal of all the defects I have mentioned, and the one I believe to be inherent in the federal system, is the relative weakness of the government of the Union. The principle on which all confederations rest is that of a divided sovereignty. The legislator may make this division less noticeable, and he may even hide it for a time from the public eye, but he cannot prevent it from existing, and a divided sovereignty must always be less powerful than a complete supremacy. The reader has seen, from my remarks on the Constitution of the United States, that the Americans have shown unusual ingenuity in combining two things. One is the restriction of the power of the Union within the narrow limits of a federal government. The other is the appearance, and to a certain extent the force, of a national government. By this means the legislators of the Union have succeeded in reducing, though not in neutralizing, the natural danger of confederations.

It has been observed that the American government does not address itself to the States but sends its commands directly to the citizens, and compels them as isolated individuals to comply with its demands. But suppose a Federal law clashed with the interests and prejudices of a State. It might be feared that all the citizens of that State would consider themselves interested in the cause of a single individual who refused to obey. Suppose all the citizens of the State were aggrieved at the same time and in the same way by the authority of the Union. The Federal government would try in vain to subdue them one by one. They would instinctively unite in a common defense, and they would draw a ready-made organization from the share of sovereignty that the institutions of their State allow them to enjoy. Fiction would give way to reality, and an organized portion of the territory might then contest the central authority. *t The same observation holds true of the Federal jurisdiction. Suppose the courts of the Union violated an important law of a State in a private case. The real contest, if not the apparent one, would then arise between the aggrieved State, represented by a citizen, and the Union, represented by its courts of justice. *u

t [ [This is precisely what occurred in 1862, and the following paragraph describes correctly the feelings and ideas of the South. General Lee held that his primary allegiance was due, not to the Union, but to Virginia.]]

u [ For instance, the Union has the right under the Constitution to sell unoccupied lands for its own profit. Suppose the State of Ohio claimed the same right for certain territories within its boundaries, on the grounds that the Constitution refers only to lands that do not belong to the jurisdiction of any particular State, and so chose to dispose of them itself. The lawsuit would be carried on in the names of the purchasers from the State of Ohio and the purchasers from the Union, and not in the names of Ohio and the Union. But what would become of this legal fiction if the Federal purchaser was confirmed in his right by the courts of the Union, while the other claimant was ordered to keep possession by the tribunals of the State of Ohio?]

He would have only a partial knowledge of the world who imagined that legal fictions can stop men from finding and using the means of gratifying their passions that have been left open to them. It may be doubted whether the American legislators, in making a collision between the two sovereigns less probable, removed the cause of such a misfortune. It may even be said that they were unable to ensure that the Federal element would prevail in a case of this kind. The Union has money and troops, but the affections and prejudices of the people lie with the States. The sovereignty of the Union is an abstract being, connected with few external objects. The sovereignty of the States is perceptible every hour, easily understood, and constantly active. And if the former is of recent creation, the latter is as old as the people itself. The sovereignty of the Union is artificial; that of the States is natural, and it draws its existence from its own simple influence, like the authority of a parent. The supreme power of the nation affects only a few of the chief interests of society. It represents an immense but remote country, and it claims a feeling of patriotism that is vague and ill defined. But the authority of the States controls every individual citizen at every hour and in all circumstances. It protects his property, his freedom, and his life. When we recall the traditions, the customs, and the prejudices of local and familiar attachment with which it is bound up, we cannot doubt the superiority of a power that is interwoven with every circumstance that makes love of one’s native country instinctive in the human heart.

Legislators cannot prevent the dangerous collisions that occur between the two sovereignties coexisting in the federal system. Their first object must therefore be, not only to dissuade the confederate States from warfare, but also to encourage institutions that may help maintain peace. It follows that the Federal compact cannot last unless the communities leagued together have a certain number of inducements to union that make their common dependence agreeable and the task of the government light. And that system cannot succeed without favorable circumstances in addition to the influence of good laws. All the peoples that have ever formed a confederation have been held together by a certain number of common interests, which served as the intellectual ties of association.

But the feelings and principles of man must be taken into account as well as his immediate interests. A certain uniformity of civilization is no less necessary to the durability of a confederation than a uniformity of interests among the States that make it up. In Switzerland, the difference between the Canton of Uri and the Canton of Vaud is equal to that between the fifteenth and the nineteenth centuries. Properly speaking, Switzerland has never had a federal government. The union between these two cantons exists only on the map, and their differences would soon be felt if a central authority tried to prescribe the same laws for the whole territory.

One of the circumstances that most powerfully helps to support the Federal government in America is that the States have not only similar interests, a common origin, and a common tongue, but have also reached the same stage of civilization, which almost always makes a union workable. I know of no European nation, however small, that shows less uniformity among its different provinces than the American people, who occupy a territory as large as half of Europe. The distance from Maine to Georgia is reckoned at about one thousand miles, but the difference between the civilization of Maine and that of Georgia is slighter than the difference between the habits of Normandy and those of Brittany. Maine and Georgia are at the opposite ends of a great empire, and they therefore have by nature more real inducements to form a confederation than Normandy and Brittany, which are separated only by a bridge.

The geographical position of the country added to the advantages that the American legislators drew from the manners and customs of the inhabitants, and it is mainly to this circumstance that the adoption and the maintenance of the Federal system are owed.

The most important event that can mark the history of a people is the outbreak of a war. In war a people struggles against foreign nations, with the energy of a single man, to defend its very existence. A skilled government, the good sense of the community, and the natural attachment men feel for their country may be enough to keep the peace within a district and to promote its internal prosperity. But a nation can carry on a great war only by making more numerous and more painful sacrifices, and to suppose that great numbers of men will comply of their own accord with these demands of the state is to show an ignorance of mankind. Every people that has had to sustain a long and serious war has therefore been led to increase the power of its government. Those that failed to do so were conquered. A long war almost always leaves nations the wretched choice of being abandoned to ruin by defeat or to despotism by victory. War therefore exposes the weakness of a government most plainly and most alarmingly; and I have shown that the inherent defect of federal governments is that they are weak.

The Federal system lacks every kind of centralized administration, and the central government itself is also imperfectly organized. This is always a major cause of inferiority when the nation faces other countries that are governed by a single authority. Under the Federal Constitution of the United States, in which the central government has more real strength, this evil is still very much felt. An example will make the matter clear to the reader.

The Constitution gives Congress the right to call out the militia to execute the laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, and repel invasions; and another article declares that the President of the United States is the commander-in-chief of the militia. In the war of 1812 the President ordered the militia of the Northern States to march to the frontiers. But Connecticut and Massachusetts, whose interests were harmed by the war, refused to obey the order. They argued that the Constitution authorizes the Federal Government to call out the militia in case of insurrection or invasion, but that in this instance there was neither invasion nor insurrection. They added that the same Constitution that gave the Union the right to call out the militia reserved to the States the right to name the officers. Consequently (as they understood the clause) no officer of the Union had any right to command the militia, even in wartime, except the President in person; and in this case the militia had been ordered to join an army commanded by someone else.
