These absurd and harmful doctrines were endorsed not only by the governors and the legislative bodies but also by the courts of justice in both States, and the Federal Government was forced to raise the troops it needed elsewhere. *v

v [ Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 244. I have chosen an example that relates to a time after the adoption of the present Constitution. If I had gone back to the days of the Confederation, I could have given still more striking instances. The whole nation was at that time in a state of enthusiastic excitement; the Revolution was embodied in a man who was the idol of the people; but even then Congress had, to tell the truth, no resources at all at its disposal. Troops and supplies were constantly lacking. The best-designed projects failed in the execution, and the Union, which was always on the verge of destruction, was saved far more by the weakness of its enemies than by its own strength. [All doubt as to the powers of the Federal Executive was, however, removed by its efforts in the Civil War, and those powers were largely extended.]]

With all the relative excellence of its laws, the American Union has only one safeguard against the dissolution that a great war would bring about: it is unlikely to suffer that calamity. The Union lies in the center of an immense continent that offers a boundless field for human industry, and it is almost as cut off from the rest of the world as if its frontiers were surrounded by the ocean. Canada has only a million inhabitants, and its population is divided into two hostile nations. The severity of the climate limits the growth of its territory and closes its ports for the six months of winter. From Canada to the Gulf of Mexico there are only a few savage tribes, which retreat, dying out as they go, before six thousand soldiers. To the south the Union touches the empire of Mexico, and it is from there that serious hostilities may one day be expected. But for a long time to come, the uncivilized state of Mexican society, the corruption of its morals, and its extreme poverty will keep that country from ranking high among nations. *w As for the Powers of Europe, they are too far away to be formidable.
w [ [War broke out between the United States and Mexico in 1846, and ended in the conquest of an immense territory, including California.]]
The great advantage of the United States, then, does not lie in a Federal Constitution that allows them to carry on great wars, but in a geographical position that makes such wars extremely unlikely.

No one is more inclined than I am to appreciate the advantages of the federal system, which I regard as one of the arrangements most favorable to human prosperity and freedom. I envy the lot of the nations that have been able to adopt it. But I cannot believe that any confederate peoples could sustain a long or an equal contest against a nation of similar strength whose government was centralized. A people that divided its sovereignty into fractional powers, in the presence of the great military monarchies of Europe, would in my opinion give up its power by that very act, and perhaps its existence and its name. But the position of the New World is so admirable that man has no enemy but himself. To be happy and free, he need only seek the gifts of prosperity and the knowledge of freedom.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — Why The People May Strictly Be Said To Govern In The United States
paragraphs: So far I have examined the institutions of the United States. I have reviewed their legislation, and I have described the present characteristics of political society in that country. But above these institutions and beyond these characteristic features there is a sovereign power that can destroy or change them as it pleases. I mean the power of the people. It remains to show how this power, which regulates the laws, acts. I must point out its inclinations and its passions, and the hidden springs that slow down, speed up, or direct its irresistible course. I must also show the effects of its unlimited authority and the destiny that probably awaits it.

In America the people appoints the legislative and the executive power, and supplies the jurors who punish every offense against the laws. American institutions are democratic not only in their principle but in all their consequences. The people elects its representatives directly, and for the most part annually, in order to keep them dependent on it. The people is therefore the real directing power. Although the form of government is representative, it is evident that the opinions, the prejudices, the interests, and even the passions of the community meet no lasting obstacle to their exercising a perpetual influence on society. In the United States the majority governs in the name of the people, as happens in every country where the people is supreme. The majority is composed mainly of peaceful citizens who, whether by inclination or by interest, sincerely desire the welfare of their country. But they are surrounded by the ceaseless agitation of parties, which try to win their cooperation and to make use of their support.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — Parties In The United States
paragraphs: A great distinction must be made between parties. Some countries are so large that the different populations living in them have conflicting interests, even though they are subjects of the same government, and they may therefore be in a perpetual state of opposition. In that case the different sections of the people are better regarded as distinct nations than as mere parties. If a civil war breaks out, the struggle is carried on by rival peoples rather than by factions within a single state.

But when citizens hold different opinions on subjects that affect the whole country equally, such as the principles on which the government should be conducted, then divisions arise that may rightly be called parties. Parties are a necessary evil in free governments, but they do not always have the same character and the same tendencies.

At certain times a nation may be oppressed by such unbearable evils that it plans to change its political constitution completely. At other times the trouble lies deeper still, and the very existence of society is in danger. These are the times of great revolutions and great parties. But between these epochs of misery and confusion there are periods when human society seems to be at rest and mankind seems to pause. This pause is only apparent, for time does not stop for nations any more than for men. They are all advancing toward a goal they do not know, and we imagine them stationary only when their progress escapes our notice, just as men walking at a slow pace seem to be standing still to those who are running.

But whatever the truth of this, there are certain epochs when the changes in the social and political constitution of nations are so slow and so imperceptible that men imagine their present condition to be final. The human mind, believing itself firmly based on certain foundations, does not extend its inquiries beyond the horizon it can see. These are the times of small parties and of intrigue.

The political parties I call great are those that cling to principles more than to their consequences, to general cases and not to particular ones, to ideas and not to men. These parties are usually marked by a nobler character, more generous passions, more genuine convictions, and bolder and more open conduct than the others. In them private interest, which always plays the chief part in political passions, is more carefully veiled under the pretext of the public good. It may even sometimes be hidden from the very people whom it excites and drives.

Minor parties, on the other hand, generally lack political faith. Because no lofty purpose sustains or dignifies them, they openly show the selfishness of their character in their actions. They glow with an artificial zeal. Their language is violent, but their conduct is timid and irresolute. The means they use are as wretched as the end they aim at. That is why, when a calm period follows a violent revolution, the leaders of society seem suddenly to vanish and the powers of the human mind seem to lie hidden. Great parties convulse society; minor ones merely agitate it. The former tear it apart, the latter degrade it. And if the great parties sometimes save it by a healthy shock, the minor ones always disturb it to no good purpose.

America has already lost the great parties that once divided the nation. Her happiness has increased considerably, but her morality has suffered from their disappearance. When the War of Independence was over and the foundations of the new government had to be laid, the nation was divided between two opinions. These two opinions are as old as the world, and they are met with perpetually, under all the forms and names that have ever existed in free communities. One tended to limit the power of the people, the other to extend it indefinitely. The conflict between them never reached in America the degree of violence it has often shown elsewhere. Both American parties were in fact agreed on the most essential points. Neither had to destroy a traditional constitution or overthrow the structure of society in order to secure its own triumph. Consequently, in neither of them were many private interests affected by success or defeat. But moral principles of a high order, such as the love of equality and of independence, were at stake in the struggle, and they were enough to kindle violent passions.

The party that wished to limit the power of the people tried to apply its doctrines especially to the Constitution of the Union, and from this it took its name of Federal. The other party, which made a show of being more exclusively attached to the cause of liberty, took the name of Republican. America is a land of democracy, and the Federalists were always in a minority. But they counted on their side almost all the great men whom the War of Independence had brought forward, and their moral influence was very considerable. Circumstances also favored their cause. The collapse of the Confederation had given the people a dread of anarchy, and the Federalists did not fail to profit from this passing mood of the multitude. For ten or twelve years they were at the head of affairs, and they were able to apply some, though not all, of their principles, for the opposing current was growing too violent day by day to be checked or resisted. In 1801 the Republicans took control of the government. Thomas Jefferson was chosen President, and he increased the influence of their party by the weight of his fame, the greatness of his talents, and the immense extent of his popularity.

The means by which the Federalists had held their position were artificial, and their resources were temporary. They had risen to power through the virtues or the talents of their leaders. When the Republicans reached that high station, their opponents were crushed by a complete defeat. An immense majority declared itself against the outgoing party, and the Federalists found themselves in so small a minority that they at once despaired of future success. From that moment the Republican or Democratic party *a has gone from conquest to conquest, until it has gained absolute supremacy in the country. The Federalists saw that they were beaten beyond recovery and isolated in the midst of the nation. They split into two groups. One joined the victorious Republicans; the other abandoned its rallying point and its name. Many years have now passed since they ceased to exist as a party.

a [ [It is scarcely necessary to remark that in more recent times the meaning of these terms has changed. The Republicans are the representatives of the old Federalists, and the Democrats of the old Republicans.—Trans. Note (1861).]] In my opinion, the rise of the Federalists to power was one of the most fortunate events that accompanied the formation of the great American Union. They resisted the inevitable tendencies of their age and country. But whether their theories were good or bad, they had the defect of being unworkable, as a system, in the society they claimed to govern, and what happened under Jefferson must therefore have happened sooner or later. Still, their government gave the new republic time to gain a certain stability, and afterward to withstand the rapid growth of the very doctrines they had fought against. A considerable number of their principles were in fact built into the political creed of their opponents, and the Federal Constitution that exists today is a lasting monument to their patriotism and their wisdom.

Great political parties, then, are not found in the United States at the present time. There are parties that threaten the future tranquillity of the Union, but none that seem to contest the present form of government or the present course of society. The parties that endanger the Union rest not on abstract principles but on material interests. These interests, scattered across the provinces of so vast an empire, may be said to form rival nations rather than parties. Thus, on a recent occasion, the North argued for a system of commercial prohibition and the South took up arms in favor of free trade, simply because the North is a manufacturing region and the South an agricultural one, and the restrictive system that benefited the one was harmful to the other. *b

b [ [The divisions between North and South have since become far more intense, and the South, though conquered, still shows a formidable spirit of opposition to Northern government.—Translator’s Note, 1875.]]

In the absence of great parties, the United States swarms with lesser controversies, and public opinion is divided into a thousand tiny shades of difference over questions of very little importance. The pains taken to create parties are beyond belief, and at present it is no easy task. In the United States there is no religious animosity, because all religion is respected and no sect is dominant. There is no jealousy of rank, because the people is everything and no one can challenge its authority. Lastly, there is no widespread poverty to supply the means of agitation, because the physical position of the country opens so wide a field to industry that a man can accomplish the most surprising undertakings with his own native resources. Nevertheless, ambitious men have an interest in creating parties, since it is hard to remove a person from office merely because others covet his place. The skill of the players in the political world therefore lies in the art of creating parties. A political aspirant in the United States begins by identifying his own interest and calculating which other interests might gather around it and combine with it. Then he manages to find some doctrine or principle that will suit the purposes of this new association, and he adopts it in order to bring his party forward and win popularity. It is like the imprimatur of a king in former days, which was bound into the volume it authorized although it had nothing to do with the book. When these preliminaries are finished, the new party is introduced into the political world.

To a stranger, all the domestic controversies of the Americans seem at first so incomprehensible and so childish that he does not know whether to pity a people that takes such arrant trifles seriously or to envy the happiness that lets it discuss them. But when he studies the secret tendencies that govern the factions of America, he easily sees that most of them are more or less connected with one or the other of those two divisions that have always existed in free communities. The deeper we look into the workings of these parties, the more we see that the aim of the one is to limit, and that of the other to extend, the authority of the people. I do not claim that the declared aim, or even the secret aim, of American parties is to promote the rule of aristocracy or of democracy in the country. But I do affirm that aristocratic or democratic passions can easily be found at the bottom of all parties, and that, although they escape superficial observation, they are the main point and the very soul of every faction in the United States.

To take a recent example: when the President attacked the Bank, the country was stirred up and parties were formed. The well-informed classes rallied to the Bank, the common people to the President. But it must not be imagined that the people had formed a reasoned opinion on a question that presents so many difficulties even to the most experienced statesmen. The Bank is a great institution with an independent existence, and the people, accustomed to making and unmaking whatever it pleases, is startled to meet this obstacle to its authority. In the midst of the constant change in society, the community is irritated by so permanent an institution and is led to attack it, to see whether it can be shaken and controlled like all the other institutions of the country.
Remains of the Aristocratic Party in the United States

Secret opposition of wealthy individuals to democracy — Their retirement — Their taste for exclusive pleasures and for luxury at home — Their simplicity in public — Their affected condescension toward the people.

It sometimes happens that, among a people with a variety of opinions, the balance between the several parties is lost, and one of them gains an irresistible preponderance. It overcomes every obstacle, harasses its opponents, and takes all the resources of society for its own purposes. The defeated citizens despair of success, and they hide their dissatisfaction in silence and general apathy. The nation seems to be governed by a single principle, and the dominant party claims the credit for having restored peace and unanimity to the country. But this apparent unanimity is merely a cloak for alarming dissension and perpetual opposition.

This is exactly what happened in America. When the democratic party gained the upper hand, it took exclusive possession of the conduct of affairs, and from that time the laws and the customs of society have been shaped to suit its whims. Today the wealthier classes are so completely removed from the direction of political affairs in the United States that wealth, far from giving a right to exercise power, is more of an obstacle than a means of reaching it. The wealthy members of the community leave the arena, unwilling to contend, and often to contend in vain, against the poorest of their fellow citizens. They concentrate all their enjoyments in the privacy of their homes, where they hold a rank they cannot assume in public, and they form a private society within the state, with its own tastes and its own pleasures. They submit to this state of things as an incurable evil, but they are careful not to show that it galls them. It is even not uncommon to hear them in public praising the delights of republican government and the advantages of democratic institutions. Next to hating their enemies, men are most inclined to flatter them.

Look, for instance, at that wealthy citizen, who is as anxious to conceal his wealth as a Jew of the Middle Ages. His dress is plain, his manner unassuming. But the inside of his house glitters with luxury, and only a few chosen guests, whom he haughtily calls his equals, are allowed into this sanctuary. No European noble is more exclusive in his pleasures, or more jealous of the smallest advantages his privileged position gives him. Yet the very same man crosses the city to reach a dark counting-house in the center of trade, where anyone who likes may approach him. If he meets his cobbler on the way, they stop and talk. The two citizens discuss the affairs of the state, in which they have an equal interest, and they shake hands before they part.

But beneath this artificial enthusiasm and these servile attentions to the dominant power, it is easy to see that the wealthy members of the community have a hearty distaste for the democratic institutions of their country. The populace is at once the object of their scorn and of their fears. If the mismanagement of the democracy ever brings on a revolutionary crisis, and if monarchical institutions ever become practicable in the United States, the truth of what I am saying will become obvious.
The two chief weapons that parties use to ensure success are the public press and the formation of associations.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Liberty Of The Press In The United States
paragraphs: The influence of the liberty of the press is not limited to political opinions. It reaches all the opinions of men, and it changes customs as well as laws. In another part of this work I shall try to determine how much influence the liberty of the press has had on civil society in the United States, to show what direction it has given to the ideas of the Anglo-Americans, and to describe the tone it has given to their character and feelings. For now, I intend only to examine the effects the liberty of the press has produced in the political world.

I confess that I do not have the firm and complete attachment to the liberty of the press that people feel for things that are supremely good in their very nature. I approve of it more because I remember the evils it prevents than because I weigh the advantages it secures.

If anyone could point out a middle position between the complete independence and the complete subjection of public expression of opinion, and one that could actually be held, I should perhaps be inclined to adopt it. But the difficulty is to find such a position. Suppose you want to correct the abuses of an unlicensed press and restore the use of orderly language. You may begin by trying the offender before a jury. But if the jury acquits him, the opinion of a single individual becomes the opinion of the whole country. So far, then, too much has been done, and too little. If you go further, you must bring the offender before a court of permanent judges. But even there the case must be heard before it can be decided, and the very principles that no book would have dared to avow are proclaimed aloud in the pleadings. What was hinted at obscurely in a single work is then repeated in a multitude of other publications. The words in which a thought is expressed are only the body of the thought, not the idea itself. Tribunals may condemn the form, but the sense and spirit of the work are too subtle for their authority. Too much has been done to turn back, and too little to reach your goal, so you must go on. If you establish a censorship of the press, the public speaker will still be heard, and you have only made the mischief worse. The powers of thought do not depend, as physical strength does, on the number of their mechanical agents, and you cannot count a host of authors the way you count the troops of an army. On the contrary, the authority of a principle is often increased by how few men express it. The words of a strong-minded man, reaching into the passions of a listening assembly, have more power than the shouting of a thousand orators. And if free speech is allowed in any one public place, the result is the same as if it were allowed in every village. The liberty of speech must therefore be destroyed as well as the liberty of the press. That is the necessary end of your efforts. But if your aim was to repress the abuses of liberty, they have brought you to the feet of a despot. You have been driven from the extreme of independence to the extreme of subjection without finding a single position along the way where you could take shelter or rest.

Some nations have special reasons for valuing the liberty of the press, apart from the general motives I have just pointed out. In certain countries that claim to enjoy the privileges of freedom, every individual agent of the government can violate the laws with impunity, because those he oppresses cannot prosecute him before the courts of justice. In that case the liberty of the press is not merely a guarantee of the citizens’ liberty and security. It is the only guarantee they possess. If the rulers of such nations proposed to abolish the independence of the press, the people would be justified in saying: Give us the right to prosecute your offenses before the ordinary tribunals, and perhaps we may then give up our right to appeal to the tribunal of public opinion.

But in countries where the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people ostensibly prevails, the censorship of the press is not only dangerous but absurd. When the right of every citizen to share in governing society is acknowledged, every citizen must be presumed able to tell the different opinions of his contemporaries apart, and to weigh the different facts from which conclusions may be drawn. The sovereignty of the people and the liberty of the press may therefore be regarded as correlative institutions. In the same way, the censorship of the press and universal suffrage are two things that are irreconcilably opposed, and that cannot long be kept together among the institutions of the same people. Not one of the twelve million people who live in the territory of the United States has yet dared to propose any restriction on the liberty of the press. The first newspaper I looked at on arriving in America contained the following article:

In all this affair the language of Jackson has been that of a heartless despot, solely occupied with the preservation of his own authority. Ambition is his crime, and it will be his punishment too: intrigue is his native element, and intrigue will confound his tricks, and will deprive him of his power: he governs by means of corruption, and his immoral practices will redound to his shame and confusion. His conduct in the political arena has been that of a shameless and lawless gamester. He succeeded at the time, but the hour of retribution approaches, and he will be obliged to disgorge his winnings, to throw aside his false dice, and to end his days in some retirement, where he may curse his madness at his leisure; for repentance is a virtue with which his heart is likely to remain forever unacquainted.

Many people in France imagine that the virulence of the press comes from the uncertain social condition of the country, its political excitement, and the general sense of the evils that follow from them. They therefore suppose that once society has regained a certain calm, the press will give up its present vehemence. I am inclined to think that these causes explain the extraordinary ascendancy the press has gained over the nation, but that they have little influence on the tone of its language. The periodical press seems to me to be driven by passions and tendencies of its own, independent of the circumstances in which it is placed, and the present state of America confirms this view.

America is perhaps, at this moment, the country in the whole world with the fewest seeds of revolution. Yet the press there is no less destructive in its principles than in France, and it shows the same violence without the same grounds for indignation. In America, as in France, the press is a singular power, so strangely made up of good and evil that it is at once indispensable to the existence of freedom and almost incompatible with the maintenance of public order. Its power is certainly much greater in France than in the United States, though nothing is rarer in the United States than to hear of a prosecution brought against it. The reason is quite simple. Having once admitted the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people, the Americans apply it with perfect consistency. They never intended to found a permanent state of things out of elements that change every day. So there is nothing criminal in attacking the existing laws, provided the attack does not involve a violent breach of them. They also believe that courts of justice are unable to check the abuses of the press. The subtlety of human language constantly escapes the severity of judicial analysis, and offenses of this kind tend to slip out of the hand that tries to seize them. They hold that to act effectively on the press, one would have to find a tribunal that was not only devoted to the existing order of things but also able to overcome the influence of public opinion. It would have to conduct its proceedings without publicity, pronounce its decrees without giving its reasons, and punish an author’s intentions even more than his language. Anyone who had the power to create and maintain such a tribunal would waste his time prosecuting the liberty of the press, for he would be the absolute master of the whole community, and he would be as free to get rid of the authors as of their writings. On this question, then, there is no middle ground between servitude and extreme license. To enjoy the priceless benefits that the liberty of the press secures, one must submit to the unavoidable evils it produces. To expect to gain the benefits and escape the evils is to cherish one of those illusions that commonly mislead nations in their times of sickness, when, tired of faction and worn out by effort, they try to combine hostile opinions and contrary principles on the same soil.
The small influence of the American journals can be attributed to several causes, among them the following.

The liberty of writing, like every other liberty, is most formidable when it is new. A people that has never been used to sharing in the conduct of State affairs places complete confidence in the first popular leader who catches its attention. The Anglo-Americans have enjoyed this liberty since the founding of the settlements. Besides, the press cannot create human passions by its own power, however skillfully it may kindle them where they already exist. In America politics are discussed with animation and a great variety of activity, but they rarely touch the deep passions that are stirred whenever the real interest of part of the community is harmed. And in the United States the interests of the community are in a most prosperous condition. A single glance at a French newspaper and an American one is enough to show the difference between the two nations on this point. In France the space given to commercial advertisements is very limited, and the news is not extensive, but the most essential part of the paper is the discussion of the politics of the day. In America, three-quarters of the enormous sheet laid before the reader are filled with advertisements, and the rest is often taken up with political news or trivial anecdotes. Only from time to time does one find a corner devoted to the kind of passionate discussion with which the journalists of France are accustomed to indulge their readers.

Observation has shown, and the natural shrewdness of the pettiest as well as the greatest despots has discovered, that the influence of a power grows in proportion as its direction is made more central. In France the press combines two kinds of centralization. Almost all its power is concentrated in the same place and held in the same hands, for its organs are far from numerous. The influence of a press organized in this way, acting on a skeptical nation, must be unbounded. It is an enemy with which a government may sign an occasional truce, but which it is hard to resist for any length of time.

Neither of these kinds of centralization exists in America. The United States has no metropolis. The intelligence and the power of the country are scattered widely, and instead of radiating from one point, they cross one another in every direction. The Americans have set up no central control over the expression of opinion, any more than over the conduct of business. These circumstances do not depend on human foresight. But it is thanks to the laws of the Union that no licenses are granted to printers, that no securities are demanded from editors as in France, and that there is no stamp duty, as there is in France and as there once was in England. As a result, nothing is easier than to start a newspaper, and a small number of readers is enough to cover the editor’s expenses.

The number of periodical and occasional publications in the United States is truly beyond belief. The best-informed Americans attribute the limited influence of the press to this excessive multiplication. It is accepted as an axiom of political science in that country that the only way to neutralize the effect of public journals is to multiply them without limit. I cannot understand why a truth so self-evident has not already been more widely accepted in Europe. It is understandable that people who hope to bring about revolutions by means of the press should want to confine its action to a few powerful organs. But it is quite incredible that the supporters of the existing state of things, the natural defenders of the law, should try to reduce the influence of the press by concentrating its authority. The governments of Europe seem to treat the press with the courtesy of the knights of old. They are eager to give it the same central power that they have found to be such a trusty weapon, so as to increase the glory of their resistance to its attacks.

In America there is hardly a hamlet that does not have its own newspaper. It is easy to see that neither discipline nor unity of purpose can be imposed on so numerous and varied a host, and so each paper fights under its own banner. All the political journals of the United States are indeed lined up on the side of the administration or against it, but they attack and defend in a thousand different ways. They cannot succeed in forming those great currents of opinion that overwhelm the most solid obstacles. This division of the press’s influence produces a number of other consequences that are almost as remarkable. The ease with which journals can be started draws a multitude of people into them. But because the amount of competition rules out any considerable profit, the most distinguished classes of society are rarely drawn to these undertakings. Yet there are so many public prints that, even if they were a source of wealth, writers of ability could not be found to run them all. The journalists of the United States are usually in a very humble position, with little education and a vulgar turn of mind. The will of the majority is the most general of laws, and it establishes certain habits that form the characteristics of each particular class of society. In this way it dictates the etiquette practiced at courts and the etiquette of the bar. The French journalist is characterized by a violent, though often eloquent and lofty, manner of discussing the politics of the day, and exceptions to this habit are only occasional. The American journalist is characterized by an open and coarse appeal to the passions of the populace. He habitually abandons the principles of political science to attack the characters of individuals, to follow them into private life, and to expose all their weaknesses and faults.

Nothing can be more deplorable than this abuse of the powers of thought. I shall have occasion later to point out the influence of the newspapers on the taste and morality of the American people, but my present subject concerns only the political world. It cannot be denied that the effects of this extreme license of the press tend, indirectly, to maintain public order. People who already hold a high place in the esteem of their fellow citizens are afraid to write in the newspapers, and so they are deprived of the most powerful instrument they could use to stir up the passions of the multitude to their own advantage. *a

a [ They write in the papers only when they choose to address the people in their own name, as, for instance, when they are called on to repel slanderous charges and to correct a misstatement of facts.]

The personal opinions of the editors carry no weight at all in the eyes of the public. The only use of a journal is that it passes on knowledge of certain facts, and it is only by altering or distorting those facts that a journalist can do anything to support his own views.

But although the press is limited to these resources, its influence in America is immense. It is the power that drives the circulation of political life through every district of that vast territory. Its eye is always open to detect the secret springs of political designs and to summon the leaders of all parties before the bar of public opinion. It rallies the interests of the community around certain principles, and it draws up the creed that factions adopt. For it provides a means of communication between parties that hear and address one another without ever having been in direct contact. When a great number of the organs of the press take the same line, their influence becomes irresistible, and public opinion, when it is constantly attacked from the same side, eventually gives way. In the United States each separate journal has little authority, but the power of the periodical press is second only to that of the people. *b
b [ See Appendix, P.]
The opinions that take hold in the United States under the empire of the liberty of the press are often more firmly rooted than those formed elsewhere under the approval of a censor.

In the United States the democracy constantly raises new individuals to the conduct of public affairs, and so the measures of the administration are seldom governed by strict rules of consistency or order. But the general principles of the government are more stable, and the opinions most widespread in society are generally more durable than in many other countries. Once the Americans have taken up an idea, whether it is well founded or not, nothing is harder than to root it out of their minds. The same tenacity of opinion has been observed in England, where for the last century there has been more freedom of conscience, and more unshakable prejudice, than in all the other countries of Europe. I attribute this result to a cause that may at first sight seem to work in the opposite direction, namely the liberty of the press. Nations in which this liberty exists are as likely to cling to their opinions out of pride as out of conviction. They cherish them because they hold them to be just, and because they used their own free will in choosing them. They maintain them not only because they are true, but because they are their own. Several other reasons lead to the same result.

A man of genius once remarked that “ignorance lies at the two ends of knowledge.” It would perhaps have been more accurate to say that absolute convictions are found at the two extremes, and that doubt lies in the middle. For the human intellect may be considered in three distinct states, which often follow one another. A man believes without question, because he adopts a proposition without inquiry. He doubts as soon as he is confronted by the objections his inquiries may have raised. But he often succeeds in resolving these doubts, and then he begins to believe afresh. He no longer grasps a truth in its dimmest and most uncertain form. He sees it clearly before him, and he goes forward by the light it gives. *c
c [ It may, however, be doubted whether this rational and self-guiding conviction arouses as much fervor or enthusiastic devotion in men as their first dogmatic belief.]

When the liberty of the press acts on men in the first of these three states, it does not immediately disturb their habit of believing without question or investigation, but it constantly changes the objects of their intuitive convictions. The human mind continues to see only one point on the whole intellectual horizon, and that point is always moving. Such are the symptoms of sudden revolutions, and of the misfortunes that are sure to befall those generations that abruptly adopt unconditional freedom of the press.

The circle of new ideas, however, is soon exhausted. Experience has touched them, and the doubt and mistrust that their uncertainty produces become universal. We may be sure that most people will either believe without knowing why, or will not know what to believe. Few can ever hope to reach that state of rational and independent conviction that true knowledge can produce in spite of the attacks of doubt.

It has been observed that in times of great religious fervor men sometimes change their religious opinions, whereas in times of general skepticism everyone clings to his own persuasion. The same thing happens in politics under the liberty of the press. In countries where all the theories of social science have been contested in turn, the citizens who have adopted one of them stick to it, not so much because they are sure of its excellence as because they are not convinced that any other is better. In the present age men are not very ready to die in defense of their opinions, but they are rarely inclined to change them. There are fewer martyrs, and also fewer apostates.

Another and still stronger reason can be given. When no abstract opinions are regarded as certain, men cling to the mere inclinations and outward interests of their position, which are naturally more tangible and more lasting than any opinions in the world.

It is not an easy question whether aristocracy or democracy is better fitted to govern a country. But it is certain that democracy annoys one part of the community and that aristocracy oppresses another. When the question is reduced to the simple form of a struggle between poverty and wealth, the tendency of each side becomes perfectly clear without further debate.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Political Associations In The United States
paragraphs: No country in the world has made more successful use of the principle of association, or applied it more freely to so many different purposes, than America. Besides the permanent associations that the law establishes under the names of townships, cities, and counties, there are a great many others that private individuals form and maintain.

From earliest childhood, the citizen of the United States is taught to rely on his own efforts to resist the evils and difficulties of life. He regards social authority with mistrust and anxiety, and he asks for its help only when he cannot possibly manage without it. One can see this habit even in the schools, where children at play follow rules they have set for themselves and punish offenses they have defined themselves. The same spirit runs through every act of social life. Suppose a blockage occurs on a public road and traffic is held up. The neighbors at once form themselves into a deliberative body, and this improvised assembly produces an executive power that removes the obstruction before anyone has thought of turning to an authority higher than the people directly concerned. If public entertainment is at stake, an association is formed to provide for its splendor and good order. Societies are formed to fight enemies of a purely moral kind and to reduce the vice of intemperance. In the United States, associations are established to promote public order, commerce, industry, morality, and religion; for there is no goal that the human will, backed by the combined efforts of individuals, despairs of reaching.

Later I shall have occasion to show what effects association has on the course of society. For the present I must limit myself to the political world. Once the right of association is recognized, citizens may use it in several different ways.

An association consists simply of the public agreement that a number of individuals give to certain doctrines, and of their commitment to promote the spread of those doctrines by their efforts. The right of association in this sense is very close to the liberty of publishing without a license, but societies formed in this way have more authority than the press. When a society represents an opinion, that opinion necessarily takes a more exact and explicit form. It counts its supporters and binds their welfare to its cause. The supporters, for their part, come to know one another, and their zeal grows with their numbers. An association brings together the efforts of minds that tend to diverge and channels them in a single direction, driving them forcefully toward the one goal that it names.

The second degree of the right of association is the power to hold meetings. When an association is allowed to set up centers of action at certain important points in the country, its activity increases and its influence spreads. People have the chance to see one another, the means of carrying out their plans are more easily combined, and opinions are held with a warmth and energy that the written word cannot match.

Finally, the exercise of the right of political association has a third degree. The supporters of an opinion may unite in electoral bodies and choose delegates to represent them in a central assembly. This is, properly speaking, the representative system applied to a party.

Thus, in the first case, a society is formed among individuals who profess the same opinion, and the tie that holds it together is purely intellectual. In the second case, small assemblies are formed that represent only a fraction of the party. In the third case, finally, the party forms a separate nation within the nation, a government within the government. Its delegates, like the true delegates of the majority, represent the whole collective force of their party, and they enjoy something of the national dignity and great influence that belong to the people’s chosen representatives. It is true that they do not have the right to make laws, but they do have the power to attack the laws that exist and to draw up in advance those that they may later get adopted.

Suppose a people is not fully accustomed to the exercise of freedom, or is exposed to violent political passions. If a deliberating minority, which confines itself to considering future laws, is set alongside the legislative majority, I cannot help believing that public tranquility runs very great risks in that nation. There is no doubt a very wide difference between proving that one law is better in itself than another and proving that the first ought to replace the second. But the imagination of the common people easily overlooks this difference, which is so plain to thoughtful minds. It sometimes happens that a nation is divided into two nearly equal parties, each of which claims to represent the majority. If another power is set up right next to the governing power, and it has almost as much moral authority, it is not to be believed that it will be content for long to speak without acting. Nor is it to be believed that it will always be held back by the abstract consideration that associations exist to guide opinion but not to enforce it, to suggest laws but not to make them.

The more we consider the independence of the press in its main consequences, the more we are convinced that it is the chief element of freedom in the modern world, and, so to speak, the one that constitutes it. A nation determined to remain free is therefore right to demand that this independence be exercised without restraint. But unrestrained liberty of political association cannot be treated as entirely the same as liberty of the press. The one is at once less necessary and more dangerous than the other. A nation may limit it without giving up any part of its self-control, and it may sometimes be obliged to do so in order to maintain its own authority.
In America the liberty of association for political purposes is unlimited. An example will show most clearly how far this privilege is tolerated.

The question of the tariff, or of free trade, produced a great display of party feeling in America. The tariff was not only a subject of debate as a matter of opinion; it also had a favorable or harmful effect on several very powerful interests of the States. The North attributed a great part of its prosperity to this system, and the South all of its sufferings. As a result, for a long time the tariff was the only source of the political animosities that agitated the Union.

In 1831, when the dispute was raging with the greatest bitterness, a private citizen of Massachusetts used the newspapers to propose that all opponents of the tariff send delegates to Philadelphia, to consult together on the means best suited to promote freedom of trade. Thanks to the power of the printing press, this proposal spread from Maine to New Orleans within a few days. The opponents of the tariff adopted it with enthusiasm, meetings were held on all sides, and delegates were named. Most of these men were well known, and some had gained considerable fame. South Carolina alone, which afterwards took up arms in the same cause, sent sixty-three delegates. On October 1, 1831, this assembly, which in the American custom had taken the name of a Convention, met at Philadelphia. It had more than two hundred members. Its debates were public, and they took on a legislative character at once. The extent of the powers of Congress, the theories of free trade, and the various clauses of the tariff were discussed in turn. After ten days of deliberation the Convention broke up, having published an address to the American people, in which it declared:
I. That Congress had not the right of making a tariff, and that the existing tariff was unconstitutional;
II. That the prohibition of free trade was prejudicial to the interests of all nations, and to that of the American people in particular.

It must be admitted that unrestrained liberty of political association has not so far produced, in the United States, the fatal consequences that one might perhaps expect from it elsewhere. The right of association was brought over from England and has always existed in America, so that the exercise of this privilege is now blended with the manners and customs of the people. At the present time the liberty of association has become a necessary guarantee against the tyranny of the majority. In the United States, as soon as a party has become dominant, all public authority passes under its control. Its private supporters fill all the offices and have the whole force of the administration at their disposal. The most distinguished supporters of the other side cannot overcome the obstacles that keep them out of power. They therefore need some means of establishing themselves on their own footing and of setting the moral authority of the minority against the physical power that dominates it. Thus a dangerous expedient is used to ward off a still more formidable danger.

The omnipotence of the majority seems to me to pose such extreme perils to the American Republics that the dangerous measure used to check it appears to do more good than harm. And here I am about to put forward a proposition that may remind the reader of what I said earlier about municipal freedom. There are no countries where associations are more needed, to prevent the despotism of faction or the arbitrary power of a prince, than those that are democratically constituted. In aristocratic nations the body of the nobles and the wealthier part of the community are themselves natural associations, which act as checks on abuses of power. In countries where such associations do not exist, if private individuals cannot create an artificial and temporary substitute for them, I can imagine no lasting protection against the most galling tyranny. A great people may then be oppressed by a small faction, or by a single individual, with impunity.

The meeting of a great political Convention (for there are Conventions of every kind) may often become a necessary measure, but it is always a serious event, even in America. The sensible friends of the country never look forward to it without alarm. This was very noticeable in the Convention of 1831, where the efforts of all the most distinguished members of the Assembly tended to moderate its language and to keep the subjects it treated within certain limits. It is probable, in fact, that the Convention of 1831 had a very great influence on the minds of the malcontents and prepared them for the open revolt against the commercial laws of the Union that took place in 1832.

No one can deny that unrestrained liberty of association for political purposes is the privilege that takes a people longest to learn how to use. Even when it does not plunge the nation into anarchy, it keeps raising the chances of that disaster. On one point, however, this dangerous liberty protects against a different kind of danger: where associations are free, secret societies are unknown. In America there are numerous factions, but no conspiracies.
Different Ways in Which the Right of Association Is Understood in Europe and in the United States — Different Use Made of It.

After the right of acting for himself, the most natural privilege of man is to combine his efforts with those of his fellow creatures and to act in common with them. I am therefore led to conclude that the right of association is almost as inalienable as the right of personal liberty. No legislator can attack it without damaging the very foundations of society. Nevertheless, the liberty of association is a fruitful source of advantages and prosperity for some nations, but others may pervert it or carry it to excess, and what gives life may be turned into a source of destruction. It may perhaps be thought useful, both to governments and to parties, to compare the different methods that associations follow in countries where they are managed with discretion and in those where liberty degenerates into license.

Most Europeans look upon an association as a weapon, to be hastily forged and tried out at once in the fight. A society is formed for discussion, but the idea of coming action dominates the minds of its members. It is in fact an army, and the time given to talk serves to count its strength and rouse the courage of the host, after which it marches against the enemy. The resources that lie within the bounds of the law may occur to its members as means of success, but never as the only means.

This, however, is not how the right of association is understood in the United States. In America, the citizens who make up the minority associate, first, to show their numerical strength and so to weaken the moral authority of the majority. Second, they associate to stimulate rivalry and to discover the arguments best suited to influence the majority; for they always hope to win their opponents over to their side and then to use the supreme power in their name. Political associations in the United States are therefore peaceable in their intentions and strictly legal in the means they use. They claim, with perfect truth, that they aim at success only by lawful means.

The difference between the Americans and ourselves depends on several causes. In Europe there are many parties so completely opposed to the majority that they can never hope to gain its support, and at the same time they think they are strong enough in themselves to struggle and to defend their cause. When a party of this kind forms an association, its object is not to conquer but to fight. In America, those whose opinions are very much opposed to the majority’s are no obstacle at all to its power, and all other parties hope in the end to win it over to their own principles. The exercise of the right of association becomes dangerous in proportion to how impossible it is for great parties to gain the majority. In a country like the United States, where differences of opinion are mere differences of shade, the right of association may remain unrestrained without bad consequences. Many European nations are inexperienced in the enjoyment of liberty, and this leads them to see the liberty of association only as a right to attack the government. The first idea that occurs to a party, as to an individual, once it has become conscious of its own strength, is that of violence. The idea of persuasion comes later and is learned only from experience. The English, who are divided into parties that differ most essentially from one another, rarely abuse the right of association, because they have long been used to exercising it. In France the passion for war is so intense that there is no undertaking so mad, or so harmful to the welfare of the state, that a man does not consider himself honored to defend it at the risk of his life.

But perhaps the most powerful of the causes that tend to soften the excesses of political association in the United States is universal suffrage. In countries where universal suffrage exists, the majority is never in doubt, because neither party can claim to represent the part of the community that has not voted. The associations that are formed know, as does the nation at large, that they do not represent the majority. This is indeed a condition inseparable from their existence; for if they did represent the dominant power, they would change the law instead of asking for its reform. The consequence is that the moral influence of the government they attack is greatly increased, and their own power is greatly weakened.

In Europe there are few associations that do not claim to represent the majority, or that do not believe they represent it. This conviction or this claim tends to increase their force enormously, and it contributes no less to making their measures seem legitimate. Violence may seem excusable in defense of the cause of oppressed right. Thus it is, in the vast labyrinth of human laws, that extreme liberty sometimes corrects the abuses of license, and that extreme democracy averts the dangers of democratic government. In Europe, associations regard themselves, to some degree, as the legislative and executive councils of the people, who are unable to speak for themselves. In America, where they represent only a minority of the nation, they argue and they petition.

The means that the associations of Europe use match the end they want to reach. The main aim of these bodies is to act and not to debate, to fight rather than to persuade. They are therefore naturally led to adopt a form of organization that differs from the ordinary customs of civil bodies and takes on the habits and maxims of military life. They centralize the direction of their resources as much as possible, and they entrust the power of the whole party to a very small number of leaders.

The members of these associations answer to a watchword, like soldiers on duty. They profess the doctrine of passive obedience; or rather, in uniting together they at once give up the exercise of their own judgment and free will. The tyrannical control these societies exercise is often far more unbearable than the authority that the government they attack holds over society. Such excesses greatly reduce their moral force, and they lose the powerful interest that a struggle between oppressors and oppressed always arouses. A man who in certain cases agrees to obey his fellows servilely, and who submits his activity and even his opinions to their control, can have no claim to be called a free citizen.

The Americans have also established certain forms of government for their associations, but these are invariably borrowed from the forms of civil administration. The independence of each individual is formally recognized. The members of the association tend toward the same end, as they do in the community at large, but they are not obliged to follow the same path. No one gives up the exercise of his reason and his free will, but everyone uses that reason and that will for the benefit of a common undertaking.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — Government Of The Democracy In America
paragraphs: I am well aware of the difficulties this part of my subject involves. Every statement I am about to make may clash, on some point or other, with the feelings of the different parties that divide my country. Even so, I will speak my mind with complete openness.

In Europe we have trouble judging the true character and the more lasting tendencies of democracy, because two opposing principles exist side by side there, and we cannot tell what belongs to the principles themselves and what to the passions they set against each other. America is different. There the people rules without any obstacle, with no dangers to fear and no injuries to avenge. In America democracy follows its own free inclinations; its course is natural and its activity unrestrained. The United States therefore offers the best opportunity for studying its real character. And no people has a more vital interest in this inquiry than the French nation, which is driven blindly onward by a daily, irresistible impulse toward a state of things that may turn out despotic or republican, but will certainly be democratic.

I have already noted that universal suffrage has been adopted in all the States of the Union. It therefore operates among populations that hold very different positions on the social scale. I have had the chance to observe its effects in different places, and among peoples who are almost strangers to one another in language, religion, and way of life: in Louisiana as in New England, in Georgia and in Canada. I have noticed that universal suffrage is far from producing in America either all the good or all the evil consequences that people in Europe assign to it, and that its effects differ very widely from those usually attributed to it.
Choice of the People, and Instinctive Preferences of the American Democracy

In the United States the ablest men are rarely placed at the head of affairs — The reason for this peculiarity — The envy that the lower orders of France feel toward the higher classes is not a French sentiment but a purely democratic one — Why the most distinguished men in America so often withdraw from public affairs.

Many people in Europe tend to believe without saying so, or to say without believing, that one of the great advantages of universal suffrage is that it puts the direction of public affairs in the hands of men who deserve the public’s confidence. They admit that the people cannot govern itself, but they assert that it is always sincerely disposed to promote the welfare of the state, and that it instinctively picks out those who share its good intentions and are best fit to hold supreme authority. I confess that what I observed in America does not agree with these opinions at all. When I arrived in the United States I was surprised to find so much distinguished talent among the governed and so little among the heads of the government. It is a well-established fact that today the ablest men in the United States are very rarely placed at the head of affairs, and it must be acknowledged that this has come about as democracy has overstepped all its former limits. The breed of American statesmen has clearly declined remarkably over the last fifty years.

Several causes may explain this phenomenon. No matter how great the effort, it is impossible to raise the intelligence of the people above a certain level. However easy it becomes to acquire information, however many simple methods and cheap forms of knowledge are on offer, the human mind can never be instructed and educated without devoting a considerable amount of time to those goals.

The greater or lesser possibility of living without labor is therefore the necessary boundary of intellectual improvement. This boundary lies farther off in some countries and closer in others, but it must exist somewhere as long as the people must work to obtain the means of physical subsistence — that is, as long as it keeps its popular character. It is therefore just as hard to imagine a State in which all the citizens are very well informed as one in which they are all wealthy; the two difficulties may be seen as correlative. It is easy to grant that the mass of citizens sincerely want to promote the welfare of their country. Indeed, one may even allow that the lower classes are less swayed by considerations of personal interest than the higher orders. But it is always more or less impossible for them to discern the best means of reaching the end they sincerely desire. Long and patient observation, together with a multitude of different ideas, is needed to form a just estimate of the character of a single individual. Can we suppose that the common people can succeed in an inquiry that misleads even the penetration of genius? The people has neither the time nor the means that an investigation of this kind requires; it forms its conclusions hastily, from a superficial look at the most prominent features of a question. Hence it often goes along with the clamor of a charlatan who knows the secret of stimulating its tastes, while its truest friends frequently fail in their efforts.

Moreover, democracy lacks not only the soundness of judgment needed to select men who really deserve its confidence; it also has neither the desire nor the inclination to find them. It cannot be denied that democratic institutions have a very strong tendency to foster the feeling of envy in the human heart. This is not so much because they give everyone the means of rising to the level of any fellow citizen, as because those means perpetually disappoint the people who use them. Democratic institutions awaken and nourish a passion for equality that they can never entirely satisfy. Complete equality slips out of the people’s grasp at the very moment it thinks it has caught it, and “flies,” as Pascal says, “with eternal flight.” The people is excited by the pursuit of an advantage that is all the more precious because it is neither remote enough to be unknown nor near enough to be enjoyed. The lower orders are stirred by the chance of success and irritated by its uncertainty. They pass from the enthusiasm of pursuit to the exhaustion of failure, and finally to the bitterness of disappointment. Whatever rises above their own level appears to them an obstacle to their desires, and there is no kind of superiority, however legitimate, that they do not find irksome.

It has been supposed that the secret instinct that leads the lower orders to keep their superiors as far as possible from the direction of public affairs is peculiar to France. This is an error. The tendency I mean belongs not to any particular nation but to democratic institutions in general. Special political circumstances may have heightened it, but it comes from a deeper cause.

In the United States the people is not inclined to hate the superior classes of society, but it is not very favorably disposed toward them either, and it carefully excludes them from the exercise of authority. It does not fear distinguished talents, but it is rarely captivated by them, and it gives its approval very sparingly to those who have risen without popular support.

While the natural tendencies of democracy lead the people to reject the most distinguished citizens as its rulers, those citizens are just as inclined to withdraw from a political career in which it is almost impossible to keep one’s independence or to advance without degrading oneself. Chancellor Kent has stated this view very frankly. Speaking with great praise of that part of the Constitution which empowers the Executive to nominate the judges, he says: “It is indeed probable that the men who are best fitted to discharge the duties of this high office would have too much reserve in their manners, and too much austerity in their principles, for them to be returned by the majority at an election where universal suffrage is adopted.” Such were the opinions printed without contradiction in America in the year 1830!
I consider it sufficiently demonstrated that universal suffrage is by no means a guarantee of wisdom in the people’s choice, and that, whatever its advantages may be, this is not one of them.

Causes Which May Partly Correct These Tendencies of the Democracy — Great dangers have opposite effects on peoples and on individuals — Why so many distinguished men stood at the head of affairs in America fifty years ago — The influence that the intelligence and the customs of the people exercise on its choice — The example of New England — The States of the Southwest — The influence of certain laws on the people’s choice — Election by an elected body — Its effect on the composition of the Senate.

When a State is threatened by serious dangers, the people often succeeds in choosing the citizens best able to save it. It has been observed that people rarely stay at their usual level when facing very critical circumstances: they rise above their ordinary condition or sink below it, and the same happens to whole nations. Extreme perils sometimes quench a people’s energy instead of stimulating it; they excite its passions without directing them, and instead of clearing its perception they confuse it. The Jews flooded the smoking ruins of their temple with the slaughter of the remnant of their army. But it is more common, for nations as for individuals, to see extraordinary virtues arise from the very nearness of danger. Great characters then stand out, as buildings hidden by the darkness of night are lit up by the glare of a fire. In those dangerous times genius no longer holds back from entering the arena, and the people, alarmed by the perils of its situation, buries its envious passions in a brief oblivion. Great names may then come out of the ballot box.

I have already observed that the American statesmen of today are far inferior to those who stood at the head of affairs fifty years ago. This is as much a result of circumstances as of the country’s laws. When America was struggling in the high cause of independence to throw off the yoke of another country, and was about to usher a new nation into the world, the spirits of its inhabitants were raised to the height that their great efforts required. In this general excitement the most distinguished men were ready to anticipate the community’s needs, and the people clung to them for support and placed them at its head. But events of this magnitude are rare, and our judgment must be formed from the ordinary course of affairs.

If passing events sometimes act as a check on the passions of democracy, the intelligence and the customs of the community exercise an influence that is no less powerful and far more lasting. This is extremely noticeable in the United States.

In New England the education and the liberties of the communities grew out of the moral and religious principles of their founders. Where society has gained enough stability to hold certain maxims and keep settled habits, the lower orders are accustomed to respect intellectual superiority and to submit to it without complaint, although they disregard all the privileges that wealth and birth have introduced among human beings. The democracy in New England therefore chooses more judiciously than it does elsewhere.

But as we move toward the South, to those States where the constitution of society is more recent and less firm, where education is less widespread, and where the principles of morality, religion, and liberty are less happily combined, we see the talents and virtues of those in authority growing steadily rarer.

Finally, when we reach the new Southwestern States, where the constitution of society dates only from yesterday and consists of a jumble of adventurers and speculators, we are amazed at the people who hold public authority. We are led to ask what force, independent of the legislation and of the men who direct it, can protect the State and make society flourish.

There are, however, certain laws of a democratic nature that help to correct, to some extent, the dangerous tendencies of democracy. On entering the House of Representatives in Washington, one is struck by the unrefined demeanor of that great assembly. The eye often fails to find a famous man within its walls. Its members are almost all obscure individuals whose names call nothing to mind: they are mostly village lawyers, tradesmen, or even people from the lower classes of society. In a country where education is very widespread, it is said that the people’s representatives do not always know how to write correctly.

A few yards from this spot is the door of the Senate, which holds within a small space a large share of the celebrated men of America. Hardly anyone in it fails to bring to mind an active and illustrious career. The Senate is made up of eloquent advocates, distinguished generals, wise magistrates, and statesmen of note, whose speeches would at any time do honor to the most remarkable parliamentary debates in Europe.

What, then, causes this strange contrast, and why are the ablest citizens found in one assembly rather than the other? Why is the first body remarkable for its lack of refinement and its poverty of talent, while the second seems to have a monopoly on intelligence and sound judgment? Both assemblies come from the people; both are chosen by universal suffrage; and no one in America has so far claimed that the Senate is hostile to the interests of the people. What, then, causes so startling a difference? The only reason that seems to me an adequate explanation is that the House of Representatives is elected directly by the populace, while the Senate is elected by elected bodies. The whole body of citizens names the legislature of each State, and the Federal Constitution turns these legislatures into so many electoral bodies, which choose the members of the Senate. Senators are thus elected by an indirect application of universal suffrage. The legislatures that name them are not aristocratic or privileged bodies exercising the vote in their own right; they are chosen by the totality of the citizens, they are generally elected every year, and new members can constantly be chosen who will use their electoral rights in accordance with the wishes of the public. But passing the people’s authority through an assembly of chosen men makes an important change in it, by refining its judgment and improving the forms it takes. Men chosen in this way accurately represent the majority of the nation that governs them, but they represent the elevated thoughts current in the community and the tendencies that prompt its nobler actions, rather than the petty passions that disturb it or the vices that disgrace it.

We can already foresee the time when the American Republics will have to use the plan of election by an elected body more often in their system of representation, or else run no small risk of perishing miserably on the shoals of democracy.

And here I have no hesitation in confessing that I regard this particular system of election as the only means of bringing the exercise of political power within reach of all classes of the people. Those thinkers who see this institution as the exclusive weapon of one party, and those who on the other hand fear to use it, seem to me to make an equally great error in either case.
Influence Which the American Democracy Has Exercised on the Laws Relating to Elections

When elections are rare, they expose the State to a violent crisis — When they are frequent, they keep up a degree of feverish excitement — The Americans have preferred the second of these two evils — Mutability of the laws — The opinions of Hamilton and Jefferson on this subject.

When elections recur at long intervals, the State is exposed to violent agitation each time they take place. Parties strain every nerve to win a prize so rarely within their reach, and since the harm is almost irreparable for the candidates who fail, the consequences of their disappointed ambition may prove disastrous. If, on the other hand, the legal struggle can be repeated within a short time, the defeated parties are patient. But when elections occur frequently, their recurrence keeps society in a perpetual state of feverish excitement and gives public affairs a constant instability.

Thus, on the one hand, the State is exposed to the perils of revolution, and on the other to perpetual change. The first system threatens the very existence of the government; the second is an obstacle to any steady and consistent policy. The Americans have preferred the second of these evils to the first. But instinct led them to this conclusion much more than reason did, for a taste for variety is one of the characteristic passions of democracy. In this way an extraordinary mutability has been introduced into their legislation. Many Americans regard the instability of their laws as a necessary consequence of a system whose general results are beneficial. But no one in the United States pretends to deny that this instability exists, or to argue that it is not a great evil.

After demonstrating the usefulness of a power that could prevent, or at least impede, the passing of bad laws, Hamilton adds: “It might perhaps be said that the power of preventing bad laws includes that of preventing good ones, and may be used to the one purpose as well as to the other. But this objection will have little weight with those who can properly estimate the mischiefs of that inconstancy and mutability in the laws which form the greatest blemish in the character and genius of our governments.” (Federalist, No. 73.) And again, in No. 62 of the same work, he observes: “The facility and excess of law-making seem to be the diseases to which our governments are most liable. . . . The mischievous effects of the mutability in the public councils arising from a rapid succession of new members would fill a volume: every new election in the States is found to change one-half of the representatives. From this change of men must proceed a change of opinions and of measures, which forfeits the respect and confidence of other nations, poisons the blessings of liberty itself, and diminishes the attachment and reverence of the people toward a political system which betrays so many marks of infirmity.”

Jefferson himself, the greatest Democrat that the democracy of America has yet produced, pointed out the same evils. “The instability of our laws,” he said in a letter to Madison, “is really a very serious inconvenience. I think that we ought to have obviated it by deciding that a whole year should always be allowed to elapse between the bringing in of a bill and the final passing of it. It should afterward be discussed and put to the vote without the possibility of making any alteration in it; and if the circumstances of the case required a more speedy decision, the question should not be decided by a simple majority, but by a majority of at least two-thirds of both houses.”

Public Officers Under the Control of the Democracy in America — The simple exterior of American public officers — No official costume — All public officers are paid — Political consequences of this system — No public career exists in America — The result of this.

Public officers in the United States mingle with the crowd of citizens; they have no palaces, no guards, and no ceremonial costumes. This simple exterior of the people in authority is connected not only with peculiarities of the American character but with the fundamental principles of that society. In the democracy’s view, a government is not a benefit but a necessary evil. Public officers must be granted a certain degree of power, for they would be of no use without it. But the outward show of authority is by no means indispensable to the conduct of affairs, and it needlessly offends the sensibilities of the public.
