The officers themselves know well that they enjoy their superiority over their fellow citizens, which comes from their authority, only on condition of putting themselves on a level with the whole community through their manners. A public officer in the United States is invariably civil, accessible to everyone, attentive to all requests, and obliging in his replies. I was pleased by these features of a democratic government, and I was struck by the manly independence of the citizens, who respect the office more than the officer and are less attached to the emblems of authority than to the man who bears them.

I am inclined to believe that the influence costumes really have, in an age like ours, has been greatly exaggerated. I never noticed that a public officer in America was any less respected while discharging his duties because nothing external set off his own merit. On the other hand, it is very doubtful that a special dress contributes to the respect public figures ought to have for their own positions, at least when they are not otherwise inclined to respect them. When a magistrate (and in France such cases are not rare) indulges his petty wit at the prisoner’s expense, or mocks the plight of an offender, it would be good to strip him of his robes of office and see whether he recalls some part of the natural dignity of mankind once he is reduced to the clothes of a private citizen.

A democracy may, however, allow a certain show of magisterial pomp and dress its officers in silk and gold without seriously compromising its principles. Privileges of this kind are temporary; they belong to the position and are distinct from the individual. But if public officers are not uniformly paid by the State, public duties must be entrusted to men of wealth and independence, who form the basis of an aristocracy; and if the people still keeps its right of election, that election can only be made from a certain class of citizens. When a democratic republic makes unpaid the offices that were formerly paid, we may safely believe that the State is moving toward monarchical institutions. And when a monarchy begins to pay officers who had until then been unpaid, it is a sure sign that it is approaching a despotic or a republican form of government. In my opinion, the substitution of paid for unpaid officials is in itself enough to constitute a serious revolution.

I regard the complete absence of unpaid officials in America as one of the most prominent signs of the absolute dominion that democracy exercises there. All public services, of whatever kind, are paid, so that everyone has not merely the right but also the means to perform them. Although in democratic States all citizens are qualified to hold positions in the government, not all are tempted to seek them. The number and abilities of the candidates are more likely to limit the electors’ choice than any conditions attached to candidacy.

In nations where the principle of election extends to every office in the State, no political career can properly be said to exist. Men are promoted as if by chance to the rank they hold, and they are by no means sure of keeping it. The consequence is that in tranquil times public offices offer few lures to ambition. In the United States the people who engage in the perplexities of political life are individuals of very moderate pretensions. The pursuit of wealth generally diverts men of great talents and great passions from the pursuit of power, and it very often happens that a man does not undertake to direct the fortunes of the State until he has found that he is incompetent to manage his own affairs. The vast number of very ordinary men in public office is as much due to these causes as to the democracy’s bad choices. In the United States I am not sure the people would elect men of superior abilities who sought its support, but it is certain that men of this kind do not come forward.
Arbitrary Power of Magistrates Under the Rule of the American Democracy
For what reason the arbitrary power of magistrates is greater in absolute monarchies and in democratic republics than in limited monarchies — The arbitrary power of the magistrates in New England.

In two different kinds of government the magistrates *a exercise a considerable degree of arbitrary power: under the absolute government of a single individual, and under that of a democracy. Nearly analogous causes produce this identical result.
a [ I use the word magistrates here in the widest sense it can have; I apply it to all the officers who are entrusted with the execution of the laws.]

In despotic States no citizen’s fortune is secure, and public officers are no safer than private individuals. The sovereign, who has under his control the lives, the property, and sometimes the honor of the men he employs, does not hesitate to give them great latitude of action, because he is convinced they will not use it against him. In despotic States the sovereign is so attached to the exercise of his power that he dislikes the constraint even of his own regulations, and he is quite content for his agents to follow a somewhat haphazard line of conduct, provided he is certain that their actions will never run counter to his wishes.

In democracies, since the majority has the right every year to remove from power the officers it has appointed, it has no reason to fear any abuse of their authority. Since the people can always make its wishes known to those who conduct the government, it prefers to leave them to make their own efforts rather than prescribe an invariable rule of conduct that would hamper both their activity and the people’s authority.

It may even be observed, on careful consideration, that under the rule of a democracy the arbitrary power of the magistrate must be still greater than in despotic States. In a despotic State the sovereign has the power to punish all the faults he learns of, but it would be vain for him to hope to learn of all those that are committed. In a democracy the sovereign power is not only supreme but present everywhere. American officials are, in fact, much more independent within the sphere of action the law marks out for them than any public officer in Europe. Very often they are simply told the object they are to accomplish, and the choice of means is left to their own discretion.

In New England, for instance, the selectmen of each township are required to draw up the list of persons who are to serve on the jury. The only rule laid down to guide their choice is that they must select citizens who have the right to vote and enjoy a fair reputation. *b In France the lives and liberties of the subjects would be thought endangered if a public officer of any kind were entrusted with so formidable a right. In New England the same magistrates are empowered to post the names of habitual drunkards in public houses and to forbid the inhabitants of the township from supplying them with liquor. *c Even the population of the most absolute monarchies would find a censorial power of this extreme kind revolting; here, however, it is accepted without difficulty.
b [ See the Act of February 27, 1813. “General Collection of the Laws of Massachusetts,” vol. ii. p. 331. It should be added that the jurors are afterward chosen by lot from these lists.]
c [ See Act of February 28, 1787. “General Collection of the Laws of Massachusetts,” vol. i. p. 302.]

Nowhere has so much been left by law to the arbitrary judgment of the magistrate as in democratic republics, because this arbitrary power brings no alarming consequences. It may even be said that the magistrate’s freedom grows as the right to vote is extended and as terms of office are shortened. Hence the great difficulty of converting a democratic republic into a monarchy. The magistrate stops being elected, but he keeps the rights and habits of an elected officer, which lead directly to despotism.

It is only in limited monarchies that the law, which prescribes the sphere in which public officers are to act, supervises all their measures. The reason is easy to see. In limited monarchies power is divided between the King and the people, and both have an interest in the stability of the magistrate. The King does not venture to place public officers under the people’s control, for fear they might be tempted to betray his interests. On the other hand, the people fears that if the magistrates were wholly dependent on the Crown, they might serve to oppress the country’s liberties. They cannot therefore be said to depend on either one or the other. The same cause that leads the king and the people to make public officers independent suggests the need for safeguards that keep that independence from encroaching on the authority of the former and the liberties of the latter. They therefore agree on the need to restrict the official to a line of conduct laid down in advance, and they both have an interest in confining him by certain regulations he cannot evade.
Instability of the Administration in the United States

In America the public acts of a community often leave fewer traces than the events of a family — Newspapers the only historical remains — The instability of the administration is harmful to the art of government.

Public men in America hold authority so briefly, and are so quickly lost again in the ever-changing population, that the acts of a community often leave fewer traces than the events of a private family. The public administration is, so to speak, oral and handed down by word of mouth. Little is written down, and that little is carried off forever by the slightest breeze, like the leaves of the Sibyl.

The only historical remains in the United States are the newspapers, but if one issue is missing, the chain of time is broken and the present is cut off from the past. I am convinced that in fifty years it will be harder to collect authentic documents about the social condition of Americans today than it is to find remains of the administration of France in the Middle Ages. And if the United States were ever invaded by barbarians, it would be necessary to turn to the history of other nations to learn anything about the people who now live there.

The instability of the administration has worked its way into the habits of the people. It even seems to suit the general taste, and no one cares what happened before his time. No methodical system is followed; no archives are kept; and no documents are gathered even when it would be very easy to do so. Where they exist, little store is set by them, and I have among my papers several original public documents that were given to me in answer to some of my inquiries. In America society seems to live from hand to mouth, like an army in the field. Nevertheless, the art of administration may undoubtedly be ranked as a science, and no science can be improved unless the discoveries and observations of successive generations are connected in the order in which they occur. One man, in the short span of his life, notices a fact; another conceives an idea; the first invents a means of carrying it out, the second reduces a truth to a fixed proposition; and mankind gathers the fruits of individual experience along its way and gradually builds up the sciences. But the people who conduct the administration in America can seldom teach each other anything, and when they take over the direction of society, they have only those attainments most widely spread in the community and no experience of their own. Democracy carried to its furthest limits is therefore harmful to the art of government, and for this reason it suits a people already practiced in administration better than a nation new to public affairs.

This remark, indeed, is not limited to the science of administration. Although a democratic government is founded on a very simple and natural principle, it always presupposes a high degree of culture and enlightenment in society. *d At first glance one might imagine it belongs to the earliest ages of the world, but closer observation will convince us that it could only come last in the sequence of human history.
d [ It hardly needs saying that I speak here of the democratic form of government as applied to a people, not merely to a tribe.]
Charges Levied by the State Under the Rule of the American Democracy

In all communities citizens can be divided into three classes — The habits of each class in directing public finances — Why public expenditure must tend to increase when the people governs — What makes the extravagance of a democracy less to be feared in America — Public expenditure under a democracy.

Before we can say whether a democratic form of government is economical or not, we must establish a suitable standard of comparison. The question would be easy to settle if we compared a democratic republic with an absolute monarchy. Public expenditure would turn out to be greater under the former than under the latter; this is true of all free States compared with those that are not free. It is certain that despotism ruins individuals by preventing them from producing wealth much more than by taking away the wealth they have produced; it dries up the source of riches while it usually respects acquired property. Freedom, on the contrary, produces far more benefits than it destroys, and nations favored with free institutions invariably find that their resources grow even faster than their taxes.
My present object is to compare free nations with one another and to point out the influence of democracy on the finances of a State.

Communities, like organic bodies, are subject to certain fixed rules in their formation that they cannot evade. They are made up of certain elements that are common to them at all times and in all circumstances. The people may always be mentally divided into three distinct classes. The first class consists of the wealthy; the second, of those in easy circumstances; and the third, of those who have little or no property and who live chiefly by the work they do for the two upper orders. The proportion of individuals in these three divisions may vary with the condition of society, but the divisions themselves can never be erased.

It is evident that each of these classes will exert, on the administration of the State’s finances, an influence peculiar to its own tendencies. If the first of the three holds the legislative power exclusively, it is likely to be free with public funds, because taxes levied on a large fortune only reduce the amount of superfluous enjoyment and are, in fact, little felt. If the second class has the power of making laws, it will certainly not be lavish with taxes, because nothing is so burdensome as a heavy tax levied on a small income. The government of the middle classes seems to me the most economical of free governments, though perhaps not the most enlightened and certainly not the most generous.

But let us now suppose that legislative authority is vested in the lowest orders. Two striking reasons show that expenditure will tend to increase, not decrease. Since the great majority of those who make the laws own no property that can be taxed, all the money spent for the community appears to be spent to their advantage, at no cost to themselves; and those who do own some small property readily find ways to arrange the taxes so that they burden the wealthy and benefit the poor, whereas the rich cannot take the same advantage when they are in possession of the government.

In countries where the poor *e alone hold the power to make the laws, no great economy in public spending should be expected. That spending will always be considerable, either because the taxes do not fall on those who impose them, or because they are laid in such a way as not to fall on those classes. In other words, the government of the democracy is the only kind of government in which the power that imposes taxes escapes paying them.

e [ The word poor is used here, and throughout the rest of this chapter, in a relative sense, not an absolute one. Poor men in America would often look rich beside the poor of Europe, but they may rightly be called poor in comparison with their wealthier countrymen.]

It may be objected (though the argument carries no real weight) that the true interest of the people is inseparably tied to that of the wealthier part of the community, since the people cannot help suffering from the harsh measures it adopts. But is it not in the true interest of kings to make their subjects happy, and in the true interest of nobles to admit new members into their order on reasonable terms? If distant advantages could prevail over the passions and pressures of the moment, there could never be a tyrannical sovereign or an exclusive aristocracy.

It may also be objected that the poor are never given the sole power of making the laws. I reply that wherever universal suffrage has been established, the majority of the community unquestionably holds the legislative authority. If it is shown that the poor always make up the majority, it may be added, with perfect truth, that in countries where they have the right to vote they hold the sole power of making laws. But it is certain that in every nation of the world the greater number has always consisted of people who own no property, or whose property is too small to spare them the need to work in order to live in modest comfort. Universal suffrage therefore does, in point of fact, place the government of society in the hands of the poor.

The harm that popular authority may sometimes do to the finances of a State was plainly visible in some of the democratic republics of antiquity, where the public treasury was drained to relieve needy citizens or to pay for the games and theatrical entertainments of the populace. It is true that the representative system was then very imperfectly understood, and that today popular passion is less felt in the conduct of public affairs. Still, it may be believed that the delegate will in the end conform to the principles of his constituents, and will indulge their inclinations as much as their interests.

The extravagance of democracy, however, is less to be feared the more the people acquire a share of property. On one hand, the contributions of the rich are then less needed; on the other, it is harder to lay on taxes that do not affect the interests of the lower classes. For this reason universal suffrage would be less dangerous in France than in England, because in England the property on which taxes may be levied is held by fewer hands. America, where the great majority of citizens own some fortune, is in a still more favorable position than France.

There are further causes that may increase public expenditure in democratic countries. When an aristocracy governs, the individuals who run the affairs of State are spared every kind of privation by their own place in society. They are content with their position; power and renown are what they strive for. Because they stand far above the more obscure mass of citizens, they do not always clearly see how the well-being of the people at large should add to their own honor. They are not indeed unfeeling toward the sufferings of the poor, but they cannot feel those miseries as keenly as if they shared them. As long as the people appear to accept their lot, the rulers are satisfied, and they ask nothing more of the government. An aristocracy is more concerned with how to keep its influence than with how to improve its condition.

When, on the contrary, the people hold supreme authority, the constant awareness of their own miseries drives the rulers of society to seek constant improvements. A thousand different things are put up for improvement; the most trivial details are sought out as open to amendment; and changes that involve considerable expense are especially pressed, since the aim is to make life more bearable for the poor, who cannot pay for themselves.
Moreover, all democratic communities are stirred by a vague excitement and a kind of feverish impatience, which give rise to a multitude of innovations, almost all of which cost money.

In monarchies and aristocracies, the rulers’ natural taste for power and renown is spurred on by ambition, and these temptations often push them into very costly undertakings. In democracies, where the rulers suffer privations, they can be won over only by means that improve their well-being, and such improvements cannot happen without spending money. When a people begins to reflect on its situation, it discovers a multitude of wants it had not felt before, and to satisfy these needs it must turn to the coffers of the State. Hence public charges grow as civilization spreads, and taxes are raised as knowledge pervades the community.

The last cause that often makes a democratic government dearer than any other is that a democracy does not always succeed in moderating its expenditure, because it does not understand the art of economy. Its plans are frequently changed, and the agents who carry them out are removed still more often, so its undertakings are often badly managed or left unfinished. In the first case the State spends sums out of all proportion to the goal it has set; in the second, the expense itself brings no return. *f

f [ The gross receipts of the Treasury of the United States in 1832 were about $28,000,000; in 1870 they had risen to $411,000,000. The gross expenditure in 1832 was $30,000,000; in 1870, $309,000,000.]
Tendencies of the American Democracy as Regards the Salaries of Public Officers

In democracies those who set high salaries have no chance of profiting by them — Tendency of the American democracy to raise the salaries of subordinate officers and to lower those of the more important officials — Reason for this — Comparison of the salaries of public officers in the United States and in France.

There is a powerful reason that usually leads democracies to economize on the salaries of public officers. In democratic countries the number of citizens who pay out the remuneration is extremely large, while the number of persons who can hope to benefit from receiving it is comparatively small. In aristocratic countries, on the contrary, the individuals who fix high salaries almost always have a vague hope of profiting by them. These appointments may be seen as capital they create for their own use, or at least as a resource for their children.

It must, however, be admitted that a democratic State is most stingy toward its principal agents. In America the secondary officers are much better paid, and the dignitaries of the administration much worse paid, than anywhere else.

The two opposite effects come from one cause. In both cases the people fixes the pay of public officers, and it measures that pay by its own needs. People think it only fair that the servants of the public should live as comfortably as the public itself. *g When the question turns to the pay of the great officers of State, however, that rule breaks down, and the popular decision is left to chance. The poor have no real idea of the needs that people in the higher classes may feel. A sum that looks small to the rich looks enormous to a poor man whose needs stop at the bare necessities of life; to him the Governor of a State, on his twelve or fifteen hundred dollars a year, is a lucky and enviable person. *h Try to persuade him that the representative of a great people ought to be able to keep up some show of splendor before foreign nations, and he may perhaps grant the point. But then he thinks of his own humble dwelling and of the hard-won earnings of his weary labor. He remembers everything he could do with a salary you call inadequate, and the sight of such uncommon wealth startles him and almost frightens him. Besides, the secondary public officer stands almost on a level with the people, while the others stand above it. The first may therefore win his interest, but the second begins to stir his envy.

g [ The comfortable circumstances of secondary officials in the United States also result from another cause, which is independent of the general tendencies of democracy. Every kind of private business is very lucrative, and the state would not be served at all if it did not pay its servants. The country is in the position of a commercial enterprise that is obliged to sustain costly competition, in spite of its taste for economy.]
h [ The State of Ohio, which has a million inhabitants, gives its Governor a salary of only $1,200 a year.]
This shows very clearly in the United States, where pay seems to fall as the authority of the people who receive it rises *i

Under the rule of an aristocracy, on the contrary, it often happens that while the high officers receive munificent salaries, the inferior ones have barely enough to procure the necessities of life. The reason is easy to find, in causes very similar to those I have just mentioned. If a democracy cannot imagine the pleasures of the rich, or watch them without envy, an aristocracy is slow to understand the privations of the poor — or, to speak more correctly, knows nothing of them. The poor man is not (if we use the term properly) the fellow of the rich one; he is a being of another kind. An aristocracy is therefore apt to care little about the fate of its subordinate agents, and their salaries are raised only when they refuse to do their work for too scanty a payment.

It is the stinginess of democracy toward its principal officers that has given rise to a belief that it is far more economical than it really is. It is true that democracy scarcely allows the individuals who conduct its affairs the means of an honorable living; but enormous sums are lavished to meet the needs of the people or to make their enjoyments easier. *j The money raised by taxation may be better spent, but it is not saved. In general, democracy gives generously to the community and very sparingly to those who govern it. The reverse is the case in aristocratic countries, where the money of the State is spent for the profit of the persons at the head of affairs.

In 1830 the State of New York had only 1,900,000 inhabitants, which is no more than double the population of the Department du Nord in France.]
Difficulty of Distinguishing the Causes Which Contribute to the Economy of the American Government

We are liable to frequent errors in researching the facts that have a serious influence on the fate of mankind, since nothing is more difficult than to appreciate their real value. One people is naturally inconsistent and enthusiastic; another is sober and calculating. These characteristics originate in their physical constitution or in remote causes we do not know.

Some nations are fond of display and the bustle of festivity, and do not regret the costly pleasures of an hour. Others, on the contrary, are attached to quieter pleasures, and seem almost ashamed of appearing to be pleased. In some countries the highest value is set on the beauty of public buildings; in others works of art are treated with indifference, and everything unproductive is looked down on with contempt. In some, renown is the ruling passion; in others, money.

Apart from the laws, all these causes combine to exercise a very powerful influence on the conduct of the finances of the State. If the Americans never spend the people’s money on galas, it is not only because the imposition of taxes is under the people’s control, but because the people take no delight in public rejoicings. If they reject all ornament in their architecture and set store only on practical and homely advantages, it is not only because they live under democratic institutions, but because they are a commercial nation. The habits of private life carry over into public life, and we ought carefully to distinguish the economy that depends on their institutions from the economy that is the natural result of their customs.
Whether the Expenditure of the United States Can Be Compared to That of France

Two points must be established to estimate the extent of the public charges, namely the national wealth and the rate of taxation — The wealth and the charges of France are not accurately known — Why the wealth and charges of the Union cannot be accurately known — The author’s researches to discover the amount of taxation in Pennsylvania — General signs that may indicate the amount of the public charges in a given nation — Result of this investigation for the Union.

Many attempts have recently been made in France to compare the public expenditure of that country with that of the United States. All of them, however, have failed, and a few words will be enough to show that they could not have had a satisfactory result.

To estimate the amount of a people’s public charges, two preliminaries are indispensable. First, we must know the wealth of that people; second, we must learn what portion of that wealth goes to the expenditure of the State. To state the amount of taxation without stating the resources set aside to meet it is a futile labor, for what we want to know is not the expenditure, but the relation of the expenditure to the revenue.

The same rate of taxation that a wealthy contributor can easily bear will reduce a poor one to extreme misery. The wealth of nations is made up of several distinct elements, of which population is the first, real property the second, and personal property the third. The first of these can be discovered without difficulty. Among civilized nations it is easy to obtain an accurate census of the inhabitants; but the other two cannot be determined so easily. It is hard to take an exact account of all the lands in a country that are under cultivation, with their natural or acquired value; and it is still more impossible to estimate the entire personal property at a nation’s disposal, which eludes the strictest analysis through the variety and number of forms it can take. And indeed we find that the oldest civilized nations of Europe, even those with the most centralized administration, have not yet succeeded in determining the exact state of their wealth.

In America no one has ever tried. How could such an investigation even be carried out in a country where society has not yet settled into regular and peaceful habits? Where the national government has no multitude of agents whose efforts it can command and direct toward a single end? Where statistics go unstudied, because nobody can gather the documents needed or find the time to read them? So the basic figures behind the French calculations cannot be had for the Union. The relative wealth of the two countries is unknown: the property of France is not accurately determined, and there is no way of computing that of America.

I therefore agree, for the sake of discussion, to abandon this necessary term of the comparison, and I confine myself to computing the actual amount of taxation, without investigating the relation between the taxation and the revenue. But the reader will see that the limits I set for my researches have not made my task any easier.

There can be no doubt that the central administration of France, assisted by all the public officers at its disposal, could determine exactly the amount of the direct and indirect taxes levied on the citizens. But this investigation, which no private individual can undertake, has not so far been completed by the French government, or at least its results have not been made public. We know the total sum of the charges of the State, and we know the amount of the departmental expenditure; but the expenses of the communal divisions have not been computed, and the amount of the public expenses of France is consequently unknown.

If we now turn to America, we find the difficulties multiplied and increased. The Union publishes an exact return of its expenditure; the budgets of the twenty-four States give similar returns of their revenues; but the expenses incurred in the affairs of the counties and the townships are unknown. *k

k [ As we have seen, the Americans keep four separate budgets, since the Union, the States, the counties, and the townships each have their own. While I was in America I tried hard to learn how much was spent publicly in the townships and counties of the principal States of the Union. The budgets of the larger townships came to me easily, but those of the smaller ones I found impossible to get. I do have some papers on county expenses which, though incomplete, are still of interest. I am grateful to Mr. Richards, Mayor of Philadelphia, for the budgets of thirteen Pennsylvania counties for the year 1830: Lebanon, Centre, Franklin, Fayette, Montgomery, Luzerne, Dauphin, Butler, Alleghany, Columbia, Northampton, Northumberland, and Philadelphia. Their population at that time was 495,207. Their expenses in 1830 came to about $361,650, or nearly 75 cents per inhabitant. Each inhabitant also paid that year about $2.55 to the Union and about 75 cents to the State of Pennsylvania. This calculation is incomplete in two ways, since it covers only one year and only one part of the public charges; but at least it is not conjecture.]

The authority of the Federal government cannot oblige the provincial governments to throw any light on this point; and even if those governments were willing to cooperate all together, it may be doubted that they have the means of giving a satisfactory answer. Apart from the natural difficulties of the task, the political organization of the country would hinder their efforts. The county and town magistrates are not appointed by the authorities of the State, and are not subject to their control. It is therefore quite reasonable to suppose that, if the State wanted to obtain the returns we require, its plan would be thwarted by the neglect of the subordinate officers it would have to employ. *l It is, in point of fact, useless to ask what the Americans might do to advance this inquiry, since it is certain that so far they have done nothing at all. There is not a single individual today, in America or in Europe, who can tell us what each citizen of the Union contributes each year to the public charges of the nation. *m [Footnote l: Those who have tried to compare the expenses of France and America have seen at once that no comparison could be drawn between the total expenditure of the two countries; but they have tried to contrast separate portions of this expenditure. It is easy to show that this second method is no less defective than the first. If I try to compare the French budget with the budget of the Union, it must be remembered that the latter covers far fewer objects than the central government of France, and that its expenditure must consequently be much smaller. If I contrast the budgets of the Departments with those of the States that make up the Union, it must be observed that, since the power and control exercised by the States are much greater than those exercised by the Departments, their expenditure is also greater. As for the budgets of the counties, nothing of the kind exists in the French system of finance; and it is again doubtful whether the corresponding expenses should be assigned to the budget of the State or to those of the municipal divisions. Municipal expenses exist in both countries, but they are not always analogous. In America the townships discharge a variety of offices that in France are reserved to the Departments or to the State. It may, moreover, be asked what is meant by the municipal expenses of America. The organization of the municipal bodies or townships differs from State to State. Are we to be guided by what happens in New England or in Georgia, in Pennsylvania or in the State of Illinois? A kind of analogy may easily be seen between certain budgets in the two countries; but since the elements that compose them always differ more or less, no fair comparison can be made between them. [The same difficulty exists, perhaps to a greater degree at the present time, when the taxation of America has largely increased. — 1874.]]

We must conclude, then, that it is no less difficult to compare the social expenditure than to estimate the relative wealth of France and America. I will even add that it would be dangerous to attempt the comparison; for when statistics are not based on strictly accurate computations, they mislead instead of guiding rightly. The mind is easily imposed on by the false show of exactness that prevails even in the misstatements of science, and it adopts with confidence errors dressed in the forms of mathematical truth.

We therefore abandon our numerical investigation, hoping to find data of another kind. In the absence of positive documents, we may form an opinion about the proportion between a people’s taxation and its real prosperity by observing whether its outward appearance is flourishing; whether, after meeting the demands of the State, the poor man keeps the means of subsistence and the rich man the means of enjoyment; and whether both classes are contented with their position, while seeking to improve it by constant exertion, so that industry is never short of capital, nor capital left unemployed by industry. An observer who draws his inferences from these signs will undoubtedly conclude that the American of the United States contributes a much smaller portion of his income to the State than the citizen of France. Nor, indeed, can the result be otherwise.

Part of the French debt comes from two successive invasions, and the Union has no such calamity to fear. A nation on the continent of Europe must keep a large standing army, while the Union’s isolated position lets it get by with only 6,000 soldiers. The French have a fleet of 300 sail; the Americans have 52 vessels. *n How, then, could the people of the Union be asked to pay as much as the people of France? The finances of two countries in such different situations cannot be compared.

n [ For details, see the Budget of the French Minister of Marine and, for America, the National Calendar of 1833, p. 228. [By 1870, however, the public debt of the United States, caused by the Civil War, amounted to $2,480,672,427, and that of France had more than doubled through the extravagance of the Second Empire and the war of 1870.]]

It is by examining what actually happens in the Union, not by comparing the Union with France, that we can discover whether the American government is really economical. Looking over the different republics that make up the confederation, I see that their governments lack perseverance in their undertakings and exercise no steady control over the men they employ. From this I naturally infer that they must often spend the people’s money to no purpose, or use more of it than their undertakings really need. Great efforts are made, in keeping with the democratic origin of society, to meet the needs of the lower orders, to open the career of power to their efforts, and to spread knowledge and comfort among them. The poor are supported, immense sums are devoted every year to public instruction, all services of whatever kind are paid for, and the most subordinate agents are liberally paid. If this kind of government seems to me useful and rational, I am nevertheless compelled to admit that it is expensive.
Wherever the poor direct public affairs and dispose of the nation’s resources, it appears certain that, since they profit by the State’s expenditure, they tend to increase it.

I conclude, therefore, without resorting to inaccurate computations and without risking a comparison that might prove wrong, that the democratic government of the Americans is not a cheap government, as is sometimes claimed. And I have no hesitation in predicting that, if the people of the United States is ever involved in serious difficulties, its taxation will quickly be raised to the level that prevails in most of the aristocracies and monarchies of Europe. *o
o [ [That is precisely what has since occurred.]]
Corruption and Vices of the Rulers in a Democracy, and Consequent Effects Upon Public Morality

In aristocracies rulers sometimes try to corrupt the people — In democracies rulers often show themselves to be corrupt — In the former their vices directly harm the morality of the people — In the latter their indirect influence is still more pernicious.

A distinction must be made when the aristocratic and the democratic principles denounce each other as tending to encourage corruption. In aristocratic governments the individuals at the head of affairs are rich men who desire only power. In democracies statesmen are poor, and they have their fortunes to make. The consequence is that in aristocratic States the rulers are rarely open to corruption and have very little craving for money, while the reverse is the case in democratic nations.

But in aristocracies, since those who want to reach the head of affairs possess considerable wealth, and since the number of persons whose help they can use to rise is comparatively small, the government is, if I may use the expression, put up to a sort of auction. In democracies, on the contrary, those who covet power are very seldom wealthy, and the number of citizens who confer that power is extremely great. Perhaps in democracies the number of men who could be bought is by no means smaller, but buyers are rarely to be found; and besides, so many persons would have to be bought at once that the attempt is made futile.

Many of the men who have held office in France during the last forty years have been accused of making their fortunes at the expense of the State or of its allies, a reproach rarely made against the public figures of the ancient monarchy. But in France the practice of bribing electors is almost unknown, whereas in England it is notoriously and publicly carried on. In the United States I never heard a man accused of spending his wealth to corrupt the populace; but I have often heard the honesty of public officers questioned, and still more often I have heard their success attributed to low intrigues and immoral practices.

So if the men who run the government of an aristocracy sometimes try to corrupt the people, the leaders of a democracy are corrupt themselves. In the first case the people’s morality is attacked directly. In the second, an indirect influence works on the people, and it is still more to be feared.

Since the rulers of democratic nations are almost always exposed to suspicion of dishonorable conduct, they in some measure lend the authority of the government to the base practices of which they are accused. They thus set an example that must discourage the struggles of virtuous independence and must feed the secret calculations of a vicious ambition. Someone may say that evil passions appear in all ranks of society, that they ascend the throne by hereditary right, and that despicable characters are to be found at the head of aristocratic nations as well as in the sphere of a democracy. This objection has little weight in my estimation. The corruption of men who have risen to power by chance has something coarse and vulgar about it that makes it contagious to the multitude. On the contrary, there is a kind of aristocratic refinement and an air of grandeur in the depravity of the great, which often keep it from spreading.

The people can never penetrate the bewildering labyrinth of court intrigue, and will always have difficulty detecting the baseness that lurks beneath elegant manners, refined tastes, and graceful language. But to plunder the public purse and to sell the favors of the State are arts that the meanest villain can understand and hope to practice in his turn.

In reality it is far less harmful to witness the immorality of the great than to witness the immorality that leads to greatness. In a democracy private citizens see a man of their own rank in life rise from that obscure position and come into riches and power within a few years. The sight excites their surprise and their envy, and they are led to ask how the person who was their equal yesterday is their ruler today. To attribute his rise to his talents or his virtues is unpleasant, for it is tacitly to acknowledge that they are themselves less virtuous and less talented than he was. They are therefore led (and not infrequently their guess is correct) to ascribe his success mainly to some one of his defects; and thus an odious mixture is formed in their minds of the ideas of baseness and power, unworthiness and success, utility and dishonor.
Efforts of Which a Democracy Is Capable

The Union has had only one struggle so far for its existence — Enthusiasm at the beginning of the war — Indifference toward its close — Difficulty of establishing military conscription or impressment of seamen in America — Why a democratic people is less capable of sustained effort than another.

Let me warn the reader that I am speaking here of a government that faithfully carries out the real wishes of a people, not of one that merely issues commands in the people’s name. Nothing is so irresistible as a tyrannical power that commands in the name of the people. It has the moral weight that belongs to the decision of the majority, and at the same time it acts with the speed and persistence of a single man.

It is difficult to say what degree of exertion a democratic government may be capable of in a crisis in the nation’s history. But no great democratic republic has so far existed in the world. To call the oligarchy that ruled France in 1793 by that name would be to insult the republican form of government. The United States offers the first example of the kind.

The American Union has now lasted half a century, and in all that time its existence has been attacked only once, namely during the War of Independence. At the beginning of that long war, various events showed an extraordinary zeal for the service of the country. *p But as the contest dragged on, signs of private egotism began to appear. No money was poured into the public treasury; few recruits could be raised for the army; the people wished to win independence but were very ill-disposed to undergo the privations by which alone it could be obtained. “Tax laws,” says Hamilton in the “Federalist” (No. 12), “have in vain been multiplied; new methods to enforce the collection have in vain been tried; the public expectation has been uniformly disappointed and the treasuries of the States have remained empty. The popular system of administration inherent in the nature of popular government, coinciding with the real scarcity of money incident to a languid and mutilated state of trade, has hitherto defeated every experiment for extensive collections, and has at length taught the different legislatures the folly of attempting them.”

p [ One of the most remarkable of these episodes was the Americans’ decision to give up the use of tea for a time. Anyone who knows that people usually cling more to their habits than to their lives will surely admire this great, though little-noticed, sacrifice made by an entire people.]

The United States has not had to fight any serious war since that period. So, to judge what sacrifices democratic nations may impose on themselves, we must wait until the American people is obliged to place half of its total income at the disposal of the government, as the English were, or until it sends a twentieth of its population onto the battlefield, as France did. *q
q [ [The Civil War showed that when necessity arose, the American people, in the North and in the South alike, were capable of making the most enormous sacrifices, both in money and in men.]]

In America conscription is unknown, and men are persuaded to enlist by bounties. The ideas and habits of the people of the United States are so opposed to compulsory enlistment that I do not think it can ever be sanctioned by the laws. What the French call the conscription is certainly the heaviest tax on the population of that country; yet how could a great continental war be fought without it? The Americans have not adopted the British practice of pressing seamen into service, and they have nothing like the French system of maritime conscription. The navy, like the merchant service, is staffed by volunteers. But it is hard to see how a nation could sustain a great naval war without resorting to one or the other of these two systems. Indeed, the Union, which has fought with some distinction at sea, has never had a very large fleet, and equipping the small number of American ships has always been extremely expensive.

I have heard American statesmen admit that the Union will have great difficulty keeping its rank at sea unless it adopts impressment or maritime conscription. But the difficulty is to get the people, who hold the supreme authority, to submit to impressment or to any compulsory system.

It is beyond dispute that in times of danger a free people shows far more energy than one that is not free. But I am inclined to think that this is especially true of those free nations in which the democratic element predominates. Democracy seems to me much better suited to the peaceful running of society, or to an occasional effort of remarkable vigor, than to the hardy and prolonged endurance of the storms that beset the political existence of nations. The reason is plain. Enthusiasm prompts men to expose themselves to dangers and privations, but they will not bear these for long without reflection. There is more calculation, even in the impulses of courage, than people generally suppose. The first efforts are inspired by passion, but perseverance is kept up by a clear view of the goal. We risk a part of what we value in order to save the rest.

But it is just this clear perception of the future, founded on sound judgment and informed experience, that democracies most often lack. The populace is more inclined to feel than to reason, and if its present sufferings are great, it is to be feared that the still greater sufferings that come with defeat will be forgotten.

Another cause tends to make the efforts of a democratic government less persevering than those of an aristocracy. The lower classes are not only less alert than the higher orders to the good or bad chances of the future, but they also suffer far more keenly from present privations. The nobleman does risk his life, but the chance of glory is as great as the chance of harm. If he gives up a large part of his income to the state, he deprives himself for a time of the pleasures of wealth. But for the poor man, death is adorned with no pomp or renown, and the taxes that are irksome to the rich are fatal to him.

This relative weakness of democratic republics is perhaps the greatest obstacle to founding a republic of this kind in Europe. For such a State to survive in one country of the Old World, similar institutions would have to be introduced into all the other nations.

I believe that a democratic government tends in the end to increase the real strength of society. But it can never gather as much power at a single point and at a given moment as an aristocracy or a monarchy can. If a democratic country lived under a republican government for a whole century, it would probably be more populous and more prosperous at the end of that time than the neighboring despotic States. But it would have run the risk of being conquered much more often than they would in that span of years.
Self-Control of the American Democracy
The American people accepts slowly, or often does not accept, what is good for its own interests — The faults of the American democracy are for the most part reparable.

A democracy has difficulty mastering its passions and setting aside the demands of the moment for the sake of the future, and this shows even in the most trivial events in the United States. The people, surrounded by flatterers, finds it very hard to overcome its inclinations. Whenever it is asked to accept a privation or any kind of inconvenience, even to reach a goal that its own reason approves, it almost always refuses at first. The Americans’ deference to the laws has been justly praised. But it must be added that in America legislation is made by the people and for the people. As a result, in the United States the law favors the very classes that elsewhere have the greatest interest in evading it. It may therefore be supposed that an onerous law, one not recognized as being of immediate usefulness, would either not be passed or not be obeyed.

In America there is no law against fraudulent bankruptcies. This is not because they are few, but because bankruptcies are so numerous. The fear of being prosecuted as a bankrupt weighs more heavily on the minds of most people than the fear of being dragged into losses or ruin by other people’s failures. And the public conscience extends a kind of guilty tolerance to an offense that everyone condemns as an individual. In the new States of the Southwest, the citizens generally take justice into their own hands, and murders are very frequent. This comes from the rough customs and the ignorance of the inhabitants of those wilderness regions, who do not see the use of giving the law adequate force and who prefer duels to prosecutions.

Someone remarked to me one day in Philadelphia that almost all crimes in America are caused by the abuse of strong liquor, which the lower classes can get in great abundance because it is so extremely cheap. “How is it,” I said, “that you do not put a duty on brandy?” “Our legislators,” my informant replied, “have often thought of this remedy. But putting it into effect is difficult. A revolt might be feared, and the members who voted for such a law would be sure to lose their seats.” “From which I am to infer,” I answered, “that the drinking population is the majority in your country, and that temperance is somewhat unpopular.”

When these things are pointed out to American statesmen, they simply assure you that time will bring about the necessary change and that the experience of evil will teach the people where its true interests lie. This is often true. A democracy is more liable to error than a monarch or a body of nobles, but its chances of regaining the right path once it has recognized its mistake are also greater. For it is rarely hampered by internal interests that conflict with those of the majority and resist the authority of reason. But a democracy can arrive at the truth only through experience, and many nations may lose their existence while they wait for the consequences of their errors.

The great privilege of the Americans lies not simply in being better educated than other nations, but in being able to repair the faults they may commit. It must be added that a democracy cannot gain real benefit from past experience unless it has reached a certain level of knowledge and civilization. There are tribes and peoples whose education has been so bad, and whose character is such a strange mixture of passion, ignorance, and mistaken ideas on every subject, that they cannot see the causes of their own misery, and they fall victim to ills they do not understand.

I have crossed vast tracts of country that were once inhabited by powerful Native American nations which are now extinct. I have myself spent some time among the shattered tribes that witness the daily decline of their numbers and of the glory of their independence, and I have heard these Native Americans themselves foresee the doom that hangs over their race. Every European can see means that would rescue these unfortunate people from certain destruction. They alone fail to see the remedy. They feel the woe that year after year heaps on their heads, but they will perish to the last man without accepting the cure. It would be necessary to use force to make them submit to the protection and the constraint of civilization.

The endless revolutions that have convulsed the South American provinces for the last quarter of a century have often been mentioned with astonishment, and people have expected those nations soon to return to their natural state. But can it be said that the turmoil of revolution is not in fact the most natural state of the South American Spaniards at present? In that country society is plunged into difficulties from which all its efforts are powerless to rescue it. The inhabitants of that fair portion of the Western Hemisphere seem obstinately bent on pursuing the work of internal destruction. If exhaustion brings them a moment of rest, that rest only prepares them for a fresh frenzy. When I consider their condition, which alternates between misery and crime, I would be inclined to believe that despotism itself would be a benefit to them, if the words despotism and benefit could ever be joined in my mind.
Conduct of Foreign Affairs by the American Democracy

Direction given to the foreign policy of the United States by Washington and Jefferson — Almost all the defects inherent in democratic institutions come to light in the conduct of foreign affairs — Their advantages are less noticeable.

We have seen that the Federal Constitution entrusts the lasting direction of the nation’s external interests to the President and the Senate, *r which to some extent removes the Union’s general foreign policy from the people’s control. It cannot therefore be said with truth that the State’s external affairs are conducted by the democracy.

r [ “The President,” says the Constitution, Art. II, sect. 2, Section 2, “shall have power, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two-thirds of the senators present concur.” The reader is reminded that the senators are elected for a term of six years and that they are chosen by the legislature of each State.]

The policy of America owes its origin to Washington, and after him to Jefferson, who established the principles that it follows today. Washington said, in the admirable letter he addressed to his fellow citizens, which may be regarded as his political legacy to the country: “The great rule of conduct for us in regard to foreign nations is, in extending our commercial relations, to have with them as little political connection as possible. So far as we have already formed engagements, let them be fulfilled with perfect good faith. Here let us stop. Europe has a set of primary interests which to us have none, or a very remote relation. Hence, she must be engaged in frequent controversies, the causes of which are essentially foreign to our concerns. Hence, therefore, it must be unwise in us to implicate ourselves, by artificial ties, in the ordinary vicissitudes of her politics, or the ordinary combinations and collisions of her friendships or enmities. Our detached and distant situation invites and enables us to pursue a different course. If we remain one people, under an efficient government, the period is not far off when we may defy material injury from external annoyance; when we may take such an attitude as will cause the neutrality we may at any time resolve upon to be scrupulously respected; when belligerent nations, under the impossibility of making acquisitions upon us, will not lightly hazard the giving us provocation; when we may choose peace or war, as our interest, guided by justice, shall counsel. Why forego the advantages of so peculiar a situation? Why quit our own to stand upon foreign ground? Why, by interweaving our destiny with that of any part of Europe, entangle our peace and prosperity in the toils of European ambition, rivalship, interest, humor, or caprice? It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world; so far, I mean, as we are now at liberty to do it; for let me not be understood as capable of patronizing infidelity to existing engagements. I hold the maxim no less applicable to public than to private affairs, that honesty is always the best policy. I repeat it; therefore, let those engagements be observed in their genuine sense; but in my opinion it is unnecessary, and would be unwise, to extend them. Taking care always to keep ourselves, by suitable establishments, in a respectable defensive posture, we may safely trust to temporary alliances for extraordinary emergencies.” Earlier in the same letter, Washington makes this admirable and just remark: “The nation which indulges toward another an habitual hatred or an habitual fondness is in some degree a slave. It is a slave to its animosity or to its affection, either of which is sufficient to lead it astray from its duty and its interest.”

Washington’s political conduct was always guided by these maxims. He succeeded in keeping his country at peace while all the other nations of the globe were at war, and he laid it down as a fundamental doctrine that the true interest of the Americans lay in perfect neutrality toward the internal quarrels of the European powers.

Jefferson went further still, and introduced into the policy of the Union a maxim which holds that “the Americans ought never to solicit any privileges from foreign nations, in order not to be obliged to grant similar privileges themselves.”

These two principles were so plain and so sound that even the populace could grasp them, and they have greatly simplified the foreign policy of the United States. Since the Union takes no part in the affairs of Europe, it has, properly speaking, no foreign interests to deal with, for it has at present no powerful neighbors on the American continent. The country is as far removed from the passions of the Old World by its position as by the policy it has chosen. It is not called upon either to reject or to embrace the conflicting interests of Europe, while the quarrels of the New World still lie hidden in the future.

The Union is free of all earlier obligations, and so it can profit from the experience of the old nations of Europe. It does not have to make the best of the past and adapt it to present circumstances, as they do, or to accept the immense inheritance they receive from their forefathers, an inheritance of glory mixed with calamities and of alliances at odds with national antipathies. By its very nature, the foreign policy of the United States is reduced to waiting for the chances of the nation’s future history, and for the present it consists more in refraining from interference than in taking action.

It is therefore very hard to say, at present, how much sagacity the American democracy will show in conducting the country’s foreign policy. On this point both its adversaries and its advocates must suspend judgment. As for myself, I do not hesitate to state my conviction that it is above all in the conduct of foreign relations that democratic governments seem to me decidedly inferior to governments run on different principles. Experience, instruction, and habit can almost always succeed in giving democracies a kind of practical discretion, and that knowledge of the daily events of life which is called good sense. Good sense may be enough to direct the ordinary course of society, and among a people whose education has been provided for, the advantages of democratic liberty in the country’s internal affairs may more than make up for the evils inherent in a democratic government. But this is not always so in the relations between foreign nations.

Foreign policy demands almost none of the qualities that a democracy possesses, and it requires, on the contrary, the full use of almost all the faculties in which a democracy is deficient. Democracy favors the growth of the State’s internal resources. It tends to spread a moderate independence. It promotes the growth of public spirit and strengthens respect for law in all classes of society. These are advantages that influence the relations of one people with another only indirectly. But a democracy is unable to manage the details of an important undertaking, to persevere in a design, and to carry it out in the face of serious obstacles. It cannot combine its measures with secrecy, and it will not wait patiently for their results. These are qualities that belong especially to an individual or to an aristocracy, and they are precisely the means by which a particular people attains a dominant position.

Look instead at the natural defects of aristocracy, and we find that their effect is comparatively harmless in directing a State’s external affairs. The chief fault with which aristocratic bodies can be charged is that they tend to serve their own advantage rather than that of the mass of the people. In foreign politics it is rare for the aristocracy’s interest to differ in any way from the people’s.

The tendency of democracies to obey the impulse of passion rather than the counsels of prudence, and to abandon a mature design to gratify a momentary whim, was very clearly seen in America when the French Revolution broke out. It was as obvious then as it is today, even to the simplest mind, that the interest of the Americans forbade them to take any part in the contest that was about to flood Europe with blood, but that could in no way harm the welfare of their own country. Nevertheless, the sympathies of the people declared themselves so violently on the side of France that nothing but the inflexible character of Washington and his immense popularity could have kept the Americans from declaring war on England. And even so, the efforts that the austere reason of that great man made to restrain the generous but imprudent passions of his fellow citizens very nearly cost him the one reward he had ever claimed, his country’s love. The majority then condemned the policy he adopted, which the nation has since approved unanimously. *s If the Constitution and the public’s favor had not entrusted the direction of the country’s foreign affairs to Washington, it is certain that the American nation would at that time have taken the very measures that it now condemns.

s [ See the fifth volume of Marshall’s “Life of Washington.” In a government constituted like that of the United States, he says, “it is impossible for the chief magistrate, however firm he may be, to oppose for any length of time the torrent of popular opinion; and the prevalent opinion of that day seemed to incline to war. In fact, in the session of Congress held at the time, it was frequently seen that Washington had lost the majority in the House of Representatives.” The violence of the language used against him in public was extreme, and at a political meeting they did not hesitate to compare him indirectly to the traitor Arnold. “By the opposition,” says Marshall, “the friends of the administration were declared to be an aristocratic and corrupt faction, who, from a desire to introduce monarchy, were hostile to France and under the influence of Britain; that they were a paper nobility, whose extreme sensibility at every measure which threatened the funds, induced a tame submission to injuries and insults, which the interests and honor of the nation required them to resist.”]

Almost all the nations that have ever had a powerful influence on the destinies of the world, by conceiving, pursuing, and carrying out vast designs, from the Romans to the English, have been governed by aristocratic institutions. This will not surprise us when we remember that nothing in the world holds to its purpose so firmly as an aristocracy. The mass of the people may be led astray by ignorance or passion. A king’s mind may be swayed, and his perseverance in his designs may be shaken; besides, a king is not immortal. But an aristocratic body is too numerous to be misled by the blandishments of intrigue, and yet not numerous enough to yield easily to the intoxicating influence of thoughtless passion. It has the energy of a firm and well-informed individual, added to the power it draws from perpetuity.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — Advantages American Society Derive From Democracy
paragraphs: What the Real Advantages Are That American Society Derives from the Government of the Democracy

Before I begin the subject of this chapter, I want to remind the reader of something I have mentioned more than once in this book. The political institutions of the United States seem to me one of the forms of government that a democracy may adopt, but I do not regard the American Constitution as the best, or as the only one, that a democratic people may establish. In showing the advantages the Americans draw from the government of the democracy, I am therefore very far from meaning, or believing, that the same advantages can be obtained only from the same laws.
General Tendency of the Laws Under the Rule of the American Democracy, and the Habits of Those Who Apply Them

The defects of a democratic government are easy to discover—Its advantages can be seen only through long observation—Democracy in America is often inexpert, but the general tendency of its laws is beneficial—In the American democracy, public officials have no permanent interests distinct from those of the majority—The result of this state of things.

The defects and weaknesses of a democratic government are very easy to discover. The most glaring examples demonstrate them, while its beneficial influence works less visibly. A single glance is enough to detect its bad consequences, but its good qualities can be seen only through long observation. The laws of the American democracy are often defective or incomplete. They sometimes attack vested rights, or give approval to others that are dangerous to the community. But even if they were good, the frequent changes they undergo would be an evil. How is it, then, that the American republics prosper and hold their position?

In judging laws, we must carefully distinguish between the end at which they aim and the means by which they pursue that end, between their absolute and their relative excellence. Suppose a legislator intends to favor the interests of the minority at the expense of the majority, and suppose the measures he takes are so arranged that they accomplish his object with the least possible expense of time and effort. Then the law may be well drafted even though its purpose is bad, and the more effective it is, the greater the harm it does.

Democratic laws generally tend to promote the welfare of the greatest possible number. They come from the majority of the citizens, who may make mistakes but cannot have an interest opposed to their own advantage. The laws of an aristocracy, on the contrary, tend to concentrate wealth and power in the hands of the minority, because an aristocracy, by its very nature, is a minority. We may therefore state as a general proposition that a democracy, in conducting its legislation, aims at something useful to a greater number of citizens than an aristocracy does. This, however, is the sum total of its advantages.

Aristocracies are infinitely more expert in the science of legislation than democracies can ever be. They possess a self-control that protects them from the errors of momentary excitement, and they form lasting designs that they bring to maturity with the help of favorable opportunities. Aristocratic government proceeds with the skill of an art; it knows how to make the combined force of all its laws converge on a given point at the same time. This is not so with democracies, whose laws are almost always ineffective or ill-timed. The means of a democracy are therefore more imperfect than those of an aristocracy, and the measures it adopts without realizing it are often opposed to its own cause. But the object it has in view is more useful.

Now imagine a community so organized, by nature or by its constitution, that it can endure the passing effects of bad laws and can wait, without being destroyed, for the general tendency of its legislation to show itself. We can then understand that a democratic government, in spite of its defects, will be best suited to promote the prosperity of such a community. This is precisely what has happened in the United States. And I repeat what I have said before: the great advantage of the Americans is that they can commit faults which they are able to repair afterward.

A similar observation can be made about public officials. It is easy to see that the American democracy often errs in choosing the individuals to whom it entrusts the power of administration, but it is harder to say why the State prospers under their rule. In the first place, we should note that if the governors in a democratic State have less honesty and less ability than elsewhere, the governed, on the other hand, are better informed and pay closer attention to their interests. Because the people in democracies are more constantly vigilant in their affairs and more jealous of their rights, they keep their representatives from abandoning the general line of conduct that their own interest prescribes. In the second place, we must remember that although the democratic magistrate is more likely to abuse his power, he holds it for a shorter time. But there is yet another reason, more general and more conclusive. It is no doubt important to the welfare of nations that they be governed by men of talent and virtue. But it is perhaps still more important that the interests of those men not differ from the interests of the community at large. For if they did, high virtues might become useless and talents might be put to bad use. I say it is important that the interests of the persons in authority not conflict with or oppose the interests of the community at large. I do not insist that they be the same as the interests of the whole population, because I know of no country where that has ever been the case.

No political form has yet been found that is equally good for the prosperity and development of every class into which society is divided. These classes remain, as it were, a number of separate nations inside one nation. Experience has shown that it is just as dangerous to leave the fate of these classes entirely in the hands of any one of them as it is to make one people the judge of another’s destiny. When the rich alone govern, the interest of the poor is always at risk, and when the poor make the laws, the rich face very serious dangers. So the advantage of democracy does not lie, as some have claimed, in promoting the prosperity of everyone, but simply in serving the well-being of the greatest possible number.

The men entrusted with directing public affairs in the United States are often inferior, both in ability and in morality, to those whom aristocratic institutions would raise to power. But their interest is identified and bound up with that of the majority of their fellow citizens. They may often be faithless and often mistaken, but they will never systematically adopt a line of conduct opposed to the will of the majority, and it is impossible for them to give the government a dangerous or exclusive tendency.

The misadministration of a democratic magistrate is a purely isolated fact, which occurs only during the short period for which he is elected. Corruption and incapacity are not common interests that can connect men permanently with one another. A corrupt or incapable magistrate will not coordinate his measures with another magistrate merely because that person is as corrupt and as incapable as himself. And these two men will never join their efforts to promote the corruption and incompetence of their distant descendants. On the contrary, the ambition and scheming of one will serve to expose the other. In democratic states, the vices of a magistrate are usually particular to his own person.

But under aristocratic governments, public men are swayed by the interest of their order. That interest is sometimes the same as the interests of the majority, but it is very often distinct from them. It is the common and lasting bond that unites these men. It leads them to join together and combine their efforts to reach an end that does not always secure the greatest happiness of the greatest number. And it serves not only to connect the persons in authority but to unite them with a considerable part of the community, since many citizens belong to the aristocracy without holding official positions. The aristocratic magistrate is therefore constantly supported by a part of the community, as well as by the government of which he is a member.

The common purpose that links the interest of the magistrates in aristocracies with that of a portion of their contemporaries also identifies it with that of future generations. Their influence belongs to the future as much as to the present. The aristocratic magistrate is urged toward the same point at once by the passions of the community, by his own, and, I might almost add, by those of his descendants. Is it any wonder, then, that he does not resist such repeated impulses? Indeed, aristocracies are often carried away by the spirit of their order without being corrupted by it, and they unconsciously shape society to their own ends and prepare it for their own descendants.

The English aristocracy is perhaps the most liberal that has ever existed, and no body of men has ever supplied, without interruption, so many honorable and educated individuals to the government of a country. Yet it cannot escape notice that in English legislation the good of the poor has been sacrificed to the advantage of the rich, and the rights of the majority to the privileges of the few. As a result, England today combines the extremes of fortune within her society, and her perils and calamities are almost equal to her power and her renown. *a

a [ [English legislation over the past forty years is certainly not fairly open to this criticism, which was written before the Reform Bill of 1832. Accordingly, Great Britain has so far escaped and overcome the perils and calamities to which she seemed to be exposed.]]

In the United States, public officials have no interests to promote that are tied to a caste, and the general and constant influence of the government is beneficial, even though the individuals who carry it on are often unskillful and sometimes contemptible. There is indeed a hidden tendency in democratic institutions to make the efforts of the citizens serve the prosperity of the community, in spite of their private vices and mistakes. In aristocratic institutions, by contrast, there is a hidden inclination that leads those who conduct the government, despite their talents and virtues, to contribute to the evils that oppress their fellow creatures. In aristocratic governments, public men may often do harm they do not intend, and in democratic states they produce benefits they never thought of.
Public Spirit in the United States

Patriotism of instinct—Patriotism of reflection—Their different characteristics—Nations ought to strive to acquire the second when the first has disappeared—The efforts of the Americans toward this end—The interest of the individual is closely connected with that of the country.

There is one kind of patriotic attachment that arises mainly from an instinctive, disinterested, and undefinable feeling that ties a man’s affections to his birthplace. This natural fondness goes together with a taste for ancient customs and a reverence for the traditions of the past. Those who feel it love their country as they love the house of their fathers. They enjoy the tranquillity it affords them. They cling to the peaceful habits they have formed within it. They are attached to the memories it awakens, and they are even pleased by the state of obedience in which they live. This patriotism is sometimes stirred up by religious enthusiasm, and then it is capable of the most prodigious efforts. It is in itself a kind of religion.
