It does not reason, but acts from the impulse of faith and feeling. Some nations have regarded the monarch as the embodiment of the country. The fervor of patriotism was then turned into the fervor of loyalty, and they took a sympathetic pride in his conquests and gloried in his power. At one time, under the ancient monarchy, the French felt a kind of satisfaction in their dependence on the arbitrary pleasure of their king, and they used to say with pride, “We are the subjects of the most powerful king in the world.”

But like all instinctive passions, this kind of patriotism is better at prompting short bursts of effort than at supplying the motives for continuous endeavor. It may save the State in a crisis, but it will often let the nation decline in time of peace. As long as the customs of a people are simple and its faith unshaken, as long as society rests steadily on traditional institutions whose legitimacy has never been questioned, this instinctive patriotism tends to last.

But there is another kind of attachment to a country that is more rational than the one we have just described. It is perhaps less generous and less ardent, but it is more fruitful and more lasting. It arises together with the spread of knowledge, it is nourished by the laws, it grows through the exercise of civil rights, and in the end it merges with the personal interest of the citizen. A man understands the influence that his country’s prosperity has on his own welfare. He knows that the laws allow him to contribute to that prosperity, and he works to promote it, first as a part of his interest and second as a part of his right.

But there are times in the life of a nation when the ancient customs of a people are changed, public morality is destroyed, religious belief is disturbed, and the spell of tradition is broken, while the spread of knowledge is still incomplete and the civil rights of the community are poorly secured or confined within very narrow limits. The country then takes on a dim and uncertain shape in the eyes of its citizens. They no longer see it in the soil they live on, for to them that soil is a dull, lifeless clod. They do not see it in the usages of their forefathers, which they have been taught to regard as a degrading yoke. They do not see it in religion, for of that they doubt. They do not see it in the laws, which do not originate in their own authority, nor in the legislator, whom they fear and despise. The country is lost to their senses. They can discover it neither under its own features nor under borrowed ones, and they shut themselves up within the dull confines of a narrow egotism. They are freed from prejudice without having acknowledged the empire of reason. They are moved neither by the instinctive patriotism of monarchical subjects nor by the thinking patriotism of republican citizens. They have stopped halfway between the two, in the midst of confusion and distress.

In this predicament, retreat is impossible. A people can no more recover the vitality of its earlier times than a man can return to the innocence and bloom of childhood. Such things may be regretted, but they cannot be renewed. The only thing left to do, then, is to go forward and hasten the union of private with public interests, since the period of disinterested patriotism has gone by forever.

I am certainly very far from claiming that, to obtain this result, the exercise of political rights should immediately be granted to all members of the community. But I maintain that the most powerful means we still possess of interesting men in the welfare of their country, and perhaps the only one, is to make them partakers in the government. At the present time, civic zeal seems to me inseparable from the exercise of political rights. And I hold that the number of citizens in Europe will be found to grow or shrink in proportion as those rights are extended.

In the United States the inhabitants were set down on the soil they now occupy only yesterday, as it were. They brought neither customs nor traditions with them. They meet one another for the first time with no previous acquaintance. In short, the instinctive love of country can scarcely exist in their minds. Yet everyone takes as zealous an interest in the affairs of his township, his county, and the whole State as if they were his own, because everyone, in his own sphere, takes an active part in the government of society.

The lower orders in the United States are aware of the influence that general prosperity has on their own welfare. Simple as this observation is, the people all too rarely make it. But in America the people regard this prosperity as the result of their own efforts. The citizen looks on the fortune of the public as his private interest, and he cooperates in its success, not so much from pride or from duty as from what I shall venture to call cupidity.

There is no need to study the institutions and the history of the Americans to see the truth of this remark, for their customs make it plain enough. Because the American takes part in everything done in his country, he thinks himself obliged to defend whatever is criticized. On these occasions it is not only his country that is attacked, but himself. The result is that his national pride resorts to a thousand artifices and to all the petty tricks of individual vanity.

Nothing is more embarrassing in the ordinary course of life than this irritable patriotism of the Americans. A stranger may be quite willing to praise many of the institutions of their country, but he asks permission to criticize some of the peculiarities he observes, and that permission is firmly refused. America is therefore a free country in which, lest anyone be hurt by your remarks, you are not allowed to speak freely of private individuals or of the state, of the citizens or of the authorities, of public or of private undertakings, or in short of anything at all, except the climate and the soil. And even then Americans will be found ready to defend one or the other, as if the inhabitants of the country had designed them.

In our times a choice must be made between the patriotism of all and the government of a few, for the force and activity that the first confers cannot be reconciled with the guarantees of tranquillity that the second provides.
Notion of Rights in the United States
No great people without a notion of rights—How the notion of rights can be given to a people—Respect for rights in the United States—Where it comes from.

After the idea of virtue, I know of no higher principle than that of right, or, to speak more precisely, these two ideas are blended into one. The idea of right is simply the idea of virtue brought into the political world. It is the idea of right that enabled men to define anarchy and tyranny, and that taught them to remain independent without arrogance and to obey without servility. The man who submits to violence is degraded by his compliance. But when he obeys the command of someone who holds that right of authority, which he acknowledges in a fellow creature, he rises in some measure above the person who gives the command. There are no great men without virtue, and there are no great nations without the notion of rights. It may almost be added that there would be no society at all without it, for what is the condition of a mass of rational and intelligent beings who are held together only by the bond of force?

I am convinced that the only means we now have of instilling the notion of rights, and of making it, as it were, palpable to the senses, is to give all members of the community the peaceful exercise of certain rights. This is very clearly seen in children, who are men without the strength and experience of manhood. When a child begins to move among the objects around him, he is instinctively led to turn everything he can lay his hands on to his own purposes. He has no notion of the property of others. But as he gradually learns the value of things and begins to see that he may in turn be deprived of his possessions, he becomes more cautious, and he respects in others the rights he wishes to have respected in himself. The principle that the child learns from possessing his toys is taught to the man by the things he can call his own. In America, the complaints against property in general that are so frequent in Europe are never heard, because in America there are no paupers. And since everyone has property of his own to defend, everyone recognizes the principle on which he holds it.

The same thing happens in the political world. In America the lowest classes have formed a very high notion of political rights, because they exercise those rights, and they refrain from attacking the rights of others so that their own will not be attacked. In Europe the same classes sometimes rebel even against the supreme power, while the American submits without a murmur to the authority of the pettiest magistrate.

This truth is shown in the most trivial details of national peculiarities. In France very few pleasures are kept for the higher classes alone. The poor are admitted wherever the rich are received, so they behave properly and respect whatever adds to the enjoyments they share. In England, where wealth monopolizes amusement as well as power, people complain that when the poor happen to sneak into the grounds set aside for the pleasures of the rich, they commit acts of wanton mischief. Is that surprising, when care has been taken that they should have nothing to lose? *b

b [ [This, too, has been remedied by much larger provisions for the amusements of the people in public parks, gardens, museums, and the like; and the conduct of the people in these places of amusement has improved in the same proportion.]]

The government of democracy brings the notion of political rights down to the level of the humblest citizens, just as the spread of wealth brings the notion of property within reach of all members of the community. I confess that, to my mind, this is one of its greatest advantages. I do not claim that it is easy to teach men to exercise political rights. But I maintain that when it can be done, the results are highly important, and I add that if there was ever a time when such an attempt should be made, that time is our own. It is clear that the influence of religious belief is shaken and that the notion of divine rights is declining. It is evident that public morality is corrupted and that the notion of moral rights is also disappearing. These are general signs of the replacement of faith by argument, and of the impulses of feeling by calculation. If, in the midst of this general breakdown, you do not succeed in connecting the notion of rights with that of personal interest, which is the only unchanging point in the human heart, what means will you have of governing the world except fear? I am told that, since the laws are weak and the populace is wild, since passions are excited and the authority of virtue is paralyzed, no measures should be taken to increase the rights of the democracy. I reply that it is for these very reasons that some measures of the kind must be taken. And I am convinced that governments have an even greater interest in taking them than society at large, because governments can be destroyed and society cannot perish.

I am not inclined, however, to exaggerate the example that America provides. In those States the people were given political rights at a time when those rights could scarcely be abused, for the citizens were few in number and simple in their customs. As they have multiplied, the Americans have not increased the power of the democracy, but they have, if I may use the expression, extended its dominions. There can be no doubt that the moment when political rights are granted to a people that had been without them is a very critical one, though a necessary one. A child may kill before he knows the value of life, and he may take another person’s property before he knows that his own can be taken from him. When the lower orders are first given political rights, they stand in relation to those rights as the child stands in relation to the whole of nature, and the famous adage may then be applied to them: Homo puer robustus. This truth can even be seen in America. The States where the citizens have enjoyed their rights longest are those where they make the best use of them.

It cannot be repeated too often that nothing is more productive of marvels than the art of being free, but nothing is harder than the apprenticeship of liberty. Despotic institutions are quite different. Despotism often promises to make up for a thousand earlier ills. It upholds the right, it protects the oppressed, and it maintains public order. The nation is lulled by the temporary prosperity that results, until it is roused to a sense of its own misery. Liberty, on the contrary, is generally established amid agitation, it is perfected by civil discord, and its benefits cannot be appreciated until it is already old.
Respect for the Law in the United States
Respect of the Americans for the law—The parental affection they feel for it—The personal interest of everyone in increasing the authority of the law.

It is not always possible to consult the whole people, directly or indirectly, in making the law. But it cannot be denied that when this is possible, the authority of the law is greatly increased. This popular origin, which lessens the excellence and wisdom of legislation, contributes enormously to its power. There is amazing strength in the expression of the determination of a whole people, and when it declares itself, the imagination of even those most inclined to resist it is overawed by its authority. Parties know this fact very well, and they therefore try to make out a majority whenever they can. If they do not have the greater number of voters on their side, they claim that the true majority abstained from voting. And if they are foiled even there, they turn to the body of those who had no votes to give.

In the United States, apart from slaves, servants, and paupers who receive relief from the townships, there is no class of persons who do not exercise the elective franchise and so contribute indirectly to making the laws. Those who intend to attack the laws must therefore either change the opinion of the nation or trample on its decision.

A second reason, still more weighty, may be added. In the United States everyone has a personal interest in enforcing the obedience of the whole community to the law. For the minority may soon win the majority over to its principles, and it therefore has an interest in professing the respect for the decrees of the legislator that it may soon need to claim for its own. However irksome an enactment may be, the citizen of the United States complies with it, not only because it is the work of the majority, but because it originates in his own authority, and he regards it as a contract to which he himself is a party.

In the United States, then, there is no numerous and turbulent multitude that always regards the law as its natural enemy and therefore looks on it with fear and distrust. On the other hand, it is impossible not to see that all classes show the utmost confidence in the legislation of their country and that they are attached to it by a kind of parental affection.

But I am wrong to say all classes, for in America the European scale of authority is inverted, and the wealthy are placed in a position like that of the poor in the Old World. It is the wealthy classes that often regard the law with suspicion. I have already observed that the advantage of democracy is not, as has sometimes been claimed, that it protects the interests of the whole community, but simply that it protects those of the majority. In the United States, where the poor rule, the rich always have some reason to fear the abuse of the poor’s power. This natural anxiety of the rich may produce a sullen dissatisfaction, but society is not disturbed by it. For the same reason that leads the rich to withhold their confidence from the legislative authority makes them obey its commands: their wealth, which prevents them from making the law, prevents them from resisting it. Among civilized nations, revolts are rarely stirred up except by people who have nothing to lose by them. And if the laws of a democracy are not always worthy of respect, at least they always obtain it. For those who usually break the laws have no excuse for not complying with enactments that they have made themselves and from which they benefit. Meanwhile the citizens whose interests might be served by breaking the laws are led, by their character and their position, to submit to the decisions of the legislature, whatever they may be. Besides, the people in America obey the law not only because it comes from the popular authority, but because that authority can change it in any point that proves vexatious. A law is obeyed because it is, first, an evil the people have imposed on themselves, and second, an evil of short duration.
Activity That Pervades All the Branches of the Body Politic in the United States; Influence It Exercises on Society

The political activity that pervades the United States is harder to imagine than the freedom and equality that reign there—The great activity that perpetually stirs the legislative bodies is only an episode in the general activity—It is difficult for an American to confine himself to his own business—Political agitation extends to all social intercourse—The commercial activity of the Americans is partly attributable to this cause—Indirect advantages that society derives from a democratic government.

When you pass from a country with free institutions to one where they do not exist, you are struck by the change. In the former all is bustle and activity, and in the latter everything is calm and motionless. In the one, improvement and progress are the general topics of inquiry. In the other, it seems as if the community aspired only to rest in the enjoyment of the advantages it has already gained. Nevertheless, the country that exerts itself so strenuously to promote its welfare is generally wealthier and more prosperous than the one that seems so content with its lot. And when we compare them, we can scarcely understand how so many new wants are felt every day in the first, while so few seem to arise in the second.

If this remark applies to those free countries in which monarchical and aristocratic institutions still exist, it is even more striking in democratic republics. In these States it is not just one part of the people that is busy improving its social condition. The whole community is engaged in the task, and provision is to be made not for the needs and convenience of a single class, but for the needs and convenience of all ranks of life.

It is not impossible to imagine the immense liberty the Americans enjoy, and some idea may also be formed of the extreme equality that exists among them. But the political activity that pervades the United States must be seen to be understood. No sooner do you set foot on American soil than you are stunned by a kind of tumult. A confused clamor rises on every side, and a thousand voices at once demand the immediate satisfaction of their social wants. Everything around you is in motion. Here, the people of one quarter of a town are meeting to decide on building a church. There, an election of a representative is under way. A little further on, the delegates of a district are hurrying to town to consult about some local improvements. In another place, the laborers of a village leave their plows to deliberate on a plan for a road or a public school. Meetings are called for the sole purpose of declaring disapproval of the government’s conduct, while in other assemblies the citizens hail the authorities of the day as the fathers of their country. Societies are formed that regard drunkenness as the principal cause of the evils from which the State suffers, and that solemnly bind themselves to set a constant example of temperance. *c

c [ While I was in the United States, the temperance societies already had more than 270,000 members. Their effect had been to cut the consumption of fermented liquors by 500,000 gallons a year in the State of Pennsylvania alone.]

The great political agitation of the American legislative bodies, which is the only kind of excitement that attracts the attention of foreign countries, is a mere episode, or a kind of continuation, of that universal movement which begins among the lowest classes of the people and spreads in turn to all ranks of society. It is impossible to put more effort into the pursuit of enjoyment.

The cares of political life take up a very prominent place in the occupations of a citizen of the United States, and almost the only pleasure an American can imagine is to take part in the government and to discuss the part he has taken. This feeling pervades even the most trifling habits of life. Even the women often attend public meetings and listen to political harangues as a recreation after their household labors. Debating clubs are, to a certain extent, a substitute for theatrical entertainments. An American cannot converse, but he can discuss, and when he tries to talk he falls into a lecture. He speaks to you as if he were addressing a meeting, and if he happens to grow warm in the course of the discussion, he will inevitably say “Gentlemen,” to the person he is talking with.

In some countries the inhabitants show a certain reluctance to use the political privileges with which the law invests them. It would seem that they set too high a value on their time to spend it on the interests of the community, and they prefer to withdraw within the exact limits of a wholesome egotism, marked out by four sunken fences and a quickset hedge. But if an American were condemned to confine his activity to his own affairs, he would be robbed of half his existence. He would feel an immense void in the life he is used to leading, and his wretchedness would be unbearable. *d I am convinced that if a despotic government is ever established in America, it will find it harder to overcome the habits that free institutions have produced than to conquer the citizens’ attachment to freedom.

d [ The same observation was made at Rome under the first Caesars. Somewhere Montesquieu mentions the excessive despondency of certain Roman citizens who, after the excitement of political life, were suddenly thrown back into the stagnation of private life.]

This ceaseless agitation, which democratic government has introduced into the political world, spreads into all of social life. I am not sure that, on the whole, this is not the greatest advantage of democracy. I am also much less inclined to praise democracy for what it does than for what it causes to be done. It cannot be denied that the people often conduct public business very badly. But the lower classes cannot take part in public business without widening the circle of their ideas and stepping outside the ordinary routine of their minds. The humblest person who is called on to help govern society gains a certain self-respect. Because he holds authority, he can command the services of minds far more educated than his own. A crowd of petitioners courts him and tries to deceive him in a thousand different ways, yet they instruct him by their very deceit. He takes part in political undertakings that he did not conceive himself, but that give him a taste for undertakings of that kind. Every day, improvements are pointed out in the property he holds in common with others, and this gives him a desire to improve the property that is more especially his own. He is perhaps neither happier nor better than those who came before him, but he is better informed and more active. I have no doubt that the democratic institutions of the United States, together with the physical character of the country, are the cause of the prodigious commercial activity of its inhabitants. They are not the direct cause, as is so often asserted, but the indirect one. The laws do not produce this activity, but the people learn how to promote it from their experience of making laws.

When the opponents of democracy say that a single individual carries out the tasks he takes on much better than the government of the community does, it seems to me that they are perfectly right. Where the two sides are equally well informed, the government of one person is more consistent, more persevering and more accurate than that of a multitude. It is also much better able to judge wisely the characters of the men it employs. Anyone who denies this has certainly never seen a democratic government, or has formed his opinion on very partial evidence. It is true that even when local circumstances and the disposition of the people allow democratic institutions to survive, they never display a regular and methodical system of government. Democratic liberty is far from carrying out all the projects it undertakes with the skill of an adroit despotism. It often abandons them before they have borne fruit, or risks them when the consequences may prove dangerous. But in the end it produces more than any absolute government does: if it does fewer things well, it does a greater number of things. Under its rule, what the public administration accomplishes is not nearly so important as what private effort accomplishes. Democracy does not give the people the most skillful kind of government, but it produces something that the most skillful governments are often unable to awaken, namely an all-pervading and restless activity, an overflowing force, and an energy that cannot be separated from it and that may, under favorable circumstances, give rise to the most amazing benefits. These are the true advantages of democracy.

In the present age, when the destinies of Christendom seem to hang in the balance, some people hurry to attack democracy as an enemy while it is still in its early growth. Others are ready with vows of worship for this new deity rising out of chaos. But both parties know very little about the object of their hatred or of their desire. They strike in the dark and land their blows by pure chance.

We must first understand what the purpose of society and the aim of government are taken to be. Suppose you intend to raise the human mind to a certain height and to teach it to look on the things of this world with generous feelings. Suppose you want to inspire in people a scorn for mere worldly advantage, to give birth to living convictions, and to keep alive the spirit of honorable devotion. Suppose you think it good to refine a nation’s habits, to improve its manners, to cultivate its arts, and to promote the love of poetry, of beauty and of renown. Suppose you want to form a people able to act with power on all other nations, and prepared for those high enterprises that, whatever the outcome of its efforts, will leave a name famous for all time. If you believe that these are the principal objects of society, you must avoid the government of democracy, which would be a very uncertain guide to the end you have in view.

But suppose you think it more useful to turn the moral and intellectual activity of man toward producing comfort and acquiring the necessities of life. Suppose you think a clear understanding is more profitable to man than genius. Suppose your aim is not to stimulate the virtues of heroism but to create habits of peace. Suppose you would rather see vices than crimes, and are content to find fewer noble deeds provided that offenses are reduced in the same proportion. Suppose that, instead of living in the midst of a brilliant society, you are content to have prosperity around you. Suppose, in short, that you hold the principal object of a government to be not to give the greatest possible share of power and glory to the nation as a body, but to ensure the greatest enjoyment and the least misery to each of the individuals who make it up. If such are your desires, you can have no surer means of satisfying them than to make conditions equal among men and to establish democratic institutions.

But suppose the time when such a choice was possible has passed, and some superhuman power drives us toward one or the other of these two kinds of government without consulting our wishes. Then let us at least try to make the best of the one that has been assigned to us. Let us examine its good and its evil tendencies closely enough that we can encourage the good and hold the evil in check as far as we can.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — Unlimited Power Of Majority, And Its Consequences
paragraphs: Unlimited Power of the Majority in the United States, and Its Consequences

The very essence of democratic government lies in the absolute sovereignty of the majority, for nothing in democratic States is able to resist it. Most of the American Constitutions have tried to increase this natural strength of the majority by artificial means. *a

a [ We observed, in examining the Federal Constitution, that the efforts of the legislators of the Union had been diametrically opposed to the present tendency. The consequence has been that the Federal government is more independent in its sphere than that of the States. But the Federal government scarcely ever interferes in anything but external affairs, and the governments of the States are in reality the authorities that direct society in America.]

Of all political institutions, the legislature is the one most easily swayed by the wishes of the majority. The Americans decided that the members of the legislature should be elected directly by the people and for a very short term. Their purpose was to subject legislators not only to the general convictions of their constituents but even to their daily passions. The members of both houses are drawn from the same class of society and are chosen in the same way. As a result, the changes in the legislative bodies are almost as rapid, and quite as irresistible, as those of a single assembly. Almost all the authority of the government has been entrusted to a legislature constituted in this way.

But while the law increased the strength of the authorities that were already strong, it weakened more and more those that were naturally weak. It deprived the representatives of the executive of all stability and independence. By subjecting them completely to the whims of the legislature, it took from them the slight influence that the nature of a democratic government might have allowed them to keep. In several States the judicial power was also placed at the discretion of the majority through election, and in all of them its very existence was made to depend on the will of the legislative authority, since the representatives were empowered to set the judges’ salaries every year.

Custom, however, has done even more than law. A practice that will in the end make all the safeguards of representative government worthless is becoming more and more common in the United States. It often happens that the electors who choose a delegate lay down a certain line of conduct for him and impose on him a number of positive obligations that he is pledged to carry out. Apart from the tumult, this amounts to the same thing as if the majority of the people held its deliberations in the marketplace.

Several other circumstances combine to make the power of the majority in America not only preponderant but irresistible. The moral authority of the majority rests partly on the idea that there is more intelligence and wisdom in a great number of men gathered together than in a single individual, and that the number of legislators matters more than their quality. In effect, the theory of equality is applied to the human mind. Human pride is thus attacked in its last refuge by a doctrine that the minority is reluctant to admit and agrees to only very slowly. Like all other powers, and perhaps more than any other, the authority of the many needs the sanction of time. At first it compels obedience by force, but its laws are not respected until they have been maintained for a long while.

The majority supposes that its right to govern society comes from its superior intelligence. This idea was brought into the United States by the first settlers. It would be enough by itself to create a free nation, and it has now merged with the customs of the people and with the small details of social life.

Under the old monarchy the French held as a maxim that the King could do no wrong, and that if he did do wrong, the blame fell on his advisers. This maxim is still a fundamental principle of the English Constitution. It was highly favorable to habits of obedience, and it allowed the subject to complain of the law without ceasing to love and honor the lawgiver. The Americans hold the same opinion about the majority.

The moral power of the majority rests on yet another principle: that the interests of the many should be preferred to those of the few. It is easy to see that the respect professed here for the rights of the majority must naturally grow or shrink according to the state of parties. When a nation is divided into several irreconcilable factions, the privilege of the majority is often disregarded, because it is intolerable to comply with its demands.

Suppose there were in America a class of citizens whom the legislating majority tried to strip of exclusive privileges they had held for ages, and to bring down from a high position to the level of the common ranks. The minority would then probably be less ready to obey the majority’s laws. But the United States was colonized by men of equal rank among themselves, and so there is as yet no natural or permanent source of conflict between the interests of its different inhabitants.

There are certain communities in which the people who make up the minority can never hope to bring the majority over to their side, because to do so they would have to give up the very point in dispute between them. Thus an aristocracy can never become a majority while it keeps its exclusive privileges, and it cannot give up its privileges without ceasing to be an aristocracy.

In the United States political questions cannot be posed in so general and absolute a way. All parties are willing to recognize the rights of the majority, because all hope to turn those rights to their own advantage at some future time. The majority in that country therefore exercises a prodigious actual authority and a moral influence that is scarcely less preponderant. No obstacles exist that can hinder its progress, or even slow it down, or make it heed the complaints of those it crushes along its path. This state of affairs is disastrous in itself and dangerous for the future.

How the Unlimited Power of the Majority Increases in America the Instability of Legislation and Administration Inherent in Democracy The Americans increase the changeableness of the laws, which is inherent in democracy, by changing the legislature every year and giving it unbounded authority. The same effect is produced on the administration. In America social improvement is pursued more energetically but less steadily than in Europe.

I have already spoken of the natural defects of democratic institutions, and every one of them grows in exact proportion to the power of the majority. Take the most obvious first. The changeableness of the laws is an evil inherent in democratic government, because it is natural for democracies to raise men to power in very rapid succession. But this evil is felt more or less strongly depending on the authority and the means of action the legislature possesses.

In America the authority exercised by the legislative bodies is supreme. Nothing prevents them from carrying out their wishes quickly and with irresistible power, and they receive new representatives every year. That is to say, the circumstances that do most to produce democratic instability, and that allow whim to be applied freely to every object in the State, are fully at work here. In keeping with this, America today is the country in the world where laws last the shortest time. Almost all the American constitutions have been amended within thirty years, so there is not a single American State that has not changed the principles of its legislation in that time. As for the laws themselves, one glance at the archives of the various States of the Union is enough to show that in America the legislator’s activity never slackens. This is not because American democracy is naturally less stable than any other. It is because American democracy is allowed to follow its capricious inclinations in making laws. *b

b [ The legislative acts issued by the State of Massachusetts alone, from the year 1780 to the present time, already fill three stout volumes. And it must not be forgotten that the collection I mean was published in 1823, when many old laws that had fallen out of use were left out. The State of Massachusetts, which is no more populous than a department of France, may be considered the most stable, the most consistent and the most sagacious in its undertakings of the whole Union.]

The omnipotence of the majority, and the rapid as well as absolute way its decisions are carried out in the United States, not only makes the law unstable. It has the same influence on the execution of the law and on the conduct of the public administration. The majority is the only power that it is important to court, so all its projects are taken up with the greatest ardor. But as soon as its attention is distracted, all this ardor dies away. In the free States of Europe, by contrast, the administration is both independent and secure, so the projects of the legislature are carried out even when its immediate attention is directed to other matters.

In America certain improvements are undertaken with much more zeal and activity than elsewhere. In Europe the same ends are advanced with much less social effort, but that effort is applied more continuously.

Some years ago several pious individuals set out to improve the condition of the prisons. The public was stirred by what they reported, and reforming criminals became a very popular cause. New prisons were built, and for the first time the idea of reforming the offender as well as punishing him became part of prison discipline. But this happy change, in which the public had taken so hearty an interest and which the efforts of citizens had irresistibly hastened, could not be completed in a moment. While the new penitentiaries were being built (and the majority wanted them finished with all possible speed), the old prisons still stood, holding a great number of offenders. These jails became more unhealthy and more corrupt as the new establishments were made more handsome and better, and the contrast is easy to understand. The majority was so busy founding the new prisons that it forgot the existing ones. Once general attention turned to a new object, the care that had been given to the old ones stopped. The beneficial rules of discipline were first relaxed and then broken. So right next to a prison that bore witness to the mild and enlightened spirit of our time, one could find dungeons that reminded the visitor of the barbarity of the Middle Ages.
Tyranny of the Majority

How the principle of the sovereignty of the people is to be understood. The impossibility of conceiving a mixed government. The sovereign power must be centered somewhere. The precautions to be taken to control its action. These precautions have not been taken in the United States. The consequences.

I hold it to be an impious and detestable maxim that, politically speaking, a people has a right to do whatever it pleases. Yet I have asserted that all authority originates in the will of the majority. Am I then contradicting myself?

A general law, which bears the name of Justice, has been made and sanctioned not only by a majority of this or that people but by a majority of mankind. The rights of every people are therefore confined within the limits of what is just. A nation may be regarded as a jury empowered to represent society at large and to apply the great and general law of justice. Should such a jury, which represents society, have more power than the society in which the laws it applies originate?

When I refuse to obey an unjust law, I do not dispute the majority’s right to command. I simply appeal from the sovereignty of the people to the sovereignty of mankind. Some have claimed that a people can never entirely overstep the boundaries of justice and reason in those affairs that are especially its own, and that full power may therefore be given without fear to the majority that represents it. But this is the language of a slave.

A majority taken collectively may be regarded as a being whose opinions, and most often whose interests, are opposed to those of another being, called a minority. If we admit that a man with absolute power may misuse it by wronging his adversaries, why should a majority not be open to the same reproach? Men do not change their character by coming together in numbers, and their patience in the face of obstacles does not grow with their awareness of their strength. *c For these reasons I can never willingly give any number of my fellow creatures the unlimited authority that I would refuse to any one of them.

c [ No one will assert that a people cannot do forcible wrong to another people. But parties may be looked on as lesser nations within a greater one, and they are strangers to each other. So if it is admitted that a nation can act tyrannically toward another nation, it cannot be denied that a party may do the same toward another party.]

I do not think it possible to combine several principles in the same government in such a way as to keep freedom and really set the principles against one another. The form of government usually called mixed has always seemed to me a mere chimera. Strictly speaking, there is no such thing as a mixed government, in the sense usually given to that term, because in every community one principle of action or another can be found that outweighs the rest. England in the last century is the example most often cited of this form of government. In fact it was an essentially aristocratic State, although it contained very powerful elements of democracy. For its laws and customs were such that the aristocracy could not fail to prevail in the end and bring the direction of public affairs under its own will. The error arose from paying too much attention to the actual struggle going on between the nobles and the people, and not considering the probable outcome of the contest, which was in reality the important point. When a community really has a mixed government, that is, when it is equally divided between two opposed principles, it must either pass through a revolution or fall into complete dissolution.

I am therefore of the opinion that one social power must always be made to predominate over the others. But I think liberty is in danger when this power meets no obstacles that might slow its course and force it to moderate its own vehemence.

Unlimited power is in itself a bad and dangerous thing. Human beings are not able to exercise it with discretion, and only God can be omnipotent, because His wisdom and His justice are always equal to His power. But no power on earth is so worthy of honor in itself, or of reverent obedience for the rights it represents, that I would agree to admit its uncontrolled and all-predominant authority. When I see the right and the means of absolute command given to a people or a king, to an aristocracy or a democracy, to a monarchy or a republic, I recognize the seed of tyranny, and I travel on to a land of more hopeful institutions.

In my opinion the main evil of the present democratic institutions of the United States does not come, as is often claimed in Europe, from their weakness, but from their overpowering strength. What alarms me most is not the excessive liberty that reigns in that country but the very inadequate safeguards against tyranny.

When an individual or a party is wronged in the United States, to whom can he turn for redress? To public opinion? Public opinion is the majority. To the legislature? It represents the majority and obeys its orders without question. To the executive power? It is appointed by the majority and remains a passive tool in its hands. The public troops are the majority under arms. The jury is the majority with the right to hear judicial cases. In certain States even the judges are elected by the majority. However unjust or absurd the wrong you complain of, you must put up with it as best you can. *d

d [ A striking instance of the excesses that the despotism of the majority can cause occurred at Baltimore in 1812. At that time the war was very popular in Baltimore. A newspaper that had taken the other side of the question aroused the anger of the inhabitants by its opposition. The crowd gathered, broke the printing presses and attacked the houses of the newspaper’s editors. The militia was called out, but no one obeyed the call. The only way to save the poor wretches threatened by the frenzy of the mob was to throw them into prison as common criminals. But even this precaution was useless. The mob gathered again during the night, and the magistrates again made a vain attempt to call out the militia. The prison was broken into, one of the editors was killed on the spot, and the others were left for dead. When the guilty parties were brought to trial, the jury acquitted them.

One day I said to an inhabitant of Pennsylvania, “Please explain to me how it happens that in a State founded by Quakers and famous for its toleration, freed Black people are not allowed to exercise civil rights. They pay taxes. Is it not fair that they should have a vote?”
“You insult us,” my informant replied, “if you imagine that our legislators could have committed so gross an act of injustice and intolerance.”
“What! Then Black people have the right to vote in this county?”
“Without the smallest doubt.”
“How does it happen, then, that at the polling place this morning I did not see a single Black person in the whole meeting?”
“This is not the fault of the law. Black people have an undisputed right to vote, but they voluntarily stay away.”
“A very pretty piece of modesty on their part!” I answered.

“Why, the truth is that they are not unwilling to vote, but they are afraid of being mistreated. In this country the law is sometimes unable to maintain its authority without the support of the majority. But in this case the majority has very strong prejudices against Black people, and the magistrates are unable to protect them in the exercise of their legal rights.”
“What! Then the majority claims the right not only to make the laws but to break the laws it has made?”]

Suppose, on the other hand, that a legislative power could be constituted so as to represent the majority without necessarily being the slave of its passions. Suppose an executive could be constituted so as to keep a certain degree of uncontrolled authority, and a judiciary so as to remain independent of the other two powers. A government would then be formed that would still be democratic without any risk of tyrannical abuse.

I do not say that tyrannical abuses often occur in America today. But I maintain that no sure barrier is set against them, and that the causes that moderate the government are to be found in the circumstances and customs of the country more than in its laws.
Effects of the Unlimited Power of the Majority on the Arbitrary Authority of American Public Officials
The liberty that American laws leave to public officials within a certain sphere, and their power.

A distinction must be drawn between tyranny and arbitrary power. Tyranny may be exercised through the law, and in that case it is not arbitrary. Arbitrary power may be exercised for the good of the community at large, and in that case it is not tyrannical. Tyranny usually uses arbitrary means, but if necessary it can rule without them.

In the United States the unbounded power of the majority favors the legal despotism of the legislature, and it equally favors the arbitrary authority of the magistrate. The majority has complete control over the law, both when it is made and when it is carried out. It has equal authority over those who hold power and over the community at large. It therefore regards public officials as its passive agents and readily entrusts the task of serving its designs to their vigilance. The details of their office and the privileges they are to enjoy are rarely defined in advance. Instead the majority treats them as a master treats servants who are always working under his eye, and whom he can direct or reprimand at any moment.

In general, American officials are far more independent than French civil officers within the sphere prescribed to them. Sometimes the popular authority even allows them to go beyond those limits. They are protected by opinion and backed by the cooperation of the majority, and so they dare to show their power in ways that astonish a European. In this way habits are formed in the heart of a free country that may one day prove fatal to its liberties.
Power Exercised by the Majority in America over Opinion

In America, when the majority has once irrevocably decided a question, all discussion ceases. The reason for this. The moral power the majority exercises over opinion. Democratic republics have taken from despotism its physical instruments. Their despotism rules the minds of men.

It is by examining how public opinion shows itself in the United States that we see clearly how far the power of the majority surpasses all the powers we know in Europe. Intellectual principles exert an influence so invisible, and often so impossible to measure, that they defeat the efforts of oppression. At the present time the most absolute monarchs in Europe cannot stop certain ideas opposed to their authority from circulating secretly throughout their dominions, and even in their courts. This is not so in America. As long as the majority is undecided, discussion goes on. But as soon as its decision is irrevocably pronounced, a submissive silence follows, and the friends of the measure and its opponents alike agree that it is right. The reason is perfectly clear. No monarch is so absolute that he can gather all the powers of society into his own hands and overcome all opposition with the energy of a majority that has the right to make and carry out the laws.

The authority of a king is purely physical. It controls the actions of the subject without subduing his private will. But the majority has a power that is both physical and moral at once. It acts on the will as well as on the actions of men, and it suppresses not only all contest but all controversy. I know of no country in which there is so little true independence of mind and freedom of discussion as in America. In any constitutional state in Europe, every kind of religious and political theory may be advocated and spread abroad. No country in Europe is so subdued by a single authority that it lacks citizens ready to shield from the consequences of his boldness the man who raises his voice for the truth. If he is unfortunate enough to live under an absolute government, the people are on his side. If he lives in a free country, he can find shelter behind the authority of the throne, should he need it. In some countries the aristocratic part of society supports him, and in others the democracy does. But in a nation with democratic institutions organized as they are in the United States, there is only one authority, one single element of strength and success, and nothing beyond it.

In America the majority raises very formidable barriers around the liberty of opinion. Within these barriers an author may write whatever he pleases, but he will regret it if he ever steps beyond them. He is not exposed to the terrors of an auto-da-fé, but he is tormented by the slights and persecutions of daily abuse. His political career is closed forever, because he has offended the only authority that can advance his success. Every kind of compensation, even that of celebrity, is refused him. Before he published his opinions, he imagined he shared them with many others. But as soon as he has declared them openly, his overbearing opponents loudly condemn him, while those who think as he does but lack the courage to say so abandon him in silence. In the end he gives way, worn down by his daily efforts, and he falls silent, as if tormented by remorse for having spoken the truth.

Chains and executioners were the crude instruments that tyranny once used. But the civilization of our age has refined the arts of despotism, which had seemed already perfected enough. The excesses of monarchical power had devised a variety of physical means of oppression. The democratic republics of the present day have made oppression as entirely a matter of the mind as the will it is meant to coerce. Under the absolute rule of a single despot, the body was attacked in order to subdue the soul, but the soul escaped the blows aimed at it and rose above the attempt. Tyranny in democratic republics takes a different course. There the body is left free, and the soul is enslaved. The sovereign can no longer say, “You shall think as I do, or die.” But he says, “You are free to think differently from me, and to keep your life, your property and all that you own. But if you choose this, you are from now on a stranger among your own people. You may keep your civil rights, but they will be useless to you, for you will never be chosen by your fellow citizens if you ask for their votes, and they will pretend to scorn you if you ask for their esteem. You will remain among men, but you will be deprived of the rights of mankind. Your fellow creatures will shun you like an unclean being, and even those who are most convinced of your innocence will abandon you too, for fear of being shunned in their turn. Go in peace! I have given you your life, but it is an existence incomparably worse than death.”

Monarchical institutions have made despotism hateful. Let us beware that democratic republics do not bring oppression back and make it less hateful and less degrading in the eyes of the many by making it still heavier for the few.

In the proudest nations of the Old World, works have been published expressly to censure the vices and mock the follies of the times. Labruyere lived in the palace of Louis XIV when he wrote his chapter on the Great, and Moliere criticized the courtiers in the very plays that were performed before the Court. But the ruling power in the United States will not be made fun of. The smallest reproach irritates its sensitivity, and the slightest joke with any foundation in truth makes it indignant. Everything, from the style of its language to the more solid virtues of its character, must be praised. No writer, whatever his eminence, can escape paying this tribute of flattery to his fellow citizens. The majority lives in the constant practice of self-praise, and there are certain truths that the Americans can learn only from strangers or from experience.

If great writers have not yet appeared in America, the reason is simply given by these facts. There can be no literary genius without freedom of opinion, and freedom of opinion does not exist in America. The Inquisition was never able to stop a vast number of anti-religious books from circulating in Spain. The empire of the majority succeeds much better in the United States, since it actually removes the wish to publish such books. There are unbelievers in America, but, to tell the truth, there is no public voice of unbelief. Some governments have tried to protect the morality of nations by banning licentious books. In the United States no one is punished for writing this sort of work, but no one is tempted to write it. This is not because all the citizens are spotless in their morals, but because the majority of the community is decent and orderly.

In these cases the advantages gained from the exercise of this power are unquestionable. I am simply discussing the nature of the power itself. This irresistible authority is a constant fact, and its wise exercise is a matter of chance.
Effects of the Tyranny of the Majority on the National Character of the Americans

Effects of the tyranny of the majority have so far been felt more in customs than in the conduct of society — They check the development of leading characters — Democratic republics organized like the United States put the practice of courting favor within the reach of the many — Proofs of this spirit in the United States — Why there is more patriotism in the people than in those who govern in its name.

The tendencies I have just mentioned are still only slightly perceptible in political society, but they are already beginning to have an unfavorable influence on the national character of the Americans. I am inclined to attribute the unusual scarcity of distinguished political figures to the ever-increasing activity of the despotism of the majority in the United States. When the American Revolution broke out, such figures appeared in great numbers, for public opinion then served not to tyrannize over individuals but to direct their efforts. Those celebrated men took a full part in the general stirring of minds common at that time. They won a high degree of personal fame, which reflected back on the nation but was by no means borrowed from it.

In absolute governments, the great nobles nearest the throne flatter the sovereign’s passions and willingly bow to his whims. But the mass of the nation does not degrade itself by servitude. It often submits from weakness, from habit or from ignorance, and sometimes from loyalty. Some nations have been known to sacrifice their own desires to those of the sovereign with pleasure and pride, and so show a kind of independence in the very act of submission. These peoples are miserable, but they are not degraded. There is a great difference between doing what one does not approve of and pretending to approve of what one does. The first is the necessary lot of a weak person, and the second suits the temper of a lackey.

In free countries, everyone is more or less called on to give his opinion on affairs of state. In democratic republics, public life is constantly mixed up with domestic affairs, the sovereign authority is accessible from every side, and its attention can almost always be caught by shouting. In such countries more people are found who play on its weaknesses and live at the expense of its passions than in absolute monarchies. This is not because men are naturally worse in these States than elsewhere, but because the temptation is both stronger and easier to reach. The result is a far more widespread debasement of the character of citizens.

Democratic republics spread the practice of currying favor with the many, and they bring it into a greater number of classes at once. This is one of the most serious reproaches that can be made against them. It is especially true in democratic States organized on the principles of the American republics, where the authority of the majority is so absolute and so irresistible that a man must give up his rights as a citizen, and almost renounce his quality as a human being, if he means to stray from the track it lays down.

In the immense crowd that throngs the avenues to power in the United States, I found very few men who showed any of that manly candor and that vigorous independence of opinion that often distinguished the Americans in former times, and that is the leading feature of distinguished characters wherever they are found. At first sight it seems as if all American minds were formed on one model, so closely do they agree in their way of judging. A stranger does sometimes meet Americans who dissent from these rigid formulas. They are men who deplore the defects of the laws and the changeableness and ignorance of democracy. They even go so far as to notice the evil tendencies that damage the national character, and to point out remedies that might be applied. But no one is there to hear these things except you, and you, to whom these private reflections are confided, are a stranger and a bird of passage. They are very ready to tell you truths that are useless to you, but in public they continue to speak a different language.

If these lines are ever read in America, I am sure of two things. First, everyone who reads them will raise his voice to condemn me. Second, very many of them will acquit me in the depths of their conscience.

I have heard talk of patriotism in the United States, and it is a virtue that can be found among the people, but never among the leaders of the people. This can be explained by analogy. Despotism debases the oppressed much more than the oppressor. In absolute monarchies the king often has great virtues, but the courtiers are invariably servile. It is true that American courtiers do not say “Sire” or “Your Majesty,” a distinction without a difference. They are forever talking about the natural intelligence of the populace they serve. They do not debate which of their master’s virtues is most worthy of admiration, for they assure him that he possesses every virtue under heaven without having acquired them, or without caring to acquire them. They do not give him their daughters and wives to be raised at his pleasure to the rank of his concubines, but by sacrificing their opinions they prostitute themselves. Moralists and philosophers in America are not obliged to hide their opinions under the veil of allegory. But before they venture a harsh truth, they say, “We know that the people we are addressing is too far above all the weaknesses of human nature to lose its temper for an instant. We would not speak this way if we were not speaking to men whose virtues and intelligence make them more worthy of freedom than all the rest of the world.” The flatterers of Louis XIV could not have flattered more skillfully. For my part, I am convinced that in all governments, whatever their nature, servility will cower before force and flattery will cling to power. The only way to keep men from degrading themselves is to give no one that unlimited authority which is the surest way of debasing them.
The Greatest Dangers of the American Republics Come from the Unlimited Power of the Majority

Democratic republics are liable to perish from a misuse of their power and not from weakness. The governments of the American republics are more centralized and more energetic than those of the monarchies of Europe. The dangers that result from this. The opinions of Hamilton and Jefferson on this point.

Governments usually fall victim either to weakness or to tyranny. In the first case their power slips away from them. In the second it is wrested from their grasp. Many observers who have witnessed the anarchy of democratic States have imagined that the government of those States was naturally weak and powerless. The truth is that once hostilities have begun between parties, the government loses its control over society. But I do not think that a democratic power is naturally without force or without resources. Rather, it is almost always through the abuse of its force and the misuse of its resources that a democratic government fails. Anarchy is almost always produced by its tyranny or its mistakes, not by its lack of strength.

It is important not to confuse stability with force, or the greatness of a thing with its duration. In democratic republics, the power that directs *e society is not stable, for it often changes hands and takes a new direction. But whichever way it turns, its force is almost irresistible. The governments of the American republics seem to me as centralized as those of the absolute monarchies of Europe, and more energetic than they are. I therefore do not imagine that they will perish from weakness. *f
e [ This power may be centered in an assembly, in which case it will be strong without being stable. Or it may be centered in an individual, in which case it will be less strong but more stable.]

f [ I assume it is hardly necessary to remind the reader, here and throughout the rest of this chapter, that I am speaking not of the Federal government but of the separate governments of each State, which the majority controls as it pleases.]

If the free institutions of America are ever destroyed, that may be attributed to the unlimited authority of the majority, which may at some future time drive the minorities to desperation and force them to resort to physical force. Anarchy will then be the result, but it will have been brought about by despotism.

Mr. Hamilton gives the same opinion in the “Federalist,” No. 51. “It is of great importance in a republic not only to guard the society against the oppression of its rulers, but to guard one part of the society against the injustice of the other part. Justice is the end of government. It is the end of civil society. It ever has been, and ever will be, pursued until it be obtained, or until liberty be lost in the pursuit. In a society, under the forms of which the stronger faction can readily unite and oppress the weaker, anarchy may as truly be said to reign as in a state of nature, where the weaker individual is not secured against the violence of the stronger: and as in the latter state even the stronger individuals are prompted by the uncertainty of their condition to submit to a government which may protect the weak as well as themselves, so in the former state will the more powerful factions be gradually induced by a like motive to wish for a government which will protect all parties, the weaker as well as the more powerful. It can be little doubted that, if the State of Rhode Island was separated from the Confederacy and left to itself, the insecurity of right under the popular form of government within such narrow limits would be displayed by such reiterated oppressions of the factious majorities, that some power altogether independent of the people would soon be called for by the voice of the very factions whose misrule had proved the necessity of it.”

Jefferson put it this way in a letter to Madison: *g “The executive power in our Government is not the only, perhaps not even the principal, object of my solicitude. The tyranny of the Legislature is really the danger most to be feared, and will continue to be so for many years to come. The tyranny of the executive power will come in its turn, but at a more distant period.” I am glad to cite Jefferson on this subject rather than anyone else, because I consider him the most powerful advocate democracy has ever produced.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — Causes Mitigating Tyranny In The United States
paragraphs: The national majority does not claim to conduct all public business. It is obliged to use the township and county magistrates to carry out its supreme decisions.

I have already pointed out the distinction between a centralized government and a centralized administration. The first exists in America, but the second is almost unknown there. Suppose the directing power of the American communities had both of these instruments of government at its disposal, and joined the habit of executing its own commands to the right of commanding. Suppose that, after establishing the general principles of government, it went down into the details of public business, and that, having regulated the great interests of the country, it could reach into the privacy of individual interests. Freedom would soon be banished from the New World.

But in the United States the majority, which so often shows the tastes and inclinations of a despot, still lacks the more perfect instruments of tyranny. In the American republics the activity of the central government has never yet extended beyond a limited number of objects prominent enough to call for its attention. It has never regulated the secondary affairs of society, and nothing so far has revealed any wish on its part to interfere in them. The majority is becoming more and more absolute, but it has not increased the prerogatives of the central government. Those great prerogatives have stayed within a certain sphere, and although the despotism of the majority may be galling on one point, it cannot be said to reach every point. However far the dominant party in the nation may be carried away by its passions, however ardently it pursues its projects, it cannot make all citizens comply with its wishes in the same manner and at the same time throughout the country. When the central government that represents the majority has issued a decree, it must entrust the carrying out of its will to agents whom it often does not control and cannot direct at every moment. The townships, municipal bodies, and counties can therefore be seen as hidden breakwaters, which check or divide the tide of popular excitement. If an oppressive law were passed, the liberties of the people would still be protected by the way in which that law would have to be put into effect. The majority cannot descend to the details, and (as I will venture to call them) the pettiness, of administrative tyranny. Nor does the people have that full awareness of its own authority which would lead it to interfere in these matters. It knows the extent of its natural powers, but it does not know the added resources that the art of government could supply.

This point deserves attention. Suppose a democratic republic like that of the United States were ever founded in a country where the power of a single individual had previously existed, and where the effects of a centralized administration had sunk deep into the habits and laws of the people. I do not hesitate to say that in such a country a more unbearable despotism would prevail than any that now exists in the monarchical States of Europe, or indeed any that could be found this side of the borders of Asia.
The Profession of the Law in the United States Serves to Counterpoise the Democracy

The usefulness of identifying the natural inclinations of the members of the legal profession—These men are called to play a prominent part in the future society—How the particular pursuits of lawyers give their ideas an aristocratic turn—Accidental causes that may check this tendency—How easily the aristocracy joins forces with legal men—The use of lawyers to a despot—The legal profession is the only aristocratic element that will combine with the natural elements of democracy—Particular causes that tend to give English and American lawyers an aristocratic turn of mind—The aristocracy of America is on the bench and at the bar—The influence of lawyers on American society—Their particular habits as magistrates affect the legislature, the administration, and even the people.

In visiting the Americans and studying their laws, we see that the authority they have entrusted to members of the legal profession, and the influence these individuals have in the government, are the most powerful existing security against the excesses of democracy. This effect seems to me to come from a general cause that is worth investigating, since it may produce similar consequences elsewhere.

Members of the legal profession have taken an important part in all the upheavals of political society in Europe during the last five hundred years. At one time they have been the instruments of those who held political authority, and at another they have succeeded in turning political authorities into their instrument. In the Middle Ages they gave powerful support to the Crown, and since then they have worked as hard as they could to limit the royal prerogative. In England they have formed a close alliance with the aristocracy. In France they have proved to be that class’s most dangerous enemies. My aim is to ask whether, in all these circumstances, lawyers have been swayed by sudden and momentary impulses, or whether they have been driven by principles that are inherent in their pursuits and that will always recur in history. What prompts me to this inquiry is the thought that this particular class of men will most likely play a prominent part in the order of things that the events of our time are bringing into being.

Men who have given themselves especially to legal pursuits take from that work certain habits of order, a liking for formalities, and an instinctive respect for the orderly connection of ideas. These make them naturally very hostile to the revolutionary spirit and to the unreflecting passions of the crowd.

The special knowledge that lawyers gain from their studies secures them a separate station in society, and they form a kind of privileged body in the scale of intelligence. The idea of their own superiority comes back to them constantly in the practice of their profession. They are the masters of a science that is necessary but not very generally known. They serve as arbiters between citizens. And the habit of steering the blind passions of parties in a lawsuit toward their own purposes gives them a certain contempt for the judgment of the multitude. It may be added that they naturally form a body, not through any prior understanding or any agreement directing them to a common end, but because the similarity of their studies and the uniformity of their procedures link their minds together as much as a common interest could unite their efforts.

Some of the tastes and habits of the aristocracy can therefore be found in the character of men in the legal profession. They share the same instinctive love of order and formalities. They feel the same repugnance toward the actions of the multitude, and the same secret contempt for the government of the people. I do not mean that the natural inclinations of lawyers are strong enough to sway them irresistibly, for they, like most other men, are governed by their private interests and the advantages of the moment.

In a state of society where lawyers are prevented from holding in the political world the rank they enjoy in private life, we may be sure they will be the foremost agents of revolution. But we must then ask whether the cause that leads them to innovate and destroy is accidental, or whether it belongs to some lasting purpose of theirs. It is true that lawyers chiefly contributed to the overthrow of the French monarchy in 1789. But it remains to be seen whether they acted that way because they had studied the laws, or because they were barred from taking part in the work of legislation.

Five hundred years ago the English nobles led the people and spoke in its name. Today the aristocracy supports the throne and defends the royal prerogative. Even so, the aristocracy has its own particular instincts and inclinations. We must be careful not to confuse isolated members of a body with the body itself. In all free governments, whatever their form, members of the legal profession will be found at the head of all parties. The same remark applies to the aristocracy, for almost all the democratic convulsions that have shaken the world have been led by nobles.

A privileged body can never satisfy the ambition of all its members. It always has more talents and more passions to satisfy and to employ than it has places to offer. As a result, one usually finds a considerable number of individuals inclined to attack the very privileges that they find impossible to turn to their own advantage.

I do not claim, then, that all members of the legal profession are at all times friends of order and opponents of innovation, but only that most of them usually are. In a community where lawyers are allowed to occupy without opposition the high station that naturally belongs to them, their general spirit will be strongly conservative and anti-democratic. When an aristocracy excludes the leaders of that profession from its ranks, it creates enemies who are all the more dangerous to its security because their industrious pursuits make them independent of the nobility. They also feel themselves its equals in intelligence, although they have less wealth and less power. But whenever an aristocracy agrees to share some of its privileges with these same individuals, the two classes combine very readily, and take on, as it were, the solidity of a single order bound by family interests.

In the same way, I am inclined to believe that a monarch will always be able to turn legal practitioners into the most useful instruments of his authority. There is a far greater affinity between lawyers and the executive power than between lawyers and the people. In the same way, there is a greater natural affinity between the nobles and the monarch than between the nobles and the people, although the higher orders of society have occasionally resisted the prerogative of the Crown together with the lower classes.

Lawyers value public order above every other consideration, and the best security of public order is authority. We must not forget that, although they prize the free institutions of their country highly, they value the legality of those institutions far more. They are less afraid of tyranny than of arbitrary power. As long as the legislature takes it upon itself to deprive men of their independence, they are not dissatisfied.

I am therefore convinced that a prince who, facing an encroaching democracy, tried to weaken the judicial authority in his dominions and to reduce the political influence of lawyers would make a great mistake. He would let the substance of authority slip away in order to grasp at its shadow. He would act more wisely by bringing men trained in the law into the government. If he entrusted them with the conduct of a despotic power that bore some marks of violence, that power would most likely take on the outward features of justice and legality in their hands.

The government of democracy favors the political power of lawyers. When the wealthy, the noble, and the prince are excluded from the government, lawyers are sure to hold the highest positions in their own right, as it were, since they are the only men of knowledge and ability, outside the sphere of the people, who can be the object of the popular choice. If their tastes lead them to join with the aristocracy and support the Crown, their interests naturally bring them into contact with the people. They like the government of democracy without sharing its inclinations and without imitating its weaknesses. From this they derive a twofold authority, from it and over it. The people in democratic states do not distrust members of the legal profession, because it is well known that they have an interest in serving the popular cause. The people listen to them without irritation, because they do not attribute any sinister designs to them. The object of lawyers is not, indeed, to overthrow the institutions of democracy, but they constantly try to give it an impulse that diverts it from its real tendency, by means that are foreign to its nature. Lawyers belong to the people by birth and interest, and to the aristocracy by habit and taste, and they may be looked upon as the natural bond and connecting link between the two great classes of society.

The legal profession is the only aristocratic element that can be blended without violence with the natural elements of democracy, and that can be combined with them advantageously and permanently.
