But I learned from what they said that men are not guilty in the eyes of God for any opinions about political government that they may sincerely profess, any more than for their mistakes in building a house or plowing a furrow. I saw that these ministers of the gospel avoided all parties with the care that people show for their own personal interest. These facts convinced me that what I had been told was true. It then became my aim to investigate the causes, and to ask how it happened that the real authority of religion was increased by a state of things that reduced its apparent strength. These causes did not long escape my inquiries.

The short span of sixty years can never satisfy the imagination of man, nor can the imperfect joys of this world satisfy his heart. Man alone, of all created beings, shows a natural contempt for existence and yet a boundless desire to exist. He scorns life, but he dreads annihilation. These conflicting feelings constantly drive his soul to contemplate a future state, and religion directs his thoughts there. Religion, then, is simply another form of hope, and it is no less natural to the human heart than hope itself. Men cannot abandon their religious faith without a kind of mental aberration and a sort of violent distortion of their true nature. But they are irresistibly brought back to more devout feelings, for unbelief is an accident, and faith is the only permanent state of mankind. If we consider religious institutions from a purely human point of view, we may say that they draw an inexhaustible source of strength from man himself, since they belong to one of the constituent principles of human nature.

I am aware that at certain times religion may reinforce this influence, which originates in itself, with the artificial power of the laws and the support of the temporal institutions that direct society. Religions closely united to the governments of the earth have been known to exercise a sovereign authority drawn from the twofold source of terror and faith. But when a religion enters into an alliance of this kind, I do not hesitate to affirm that it makes the same mistake as a man who would sacrifice his future to his present welfare. In gaining a power to which it has no claim, it puts at risk the authority that is rightfully its own. When a religion founds its empire on the desire for immortality that lives in every human heart, it may aspire to universal dominion. But when it attaches itself to a government, it must necessarily adopt maxims that apply only to certain nations. Thus, by forming an alliance with a political power, religion increases its authority over a few and gives up the hope of reigning over all.

As long as a religion rests on those feelings that console every affliction, it can win the affections of mankind. But if it becomes mixed up with the bitter passions of the world, it may be forced to defend allies given to it by its interests and not by the principle of love, or to repel as enemies men who are still attached to its spirit, however opposed they may be to the powers with which it is allied. The Church cannot share the temporal power of the state without becoming the object of some of the animosity that the state arouses.

The political powers that seem most firmly established often have no better guarantee of their duration than the opinions of a generation, the interests of the time, or the life of one individual. A law can change the social condition that seems most fixed and settled, and when the social condition changes, everything else must change with it. The powers of society are more or less fleeting, like the years we spend on earth. They follow one another rapidly, like the passing cares of life, and no government has ever yet been founded on an unchanging disposition of the human heart or on an imperishable interest.

As long as a religion is sustained by those feelings, tendencies, and passions that occur in the same forms in every period of history, it can defy the efforts of time. At the least, it can be destroyed only by another religion. But when religion clings to the interests of the world, it becomes almost as fragile as the powers of the earth. It is the only one of them all that can hope for immortality. But if it is tied to their ephemeral authority, it shares their fortunes, and may fall along with the transient passions that supported them for a day. The alliance that religion makes with political powers must be burdensome to itself, since it does not need their help to live, and by giving them its help it may expose itself to decay.

The danger I have just pointed out always exists, but it is not always equally visible. In some ages governments seem imperishable; in others, the existence of society seems more precarious than the life of a man. Some constitutions plunge the citizens into a lethargic drowsiness, and others rouse them to feverish excitement. When governments seem so strong and laws so stable, men do not see the dangers that may arise from a union of Church and State. When governments show so much weakness and laws so much inconstancy, the danger is obvious, but by then it can no longer be avoided. To be effective, measures must be taken to detect its approach.

The more a nation takes on a democratic social condition, and the more communities show democratic tendencies, the more dangerous it becomes to connect religion with political institutions. For the time is coming when authority will be tossed from hand to hand, when political theories will succeed one another, and when men, laws, and constitutions will disappear or be modified from day to day, and this not for a season only but unceasingly. Agitation and instability are inherent in the nature of democratic republics, just as stagnation and inertia are the law of absolute monarchies.

The Americans change the head of the government once in four years, elect new legislators every two years, and renew the provincial officers every twelve months. They have abandoned the political world to the attempts of innovators. If they had not placed religion beyond the innovators’ reach, where could it abide in the ebb and flow of human opinions? Where would the respect that belongs to it be paid, amid the struggles of faction? And what would become of its immortality, in the midst of perpetual decay? The American clergy were the first to see this truth and to act on it. They saw that they must give up their religious influence if they were to strive for political power, and they chose to give up the support of the state rather than share its changing fortunes.

Perhaps religion in America has less power than it has held at certain times among certain peoples, but its influence lasts longer. It relies only on its own resources, and no one can take those away. It operates within a narrow circle of principles, yet those principles belong wholly to it, and nobody disputes its authority over them.

On every side in Europe we hear voices complaining of the absence of religious faith and asking how to restore to religion some remnant of its original authority. It seems to me that we must first consider carefully what ought to be the natural state of men with regard to religion at the present time. When we know what we have to hope and to fear, we may see the end toward which our efforts ought to be directed.

The two great dangers that threaten the existence of religions are schism and indifference. In ages of fervent devotion, men sometimes abandon their religion, but they shake it off only in order to adopt another. Their faith changes its objects, but it suffers no decline. The old religion then arouses enthusiastic attachment or bitter enmity on either side. Some leave it in anger, others cling to it with increased devotion, and although persuasions differ, irreligion is unknown. This is not the case, however, when a religious belief is secretly undermined by doctrines that may be called negative, since they deny the truth of one religion without affirming that of any other. Prodigious revolutions then take place in the human mind, without the apparent cooperation of human passions and almost without man’s knowledge. Men lose the objects of their fondest hopes as if through forgetfulness. They are carried away by an imperceptible current that they lack the courage to resist, but which they follow with regret, since it bears them from a faith they love to a skepticism that plunges them into despair.

In ages that fit this description, men desert their religious opinions out of lukewarmness rather than dislike. They do not reject them, but the feelings that once sustained them disappear. Yet although the unbeliever does not admit religion to be true, he still considers it useful. Looking at religious institutions from a human point of view, he acknowledges their influence on customs and on legislation. He admits that they may help men live in peace with one another and prepare them gently for the hour of death. He regrets the faith he has lost. Since he has been deprived of a treasure whose full value he has learned to recognize, he hesitates to take it from those who still possess it.

On the other hand, those who continue to believe are not afraid to avow their faith openly. They look on those who do not share their persuasion as more deserving of pity than of opposition, and they know that to win the esteem of unbelievers they need not follow their example. They are hostile to no one in the world. They do not consider the society in which they live as an arena in which religion is bound to face its thousand deadly foes, and so they love their contemporaries while they condemn their weaknesses and lament their errors.

Since those who do not believe conceal their unbelief, and those who believe display their faith, public opinion declares itself in favor of religion. Love, support, and honor are bestowed on it, and only by searching the human soul can we detect the wounds it has received. The mass of mankind, who are never without a religious feeling, see nothing at odds with the established faith. The instinctive desire for a future life brings the crowd to the altar and opens men’s hearts to the precepts and consolations of religion.

But this picture does not apply to us. Among us there are men who have ceased to believe in Christianity without adopting any other religion; others who are in the perplexities of doubt and who already pretend not to believe; and still others who are afraid to avow the Christian faith that they secretly cherish.

Amid these lukewarm partisans and ardent opponents there exists a small number of believers who are ready to brave all obstacles and to scorn all dangers in defense of their faith. They have done violence to human weakness in order to rise above public opinion. Excited by the effort they have made, they scarcely know where to stop. They know that the first use the French made of independence was to attack religion, so they look on their contemporaries with dread and recoil in alarm from the liberty their fellow citizens are seeking to obtain. Because unbelief appears to them a novelty, they include everything new in one indiscriminate hostility. They are at war with their age and country, and they regard every opinion put forward there as the necessary enemy of the faith.

Men today are not naturally in this condition with regard to religion. Some extraordinary or accidental cause must be at work in France, preventing the human mind from following its original tendencies and pushing it past the point where it would naturally stop. I am profoundly convinced that this extraordinary and accidental cause is the close tie between politics and religion. Europe’s unbelievers attack Christians as their political opponents rather than as their religious adversaries. They hate the Christian religion as the opinion of a party far more than as a mistaken belief, and they reject the clergy less because the clergy are the representatives of the Divinity than because they are the allies of authority.

In Europe, Christianity has been closely united to the powers of the earth. Those powers are now in decay, and Christianity is, as it were, buried under their ruins. The living body of religion has been bound to the dead corpse of an outworn political order. Cut the bonds that hold it, and what is alive will rise once more. I do not know what could restore the Christian Church of Europe to the energy of its earlier days. That power belongs to God alone. But it may be within the reach of human policy to leave the faith free to exercise the full strength that it still retains.
How the Instruction, the Habits, and the Practical Experience of the Americans Promote the Success of Their Democratic Institutions

What is meant by the education of the American people — The human mind more superficially educated in the United States than in Europe — No one completely uneducated — The reason for this — How quickly opinions spread even in the uncultivated States of the West — Practical experience more useful to the Americans than book learning.
I have very little to add to what I have already said about the influence that the education and habits of the Americans have on the maintenance of their political institutions.

America has so far produced very few distinguished writers. It has no great historians and not a single eminent poet. Its inhabitants regard what are properly called literary pursuits with a kind of disapproval, and there are towns of quite secondary importance in Europe that publish more literary works each year than the twenty-four States of the Union put together. The Americans’ cast of mind is averse to general ideas, and it does not seek theoretical discoveries. Neither politics nor manufacturing directs them to such pursuits. And although new laws are constantly being enacted in the United States, no great writers have yet inquired into the general principles of their legislation. The Americans have lawyers and commentators but no jurists, *h and they offer the world examples rather than lessons. The same observation applies to the mechanical arts. In America the inventions of Europe are adopted with shrewdness; they are perfected and adapted with admirable skill to the needs of the country. Manufactures exist, but the science of manufacturing is not cultivated, and the Americans have good workmen but very few inventors. Fulton had to offer his services to foreign nations for a long time before he was able to devote them to his own country.
h [ [This cannot truthfully be said of the country of Kent, Story, and Wheaton.]]

An observer who wants to form an opinion about the state of education among the Anglo-Americans must look at the same subject from two different points of view. If he singles out only the learned, he will be astonished to find how rare they are. But if he counts the ignorant, the American people will appear to be the most educated community in the world. The whole population, as I observed elsewhere, lies between these two extremes. In New England every citizen receives the basics of human knowledge. He is also taught the doctrines and evidences of his religion, the history of his country, and the leading features of its Constitution. In the States of Connecticut and Massachusetts it is extremely rare to find a man imperfectly acquainted with all these things, and a person wholly ignorant of them is a kind of phenomenon.

When I compare the Greek and Roman republics with these American States — the manuscript libraries of the former and their rude population with the innumerable journals and the educated people of the latter — and when I recall all the attempts that are made to judge the modern republics by the help of those of antiquity, and to infer what will happen in our time from what took place two thousand years ago, I am tempted to burn my books so that I may apply only new ideas to so new a condition of society.

What I have said of New England must not, however, be applied indiscriminately to the whole Union. As we advance toward the West or the South, the education of the people declines. In the States bordering the Gulf of Mexico, a certain number of individuals may be found, as in our own countries, who lack the rudiments of education. But there is not a single district in the United States sunk in complete ignorance, and for a very simple reason. The peoples of Europe started from the darkness of a barbarous condition to advance toward the light of civilization. Their progress has been unequal: some of them have improved rapidly, while others have lingered on the way, and some have stopped and are still sleeping beside it. *i

i [ [In the Northern States the number of people with no education is small, the largest being 241,152 in the State of New York (according to Spaulding’s “Handbook of American Statistics” for 1874). But in the South no fewer than 1,516,339 whites and 2,671,396 Black people are returned as “illiterate.”]]

This has not been the case in the United States. The Anglo-Americans settled in a state of civilization on the territory their descendants now occupy. They did not have to begin to learn; it was enough for them not to forget. Now the children of these same Americans are the people who, year by year, move their dwellings into the wilds, and with their dwellings they carry their acquired knowledge and their esteem for learning. Education has taught them the usefulness of instruction and has enabled them to pass that instruction on to their children. In the United States society has no infancy; it is born grown up.

The Americans never use the word “peasant,” because they have no idea of the distinct class that the word describes. The ignorance of earlier ages, the simplicity of country life, and the rustic manners of the villager have not survived among them. They are equally strangers to the virtues, the vices, the coarse habits, and the simple graces of an early stage of civilization. At the far borders of the Confederate States, where society meets the wilderness, a population of bold adventurers has settled. They push into the solitude of the American forests and look for a new country there, to escape the poverty that awaited them in their native provinces. As soon as the pioneer reaches the spot that is to be his refuge, he fells a few trees and builds a log house. Nothing could look more wretched than these isolated dwellings. A traveler who approaches one of them toward nightfall sees the flicker of the hearth fire through the chinks in the walls. At night, if the wind rises, he hears the roof of boughs shaking to and fro among the great forest trees. Who would not take this poor hut for a refuge of crudeness and ignorance? Yet no comparison can be drawn between the pioneer and the dwelling that shelters him. Everything around him is primitive and unformed, but he himself is the product of the labor and experience of eighteen centuries. He dresses and speaks like the people of the cities. He knows the past, is curious about the future, and is ready to argue about the present. In short, he is a highly civilized man who agrees, for a time, to live in the backwoods, and who enters the wilds of the New World with a Bible, an axe, and a bundle of newspapers.

It is hard to imagine the incredible speed with which public opinion travels in the middle of these deserts. *j I do not think that so much intellectual exchange takes place even in the most educated and populous districts of France. *k There can be no doubt that, in the United States, the education of the people contributes powerfully to the support of a democratic republic. I believe this must always be so where education that awakens the understanding is not separated from moral training that improves the heart. But I do not exaggerate this benefit at all, and I am even further from thinking, as so many people in Europe do, that men can be turned into citizens at once by teaching them to read and write. True knowledge comes mainly from experience. If the Americans had not been gradually accustomed to governing themselves, their book learning would not help them much today.

j [ I traveled along part of the frontier of the United States in a kind of cart called the mail. Day and night we rolled along at great speed on barely marked roads through immense forests. When the darkness of the woods became too thick to see through, the driver lit branches of fir, and we went on by their light. Every so often we came to a hut in the middle of the forest, which was a post office. The mail dropped an enormous bundle of letters at the door of this lonely dwelling, and we went on at full gallop, leaving the people from the neighboring log houses to come and collect their share of the treasure.

[When the author visited America the locomotive and the railroad were scarcely invented, and not yet introduced in the United States. It is superfluous to point out the immense effect of those inventions in extending civilization and developing the resources of that vast continent. In 1831 there were 51 miles of railway in the United States; in 1872 there were 60,000 miles of railway.]]

I have lived a great deal among the people of the United States, and I cannot say how much I admire their experience and their good sense. An American should never be allowed to speak of Europe, for then he will probably show a great deal of presumption and very foolish pride. He will fall back on those crude and vague ideas that are so useful to ignorant people all over the world. But if you ask him about his own country, the cloud that dimmed his intelligence lifts at once. His language becomes as clear and precise as his thoughts. He will tell you what his rights are and how he exercises them. He can point out the customs that prevail in the political world. You will find that he knows the rules of the administration well and is familiar with the workings of the laws. The citizen of the United States does not get his practical knowledge and his firm ideas from books. The schooling he has received may have prepared him to take in those ideas, but it did not supply them. The American learns the laws by taking part in making them, and he learns the forms of government by governing. The great work of society is always going on before his eyes and, as it were, under his hands.

In the United States, politics is the end and aim of education. In Europe, its main purpose is to fit men for private life. Citizens there take part in public affairs too rarely for education to anticipate it. A glance over society in the two hemispheres shows these differences even in its outward appearance.

In Europe we often carry the ideas and habits of private life into public affairs. Since we pass at once from the family circle to the government of the state, we can often be heard discussing the great interests of society in the same way we talk with our friends. The Americans, on the other hand, carry the habits of public life over into their private customs. In their country the jury system is brought into the games of schoolboys, and parliamentary rules are followed in arranging a feast.
The Laws Contribute More to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States Than the Physical Circumstances of the Country, and the Manners More Than the Laws

All the nations of America have a democratic state of society — Yet democratic institutions survive only among the Anglo-Americans — The Spaniards of South America, as favored by physical causes as the Anglo-Americans, are unable to maintain a democratic republic — Mexico, which has adopted the Constitution of the United States, is in the same situation — The Anglo-Americans of the West are less able to maintain it than those of the East — The reason for these different results.

I have observed that the maintenance of democratic institutions in the United States is due to the circumstances, the laws, and the customs of that country. *l Most Europeans know only the first of these three causes, and they tend to give it an overriding importance that it does not really have.
l [ Let me remind the reader what I mean by the word “manners” in general: the moral and intellectual characteristics of men living in society, considered as a whole.]

It is true that the Anglo-Saxons settled in the New World in a state of social equality. The low-born and the noble were not to be found among them, and prejudices of profession were always as completely unknown as prejudices of birth. So, since the condition of society was democratic, democracy came to rule without difficulty. But this circumstance is by no means unique to the United States. Almost all the colonies across the Atlantic were founded by men who were equal among themselves, or who became so by living there. Nowhere in the New World have Europeans managed to create an aristocracy. Yet democratic institutions thrive nowhere but in the United States.

The American Union has no enemies to fight. It sits in the wilderness like an island in the ocean. But nature isolated the Spaniards of South America just as much, and that has not spared them the burden of standing armies. When they have no foreign enemies, they make war on each other. The Anglo-American democracy is the only one that has so far managed to stay at peace. *m
m [ [A remark which, since the great Civil War of 1861-65, ceases to be applicable.]]

The territory of the Union offers a boundless field to human activity and inexhaustible materials for industry and labor. The passion for wealth takes the place of ambition, and the heat of faction is cooled by a sense of prosperity. But where in the world shall we find more fertile plains, mightier rivers, or more unexplored and inexhaustible riches than in South America?

Nevertheless, South America has been unable to maintain democratic institutions. Suppose the welfare of nations depended on being placed far away, with an unlimited expanse of habitable land before them. Then the Spaniards of South America would have no reason to complain of their lot. They might enjoy less prosperity than the people of the United States, and still their situation might be one that some nations in Europe would envy. Yet no nations on earth are more miserable than those of South America.

Thus physical causes are not only unable to produce results like those that occur in North America; they cannot even raise the population of South America to the level of the States of Europe, where they work in the opposite direction. Physical causes, therefore, do not affect the destiny of nations as much as has been supposed.

In New England I met men who were about to leave a country where they could have lived comfortably, to seek their fortune in the wilds. Not far from there, in Canada, I found a French population crowded into a narrow strip of land even though the same wilds lay close by. The emigrant from the United States bought a large estate with what he earned in a short period of work, while the Canadian paid as much for land as he would have paid in France. Nature offers the solitudes of the New World to Europeans, but they do not always know how to turn her gifts to account. Other peoples of America have the same physical conditions for prosperity as the Anglo-Americans, but without their laws and their customs, and these peoples are wretched. The laws and customs of the Anglo-Americans are therefore the effective cause of their greatness, which is the object of my inquiry.

I am far from supposing that the American laws are excellent in themselves. I do not think they apply to all democratic peoples, and several of them seem dangerous to me, even in the United States. Still, no one can deny that American legislation, taken as a whole, suits the genius of its people and the nature of its country extremely well. The American laws are therefore good, and a large share of the success of democratic government in America must be credited to them. But I do not believe they are the main cause of that success. They seem to me to have more influence on the social happiness of the Americans than the nature of the country does. Yet there is reason to believe that their effect is still smaller than that of the customs of the people.

The Federal laws are undoubtedly the most important part of the legislation of the United States. Mexico, which is no less fortunately situated than the Anglo-American Union, has adopted the same laws, yet it cannot accustom itself to democratic government. Some other cause is therefore at work, besides the physical circumstances and the particular laws that enable democracy to rule in the United States.

Here is another, still more striking proof. Almost all the inhabitants of the territory of the Union descend from a common stock. They speak the same language, worship God in the same way, are affected by the same physical causes, and obey the same laws. Where, then, do their characteristic differences come from? Why, in the Eastern States, does republican government show vigor and regularity and proceed with mature deliberation? Where does it get the wisdom and durability that mark its acts, while in the Western States society seems to be ruled by chance? There, public business is conducted irregularly and with a passionate, feverish excitement that does not promise a long or secure life.

I am no longer comparing the Anglo-American States with foreign nations. I am contrasting them with each other and trying to discover why they are so unlike. The arguments drawn from the nature of the country and from differences in legislation are all set aside here. Some other cause must be found, and what other cause can there be except the customs of the people?

The Anglo-Americans of the Eastern States have been used to democratic government longest, and they have formed the habits and conceived the ideas most favorable to keeping it. Democracy has gradually worked its way into their customs, their opinions, and the forms of their social life. It is found in all the details of daily life as much as in the laws. In the Eastern States the education and practical training of the people have reached their fullest development, and religion has been most thoroughly joined with liberty. Now these habits, opinions, customs, and convictions are exactly the elements of what I have called manners.

In the Western States, by contrast, some of these same advantages are still missing. Many of the Americans of the West were born in the woods, and they mix the ideas and customs of savage life with the civilization of their parents. Their passions are stronger, their religious morality has less authority, and their convictions are less secure. The inhabitants exercise no control over their fellow citizens, because they hardly know each other. The nations of the West show, to some extent, the inexperience and rough habits of a people in its infancy. For although they are made up of old elements, they have only recently come together.

The customs of the Americans of the United States are, then, the real reason why that people alone, among the American nations, can sustain a democratic government. It is the influence of customs that produces the different degrees of order and prosperity that can be seen in the several Anglo-American democracies. Europe, therefore, exaggerates what the geographical position of a country can do for the durability of democratic institutions. It gives too much weight to legislation and too little to customs. These three great causes no doubt help to regulate and direct the American democracy. But if I had to rank them in their proper order, I would say that physical circumstances count for less than the laws, and the laws are greatly subordinate to the customs of the people. I am convinced that the most favorable situation and the best possible laws cannot sustain a constitution against the customs of a country, while customs can turn even the most unfavorable situations and the worst laws to some advantage. The importance of customs is a common truth to which study and experience keep bringing us back. It may be regarded as the central point in the range of human observation, and the place where all inquiry finally ends. I insist on this point so seriously that, if I have failed to make the reader feel the great influence I attribute to the practical experience, the habits, the opinions, in short the customs of the Americans, on the survival of their institutions, then I have failed in the main object of my work.
Whether Laws and Manners Are Sufficient to Maintain Democratic Institutions in Other Countries Besides America

The Anglo-Americans, if transported into Europe, would be obliged to modify their laws — A distinction must be made between democratic institutions and American institutions — Democratic laws may be conceived that are better than, or at least different from, those the American democracy has adopted — The example of America only proves that it is possible to regulate democracy with the help of customs and legislation.

I have asserted that the success of democratic institutions in the United States depends more on the laws themselves and the customs of the people than on the nature of the country. But does it follow that the same causes would produce the same results if they were put to work elsewhere? And if the country is no adequate substitute for laws and customs, can laws and customs in their turn substitute for the country? We can easily see that we lack what we would need to answer this question. There are other peoples in the New World besides the Anglo-Americans, and since the same physical circumstances affect them, they can fairly be compared with the Anglo-Americans. But no nations outside America have adopted the same laws and customs while lacking the physical advantages that belong to the Anglo-Americans. So there is no standard of comparison, and we can only venture an opinion on this subject.

First, it seems to me that we must carefully distinguish the institutions of the United States from democratic institutions in general. When I think about Europe, with its mighty nations, populous cities, and formidable armies, and with the complexity of its politics, I cannot suppose that even the Anglo-Americans could live in our hemisphere with their ideas, their religion, and their customs and not alter their laws considerably. But we can imagine a democratic nation organized differently from the American people. It is not impossible to conceive of a government truly founded on the will of the majority, in which the majority nevertheless holds back its natural leaning toward equality. For the sake of order and stability in the state, it would consent to give a family or an individual all the prerogatives of the executive. A democratic society might exist in which the forces of the nation were more centralized than they are in the United States. The people would then have a less direct and less irresistible influence on public affairs, and yet every citizen, invested with certain rights, would still take part, within his own sphere, in running the government. What I observed among the Anglo-Americans leads me to believe that democratic institutions of this kind, if prudently introduced so that they gradually blend with the habits and mingle with the opinions of the people, might survive in other countries besides America. If the laws of the United States were the only democratic laws one could imagine, or the most perfect, I would admit that their success proves nothing about the success of democratic institutions in general in a country less favored by nature. But the laws of America seem to me defective in several ways, and I can easily imagine others of the same general kind. So the particular advantages of that country do not prove that democratic institutions cannot succeed in a nation less favored by circumstances, if it is ruled by better laws.

Suppose human nature were different in America from what it is elsewhere. Or suppose the social condition of the Americans produced among them habits and opinions different from those that arise from the same social condition in the Old World. Then the American democracies would give us no means of predicting what may happen in other democracies. Suppose, again, that the Americans showed the same propensities as all other democratic nations, and their legislators had counted on the nature of the country and the favor of circumstances to keep those propensities within proper bounds. Then the prosperity of the United States would be due entirely to physical causes, and it would give no encouragement to a people inclined to imitate their example without sharing their natural advantages. But the facts support neither of these suppositions.

In America we find the same passions as in Europe, some arising from human nature, others from the democratic condition of society. Thus in the United States I found the restlessness of heart that is natural to men when all ranks are nearly equal and everyone has the same chance of rising. I found the democratic feeling of envy expressed in a thousand different forms. I saw that the people often showed, in the conduct of affairs, a perfect mixture of ignorance and presumption, and I concluded that in America men are subject to the same failings and the same absurdities as among ourselves. But when I looked at the state of society more closely, I soon discovered that the Americans had made great and successful efforts to counteract these imperfections of human nature and to correct the natural defects of democracy. Their various municipal laws seemed to me a way of keeping the ambition of the citizens within a narrow sphere, and of turning those same passions that might have wreaked havoc in the state to the good of the township or the parish. The American legislators have succeeded, to a certain extent, in setting the notion of rights against the feelings of envy; the stability of the religious world against the constant shifting of politics; the experience of the people against its theoretical ignorance; and its practical knowledge of business against the impatience of its desires.

The Americans, then, have not relied on the nature of their country to counterbalance the dangers that arise from their Constitution and their political laws. To evils common to all democratic peoples they have applied remedies that no one but themselves had ever thought of before. Although they were the first to make the experiment, they have succeeded in it.

The customs and laws of the Americans are not the only ones that may suit a democratic people. But the Americans have shown that it would be wrong to despair of regulating democracy with the help of customs and laws. Suppose other nations take this general and fruitful idea from the Americans, without meaning to copy the particular way they have applied it. Suppose they try to prepare themselves for the social condition that Providence seems to impose on the generations of this age, and so to escape the despotism or the anarchy that threatens them. What reason is there to suppose that their efforts would fail? The organization and establishment of democracy in Christendom is the great political problem of the time. The Americans, unquestionably, have not solved this problem, but they supply useful data to those who undertake the task.
Importance of What Precedes With Respect to the State of Europe

It is easy to see why I undertook the inquiries above. The question discussed here interests not only the United States but the whole world. It concerns not one nation but all mankind. If nations whose social condition is democratic could remain free only while they lived in the wilds, we could only despair of the future of the human race. For democracy is rapidly extending its sway, and the wilds are gradually filling with people. If it were true that laws and customs are not enough to maintain democratic institutions, what refuge would remain open to nations except the despotism of a single individual? I know that there are many worthy people today who are not alarmed by this alternative, and who are so tired of liberty that they would be glad of rest, far from the storms that accompany it. But these people do not know well the harbor toward which they are headed. Their memories deceive them so much that they judge the tendency of absolute power by what it was in the past, and not by what it might become today.

If absolute power were re-established among the democratic nations of Europe, I am persuaded that it would take a new form and appear with features unknown to our forefathers. There was a time in Europe when the laws and the consent of the people had given princes almost unlimited authority, but they hardly ever made use of it. I am not speaking of the prerogatives of the nobility, of the authority of the supreme courts of justice, of corporations and their chartered rights, or of provincial privileges. These softened the blows of the sovereign authority and kept a spirit of resistance alive in the nation. Apart from these political institutions, which kept the love of freedom alive in the public mind, however opposed they may have been to personal liberty, and which may be considered useful in that respect, the customs and opinions of the nation confined royal authority within barriers that were no less powerful for being less conspicuous. Religion, the affections of the people, the kindness of the prince, the sense of honor, family pride, provincial prejudices, custom, and public opinion all limited the power of kings and held their authority within an invisible circle. The constitution of nations was despotic at that time, but their customs were free. Princes had the right, but they had neither the means nor the desire, to do whatever they pleased.

But what remains now of those barriers that once stopped the aggressions of tyranny? Religion has lost its empire over the souls of men, so the most prominent boundary between good and evil has been overthrown. The very elements of the moral world are uncertain. The princes and the peoples of the earth are guided by chance, and no one can define the natural limits of despotism or the bounds of license. Long revolutions have destroyed forever the respect that once surrounded the rulers of the state. Now that they have been relieved of the burden of public esteem, princes may from now on give themselves up without fear to the temptations of arbitrary power.

When kings find that the hearts of their subjects are turned toward them, they are merciful, because they are conscious of their strength. They are careful of the affection of their people, because that affection is the bulwark of the throne. A mutual exchange of goodwill then takes place between the prince and the people, like the gracious relations of a family. The subjects may grumble at the sovereign’s decree, but they are grieved to displease him, and the sovereign punishes his subjects with the light hand of parental affection.

But once the spell of royalty is broken in the tumult of revolution, and successive monarchs have passed across the throne, alternately showing the people the weakness of their right and the harshness of their power, the sovereign is no longer regarded by anyone as the Father of the State, and he is feared by all as its master. If he is weak, he is despised. If he is strong, he is hated. He himself is full of animosity and alarm. He finds that he is a stranger in his own country, and he treats his subjects like conquered enemies.

When the provinces and the towns formed so many different nations within their common country, each of them had a will of its own, opposed to the general spirit of subjection. But now all the parts of the same empire have lost their immunities, their customs, their prejudices, their traditions, and their names, and have been subjected and accustomed to the same laws. It is no more difficult to oppress them all together than it was once to oppress them one by one.

While the nobles held their power, and indeed long after they had lost it, the honor of aristocracy gave extraordinary force to their personal opposition. There are instances of men who, despite their weakness, still held a high opinion of their personal worth and dared to stand alone against the efforts of the public authority. But today all ranks are more and more mixed together, the individual disappears in the crowd and is easily lost in a common obscurity, the honor of monarchy has almost lost its empire without being replaced by public virtue, and nothing enables a man to rise above himself. Who can say at what point the demands of power and the servility of weakness will stop?

As long as family feeling was alive, the man who opposed oppression was never alone. He looked around him and found his clients, his hereditary friends, and his relatives. If this support was lacking, his ancestors sustained him and his descendants inspired him. But when inherited estates are divided, and a few years are enough to blur the distinctions of a race, where can family feeling be found? What force can there be in the customs of a country that has changed and is still constantly changing its face? In such a country every act of tyranny has a precedent and every crime an example. Nothing is so old that its age can save it from destruction, and nothing so unheard of that its novelty can prevent it from being done. What resistance can customs offer when they are so pliant that they have already often given way? What strength can even public opinion have kept, when no twenty persons are connected by a common tie? When not a single man, family, chartered corporation, class, or free institution has the power to represent or assert that opinion? When every citizen, equally weak, equally poor, and equally dependent, has only his personal helplessness to set against the organized force of the government?

The annals of France offer nothing like the condition into which that country might then be thrown. It is better compared to the times of old, to those hideous eras of Roman oppression, when the customs of the people were corrupted, their traditions wiped out, their habits destroyed, and their opinions shaken. Freedom, driven out of the laws, could find no refuge in the land. Nothing protected the citizens, and the citizens no longer protected themselves. Human nature was the plaything of man, and princes wore out the mercy of Heaven before they exhausted the patience of their subjects. Those who hope to revive the monarchy of Henry IV or of Louis XIV seem to me to be afflicted with mental blindness. When I consider the present condition of several European nations, a condition toward which all the others are tending, I am led to believe that they will soon be left with no other alternative than democratic liberty or the tyranny of the Caesars. *n
n [ [This prediction of the return of France to imperial despotism, and of the true character of that despotic power, was written in 1832, and realized to the letter in 1852.]]

And indeed it deserves consideration whether men are to be entirely emancipated or entirely enslaved, whether their rights are to be made equal or wholly taken away from them. Suppose the rulers of society were reduced either to raising the crowd gradually to their own level or to pushing the citizens below the level of humanity. Would not the doubts of many be resolved, the consciences of many be healed, and the community be prepared to make great sacrifices with little difficulty? In that case, the gradual growth of democratic customs and institutions should be regarded not as the best means of preserving freedom but as the only one. Even without liking democratic government, one might adopt it as the most workable and the fairest remedy for the present ills of society.

It is difficult to draw a people into the work of government, but it is still more difficult to give it the experience and to inspire in it the feelings it needs in order to govern well. I grant that the caprices of democracy are perpetual, its instruments crude, its laws imperfect. But suppose it were true that soon no just middle ground would exist between the empire of democracy and the dominion of a single arm. Should we not rather incline toward the former than submit voluntarily to the latter? And if complete equality is to be our fate, is it not better to be leveled by free institutions than by despotic power?

Anyone who, after reading this book, imagines that I wrote it to hold up the laws and customs of the Anglo-Americans as a model for all democratic peoples would be making a very great mistake. Such a reader must have paid more attention to the form of my ideas than to their substance. My aim has been to show, by the example of America, that there may be laws, and especially customs, that allow a democratic people to remain free. But I am very far from thinking that we should follow the example of the American democracy and copy the means it has used to reach its ends. I am well aware of the influence that the nature of a country and its political precedents have on a constitution, and I would regard it as a great misfortune for mankind if liberty were to exist all over the world in the same forms.

But I am of the opinion that if we do not succeed in gradually introducing democratic institutions into France, and if we give up hope of giving the citizens the ideas and feelings that first prepare them for freedom and then let them enjoy it, there will be no independence for anyone, whether the middle classes or the nobility, the poor or the rich, but an equal tyranny over all. And I foresee that if the peaceable empire of the majority is not established among us in time, we shall sooner or later arrive at the unlimited authority of a single despot.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — Future Condition Of Three Races In The United States
paragraphs: The Present and Probable Future Condition of the Three Races Which Inhabit the Territory of the United States

I have now completed the main task I set for myself. I have shown, as well as I could, the laws and the customs of American democracy. I could stop here, but the reader might feel that I have not met his expectations.

The absolute supremacy of democracy is not the only thing one finds in America; the inhabitants of the New World can be viewed from more than one angle. In the course of this work my subject has often led me to mention the Native Americans and Black Americans, but I have never been able to stop and show what place these two races hold within the democratic people I was describing. I have said in what spirit and under what laws the Anglo-American Union was formed, but I could only glance at the dangers that threaten that confederation, and it was equally impossible for me to give a detailed account of its chances of lasting, apart from its laws and customs. When I spoke of the united republican States, I made no guesses about whether republican forms would endure in the New World. And when I often referred to the commercial activity that prevails in the Union, I could not inquire into the future condition of the Americans as a commercial people.

These subjects are connected with my topic only indirectly, without being part of it. They are American without being democratic, and my main aim has been to portray democracy. I therefore had to put these questions off, and I now take them up as the fitting end of my work.

The territory now occupied or claimed by the American Union stretches from the shores of the Atlantic to those of the Pacific Ocean. To the east and west, its limits are those of the continent itself. To the south it reaches nearly to the tropics, and to the north it extends into the icy regions. The human beings scattered over this space do not form, as in Europe, so many branches of the same stock. At first glance one can pick out three races among them, naturally distinct and, I might almost say, hostile to one another. Education and law, as well as origin and outward appearance, had raised almost insurmountable barriers between them. But fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, although they are mixed, they do not blend, and each race fulfills its destiny apart.

Among these widely different families of men, the first to attract attention, superior in intelligence, power, and enjoyment, is the white or European, the preeminent man. Below him, in lower ranks, come the Black American and the Native American. These two unfortunate races have nothing in common: not birth, not features, not language, not habits. Their only likeness lies in their misfortunes. Both hold an inferior rank in the country they inhabit; both suffer under tyranny; and if their wrongs are not the same, they come, at any rate, from the same authors.

If we reasoned from what goes on in the world, we might almost say that the European is to the other races of mankind what man is to the lower animals. He makes them serve his purposes, and when he cannot subdue them, he destroys them. Oppression has, at one stroke, stripped the descendants of Africans of almost all the privileges of humanity. The Black American in the United States has lost all memory of his country. The language his forefathers spoke is never heard around him. He gave up their religion and forgot their customs when he ceased to belong to Africa, without gaining any claim to European privileges. So he remains halfway between the two communities, sold by one and rejected by the other, finding no spot in the universe to call his country, except the faint image of a home that his master’s roof provides.

The Black American has no family; woman is merely the temporary companion of his pleasures, and his children are his equals from the moment they are born. Should I call it a proof of God’s mercy or a visitation of his wrath, that in certain conditions man seems insensible to his extreme wretchedness, and almost develops a perverse fondness for the cause of his misfortunes? The Black American, plunged in this abyss of evils, scarcely feels his own calamitous situation. Violence made him a slave, and the habit of servitude gives him a slave’s thoughts and desires. He admires his tyrants more than he hates them, and finds his joy and pride in servile imitation of those who oppress him. His understanding has been degraded to the level of his soul.

The Black American enters slavery the moment he is born. Indeed, he may have been bought in the womb and begun his slavery before he began his existence. With no wants and no enjoyments, and useless to himself, he learns with his first ideas of existence that he is another man’s property, that this man has an interest in keeping him alive, and that the care of his life does not fall to himself. Even the power of thought appears to him a useless gift of Providence, and he quietly enjoys the privileges of his degradation. If he becomes free, he often finds independence a heavier burden than slavery. For he has learned in the course of his life to submit to everything except reason, and he knows too little of her dictates to obey them. A thousand new desires beset him, and he lacks the knowledge and energy to resist them. These are masters that must be fought, and he has learned only to submit and obey. In short, he sinks to such a depth of wretchedness that while servitude brutalizes him, liberty destroys him.

Oppression has been no less fatal to the Native Americans than to Black Americans, but its effects are different. Before white men arrived in the New World, the inhabitants of North America lived quietly in their woods, going through the changes of fortune, and practicing the virtues and vices, common to savage nations. The Europeans scattered the tribes, drove them into the wilderness, and condemned them to a wandering life full of inexpressible sufferings.

Savage nations are governed only by opinion and custom. The Native Americans lost their sense of attachment to their country; their families were dispersed, their traditions obscured, and the chain of their memories broken. All their habits were changed, and their wants grew beyond measure. European tyranny made them more disorderly and less civilized than they had been before. The moral and physical condition of the tribes kept getting worse, and they became more barbarous as they became more wretched. Nevertheless, the Europeans have not been able to transform the character of the Native Americans. They have had the power to destroy them, but they have never been able to make them submit to the rules of civilized society.

The lot of the Black American lies at the extreme limit of servitude, while that of the Native American lies at the farthest edge of liberty. Slavery does not produce more fatal effects on the first than independence does on the second. The Black slave has lost all property in his own person, and he cannot dispose of his own existence without committing a kind of fraud. But the savage is his own master as soon as he is able to act. He scarcely knows parental authority; he has never bent his will to that of any other person, nor learned the difference between voluntary obedience and shameful subjection; and the very name of law is unknown to him. To be free, for him, means to escape every shackle of society. He delights in this barbarous independence and would rather die than give up the least part of it, so civilization has little power over him.

The Black American makes a thousand fruitless efforts to work his way in among men who reject him. He conforms to the tastes of his oppressors, adopts their opinions, and hopes by imitating them to become part of their community. He has been told from infancy that his race is naturally inferior to the whites, and he accepts the claim and is ashamed of his own nature. In each of his features he finds a trace of slavery, and if it were in his power, he would gladly rid himself of everything that makes him what he is.

The Native American, on the contrary, has an imagination swollen with the supposed nobility of his origin, and he lives and dies amid these dreams of pride. Far from wanting to conform his habits to ours, he loves his savage life as the distinguishing mark of his race, and he rejects every step toward civilization, perhaps less from hatred of it than from dread of resembling the Europeans. *a He has nothing to set against our perfection in the arts but the resources of the wilderness, and nothing to set against our tactics but undisciplined courage. Our carefully worked-out plans are met only by the spontaneous instincts of savage life. Who can wonder if he fails in this unequal contest?

a [ The native of North America holds on to his opinions and even the most insignificant of his habits with a tenacity that has no parallel in history. For more than two hundred years the wandering tribes of North America have been in daily contact with the whites, and they have never taken from them either a custom or an idea. Yet the Europeans have had a powerful influence over the savages: they have made them more licentious, but not more European. In the summer of 1831 I happened to be beyond Lake Michigan, at a place called Green Bay, which serves as the farthest frontier between the United States and the Native Americans on the northwestern side. There I met an American officer, Major H., who talked to me at length about the inflexibility of the Native American character and then related the following fact: “I formerly knew a young Indian,” he said, “who had been educated at a college in New England, where he had greatly distinguished himself, and had acquired the external appearance of a member of civilized society. When the war broke out between ourselves and the English in 1810, I saw this young man again; he was serving in our army, at the head of the warriors of his tribe, for the Indians were admitted among the ranks of the Americans, upon condition that they would abstain from their horrible custom of scalping their victims. On the evening of the battle of . . ., C. came and sat himself down by the fire of our bivouac. I asked him what had been his fortune that day: he related his exploits; and growing warm and animated by the recollection of them, he concluded by suddenly opening the breast of his coat, saying, ‘You must not betray me — see here!’ And I actually beheld,” said the Major, “between his body and his shirt, the skin and hair of an English head, still dripping with gore.”]

The Black American, who earnestly wishes to mingle his race with the European, cannot do so, while the Native American, who might succeed to a certain extent, disdains even to try. The servility of the one dooms him to slavery; the pride of the other dooms him to death.

I remember that while I was traveling through the forests that still cover the State of Alabama, I came one day to the log house of a pioneer. I did not want to go into the American’s home, so I withdrew to rest for a while by a spring not far off in the woods. While I was there (it was near the Creek territory), a Native American woman appeared, followed by a Black woman and holding by the hand a little white girl of five or six, whom I took to be the pioneer’s daughter. A kind of barbarous luxury adorned the Native American woman’s dress: metal rings hung from her nostrils and ears; her hair, decorated with glass beads, fell loose on her shoulders; and I saw that she was not married, for she still wore the necklace of shells that a bride always lays on the marriage bed. The Black woman was dressed in shabby European clothes. All three came and sat down on the bank of the spring. The young Native American woman took the child in her arms and gave her the fond caresses a mother gives, while the Black woman tried by various small tricks to attract the attention of the young Creole.

In her slightest gestures the child showed a consciousness of superiority that contrasted strangely with her childish weakness, as if she received the attentions of her companions with a kind of condescension. The Black woman sat on the ground before her mistress, watching her smallest wishes, and seemingly torn between strong affection for the child and servile fear. The savage, in the midst of her tenderness, showed an air of freedom and pride that was almost ferocious. I had approached the group and was watching them in silence, but my curiosity probably displeased the Native American woman, for she suddenly rose, pushed the child roughly away from her, and, giving me an angry look, plunged into the thicket. I had often happened to see people of the three races that populate North America gathered in the same place. I had noticed in many different ways the preponderance of the whites. But in the scene I have just described there was something especially touching. A bond of affection united the oppressors with the oppressed here, and nature’s effort to bring them together made the immense distance that prejudice and law had placed between them all the more striking.
The Present and Probable Future Condition of the Native American Tribes Which Inhabit the Territory Possessed by the Union

Gradual disappearance of the native tribes — How it takes place — The miseries that accompany the forced migrations of the Native Americans — The savages of North America had only two ways of escaping destruction: war or civilization — They are no longer able to make war — Why they refused to become civilized when it was in their power, and why they cannot become so now that they want to — The example of the Creeks and Cherokees — The policy of the individual States toward these tribes — The policy of the Federal government.

None of the Native American tribes that once lived in the territory of New England — the Naragansetts, the Mohicans, the Pecots — exists any longer except in human memory. The Lenapes, who received William Penn on the banks of the Delaware a hundred and fifty years ago, have disappeared; and I myself met the last of the Iroquois, who were begging for alms. The nations I have named once covered the country all the way to the seacoast, but today a traveler must go more than a hundred leagues into the interior of the continent to find a Native American. These wild tribes have not only withdrawn; they have been destroyed. *b And as they give way or perish, an immense and growing people takes their place. There is no recorded instance of such prodigious growth or such rapid destruction, and it is not hard to describe how the destruction takes place.

b [ In the thirteen original States there are only 6,273 Native Americans remaining. (See Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, p. 90.) [The decrease is now far greater, and is verging on extinction. See page 360 of this volume.]]

When the Native Americans were the only inhabitants of the wilds from which they have since been driven out, their wants were few. They made their own weapons, their only drink was the water of the brook, and their clothes were the skins of the animals whose flesh fed them.

The Europeans brought firearms, strong liquor, and iron to the savages of North America. They taught them to exchange manufactured cloth for the rough garments that had satisfied their untutored simplicity before. The Native Americans had acquired new tastes without the skills to satisfy them, so they had to turn to the whites’ workmanship. But in return for these goods the savage had nothing to offer except the rich furs that still abounded in his woods. Hunting therefore became necessary, not only to feed himself but to obtain the only goods he could supply to Europe in barter. *c While the natives’ wants were thus increasing, their resources kept shrinking.

c [ In their Report to Congress on February 4, 1829, p. 23, Messrs. Clarke and Cass put it this way: “The time when the Indians generally could supply themselves with food and clothing, without any of the articles of civilized life, has long since passed away. The more remote tribes, beyond the Mississippi, who live where immense herds of buffalo are yet to be found and who follow those animals in their periodical migrations, could more easily than any others recur to the habits of their ancestors, and live without the white man or any of his manufactures. But the buffalo is constantly receding. The smaller animals, the bear, the deer, the beaver, the otter, the muskrat, etc., principally minister to the comfort and support of the Indians; and these cannot be taken without guns, ammunition, and traps. Among the Northwestern Indians particularly, the labor of supplying a family with food is excessive. Day after day is spent by the hunter without success, and during this interval his family must subsist upon bark or roots, or perish. Want and misery are around them and among them. Many die every winter from actual starvation.”

The Native Americans will not live as Europeans do, and yet they can neither survive without them nor live exactly as their fathers did. A fact that I likewise give on official authority shows this. Some members of a tribe on the banks of Lake Superior had killed a European. The American government forbade all trade with the tribe the guilty men belonged to until they were handed over to justice. The measure had the desired effect.]

As soon as a European settlement is formed near the territory the Native Americans occupy, the game animals take alarm. *d Thousands of savages wandering through the forests with no fixed dwelling did not disturb them. But as soon as they hear the continuous sounds of European labor nearby, they begin to flee and retreat to the West, where their instinct tells them they will find deserts of immeasurable extent. “The buffalo is constantly receding,” say Messrs. Clarke and Cass in their Report of the year 1829; “a few years since they approached the base of the Alleghany; and a few years hence they may even be rare upon the immense plains which extend to the base of the Rocky Mountains.” I have been assured that the approach of the whites is often felt in this way at two hundred leagues’ distance from their frontier. Their influence thus reaches tribes whose names are unknown to them, and who suffer the evils of usurpation long before they know who is responsible for their distress. *e

d [ “Five years ago,” says Volney in his “Tableau des Etats-Unis,” p. 370, “in going from Vincennes to Kaskaskia, a territory which now forms part of the State of Illinois, but which at the time I mention was completely wild (1797), you could not cross a prairie without seeing herds of from four to five hundred buffaloes. There are now none remaining; they swam across the Mississippi to escape from the hunters, and more particularly from the bells of the American cows.”]

e [ You can easily confirm what I am saying here by consulting the tabular statement of the Native American tribes living in the United States and its territories. (Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, pp. 90–105.) It shows that the tribes in the center of America are rapidly decreasing, even though the Europeans are still at a considerable distance from them.]

Bold adventurers soon move into the country the Native Americans have abandoned. When they have advanced about fifteen or twenty leagues beyond the outermost frontier of the whites, they begin building homes for civilized beings in the middle of the wilderness. This is done without difficulty, because the territory of a hunting nation is poorly defined. It is the common property of the tribe and belongs to no one in particular, so no individual interests are involved in protecting any part of it.

A few European families, settled in different places at a considerable distance from one another, soon drive away the wild animals that remain between their homes. The Native Americans, who had lived in a kind of abundance, then find it hard to survive, and harder still to obtain the goods for barter that they need.

Driving away their game deprives them of their means of existence, just as effectively as if our farmers’ fields were struck with barrenness. They are reduced, like starving wolves, to prowl through the abandoned woods looking for prey. Their instinctive love of their country attaches them to the soil that gave them birth, *f even after it has stopped yielding anything but misery and death. In the end they are forced to give in and leave. They follow the tracks of the elk, the buffalo, and the beaver, and these wild animals guide them in choosing their future country. Strictly speaking, then, it is not the Europeans who drive away the native inhabitants of America; it is famine that forces them to withdraw. This is a happy distinction that escaped the casuists of former times, and we owe it to modern discovery!

f [ “The Indians,” say Messrs. Clarke and Cass in their Report to Congress, p. 15, “are attached to their country by the same feelings which bind us to ours; and, besides, there are certain superstitious notions connected with the alienation of what the Great Spirit gave to their ancestors, which operate strongly upon the tribes who have made few or no cessions, but which are gradually weakened as our intercourse with them is extended. ‘We will not sell the spot which contains the bones of our fathers,’ is almost always the first answer to a proposition for a sale.”]

It is impossible to imagine how much suffering these forced emigrations involve. A people already exhausted and reduced undertake them, and the countries the newcomers go to are inhabited by other tribes, who receive them with jealous hostility. Hunger follows behind them, war awaits them ahead, and misery besets them on every side. Hoping to escape such a host of enemies, they separate, and each individual tries to find the means of supporting his existence in solitude and secrecy, living in the vastness of the wilderness like an outcast in civilized society. The social tie, which distress had long since weakened, then dissolves. They have lost their country, and soon their people desert them. Their very families are wiped out; the names they bore in common are forgotten; their language dies; and every trace of their origin disappears. Their nation has ceased to exist, except in the memory of the antiquaries of America and a few scholars of Europe.

I would be sorry if my reader supposed that I am coloring the picture too strongly. I saw with my own eyes several of the cases of misery I have described, and I witnessed sufferings I have no power to portray.

At the end of the year 1831, while I was on the left bank of the Mississippi at a place the Europeans named Memphis, a numerous band of Choctaws arrived (or Chactas, as the French in Louisiana call them). These savages had left their country and were trying to reach the right bank of the Mississippi, where they hoped to find the refuge the American government had promised them. It was the middle of winter, and the cold was unusually severe. The snow had frozen hard on the ground, and the river was carrying huge masses of ice. The Native Americans had their families with them, and they brought in their train the wounded and the sick, newborn children, and old men on the verge of death. They had neither tents nor wagons, only their weapons and some provisions. I watched them embark to cross the mighty river, and that solemn sight will never fade from my memory. No cry, no sob was heard among the assembled crowd; all were silent. Their calamities were of long standing, and they knew them to be beyond remedy. The Native Americans had all stepped into the boat that was to carry them across, but their dogs remained on the bank. As soon as these animals saw that their masters were leaving the shore for good, they set up a dismal howl and, plunging all together into the icy waters of the Mississippi, swam after the boat.

The ejection of the Native Americans very often takes place today in a regular and, so to speak, legal manner. When the European population begins to approach the edge of the wilderness inhabited by a savage tribe, the government of the United States usually sends envoys to them. The envoys gather the Native Americans on a large plain, eat and drink with them first, and then address them in the following way: “What have you to do in the land of your fathers? Before long, you must dig up their bones in order to live. In what respect is the country you inhabit better than another? Are there no woods, marshes, or prairies, except where you dwell? And can you live nowhere but under your own sun? Beyond those mountains which you see at the horizon, beyond the lake which bounds your territory on the west, there lie vast countries where beasts of chase are found in great abundance; sell your lands to us, and go to live happily in those solitudes.” After saying this, they lay out before the eyes of the Native Americans firearms, woolen garments, kegs of brandy, glass necklaces, tinsel bracelets, earrings, and mirrors. *g If, after seeing all these riches, the Native Americans still hesitate, it is hinted that they have no means of refusing the consent that is demanded, and that the government itself will soon be unable to protect their rights. What are they to do? Half convinced and half forced, they go to live in new deserts, where the importunate whites will not let them stay in peace for ten years. This is how the Americans obtain, at a very low price, whole provinces that the richest sovereigns of Europe could not buy. *h

g [ See, in the Legislative Documents of Congress (Doc. 117), the account of what happens on these occasions. This curious passage comes from the report mentioned above, made to Congress by Messrs. Clarke and Cass in February, 1829. Mr. Cass is now the Secretary of War.

“The Indians,” says the report, “reach the treaty-ground poor and almost naked. Large quantities of goods are taken there by the traders, and are seen and examined by the Indians. The women and children become importunate to have their wants supplied, and their influence is soon exerted to induce a sale. Their improvidence is habitual and unconquerable. The gratification of his immediate wants and desires is the ruling passion of an Indian. The expectation of future advantages seldom produces much effect. The experience of the past is lost, and the prospects of the future disregarded. It would be utterly hopeless to demand a cession of land, unless the means were at hand of gratifying their immediate wants; and when their condition and circumstances are fairly considered, it ought not to surprise us that they are so anxious to relieve themselves.”]

h [ On May 19, 1830, Mr. Edward Everett stated before the House of Representatives that the Americans had already acquired by treaty, to the east and west of the Mississippi, 230,000,000 acres. In 1808 the Osages gave up 48,000,000 acres for an annual payment of $1,000. In 1818 the Quapaws gave up 29,000,000 acres for $4,000. They kept for themselves a territory of 1,000,000 acres as a hunting ground. A solemn oath was taken that it would be respected, but before long it was invaded like the rest. Mr. Bell, in his Report of the Committee on Indian Affairs, February 24, 1830, has these words: “To pay an Indian tribe what their ancient hunting-grounds are worth to them, after the game is fled or destroyed, as a mode of appropriating wild lands claimed by Indians, has been found more convenient, and certainly it is more agreeable to the forms of justice, as well as more merciful, than to assert the possession of them by the sword. Thus the practice of buying Indian titles is but the substitute which humanity and expediency have imposed, in place of the sword, in arriving at the actual enjoyment of property claimed by the right of discovery, and sanctioned by the natural superiority allowed to the claims of civilized communities over those of savage tribes. Up to the present time so invariable has been the operation of certain causes, first in diminishing the value of forest lands to the Indians, and secondly in disposing them to sell readily, that the plan of buying their right of occupancy has never threatened to retard, in any perceptible degree, the prosperity of any of the States.” (Legislative Documents, 21st Congress, No. 227, p. 6.)]

These are great evils, and I must add that they seem to me beyond remedy. I believe that the native nations of North America are doomed to perish, and that once the Europeans are established on the shores of the Pacific Ocean, that race of men will be no more. *i The Native Americans had only two alternatives, war or civilization. In other words, they had to either destroy the Europeans or become their equals.

i [ Almost all American statesmen seem, in fact, to hold this opinion. “Judging of the future by the past,” says Mr. Cass, “we cannot err in anticipating a progressive diminution of their numbers, and their eventual extinction, unless our border should become stationary, and they be removed beyond it, or unless some radical change should take place in the principles of our intercourse with them, which it is easier to hope for than to expect.”]

When the colonies were first settled, the Native Americans might have been able, by uniting their forces, to rid themselves of the small bodies of strangers landing on their continent. *j They tried several times and were on the point of succeeding. But today the disproportion between their resources and those of the whites is too great for such an undertaking to be considered.
