Nevertheless, from time to time men of penetration do arise among them who foresee the final destiny awaiting the native population and who strive to unite all the tribes in common hostility to the Europeans. Their efforts are in vain. The tribes near the whites are too weakened to offer effective resistance. The others give way to the childish carelessness about tomorrow that marks savage life, and wait until danger is close before preparing to meet it. Some are unable to make the effort, the others unwilling.

j [ Among other warlike enterprises was one by the Wampanaogs and other confederate tribes under Metacom in 1675 against the colonists of New England; the English were also engaged in war in Virginia in 1622.]
It is easy to foresee that the Native Americans will never adapt to civilization, or that it will be too late whenever they may be inclined to try.

Civilization is the result of a long social process that takes place in one spot and is handed down from one generation to the next, each profiting from the experience of the one before. Of all nations, those that live habitually by hunting submit to civilization with the most difficulty. Pastoral tribes, it is true, often change their place of abode, but they follow a regular order in their migrations and often return to their old stations, whereas the hunter’s dwelling changes with that of the animals he pursues.

Several attempts have been made to spread knowledge among the Native Americans without controlling their wandering tendencies, by the Jesuits in Canada and by the Puritans in New England. *k None of these efforts was crowned with any lasting success. Civilization began in the cabin, but it soon withdrew to die in the woods. The great error of these lawgivers to the Native Americans was that they did not understand that, to civilize a people, one must first make it settle, and this cannot be done without inducing it to cultivate the soil. The Native Americans should first have been accustomed to agriculture. But not only do they lack this indispensable first step toward civilization, they would have great difficulty acquiring it. Men who have once given themselves up to the restless and adventurous life of the hunter feel an insurmountable disgust for the constant and regular labor that farming requires. We see this proved within our own society, but it is far more visible among peoples whose fondness for the chase is part of their national character.
k [ See the “Histoire de la Nouvelle France,” by Charlevoix, and the work entitled “Lettres edifiantes.”]

Apart from this general difficulty, there is another that applies especially to the Native Americans: they consider labor not merely an evil but a disgrace, so that their pride keeps them from becoming civilized as much as their indolence does. *l

l [ “In all the tribes,” says Volney, in his “Tableau des Etats-Unis,” p. 423, “there still exists a generation of old warriors, who cannot forbear, when they see their countrymen using the hoe, from exclaiming against the degradation of ancient manners, and asserting that the savages owe their decline to these innovations; adding, that they have only to return to their primitive habits in order to recover their power and their glory.”]

There is no Native American so wretched that he does not keep, under his hut of bark, a lofty idea of his personal worth. He considers the cares of industry and labor degrading occupations. He compares the farmer to the ox that draws the furrow, and even in our most ingenious handicrafts he sees nothing but the work of slaves. It is not that he lacks admiration for the power and intellectual greatness of the whites. But although the results of our efforts amaze him, he despises the means by which we achieve them, and while he acknowledges our ascendancy, he still believes in his own superiority. War and hunting are the only pursuits that seem to him worthy of a man. *m In the dreary solitude of his woods, the Native American cherishes the same ideas and opinions as the noble of the Middle Ages in his castle, and to complete the resemblance he needs only to become a conqueror. Thus, strange as it may seem, it is in the forests of the New World, and not among the Europeans who populate its coasts, that the ancient prejudices of Europe still survive.

m [ The following description appears in an official document: “Until a young man has been engaged with an enemy, and has performed some acts of valor, he gains no consideration, but is regarded nearly as a woman. In their great war-dances all the warriors in succession strike the post, as it is called, and recount their exploits. On these occasions their auditory consists of the kinsmen, friends, and comrades of the narrator. The profound impression which his discourse produces on them is manifested by the silent attention it receives, and by the loud shouts which hail its termination. The young man who finds himself at such a meeting without anything to recount is very unhappy; and instances have sometimes occurred of young warriors, whose passions had been thus inflamed, quitting the war-dance suddenly, and going off alone to seek for trophies which they might exhibit, and adventures which they might be allowed to relate.”]

More than once in the course of this work I have tried to explain the prodigious influence that social condition seems to have on the laws and customs of men, and I ask leave to add a few words on the same subject.

When I perceive the resemblance between the political institutions of our ancestors the Germans and those of the wandering tribes of North America, and between the customs described by Tacitus and those I have sometimes witnessed, I cannot help thinking that the same cause has produced the same results in both hemispheres. I think that amid the apparent diversity of human affairs, a certain number of primary facts can be discovered from which all the others derive. In what we usually call the German institutions, then, I am inclined to see only barbarian habits, and in what we call feudal principles, the opinions of savages.

However strongly the vices and prejudices of the Native Americans of North America may stand in the way of their becoming farmers and civilized, necessity sometimes forces them to it. Several of the Southern nations, among them the Cherokees and the Creeks, *n found themselves surrounded by Europeans. These Europeans had landed on the shores of the Atlantic, and, whether they came down the Ohio or up the Mississippi, they reached the tribes’ borders at the same time. These tribes have not been driven from place to place, as their Northern brethren were. Instead, they have been gradually hemmed into narrow limits, like game in a thicket before the hunters plunge into the interior. Placed between civilization and death, they found themselves obliged to live by degrading labor, like the whites. They took up agriculture, and, without entirely giving up their old habits and customs, they sacrificed only as much as was necessary to survive.

n [ These nations are now absorbed into the States of Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, and Mississippi. The South once had four great nations (remnants of which still survive): the Choctaws, the Chickasaws, the Creeks, and the Cherokees. In 1830 the remnants of these four nations numbered about 75,000 individuals. It is estimated that about 300,000 Native Americans now remain in the territory occupied or claimed by the Anglo-American Union. (See Proceedings of the Indian Board in the City of New York.) The official documents supplied to Congress put the number at 313,130. A reader who wants to know the names and numerical strength of all the tribes living in Anglo-American territory should consult the documents I refer to. (Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, pp. 90–105.) [In the Census of 1870 it is stated that the Indian population of the United States is only 25,731, of whom 7,241 are in California.]]

The Cherokees went further. They created a written language and established a permanent form of government. And since everything moves fast in the New World, they set up a newspaper before they all had clothes. *o
o [ I brought back with me to France one or two copies of this unusual publication.]

The growth of European habits among these Native Americans has been remarkably speeded up by the mixed race that has arisen among them. *p Drawing its education from the father’s side, without entirely losing the savage customs of the mother, the person of mixed race forms the natural link between civilization and barbarism. Wherever this mixed race has multiplied, the savage state has been modified, and a great change has taken place in the customs of the people. *q

p [ See in the Report of the Committee on Indian Affairs, 21st Congress, No. 227, p. 23, why the number of people of mixed blood has grown among the Cherokees. The main cause goes back to the War of Independence. Many Anglo-Americans in Georgia had sided with England and had to flee to the Native Americans, among whom they married.]

q [ Unhappily the mixed race has been less numerous and less influential in North America than in any other country. The American continent was peopled by two great nations of Europe, the French and the English. The French were quick to form ties with the daughters of the natives. But there was an unfortunate affinity between the Native American character and their own. Instead of giving the savages the tastes and habits of civilized life, the French too often became passionately fond of the wild freedom they found them in. They became the most dangerous inhabitants of the wilderness, and won the friendship of the Native Americans by exaggerating both their vices and their virtues. M. de Senonville, the governor of Canada, wrote to Louis XIV in 1685: “It has long been believed that in order to civilize the savages we ought to draw them nearer to us. But there is every reason to suppose we have been mistaken. Those which have been brought into contact with us have not become French, and the French who have lived among them are changed into savages, affecting to dress and live like them.” (“History of New France,” by Charlevoix, vol. ii., p. 345.) The Englishman, by contrast, stayed stubbornly attached to the customs and even the most trivial habits of his forefathers. He has remained in the midst of the American wilderness just what he was in the heart of European cities. He would allow no contact with savages whom he despised, and he carefully avoided any union of his race with theirs. Thus, while the French exercised no wholesome influence over the Native Americans, the English have always remained strangers to them.]

The success of the Cherokees proves that Native Americans are capable of civilization, but it does not prove that they will succeed in it. The difficulty they find in submitting to civilization comes from a general cause, which it is almost impossible for them to escape. A careful look at history shows that, in general, barbarous nations have raised themselves to civilization gradually, and by their own efforts. Whenever they have drawn knowledge from a foreign people, they have stood toward it as conquerors, not as a conquered nation. When the conquered nation is educated and the conquerors are half savage, as when the Northern nations invaded Rome or the Mongols invaded China, the power that victory gives the barbarian is enough to keep up his importance among civilized men and to let him rank as their equal until he becomes their rival. The one has might on his side, the other has intelligence; the former admires the knowledge and the arts of the conquered, and the latter envies the power of the conquerors. The barbarians at length admit civilized man into their palaces, and he in turn opens his schools to the barbarians. But when the side that holds the physical force also holds the intellectual advantage, the conquered party seldom becomes civilized: it retreats, or is destroyed. It may therefore be said, in a general way, that savages go out in arms to seek knowledge, but that they do not accept it when it comes to them.

If the Native American tribes that now live in the heart of the continent could summon up enough energy to try to civilize themselves, they might possibly succeed. Already superior to the barbarous nations around them, they would gradually gain strength and experience. When the Europeans appeared on their borders, they would be in a position, if not to maintain their independence, at least to assert their right to the soil and to merge with the conquerors. But the misfortune of the Native Americans is that they have come into contact with a civilized people that is also (it must be admitted) the most avaricious nation on the globe, while they are still semi-barbarous. They find despots in their teachers, and they receive knowledge from the hand of oppression. Living in the freedom of the woods, the Native American of North America was poor, but he felt inferior to no one. As soon as he wants to enter the social scale of the whites, however, he takes the lowest rank in society, for he enters the circle of science and wealth ignorant and poor. He has led a life of agitation, beset with evils and dangers but filled at the same time with proud emotions. *r Now he is obliged to submit to a wearisome, obscure, and degraded state, and to earn the bread that feeds him by hard and ignoble labor. In his eyes these are the only results civilization can boast of, and even this much he is not sure to obtain.

r [ The adventurous life of the hunter has a certain irresistible charm, which seizes the heart of man and carries him away in spite of reason and experience. The memoirs of Tanner show this plainly. Tanner is a European who was carried off by Native Americans at the age of six and remained with them in the woods for thirty years. Nothing can be imagined more appalling than the miseries he describes. He tells us of tribes without a chief, families without a nation to call their own, men in a state of isolation, and the wrecks of powerful tribes wandering at random amid the ice and snow and desolate solitudes of Canada. Hunger and cold pursue them, and every day their lives are in danger. Among these men, customs have lost their hold and traditions are without power. They become more and more savage. Tanner shared in all these miseries. He knew he was of European origin. He was not kept away from the whites by force; on the contrary, he came every year to trade with them, entered their homes, and saw their comforts. He knew that whenever he chose to return to civilized life he was perfectly able to do so, and he remained thirty years in the wilderness. When he came into civilized society, he declared that the rough existence he described had a secret charm for him that he could not define. He went back to it again and again. At length he abandoned it with bitter regret, and when he was finally settled among the whites, several of his children refused to share his calm and easy situation. I saw Tanner myself at the lower end of Lake Superior; he seemed to me more like a savage than a civilized man. His book is written without either taste or order, but, even unintentionally, it gives a vivid picture of the prejudices, the passions, the vices, and above all the destitution in which he lived.]

When Native Americans try to imitate their European neighbors and to till the earth as the settlers do, they are immediately exposed to very formidable competition. The white man is skilled in the craft of agriculture; the Native American is a rough beginner in an art he does not know. The white man reaps abundant crops without difficulty, while the Native American meets a thousand obstacles in raising the fruits of the earth.

The European lives among a population whose wants he knows and shares. The savage is isolated in the midst of a hostile people, with whose customs, language, and laws he is imperfectly acquainted, but without whose help he cannot live. He can obtain the means of comfort only by bartering his goods for the goods of the European, since the help of his own countrymen is wholly insufficient to meet his wants. When the Native American wants to sell the produce of his labor, he cannot always find a buyer, while the European readily finds a market. And the former can produce only at considerable cost what the latter sells at a very low price. Thus the Native American has no sooner escaped the evils to which barbarous nations are exposed than he is subjected to the still greater miseries of civilized communities. He finds it scarcely less difficult to live in the midst of our abundance than in the depths of his own wilderness.

He has not yet lost the habits of his wandering life; the traditions of his fathers and his passion for the chase are still alive within him. The wild pleasures that once animated him in the woods painfully excite his troubled imagination, and his former hardships seem less harsh to him, his former dangers less appalling. He contrasts the independence he enjoyed among his equals with the servile position he holds in civilized society. On the other hand, the wilderness that was so long his free home is still close at hand; a few hours’ march will bring him back to it. The whites offer him a sum, which seems considerable to him, for the ground he has begun to clear. This money from the Europeans may possibly give him the means of a happy and peaceful living in remoter regions. So he leaves the plow, takes up his native weapons again, and returns to the wilderness forever. *s The condition of the Creeks and Cherokees, to which I have already alluded, fully confirms the truth of this sad picture.

s [ The Europeans themselves have shown how destructive the influence of highly civilized nations can be upon less civilized ones. About a century ago the French founded the town of Vincennes on the Wabash, in the middle of the wilderness, and lived there in great plenty until the American settlers arrived. The Americans first ruined the earlier inhabitants through competition and then bought their lands at a very low price. When M. de Volney, from whom I borrow these details, passed through Vincennes, the number of the French was reduced to a hundred individuals, most of whom were about to move to Louisiana or to Canada. These French settlers were worthy people, but idle and uneducated; they had picked up many of the habits of savages. The Americans, who were perhaps their inferiors from a moral point of view, were immeasurably superior to them in intelligence: they were industrious, well informed, rich, and used to governing their own community.

I myself saw in Canada, where the intellectual difference between the two races is less striking, that the English are the masters of commerce and manufacturing in the Canadian country. They spread on all sides and confine the French within limits that scarcely suffice to hold them. In the same way, in Louisiana, almost all activity in commerce and manufacturing is concentrated in the hands of the Anglo-Americans.

But the case of Texas is still more striking. The State of Texas is a part of Mexico and lies on the frontier between that country and the United States. In the last few years the Anglo-Americans have moved into this province, which is still thinly peopled. They buy land, they produce the commodities of the country, and they replace the original population. It is easy to foresee that if Mexico takes no steps to check this change, the province of Texas will very shortly cease to belong to that government.

If the different degrees of European civilization, which differ comparatively little, produce results of such magnitude, we can readily imagine the consequences that must follow when the most advanced European civilization collides with Native American savages.]

In the little they have done, the Native Americans have unquestionably shown as much natural genius as the peoples of Europe in their most important undertakings. But nations, like individuals, need time to learn, whatever their intelligence and zeal. While the savages were engaged in the work of civilization, the Europeans kept surrounding them on every side and confining them within narrower limits. The two races gradually met, and they now stand in immediate juxtaposition. The Native American is already superior to his barbarous parent, but he is still very far below his white neighbor. With their resources and acquired knowledge, the Europeans soon took for themselves most of the advantages the natives might have drawn from owning the soil. They have settled in the country; they have bought land at a very low price or occupied it by force; and the Native Americans have been ruined by a competition they had no means of resisting. They were isolated in their own country, and their race was only a colony of troublesome aliens in the midst of a numerous and domineering people. *t

t [ See in the Legislative Documents (21st Congress, No. 89) instances of every kind of excess committed by the whites on the territory of the Native Americans. The whites took possession of part of their lands until the troops of Congress forced them to withdraw, or they carried off their cattle, burned their houses, cut down their corn, and did violence to their persons. It appears nevertheless from all these documents that the claims of the natives are constantly protected by the government against the abuse of force. The Union has a representative agent continually employed to reside among the Native Americans, and the report of the Cherokee agent, which is among the documents I have referred to, is almost always favorable to them. “The intrusion of whites,” he says, “upon the lands of the Cherokees would cause ruin to the poor, helpless, and inoffensive inhabitants.” And he further remarks, about the attempt of the State of Georgia to establish a division line limiting the boundaries of the Cherokees, that the line drawn, having been made by the whites and entirely upon ex parte evidence of their several rights, was of no validity whatever.]

Washington said in one of his messages to Congress, “We are more enlightened and more powerful than the Indian nations, we are therefore bound in honor to treat them with kindness and even with generosity.” That virtuous and high-minded policy has not been followed. The settlers’ greed is usually backed by the tyranny of the government. The Cherokees and the Creeks are established on the territory they inhabited before the Europeans settled, and the Americans have often treated with them as with foreign nations. Even so, the surrounding States have not agreed to recognize them as independent peoples, and attempts have been made to subject these children of the woods to Anglo-American magistrates, laws, and customs. *u Destitution had driven these unfortunate people to civilization, and oppression now drives them back to their former condition. Many of them abandon the soil they had begun to clear and return to their savage way of life.
u [ In 1829 the State of Alabama split the Creek territory into counties and placed the Native American population under the authority of European magistrates.

In 1830 the State of Mississippi assimilated the Choctaws and Chickasaws to the white population, and declared that any of them who took the title of chief would be punished by a fine of $1,000 and a year’s imprisonment. When these laws were enforced upon the Choctaws, who lived in that district, the tribe assembled. Their chief told them what the whites intended and read them some of the laws they were meant to submit to. They unanimously declared that it was better to retreat into the wilds again at once.]
Chapter XVIII: Future Condition of Three Races — Part III

If we consider the tyrannical measures adopted by the legislatures of the Southern States, the conduct of their Governors, and the decrees of their courts of justice, we shall be convinced that the final aim of their policy is the complete expulsion of the Native Americans. The Americans of that part of the Union look on the aborigines with jealousy. *v They know that these tribes have not yet lost the traditions of savage life, and before civilization has fixed them permanently to the soil, they intend to force them to withdraw by driving them to despair. The Creeks and Cherokees, oppressed by the several States, have appealed to the central government. It is by no means indifferent to their misfortunes and sincerely wants to save the remnant of the natives and keep them in free possession of the territory that the Union is pledged to respect. *w But the several States offer such formidable resistance to carrying out this plan that the government is obliged to consent to the destruction of a few barbarous tribes, so as not to endanger the safety of the American Union.

v [ The Georgians, who are so troubled by having Native Americans nearby, live in a territory that at present has no more than seven inhabitants to the square mile. In France the same area holds one hundred and sixty-two inhabitants.]

w [ In 1818 Congress appointed commissioners to visit the Arkansas Territory, accompanied by a deputation of Creeks, Choctaws, and Chickasaws. This expedition was commanded by Messrs. Kennerly, M’Coy, Wash Hood, and John Bell. See the different reports of the commissioners, and their journal, in the Documents of Congress, No. 87, House of Representatives.]

But the federal government, which cannot protect the Native Americans, would gladly ease the hardships of their lot. With this intention, proposals have been made to transport them at public expense to more remote regions.

Between the thirty-third and thirty-seventh degrees of north latitude lies a vast tract of country, which has taken the name of Arkansas from the principal river that waters it. It is bounded on one side by the borders of Mexico and on the other by the Mississippi. Numberless streams cross it in every direction; the climate is mild and the soil productive, but only a few wandering hordes of savages live there. The government of the Union wants to transport the broken remnants of the indigenous population of the South to the part of this country nearest Mexico and at a great distance from the American settlements.

We were assured, toward the end of the year 1831, that 10,000 Native Americans had already gone down to the shores of the Arkansas, and fresh detachments were constantly following them. But Congress has been unable to arouse a unanimous determination in those it wants to protect. Some, indeed, are willing to leave the seat of oppression, but the most educated members of the community refuse to abandon their new homes and their growing crops. They believe that the work of civilization, once interrupted, will never be resumed. They fear that the domestic habits they have so recently acquired may be irretrievably lost in a country that is still barbarous, where nothing is prepared for the support of an agricultural people. They know that hostile hordes will oppose their entry into those wilds, and that they have lost the energy of barbarians without gaining the resources of civilization to resist their attacks. Moreover, they readily see that the settlement proposed to them is merely a temporary expedient. Who can assure them that they will at length be allowed to live in peace in their new retreat? The United States pledges itself to keep its obligation, but the territory they now occupy was formerly secured to them by the most solemn oaths of Anglo-American good faith. *x The American government does not indeed rob them of their lands, but it allows constant incursions upon them. In a few years the same white population that now crowds around them will track them to the solitudes of the Arkansas. They will then be exposed to the same evils without the same remedies, and since the limits of the earth will at last fail them, their only refuge is the grave.

x [ The fifth article of the treaty made with the Creeks in August, 1790, reads as follows: — “The United States solemnly guarantee to the Creek nation all their land within the limits of the United States.”

The seventh article of the treaty concluded in 1791 with the Cherokees says: — “The United States solemnly guarantee to the Cherokee nation all their lands not hereby ceded.” The next article declared that if any citizen of the United States, or any other settler not of the Indian race, should settle on Cherokee territory, the United States would withdraw its protection from that person and hand him over to be punished as the Cherokee nation saw fit.]

The Union treats the Native Americans with less greed and harshness than the policy of the several States does, but the two governments are equally lacking in good faith. The States extend to the tribes what they are pleased to call the benefits of their laws, believing that the tribes will withdraw rather than submit. And the central government, which promises these unhappy people a permanent refuge, is well aware that it cannot secure it to them. *y

y [ That does not stop them from promising it in the most solemn manner. See the letter of the President addressed to the Creek Indians, March 23, 1829 (Proceedings of the Indian Board, in the city of New York, p. 5): “Beyond the great river Mississippi, where a part of your nation has gone, your father has provided a country large enough for all of you, and he advises you to remove to it. There your white brothers will not trouble you; they will have no claim to the land, and you can live upon it, you and all your children, as long as the grass grows, or the water runs, in peace and plenty. It will be yours forever.”

The Secretary of War, in a letter written to the Cherokees on April 18, 1829 (see the same work, p. 6), tells them that they cannot expect to keep possession of the lands they then occupied. But he gives them the most positive assurance of uninterrupted peace if they will move beyond the Mississippi. It is as if the power that could not protect them then would be able to protect them later!]

Thus the tyranny of the States forces the savages to retire, and the Union, by its promises and resources, makes their retreat easier. These measures tend to precisely the same end. *z “By the will of our Father in Heaven, the Governor of the whole world,” said the Cherokees in their petition to Congress, *a “the red man of America has become small, and the white man great and renowned. When the ancestors of the people of these United States first came to the shores of America they found the red man strong: though he was ignorant and savage, yet he received them kindly, and gave them dry land to rest their weary feet. They met in peace, and shook hands in token of friendship. Whatever the white man wanted and asked of the Indian, the latter willingly gave. At that time the Indian was the lord, and the white man the suppliant. But now the scene has changed. The strength of the red man has become weakness. As his neighbors increased in numbers his power became less and less, and now, of the many and powerful tribes who once covered these United States, only a few are to be seen — a few whom a sweeping pestilence has left. The northern tribes, who were once so numerous and powerful, are now nearly extinct. Thus it has happened to the red man of America. Shall we, who are remnants, share the same fate?”

z [ To form a correct idea of the policy followed by the several States and the Union toward the Native Americans, one must consult: 1st, “The Laws of the Colonial and State Governments relating to the Indian Inhabitants.” (See the Legislative Documents, 21st Congress, No. 319.) 2nd, The Laws of the Union on the same subject, and especially that of March 30, 1802. (See Story’s “Laws of the United States.”) 3rd, The Report of Mr. Cass, Secretary of War, relative to Indian Affairs, November 29, 1823.]
a [ December 18, 1829.]

“The land on which we stand we have received as an inheritance from our fathers, who possessed it from time immemorial, as a gift from our common Father in Heaven. They bequeathed it to us as their children, and we have sacredly kept it, as containing the remains of our beloved men. This right of inheritance we have never ceded nor ever forfeited. Permit us to ask what better right can the people have to a country than the right of inheritance and immemorial peaceable possession? We know it is said of late by the State of Georgia and by the Executive of the United States, that we have forfeited this right; but we think this is said gratuitously. At what time have we made the forfeit? What great crime have we committed, whereby we must forever be divested of our country and rights? Was it when we were hostile to the United States, and took part with the King of Great Britain, during the struggle for independence? If so, why was not this forfeiture declared in the first treaty of peace between the United States and our beloved men? Why was not such an article as the following inserted in the treaty: — ‘The United States give peace to the Cherokees, but, for the part they took in the late war, declare them to be but tenants at will, to be removed when the convenience of the States, within whose chartered limits they live, shall require it’? That was the proper time to assume such a possession. But it was not thought of, nor would our forefathers have agreed to any treaty whose tendency was to deprive them of their rights and their country.”

Such is the language of the Native Americans. Their assertions are true and their forebodings unavoidable. From whichever side we consider the destiny of the aborigines of North America, their calamities appear beyond remedy. If they remain barbarous, they are forced to retire. If they try to civilize their customs, contact with a more civilized community subjects them to oppression and destitution. They perish if they keep wandering from waste to waste, and if they try to settle, they must still perish. The help of Europeans is necessary to teach them, but the approach of Europeans corrupts them and drives them back into savage life. They refuse to change their habits as long as their wilderness is their own, and it is too late to change them when they are forced to submit.

The Spaniards hunted the Native Americans with bloodhounds, like wild beasts. They sacked the New World with no more restraint or compassion than a city taken by storm. But destruction must cease and frenzy must end. The remnant of the Native American population that had escaped the massacre mixed with its conquerors and in the end adopted their religion and their customs. *b The conduct of the Americans of the United States toward the aborigines, on the other hand, is marked by a singular attachment to the formalities of law. As long as the Native Americans remain in their barbarous condition, the Americans take no part in their affairs. They treat them as independent nations, and they do not take possession of their hunting grounds without a treaty of purchase. And if a Native American nation happens to be so encroached upon that it cannot live on its territory, they give it brotherly help in transporting it to a grave far enough away from the land of its fathers.

b [ The honor of this result, however, is by no means due to the Spaniards. If the Native American tribes had not been tillers of the ground when the Europeans arrived, they would unquestionably have been destroyed in South America as well as in North America.]

The Spaniards could not wipe out the Native American race, even by those unparalleled atrocities that brand them with lasting shame, nor did they entirely succeed in stripping it of its rights. The Americans of the United States have achieved both aims with remarkable ease: quietly, legally, philanthropically, without shedding blood, and without breaking a single great principle of morality in the eyes of the world. *c It is impossible to destroy men with more respect for the laws of humanity.

c [ See, among other documents, the report made by Mr. Bell in the name of the Committee on Indian Affairs, February 24, 1830, in which it is most logically established and most learnedly proved that “the fundamental principle that the Indians had no right by virtue of their ancient possession either of will or sovereignty, has never been abandoned either expressly or by implication.” Anyone reading this report, which was clearly written by an experienced hand, is astonished at how easily the author sweeps aside every argument based on reason and natural right, which he calls abstract and theoretical principles. The more I think about how civilized and uncivilized man differ in their approach to the principles of justice, the more I see that the former disputes the justice of the very rights that the latter simply violates.]

[I leave this chapter entirely unchanged, because it has always seemed to me one of the most eloquent and moving parts of this book. But it is no longer a prophecy: the destruction of the Native American race in the United States has already been carried out. In 1870 only 25,731 Native Americans remained in the whole territory of the Union, and by far the largest part of them live in California, Michigan, Wisconsin, Dakota, and New Mexico and Nevada. In New England, Pennsylvania, and New York the race is extinct, and the predictions of M. de Tocqueville are fulfilled. — Translator’s Note.]
Situation of the Black Population in the United States, and Dangers with Which Its Presence Threatens the Whites

Why it is more difficult to abolish slavery, and to efface all traces of it, among the moderns than it was among the ancients — In the United States the prejudices of whites against Black people seem to increase in proportion as slavery is abolished — Situation of Black people in the Northern and Southern States — Why the Americans abolish slavery — Servitude, which debases the slave, impoverishes the master — Contrast between the left and the right bank of the Ohio — To what this is attributable — The Black race, as well as slavery, recedes toward the South — Explanation of this fact — Difficulties attendant upon the abolition of slavery in the South — Dangers to come — General anxiety — Foundation of a Black colony in Africa — Why the Americans of the South increase the hardships of slavery, while they are distressed at its continuance.

The Native Americans will perish in the same isolation in which they have lived. But the destiny of Black people is to some extent interwoven with that of the Europeans. These two races are attached to each other without intermingling, and they are equally unable either to separate entirely or to combine. The most formidable of all the ills that threaten the future existence of the Union comes from the presence of a Black population on its territory. When the observer looks for the cause of the present embarrassments or the future dangers of the United States, he is invariably led to this as a primary fact.

The lasting evils that afflict mankind are usually produced by the violent or growing efforts of men. But there is one calamity that crept stealthily into the world and was at first scarcely distinguishable amid the ordinary abuses of power. It began with an individual whose name history has not preserved. It was carried like some accursed seed to one portion of the soil, but afterward it fed itself, grew without effort, and spreads naturally with the society to which it belongs. I need hardly add that this calamity is slavery. Christianity suppressed slavery, but the Christians of the sixteenth century reestablished it, as an exception, indeed, to their social system, and restricted to one of the races of mankind. Yet the wound thus inflicted on humanity, though less extensive, was at the same time made far harder to cure.

It is important to distinguish accurately between slavery itself and its consequences. The immediate evils produced by slavery were very nearly the same in antiquity as they are among the moderns, but the consequences of these evils were different. Among the ancients, the slave belonged to the same race as his master and was often the superior of the two in education *d and learning. Freedom was the only distinction between them, and when freedom was granted they were easily blended together. The ancients, then, had a very simple means of avoiding slavery and its evil consequences, which was emancipation; and they succeeded as soon as they adopted this measure generally. This is not to say that in ancient States no traces of servitude lingered for some time after servitude itself was abolished. There is a natural prejudice that leads men to despise anyone who was once their inferior long after he has become their equal. The real inequality produced by fortune or by law is always followed by an imaginary inequality planted in the customs of the people. Nevertheless, among the ancients this secondary consequence of slavery lasted only a limited time, for the freedman so completely resembled those born free that it soon became impossible to tell him apart from them.

d [ It is well known that several of the most distinguished authors of antiquity, among them Aesop and Terence, were or had been slaves. Slaves were not always taken from barbarous nations; the fortunes of war also reduced highly civilized men to servitude.]

The greatest difficulty in antiquity was changing the law; among the moderns it is changing the customs. And as far as we are concerned, the real obstacles begin where those of the ancients ended. This comes from the fact that, among the moderns, the abstract and transient fact of slavery is fatally joined to the physical and permanent fact of color. The tradition of slavery dishonors the race, and the distinctiveness of the race keeps the tradition of slavery alive. No African has ever voluntarily emigrated to the shores of the New World, and from this it must be inferred that all the Black people now found in that hemisphere are either slaves or freedmen. Thus the Black person passes the eternal mark of his disgrace on to all his descendants, and although the law may abolish slavery, God alone can erase the traces of its existence.

The modern slave differs from his master not only in his condition but in his origin. You can set a Black person free, but you cannot make him anything other than a foreigner to the European. Nor is this all. We scarcely recognize the common features of humanity in this child of degradation whom slavery has brought among us. His face seems hideous to us, his understanding weak, his tastes low; and we are almost inclined to regard him as a being halfway between man and the brutes. *e Thus, once the moderns have abolished slavery, they have three prejudices to fight, which are harder to attack and far harder to overcome than the mere fact of servitude: the prejudice of the master, the prejudice of race, and the prejudice of color.

e [ For the whites to give up the opinion they have formed of the moral and intellectual inferiority of their former slaves, Black people would have to change; but as long as that opinion lasts, change is impossible.]

It is hard for us, who have been fortunate enough to be born among men who are like us by nature and equal to us by law, to grasp the irreconcilable differences that separate Black Americans from Europeans in America. But we can form a faint idea of them by analogy. France was once a country with many distinctions of rank that had been created by legislation. Nothing is more artificial than a purely legal inferiority; nothing is more contrary to the instinct of mankind than these permanent divisions set up between beings who are plainly alike. Yet these divisions lasted for ages; in many places they still last; and everywhere they have left imaginary traces that only time can wear away. If it is so hard to root out an inequality that originates solely in the law, how can we destroy distinctions that seem to rest on the unchangeable laws of Nature herself? When I recall how extremely difficult it is for aristocratic bodies, of whatever kind, to blend with the mass of the people, and how very carefully they guard the ideal boundaries of their caste, I despair of seeing an aristocracy disappear when it is founded on visible and indelible signs. Those who hope that Europeans will ever mix with Black people seem to me to deceive themselves; neither my own reason nor the evidence of facts leads me to any such conclusion.

Until now, wherever the whites have been the most powerful, they have kept Black people in a subordinate or servile position; wherever Black people have been strongest, they have destroyed the whites. That is the only retribution that has ever taken place between the two races.

I see that in one part of the territory of the United States today, the legal barrier between the two races is tending to fall away, but not the barrier that exists in the customs of the country. Slavery recedes, but the prejudice it gave birth to stays where it was. Anyone who has lived in the United States must have noticed that in the parts of the Union where Black people are no longer slaves, they have in no way drawn closer to the whites. On the contrary, race prejudice appears stronger in the States that have abolished slavery than in those where it still exists; and nowhere is it so intolerant as in the States where servitude has never been known.

It is true that in the North of the Union marriages between Black people and whites may be legally contracted; but public opinion would condemn as infamous a man who married a Black woman, and it would be hard to find a single instance of such a union. The right to vote has been granted to Black people in almost all the States that have abolished slavery; but if they come forward to vote, their lives are in danger. If they are wronged, they may bring a lawsuit, but they will find only whites among their judges; and although they may legally serve as jurors, prejudice drives them away from that duty. The same schools do not admit the Black child and the European child. In the theaters, no amount of gold can buy a seat for the servile race beside their former masters; in the hospitals they lie apart; and although they are allowed to call on the same God as the whites, it must be at a different altar, in their own churches, with their own clergy. The gates of Heaven are not closed against these unhappy people; but their inferiority follows them to the very edge of the other world. When a Black man dies, his bones are cast aside, and the distinction of condition prevails even in the equality of death. The Black man is free, but he can share neither the rights, nor the pleasures, nor the labor, nor the sorrows, nor the tomb of the man whose equal he has been declared to be; and he cannot meet him on fair terms in life or in death.

In the South, where slavery still exists, Black people are kept apart less carefully. They sometimes share the labor and the recreations of the whites; the whites agree to mix with them to a certain extent; and although the legislation treats them more harshly, the habits of the people are more tolerant and compassionate. In the South the master is not afraid to raise his slave to his own level, because he knows he can reduce him to the dust in a moment whenever he pleases. In the North the white man no longer sees clearly the barrier that separates him from the degraded race, and he avoids Black people all the more stubbornly because he fears that one day they might be confused with him.

Among the Americans of the South, nature sometimes claims her rights again and brings back a fleeting equality between Black people and whites; in the North, though, pride holds in check the most commanding of human passions. The American of the Northern States would perhaps allow a Black woman to share his licentious pleasures, if the laws of his country did not declare that she may aspire to be the lawful partner of his bed; but he recoils in horror from the woman who might become his wife.

Thus it is that in the United States the prejudice that repels Black people seems to grow in proportion as they are emancipated, and inequality is sanctioned by the customs of the country while it is erased from its laws. But if the relative position of the two races living in the United States is what I have described, it may be asked why the Americans have abolished slavery in the North of the Union, why they maintain it in the South, and why they make its hardships worse there. The answer is easily given. It is not for the good of Black people but for that of the whites that measures are taken to abolish slavery in the United States.

The first Black people were brought into Virginia about the year 1621. *f In America, therefore, as in the rest of the world, slavery began in the South. From there it spread from one settlement to another; but the number of slaves fell off toward the Northern States, and the Black population was always very small in New England. *g

f [ See Beverley’s “History of Virginia.” See also, in Jefferson’s “Memoirs,” some interesting details about how Black people were first brought into Virginia, and about the first Act, passed in 1778, that prohibited their importation.]

g [ The number of slaves was smaller in the North, but the advantages that came from slavery were no more disputed there than in the South. In 1740, the legislature of the State of New York declared that the direct importation of slaves ought to be encouraged as much as possible, and smuggling severely punished, so as not to discourage the honest trader. (Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. ii. p. 206.) Curious research by Belknap on slavery in New England can be found in the “Historical Collection of Massachusetts,” vol. iv. p. 193. It appears that Black people were brought there in 1630, but that the legislation and the customs of the people were opposed to slavery from the first; see also, in the same work, how public opinion, and afterward the laws, finally put an end to slavery.]

Scarcely a century had passed since the founding of the colonies when the planters were struck by an extraordinary fact: the provinces with comparatively few slaves grew in population, wealth, and prosperity more rapidly than those with the greatest number of Black people. In the former, it is true, the inhabitants had to cultivate the soil themselves or by hired laborers; in the latter they were supplied with hands for which they paid no wages. Yet although labor and expense were on one side, and ease with economy on the other, the former provinces had the more advantageous system. This result seemed all the harder to explain because the settlers all belonged to the same European race, and had the same habits, the same civilization, and the same laws, and their differences were extremely slight.

Time went on, however, and the Anglo-Americans spread beyond the coasts of the Atlantic Ocean and pushed farther and farther into the wilderness of the West. They met with new soil and an unfamiliar climate; the obstacles in their way were of the most varied kind; their races intermingled; the inhabitants of the South went north, and those of the North went south. But amid all these causes, the same result appeared at every step, and in general the colonies without slaves became more populous and richer than those where slavery flourished. The further progress went, the more it was shown that slavery, so cruel to the slave, is harmful to the master.

But this truth was demonstrated most fully when civilization reached the banks of the Ohio. The river that the Native Americans called Ohio, or Beautiful River, waters one of the most magnificent valleys ever made the home of man. Rolling land stretches along both shores of the Ohio, and its soil offers inexhaustible treasures to the farmer. On either bank the air is healthy and the climate mild, and each bank forms the far frontier of a vast State. The one that follows the many windings of the Ohio on the left is called Kentucky; the one on the right bears the name of the river. These two States differ in only one respect: Kentucky has admitted slavery, but the State of Ohio has forbidden slaves within its borders. *h
h [ Not only is slavery prohibited in Ohio, but no free Black people are allowed to enter the territory of that State, or to hold property in it. See the Statutes of Ohio.]

Thus the traveler who floats down the Ohio to the place where it flows into the Mississippi may be said to sail between liberty and servitude; and a quick look at the surrounding scene will convince him which of the two is more favorable to mankind. On the left bank the population is sparse; from time to time one sees a band of slaves loitering in the half-deserted fields; the primeval forest returns at every turn; society seems asleep and man idle, and nature alone offers a scene of activity and life. From the right bank, by contrast, a confused hum is heard that announces the presence of industry; the fields are covered with abundant harvests; the elegance of the dwellings shows the taste and activity of the farmer; and man appears to enjoy the wealth and contentment that are the reward of labor. *i

i [ Ohio’s energy is not limited to individuals; the State’s own undertakings are remarkably large. A canal now links Lake Erie to the Ohio, so that the valley of the Mississippi is connected with the river of the North, and European goods landed at New York can travel by water all the way to New Orleans, across five hundred leagues of continent.]

The State of Kentucky was founded in 1775, the State of Ohio only twelve years later; but twelve years count for more in America than half a century in Europe, and today the population of Ohio exceeds that of Kentucky by two hundred and fifty thousand souls. *j These opposite consequences of slavery and freedom are easy to understand, and they are enough to explain many of the differences we see between the civilization of antiquity and that of our own time.
j [ The exact numbers given by the census of 1830 were: Kentucky, 688,-844; Ohio, 937,679. [In 1890 the population of Ohio was 3,672,316, that of Kentucky, 1,858,635.]]

On the left bank of the Ohio, labor is associated with the idea of slavery; on the right bank, it is identified with prosperity and improvement. On the one side it is degraded, on the other it is honored. In the former territory no white laborers can be found, for they would be afraid of being assimilated to Black people; in the latter no one is idle, for the white population brings its activity and its intelligence to every kind of employment. Thus the men whose task is to cultivate the rich soil of Kentucky are ignorant and lukewarm, while those who are active and educated either do nothing or move over to the State of Ohio, where they can work without dishonor.

It is true that in Kentucky the planters do not have to pay wages to the slaves they employ; but they get small profits from their labor, whereas the wages paid to free workmen would come back with interest in the value of their services. The free workman is paid, but he does his work faster than the slave, and speed of execution is one of the great elements of economy. The white man sells his services, but they are bought only when they happen to be useful; the Black man can claim no payment for his toil, but the cost of his upkeep never stops. He must be supported in his old age as well as in the prime of manhood, in his unprofitable childhood as well as in the productive years of youth. Payment must be made equally to obtain the services of either class of men: the free workman receives his wages in money, the slave in education, food, care, and clothing. The money a master spends on the upkeep of his slaves goes out gradually and in small amounts, so that it is scarcely noticed; the free workman’s wage is paid in a lump sum, which seems only to enrich the person who receives it. But in the end the slave has cost more than the free servant, and his labor is less productive. *k

k [ Apart from these causes, which make free labor more productive and more economical than slave labor wherever free workmen are plentiful, another cause can be pointed out that is particular to the United States: the sugar cane has until now been cultivated successfully only on the banks of the Mississippi, near the mouth of that river in the Gulf of Mexico. In Louisiana the cultivation of sugar cane is extremely profitable, and nowhere does a laborer earn so much by his work; and since there is always a certain relation between the cost of production and the value of the produce, the price of slaves is very high in Louisiana. But Louisiana is one of the confederated States, and slaves may be carried there from all parts of the Union; the price paid for slaves in New Orleans therefore raises the value of slaves in all the other markets. The consequence is that in the countries where the land is less productive, the cost of slave labor is still very considerable, which gives free labor an additional advantage in competition.]

The influence of slavery goes further still: it affects the character of the master and gives a particular bent to his ideas and tastes. On both banks of the Ohio the inhabitants are enterprising and energetic, but this vigor is used very differently in the two States. The white inhabitant of Ohio, who has to live by his own efforts, regards material prosperity as the main aim of his existence. The country he lives in offers inexhaustible resources to his industry and ever-changing temptations to his activity, so his eagerness to acquire goes beyond the ordinary limits of human greed. He is tormented by the desire for wealth, and he boldly takes every path that fortune opens to him. He becomes a sailor, a pioneer, an artisan, or a laborer with equal indifference, and he endures with equal constancy the hardships and dangers of these various professions. The resources of his intelligence are astonishing, and his eagerness in pursuit of gain amounts to a kind of heroism.

But the Kentuckian scorns not only labor but all the undertakings that labor promotes. Because he lives in idle independence, his tastes are those of an idle man; money loses part of its value in his eyes; he covets wealth much less than pleasure and excitement; and the energy his neighbor devotes to making money turns, in him, into a passionate love of field sports and military exercises. He delights in violent bodily exertion, he is familiar with the use of arms, and from a very early age he is accustomed to risk his life in single combat. Thus slavery not only keeps the whites from becoming wealthy, it keeps them even from wishing to be.

The same causes have been producing opposite effects continually for the last two centuries in the British colonies of North America, and they have established a very striking difference between the commercial capacity of the inhabitants of the South and that of the North. Today only the Northern States possess shipping, manufactures, railroads, and canals. This difference can be seen not only in comparing the North with the South but also in comparing the several Southern States. Almost all the individuals who carry on commercial operations, or who try to turn slave labor to account, in the most southern districts of the Union have emigrated from the North. The natives of the Northern States are constantly spreading over the part of American territory where they have less competition to fear. They discover resources there that escaped the notice of the inhabitants; and since they go along with a system they do not approve of, they succeed in turning it to better advantage than the people who first founded it and still maintain it.

If I wished to continue this comparison, I could easily prove that almost all the differences we notice between the characters of the Americans in the Southern and the Northern States have originated in slavery; but that would take me away from my subject, and my present intention is to point out not all the consequences of servitude but only the effects it has had on the prosperity of the countries that have admitted it.

The influence of slavery on the production of wealth must have been understood very imperfectly in antiquity, since slavery then prevailed throughout the civilized world, and the nations that did not have it were barbarous. And indeed Christianity abolished slavery only by pleading the cause of the slave; at the present time it can be attacked in the name of the master, and on this point self-interest is reconciled with morality.

As these truths became plain in the United States, slavery gave way before the progress of experience. Servitude had begun in the South and had spread from there toward the North; but now it is retreating again. Freedom, which started from the North, now moves steadily down toward the South. Among the large States, Pennsylvania now forms the northern limit of slavery; but even within those limits the slave system is shaken. Maryland, which lies immediately below Pennsylvania, is preparing for its abolition; and Virginia, which comes next to Maryland, is already debating its usefulness and its dangers. *l

l [ One particular reason helps turn the last two States away from the cause of slavery. This part of the Union used to draw its wealth mainly from growing tobacco. That crop is grown especially by slaves; but in the last few years the market price of tobacco has dropped, while the value of slaves has stayed the same. So the ratio between the cost of production and the value of the produce has shifted. The people of Maryland and Virginia are therefore more willing than they were thirty years ago to give up slave labor in tobacco growing, or to give up slavery and tobacco together.]

No great change takes place in human institutions without the law of inheritance being among its causes. When the law of primogeniture prevailed in the South, each family was represented by one wealthy individual, who was neither forced nor encouraged to work. He was surrounded, like a tree by parasitic plants, by the other members of his family, who were then excluded by law from sharing the common inheritance and who lived the same kind of life as he did. The very same thing happened then in all the families of the South as still happens in the wealthy families of some European countries: the younger sons remain in the same state of idleness as their elder brother, without being as rich as he is. This identical result seems to be produced in Europe and in America by wholly similar causes. In the South of the United States the whole white race formed an aristocratic body, headed by a certain number of privileged individuals whose wealth was permanent and whose leisure was hereditary. These leaders of the American nobility kept alive the traditional prejudices of the white race, whose representatives they were, and upheld the honor of an inactive life. This aristocracy contained many who were poor, but none who would work; its members preferred want to labor. Consequently no competition arose against Black laborers and slaves, and whatever opinion might be held about the usefulness of their efforts, it was necessary to employ them, since there was no one else to work.

As soon as the law of primogeniture was abolished, fortunes began to shrink, and all the families of the country were reduced at the same time to a state in which labor became necessary to earn a living. Several of them have since disappeared entirely, and all of them learned to look ahead to the time when everyone would have to provide for his own needs. Wealthy individuals can still be found, but they no longer form a close-knit, hereditary body, nor have they been able to adopt a line of conduct that they could keep up and spread through all ranks of society. The prejudice that stigmatized labor was first abandoned by common consent; the number of needy men increased; and the needy were allowed to earn a hard living without blushing for their efforts. Thus one of the most immediate consequences of the division of estates has been to create a class of free laborers. As soon as competition began between the free laborer and the slave, the slave’s inferiority became obvious, and slavery was attacked at its fundamental principle, which is the interest of the master.

As slavery recedes, the Black population follows its backward course and returns with it toward the tropical regions from which it originally came. However odd this fact may seem at first, it is easily explained. Although the Americans abolish the principle of slavery, they do not set their slaves free. To illustrate this remark, I will take the example of the State of New York. In 1788 the State of New York prohibited the sale of slaves within its limits, which was an indirect way of prohibiting the importation of Black people. From then on the number of Black people could increase only at the rate of natural population growth. But eight years later a more decisive measure was taken, and it was enacted that all children born of slave parents after July 4, 1799, should be free. No increase could then take place; and although slaves still existed, slavery could be said to be abolished.

Once a Northern State prohibited the importation of slaves, no more slaves were brought from the South to be sold in its markets. On the other hand, because the sale of slaves was forbidden in that State, an owner could no longer rid himself of a slave who had become a burden, except by taking him to the South. And when a Northern State declared that a slave’s son should be born free, the slave lost a large share of his market value, since his descendants were no longer part of the bargain; the owner then had a strong interest in taking him to the South. Thus the same law keeps the slaves of the South from coming to the Northern States, and drives those of the North to the South.

A State feels the lack of free hands more as its slaves become fewer. But the more the work is done by free hands, the less productive slave labor becomes; the slave is then a useless or burdensome possession, and it is important to send him off to those Southern States where the same competition is not to be feared. Thus the abolition of slavery does not set the slave free: it merely transfers him from one master to another, and from the North to the South.

The emancipated Black people, and those born after the abolition of slavery, do not, indeed, move from the North to the South; but their situation in relation to the Europeans is not unlike that of the native peoples of America. They remain half civilized and deprived of their rights in the midst of a population far superior to them in wealth and in knowledge, where they are exposed to the tyranny of the laws *m and the intolerance of the people. In some respects they are even more to be pitied than the Native Americans, since they are haunted by the memory of slavery and cannot claim possession of a single piece of the soil. Many of them perish miserably, *n and the rest crowd into the large towns, where they do the lowest jobs and lead a wretched and precarious existence.

m [ States that have abolished slavery usually do whatever they can to make their territory an unpleasant place for Black people to live; and since the different States rival one another in this, these unhappy people can only choose the least of the evils surrounding them.]

n [ Death rates differ greatly between Black people and whites in the States that have abolished slavery. From 1820 to 1831 only one out of forty-two individuals of the white population died in Philadelphia, but one Black person out of twenty-one individuals of the Black population died in the same period. Among Black people who are still slaves, mortality is by no means so high. (See Emerson’s “Medical Statistics,” p. 28.)]

But even if the number of Black people continued to increase as fast as when they were still in slavery, the number of whites has grown twice as fast since the abolition of slavery, so Black people would soon be, as it were, lost in the midst of a foreign population.

A district cultivated by slaves is generally more thinly populated than a district cultivated by free labor. Moreover, America is still a new country, and a State is therefore not half populated when it abolishes slavery. As soon as slavery is ended, the lack of free labor is felt, and a crowd of enterprising adventurers arrives at once from all parts of the country, hurrying to profit from the fresh resources then opened to industry. The soil is soon divided among them, and a family of white settlers takes possession of each tract of land. Besides, European emigration goes exclusively to the free States; for what would be the fate of a poor emigrant who crosses the Atlantic in search of comfort and happiness if he landed in a country where labor is stigmatized as degrading?

Thus the white population grows by natural increase and, at the same time, by the immense influx of emigrants, while the Black population receives no emigrants and is declining. The proportion between the two races is soon reversed. Black people become a small remnant, a poor tribe of wanderers, lost in the midst of an immense people in full possession of the land; and their presence is marked only by the injustice and hardships of which they are the unhappy victims.

In several of the Western States the Black race never appeared, and in all the Northern States it is declining rapidly. Thus the great question of its future condition is confined within a narrow circle, where it becomes less formidable, though no easier to solve.
The farther south we go, the more difficult it becomes to abolish slavery with advantage; and this arises from several physical causes that are important to point out.

The first of these causes is the climate. It is well known that the closer Europeans come to the tropics, the more they suffer from labor. Many Americans even claim that within a certain latitude the exertions a Black man can make without danger are fatal to them; *o but I do not think that this opinion, which is so convenient for the idleness of the inhabitants of southern regions, is confirmed by experience. The southern parts of the Union are not hotter than the South of Italy and of Spain; *p and it may be asked why the European cannot work as well there as in those two countries. If slavery has been abolished in Italy and in Spain without destroying the masters, why should the same thing not happen in the Union? I cannot believe that nature has forbidden Europeans in Georgia and the Floridas, on pain of death, to raise their means of subsistence from the soil; but their labor would unquestionably be more tiresome and less productive for them than for the inhabitants of New England. Since the free workman thus loses part of his superiority over the slave in the Southern States, there are fewer inducements to abolish slavery.

o [ This is true of the places where rice is cultivated; rice grounds, which are unhealthy in all countries, are particularly dangerous in regions exposed to the rays of a tropical sun. Europeans would not find it easy to cultivate the soil in that part of the New World if it had to be made to produce rice; but may they not live without rice grounds?]
p [ These States are nearer to the equator than Italy and Spain, but the temperature of the continent of America is very much lower than that of Europe.

The Spanish government once had a certain number of peasants from the Azores transported to a district of Louisiana called Attakapas, as an experiment. These settlers still cultivate the soil without the help of slaves, but their industry is so sluggish that it barely supplies their most necessary wants.]

All the plants of Europe grow in the northern parts of the Union; the South has special products of its own. It has been observed that slave labor is a very expensive way of cultivating corn. The farmer of corn land in a country where slavery is unknown keeps a small number of laborers in his service all the time, and at seed time and harvest he hires several additional hands, who live at his expense only for a short period. But the farmer in a slave State has to keep a large number of slaves all year round, in order to sow his fields and bring in his crops, although their services are needed for only a few weeks. Slaves cannot wait until they are hired and support themselves by their own labor in the meantime, as free laborers do; to have their services, they must be bought. Slavery, apart from its general disadvantages, is therefore even less suited to countries where corn is grown than to those that produce other kinds of crops. The cultivation of tobacco, of cotton, and especially of sugar cane, on the other hand, demands constant attention; and women and children are employed in it, whose services are of little use in growing wheat. Thus slavery is naturally better suited to the countries from which these products come. Tobacco, cotton, and sugar cane are grown exclusively in the South, and they are among the principal sources of wealth of those States. If slavery were abolished, the inhabitants of the South would be forced to choose between two alternatives. Either they would have to change their system of cultivation, and then they would come into competition with the more active and more experienced inhabitants of the North; or, if they kept growing the same produce without slave labor, they would have to face the competition of the other Southern States that might still keep their slaves. Thus there are particular reasons for maintaining slavery in the South that do not operate in the North.

But there is yet another motive, more compelling than all the others. Strictly speaking, the South could abolish slavery; but how would it rid its territory of the Black population? Slaves and slavery are driven from the North by the same law, but this twofold result cannot be hoped for in the South.

The arguments I have given, showing that slavery is more natural and more profitable in the South than in the North, are enough to prove that slaves must be far more numerous in the southern districts. It was to the southern settlements that the first Africans were brought, and it is there that the greatest number of them have always been imported. As we advance toward the South, the prejudice that sanctions idleness grows stronger. In the States nearest the tropics there is not a single white laborer; Black people are consequently much more numerous in the South than in the North. And, as I have already observed, this disproportion grows daily, since Black people are transferred to one part of the Union as soon as slavery is abolished in the other. Thus the Black population increases in the South not only by its natural fertility but by the forced emigration of Black people from the North; and the African race has causes of increase in the South very similar to those that so powerfully speed the growth of the European race in the North.

In the State of Maine there is one Black person in 300 inhabitants; in Massachusetts, one in 100; in New York, two in 100; in Pennsylvania, three in the same number; in Maryland, thirty-four; in Virginia, forty-two; and lastly, in South Carolina, *q fifty-five percent. Such was the proportion of the Black population to the whites in the year 1830. But the proportion keeps changing: it falls steadily in the North and rises in the South.

q [ We find it asserted in an American work entitled “Letters on the Colonization Society,” by Mr. Carey, 1833, “That for the last forty years the black race has increased more rapidly than the white race in the State of South Carolina; and that if we take the average population of the five States of the South into which slaves were first introduced, viz., Maryland, Virginia, South Carolina, North Carolina, and Georgia, we shall find that from 1790 to 1830 the whites have augmented in the proportion of 80 to 100, and the blacks in that of 112 to 100.”
In the United States, in 1830, the population of the two races stood as follows:—

In the States where slavery is abolished: 6,565,434 whites; 120,520 Black people. In the slave States: 3,960,814 whites; 2,208,102 Black people. [In 1890 the United States contained a population of 54,983,890 whites, and 7,638,360 Black people.]]

It is clear that the southernmost States of the Union cannot abolish slavery without running very great dangers, ones the North had no reason to fear when it freed its Black population. We have already described how the Northern States manage the transition from slavery to freedom: they keep the present generation in chains and set their descendants free. In this way Black people are brought into society gradually. While the men who might abuse their freedom remain in servitude, those who are freed can learn the art of being free before they become their own masters. But this method would be hard to apply in the South. To declare that all Black people born after a certain date shall be free is to introduce the principle and the idea of liberty into the heart of slavery. The Black people whom the law keeps enslaved, while their children are released from that condition, are astonished at so unequal a fate, and their astonishment is only the prelude to impatience and resentment. From then on, slavery loses in their eyes the kind of moral power it drew from time and habit; it is reduced to a plain abuse of force. The Northern States had nothing to fear from this contrast, because Black people there were few and the white population was very large. But if this faint dawn of freedom were to show two million men their true position, the oppressors would have reason to tremble. Once they had freed the children of their slaves, the Europeans of the Southern States would very soon be obliged to extend the same benefit to the entire Black population.

In the North, as I have already remarked, a twofold migration follows the abolition of slavery, or even precedes it when circumstances have made abolition likely. The slaves leave the country to be transported southward, and the whites of the Northern States, along with emigrants from Europe, hurry to fill their place. But these two causes cannot work in the same way in the Southern States. On the one hand, the mass of slaves is too great for anyone to expect that they could ever be removed from the country. On the other hand, the Europeans and the Anglo-Americans of the North are afraid to settle in a country where labor has not yet been restored to its rightful honor. Besides, they very justly regard the States in which Black people equal or outnumber whites as exposed to very great dangers, and they refrain from directing their energies there.

Thus the people of the South could not, like their Northern countrymen, introduce the slaves gradually to freedom by abolishing slavery. They have no way of noticeably reducing the Black population, and they would be left without support to restrain its excesses. So within a few years a great population of free Black people would exist in the heart of a white nation of equal size.

The same abuses of power that still sustain slavery would then become the source of the most alarming perils the white population of the South might have to fear.
