At present the descendants of the Europeans are the sole owners of the land, the absolute masters of all labor, and the only people who possess wealth, knowledge, and arms. The Black man has none of these advantages, but he gets by without them because he is a slave. If he were free and had to provide for his own subsistence, would it be possible for him to go without these things and still stay alive? Or would not the very instruments of the white man’s present superiority, while slavery lasts, expose him to a thousand dangers if slavery were abolished?

As long as the Black man remains a slave, he can be kept in a condition not very far from that of the animals. But with his liberty he cannot fail to acquire enough instruction to appreciate his misfortunes and to see a remedy for them. Moreover, there is a peculiar principle of relative justice that is very firmly planted in the human heart. People are struck much more forcibly by inequalities within the same class than by those between different classes. It is easier for them to accept slavery than to allow several million citizens to live under a load of eternal infamy and hereditary wretchedness. In the North the population of freed Black people feels these hardships and resents these indignities, but its numbers and its power are small; in the South it would be numerous and strong.

Once it is admitted that whites and emancipated Black people live on the same territory as two foreign communities, it is easy to see that the future holds only two alternatives: Black people and whites must either separate completely or mingle completely. I have already stated my conviction about the latter. *r I do not imagine that the white and Black races will ever live on an equal footing in any country. But I believe the difficulty to be even greater in the United States than elsewhere. An isolated individual may overcome the prejudices of religion, of country, or of race, and if that individual is a king he may bring about surprising changes in society; but a whole people cannot rise, as it were, above itself. A despot who made the Americans and their former slaves bear the same yoke might perhaps succeed in blending their races. But as long as the American democracy remains at the head of affairs, no one will undertake so difficult a task, and it can be foreseen that the freer the white population of the United States becomes, the more isolated it will remain. *s

r [ This opinion is backed by authorities infinitely weightier than anything I can say. For instance, the “Memoirs of Jefferson” (as collected by M. Conseil) state: “Nothing is more clearly written in the book of destiny than the emancipation of the blacks; and it is equally certain that the two races will never live in a state of equal freedom under the same government, so insurmountable are the barriers which nature, habit, and opinions have established between them.”]
s [ If the British West India planters had governed themselves, they would certainly not have passed the Slave Emancipation Bill that the mother country has recently imposed on them.]

I have observed earlier that the mixed race is the true bond of union between the Europeans and the Native Americans. In the same way, people of mixed race are the true means of transition between the white and the Black man, so that wherever they are numerous, the intermixture of the two races is not impossible. In some parts of America the European and Black races have crossed so much that it is rare to meet a man who is entirely Black or entirely white. When they have reached this point, the two races may truly be said to be combined, or rather to have been absorbed into a third race, which is connected with both without being identical with either.

Of all the Europeans, the English are the ones who have mixed least with Black people. More people of mixed race are seen in the South of the Union than in the North, but they are still infinitely scarcer than in any other European colony. They are by no means numerous in the United States; they have no strength of their own, and when quarrels arising from differences of color break out, they generally side with the whites, just as the lackeys of the great in Europe take on the contemptuous airs of the nobility toward the lower orders.

The pride of origin natural to the English is singularly increased by the personal pride that democratic liberty fosters among the Americans. The white citizen of the United States is proud of his race and proud of himself. But if whites and Black people do not intermingle in the North of the Union, how would they mix in the South? Can anyone suppose for a moment that an American of the Southern States, placed as he must forever be between the white man with all his physical and moral superiority and the Black man, will ever think of preferring the latter? The Americans of the Southern States have two powerful passions that will always keep them apart: the first is the fear of being made like Black people, their former slaves; the second is the dread of sinking below the whites, their neighbors.

If I were asked to predict what will probably happen at some future time, I would say that the abolition of slavery in the South will, in the ordinary course of things, increase the white population’s repugnance toward people of color. I base this opinion on a similar observation I had already made in the North. I noticed there that the white inhabitants of the North avoid Black people with increasing care as the legal barriers of separation are removed by the legislature. Why should the same result not occur in the South? In the North, whites are deterred from mixing with Black people by fear of an imaginary danger; in the South, where the danger would be real, I cannot imagine that the fear would be less widespread.

Suppose, on the one hand, it is admitted (and the fact is unquestionable) that the Black population keeps accumulating in the extreme South and that it increases more rapidly than the white population. Suppose, on the other hand, it is granted that no one can foresee a time when whites and Black people will be so intermingled as to draw the same benefits from society. Must we not conclude that Black people and whites will sooner or later come to open conflict in the Southern States of the Union? But if one asks what the outcome of the struggle is likely to be, it is easy to see that we can form only a very vague guess at the truth. The human mind may succeed in drawing a wide circle, as it were, that includes the course of future events; but within that circle a thousand different chances and circumstances may steer it in as many different directions, and every picture of the future contains a dim spot that the eye of the understanding cannot penetrate. It appears, however, extremely probable that in the West Indian Islands the white race is destined to be overcome, and the Black population on the continent to share the same fate.

In the West India Islands the white planters are surrounded by an immense Black population. On the continent, Black people are placed between the ocean and an innumerable people that already spreads over them in a dense mass, from the icy borders of Canada to the frontiers of Virginia, and from the banks of the Missouri to the shores of the Atlantic. If the white citizens of North America remain united, we cannot suppose that Black people will escape the destruction that threatens them; they must be subdued by want or by the sword. But the Black population accumulated along the coast of the Gulf of Mexico has a chance of success if the American Union is dissolved when the struggle between the two races begins. If the federal tie were broken, the citizens of the South would be wrong to rely on any lasting help from their Northern countrymen. The Northerners know well that the danger can never reach them, and unless they are compelled to march to the South’s assistance by a formal obligation, it can be foreseen that the sympathy of color will not be enough to spur them to effort.

Yet whenever the conflict may break out, the whites of the South, even if left to their own resources, will enter the contest with an immense superiority in knowledge and in the means of warfare. But Black people will have numerical strength and the energy of despair on their side, and these are powerful resources for men who have taken up arms. The fate of the white population of the Southern States will perhaps be like that of the Moors in Spain. After occupying the land for centuries, it will perhaps be forced to withdraw to the country its ancestors came from, and to leave to Black people the possession of a territory that Providence seems to have destined more particularly for them, since they can live and work in it more easily than whites.

The danger of a conflict between the white and Black inhabitants of the Southern States of the Union — a danger that, however remote, is inevitable — haunts the imagination of the Americans without rest. The people of the North make it a common topic of conversation, although they have no direct injury to fear from the struggle, but they try in vain to devise some means of avoiding the misfortunes they foresee. In the Southern States the subject is not discussed. The planter does not mention the future when talking with strangers; the citizen does not share his apprehensions with his friends; he tries to hide them from himself. But there is something more alarming in the silent forebodings of the South than in the loud fears of the Northern States.

This all-pervading anxiety has given birth to an undertaking that is little known but may change the fate of a portion of the human race. Out of apprehension of the dangers I have just described, a certain number of American citizens have formed a society to export to the coast of Guinea, at their own expense, any free Black people who are willing to escape the oppression to which they are subject. *t In 1820 the society I am speaking of founded a settlement in Africa, at the seventh degree of north latitude, which bears the name of Liberia. The most recent information tells us that 2,500 Black people are gathered there. They have introduced the democratic institutions of America into the country of their forefathers. Liberia has a representative system of government, Black jurymen, Black magistrates, and Black priests; churches have been built, newspapers founded, and, by a strange reversal in the course of the world’s affairs, white men are forbidden to stay within the settlement. *u

t [ This society took the name “The Society for the Colonization of the Blacks.” See its annual reports, and especially the fifteenth. See also the pamphlet already mentioned, titled “Letters on the Colonization Society, and on its probable Results,” by Mr. Carey, Philadelphia, 1833.]

u [ The founders of the settlement laid down this last rule. They feared that a state of things might arise in Africa like the one on the frontiers of the United States, and that if Black people, like the Native Americans, were brought into collision with a people better educated than themselves, they would be destroyed before they could be civilized.]

This is indeed a strange caprice of fortune. Two hundred years have now passed since the people of Europe set out to tear the Black man from his family and his home in order to carry him to the shores of North America. Today the European settlers are busy sending the descendants of those same Black people back to the Continent from which they were first taken. The barbarous Africans have been brought into contact with civilization in the midst of bondage, and have become acquainted with free political institutions in slavery. Until now Africa has been closed to the arts and sciences of the whites; but perhaps the inventions of Europe will now penetrate those regions, since Africans themselves are introducing them. The settlement of Liberia is founded on a lofty and most fruitful idea; but whatever its results may be for the Continent of Africa, it can offer no remedy to the New World.

In twelve years the Colonization Society has transported 2,500 Black people to Africa; in the same period about 700,000 Black people were born in the United States. Suppose the colony of Liberia were situated so that it could receive thousands of new inhabitants every year, and suppose Black people were in a condition to be sent there with advantage. Suppose the Union gave the society annual subsidies *v and carried Black people to Africa in the vessels of the state. It would still be unable to offset the natural increase of the Black population. And since it could not remove in a year as many people as are born on its territory in the same time, it would fail to halt the growth of the evil, which increases daily in the States. *w The Black race will never leave those shores of the American continent to which it was brought by the passions and vices of Europeans, and it will not disappear from the New World as long as it continues to exist. The inhabitants of the United States may delay the calamities they fear, but they cannot now destroy their efficient cause.

v [ Nor would these be the only difficulties of the undertaking. If the Union set out to buy up the Black people now in America in order to transport them to Africa, the price of slaves, rising with their scarcity, would soon become enormous, and the Northern States would never agree to spend such great sums for a purpose that would bring them so little advantage. If the Union seized the slaves in the Southern States by force, or at a price fixed by law, insurmountable resistance would arise in that part of the country. Both alternatives are equally impossible.]

w [ In 1830 there were in the United States 2,010,327 slaves and 319,439 free Black people, 2,329,766 Black people in all, who formed about one-fifth of the total population of the United States at that time.]

I am obliged to confess that I do not regard the abolition of slavery as a means of warding off the struggle between the two races in the United States. Black people may remain slaves for a long time without complaining; but once they are raised to the level of free men, they will soon revolt at being deprived of all their civil rights, and since they cannot become the equals of the whites, they will soon declare themselves enemies. In the North everything helped to make emancipation easy, and slavery was abolished without putting free Black people in a position that could become formidable, since their number was too small for them ever to claim the exercise of their rights. But the South is different. For the slave-owners of the North, the question of slavery was a question of commerce and manufacturing; for those of the South it is a question of life and death. God forbid that I should try to justify the principle of the enslavement of Black people, as some American writers have done! I only observe that not all the countries that once adopted that execrable principle are equally able to abandon it at present.

When I consider the condition of the South, I can see only two courses open to the white inhabitants of those States: either to emancipate Black people and mingle with them, or, remaining separate from them, to keep them in slavery as long as possible. All intermediate measures seem to me likely to end, and soon, in the most horrible of civil wars, and perhaps in the extermination of one of the two races. This is how the Americans of the South view the question, and they act consistently with it. Since they are determined not to mingle with Black people, they refuse to emancipate them.

It is not that the people of the South regard slavery as necessary to the planter’s wealth. On this point many of them agree with their Northern countrymen in freely admitting that slavery is harmful to their interest. But they are convinced that, however harmful it may be, they hold their lives on no other terms. The education now spreading in the South has convinced the inhabitants that slavery is injurious to the slave-owner, but it has also shown them, more clearly than before, that there is no way of getting rid of its bad consequences. Hence arises a strange contrast: the more the usefulness of slavery is disputed, the more firmly it is established in the laws; and while the principle of servitude is gradually abolished in the North, that very principle gives rise to harsher and harsher consequences in the South.

The legislation of the Southern States concerning slaves presents today such unparalleled atrocities that they suffice to show how radically the laws of humanity have been perverted, and to reveal the desperate position of the community in which that legislation was enacted. The Americans of this part of the Union have not, indeed, increased the hardships of slavery; on the contrary, they have improved the physical condition of the slaves. The only means by which the ancients maintained slavery were fetters and death; the Americans of the South of the Union have discovered more intellectual safeguards for the duration of their power. They have turned their despotism and violence against the human mind. In antiquity, precautions were taken to keep the slave from breaking his chains; today measures are taken to deprive him even of the desire for freedom. The ancients held the bodies of their slaves in bondage, but they placed no restraint on the mind and no check on education; and they acted consistently with their established principle, since slavery then had a natural end, and one day or another the slave might be set free and become the equal of his master. But the Americans of the South, who do not admit that Black people can ever be blended with themselves, have forbidden them, under severe penalties, to be taught to read or write; and since they will not raise them to their own level, they push them down as nearly as possible to that of animals.

The slave had always been allowed the hope of liberty to lighten the hardships of his condition. But the Americans of the South are well aware that emancipation cannot fail to be dangerous when the freed man can never be assimilated to his former master. To give a man his freedom and leave him in wretchedness and disgrace is nothing less than to prepare a future leader of a slave revolt. Moreover, it has long been noticed that the presence of a free Black person vaguely disturbs the minds of his less fortunate brethren and gives them a dim idea of their rights. The Americans of the South have therefore taken measures to prevent slave-owners, in most cases, from emancipating their slaves — not, indeed, by a positive prohibition, but by subjecting that step to various formalities that are hard to satisfy. I happened to meet an old man in the South of the Union who had lived in an illicit relationship with one of his Black female slaves and had had several children by her, who were born the slaves of their father. He had indeed often thought of leaving them at least their liberty in his will; but years had passed without his being able to overcome the legal obstacles to their emancipation, and in the meantime old age had come and he was about to die. He pictured his sons dragged from market to market, passing from a parent’s authority to the rod of a stranger, until these horrible forebodings drove his dying imagination to frenzy. When I saw him he was a prey to all the anguish of despair, and he made me feel how awful is nature’s retribution on those who have broken her laws.

These evils are unquestionably great; but they are the necessary and foreseen consequence of the very principle of modern slavery. When the Europeans chose their slaves from a race different from their own, which many of them considered inferior to the other races of mankind, and which they all rejected with horror at any thought of intimate connection, they must have believed that slavery would last forever. For no intermediate state can be lasting between the excessive inequality produced by servitude and the complete equality that originates in independence. The Europeans did dimly feel this truth, but without acknowledging it even to themselves. Whenever they have had dealings with Black people, their conduct has been dictated either by their interest and pride or by their compassion. They first violated every right of humanity in their treatment of Black people, and afterward they informed them that those rights were precious and inviolable. They pretended to open their ranks to the slaves, but Black people who tried to enter the community were driven back with scorn; and they have been led, carelessly and unintentionally, to accept freedom in place of slavery, without having the courage to be either wholly wicked or wholly just.

Suppose no one can foresee a time when the Americans of the South will mix their blood with that of Black people. Can they then let their slaves go free without putting their own safety at risk? And if they are obliged to keep that race in bondage to save their own families, may they not be excused for using the means best suited to that end? What is happening in the Southern States of the Union strikes me as both the most horrible and the most natural result of slavery. When I see the order of nature overturned, and when I hear the cry of humanity struggling in vain against the laws, my indignation does not fall on the men of our own time who are the instruments of these outrages. I reserve my execration for those who, after a thousand years of freedom, brought slavery back into the world once more.

Whatever efforts the Americans of the South make to maintain slavery, they will not always succeed. Slavery is now confined to a single region of the civilized earth; Christianity attacks it as unjust and political economy as harmful; and it now stands in contrast with democratic liberties and the knowledge of our age. It cannot survive. By the master’s choice or by the slave’s will, it will end; and in either case great calamities may be expected to follow. If liberty is refused to the Black people of the South, they will in the end seize it by force; if it is given, they will before long abuse it. *x

Thus in South Carolina there were in 1870, 289,667 whites and 415,814 Black people. What Are the Chances in Favor of the Duration of the American Union, and What Dangers Threaten It *y

The survival of the existing institutions of the several States depends to some extent on the survival of the Union itself. It is therefore important to begin by inquiring into the probable fate of the Union. One point may indeed be assumed at once: if the present confederation were dissolved, it seems to me beyond dispute that the States now composing it would not return to their original isolated condition, but that several unions would then be formed in place of one. I do not intend to inquire into the principles on which these new unions would probably be established, but only to show what causes may bring about the breakup of the existing confederation.

For this purpose I shall have to retrace some of the steps I have already taken and return to topics I have discussed before. I know the reader may accuse me of repetition, but the importance of the matter still to be treated is my excuse. I would rather say too much than too little to be fully understood, and I prefer to harm the author rather than slight the subject.

The legislators who framed the Constitution of 1789 tried to give the federal power a distinct and preponderating authority. But they were limited by the nature of the task they had undertaken. They were not appointed to constitute the government of a single people, but to regulate the association of several States; and whatever their inclinations might be, they could not avoid dividing the exercise of sovereignty in the end.

To understand the consequences of this division, it is necessary to draw a short distinction among the affairs of government. Some matters are national by their very nature; that is, they affect the nation as a body and can be entrusted only to the man or the assembly of men who most completely represent the entire nation. War and diplomacy may be counted among these. Other matters are provincial by their very nature; that is, they affect only certain localities and can be handled properly only in that locality. The budget of a municipality is an example. Lastly, there are certain matters of a mixed nature, which are national in that they affect all the citizens who make up the nation, and provincial in that the nation itself need not provide for all of them. Such are the rights that regulate the civil and political condition of the citizens. No society can exist without civil and political rights. These rights therefore concern all citizens alike; but it is not always necessary to the existence and prosperity of the nation that these rights be uniform, nor, consequently, that the central authority regulate them.

There are, then, two distinct categories of matters placed under the direction of the sovereign power, and these categories are found in all well-constituted communities, whatever the basis of the political constitution may otherwise be. Between these two extremes lie the matters I have called mixed. Since these matters are neither exclusively national nor entirely provincial, they may be handled by a national or by a provincial government, according to the agreement of the contracting parties, without in any way impairing the contract of association.

The sovereign power is usually formed by the union of separate individuals who make up a people; and individual powers or collective forces, each representing a very small portion of the sovereign authority, are the only elements subject to the general government of their choice. In this case the general government is more naturally called upon to regulate not only the affairs of essential national importance but also those of more local interest, and the local governments are reduced to the small share of sovereign authority indispensable to their prosperity.

But sometimes the sovereign authority is composed of political bodies already organized, by virtue of circumstances that predate their union. In this case the provincial governments take control not only of the affairs that more particularly belong to their province, but of all or part of the mixed affairs mentioned above. For the confederate nations, which were independent sovereign States before their union and still represent a very considerable share of the sovereign power, have consented to cede to the general government only the exercise of those rights indispensable to the Union.

When the national government, besides the prerogatives inherent in its nature, is invested with the right to regulate affairs that relate partly to general and partly to local interests, it has a preponderating influence. Not only are its own rights extensive, but all the rights it does not hold exist only by its sufferance, and it may be feared that its influence will deprive the provincial governments of their natural and necessary prerogatives.

Now suppose the opposite arrangement, in which the provincial governments are given the power to regulate those same affairs of mixed interest. Society then leans the other way. The stronger force sits in the province rather than in the nation, and it is to be feared that the national government may in the end be stripped of the privileges it needs in order to exist.
Independent nations, then, naturally tend toward centralization, and confederations naturally tend toward dismemberment.

All that remains is to apply these general principles to the American Union. The several States necessarily held the right to regulate every affair that is purely provincial. They also kept the right to decide who is competent to act as a citizen in civil and political matters, to regulate the relations of the members of the community with one another, and to dispense justice. These rights are general in nature, yet they do not necessarily belong to a national government. We have seen that the government of the Union has the power to act in the name of the whole nation when the nation must appear as a single, undivided power: in foreign relations, for instance, and in joint resistance to a common enemy. In short, it handles the affairs I have called exclusively national.

At first glance, the Union seems to hold a larger share of sovereignty than the States do. A closer look shows that it holds a smaller one. The Union’s undertakings are more vast, but its influence is felt less often. The provincial governments’ undertakings are comparatively small, but they never stop, and they keep alive the authority behind them. The government of the Union looks after the general interests of the country. Yet the general interests of a people have a very doubtful effect on individual happiness, whereas provincial interests bear immediately on the well-being of the inhabitants. The Union secures the independence and greatness of the nation, which private citizens do not feel directly. The several States, by contrast, preserve each citizen’s liberty, regulate his rights, protect his property, and secure his life and his whole future prosperity.

The federal government stands very far from the people it governs, while the provincial governments are within everyone’s reach and ready to hear the smallest appeal. The central government has behind it the passions of a few superior men who aspire to run it. The provincial governments have behind them the interests of all the second-rate men who can hope for power only inside their own State. These men nevertheless hold the largest share of authority over the people, because they stand closest to the people’s own level. So the Americans have much more to hope for and to fear from the States than from the Union, and, following the natural bent of the human mind, they are more likely to attach themselves to the former than to the latter. On this point their habits and feelings agree with their interests.

Suppose a compact nation divides its sovereignty and adopts a confederate form of government. For a long time the people’s traditions, habits, and mores will conflict with their laws, and those traditions and habits will tend to give the central government more influence than the laws allow it. Now suppose several confederate states unite to form a single nation. The same causes then work in the opposite direction. I have no doubt that if France became a confederate republic like the United States, its government would at first show more energy than the government of the Union does. And if the Union changed its constitution to a monarchy like the French one, I think the American government would need a long time to gain the force that now governs France. When the Anglo-Americans began their national existence, their provincial existence was already old. Necessary ties had formed between the townships and between the individual citizens of each State. The people were used to treating some matters as common to all, and to handling other affairs as concerning only their own particular interests.

The Union is a vast body, and it gives patriotic feeling no definite object to attach to. The State, by contrast, has distinct and limited forms and boundaries. It stands for a certain number of things that its citizens know well and that everyone loves. It is bound up with the soil itself, with the right of property and the affections of home, with the memories of the past, the labors of the present, and the hopes of the future. Patriotism is often only individual egotism extended, and it still turns toward the State; the Union does not arouse it. Thus the interests, habits, and feelings of the people all tend to center political activity in the States rather than in the Union.

One can easily measure the relative strength of the two governments by watching how each performs its functions. When the government of a State has to speak to an individual or to a gathering of individuals, its language is clear and commanding. The federal government uses the same tone with individuals. But as soon as it has any business with a State, it starts to parley. It explains its motives and justifies its conduct, argues and advises, and does anything except command. If doubts arise over the limits of each government’s constitutional powers, the provincial government states its claim boldly and takes quick, vigorous steps to back it up. The government of the Union, meanwhile, reasons. It appeals to the nation’s interests, its good sense, and its glory; it stalls and negotiates, and it will not agree to act until it is driven to the last extremity. At first sight one might easily suppose that the provincial government is the one armed with the nation’s authority, and that Congress speaks for a single State.

The federal government is therefore, whatever precautions its founders took, so weak by nature that it particularly requires the free consent of the governed in order to survive. It is easy to see that its purpose is to help the States carry out, without difficulty, their resolve to stay united. As long as that resolve exists, its authority is great, moderate, and effective. The Constitution equips the government to control individuals and to overcome without trouble whatever obstacles they may try to put in its way. It was by no means established with the possible separation of one or more States from the Union in view.

Suppose the sovereignty of the Union entered into a struggle with that of the States today. One can confidently predict that the Union would lose, and a struggle of that kind is unlikely ever to be seriously attempted. Whenever the federal government meets steady resistance, it gives way. Experience so far shows that a State that has demanded something with perseverance and resolution has always got it, and that when a separate government has plainly refused to act, it has been left to do as it saw fit. *z

z [ See the conduct of the Northern States in the war of 1812. “During that war,” says Jefferson in a letter to General Lafayette, “four of the Eastern States were only attached to the Union, like so many inanimate bodies to living men.”]

Even if the government of the Union had some strength of its own, the physical situation of the country would make that strength hard to use. *a The United States covers an immense territory. Great distances separate the States from one another, and the population is scattered across a country that is still half wilderness. If the Union tried to compel the confederate States to obey by force of arms, it would find itself in a position much like England’s during the War of Independence.

a [ The profound peace of the Union gives no pretext for a standing army; and without a standing army a government is not prepared to take advantage of a favorable opportunity to overcome resistance and seize the sovereign power by surprise. [The results of the Civil War have shown that this note, and the paragraph in the text that precedes it, were a misconception on the writer’s part.]]

No government, however strong, can easily escape the consequences of a principle it has once accepted as the foundation of its constitution. The States formed the Union by voluntary agreement. In uniting, they did not give up their nationality, and they were not reduced to being one and the same people. If one State chose to withdraw from the contract, it would be hard to disprove its right to do so, and the federal government would have no direct way to uphold its claims, whether by force or by right. For the federal government to overcome easily the resistance of any one of its members, one or more of the others would have to have a special stake in the existence of the Union. That has often been the case in the history of confederations.

Suppose that among the States joined by the federal tie, some alone enjoy the main advantages of union, or depend for their prosperity on its lasting. It is certain that these States will always be ready to back the central government when it forces the others to obey. But the government would then be using a force that does not come from itself, and that comes instead from a principle contrary to its nature. States form confederations in order to gain equal advantages from union. In the case just described, the federal government would draw its power from the unequal distribution of those advantages among the States.

Suppose one of the confederate States has gained such a preponderance that it can take exclusive possession of the central authority. It will then treat the other States as subject provinces and will have its own supremacy respected under the borrowed name of the sovereignty of the Union. Great things may be done in the name of the federal government, but in reality that government will have ceased to exist. *b In both cases, the power acting in the confederation’s name grows stronger the further it departs from the natural state and the accepted principles of confederations.

b [ Thus the province of Holland in the republic of the Low Countries, and the Emperor in the Germanic Confederation, have sometimes put themselves in the place of the union and used the federal authority to their own advantage.]

In America the existing Union benefits every State, but it is not indispensable to any one of them. Several of them could break the federal tie without harming the welfare of the rest, though their own prosperity would suffer. The existence and happiness of none of them depend wholly on the present Constitution, so none of them would be inclined to make great personal sacrifices to preserve it. On the other hand, no State seems so far to have its ambition much bound up with keeping the existing Union in being. They certainly do not all have equal influence in the federal councils, but none can hope to lord it over the others or to treat them as inferiors or subjects.

I find it beyond doubt that if any part of the Union seriously wanted to separate from the other States, the rest could not stop it, and indeed would not try. The present Union will last only as long as the States that make it up choose to remain in the confederation. Once this point is granted, the question becomes less difficult. We are not asking whether the States of the existing Union are able to separate. We are asking whether they will choose to stay united.

Of the many reasons that make the existing Union useful to the Americans, two principal ones stand out to an observer. The Americans are, in a sense, alone on their continent, yet their trade makes them neighbors of every nation they deal with. Their isolation is only apparent. They need a certain degree of strength, and they can keep it only by staying united with one another. If the States were to split apart, they would not only reduce the strength they can now show toward foreign nations; they would soon create foreign powers on their own soil. Inland customs barriers would go up, imaginary boundary lines would cut across the valleys, territorial distinctions would restrict the courses of the rivers, and countless hindrances would keep the Americans from exploring the whole of the vast continent that Providence has given them to rule. For now they have no invasion to fear, and so they have no standing armies to maintain and no taxes to levy. If the Union dissolved, all these burdensome measures might soon be required. The Americans therefore have a very strong interest in keeping their Union. On the other hand, one can hardly find any material interest that would now tempt a part of the Union to break away from the rest.

Looking at a map of the United States, we see the chain of the Alleghany Mountains running from northeast to southwest across nearly a thousand miles of country. We are tempted to think Providence meant to raise between the valley of the Mississippi and the Atlantic coast one of those natural barriers that cut off contact between peoples and mark the necessary limits of different States. But the Alleghanies average no more than 2,500 feet in height, and their highest point is not above 4,000 feet. Their rounded summits, and the broad valleys hidden in their passes, can be entered easily from several sides. Besides this, the principal rivers that empty into the Atlantic Ocean — the Hudson, the Susquehanna, and the Potomac — all begin beyond the Alleghanies, in an open district that borders the valley of the Mississippi. They leave that region and break through the barrier that seems to turn them westward, and as they wind through the mountains they give people an easy, natural way across. There is no natural barrier anywhere in the regions the Anglo-Americans now inhabit. The Alleghanies, far from separating nations, do not even serve as a frontier between States. New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia take them within their borders, and those States reach as far west of the line as east of it. The territory now held by the twenty-four States of the Union, together with the three great districts that already have inhabitants but have not yet been given the rank of States, covers 1,002,600 square miles, *c which is about five times the size of France. Within these limits the soil, the temperature, and the produce of the country vary enormously. The great extent of territory held by the Anglo-American republics has raised doubts about whether their Union can last. Here we must draw a distinction. In a vast empire, opposing interests sometimes arise in different provinces and often end in open conflict, and then the size of the country does the greatest harm to the power of the State. But if the inhabitants of such vast regions are not divided by opposing interests, the size of the territory may help their prosperity. Unity of government encourages the exchange of the soil’s different products, and it raises their value by making them easier to consume.

c [ See “Darby’s View of the United States,” p. 435. [In 1890 the number of States and Territories had increased to 51, the population to 62,831,900, and the area of the States to 3,602,990 square miles. This does not include the Philippine Islands, Hawaii, or Porto Rico. A conservative estimate of the population of the Philippine Islands is 8,000,000; that of Hawaii, by the census of 1897, was given as 109,020; and the present estimated population of Porto Rico is 900,000. The area of the Philippine Islands is about 120,000 square miles, that of Hawaii is 6,740 square miles, and the area of Porto Rico is about 3,600 square miles.]]

Different interests are indeed easy to find in the different parts of the Union, but I know of none that are hostile to one another. The Southern States are almost wholly agricultural. The Northern States are especially commercial and manufacturing. The Western States are agricultural and manufacturing at once. In the South the crops are tobacco, rice, cotton, and sugar; in the North and West they are wheat and maize. These are different sources of wealth, but union is the means that opens them all to everyone and makes each equally profitable to every district.

The North carries the produce of the Anglo-Americans to every part of the world and brings the world’s produce back to the Union. It plainly has an interest in keeping the confederation as it now stands, so that the number of American producers and consumers stays as large as possible. The North is the most natural go-between linking the South and West of the Union with the rest of the world. It therefore has an interest in the union and prosperity of the South and West, so that they may keep supplying raw materials for its factories and cargoes for its ships.

The South and the West, for their part, have an even more direct interest in preserving the Union and in the North’s prosperity. Most of the South’s produce is shipped overseas, so the South and the West both depend on the North’s commercial resources. They also have an interest in the Union keeping a powerful fleet to protect them effectively. The South and West own no ships, but they cannot refuse to pay willingly toward the navy’s expenses. If the fleets of Europe blockaded the ports of the South and the mouth of the Mississippi, what would become of the rice of the Carolinas, the tobacco of Virginia, and the sugar and cotton grown in the Mississippi valley? Every part of the federal budget thus helps to maintain material interests shared by all the confederate States.

Besides this commercial usefulness, the South and the West gain great political advantages from their connection with the North. The South has an enormous slave population, one that is already alarming and will be more formidable still in the future. The Western States lie at the far end of a single valley. All the rivers that cross their territory rise in the Rocky Mountains or the Alleghanies and flow into the Mississippi, which carries them on to the Gulf of Mexico. Their position therefore cuts the Western States off entirely from the traditions of Europe and the civilization of the Old World. So the people of the South have reason to support the Union in order to have its protection against Black people. The people of the West have reason to support it so as not to lose free communication with the rest of the world and be shut up in the wilds of central America. And the North cannot help wanting the Union kept in being, so that it can remain, as it is now, the link between that vast body and the rest of the world.
The material interests of all the parts of the Union, then, are closely tied together. The same is true of those opinions and feelings that may be called the immaterial interests of men.

The people of the United States talk a great deal about their love of country. I confess that I do not rely on that calculating patriotism, which rests on interest and which a change in the interests at stake can wipe out. Nor do I give much weight to the Americans’ words when, in daily conversation, they declare their intention to maintain the federal system their forefathers adopted. A government holds its sway over a great number of citizens far less through the voluntary, reasoned consent of the multitude than through an instinctive and, to some extent, involuntary agreement that comes from similar feelings and resemblances of opinion. I will never grant that men form a social body merely because they obey the same head and the same laws. Society can exist only when a great number of men see a great number of things from the same point of view, hold the same opinions on many subjects, and have the same thoughts and impressions suggested to them by the same events.

An observer who examines the present condition of the United States by this principle will readily see that, although the citizens are divided into twenty-four distinct sovereignties, they still form a single people. He may perhaps be led to think that the Anglo-American Union is more truly a society than certain nations of Europe that live under the same laws and the same prince.

The Anglo-Americans belong to several religious sects, yet they all look at religion in the same way. They do not always agree about which measures best serve good government, and they differ over some of the forms of government worth adopting. But they are unanimous about the general principles that should govern human society. From Maine to the Floridas, and from the Missouri to the Atlantic Ocean, the people is held to be the legitimate source of all power. Everywhere the same ideas are held about liberty and equality, the liberty of the press, the right of association, trial by jury, and the responsibility of the agents of government.

If we leave their political and religious opinions and turn to the moral and philosophical principles that shape the actions of daily life and guide their conduct, we find the same uniformity. The Anglo-Americans *d recognize the absolute moral authority of the community’s reason, just as they recognize the political authority of the mass of citizens, and they hold that public opinion is the surest judge of what is allowed or forbidden, true or false. Most of them believe that a man will be led to do what is just and good by following his own self-interest properly understood. They hold that every man is born with the right to govern himself, and that no one has the right to force his fellow creatures to be happy. They all have a lively faith in human perfectibility. They think that the spread of knowledge must have good effects and that ignorance must have fatal ones. They all see society as a body that is improving, and humanity as a changing scene in which nothing is, or should be, permanent. And they admit that what seems good to them today may be replaced tomorrow by something better. I do not offer all these opinions as true. I cite them as characteristic of the Americans.

d [ I hardly need point out that by the expression Anglo-Americans I mean only the great majority of the nation; for a certain number of isolated individuals are of course to be found holding very different opinions.]

These shared opinions are not all that unites the Anglo-Americans. A common feeling of pride also sets them apart from every other nation. For the last fifty years, no effort has been spared to persuade the people of the United States that they alone are religious, enlightened, and free. They see that for the moment their own democratic institutions succeed while those of other countries fail. They therefore form an inflated opinion of their own superiority, and they are not far from believing that they belong to a different race of mankind.

The dangers that threaten the American Union come not from diversity of interests or opinions but from the differing characters and passions of the Americans. The men who live across the vast territory of the United States are almost all descended from one common stock. But climate, and above all slavery, have gradually produced very striking differences between the British settler in the Southern States and the British settler in the North. In Europe it is generally believed that slavery has set the interests of one part of the Union against those of another. I did not find this to be so at all. Slavery has not created interests in the South opposed to those of the North. What it has done is change the character and habits of the South’s native-born people.

I have already explained how slavery has affected the commercial ability of the Southern Americans, and the same influence extends equally to their mores. The slave is a servant who never protests and who submits to everything without complaint. He may sometimes murder his master, but he never stands up to him. In the South no family is too poor to own slaves. From his earliest years the Southern citizen holds a kind of domestic dictatorship. The first idea he gets in life is that he was born to command, and the first habit he forms is that of being obeyed without resistance. His upbringing thus tends to make him haughty and hasty: irascible, violent, and ardent in his desires, impatient with obstacles, yet easily discouraged if he fails at his first attempt.

The American of the Northern States grows up with no slaves around him, and not even free servants to wait on him, and he usually has to provide for his own needs. As soon as he enters the world, the idea of necessity presses on him from every side. He quickly learns exactly where the natural limit of his authority lies. He never expects to subdue by force those who resist him, and he knows that the surest way to win the support of his fellow creatures is to earn their favor. So he becomes patient, thoughtful, tolerant, slow to act, and steady in his plans.

In the Southern States the more pressing needs of life are always provided for. The people there are not occupied with the material cares of life, since others always attend to them, and their imagination turns to more captivating and less definite objects. The Southerner loves grandeur, luxury, and renown, gaiety and pleasure, and above all idleness. Nothing forces him to exert himself to make a living, and since he has no necessary occupation, he gives in to laziness and does not even try what would be useful.

In the North, however, equality of fortunes and the absence of slavery plunge people into the same cares of daily life that the white population of the South looks down on. From infancy they are taught to fight want and to put comfort above every pleasure of the mind or heart. Imagination is stifled by the petty details of life, and ideas grow fewer and less general, though far more practical and precise. Since prosperity is the only aim of their efforts, they reach it superbly. Nature and mankind are turned to the best financial account, and society is cleverly made to serve the welfare of each of its members, so that individual egotism becomes the source of general happiness.

The Northerner has not only experience but knowledge, and yet he values the pleasures of knowledge very little. To him it is a means to an end, and he is eager only to seize its most profitable uses. The Southerner is more inclined to act on impulse. He is cleverer, more open, more generous, more intellectual, and more brilliant. The Northerner has more activity, common sense, information, and general ability, and he has the characteristic virtues and vices of the middle classes. The Southerner has the tastes, prejudices, weaknesses, and magnanimity of every aristocracy. Take two men who share a society and have the same interests and, to some degree, the same opinions, but who differ in character, in what they have learned, and in their style of civilization. They will probably not agree. The same holds for a society of nations. Slavery, then, does not attack the American Union directly through its interests, but indirectly through its mores.

Thirteen States gave their assent to the federal contract in 1790. The Union now has thirty-four members. The population, nearly 4,000,000 in 1790, more than tripled in forty years and reached nearly 13,000,000 in 1830. *e Changes on this scale cannot take place without some danger.

A society of nations, like a society of individuals, owes its main chances of lasting to the wisdom of its members, their individual weakness, and their small number. The Americans who leave the Atlantic coast and plunge into the western wilderness are adventurers who cannot bear restraint, who are greedy for wealth, and who are often men driven out of the States where they were born. When they reach the wilds, they are strangers to one another, and they have no traditions, no family feeling, and no example to hold their excesses in check. Among them the rule of law is weak, and that of morality weaker still. The settlers who keep filling the Mississippi valley are thus in every respect far inferior to the Americans of the older parts of the Union. Yet they already have great influence in its councils, and they come to govern the commonwealth before they have learned to govern themselves. *f
f [ This is indeed only a temporary danger. I have no doubt that in time society will acquire as much stability and regularity in the West as it already has on the coast of the Atlantic Ocean.]

The weaker each party to a contract is individually, the better the chances that the contract will last, since their safety then depends on staying united. In 1790 the most populous of the American republics had fewer than 500,000 inhabitants. *g Each felt how insignificant it was as an independent people, and that feeling made it easier to comply with the federal authority. But consider a confederate State like New York, which counts 2,000,000 inhabitants and covers a territory equal to a quarter of France. *h Such a State feels its own strength. It may keep supporting the Union because the Union helps its prosperity, but it no longer sees the Union as necessary to its existence. And while it remains a party to the federal compact, it soon aims at preponderance in the federal assemblies. The likelihood of unanimity among the States diminishes as their number grows. Today the interests of the different parts of the Union do not conflict. But who can foresee the many changes still to come in a country where towns are founded from one day to the next, and States almost from one year to the next?
g [ Pennsylvania contained 431,373 inhabitants in 1790 [and 5,258,014 in 1890.]]
h [ The area of the State of New York is 49,170 square miles. [See U. S. census report of 1890.]]

Ever since the British colonies were first settled, their population has roughly doubled every twenty-two years. I can see nothing likely to halt this steady growth of the Anglo-American population during the next hundred years. Before that time is up, I believe, the territories and dependencies of the United States will hold more than 100,000,000 inhabitants and be divided into forty States. *i I grant that these 100,000,000 men will have no hostile interests. I even suppose that they all have an equal stake in keeping the Union. Still, I hold that with 100,000,000 men and forty distinct nations of unequal strength, the survival of the federal government can only be a lucky accident.

i [ If the population continues to double every twenty-two years, as it has done for the last two hundred years, the number of inhabitants in the United States in 1852 will be twenty millions; in 1874, forty-eight millions; and in 1896, ninety-six millions. This may still be the case even if the lands on the western slope of the Rocky Mountains turn out to be unfit for cultivation. The territory already occupied can easily hold this number of inhabitants. One hundred millions of men spread over the surface of the twenty-four States and the three dependencies that make up the Union would give only 762 inhabitants to the square league. This is far below the mean population of France, which is 1,063 to the square league, or of England, which is 1,457; and it would even be below the population of Switzerland, for that country, despite its lakes and mountains, has 783 inhabitants to the square league. See “Malte Brun,” vol. vi. p. 92.

[The actual result has fallen somewhat short of these calculations, despite the vast territorial acquisitions of the United States; but in 1899 the population is probably about eighty-seven millions, including the population of the Philippines, Hawaii, and Porto Rico.]]

However much faith I have in human perfectibility, I will refuse to believe that a government can last when it is asked to hold together forty different peoples spread over a territory half the size of Europe, to prevent all rivalry, ambition, and conflict among them, and to direct their independent activity toward the same ends. I will keep refusing until human nature changes and men are wholly transformed.

But the greatest danger the Union faces from its growth comes from the constant shifting of its internal strength. From Lake Superior to the Gulf of Mexico the distance runs from the 47th to the 30th degree of latitude, more than 1,200 miles in a straight line. The frontier of the United States winds along this whole immense line, sometimes falling inside it, but more often reaching far beyond it into the wilderness. It has been calculated that the whites advance an average of seventeen miles a year along this entire vast boundary. *j Now and then they meet obstacles: an unproductive district, a lake, or a Native American nation they did not expect to find. The advancing column then halts for a while. Its two ends fall back on themselves, and as soon as they have joined up again, they move forward. This slow, unbroken progress of the European race toward the Rocky Mountains has the solemnity of a providential event. It is like a flood of men that keeps rising and is driven forward every day by the hand of God.
j [ See Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, p. 105.]

Within this first line of conquering settlers, towns are built and great States founded. In 1790 only a few thousand pioneers were scattered along the valleys of the Mississippi. Today those valleys hold as many people as the entire Union held in 1790. Their population is nearly 4,000,000. *k The city of Washington was founded in 1800 at the very center of the Union. But so much has changed that it now lies at one of the extremities, and the delegates from the most remote Western States already have to make a journey as long as the one from Vienna to Paris. *l
l [ The distance from Jefferson, the capital of the State of Missouri, to Washington is 1,019 miles. (“American Almanac,” 1831, p. 48.)]

All the States are carried forward together along the road to fortune, but they naturally do not all grow and prosper at the same rate. In the North, the outlying branches of the Alleghany chain run all the way to the Atlantic Ocean and form spacious roadsteads and ports that vessels of the greatest burden can always enter. But from the Potomac to the mouth of the Mississippi the coast is sandy and flat. In this part of the Union the mouths of nearly all the rivers are blocked, and the few harbors among the lagoons offer ships much shallower water and far fewer commercial advantages than those of the North.

This first natural cause of inferiority is joined by another that comes from the laws. We have already seen that slavery, which has been abolished in the North, still exists in the South, and I have pointed out its fatal consequences for the prosperity of the planter himself.

The North is therefore superior to the South in both commerce *m and manufacturing, and the natural result is a more rapid growth of population and wealth within its borders. The States on the shores of the Atlantic Ocean are already half-peopled. Most of the land there has an owner, so these districts cannot take in as many emigrants as the Western States, where a boundless field is still open to their efforts. The valley of the Mississippi is far more fertile than the Atlantic coast. This reason, added to all the others, drives Europeans westward — a fact that can be demonstrated rigorously with figures. The total population of all the United States has roughly tripled over forty years. But in the new States next to the Mississippi, the population has grown thirty-one-fold in the same period. *n
m [ The following figures will be enough to show the difference between the commerce of the South and that of the North: —

In 1829 the combined tonnage of all the merchant vessels belonging to Virginia, the two Carolinas, and Georgia (the four great Southern States) came to only 5,243 tons. In the same year the tonnage of the vessels of the State of Massachusetts alone came to 17,322 tons. (See Legislative Documents, 21st Congress, 2d session, No. 140, p. 244.) So Massachusetts had three times as much shipping as the four States just named. Yet the area of Massachusetts is only 7,335 square miles, and its population is 610,014 inhabitants [2,238,943 in 1890], while the area of the four other States I have cited is 210,000 square miles and their population 3,047,767. (See “Darby’s View of the United States.”) Slavery harms the commercial prosperity of the South in several ways: it weakens the spirit of enterprise among the whites, and it prevents them from finding as large a class of sailors as they need. They cannot serve as well as a white crew, and there would always be fear that they would mutiny in mid-ocean or escape in the foreign countries where they might put in.]
n [ “Darby’s View of the United States,” p. 444.]

The relative position of the central federal power is continually shifting. Forty years ago most of the citizens of the Union lived on the Atlantic coast, in the area around the spot where Washington now stands. But the great body of the people is now moving inland and to the north, so that within twenty years the majority will undoubtedly be on the western side of the Alleghanies. If the Union continues to exist, the basin of the Mississippi is clearly marked out, by its fertility and its size, as the future center of the Federal Government. In thirty or forty years that region will have taken the rank that naturally belongs to it. It is easy to calculate that its population, compared to that of the Atlantic coast, will be, in round numbers, as 40 to 11. In a few years the States that founded the Union will lose the direction of its policy, and the population of the valley of the Mississippi will predominate in the federal assemblies.

This constant shift of federal power and influence toward the northwest shows itself every ten years, when a general census is taken and the number of delegates each State sends to Congress is set anew. *o In 1790 Virginia had nineteen representatives in Congress. That number kept rising until 1813, when it reached twenty-three; from then on it declined, and in 1833 Virginia elected only twenty-one representatives. *p Over the same period the State of New York moved in the opposite direction: in 1790 it had ten representatives in Congress; in 1813, twenty-seven; in 1823, thirty-four; and in 1833, forty. The State of Ohio had only one representative in 1803, and in 1833 it already had nineteen.

o [ It can be seen that over the last ten years (1820–1830) the population of one district, for instance the State of Delaware, has grown by five percent, while that of another, such as the territory of Michigan, has grown by 250 percent. Likewise the population of Virginia had increased thirteen percent, and that of the border State of Ohio sixty-one percent, in the same period. The general table of these changes, given in the “National Calendar,” presents a striking picture of the unequal fortunes of the different States.]

p [ It was just said that in the last period the population of Virginia grew thirteen percent. It is necessary to explain how the number of representatives for a State can fall when the State’s population, far from shrinking, is actually growing. I take the State of Virginia, which I have already mentioned, as my point of comparison. The number of Virginia’s representatives in 1823 was proportional to the total number of representatives of the Union and to the ratio of its population to that of the whole Union. In 1833 the number of Virginia’s representatives was likewise proportional to the total number of representatives of the Union and to the ratio of its population, enlarged over ten years, to the enlarged population of the Union over the same time. The new number of Virginian representatives will then stand to the old number, on the one hand, as the new total number of representatives stands to the old; and, on the other hand, as the growth of Virginia’s population stands to the growth of the whole population of the country. Thus, if the growth of the smaller country’s population stands to that of the larger in exact inverse ratio to the proportion between the new and old totals of representatives, the number of Virginia’s representatives will stay the same. And if the growth of the Virginian population stands to that of the whole Union in a weaker ratio than the new number of the Union’s representatives to the old number, the number of Virginia’s representatives must fall. [Thus, to the 56th Congress in 1899, Virginia and West Virginia send only fourteen representatives.]]

It is hard to imagine a lasting union between a rich, strong people and a poor, weak one, even if it were proved that the strength and wealth of the one are not the causes of the weakness and poverty of the other. But union is harder still to maintain when one party is losing strength and the other is gaining it. This rapid and disproportionate growth of certain States threatens the independence of the others. New York, with its 2,000,000 inhabitants and its forty representatives, might perhaps succeed in dictating to the other States in Congress. But even if the more powerful States make no attempt to overbear the lesser ones, the danger remains, for the possibility of the act matters almost as much as the act itself. The weak generally distrust the justice and the reason of the strong. The States that grow less rapidly than the others look with envy and suspicion on those that fortune favors more. Hence come the deep-seated uneasiness and vague agitation that can be observed in the South, and that contrast so sharply with the confidence and prosperity common to other parts of the Union. I am inclined to think that the hostile measures taken by the Southern provinces on a recent occasion are due to no other cause. Of all Americans, the inhabitants of the Southern States have the greatest interest in maintaining the Union; they would surely suffer most from being left to themselves; and yet they are the only citizens who threaten to break the bond of confederation. But it is easy to see that the South has given the Union four Presidents, Washington, Jefferson, Madison, and Monroe; that it perceives it is losing its federal influence; that the number of its representatives in Congress is shrinking from year to year, while those of the Northern and Western States are growing; and that the South, which is peopled with ardent and irascible men, is becoming more and more irritated and alarmed. Its citizens reflect on their present position and remember their past influence, with the melancholy uneasiness of men who suspect oppression. If they find a law of the Union that is not unequivocally favorable to their interests, they protest against it as an abuse of force; and if their ardent remonstrances go unheard, they threaten to leave an association that loads them with burdens while it deprives them of their due profits. “The tariff,” said the inhabitants of Carolina in 1832, “enriches the North, and ruins the South; for if this were not the case, to what can we attribute the continually increasing power and wealth of the North, with its inclement skies and arid soil; while the South, which may be styled the garden of America, is rapidly declining?” *q
q [ See the report of its committee to the Convention which proclaimed the nullification of the tariff in South Carolina.]

If the changes I have described were gradual, so that each generation at least had time to pass away along with the order of things it had lived under, the danger would be smaller. But the progress of society in America is precipitate and almost revolutionary. The same citizen may live to see his State take the lead in the Union and then become powerless in the federal assemblies; and an Anglo-American republic has been known to grow as fast as a man passing from birth and infancy to maturity in thirty years. It must not be imagined, however, that States that lose their predominance also lose their population or their wealth. Their prosperity is not halted, and they even go on growing faster than any kingdom in Europe. *r But they believe themselves impoverished because their wealth does not grow as fast as their neighbors’, and they think their power is lost because they have suddenly run up against a power greater than their own. *s Thus they are hurt more in their feelings and passions than in their interests. But that is amply enough to endanger the maintenance of the Union. If kings and peoples had only ever looked to their true interests since the beginning of the world, the name of war would scarcely be known among mankind.

r [ The population of a country is surely the first element of its wealth. In the ten years (1820–1830) during which Virginia lost two of its representatives in Congress, its population grew by 13.7 percent, that of Carolina by fifteen percent, and that of Georgia by 15.5 percent. (See the “American Almanac,” 1832, p. 162) But the population of Russia, which grows faster than that of any other European country, increases in ten years at only 9.5 percent; in France, at seven percent; and in Europe in general, at 4.7 percent. (See “Malte Brun,” vol. vi. p. 95)]

s [ It must be admitted, however, that the fall in the value of tobacco over the last fifty years has notably reduced the opulence of the Southern planters; but this circumstance is as independent of the will of their Northern brethren as it is of their own.]

So the prosperity of the United States is the source of the gravest dangers that threaten them. It tends to produce, in some of the confederate States, the feverish excitement that comes with fast-growing fortunes, and to awaken in others the envy, mistrust, and regret that usually follow when such fortunes are lost. The Americans watch this extraordinary and hurried progress with exultation, but they would be wiser to watch it with sorrow and alarm. The Americans of the United States are bound to become one of the greatest nations in the world. Their offshoot will cover almost all of North America, and the continent they live on is their dominion, which cannot slip away from them. What drives them to seize it so soon? Riches, power, and renown will certainly be theirs someday, yet they rush toward their fortune as though only a moment were left to make it their own.

I think I have shown that the existence of the present confederation depends entirely on the continued assent of all the confederates, and, starting from this principle, I have inquired into the causes that may lead the several States to separate from the others. The Union may, however, perish in two different ways. One of the confederate States may choose to withdraw from the compact and so forcibly sever the federal tie; most of my remarks so far apply to this supposition. Or the authority of the Federal Government may be gradually eroded by the simultaneous tendency of the united republics to take back their independence. The central power, stripped one by one of all its prerogatives and reduced to impotence by tacit consent, would become unable to fulfill its purpose, and the second Union would perish, like the first, from a kind of senile incapacity. The gradual weakening of the federal tie, which may finally lead to the dissolution of the Union, is a separate matter, and it may produce a variety of lesser consequences before it brings about so violent a change. The confederation might still subsist even if its government were reduced to such a state of inanition that it paralyzed the nation, caused internal anarchy, and checked the general prosperity of the country.

Having investigated the causes that may lead the Anglo-Americans to disunite, it is important to ask whether, if the Union continues to exist, their government will widen or narrow its sphere of action, and whether it will become more energetic or weaker.

The Americans are evidently disposed to view their future condition with alarm. They see that in most nations of the world the exercise of the rights of sovereignty tends to fall under the control of a few individuals, and they are dismayed by the idea that the same will happen in their own country. Even statesmen feel these fears, or pretend to; for in America centralization is by no means popular, and there is no surer way of courting the majority than to inveigh against the encroachments of the central power. The Americans do not notice that the countries where this alarming tendency to centralization exists are inhabited by a single people, while the fact that the Union is composed of different confederate communities is enough to defeat all the inferences that might be drawn from analogous circumstances. I confess that I am inclined to consider the fears of a great number of Americans as purely imaginary; and far from sharing their dread of power being consolidated in the hands of the Union, I think that the Federal Government is visibly losing strength.
To prove this assertion I shall not turn to any remote events, but to circumstances that I have witnessed myself and that belong to our own time.

A careful look at what is going on in the United States will easily convince us that two opposite tendencies exist in that country, like two distinct currents flowing in opposite directions in the same channel. The Union has now existed for forty-five years, and in that time a vast number of provincial prejudices, which at first were hostile to its power, have died away. The patriotic feeling that attached each American to his native State has become less exclusive, and the different parts of the Union have become more closely connected the better they have come to know each other. The post, *t that great instrument of intellectual communication, now reaches into the backwoods, and steamboats have established daily connections between the different points of the coast. An inland navigation of unexampled speed carries goods up and down the rivers of the country. *u To these advantages of nature and art we may add those restless cravings, that busy-mindedness, and that love of money, which constantly drive the American into active life and bring him into contact with his fellow citizens. He crosses the country in every direction; he visits all the various populations of the land; and there is not a province in France whose natives know each other as well as the 13,000,000 men who cover the territory of the United States.

t [ In 1832 the district of Michigan, which has only 31,639 inhabitants and is still nearly unexplored wilderness, already had 940 miles of mail-roads. The territory of Arkansas, which is even less settled, was already crossed by 1,938 miles of mail-roads. (See the report of the General Post Office, November 30, 1833.) The postage on newspapers alone in the whole Union came to $254,796.]

u [ In the ten years from 1821 to 1831, 271 steamboats were launched on the rivers that water the valley of the Mississippi alone. In 1829, 259 steamboats existed in the United States. (See Legislative Documents, No. 140, p. 274.)]

But as the Americans intermingle, they come to resemble each other more. The differences that result from their climate, their origin, and their institutions grow smaller, and they all draw nearer and nearer to a common type. Every year, thousands of men leave the North to settle in different parts of the Union. They bring with them their faith, their opinions, and their customs; and as they are better educated than the men among whom they are about to live, they soon rise to the head of affairs and shape society to their own advantage. This continual emigration from the North to the South is particularly favorable to the fusion of all the different provincial characters into one national character. The civilization of the North appears to be the common standard to which the whole nation will one day be assimilated.

The commercial ties that unite the confederate States are strengthened by the Americans’ growing manufactures, and the union that began to exist in their opinions gradually becomes part of their habits. The passage of time has swept away the bugbear fears that haunted the imaginations of citizens in 1789. The federal power has not become oppressive; it has not destroyed the independence of the States; it has not subjected the confederates to monarchical institutions; and the Union has not made the lesser States dependent on the larger ones. Instead the confederation has gone on growing in population, wealth, and power.
