As they are accustomed to rely on their own testimony, they like to see the object that engages their attention with extreme clearness. They therefore strip away as much as possible of all that covers it, rid themselves of whatever separates them from it, and remove whatever hides it from sight, in order to view it more closely and in the broad light of day. This disposition of mind soon leads them to despise forms, which they regard as useless and inconvenient veils placed between them and the truth.

The Americans, then, have not needed to draw their philosophical method from books; they have found it in themselves. The same thing can be observed in what has happened in Europe. This same method has been established and made popular in Europe only to the degree that the condition of society has become more equal and people have grown more like each other. Let us consider for a moment how the periods in which this change can be traced are connected. In the sixteenth century the Reformers subjected some of the dogmas of the ancient faith to the scrutiny of private judgment, but they still withheld all the rest from it. In the seventeenth century, Bacon in the natural sciences and Descartes in philosophy in the strict sense abolished accepted formulas, destroyed the empire of tradition, and overthrew the authority of the schools. The philosophers of the eighteenth century finally generalized the same principle and undertook to submit to the private judgment of each man all the objects of his belief.

Who does not see that Luther, Descartes, and Voltaire used the same method, and that they differed only in how far each said it should be applied? Why did the Reformers keep so closely within the circle of religious ideas? Why did Descartes, who chose to apply his method only to certain matters even though he had made it fit for all, declare that men might judge for themselves in matters philosophical but not in matters political? How did it happen that in the eighteenth century those general applications were suddenly drawn from this same method, which Descartes and his predecessors had either not noticed or had rejected? And finally, how are we to explain that at this period the method we are speaking of suddenly left the schools, entered society, and became the common standard of intelligence; and that, once it had become popular among the French, it was openly adopted or secretly followed by all the nations of Europe?

The philosophical method described here may have been produced in the sixteenth century; it may have been more accurately defined and more widely applied in the seventeenth. But in neither century could it be commonly adopted. Political laws, the condition of society, and the habits of mind that derive from these causes were still opposed to it. It was discovered at a time when men were beginning to equalize and assimilate their conditions. It could be generally followed only in ages when those conditions had at last become nearly equal and men nearly alike.

The philosophical method of the eighteenth century is therefore not only French but democratic, and this explains why it was so readily accepted throughout Europe, where it has contributed so powerfully to changing the face of society. The French did not convulse the world because they changed their former opinions and altered their former customs. They did so because they were the first to generalize and bring to light a philosophical method that made it easy to attack all that was old and to open a path to all that was new.

If it is asked why this same method is today more rigorously followed and more frequently applied by the French than by the Americans, although the principle of equality is no less complete among the latter and is of more ancient date, the fact may be attributed to two circumstances, which it is essential to understand clearly at the outset. It must never be forgotten that religion gave birth to Anglo-American society. In the United States, therefore, religion is blended with all the habits of the nation and all the feelings of patriotism, and this gives it a particular force. To this powerful reason another of no less intensity may be added: in America religion has, as it were, set its own limits. Religious institutions have remained wholly distinct from political institutions, so that former laws have been easily changed while former belief has remained unshaken. Christianity has therefore kept a strong hold on the public mind in America. I would particularly remark that its sway is not only that of a philosophical doctrine adopted after inquiry, but of a religion that is believed without discussion. In the United States Christian sects are infinitely diversified and perpetually modified, but Christianity itself is a fact so irresistibly established that no one undertakes either to attack or to defend it. The Americans, having accepted the principal doctrines of the Christian religion without inquiry, are obliged to accept in the same way a great number of moral truths that originate in it and are connected with it. Hence the activity of individual analysis is restrained within narrow limits, and many of the most important human opinions are removed from its influence.

The second circumstance I mentioned is this: the social condition and the constitution of the Americans are democratic, but they have not had a democratic revolution. They arrived on the soil they now occupy in almost the condition in which we see them today, and this matters a great deal.

No revolution fails to shake existing belief, weaken authority, and cast doubt on commonly received ideas. The effect of all revolutions is therefore, more or less, to surrender men to their own guidance and to open to the mind of every man a void and almost unlimited range of speculation. When equality of conditions follows a protracted conflict between the different classes that made up the older society, envy, hatred, and uncharitableness, pride, and exaggerated self-confidence tend to seize the human heart and hold sway there for a time. Independently of equality itself, this tends powerfully to divide men — to lead them to mistrust the judgment of others and to seek the light of truth nowhere but in their own understandings. Everyone then tries to be his own sufficient guide and makes it his boast to form his own opinions on all subjects. Men are no longer bound together by ideas but by interests, and it would seem that human opinions are reduced to a kind of intellectual dust, scattered on every side, unable to collect, unable to cohere.

Thus the independence of mind that equality presupposes is never so great, and never seems so excessive, as when equality is beginning to establish itself and during the painful labor by which it is established. The kind of intellectual freedom that equality may give must therefore be very carefully distinguished from the anarchy that revolution brings. Each of these two things must be considered separately, so as not to form exaggerated hopes or fears about the future.

I believe that people living under the new forms of society will often use their private judgment, but I am far from thinking that they will often abuse it. This is due to a cause that applies more generally to all democratic countries, and that in the long run must keep the independence of individual speculation within fixed, and sometimes narrow, limits. I shall point out this cause in the next chapter.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Of The Principal Source Of Belief Among Democratic Nations
paragraphs: The amount of dogmatic belief varies from one period to another. It arises in different ways, and it may change its object or its form. But dogmatic belief will never cease to exist under any circumstances. In other words, people will never stop holding some opinions on trust, without testing them by actual discussion. If everyone set out to form his own opinions and to seek the truth by paths he had cut for himself alone, we could not suppose that any considerable number of people would ever come to share a common belief. Yet it is obvious that without such a common belief no society can prosper — or rather, no society can survive. For without ideas held in common there is no common action, and without common action there may still be individuals, but there is no social body. For a society to exist, and all the more for it to prosper, the minds of its citizens must be drawn together and held together by certain dominant ideas. That cannot happen unless each citizen sometimes draws his opinions from the common source and agrees to accept certain beliefs from the community.

If I now consider man as an individual, I find that dogmatic belief is just as indispensable to him for living alone as it is for cooperating with his fellow creatures. If a man had to prove to himself every truth he uses in daily life, his task would never end. He would exhaust his strength on preliminary exercises and never get beyond them. His life is too short for this, and his intelligence too limited. So he is reduced to taking on trust a number of facts and opinions that he has had neither the time nor the ability to verify himself, but which people of greater ability have worked out, or which the world has adopted. On this foundation he builds the structure of his own thoughts. He does not proceed this way so much by choice as because the inflexible law of his condition forces him to. No philosopher in the world is so gifted that he does not believe a million things on the word of other people, and assume many more truths than he proves. This is not only necessary but desirable. A man who undertook to investigate everything for himself could give each thing only a little time and attention. His task would keep his mind in constant turmoil, which would stop him from penetrating to the depths of any truth or fastening his mind firmly to any conviction. His intellect would be at once independent and powerless. He must therefore choose among the various objects of human belief, and he must adopt many opinions without discussion, so that he can examine more thoroughly the smaller number he sets aside for investigation. It is true that whoever accepts an opinion on another person’s word thereby puts his mind in bondage to that extent. But it is a salutary bondage, one that lets him make good use of his freedom.

A principle of authority must therefore always be present, whatever the circumstances, in some part of the moral and intellectual world. Its place may vary, but it necessarily has one. The independence of individual minds may be greater or smaller, but it can never be unlimited. So the question is not whether any intellectual authority exists in the ages of democracy. It is simply where that authority resides and by what standard it is to be measured.

I showed in the preceding chapter how the equality of conditions leads men to a kind of instinctive disbelief in the supernatural, and to a very high and often exaggerated opinion of the human understanding. People who live in a period of social equality are therefore not easily led to place the intellectual authority they bow to beyond or above humanity. They usually look for the sources of truth in themselves, or in those who are like themselves. This alone would be enough to prove that no new religion could be established in such periods, and that any scheme for founding one would be not only impious but absurd and irrational. We can foresee that a democratic people will not easily believe in divine missions, that they will readily make fun of modern prophets, and that they will look for the chief judge of their beliefs within the limits of mankind, not beyond them.

When the ranks of society are unequal and people differ in condition, some individuals hold all the power of superior intelligence, learning, and education, while the multitude is sunk in ignorance and prejudice. People who live in these aristocratic periods are therefore naturally led to shape their opinions by the higher standard of one person or one class, and they are reluctant to recognize the infallibility of the mass of the people.

The opposite happens in ages of equality. The closer citizens come to the common level of an equal and similar condition, the less inclined each of them is to place unquestioning faith in a particular man or a particular class. But his readiness to believe the multitude grows, and opinion becomes more than ever the mistress of the world. Among a democratic people, common opinion is not only the one guide that private judgment retains. It also has a power there far beyond what it has anywhere else. In times of equality, people have no faith in one another, because they all resemble one another. But this same resemblance gives them almost unlimited confidence in the judgment of the public. For they all have equal means of judging, so it hardly seems likely that the greater truth would fail to lie with the greater number.

When the inhabitant of a democratic country compares himself individually with all those around him, he feels with pride that he is the equal of any one of them. But when he surveys the whole body of his fellows and sets himself against so huge a mass, he is at once overwhelmed by the sense of his own insignificance and weakness. The same equality that makes him independent of each of his fellow citizens taken one by one leaves him alone and unprotected against the influence of the greater number. Among a democratic people, then, the public has a singular power, of which aristocratic nations could never even form an idea. For it does not persuade people to adopt certain opinions. It enforces them, and instills them into the faculties by a kind of enormous pressure of the minds of all upon the reason of each.

In the United States the majority undertakes to supply individuals with a multitude of ready-made opinions, and so relieves them of the need to form opinions of their own. Everyone there adopts great numbers of theories on philosophy, morals, and politics without inquiry, on public trust. And if we look very closely, we will see that religion herself holds sway there much less as a doctrine of revelation than as a commonly received opinion. The political laws of the Americans give the majority sovereign rule over the community, and this materially increases the power the majority naturally exercises over the mind. For nothing is more common in man than to recognize superior wisdom in the person of his oppressor. This political omnipotence of the majority in the United States undoubtedly increases the influence that public opinion would have over each member of the community even without it. But the foundations of that influence do not rest on it. They must be sought in the principle of equality itself, not in the more or less popular institutions that people living under that condition may give themselves. The intellectual dominion of the greater number would probably be less absolute among a democratic people governed by a king than in a pure democracy, but it will always be extremely absolute. And whatever political laws govern people in the ages of equality, we can foresee that faith in public opinion will become a kind of religion there, with the majority as its ministering prophet.

Intellectual authority will therefore be different, but it will not be diminished. Far from thinking that it will disappear, I predict that it may easily gain too much weight and confine the action of private judgment within narrower limits than are suited either to the greatness or to the happiness of the human race. In the principle of equality I see two tendencies very clearly. One leads the mind of every man toward untried thoughts. The other would forbid him to think at all. And I can see how, under certain laws, democracy would extinguish that liberty of the mind to which a democratic social condition is favorable. After breaking every bond once imposed on it by ranks or by individuals, the human mind would then be tightly bound to the general will of the greatest number.

Suppose democratic nations were to replace all the different powers that checked or slowed the energy of individual minds too much with the absolute power of the majority. The evil would only have changed its symptoms. People would not have found a way to live independently. They would simply have invented (and it is no easy task) a new dress for servitude. There is here — and I cannot repeat it too often — much for deep reflection by those who regard freedom as a holy thing, and who hate not only the despot but despotism. For my own part, when I feel the hand of power pressing heavily on my brow, I care little who is oppressing me. And I am no more willing to bow beneath the yoke because a million arms hold it out to me.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Why The Americans Display More Readiness And More Taste For General Ideas Than Their Forefathers, The English.
paragraphs: General Ideas Than Their Forefathers, the English.

God does not regard the human race as a whole. He surveys all the beings that make up mankind at a single glance and one by one. In each person he sees both the resemblances that tie him to his fellows and the differences that set him apart from them. God therefore has no need of general ideas. That is, he never feels any need to gather a large number of similar things under one form to make thinking easier. Man is in a different position. If the human mind tried to examine and judge every individual case that came before it, the sheer mass of detail would soon lead it astray and confuse its judgment. In this difficulty man turns to an expedient that is imperfect but necessary, and that both helps him and exposes his weakness. He considers a certain number of things superficially and notices that they resemble one another. Then he gives them a common name, sets them apart, and moves on.

General ideas are no proof of the strength of the human intellect. They show rather its inadequacy. For nature contains no two beings exactly alike, no two things precisely identical, and no rule that applies indiscriminately and equally to several objects at once. The chief merit of general ideas is that they let the human mind pass a quick judgment on a great many objects at once. On the other hand, the notions they convey are always incomplete, and they always make the mind lose as much in accuracy as it gains in breadth. As societies advance in civilization, they learn new facts, and each day they pick up, almost without noticing, some particular truths. The more truths of this kind a man grasps, the more general ideas he is naturally led to form. A multitude of particular facts cannot be seen separately without eventually revealing the common tie that connects them. Several individuals lead to the perception of the species, and several species to that of the genus. The habit and the taste for general ideas will therefore always be strongest among a people of long-established culture and extensive knowledge.
But there are other reasons that push men to generalize their ideas, or hold them back from doing so.

The Americans are much more given to the use of general ideas than the English, and have a much greater taste for them. At first sight this seems very strange, when we remember that the two nations have the same origin, that they lived for centuries under the same laws, and that they still constantly exchange their opinions and their customs. The contrast becomes much more striking if we look at our own part of the world and compare the two most educated nations that live in it. The English mind seems able to tear itself away from the observation of particular facts, and rise from them to their causes, only reluctantly and painfully. It seems to generalize only in spite of itself. Among the French, on the contrary, the taste for general ideas seems to have grown into so ardent a passion that it must be satisfied on every occasion. Every morning when I wake I am told that some general and eternal law has just been discovered, one I had never heard mentioned before. There is not a mediocre scribbler who does not try his hand at discovering truths that apply to a great kingdom, and who is not very displeased with himself if he fails to squeeze the human race into the space of an article. It surprises me that two very educated nations should differ so much. If I turn my attention back to England and look at the events there over the last half-century, I think I can affirm that the taste for general ideas grows in that country in proportion as its ancient constitution weakens.

The state of civilization is therefore not enough by itself to explain what prompts the human mind to love general ideas or turns it away from them. When the conditions of men are very unequal, and inequality is the permanent state of society, individuals gradually become so unlike one another that each class takes on the appearance of a separate race. Only one of these classes is in view at any moment. People lose sight of the general tie that binds them all within the vast bosom of mankind, and their observation always settles not on man but on certain men. Those who live in this aristocratic state of society therefore never form very general ideas about themselves. That is enough to give them a habitual distrust of such ideas and an instinctive aversion to them. The man who lives in a democratic country, on the contrary, sees men all around him who differ very little from one another. He cannot turn his mind to any one part of mankind without his thought expanding until it takes in the whole. All the truths that apply to himself seem to him equally and similarly applicable to each of his fellow citizens and fellow men. He acquires the habit of generalizing his ideas in the study that occupies him most and interests him more than any other, and he carries the same habit into all his pursuits. This is how the craving to discover general laws in everything, to bring a great number of objects under a single formula, and to explain a mass of facts by one cause becomes an ardent and sometimes undiscerning passion of the human mind.

Nothing shows the truth of this proposition more clearly than the opinions the ancients held about their slaves. The deepest and most capacious minds of Rome and Greece never managed to reach the idea, at once so general and so simple, that all men are alike and that each has the same birthright to freedom. They tried to prove that slavery was part of the order of nature and would always exist. More than that, everything shows that those among the ancients who had passed from slavery to freedom, many of whom have left us excellent writings, themselves viewed servitude in no other light.

All the great writers of antiquity belonged to the aristocracy of masters, or at least saw that aristocracy established and uncontested before their eyes. Their minds, after expanding in several directions, were blocked from further progress in this one. The coming of Jesus Christ to earth was needed to teach that all members of the human race are by nature equal and alike.

In ages of equality all men are independent of one another, isolated and weak. The movements of the multitude are not permanently guided by the will of any individuals. At such times humanity seems always to advance by itself. To explain what is happening in the world, a man is therefore driven to look for some great causes that act in the same way on all his fellow creatures and so push them all, against their will, along the same track. This in turn naturally leads the human mind to form general ideas, and gives it a taste for them.

I have already shown how the equality of conditions leads every man to investigate truths for himself. It is easy to see that a method of this kind must gradually and imperceptibly produce a tendency toward general ideas in the human mind. When I reject the traditions of rank, profession, and birth, and when I escape the authority of example to find the path I should follow by the sole effort of my own reason, I am inclined to draw the grounds of my opinions from human nature itself. This leads me necessarily, and almost without noticing, to adopt a great number of very general notions.

All that I have said here explains why the English show much less readiness and taste for generalizing ideas than their American offspring, and still less than their French neighbors. It also explains why the English of today show more of these qualities than their forefathers did. The English have long been a very educated and very aristocratic nation. Their education urged them constantly to generalize, and their aristocratic habits confined them to particulars. From this came the philosophy, at once bold and timid, broad and narrow, that has prevailed in England until now, and that still obstructs and stagnates so many minds in that country.

Apart from the causes I have pointed out above, others can be discerned that are less obvious but no less effective, and that give almost every democratic people a taste, and often a passion, for general ideas. A careful distinction must be made between ideas of this kind. Some are the result of slow, detailed, and conscientious labor of the mind, and these widen the sphere of human knowledge. Others spring up at once from the first quick exercise of the wits, and produce only very superficial and very uncertain notions. People who live in ages of equality have a great deal of curiosity and very little leisure. Their lives are so practical, so confused, so excited, and so active that little time is left to them for thought. Such people are drawn to general ideas because these spare them the trouble of studying particulars. General ideas contain, so to speak, a great deal in a small space, and give a large return in a short time. So if a brief and inattentive investigation leads them to think they have detected a common relation among certain objects, they push the inquiry no further. Without examining in detail how far these different objects differ or agree, they quickly arrange them under one formula so that they can move on to another subject.

One of the distinguishing characteristics of a democratic period is the taste all men have at such times for easy success and immediate enjoyment. This is true of the pursuits of the intellect as of all others. Most of those who live in a time of equality are full of an ambition that is at once aspiring and slack. They would like to succeed brilliantly and at once, but they would be excused from great efforts to achieve success. These conflicting tendencies lead straight to the pursuit of general ideas. With the help of such ideas they flatter themselves that they can cut a very important figure at small expense and attract the public’s attention with very little trouble. And I do not know whether they are wrong to think so. For their readers are as unwilling to investigate anything to the bottom as they are themselves, and what people generally look for in the products of the mind is easy pleasure and information without labor.

Aristocratic nations do not make enough use of general ideas, and they often treat them with thoughtless disdain. It is true, on the other hand, that a democratic people is always ready to carry ideas of this kind to excess and to embrace them with injudicious warmth.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — Why The Americans Have Never Been So Eager As The French For General Ideas In Political Matters
paragraphs: General Ideas in Political Matters

I observed in the last chapter that the Americans have a less decided taste for general ideas than the French, and that this is especially true in political matters. The Americans put infinitely more general ideas into their legislation than the English do, and they pay much more attention than the English to adjusting the practice of affairs to theory. Even so, no political body in the United States has ever shown so warm an attachment to general ideas as the Constituent Assembly and the Convention in France. At no time has the American people seized on such ideas with the passionate energy of the French people in the eighteenth century, or shown the same blind confidence in the value and absolute truth of any theory. This difference between the Americans and the French has several causes, but chiefly the following one. The Americans are a democratic people who have always directed public affairs themselves. The French are a democratic people who for a long time could only speculate about the best way to conduct them. The social condition of France led the French to form very general ideas about government, while its political constitution kept them from correcting those ideas by experiment and gradually detecting their inadequacy. In America, by contrast, the two things constantly balance and correct each other.

At first sight this may seem to contradict what I said earlier, that democratic nations draw their love of theory from the excitement of their active life. A closer examination will show that the two statements do not conflict. People who live in democratic countries seize eagerly on general ideas because they have little leisure and because these ideas spare them the trouble of studying particulars. This is true, but it should be understood to apply only to matters that are not the necessary and habitual subjects of their thought. Merchants will eagerly take up, without very close scrutiny, any general ideas on philosophy, politics, science, or the arts that are put before them. But ideas that relate to commerce they will not accept without inquiry or adopt without reservation. The same is true of statesmen with regard to general ideas in politics. So if there is a subject on which a democratic people is especially liable to give itself up blindly and extravagantly to general ideas, the best corrective is to make that subject part of the people’s daily practical business. The people will then be forced to enter into its details, and the details will teach them the weak points of the theory. This remedy may often be a painful one, but its effect is certain.

So it happens that democratic institutions, which compel every citizen to take a practical part in government, moderate the excessive taste for general theories in politics that the principle of equality suggests.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Of The Manner In Which Religion In The United States Avails Itself Of Democratic Tendencies
paragraphs: Itself of Democratic Tendencies

I argued in an earlier chapter that people cannot do without dogmatic belief, and that it is very much to be desired that they hold it. I now add that, of all the kinds of dogmatic belief, the one that seems to me most desirable is dogmatic belief in matters of religion. This follows clearly even if we consider nothing higher than the interests of this world. Hardly any human action, however particular its character, fails to originate in some very general idea that people have formed of God, of his relation to humanity, of the nature of their own souls, and of their duties to their fellow human beings. Nothing can prevent these ideas from being the common source from which everything else flows. People therefore have an immense stake in acquiring fixed ideas of God, of the soul, and of their common duties to their Creator and to one another. For doubt about these first principles would leave all their actions to the impulse of chance, and would condemn them to live, to a certain extent, powerless and undisciplined.

This, then, is the subject on which it is most important for each of us to hold fixed ideas. Unhappily, it is also the subject on which it is hardest for each of us, left alone, to settle our opinions by the force of reason alone. Only minds unusually free from the ordinary anxieties of life, minds that are at once penetrating, subtle, and trained in thinking, can sound the depths of these most necessary truths, even with the help of much time and care. Indeed, we see that these philosophers are themselves almost always wrapped in uncertainties. At every step the natural light that illuminates their path grows dimmer and less secure. In spite of all their efforts, they have so far discovered only a small number of conflicting ideas, on which the human mind has been tossed about for thousands of years without getting a firmer grip on the truth or even finding anything new in its errors. Studies of this kind are far above the average capacity of people. And even if most of mankind were capable of such pursuits, it is clear that they would still lack the leisure to pursue them. Fixed ideas of God and of human nature are indispensable to the daily conduct of people’s lives, but the conduct of their lives prevents them from acquiring such ideas.

I think the difficulty has no parallel. Among the sciences, some are useful to the mass of mankind and within its reach. Others can be approached only by a few, and the many do not study them, since they need nothing beyond their more remote applications. But the daily practice of the science I am speaking of is indispensable to everyone, even though the study of it is out of reach for the great majority.

General ideas about God and human nature are therefore, above all others, the ideas that it is most fitting to withdraw from the habitual action of private judgment, and the ones in which there is most to gain and least to lose by recognizing a principle of authority. The first object of religions, and one of their principal advantages, is to give each of these fundamental questions an answer that is clear, precise, intelligible to the mass of mankind, and lasting. Some religions are very false and very absurd. Yet it may be affirmed that any religion that stays within the circle I have just traced, without aspiring to go beyond it (as many religions have tried to do, in order to fence in the free progress of the human mind on every side), imposes a salutary restraint on the intellect. And it must be admitted that, even if such a religion does not save people in another world, it is at least very conducive to their happiness and greatness in this one. This is especially true of people living in free countries. When a people’s religion is destroyed, doubt takes hold of the highest part of the intellect and half paralyzes all the rest of its powers. Everyone grows used to holding only confused and shifting ideas on the subjects that matter most to himself and his fellow human beings. His opinions are poorly defended and easily abandoned. Despairing of ever solving by himself the hardest problems of human destiny, he ignobly resigns himself to thinking no more about them. Such a condition cannot fail to weaken the soul, loosen the springs of the will, and prepare a people for servitude. In such a case people do not merely allow their freedom to be wrested from them; they often give it up themselves. When there is no longer any principle of authority in religion, any more than in politics, people are soon frightened by the sight of this unbounded independence. The constant agitation of everything around them alarms and exhausts them. Since everything in the realm of the intellect is adrift, they decide at least that the machinery of society should be firm and fixed. And since they cannot return to their old belief, they take a master.

For my own part, I doubt that a person can ever bear complete religious independence and entire public freedom at the same time. And I am inclined to think that if he lacks faith, he must serve, and if he is free, he must believe.

Perhaps, however, this great usefulness of religions is even more obvious among nations where equality of conditions prevails than among others. It must be acknowledged that equality, though it brings great benefits into the world, also suggests to people (as will be shown later) some very dangerous tendencies. It tends to isolate them from one another and to fix each person’s attention on himself, and it opens the soul to an immoderate love of material gratification. The greatest advantage of religion is that it inspires exactly the opposite principles. There is no religion that does not place the object of human desire above and beyond the treasures of the earth, and that does not naturally lift the soul to regions far above those of the senses. Nor is there any that does not impose on a person some duties toward his fellow human beings, and so draw him at times out of the contemplation of himself. This is true even of the most false and dangerous religions. Religious nations are therefore naturally strong at the very point where democratic nations are weak. This shows how important it is for people to keep their religion as their conditions become more equal.

I have neither the right nor the intention to examine the supernatural means by which God instills religious belief in the human heart. At this moment I am considering religions from a purely human point of view. My aim is to ask by what means they can most easily keep their hold in the democratic ages we are entering. It has been shown that in times of general education and equality, the human mind accepts dogmatic opinions only with reluctance, and feels the need of them keenly only in spiritual matters. This proves, first, that in such times religions ought to confine themselves within their own bounds more carefully than at any other time. For in seeking to extend their power beyond religious matters, they risk not being believed at all. The circle within which they try to confine the human intellect should therefore be drawn carefully, and beyond its edge the mind should be left entirely free to follow its own guidance. Muhammad claimed to receive from Heaven, and put into the Koran, not only a body of religious doctrines but also political maxims, civil and criminal laws, and theories of science. The Gospel, by contrast, speaks only of the general relations of people to God and to one another, and beyond that it teaches and imposes no article of faith. This alone, besides a thousand other reasons, would be enough to prove that the first of these religions will never long dominate an educated and democratic age, while the second is destined to keep its hold in such an age as in all others.

But to pursue this part of the subject, I find that for religions to keep their authority, humanly speaking, in democratic ages, they must do more than confine themselves strictly to the circle of spiritual matters. Their power also depends very much on the nature of the belief they teach, on the external forms they take, and on the obligations they impose. My earlier observation that equality leads people to very general and very broad ideas applies principally to the question of religion. People who live in a similar and equal condition in the world easily conceive the idea of one God, who governs every person by the same laws and grants every person future happiness on the same terms. The idea of the unity of mankind constantly leads them back to the idea of the unity of the Creator. In a state of society where people are broken up into very unequal ranks, by contrast, they tend to invent as many deities as there are nations, castes, classes, or families, and to trace out a thousand private roads to heaven.

It cannot be denied that Christianity itself has felt, to a certain extent, the influence that social and political conditions have on religious opinions. When the Christian religion appeared on earth, Providence, which had doubtless prepared the world for its coming, had gathered a large part of the human race, like an immense flock, under the scepter of the Caesars. The people who made up this multitude differed in many ways, but they had this much in common: they all obeyed the same laws, and every subject was so weak and insignificant beside the imperial ruler that all appeared equal when their condition was compared with his. This new and peculiar state of mankind necessarily predisposed people to listen to the general truths that Christianity teaches, and it may help explain the ease and speed with which those truths then penetrated the human mind. The opposite state of things appeared after the destruction of the empire. The Roman world was then, as it were, shattered into a thousand fragments, and each nation went back to its original individuality. An endless scale of ranks soon grew up within these nations. The different races were more sharply defined, and castes divided each nation into several peoples. In the midst of this common effort, which seemed to drive human society toward the greatest imaginable degree of voluntary subdivision, Christianity did not lose sight of the leading general ideas it had brought into the world. But it seemed nonetheless to adapt itself, as far as it could, to the new tendencies that the fragmentation of mankind had produced. People continued to worship one God, the Creator and Preserver of all things. But every people, every city, and, so to speak, every individual thought of obtaining some distinct privilege and winning the favor of a special patron at the foot of the Throne of Grace. Unable to divide the Deity, they multiplied the divine agents and wrongly inflated their importance. The homage due to saints and angels became an almost idolatrous worship for most of the Christian world, and for a moment there was reason to fear that the religion of Christ would slide back toward the superstitions it had conquered. It seems clear that the more the barriers are removed that separate nation from nation among mankind, and citizen from citizen within a people, the stronger the human mind’s bent becomes, as if by its own impulse, toward the idea of a single, all-powerful Being who dispenses equal laws in the same way to every person. In democratic ages, then, it is especially important not to let the homage paid to secondary agents be confused with the worship due to the Creator alone.

Another truth is no less clear: religions ought to take on fewer external observances in democratic periods than in any others. In speaking of philosophical method among the Americans, I showed that in an age of equality nothing is more repugnant to the human mind than the idea of submitting to forms. People living in such times are impatient with figures of speech. To them, symbols seem a childish device for hiding or dressing up truths that would more naturally be laid bare in the light of day. They are unmoved by ceremonial observances, and they are inclined to give only secondary importance to the details of public worship. Those who have the task of regulating the external forms of religion in a democratic age should pay close attention to these natural tendencies of the human mind, so as not to run against them needlessly. I firmly believe in the necessity of forms, which hold the human mind fixed on the contemplation of abstract truths, spur its ardor in pursuing them, and strengthen its power to hold them steadily. Nor do I suppose that it is possible to maintain a religion without external observances. But on the other hand, I am convinced that in the ages we are entering it would be especially dangerous to multiply them beyond measure, and that they should rather be limited to what is absolutely necessary to perpetuate the doctrine itself, which is the substance of religions, of which the ritual is only the form. *a A religion that became more minute, more rigid, and more loaded with petty observances at a time when people are becoming more equal would soon find itself reduced to a band of fanatical zealots in the midst of an unbelieving people.

[Footnote a: In all religions there are some ceremonies which are inherent in the substance of the faith itself, and in these nothing should, on any account, be changed. This is especially the case with Roman Catholicism, in which the doctrine and the form are frequently so closely united as to form one point of belief.]

I anticipate the objection that, since all religions have general and eternal truths as their object, they cannot adapt themselves to the shifting spirit of every age without giving up their claim to certainty in the eyes of mankind. To this I reply again that the principal opinions that make up belief, which theologians call articles of faith, must be carefully distinguished from the accessories attached to them. Religions are obliged to hold fast to the former, whatever the particular spirit of the age. But they should take good care not to bind themselves in the same way to the latter, at a time when everything is in transition, and when the mind, accustomed to the moving pageant of human affairs, reluctantly puts up with any attempt to fix it to a given point. The fixity of external and secondary things can offer a chance of lasting only when civil society is itself fixed. Under any other circumstances I consider it perilous.

We shall have occasion to see that, of all the passions that originate in equality or are fostered by it, there is one that it makes especially intense, and that it instills at the same time in the heart of every person. I mean the love of well-being. The taste for well-being is the prominent and indelible feature of democratic ages. It may be believed that a religion that undertook to destroy so deep-seated a passion would in the end be destroyed by it. And if such a religion tried to wean people entirely from thinking about the good things of this world, in order to devote their faculties exclusively to thinking about another, it can be foreseen that the soul would eventually escape its grasp and plunge into the exclusive enjoyment of present, material pleasures. The chief concern of religions is to purify, regulate, and restrain the excessive and exclusive taste for well-being that people feel in periods of equality. But they would be mistaken to try to control it completely or to root it out. They will not succeed in curing people of the love of riches, but they can still persuade them to enrich themselves only by honest means.

This brings me to a final consideration, which includes, as it were, all the others. The more the conditions of people are equalized and made alike, the more important it is for religions, while they carefully keep out of the daily turmoil of secular affairs, not to run needlessly against the ideas that generally prevail or the permanent interests that exist among the mass of the people. For as public opinion grows more and more clearly the first and most irresistible of existing powers, the religious principle has no outside support strong enough to let it resist public opinion’s attacks for long. This is just as true of a democratic people ruled by a despot as of a republic. In ages of equality, kings may often command obedience, but the majority always commands belief. Deference is therefore to be paid to the majority in everything that is not contrary to the faith.

I showed in my earlier volumes how the American clergy keep aloof from secular affairs. This is the most obvious example of their self-restraint, but it is not the only one. In America, religion is a separate sphere, in which the priest is sovereign but which he takes care never to leave. Within its limits he is master of the mind. Beyond them he leaves people to themselves and surrenders them to the independence and instability that belong to their nature and their age. I have seen no country in which Christianity is clothed with fewer forms, figures, and observances than in the United States, or where it presents the mind with ideas that are more distinct, more simple, or more general. Although the Christians of America are divided into a multitude of sects, they all look at their religion in the same light. This applies to Roman Catholicism as well as to the other forms of belief. There are no Roman priests who show less taste for minute individual observances, for extraordinary or peculiar means of salvation, or who cling more to the spirit and less to the letter of the law, than the Roman Catholic priests of the United States. Nowhere is the Church’s doctrine that forbids offering to the saints the worship reserved for God alone more clearly taught or more generally followed. Yet the Roman Catholics of America are very submissive and very sincere.

Another remark applies to the clergy of every denomination. The American ministers of the gospel do not try to draw all of a person’s thoughts toward the life to come or to fix them there. They are willing to leave a portion of his heart to the cares of the present, and they seem to regard the goods of this world as important, though secondary, objects. If they take no part themselves in productive labor, they are at least interested in its progress and ready to applaud its results. And while they never cease to point to the other world as the great object of the believer’s hopes and fears, they do not forbid him to seek prosperity honestly in this one. Far from trying to show that these things are separate and opposed to each other, they rather study to find the point at which they are most closely connected.

All the American clergy know and respect the intellectual supremacy exercised by the majority, and they engage in only those conflicts with it that are necessary. They take no part in the quarrels of parties, but they readily adopt the general opinions of their country and their age. They let themselves be carried along, without resistance, in the current of feeling and opinion that sweeps along everything around them. They try to improve their contemporaries, but they do not break off fellowship with them. Public opinion is therefore never hostile to them; it rather supports and protects them. Their belief owes its authority both to the strength that is its own and to the strength that it borrows from the opinions of the majority. Thus, by respecting all democratic tendencies that are not absolutely contrary to herself, and by making use of several of them for her own purposes, religion carries on an advantageous struggle against that spirit of individual independence which is her most dangerous opponent.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Of The Progress Of Roman Catholicism In The United States
paragraphs: America is the most democratic country in the world, and at the same time it is (according to reports worthy of belief) the country in which the Roman Catholic religion is making the most progress. At first sight this is surprising. Two things must be carefully distinguished here. Equality inclines people to want to form their own opinions. But on the other hand, it gives them a taste for, and an idea of, unity, simplicity, and impartiality in the power that governs society. People living in democratic ages are therefore very prone to throw off all religious authority. But if they consent to submit to any authority of this kind, they insist at least that it be single and uniform. Religious powers that do not radiate from a common center are naturally repugnant to their minds, and they can almost as easily imagine that there should be no religion as that there should be several. Today, more than in any earlier age, Roman Catholics are seen sliding into unbelief and Protestants converting to Roman Catholicism. Looked at within the bounds of the church, the Roman Catholic faith seems to be losing ground; outside those bounds, it seems to be gaining. Nor is this hard to explain. The people of our time are naturally disposed to believe. But as soon as they have any religion, they find in themselves a hidden tendency that pushes them, without their realizing it, toward Catholicism. Many of the doctrines and practices of the Church of Rome astonish them, but they feel a secret admiration for its discipline, and its great unity attracts them. If Catholicism could at last withdraw from the political animosities it has stirred up, I have hardly any doubt that the same spirit of the age that now seems so opposed to it would become so favorable as to allow it to advance greatly and suddenly. One of the most common weaknesses of the human intellect is to try to reconcile contrary principles and to buy peace at the expense of logic. Thus there have always been, and always will be, people who submit some part of their religious belief to the principle of authority, but try to exempt several other parts of their faith from its influence, and keep their minds floating at random between liberty and obedience. But I am inclined to believe that the number of such thinkers will be smaller in democratic ages than in others, and that our descendants will tend more and more to divide simply into two groups: some giving up Christianity entirely, and others returning to the bosom of the Church of Rome.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Of The Cause Of A Leaning To Pantheism Amongst Democratic Nations
paragraphs: I shall have occasion later to show in what form the dominant taste of a democratic people for very general ideas shows itself in politics. But at this stage of my work I want to point out its principal effect on philosophy. It cannot be denied that pantheism has made great progress in our age. The writings of part of Europe bear visible marks of it: the Germans introduce it into philosophy, and the French into literature. Most of the works of imagination published in France contain some opinions, or some tinge, taken from pantheistic doctrines, or show in their authors some leaning toward such doctrines. This seems to me to come not from an accidental cause but from a permanent one.

When the conditions of society are becoming more equal, and each individual becomes more like all the rest, weaker and more insignificant, a habit grows up of no longer noticing citizens in order to consider only the people, and of overlooking individuals in order to think only of their kind. At such times the human mind seeks to take in a multitude of different objects at once, and it constantly strives to link a variety of effects to a single cause. The idea of unity takes such hold of a person, and he seeks it so universally, that if he thinks he has found it, he readily settles down to rest in that belief. Nor is he content with the discovery that there is nothing in the world but a creation and a Creator. Still troubled by this first division of things, he tries to broaden and simplify his conception by including God and the universe in one great whole. Suppose there is a philosophical system that teaches that all things, material and immaterial, visible and invisible, that the world contains are only to be considered as the several parts of one immense Being, which alone stays unchanged amid the continual change and ceaseless transformation of everything that makes it up. We may readily infer that such a system will have secret charms for people living in democracies, even though it destroys the individuality of man, or rather precisely because it destroys that individuality. All their habits of thought prepare them to conceive it and predispose them to adopt it. It naturally attracts and holds their imagination; it feeds the pride of their minds while it soothes their laziness. Among the different systems by which philosophy tries to explain the universe, I believe pantheism to be one of those best fitted to seduce the human mind in democratic ages. All who remain attached to the true greatness of man should struggle against it and unite against it.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — The Principle Of Equality Suggests To The Americans The Idea Of The Indefinite Perfectibility Of Man
paragraphs: Idea of the Indefinite Perfectibility of Man

Equality suggests to the human mind several ideas that would not have come from any other source, and it modifies almost all the ideas held before. I take as an example the idea of human perfectibility, because it is one of the principal notions the intellect can conceive, and because it is in itself a great philosophical theory, whose consequences can be traced at every moment in the conduct of human affairs. Man has many points of resemblance with the animals, but one characteristic belongs to him alone: he improves, and they cannot. Mankind could not fail to notice this difference from its earliest period. The idea of perfectibility is therefore as old as the world. Equality did not give birth to it, though it has given it a new character.

When the citizens of a community are classed by rank, profession, or birth, and when everyone is forced to follow whatever career happens to open before him, each person thinks that the utmost limits of human power lie close at hand, and no one seeks any longer to resist the inevitable law of his destiny. It is not that an aristocratic people absolutely denies man’s capacity for self-improvement, but they do not hold it to be indefinite. They conceive of improvement, but not of change. They imagine that the future condition of society may be better, but not essentially different. And while they admit that mankind has made vast strides in improvement and may still have some to make, they fix certain impassable limits for it in advance. Thus they do not presume that they have reached the supreme good or absolute truth (what people or what person was ever foolish enough to imagine that?), but they are convinced that they have pretty nearly reached the degree of greatness and knowledge that our imperfect nature allows. Since nothing moves around them, they are willing to fancy that everything is in its proper place. Then it is that the legislator pretends to lay down eternal laws, that kings and nations will raise only monuments meant to last forever, and that the present generation undertakes to spare future generations the task of regulating their own destinies.

As castes disappear and the classes of society draw closer together, as mores, customs, and laws change through the tumultuous contact of people with one another, as new facts arise, as new truths come to light, as ancient opinions fade and others take their place, the image of an ideal perfection, always on the wing, presents itself to the human mind. Continual changes then occur at every moment under everyone’s eyes. The position of some is made worse, and he learns only too well that no people and no individual, however enlightened, can claim to be infallible. The condition of others is improved, and from this he infers that man is endowed with an indefinite capacity for improvement. His setbacks teach him that no one may hope to have found absolute good; his successes spur him to pursue it without end. Thus, always seeking, always falling to rise again, often disappointed but not discouraged, he moves unceasingly toward that immeasurable greatness, so dimly visible at the end of the long road that humanity has yet to travel. It is hard to believe how many facts flow naturally from the philosophical theory of the indefinite perfectibility of man, or how strong an influence it has even on people who live entirely for action and not for thought, and who seem to conform their actions to it without knowing anything about it. I stop an American sailor and ask why the ships of his country are built to last such a short time. He answers without hesitation that the art of navigation is making such rapid progress every day that the finest vessel would become almost useless if it lasted beyond a certain number of years. In these words, which fell by chance and on a particular subject from a man of rough education, I recognize the general and systematic idea on which a great people directs all its affairs.
Aristocratic nations are naturally too apt to narrow the scope of human perfectibility; democratic nations, to expand it beyond all limits.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — The Example Of The Americans Does Not Prove That A Democratic People Can Have No Aptitude And No Taste For Science, Literature, Or Art
paragraphs: Democratic People Can Have No Aptitude and No Taste for Science, Literature, or Art

It must be acknowledged that few of the civilized nations of our time have made less progress in the higher sciences than the United States, and few have produced fewer great artists, fine poets, or celebrated writers. Many Europeans, struck by this fact, have seen it as a natural and inevitable result of equality. They have supposed that if a democratic state of society and democratic institutions ever came to prevail over the whole earth, the human mind would gradually see its guiding lights grow dim, and people would fall back into an age of darkness. To reason this way is, I think, to confuse several ideas that it is important to separate and examine one by one. It is to mix together, without intending to, what is democratic with what is merely American.

The religion professed by the first emigrants and handed down by them to their descendants is simple in its worship, austere and almost harsh in its principles, and hostile to outward symbols and ceremonial pomp. It is naturally unfavorable to the fine arts, and it only grudgingly tolerates the pleasures of literature. The Americans are a very old and very educated people who have come upon a new and boundless country, where they can spread out as they please and which they can make fertile without difficulty. This situation has no parallel in the history of the world. In America, then, everyone finds opportunities, unknown elsewhere, to make or increase a fortune. The spirit of gain is always strained to the utmost, and the human mind, constantly drawn away from the pleasures of the imagination and the labors of the intellect, is moved there by no impulse but the pursuit of wealth. The United States has its manufacturing and commercial classes, as every other country does. But what has never happened elsewhere is that the whole community is engaged at once in productive industry and commerce. I am convinced that if the Americans had been alone in the world, with the freedom and knowledge their forefathers acquired and the passions that are their own, they would not have been slow to discover that progress in the application of the sciences cannot long continue without cultivating the theory behind them, and that all the arts are perfected by one another. However absorbed they might have been in pursuing the main object of their desires, they would soon have admitted that they must turn aside from it now and then, in order to reach it better in the end.

The taste for the pleasures of the mind is, moreover, so natural to the heart of civilized man that even among refined nations least inclined to give themselves up to such pursuits, a certain number of citizens are always found who take part in them. Once felt, this intellectual craving would very soon have been satisfied. But at the very time when the Americans were naturally inclined to ask nothing of science except its specific applications to the useful arts and the means of making life comfortable, learned and literary Europe was exploring the common sources of truth and, at the same time, improving everything that can serve the pleasures or meet the needs of man. Among the educated nations of the Old World, the inhabitants of the United States singled out one in particular, to which they were closely tied by a common origin and by kindred habits. Among this people they found distinguished men of science, skilled artists, and eminent writers, and they were able to enjoy the treasures of the intellect without having to labor to gather them. I cannot agree to separate America from Europe, in spite of the ocean between them. I regard the people of the United States as the part of the English people that has been given the task of exploring the wilds of the New World, while the rest of the nation, with more leisure and less worn down by the drudgery of life, can devote its energies to thought and extend the empire of the mind in every direction. The position of the Americans is therefore quite exceptional, and it may be believed that no democratic people will ever be placed in a similar one. Their strictly Puritan origin, their exclusively commercial habits, even the country they inhabit, which seems to draw their minds away from science, literature, and the arts, and the nearness of Europe, which lets them neglect these pursuits without falling back into barbarism, along with a thousand particular causes of which I have been able to point out only the most important, have all come together to fix the American’s mind on purely practical objects. His passions, his needs, his education, and everything around him seem to join in pulling the native of the United States toward the earth. His religion alone bids him turn, from time to time, a brief and distracted glance toward heaven. Let us stop, then, viewing all democratic nations through the mask of the American people, and let us try at last to look at them with their own proper features.

It is possible to imagine a people not divided into any castes or scale of ranks, in which the law recognizes no privileges and divides inherited property into equal shares, but which at the same time lacks both knowledge and freedom. Nor is this an empty hypothesis. A despot may find it in his interest to make his subjects equal and to leave them ignorant, so as to keep them more easily enslaved. A democratic people of this kind would show neither aptitude nor taste for science, literature, or art, and it would probably never come to possess them. The law of descent would by itself destroy fortunes in each succeeding generation, and no one would acquire new ones. The poor man, with neither knowledge nor freedom, would not even conceive the idea of raising himself to wealth, and the rich man would let himself be reduced to poverty without any thought of defending himself. Between these two members of the community a complete and unshakable equality would soon be established.

No one would then have the time or the taste to devote himself to the pursuits or pleasures of the intellect. All men would remain paralyzed in a state of common ignorance and equal servitude. When I picture a democratic society of this kind, I imagine myself in one of those low, close, gloomy dwellings where the light that breaks in from outside soon grows faint and fades away. A sudden heaviness overcomes me, and I grope through the surrounding darkness to find the opening that will bring me back to daylight and fresh air.

But none of this applies to men who are already educated and who keep their freedom after abolishing among themselves those particular, hereditary rights that kept property permanently in the hands of certain individuals or certain bodies. When men living in a democratic state of society are educated, they readily see that no limits confine them or force them to put up with their present fortune. They therefore all conceive the idea of increasing it. If they are free, they all try, but they do not all succeed in the same way. The legislature, it is true, no longer grants privileges, but nature bestows them. Since natural inequality is very great, fortunes become unequal as soon as every man uses all his faculties to get rich. The law of descent prevents the establishment of wealthy families, but it does not prevent the existence of wealthy individuals. It constantly brings the members of the community back to a common level, and they constantly escape from it. The inequality of fortunes grows in proportion as knowledge spreads and liberty increases.

A sect that arose in our time, famous for its talents and its extravagance, proposed to concentrate all property in the hands of a central power, whose job it would then be to parcel it out to individuals according to their capacity. This would have been a way of escaping the complete and eternal equality that seems to threaten democratic society. But it would be a simpler and less dangerous remedy to grant no privilege to anyone, giving all people equal education and equal independence, and leaving each to determine his own position. Natural inequality will very soon make its own way, and wealth will pass of itself into the hands of the most capable.

Free and democratic communities, then, will always contain a considerable number of people who enjoy wealth or a comfortable competence. These wealthy people will not be as closely linked to one another as the members of the old aristocratic class were. Their tendencies will be different, and they will scarcely ever enjoy leisure that is as secure or as complete. But they will be far more numerous than the members of that class could ever be. These people will not be strictly confined to the cares of practical life, and they will still be able, though in different degrees, to indulge in the pursuits and pleasures of the intellect. And they will indulge in them. For if it is true that the human mind leans on one side toward the narrow, the practical, and the useful, it naturally rises on the other side toward the infinite, the spiritual, and the beautiful. Physical needs tie it to the earth, but as soon as the tie is loosened, it will relax and rise again.

Not only will the number of people who can take an interest in the products of the mind grow, but the taste for intellectual enjoyment will spread, step by step, even to those who in aristocratic societies seem to have neither the time nor the ability to indulge in it. When hereditary wealth, the privileges of rank, and the prerogatives of birth have ceased to exist, and when every man draws his strength from himself alone, it becomes evident that the chief cause of the differences between men’s fortunes is the mind. Whatever tends to strengthen, extend, or adorn the mind instantly becomes very valuable. The usefulness of knowledge becomes strikingly obvious even to the multitude. Those who have no taste for its charms still value its results and make some effort to acquire it. In free and educated democratic ages, nothing separates men from one another or keeps them in their own particular sphere. They rise and fall with extreme rapidity. All classes live in constant contact because they are so close together. They talk and mingle every day, and they imitate and envy one another. This suggests to the people many ideas, notions, and desires that they would never have had if the distinctions of rank had been fixed and society at rest. In such nations the servant never regards himself as a complete stranger to the pleasures and toils of his master, nor the poor man to those of the rich. The rural population grows to resemble that of the towns, and the provinces that of the capital. No one easily lets himself be reduced to the merely material cares of life, and the humblest artisan now and then casts an eager, furtive glance into the higher regions of the intellect. People do not read with the same ideas or in the same way as in an aristocratic community, but the circle of readers keeps widening until it includes all the citizens.

As soon as the multitude begins to take an interest in the labors of the mind, it finds that excelling in some of them is a powerful way to gain fame, power, or wealth. The restless ambition that equality produces at once takes this direction, as it does every other. The number of people who cultivate science, letters, and the arts becomes immense. The intellectual world springs into prodigious activity. Everyone tries to open a path there for himself and to draw the eyes of the public after him. Something similar occurs in the intellectual world to what happens in American society politically. What is done is often imperfect, but the attempts are countless. And although the results of individual effort are usually very small, the total is always very large.

It is therefore not true to claim that men living in democratic ages are naturally indifferent to science, literature, and the arts. It must only be admitted that they cultivate them in their own way, and bring to the task their own particular strengths and weaknesses.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — Why The Americans Are More Addicted To Practical Than To Theoretical Science
paragraphs: If a democratic state of society and democratic institutions do not halt the course of the human mind, they undeniably steer it in one direction rather than another. Their effects, though limited in this way, are still very great, and I hope I may be forgiven for pausing a moment to examine them. When we spoke of the philosophical method of the American people, we made several observations that must be put to use here.

Equality gives man the desire to judge everything for himself. It gives him, in all things, a taste for the tangible and the real, and a contempt for tradition and for forms. These general tendencies show up especially in the particular subject of this chapter. Those who cultivate the sciences among a democratic people are always afraid of losing their way in visionary speculation. They distrust systems. They hold closely to facts, and to the study of facts with their own senses. Since they do not easily defer to the mere name of any fellow man, they are never inclined to rest on anyone’s authority. On the contrary, they work tirelessly to point out the weak points in their neighbors’ opinions. Scientific precedents carry very little weight with them. They are never held up for long by the subtleties of the schools, and they are not ready to accept big words as sterling coin. They penetrate as far as they can into the main parts of the subject that occupies them, and they explain those parts in everyday language. Scientific pursuits then follow a freer and safer course, but a less lofty one.

The mind may, it seems to me, divide science into three parts. The first comprises the most theoretical principles and the more abstract notions, whose application is either unknown or very remote. The second consists of those general truths that still belong to pure theory but nevertheless lead by a straight, short road to practical results. The third is made up of methods of application and means of execution. Each of these portions of science may be cultivated separately, although reason and experience show that none of them can flourish for long if it is entirely cut off from the other two.

In America the purely practical part of science is admirably understood, and careful attention is paid to the portion of theory that is immediately needed for application. In this the Americans always show a clear, free, original, and inventive power of mind. But hardly anyone in the United States devotes himself to the essentially theoretical and abstract part of human knowledge. In this respect the Americans carry to excess a tendency that I think can be seen, though to a lesser degree, among all democratic nations.

Nothing is more necessary to the cultivation of the higher sciences, or of the more elevated branches of science, than meditation, and nothing is less suited to meditation than the structure of democratic society. There we do not find, as among an aristocratic people, one class that clings to repose because it is well off, and another that does not dare to stir because it despairs of improving its condition. Everyone is actively in motion, some in pursuit of power, others of gain. In the midst of this universal tumult, this incessant clash of conflicting interests, this continual rush of men after fortune, where is the calm to be found that the deeper workings of the intellect require? How can the mind dwell on any single point when everything whirls around it, and when man himself is swept and battered onward by the headlong current that carries everything along with it? But the permanent agitation that exists in the heart of a peaceable and established democracy must be distinguished from the tumultuous, revolutionary movements that almost always accompany the birth and growth of democratic society. When a violent revolution occurs among a highly civilized people, it cannot fail to give a sudden impulse to their feelings and their opinions. This is especially true of democratic revolutions, which stir up all the classes that make up a people and at the same time produce an immoderate ambition in the breast of every member of the community. The French made most surprising advances in the exact sciences at the very time when they were finishing the destruction of the remains of their former feudal society. Yet this sudden fertility should not be attributed to democracy, but to the unprecedented revolution that accompanied its growth. What happened at that time was a special incident, and it would be unwise to take it as the test of a general principle. Great revolutions are not more common among democratic nations than among others. I am even inclined to believe that they are less common. But among these populations there prevails a small, distressing motion, a kind of incessant jostling of men, which annoys and disturbs the mind without exciting or elevating it. Men who live in democratic communities not only seldom indulge in meditation, but they naturally hold it in very little esteem. A democratic state of society and democratic institutions plunge most men into constant active life, and the habits of mind suited to an active life are not always suited to a contemplative one. The man of action is often obliged to settle for the best he can get, because he would never achieve his purpose if he insisted on carrying every detail to perfection. He constantly has to rely on ideas that he has not had the leisure to search to the bottom. He is much more often helped by the timeliness of an idea than by its strict accuracy, and in the long run he risks less by using some false principles than by spending his time establishing all his principles on the basis of truth. The world is not led by long or learned demonstrations. A rapid glance at particular events, the daily study of the fleeting passions of the multitude, the accidents of the moment, and the art of turning them to account decide all its affairs.

In ages when active life is the condition of almost everyone, men are therefore generally led to put an excessive value on the quick flashes and superficial conceptions of the intellect, and, on the other hand, to rate its slower and deeper labors far below their true worth. This opinion of the public influences the judgment of the men who cultivate the sciences. They are persuaded that they can succeed in those pursuits without meditation, or they are deterred from the pursuits that require it.

There are several ways of studying the sciences. Among a multitude of men you will find a selfish, mercantile, trading taste for the discoveries of the mind, which must not be confused with the disinterested passion that is kindled in the hearts of a few. A desire to make use of knowledge is one thing. The pure desire to know is another. I do not doubt that in a few minds, scattered far apart, an ardent, inexhaustible love of truth springs up, sustains itself, and lives in ceaseless enjoyment without ever reaching the satisfaction it seeks. It is this ardent love, this proud, disinterested love of what is true, that raises men to the abstract sources of truth, to draw their mother-knowledge from there. If Pascal had had nothing in view but some large gain, or even if he had been driven by the love of fame alone, I cannot imagine that he would ever have been able to rally all the powers of his mind, as he did, to discover more fully the most hidden things of the Creator.
