When I see him, as it were, tear his soul away from all the cares of life to devote it wholly to these researches, and, snapping prematurely the links that bind the body to life, die of old age before forty, I stand amazed, and I see that no ordinary cause is at work to produce such extraordinary efforts.

The future will show whether these passions, at once so rare and so productive, come into being and grow as easily in democratic communities as in aristocratic ones. For myself, I confess that I am slow to believe it. In aristocratic society, the class that sets the tone of opinion and holds the supreme direction of affairs is placed permanently and hereditarily above the multitude. It naturally forms a lofty idea of itself and of man. It loves to invent noble pleasures for him and to carve out splendid objects for his ambition. Aristocracies often commit very tyrannical and very inhuman actions, but they rarely entertain base thoughts, and they show a kind of haughty contempt for petty pleasures, even while they indulge in them. The effect is greatly to raise the general pitch of society. In aristocratic ages, people commonly hold vast ideas of the dignity, the power, and the greatness of man. These opinions influence those who cultivate the sciences as well as the rest of the community. They help the mind’s natural impulse toward the highest regions of thought, and they naturally prepare it to conceive a sublime, even almost divine, love of truth. Men of science at such times are consequently carried away by theory, and it even happens that they often conceive a thoughtless contempt for the practical part of learning. “Archimedes,” says Plutarch, “was of so lofty a spirit that he never condescended to write any treatise on the manner of constructing all these engines of offense and defense. And as he held this science of inventing and putting together engines, and all arts generally speaking which tended to any useful end in practice, to be vile, low, and mercenary, he spent his talents and his studious hours in writing of those things only whose beauty and subtlety had in them no admixture of necessity.” Such is the aristocratic aim of science. In democratic nations it cannot be the same.

Most of the men who make up these nations are extremely eager in the pursuit of actual, physical gratification. Since they are always dissatisfied with the position they hold and always free to leave it, they think of nothing but the means of changing their fortune or increasing it. To minds so disposed, every new method that leads by a shorter road to wealth, every machine that spares labor, every instrument that lowers the cost of production, and every discovery that makes pleasures easier or increases them seems the grandest effort of the human intellect. It is chiefly from these motives that a democratic people takes up scientific pursuits, understands them, and respects them. In aristocratic ages, science is called upon above all to provide gratification to the mind. In democracies, it is called upon to provide it to the body. You may be sure that the more democratic, educated, and free a nation is, the greater will be the number of these promoters of scientific genius who act out of interest, and the more discoveries that can be applied at once to productive industry will bring gain, fame, and even power to their authors. For in democracies the working class takes part in public affairs, and public honors, as well as financial rewards, may be given to those who deserve them. In a community organized in this way, it is easy to see that the human mind may be led, without noticing, to neglect theory, and that it is driven, on the contrary, with unparalleled vehemence toward the applications of science, or at least toward that portion of theoretical science which is necessary to those who make such applications. In vain will some innate inclination raise the mind toward the loftier spheres of the intellect: interest draws it down to the middle zone. There it can develop all its energy and restless activity, and there it can produce all its wonders. These very Americans, who have not discovered a single one of the general laws of mechanics, have introduced into navigation an engine that is changing the face of the world.

Assuredly I do not contend that the democratic nations of our time are destined to see the great luminaries of man’s intelligence go out, or even that no new lights will ever appear. At the age the world has now reached, and among so many cultivated nations, all perpetually fired by the fever of productive industry, the bonds that connect the different parts of science cannot fail to strike the observer. And the taste for practical science itself, if it is educated, ought to lead men not to neglect theory. Amid such countless attempted applications of so many experiments, repeated every day, it is almost impossible that general laws should not often be brought to light, so that great discoveries would be frequent, though great inventors might be rare. I believe, moreover, in the high calling of scientific minds. If the democratic principle does not, on the one hand, lead men to cultivate science for its own sake, on the other hand it enormously increases the number of those who do cultivate it. Nor is it credible that, among so great a multitude, no speculative genius should arise from time to time, inflamed by the love of truth alone. Such a person, we may be sure, would dive into the deepest mysteries of nature, whatever the spirit of his country or his age. He needs no help in his course. It is enough that he is not hindered in it.

All I mean to say is this: permanent inequality of conditions leads men to confine themselves to the arrogant and sterile search for abstract truths, while the social condition and the institutions of democracy prepare them to seek the immediate, useful, practical results of the sciences. This tendency is natural and inevitable. It is worth knowing about, and it may be necessary to point it out. If those who are called upon to guide the nations of our time clearly saw from afar these new tendencies, which will soon be irresistible, they would understand that men living in democratic ages, possessing education and freedom, cannot fail to improve the industrial part of science, and that from now on all the efforts of the constituted authorities ought to be directed to supporting the highest branches of learning and to fostering the nobler passion for science itself. In the present age the human mind must be forced into theoretical studies. It runs of its own accord to practical applications, and instead of perpetually sending it back to the minute examination of secondary effects, it is good sometimes to turn it away from them, in order to raise it to the contemplation of primary causes. Because the civilization of ancient Rome perished as a result of the invasion of the barbarians, we are perhaps too ready to think that civilization cannot perish in any other way. If the light by which we are guided is ever extinguished, it will dwindle by degrees and die out of itself. By sticking closely to mere applications, people would lose sight of principles. When the principles were wholly forgotten, the methods derived from them would be badly pursued. New methods could no longer be invented, and men would go on applying, without intelligence and without art, scientific processes that were no longer understood.

Three hundred years ago, when Europeans first reached China, they found that nearly all the arts had attained a certain degree of perfection there. They were surprised that a people who had come so far had never gone further. Later they found some traces of the higher branches of science, which had been lost. The nation was wrapped up in productive industry. Most of its scientific processes had been kept, but science itself no longer existed. That explained the strangely motionless state in which they found the Chinese mind. The Chinese, following in their forefathers’ footsteps, had forgotten the reasons that had guided those forefathers. They still used the formula without asking what it meant. They kept the instrument, but they had lost the art of altering or renewing it. The Chinese, then, had lost the power of change, and improvement was impossible for them. At all times and in all things they had to imitate their predecessors, for fear that by straying for a moment from the path laid down for them they would wander into total darkness. The source of human knowledge was almost dry. The stream still flowed, but it could neither swell its waters nor change its course. Even so, China had lasted in peace for centuries. The invaders who had conquered the country had taken on the customs of its inhabitants, and order prevailed. A kind of physical prosperity was visible everywhere. Revolutions were rare, and war was, so to speak, unknown.

It is therefore a delusion to comfort ourselves with the thought that the barbarians are still far from us. For if some nations allow civilization to be torn from their grasp, there are others who trample it underfoot themselves.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Of The Spirit In Which The Americans Cultivate The Arts
paragraphs: I would be wasting my readers’ time and my own if I tried to demonstrate how the general mediocrity of fortunes, the absence of excess wealth, the universal desire for comfort, and the constant effort everyone makes to obtain it cause the taste for the useful to outweigh the love of the beautiful in the human heart. Democratic nations, where all these conditions exist, will therefore cultivate the arts that make life easy rather than those whose aim is to adorn it. They will habitually prefer the useful to the beautiful, and they will demand that the beautiful also be useful. But I mean to go further. Having pointed out this first feature, I want to sketch several others.

In ages of privilege, it commonly happens that the practice of almost all the arts becomes a privilege, and that every profession is a separate path that not everyone is allowed to enter. Even when productive industry is free, the fixed character of aristocratic nations gradually separates all the people who practice the same art, until they form a distinct class, always made up of the same families. Its members all know one another, and a public opinion of their own and a kind of corporate pride soon arise among them. In a class or guild of this kind, each artisan has not only his fortune to make but also his reputation to protect. He is guided not only by his own interest, or even by that of his customer, but by that of the body to which he belongs. And the interest of that body is that each artisan should produce the best possible work. In aristocratic ages, then, the aim of the arts is to manufacture as well as possible, not as quickly or as cheaply as possible.

When, on the contrary, every profession is open to all, when a multitude of people are constantly entering and leaving it, and when its members are strangers to one another, indifferent, and so numerous that they hardly see one another, the social bond is destroyed. Each workman, standing alone, simply tries to earn as much money as he can at the least possible cost. The customer’s will is then his only limit. But at the same time a corresponding revolution takes place in the customer. In countries where wealth as well as power is concentrated in the hands of a few and stays there, the enjoyment of most of this world’s goods belongs to a small number of individuals, who are always the same. Necessity, public opinion, or moderate desires keep everyone else from enjoying them. Since this aristocratic class stays fixed at the pinnacle of greatness where it stands, neither shrinking nor growing, it is always moved by the same wants and affected by them in the same way. The men who make it up naturally draw from their superior, hereditary position a taste for what is extremely well made and durable. This shapes the general way the nation thinks about the arts. Among such a people it often happens that even the peasant would rather go without the thing he longs for than get it in an imperfect state. In aristocracies, then, craftsmen work for only a limited number of very demanding customers, and the profit they hope to make depends mainly on the perfection of their work.

This is no longer the case when all privileges have been abolished, ranks are mixed together, and people are forever rising or sinking on the ladder of society. Among a democratic people there are always a number of citizens whose inheritance is being divided up and is dwindling. Under more prosperous circumstances they acquired certain wants, which remain after the means of satisfying them are gone, and they anxiously look for some underhanded way of providing for them. On the other hand, democracies always have a large number of men whose fortunes are growing, but whose desires grow much faster than their fortunes. They gloat over the gifts of wealth in anticipation, long before they have the means to command them. Such men are eager to find some shortcut to these gratifications, which already seem almost within their reach. The combined result of these causes is that in democracies there are always a multitude of individuals whose wants exceed their means, and who are very willing to settle for an imperfect satisfaction rather than give up what they desire.

The artisan readily understands these passions, because he shares them. In an aristocracy he would try to sell his work at a high price to a few people. Now he sees that the quicker way to get rich is to sell at a low price to everyone. But there are only two ways of lowering the price of goods. The first is to discover a better, shorter, and more ingenious method of producing them. The second is to manufacture a larger quantity of goods that are nearly the same but of lower value. Among a democratic population, all the intellectual faculties of the workman are directed to these two objects. He strives to invent methods that will let him work not only better but also faster and more cheaply. Or, if he cannot manage that, he tries to reduce the intrinsic quality of what he makes, without making it entirely unfit for its intended use. When only the wealthy had watches, almost all of them were very good ones. Few watches are now made that are worth much, but everybody has one in his pocket. Thus the democratic principle not only tends to turn the human mind toward the useful arts, but it also leads the artisan to produce a quantity of imperfect goods more rapidly, and the consumer to be satisfied with those goods.

This does not mean that the arts in democracies are incapable of producing very admirable works when they are called for. That may occasionally happen, if customers appear who are willing to pay for time and effort. In this rivalry of every kind of industry, in the midst of this immense competition and these countless experiments, some excellent workmen emerge who reach the utmost limits of their craft. But they rarely have a chance to show what they can do. They are scrupulously sparing with their powers. They remain in a state of accomplished mediocrity, which condemns itself and, although it is perfectly able to shoot past the mark before it, aims only at what it hits. In aristocracies, by contrast, workmen always do all they can, and when they stop, it is because they have reached the limit of their skill.

When I arrive in a country and find some of the finest products of the arts there, I learn nothing from that fact about the social condition or the political constitution of the country. But if I see that the products of the arts are generally of inferior quality, very abundant, and very cheap, I am convinced that among that people privilege is declining, that ranks are beginning to mix, and that they will soon be completely confused.

The craftsmen of democratic ages strive not only to bring their useful products within reach of the whole community but also to give all their goods attractive qualities that they do not really have. In the confusion of all ranks, everyone hopes to appear what he is not, and makes great efforts to succeed. This feeling, which is only too natural to the human heart, does not originate in the democratic principle, but that principle applies it to material objects. Mimicking virtue belongs to every age, but the hypocrisy of luxury belongs more particularly to the ages of democracy.

To satisfy these new cravings of human vanity, the arts turn to every kind of imposture, and these devices sometimes go so far as to defeat their own purpose. Imitation diamonds are now made that can easily be mistaken for real ones. As soon as the art of making false diamonds reaches such a degree of perfection that they cannot be told apart from real ones, it is probable that both will be abandoned and become mere pebbles again.

This leads me to speak of the arts that are called the fine arts, to set them apart from the others. I do not believe that a democratic social condition and democratic institutions necessarily reduce the number of men who cultivate the fine arts. But these causes have a very powerful influence on the way the fine arts are cultivated. Many of those who had already acquired a taste for the fine arts are impoverished. On the other hand, many who are not yet rich begin to form that taste, at least by imitation. The number of consumers increases, but wealthy and demanding consumers become scarcer. Something similar to what I have already pointed out in the useful arts then takes place in the fine arts. Artists produce more works, but the merit of each work is lessened. No longer able to rise to what is great, they cultivate what is pretty and elegant, and appearance gets more attention than reality. In aristocracies a few great paintings are produced; in democratic countries, a vast number of insignificant ones. In the former, statues are cast in bronze; in the latter, they are modeled in plaster.

When I first arrived at New York, by the part of the Atlantic Ocean called the Narrows, I was surprised to see along the shore, some distance from the city, a considerable number of little palaces of white marble, several of them built on the models of ancient architecture. The next day I went to examine more closely the building that had particularly caught my attention, and I found that its walls were of whitewashed brick and its columns of painted wood. All the buildings I had admired the night before were of the same kind.

The social condition and the institutions of democracy also give certain distinctive tendencies to all the imitative arts, and these are easy to point out. They often draw the arts away from depicting the soul and fix them exclusively on depicting the body. They substitute the representation of motion and sensation for that of feeling and thought. In a word, they put the real in the place of the ideal. I doubt whether Raphael studied the minutest details of the mechanism of the human body as thoroughly as the draftsmen of our own time. He did not attach the same importance to rigorous accuracy on this point as they do, because he aspired to surpass nature. He sought to make of man something superior to man, and to make beauty itself more beautiful. David and his pupils, on the contrary, were as good anatomists as they were good painters. They depicted the models before their eyes wonderfully well, but they rarely imagined anything beyond them. They followed nature faithfully, while Raphael sought something better than nature. They have left us an exact portrait of man, but in his works Raphael gives a glimpse of the Divinity. This remark about the manner of treating a subject applies just as much to the choice of subject. The painters of the Middle Ages generally looked far above themselves, and far from their own time, for grand subjects that left their imagination an unbounded range. Our painters often use their talents to imitate exactly the details of private life, which they always have before their eyes, and they are forever copying trivial objects, whose originals are only too abundant in nature.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Why The Americans Raise Some Monuments So Insignificant, And Others So Important
paragraphs: And Others So Important

I have just observed that in democratic ages monuments of the arts tend to become more numerous and less important. I now hasten to point out the exception to this rule. In a democratic community individuals are very powerless, but the State, which represents them all and holds them all in its grasp, is very powerful. Nowhere do citizens appear so insignificant as in a democratic nation. Nowhere does the nation itself appear greater, or the mind more easily take in a broad general view of it. In democratic communities the imagination shrinks when men consider themselves, and expands without limit when they think of the State. This is why the same men who live on a small scale in narrow dwellings often aspire to gigantic splendor in building their public monuments.

The Americans marked out the boundary of an immense city on the site they intended for their capital. Up to now it is hardly more densely populated than Pontoise, though according to them it will one day hold a million inhabitants. They have already uprooted trees for ten miles around, so that they would not get in the way of the future citizens of this imaginary metropolis. They have built a magnificent palace for Congress in the center of the city and given it the pompous name of the Capitol. The several States of the Union are every day planning and building prodigious undertakings that would astonish the engineers of the great European nations. Thus democracy not only leads men to a vast number of unimportant productions; it also leads them to raise some monuments on the largest scale. But between these two extremes there is a blank. A few scattered remains of enormous buildings can therefore teach us nothing about the social condition and the institutions of the people who raised them. I may add, though the remark takes me outside my subject, that they do not tell us any more about that people’s greatness, its civilization, or its real prosperity. Whenever a power of any kind is able to make a whole people cooperate in a single undertaking, that power, with a little knowledge and a great deal of time, will manage to obtain something enormous from the cooperation of so many efforts. But this does not lead to the conclusion that the people was very happy, very educated, or even very strong.

When the Spaniards reached the City of Mexico, they found it full of magnificent temples and vast palaces. That did not stop Cortes from conquering the Mexican Empire with 600 foot soldiers and sixteen horses. Had the Romans understood the laws of hydraulics better, they would not have built all the aqueducts whose remains surround their ruined cities, and they would have put their power and wealth to better use. Had they invented the steam engine, perhaps they would not have stretched those long artificial roads, the so-called Roman roads, out to the far edges of their empire. These works are at once splendid memorials of their ignorance and of their greatness. A people that left behind no other trace of its passage than a few lead pipes in the ground and a few iron rods on the surface might have been more truly the master of nature than the Romans were.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — Literary Characteristics Of Democratic Ages
paragraphs: When a traveler goes into a bookshop in the United States and looks over the American books on the shelves, the number of works seems extremely large, while the number of known authors seems, on the contrary, extremely small. He will first come across a number of elementary textbooks meant to teach the basics of human knowledge. Most of these books are written in Europe, and the Americans reprint them, adapting them to their own country. Next comes an enormous quantity of religious works: Bibles, sermons, edifying anecdotes, theological controversy, and reports of charitable societies. Last comes the long catalogue of political pamphlets. In America, parties do not write books to fight each other’s opinions. They write pamphlets, which circulate with incredible speed for a day and then die. In the midst of all these obscure products of the human brain are the more remarkable works of that small number of authors whose names are, or ought to be, known to Europeans.

Although America is perhaps, in our day, the civilized country where literature gets the least attention, a large number of people there nevertheless take an interest in the products of the mind, and make them, if not the study of their lives, at least the charm of their leisure hours. But England supplies these readers with most of the books they need. Almost all important English books are republished in the United States. The literary genius of Great Britain still shoots its rays into the recesses of the forests of the New World. There is hardly a pioneer’s hut that does not contain a few odd volumes of Shakespeare. I remember that I read the feudal play of Henry V for the first time in a log cabin.

Not only do the Americans constantly draw on the treasures of English literature, but it may truly be said that they find English literature growing on their own soil. Most of the small number of men in the United States who are engaged in writing literary works are English in substance, and still more so in form. Thus they carry into the midst of democracy the ideas and literary fashions current among the aristocratic nation they have taken as their model. They paint with colors borrowed from foreign customs, and since they hardly ever portray the country they were born in as it really is, they are seldom popular there. The citizens of the United States are themselves so convinced that books are not published for them that, before they can make up their minds about the merit of one of their authors, they generally wait until his fame has been confirmed in England, just as, in paintings, the author of an original is held to be entitled to judge the merit of a copy. The inhabitants of the United States, then, have at present, properly speaking, no literature. The only authors I acknowledge as American are the journalists. They are not, indeed, great writers, but they speak the language of their countrymen and make themselves heard by them. Other authors are foreigners. They are to the Americans what the imitators of the Greeks and Romans were to us at the revival of learning: an object of curiosity, not of general sympathy. They amuse the mind, but they do not act upon the customs of the people.

As I have already said, this state of affairs does not come from democracy alone. Its causes lie in several particular circumstances that have nothing to do with the democratic principle. Suppose the Americans had kept the same laws and social condition but had come from a different origin and been settled in another country. I do not doubt that they would have had a literature. Even as they now are, I am convinced that they will eventually have one. But its character will differ from that of the American writing of our time, and that character will be its own. It is not impossible to trace it in advance.

Suppose an aristocratic people among whom letters are cultivated. The labors of the mind, like the affairs of state, are directed by a ruling class in society. The literary career, like the political one, is almost entirely confined to this class, or to those nearest to it in rank. These premises are enough to give me the key to all the rest. When a small number of the same men are engaged at the same time on the same subjects, they easily agree with one another and settle certain leading rules to govern them all. If the subject that attracts the attention of these men is literature, they will soon subject the products of the mind to precise canons from which it will no longer be permitted to depart. If these men hold a hereditary position in the country, they will naturally be inclined not only to adopt a certain number of fixed rules for themselves but also to follow those their forefathers laid down for their own guidance. Their code will be at once strict and traditional. They are not necessarily absorbed by the cares of daily life, and they never have been, any more than their fathers were before them. For several generations, therefore, they have learned to take an interest in the labors of the mind. They have learned to understand literature as an art, to love it in the end for its own sake, and to feel a scholar’s satisfaction in seeing men follow its rules. Nor is this all. The men I am speaking of began their lives, and will end them, in easy or wealthy circumstances. Hence they have naturally acquired a taste for choice gratifications and a love of refined and delicate pleasures. Moreover, a kind of indolence of mind and heart, which they often fall into amid this long and peaceful enjoyment of so much well-being, leads them to set aside, even from their pleasures, anything too startling or too sharp. They would rather be amused than intensely excited. They want to be interested, but not carried away.

Now let us imagine a great number of literary works produced by, or for, the men I have just described, and we will easily conceive a style of literature in which everything is regular and planned in advance. The slightest work will be carefully finished in its smallest details. Art and labor will be visible in everything. Each kind of writing will have rules of its own, from which it will not be allowed to swerve and which distinguish it from all others. Style will be thought almost as important as thought, and form will be considered no less than substance. The diction will be polished, measured, and uniform. The tone of the mind will always be dignified and seldom very lively, and writers will care more about perfecting what they produce than about producing a great deal. It will sometimes happen that the members of the literary class, always living among themselves and writing for themselves alone, will lose sight of the rest of the world, which will infect them with a false and labored style. They will lay down minute literary rules for their exclusive use, which will imperceptibly lead them away from common sense and finally across the bounds of nature. By straining after a way of speaking different from the common one, they will arrive at a kind of aristocratic jargon that is hardly less distant from pure language than the coarse dialect of the people. Such are the natural perils of literature in aristocracies. Every aristocracy that keeps itself entirely apart from the people becomes powerless, and this is as true in literature as in politics. *a

[Footnote a: All this is especially true of the aristocratic countries that have long and peacefully been subject to a monarchical government. When liberty prevails in an aristocracy, the higher ranks are constantly obliged to make use of the lower classes, and when they use them, they come closer to them. This frequently brings something of a democratic spirit into an aristocratic community. Moreover, in a privileged body that governs with energy and a habitually bold policy, a taste for stir and excitement springs up, which must inevitably affect all literary works.]

Let us now turn the picture around and look at the other side. Let us move into the midst of a democracy that is not unprepared, by ancient traditions and present culture, to share in the pleasures of the mind. Ranks there are mixed together and confused. Knowledge and power are both infinitely divided and, if I may put it this way, scattered on every side. Here, then, is a motley multitude whose intellectual wants must be supplied. These new devotees of the pleasures of the mind have not all received the same education. They do not have the same degree of culture as their fathers, nor any resemblance to them. In fact, they continually differ from themselves, for they live in a state of incessant change of place, feelings, and fortunes. The mind of each member of the community is therefore not attached to that of his fellow citizens by tradition or common habits, and they have never had the power, the inclination, or the time to agree among themselves. Yet it is from the midst of this mixed and restless mass that authors come, and from the same source their profits and their fame are handed out. I can easily understand that in these circumstances I must expect to find in the literature of such a people few of those strict conventional rules that readers and writers accept in aristocratic ages. Even if the men of one period should happen to agree on some such rules, that would prove nothing for the next period, for among democratic nations each new generation is a new people. Among such nations, then, literature will not easily be subjected to strict rules, and it is impossible that any such rules should ever be permanent.

In democracies, it is by no means the case that all the men who cultivate literature have received a literary education. Most of those who have some tinge of fine letters are either engaged in politics or in a profession that allows them to taste the pleasures of the mind only occasionally and by stealth. These pleasures, therefore, are not the principal charm of their lives. They are regarded as a passing and necessary recreation amid the serious labors of life. Such a man can never gain a knowledge of the art of literature intimate enough to appreciate its more delicate beauties, and the finer shades of expression must escape him. Since the time he can give to letters is very short, he tries to make the best use of all of it. He prefers books that can be easily obtained and quickly read, and that need no learned research to be understood. He asks for beauties that offer themselves and are easily enjoyed. Above all, he must have what is unexpected and new. Accustomed to the struggle, the setbacks, and the monotony of practical life, he requires quick emotions and startling passages, truths or errors brilliant enough to rouse him and plunge him at once, as if by force, into the middle of a subject.

Why should I say more? Who does not understand what is about to follow before I have said it? Taken as a whole, literature in democratic ages can never present, as it does in periods of aristocracy, an appearance of order, regularity, learning, and art. Its form will, on the contrary, ordinarily be neglected and sometimes despised. Style will often be fantastic, incorrect, overburdened, and loose, and almost always vehement and bold. Authors will aim at speed of execution more than at perfection of detail. Short productions will be more common than bulky books. There will be more wit than erudition and more imagination than depth. Literary works will bear the marks of an untrained and rough vigor of thought, often of great variety and remarkable fertility. The aim of authors will be to astonish rather than to please, and to stir the passions more than to charm the taste. Here and there, no doubt, writers will appear who choose a different track, and who, if they are gifted with superior abilities, will succeed in finding readers in spite of their defects or their better qualities. But these exceptions will be rare, and even the authors who depart in this way from accepted practice in the main subject of their works will always fall back into it in some lesser details.

I have just described two extreme conditions. The transition by which a nation passes from the one to the other is not sudden but gradual, and it is marked by shades of very different intensity. In the passage that leads a literate people from the one to the other, there is almost always a moment when the literary genius of democratic nations meets that of aristocracies, and both seek to establish their joint sway over the human mind. Such epochs are short-lived but very brilliant. They are fertile without excess and lively without confusion. The French literature of the eighteenth century may serve as an example.

I would be saying more than I mean if I asserted that the literature of a nation is always subordinate to its social condition and its political constitution. I am aware that, apart from these causes, there are several others that give certain characteristics to literary works. But these seem to me the chief ones. The relations between the social and political condition of a people and the genius of its authors are always very numerous. Whoever knows the one is never completely ignorant of the other.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — The Trade Of Literature
paragraphs: Democracy not only spreads a taste for letters among the trading classes but also introduces a trading spirit into literature. In aristocracies, readers are fastidious and few in number. In democracies, they are far more numerous and far less difficult to please. The consequence is that among aristocratic nations no one can hope to succeed without immense exertion, and that this exertion may bring a great deal of fame but can never earn much money. Among democratic nations, on the other hand, a writer may flatter himself that he will cheaply obtain a modest reputation and a large fortune. For this purpose he need not be admired; it is enough that he is liked. The ever-growing crowd of readers, and their constant craving for something new, assure the sale of books that nobody much esteems.

In democratic periods the public often treats authors as kings treat their courtiers: they enrich them and they despise them. What more do the venal souls born in courts, or worthy of living there, need? Democratic literature is always infested with a tribe of writers who regard letters as a mere trade, and for the few great authors who adorn it, you may count thousands of idea-peddlers.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — The Study Of Greek And Latin Literature Peculiarly Useful In Democratic Communities
paragraphs: Democratic Communities

What was called the People in the most democratic republics of antiquity was very unlike what we mean by that term. In Athens all the citizens took part in public affairs, but there were only 20,000 citizens among more than 350,000 inhabitants. All the rest were slaves, and they carried out most of the duties that belong today to the lower or even the middle classes. Athens, then, with her universal suffrage, was after all merely an aristocratic republic in which all the nobles had an equal right to govern. The struggle between the patricians and plebeians of Rome must be seen in the same light. It was simply an internal feud between the older and younger branches of the same family. All the citizens belonged, in fact, to the aristocracy and shared its character.

It should also be noted that among the ancients books were always scarce and expensive, and that very great difficulties stood in the way of publishing and circulating them. These circumstances confined literary tastes and habits to a small number of men, who formed a small literary aristocracy drawn from the choicer spirits of the great political aristocracy. Accordingly, nothing suggests that literature was ever treated as a trade among the Greeks and Romans.

These peoples were not only aristocracies but also very polished and free nations, so they naturally gave their literary productions the defects and the merits that mark the literature of aristocratic ages. Indeed, a very superficial look at the literary remains of the ancients is enough to convince us of this. Those writers were sometimes lacking in variety, or in fertility of subject, or in boldness, liveliness, or power of generalization in their thoughts, but they always showed exquisite care and skill in their details. Nothing in their works seems done hastily or at random. Every line is written for the eye of the connoisseur and is shaped by some conception of ideal beauty. No literature shows more boldly than that of the ancients the fine qualities in which the writers of democracies are naturally deficient. No literature, therefore, ought to be studied more in democratic ages. This study is better suited than any other to fight the literary defects inherent in those ages. As for their more praiseworthy literary qualities, these will spring up of their own accord, without any need to learn how to acquire them.

It is important that this point be clearly understood. A particular study may be useful to the literature of a people without being suited to its social and political needs. Suppose people persisted in teaching nothing but the literature of the dead languages in a community where everyone is habitually driven to make vehement efforts to increase or maintain his fortune. The result would be a very polished but very dangerous race of citizens. Their social and political condition would make them feel, every day, wants that their education would never teach them to supply. They would disturb the State in the name of the Greeks and Romans, instead of enriching it by their productive industry.

Clearly, in democratic communities both the interest of individuals and the safety of the commonwealth require that most people receive a scientific, commercial, and industrial education rather than a literary one. Greek and Latin should not be taught in every school. But those whose natural disposition or fortune destines them to cultivate letters, or prepares them to enjoy letters, must be able to find schools where they can gain a complete knowledge of ancient literature and where the true scholar can be formed. A few excellent universities would do more toward this goal than a vast number of poor grammar schools, where unnecessary subjects, badly learned, get in the way of sound instruction in necessary ones.

All who aspire to literary excellence in democratic nations ought often to refresh themselves at the springs of ancient literature. There is no more wholesome course for the mind. I do not hold that the literary productions of the ancients are beyond reproach. But I think they have some special merits, admirably suited to counterbalance our particular defects. They are a prop on the side where we are in most danger of falling.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — The Effect Of Democracy On Language
paragraphs: If the reader has rightly understood what I have already said about literature in general, he will have no difficulty seeing what kind of influence a democratic social condition and democratic institutions can have on language itself, which is the chief instrument of thought.

American authors can truly be said to live more in England than in their own country, since they constantly study the English writers and take them as their models every day. But this is not true of the bulk of the population, which is more directly exposed to the particular causes at work in the United States. So it is not the written language but the spoken language that we must watch, if we want to detect the changes an aristocratic people’s idiom may undergo when it becomes the language of a democracy.

Educated Englishmen, who are better judges than I am of the finer shades of expression, have often assured me that the language of the educated classes in the United States is noticeably different from that of the educated classes in Great Britain. They complain not only that the Americans have brought a number of new words into use — the difference and the distance between the two countries might be enough to explain that much — but that these new words are drawn especially from the jargon of parties, the mechanical arts, or the language of trade. They also say that the Americans often use old English words in new senses. Finally, they say that the inhabitants of the United States frequently mix their phrasing in the strangest way, and sometimes put together words that are always kept apart in the language of the mother country. These remarks were made to me at various times by people who seemed to deserve credit, and they led me to reflect on the subject. My reflections brought me, by theoretical reasoning, to the same point that my informants had reached by practical observation.

In aristocracies, language must naturally share in the state of repose in which everything else stays. Few new words are coined, because few new things are made; and even if new things were made, they would be called by familiar words whose meaning has been fixed by tradition. If the human mind does at last stir itself, or is roused by light breaking in from outside, the new expressions it introduces carry a degree of learning, intelligence, and philosophy that shows they do not originate in a democracy. After the fall of Constantinople turned the tide of science and literature toward the west, the French language was almost immediately flooded with a multitude of new words, all with Greek or Latin roots. A learned neologism then sprang up in France. It stayed within the educated classes and had no noticeable effect on the people, or at most a very gradual one. All the nations of Europe showed the same change in turn. Milton alone introduced more than six hundred words into the English language, almost all of them derived from Latin, Greek, or Hebrew. In a democratic community, by contrast, the constant agitation tends unceasingly to change the character of the language, just as it changes the look of public affairs. In the midst of this general stir and rivalry of minds, a great number of new ideas are formed. Old ideas are lost, or reappear, or are subdivided into an infinite variety of minor shades. The result is that many words must fall out of use, and others must be brought in.

Democratic nations love change for its own sake, and this shows in their language as much as in their politics. Even when they have no need to change words, they sometimes feel a wish to transform them. The genius of a democratic people shows itself not only in the great number of words they bring into use, but also in the nature of the ideas those new words stand for. Among such a people the majority lays down the law in language as it does in everything else, and its prevailing spirit is as plain there as anywhere. But the majority is more occupied with business than with study, with political and commercial interests than with philosophical speculation or literary pursuits. Most of the words coined or adopted for its use will therefore bear the mark of these habits. They will mainly serve to express the needs of business, the passions of party, or the details of public administration. In these areas the language will keep spreading, while in metaphysics and theology it will gradually lose ground.

The source from which democratic nations usually draw their new expressions, and the way they go about coining them, are both easy to describe. People living in democratic countries know little of the language spoken at Athens and Rome, and they do not care to dig into the lore of antiquity to find the expression they happen to want. If they sometimes turn to learned etymologies, vanity will lead them to search the roots of the dead languages, but erudition does not naturally supply them with its resources. It sometimes happens that the most ignorant make the most use of them. The eminently democratic desire to rise above one’s own sphere will often lead them to dignify a common profession with a Greek or Latin name. The lower the calling and the further from learning, the more pompous and learned its name. Thus the French rope-dancers have transformed themselves into acrobates and funambules.

Lacking knowledge of the dead languages, democratic nations are inclined to borrow words from living tongues, for their dealings with one another become constant, and the inhabitants of different countries imitate each other more readily as they grow more alike every day.

But it is chiefly in their own languages that democratic nations attempt innovations. From time to time they take forgotten expressions out of their vocabulary and bring them back into use. Or they borrow from some particular class of the community a term peculiar to it and introduce it, with a figurative meaning, into the language of daily life. Many expressions that originally belonged to the technical language of a profession or a party are drawn in this way into general circulation.

The most common way democratic nations innovate in language is to give an unusual meaning to an expression already in use. This method is very simple, quick, and convenient. No learning is required to use it correctly, and ignorance itself rather helps the practice. But that practice is most dangerous to the language. When a democratic people doubles the meaning of a word in this way, they sometimes make the meaning it keeps as ambiguous as the one it gains. An author begins by slightly bending a known expression away from its original meaning, and he adapts it, thus modified, as well as he can to his subject. A second writer twists the sense of the expression in another direction; a third takes it over for another purpose. Since there is no common appeal to the judgment of a permanent tribunal that could settle the meaning of the word once and for all, it remains ambiguous. The consequence is that writers hardly ever seem to dwell on a single thought. They always seem to aim at a knot of ideas, leaving the reader to judge which of them has been hit. This is a deplorable consequence of democracy. I would rather have the language made hideous with words imported from the Chinese, the Tartars, or the Hurons than have the meaning of a word in our own language become indeterminate. Harmony and uniformity are only secondary beauties in composition. Many of these things are conventional, and strictly speaking it is possible to do without them. But without clear phrasing there is no good language.

The principle of equality necessarily introduces several other changes into language. In aristocratic ages, each nation tends to stand apart from all others and likes to have distinct characteristics of its own. It often happens, then, that several peoples with a common origin become estranged from one another, so that, without ceasing to understand the same language, they no longer all speak it in the same way. In these ages each nation is divided into a certain number of classes that see little of each other and do not mingle. Each of these classes acquires, and invariably keeps, habits of mind peculiar to itself, and chooses certain words and terms that afterward pass from generation to generation, like their estates. The same idiom then includes a language of the poor and a language of the rich, a language of the citizen and a language of the nobility, a learned language and a vulgar one. The deeper the divisions and the more impassable the barriers of society, the more this must be so. I would wager that among the castes of India there are amazing variations of language, and that there is almost as much difference between the language of the pariah and that of the Brahmin as there is in their dress. When, on the contrary, people are no longer restrained by ranks and meet on terms of constant contact — when castes are destroyed and the classes of society are recruited from one another and intermixed — all the words of a language are mingled. Those unsuitable to the greater number die out. The rest form a common store, from which everyone chooses pretty much at random. Almost all the different dialects that divided the idioms of the European nations are clearly declining. There is no patois in the New World, and it is disappearing every day from the old countries.

This revolution in social conditions affects style as much as it affects phrasing. Not only does everyone use the same words, but a habit grows up of using them without discrimination. The rules that style had set up are almost abolished. The line ceases to be drawn between expressions that seem vulgar by their very nature and others that seem refined. People who come from different ranks of society carry the terms and expressions they are used to into whatever circumstances they pass into. Thus the origin of words is lost, like the origin of individuals, and there is as much confusion in language as there is in society.

I am aware that in the classification of words there are rules that belong to no one form of society more than another, but come from the nature of things. Some expressions and phrases are vulgar because the ideas they are meant to express are low in themselves. Others are of a higher character because the objects they are meant to designate are naturally elevated. No mixing of ranks will ever erase these differences. But the principle of equality cannot fail to root out whatever is merely conventional and arbitrary in the forms of thought. Perhaps the necessary classification I pointed out in the last sentence will always be less respected by a democratic people than by any other. For among such a people there are no men permanently disposed, by education, culture, and leisure, to study the natural laws of language, and who make those laws respected by observing them themselves.

I will not leave this topic without touching on a feature of democratic languages that is perhaps more characteristic of them than any other. It has already been shown that democratic nations have a taste, and sometimes a passion, for general ideas, and that this arises from their particular merits and defects. This liking for general ideas shows itself in democratic languages through the continual use of generic terms or abstract expressions, and through the way they are used. This is the great merit and the great imperfection of these languages. Democratic nations are passionately fond of generic terms and abstract expressions, because these modes of speech enlarge thought and assist the operations of the mind by letting it include several objects in a small compass. A French democratic writer will be inclined to say capacites in the abstract for men of capacity, without specifying the objects to which their capacity is applied. He will talk about actualities to designate in one word the things passing before his eyes at that moment, and he will take in under the term eventualities whatever may happen in the universe from the moment he speaks. Democratic writers are perpetually coining words of this kind, in which they refine the already abstract terms of the language into still further abstraction. What is more, to make their mode of speech more concise, they personify the subject of these abstract terms and make it act like a real entity. Thus they would say in French, “La force des choses veut que les capacites gouvernent.”

I cannot illustrate what I mean better than by my own example. I have often used the word “equality” in an absolute sense. Indeed, I have personified equality in several places, saying that equality does such and such things, or refrains from doing others. It may be affirmed that the writers of the age of Louis XIV would not have used these expressions. They would never have thought of using the word “equality” without applying it to some particular object, and they would rather have given up the term altogether than agree to make a living person of it.

These abstract terms, which abound in democratic languages and are used on every occasion without being attached to any particular fact, enlarge and obscure the thoughts they are meant to convey. They make the mode of speech more concise and the idea in it less clear. But where language is concerned, democratic nations prefer obscurity to labor. In fact, I wonder whether this loose style does not have some secret charm for those who speak and write among these nations. The men who live there are frequently left to the efforts of their own individual minds, so they are almost always prey to doubt. And since their situation in life is forever changing, they are never held fast to any of their opinions by the secure tenure of their fortunes. People living in democratic countries are therefore inclined to have unsettled ideas, and they need loose expressions to convey them. They never know whether the idea they express today will suit the new position they may occupy tomorrow, so they naturally develop a liking for abstract terms. An abstract term is like a box with a false bottom: you may put in it whatever ideas you please, and take them out again without being noticed.

Among all nations, generic and abstract terms form the basis of language. I do not, therefore, pretend to banish these terms from democratic languages. I simply remark that in the ages of democracy people have a special tendency to multiply words of this kind. They tend to take them always by themselves in their most abstract sense, and to use them on all occasions, even when the nature of the discourse does not require them.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — Of Some Of The Sources Of Poetry Amongst Democratic Nations
paragraphs: The word “poetry” has been given several different meanings. It would weary my readers if I led them into a discussion of which of these definitions should be chosen. I prefer to tell them at once which one I have chosen. In my opinion, poetry is the search for and the portrayal of the ideal. The poet is the one who completes and extends the work of nature. He does so by suppressing part of what exists, by adding some imaginary touches to the picture, and by combining certain real circumstances that do not in fact occur together. Thus the object of poetry is not to represent what is true, but to adorn it and to present to the mind some loftier imagery. Verse, regarded as the ideal beauty of language, may be eminently poetic, but verse by itself does not constitute poetry.

I now go on to ask whether, among the actions, feelings, and opinions of democratic nations, there are any that lead to a conception of ideal beauty, and that may for this reason be considered natural sources of poetry. We must first acknowledge that the taste for ideal beauty, and the pleasure of expressing it, are never so intense or so widespread among a democratic people as among an aristocratic one. In aristocratic nations it sometimes happens that the body goes on acting, as it were, spontaneously, while the higher faculties are bound and weighed down by repose. Among these nations the people very often show poetic tastes, and sometimes let their fancy range beyond and above what surrounds them. But in democracies the love of physical gratification, the idea of bettering one’s condition, the excitement of rivalry, and the charm of anticipated success are so many spurs driving men forward in the active professions they have taken up, without letting them stray from the track for an instant. The main stress of the faculties is directed to this point. The imagination is not extinct, but its chief function is to devise what may be useful and to represent what is real.

The principle of equality not only turns men away from portraying ideal beauty; it also reduces the number of objects to be portrayed. Aristocracy holds society in a fixed position. This favors the solidity and duration of positive religions, as well as the stability of political institutions. It not only keeps the human mind within a certain sphere of belief, but also predisposes it to adopt one faith rather than another. An aristocratic people will always be inclined to place intermediate powers between God and man. In this respect it may be said that the aristocratic element is favorable to poetry. When the universe is peopled with supernatural creatures, not perceptible to the senses but discovered by the mind, the imagination ranges freely. Poets then find a thousand subjects to portray, and they also find a countless audience interested in their works. In democratic ages, on the contrary, it sometimes happens that men are as adrift in matters of belief as they are in their laws. Skepticism then draws the poets’ imagination back to earth and confines them to the real and visible world. Even when the principle of equality does not disturb religious belief, it tends to simplify it, and to turn attention away from secondary agents and fix it chiefly on the Supreme Power. Aristocracy naturally leads the human mind to contemplate the past and holds it there. Democracy, on the contrary, gives men a kind of instinctive distaste for what is ancient. In this respect aristocracy is far more favorable to poetry, for things commonly grow larger and more obscure the more remote they are. For this twofold reason they are better suited to the portrayal of the ideal.

Having deprived poetry of the past, the principle of equality robs it in part of the present. Among aristocratic nations there are a certain number of privileged persons whose situation is, as it were, outside and above the condition of man. Power, wealth, fame, wit, refinement, and distinction in all things appear to belong especially to them. The crowd never sees them very closely, or does not watch them in minute detail, and little is needed to make the description of such men poetic. On the other hand, among the same people you will find classes so ignorant, low, and enslaved that they are no less fit objects for poetry, because of the extremity of their rudeness and wretchedness, than the former are because of their greatness and refinement. Besides, the different classes that make up an aristocratic community are widely separated and imperfectly acquainted with each other. The imagination can therefore always represent them with something added to, or subtracted from, what they really are. In democratic communities, where men are all insignificant and very much alike, each man sees all his fellows the moment he looks at himself. The poets of democratic ages can therefore never take any one man as the subject of a piece. An object of slight importance, seen distinctly on all sides, will never lend itself to an ideal conception. Thus, as the principle of equality has established itself in the world, it has dried up most of the old springs of poetry. Let us now try to show what new ones it may open.

Skepticism had emptied heaven, and the progress of equality had reduced each individual to smaller and better known proportions. The poets did not yet know what they could put in place of the great themes that were departing along with the aristocracy, so they turned their eyes to inanimate nature. As they lost sight of gods and heroes, they set themselves to describe streams and mountains. This is the origin, in the last century, of the kind of poetry that has been called, by way of distinction, descriptive. Some have thought that this sort of portrayal, embellished with all the physical and inanimate objects that cover the earth, was the kind of poetry peculiar to democratic ages. But I believe this is a mistake, and that it belongs only to a period of transition.

I am convinced that in the end democracy turns the imagination away from everything external to man and fixes it on man alone. Democratic nations may amuse themselves for a while by considering the productions of nature, but they are truly excited only by a survey of themselves. Here, and here alone, are the true sources of poetry among such nations to be found. It may be believed that poets who neglect to draw their inspiration from this source will lose all sway over the minds they want to enchant, and will be left in the end with none but unmoved spectators of their raptures. I have shown how the ideas of progress and of the indefinite perfectibility of the human race belong to democratic ages. Democratic nations care little for what has been, but they are haunted by visions of what will be. In this direction their unbounded imagination grows and expands beyond all measure. Here, then, is the wildest range open to the genius of poets, which lets them place their works at a sufficient distance from the eye. Democracy shuts the past against the poet, but opens the future before him. All the citizens who make up a democratic community are nearly equal and alike, so the poet cannot dwell on any one of them. But the nation itself invites the exercise of his powers. The general similarity of individuals makes any one of them, taken separately, an improper subject of poetry. Yet it allows poets to include them all in the same imagery and to take a general survey of the people itself. Democratic nations have a clearer perception than any others of their own aspect, and an aspect so imposing is admirably suited to the portrayal of the ideal.

I readily admit that the Americans have no poets, but I cannot allow that they have no poetic ideas. In Europe people talk a great deal about the wilds of America, but the Americans themselves never think about them. They are insensible to the wonders of inanimate nature, and it may be said that they do not notice the mighty forests that surround them until they fall beneath the hatchet. Their eyes are fixed on another sight. The American people sees itself marching across these wilds, draining swamps, turning the course of rivers, peopling solitudes, and subduing nature. This magnificent image of themselves does not meet the gaze of the Americans only at intervals. It may be said to haunt every one of them in his smallest as well as his most important actions, and to be always flitting before his mind. Nothing imaginable is so petty, so insipid, so crowded with paltry interests — in a word, so anti-poetic — as the life of a man in the United States. But among the thoughts it suggests there is always one full of poetry, and that is the hidden nerve that gives vigor to the whole frame.

In aristocratic ages each people, like each individual, tends to stand separate and aloof from all others. In democratic ages, the extreme restlessness of men and the impatience of their desires keep them perpetually on the move. The inhabitants of different countries therefore mingle, and they see, listen to, and borrow from each other’s stores. It is not only the members of the same community who grow more alike. Communities themselves become assimilated to one another, and the whole assemblage presents to the eye of the spectator one vast democracy, each citizen of which is a people. This shows the aspect of mankind in the broadest light for the first time. All that belongs to the existence of the human race taken as a whole, to its changes of fortune and to its future, becomes an abundant mine of poetry. The poets who lived in aristocratic ages were eminently successful in portraying certain incidents in the life of a people or a man. But none of them ever ventured to include the destinies of mankind in his works, a task that poets writing in democratic ages may attempt. At the same time that every man, raising his eyes above his country, begins at last to see mankind at large, the Divinity becomes more and more visible to the human mind in full and entire majesty. In democratic ages, faith in positive religions is often shaken, and belief in intermediate agents, by whatever name they are called, is clouded. On the other hand, men are inclined to form a far broader idea of Providence itself, and its interference in human affairs takes on a new and more imposing appearance in their eyes. Looking at the human race as one great whole, they easily conceive that its destinies are governed by a single design. In the actions of every individual they are led to recognize a trace of that universal and eternal plan by which God rules our race. This consideration may be taken as another rich source of poetry opened in democratic ages. Democratic poets will always appear trivial and frigid if they try to give gods, demons, or angels bodily forms, or if they attempt to draw them down from heaven to dispute the supremacy of earth. But suppose they strive to connect the great events they commemorate with the general providential designs that govern the universe, and, without showing the finger of the Supreme Governor, reveal the thoughts of the Supreme Mind. Then their works will be admired and understood, for the imagination of their contemporaries takes this direction of its own accord.

In the same way, it may be foreseen that poets living in democratic ages will prefer portraying passions and ideas to portraying persons and achievements. The language, the dress, and the daily actions of men in democracies are repugnant to ideal conceptions. These things are not poetic in themselves. And if it were otherwise, they would cease to be poetic, because they are too familiar to all those to whom the poet would speak of them. This forces the poet constantly to search below the external surface that the senses can perceive, in order to read the inner soul. Nothing lends itself more to the portrayal of the ideal than the scrutiny of the hidden depths in the immaterial nature of man. I do not need to wander over earth and sky to discover a wondrous object woven of contrasts, of infinite greatness and littleness, of intense gloom and amazing brightness, capable at once of exciting pity, admiration, terror, and contempt. I find that object in myself. Man springs out of nothing, crosses time, and disappears forever in the bosom of God. He is seen only for a moment, staggering on the verge of the two abysses, and there he is lost. If man were wholly ignorant of himself, he would have no poetry in him, for it is impossible to describe what the mind does not conceive. If man clearly saw his own nature, his imagination would remain idle and would have nothing to add to the picture. But the nature of man is disclosed enough for him to grasp something of himself, and obscure enough for all the rest to be plunged in thick darkness, in which he gropes forever, and forever in vain, to lay hold of some fuller notion of his being.

Among a democratic people, poetry will not be fed on legendary lays or the memorials of old traditions. The poet will not attempt to people the universe with supernatural beings in whom his readers and his own fancy have ceased to believe. Nor will he present virtues and vices in the mask of frigid personification, when they are better received under their own features. All these resources fail him, but Man remains, and the poet needs no more. The destinies of mankind will become the chief theme of poetry among these nations, if not the only one. By this I mean man himself, taken apart from his age and his country, standing in the presence of Nature and of God, with his passions, his doubts, his rare prosperities, and his inconceivable wretchedness. Experience may confirm this assertion if we consider the works of the greatest poets who have appeared since the world turned to democracy. The authors of our age who have so admirably portrayed the features of Faust, Childe Harold, Rene, and Jocelyn did not seek to record the actions of an individual. They sought to enlarge and to throw light on some of the obscurer recesses of the human heart. Such are the poems of democracy. The principle of equality, then, does not destroy all the subjects of poetry. It makes them fewer, but more vast.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — Of The Inflated Style Of American Writers And Orators
paragraphs: I have often noticed that the Americans generally treat business in clear, plain language, free of any ornament and so extremely simple as to be often coarse. Yet they are apt to become inflated as soon as they attempt a more poetic diction. They then vent their pomposity from one end of a speech to the other. To hear them lavish imagery on every occasion, one might think they never spoke of anything simply. The English are more rarely given to a similar failing. The cause of this can be pointed out without much difficulty. In democratic communities each citizen is habitually occupied with contemplating a very puny object, namely himself. If he ever raises his eyes higher, he sees nothing but the immense form of society at large, or the still more imposing aspect of mankind. His ideas are either extremely small and clear, or extremely general and vague. What lies between is an open void. When he has been drawn out of his own sphere, therefore, he always expects some amazing object to be offered to his attention. Only on these terms does he consent to tear himself, for an instant, from the petty, complicated cares that form the charm and the excitement of his life. This seems to me enough to explain why men in democracies, whose concerns are in general so paltry, call on their poets for conceptions so vast and descriptions so unlimited.

The authors, for their part, do not fail to obey a tendency they share themselves. They perpetually inflate their imaginations and expand them beyond all bounds, and they not infrequently abandon the great in order to reach the gigantic. By these means they hope to attract the attention of the multitude and to fix it easily upon themselves. Nor are their hopes disappointed, for as the multitude looks for nothing in poetry but subjects of very vast dimensions, it has neither the time to measure accurately the proportions of all the subjects set before it, nor a taste correct enough to perceive at once in what respect they are out of proportion. The author and the public corrupt one another at the same time.

As we have just seen, the sources of poetry among democratic nations are grand but not abundant. They run dry quickly. Poets then cannot find the elements of the ideal in what is real and true, so they drop reality entirely and invent monsters. I am not afraid that the poetry of democratic nations will turn out too dull or hug the ground too closely. My fear is rather that it will keep losing itself in the clouds and will finally wander into purely imaginary regions. I fear that democratic poets’ works may often be crammed with immense and incoherent imagery, exaggerated descriptions, and strange creations, and that the fantastic beings of their imagination may sometimes make us long for the world of reality.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — Some Observations On The Drama Amongst Democratic Nations
paragraphs: When the revolution that overturns the social and political state of an aristocratic people begins to reach literature, it usually shows itself first in the drama, and it always remains most visible there. A spectator at a play is, to some extent, taken by surprise by the impression it makes on him. He has no time to consult his memory or to ask people better qualified to judge than he is. It does not occur to him to resist the new literary tendencies he begins to feel; he gives in to them before he knows what they are. Authors are very quick to discover which way the public’s taste is secretly turning. They shape their works accordingly, and the literature of the stage, after serving as a sign of the coming literary revolution, soon carries it through. If you want to judge in advance the literature of a people that is sliding into democracy, study its plays.

Moreover, even among aristocratic nations, the literature of the stage is the most democratic part of their literature. No kind of literary pleasure is so easily within the reach of the multitude as the pleasure of watching a theatrical performance. It requires neither preparation nor study to enjoy; it takes hold of you in the midst of your prejudices and your ignorance. When an as yet untutored love of the pleasures of the mind begins to stir in one class of the community, it draws that class straight to the stage. The theaters of aristocratic nations have always been full of spectators who did not belong to the aristocracy. The theater is the only place where the higher ranks mix with the middle and lower classes, and the only place where the higher ranks agree to listen to the opinions of the others, or at least allow them to have an opinion at all. In the theater, cultivated men with literary accomplishments have always had more trouble than anywhere else in making their taste prevail over that of the people, and in avoiding being swept along by it. The pit has often made laws for the boxes.

If it is hard for an aristocracy to keep the people from getting the upper hand in the theater, it is easy to see that the people will be supreme there once democratic principles have worked their way into the laws and customs. That happens when ranks are mixed together, when minds as well as fortunes are drawn closer, and when the upper class has lost its hereditary wealth along with its power, its precedents, and its leisure. The tastes and inclinations that come naturally to democratic nations in literature will therefore show themselves first in the drama, and we can foresee that they will burst out there with great force. In written works, the literary rules of aristocracy will be modified gently, gradually, and, so to speak, legally; in the theater they will be overthrown in a riot. The drama brings out most of the good qualities and almost all the faults that are inherent in democratic literature. Democratic peoples place a very low value on learning and care little about what happened in Rome and Athens. They want to hear something that concerns themselves, and what they demand is a portrayal of the present age.

When the heroes and customs of antiquity are often brought onto the stage, and playwrights faithfully follow the rules of old precedent, that is enough to conclude that the democratic classes have not yet gained the upper hand in the theaters. In the preface to “Britannicus,” Racine very humbly apologizes for having placed Junia among the Vestals, who, according to Aulus Gellius, he says, “admitted no one below six years of age nor above ten.” We may be sure he would neither have accused himself of this offense nor defended himself against criticism if he had been writing for our contemporaries. A fact of this kind shows the state of literature at the time, and it shows the state of society itself as well. A democratic stage does not prove that the nation is in a state of democracy, because, as we have just seen, even in aristocracies democratic tastes may influence the drama. But when the spirit of aristocracy reigns exclusively on the stage, that fact proves beyond refutation that the whole of society is aristocratic. One may boldly infer that the same lettered and learned class that sways the playwrights also commands the people and governs the country.

The refined tastes and arrogant bearing of an aristocracy will rarely fail to lead it, when it controls the stage, to make a kind of selection within human nature. Some conditions of society hold its chief interest, and the scenes that depict their customs are preferred on the stage. Certain virtues, and even certain vices, are thought to deserve a place there more than others, and these are applauded while all the rest are shut out. On the stage as elsewhere, an aristocratic audience wants to meet only people of quality and to share the emotions of kings. The same goes for style: an aristocracy tends to impose on playwrights certain modes of expression that set the key in which everything must be delivered. In this way the stage often comes to depict only one side of man, or sometimes even to represent what cannot be found in human nature at all, rising above nature and going beyond it.

In democratic communities the spectators have no such favorites, and they rarely show such dislikes.
