They like to see on the stage the medley of conditions, feelings, and opinions that they see before their own eyes. The drama becomes more striking, more ordinary, and more true. Sometimes, however, those who write for the stage in democracies also go beyond the limits of human nature, but on a different side from their predecessors. In trying to represent in minute detail the small oddities of the moment and the particular traits of certain characters, they forget to portray the general features of the race.

When the democratic classes rule the stage, they bring as much license into the way subjects are treated as into the choice of them. The love of the drama is, of all literary tastes, the one most natural to democratic nations, so in these communities the number of authors, of spectators, and of theatrical performances keeps growing. A multitude made up of such different elements, and scattered over so many different places, cannot recognize the same rules or submit to the same laws. No agreement is possible among so many judges, who do not know when they will meet again, and so each one pronounces his own sentence on the play. If the effect of democracy is generally to call into question the authority of all literary rules and conventions, on the stage it abolishes them altogether and puts nothing in their place but the whim of each author and each public.

The drama also shows in a particular way the truth of what I said earlier, when I spoke more generally about style and art in democratic literature. Read the criticisms provoked by the plays of the age of Louis XIV, and you are surprised to notice how much stress the public put on the probability of the plot. You notice the importance attached to the perfect consistency of the characters, and to their doing nothing that could not be easily explained and understood. The value placed on forms of language at that time, and the petty quarrels over words with which playwrights were attacked, are no less surprising. It seems that the men of the age of Louis XIV attached exaggerated importance to details that can be noticed in the study but escape attention on the stage. For, after all, the main purpose of a play is to be performed, and its chief merit is to move the audience. But in that age the audience and the readers were the same people: on leaving the theater, they summoned the author to judgment at their own firesides. In democracies, plays are listened to but not read. Most of those who go to the theater do not go to look for the pleasures of the mind but for the keen emotions of the heart. They do not expect to hear a fine piece of literature but to see a play. As long as the author writes his country’s language correctly enough to be understood, and his characters arouse curiosity and awaken sympathy, the audience is satisfied. They ask nothing more of fiction and go straight back to real life. Correctness of style is therefore less required, because careful observance of its rules is less noticeable on the stage. As for the probability of the plot, it is incompatible with constant novelty, surprise, and quickness of invention. It is therefore neglected, and the public excuses the neglect. You may be sure that if you bring your audience face to face with something that moves them, they will not care by what road you brought them there, and they will never reproach you for stirring their emotions in spite of the rules of drama.

The Americans show very clearly all the different inclinations I have just described when they go to the theater. But it must be admitted that so far very few of them go to the theater at all. Playgoers and plays have increased enormously in the United States over the last forty years, yet the population indulges in this kind of amusement with the greatest reserve. This is due to particular causes that the reader already knows, and a few words will be enough to remind him of them. The Puritans who founded the American republics were not only enemies of amusements; they professed a special horror of the stage. They regarded it as an abominable pastime, and as long as their principles held undivided sway, theatrical performances were completely unknown among them. These opinions of the first fathers of the colony have left very deep marks on the minds of their descendants. The extreme regularity of habits and great strictness of customs seen in the United States have so far put further obstacles in the way of the growth of dramatic art. There are no dramatic subjects in a country that has seen no great political catastrophes and where love always leads by a straight and easy road to marriage. People who spend every weekday making money and Sunday going to church have nothing to attract the muse of Comedy.

One fact is enough to show that the stage is not very popular in the United States. The Americans, whose laws allow the utmost freedom and even license of language in every other respect, have nevertheless subjected their playwrights to a kind of censorship. Theatrical performances can only take place with the permission of the municipal authorities. This may show how much communities resemble individuals. They surrender without scruple to their ruling passions, and then take the greatest care not to yield too much to the force of tastes they do not have.

No part of literature is joined by closer or more numerous ties to the present condition of society than the drama. The drama of one period can never suit the following age if, in the meantime, an important revolution has changed the nation’s customs and laws. The great authors of an earlier age may still be read, but plays written for a different public will not be followed. The playwrights of the past live only in books. The traditional taste of certain individuals, vanity, fashion, or the genius of an actor may sustain or revive the aristocratic drama for a time in a democracy. But it will soon fall away of its own accord, not overthrown but abandoned.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 — Characteristics Of Historians In Democratic Ages
paragraphs: Historians who write in aristocratic ages usually trace every event back to the particular will or temperament of certain individuals, and they tend to attribute the most important revolutions to very slight accidents. They follow the smallest causes with great shrewdness and often fail to notice the greatest. Historians who live in democratic ages show exactly the opposite tendencies. Most of them attribute hardly any influence to the individual over the destiny of the human race, or to citizens over the fate of a people. On the other hand, they assign great general causes to every petty incident. These opposite tendencies explain each other.

When the historian of aristocratic ages looks over the theater of the world, he immediately sees a very small number of leading actors who manage the whole play. These great figures stand at the front of the stage, and they catch his attention and hold it. While the historian is intent on uncovering the secret motives that make them speak and act, he forgets the rest. The importance of what some men are seen to do gives him an exaggerated idea of the influence one man can have. It naturally leads him to think that, to explain the impulses of the multitude, he must trace them back to the particular influence of some one individual.

When, on the contrary, all the citizens are independent of one another and each of them is individually weak, no one is seen to exercise great power over the community, much less lasting power. At first sight, individuals seem to have no influence over it at all, and society seems to advance by itself, through the free and voluntary cooperation of all the men who make it up. This naturally pushes the mind to look for the general reason that acts on the faculties of so many men at the same time and turns them all in the same direction at once.

I am fully convinced that even among democratic nations, the genius, vices, or virtues of certain individuals slow down or speed up the natural course of a people’s history. But causes of this secondary and accidental kind are infinitely more varied, more hidden, more complex, less powerful, and therefore harder to trace in periods of equality than in ages of aristocracy. In an aristocratic age the historian’s task is simply to pick out, from the mass of general events, the particular influences of one man or a few men. In a democratic age the historian is soon worn out by the labor, and his mind gets lost in the maze. Unable to discern clearly, or to point out plainly, the influence of individuals, he denies that it exists. He prefers to talk about the characteristics of a race, the physical features of the country, or the genius of civilization. This shortens his own labor and satisfies his reader far better at less cost.

M. de Lafayette says somewhere in his “Memoirs” that the exaggerated system of general causes offers surprising consolations to second-rate statesmen. I will add that it consoles second-rate historians just as much. It can always supply a few mighty reasons to get them out of the most difficult part of their work. It indulges the laziness or incapacity of their minds, while it gives them credit for deep thinking.

For my part, I am of the opinion that at all times one large portion of the events of this world is due to general facts and another to particular influences. These two kinds of cause are always at work; only their proportion varies. General facts explain more things in democratic ages than in aristocratic ones, and fewer things can then be assigned to particular influences. In periods of aristocracy the reverse holds: particular influences are stronger and general causes weaker, unless we count as a general cause the very fact of the inequality of conditions, which allows some individuals to thwart the natural tendencies of all the rest. Historians who try to describe what happens in democratic societies are therefore right to assign much to general causes and to give most of their attention to finding them. But they are wrong to deny entirely the particular influence of individuals just because they cannot easily trace or follow it.

Historians who live in democratic ages are not only inclined to assign a great cause to every incident; they are also inclined to connect incidents with one another so as to draw a system from them. In aristocratic ages the attention of historians is constantly drawn to individuals, so the connection between events escapes them, or rather, they do not believe in any such connection. To them the thread of history seems to be crossed and broken at every moment by the footstep of man. In democratic ages, on the contrary, the historian sees much more of actions than of actors, and so he can easily establish some kind of sequence and methodical order among the actions. Ancient literature is so rich in fine historical writing, yet it does not contain a single great historical system, while the poorest of modern literatures are full of them. It seems that the ancient historians did not make enough use of the general theories that our historical writers are always ready to carry to excess.

Those who write in democratic ages have another, more dangerous tendency. When the traces of individual action on nations are lost, it often happens that the world keeps moving although the agent that moves it can no longer be found. It becomes extremely difficult to discern and analyze the reasons that act separately on the will of each member of the community and in the end combine to set the old mass in motion. Men are therefore led to believe that this movement is involuntary, and that societies unconsciously obey some superior force ruling over them. But even when the general fact that governs the private will of every individual is supposed to have been discovered on earth, the principle of human free will is not safe. A cause wide enough to affect millions of men at once, and strong enough to bend them all together in the same direction, may well seem irresistible. Having seen that mankind does yield to it, the mind is close to concluding that mankind cannot resist it.

Historians who live in democratic ages, then, not only deny that the few have any power to act on the destiny of a people. They also deprive the people themselves of the power to change their own condition, and they subject them either to an inflexible Providence or to some blind necessity. According to them, each nation is indissolubly bound by its position, its origin, its precedents, and its character to a certain lot that no effort can ever change. They link generation to generation. Going back in this way from age to age and from necessity to necessity, all the way to the origin of the world, they forge a close and enormous chain that girds and binds the human race. It is not enough for them to show what events have occurred; they want to show that events could not have occurred otherwise. They take a nation that has reached a certain stage of its history and assert that it could not have failed to follow the track that brought it there. It is easier to make such an assertion than to show how the nation might have taken a better course.

When you read the historians of aristocratic ages, and especially those of antiquity, it seems that to be master of his lot and to govern his fellow creatures, a man needs only to be master of himself. When you read the historical works our age has produced, it seems that man is utterly powerless over himself and over everything around him. The historians of antiquity taught how to command; those of our time teach only how to obey. In their writings the author often appears great, but humanity is always small. Suppose this doctrine of necessity, which is so attractive to those who write history in democratic ages, passes from authors to their readers, until it infects the whole mass of the community and takes possession of the public mind. It will soon paralyze the activity of modern society and reduce Christians to the level of the Turks. I would observe, moreover, that such principles are especially dangerous at the point we have now reached. Our contemporaries are only too inclined to doubt human free will, because each of them feels himself hemmed in on every side by his own weakness. But they are still willing to acknowledge the strength and independence of men united in society. Let us not lose sight of this principle, for the great goal in our time is to raise the faculties of men, not to complete their prostration.

chapters.title: Chapter 21 — Of Parliamentary Eloquence In The United States
paragraphs: Among aristocratic nations all the members of the community are connected with one another and depend on one another. The graduated scale of ranks acts as a tie that keeps everyone in his proper place and the whole body in subordination. Something of the same kind always happens in the political assemblies of these nations. Parties naturally group themselves under certain leaders, whom they obey by a kind of instinct that is only the result of habits formed elsewhere. They carry the habits and customs of general society into the smaller gathering.

In democratic countries it often happens that a great number of citizens are heading toward the same point, but each one moves there of his own accord, or at least flatters himself that he does. He is used to governing his actions by personal impulse alone, and he does not willingly submit to dictation from outside. This taste and habit of independence goes with him into the councils of the nation. If he agrees to join with other men in pursuing the same purpose, he still insists on remaining free to contribute to the common success in his own way. This is why, in democratic countries, parties are so impatient of control and can be managed only in moments of great public danger. Even then, the authority of leaders may be able to make men act or speak, but it hardly ever reaches the point of making them keep silent.

In aristocratic nations, the men who sit in political assemblies also belong to the aristocracy. Each has a high, settled rank of his own, and his seat in the assembly often matters less to him than his standing in the country. That standing comforts him when he takes no part in debates on public affairs, and it keeps him from trying too eagerly to take a trivial part.

In America, it generally happens that a Representative becomes somebody only through his position in the Assembly. He is therefore constantly haunted by a craving to gain importance there, and he feels a restless desire to keep pushing his opinions on the House. His own vanity is not the only thing urging him along this course; so are his constituents, and so is the constant need to win their favor. Among aristocratic nations a member of the legislature is rarely strictly dependent on his constituents. He is often, to them, a kind of unavoidable representative; sometimes they are themselves strictly dependent on him. If they finally reject him, he can easily get elected elsewhere, or, retiring from public life, he can still enjoy the pleasures of a splendid idleness. In a democratic country like the United States, a Representative hardly ever has a lasting hold on the minds of his constituents. However small an electoral body may be, the shifting currents of democracy are constantly changing its character, so it must be courted without end. He is never sure of his supporters, and if they abandon him he is left without any resource. His natural position is not high enough for him to be easily known to people who are not close to him, and, given the complete independence prevailing among the people, he cannot hope that his friends or the government will send him down to be returned by an electoral body that does not know him. The seeds of his fortune are therefore sown in his own neighborhood. From that corner of the earth he must start, to raise himself to the command of a people and to influence the destinies of the world. So it is natural that in democratic countries the members of political assemblies think more of their constituents than of their party, whereas in aristocracies they think more of their party than of their constituents.

But what ought to be said to please constituents is not always what ought to be said to serve the party to which Representatives profess to belong. The general interest of a party often requires that its members not speak on great questions they understand imperfectly. It requires that they speak little on those minor questions that get in the way of the great ones. Finally, and in most cases, it requires that they not speak at all. Keeping silent is the most useful service a mediocre speaker can render to the commonwealth. Constituents, however, do not think so. The people of a district send a representative to take part in the government of the country because they hold a very high opinion of his merits. Men appear greater in proportion to the smallness of the things around them, so we may assume that the opinion held of the delegate will be higher the rarer talents are among his constituents. It will therefore often happen that the less his constituents have to expect from their representative, the more they will expect from him. However unfit he may be, they will not fail to call on him for remarkable efforts that match the rank they have given him.

Apart from his position as a legislator of the State, electors also regard their Representative as the natural patron of the constituency in the legislature. They almost consider him the proxy of each of his supporters, and they flatter themselves that he will be no less zealous in defending their private interests than those of the country. Electors are therefore quite sure in advance that the Representative of their choice will be an orator. They expect him to speak often if he can. If he is forced to hold back, they expect him at least to squeeze into his rarer speeches a review of all the great questions of state, together with an account of all the petty grievances they themselves have to complain of. Even if he cannot come forward often, he should prove what he is capable of on each occasion. Instead of constantly lavishing his powers, he should now and then condense them into a small space, so as to give a complete and brilliant summary of his constituents and of himself. On these terms they will vote for him at the next election. These conditions drive worthy men of modest abilities to despair; knowing their own powers, they would never have come forward voluntarily. But pushed on in this way, the Representative begins to speak, to the great alarm of his friends. Rushing recklessly into the midst of the most celebrated orators, he muddles the debate and wearies the House.

All laws that tend to make the Representative more dependent on the elector affect not only the conduct of legislators, as I have remarked elsewhere, but also their language. They influence at once the business itself and the manner in which the business is discussed.

There is hardly a member of Congress who can bring himself to go home without having sent at least one speech to his constituents. None of them will put up with any interruption until he has worked into his harangue whatever useful suggestions may be made about the four-and-twenty States of which the Union is composed, and especially about the district he represents. He therefore presents his listeners with a succession of great general truths, which he himself understands and expresses only confusedly, and of petty details, which he is only too able to discover and point out. The result is that the debates of that great assembly are often vague and confused, and seem to drag their slow length along rather than advance toward a clear object. Some such state of things will, I believe, always arise in the public assemblies of democracies.

Favorable circumstances and good laws might succeed in drawing to the legislature of a democratic people men far superior to those the Americans send to Congress. But nothing will ever prevent the men of slender abilities who sit there from pushing themselves complacently, and in every way, on the public. The evil does not seem to me capable of a complete cure, because it originates not only in the procedures of that assembly but in its constitution and in that of the country. The inhabitants of the United States themselves seem to see the matter this way. They show their long experience of parliamentary life not by refraining from making bad speeches but by courageously submitting to hear them. They are resigned to it, as to an evil they know to be unavoidable.

We have shown the petty side of political debates in democratic assemblies; let us now show the more imposing side. The proceedings of the Parliament of England for the last one hundred and fifty years have never caused any great stir outside that country. The opinions and feelings expressed by the speakers have never awakened much sympathy, even among the nations placed nearest to the great arena of British liberty. Europe, by contrast, was excited by the very first debates held in the small colonial assemblies of America at the time of the Revolution. This was due not only to particular and accidental circumstances but to general and lasting causes. I can imagine nothing more admirable or more powerful than a great orator debating great questions of state in a democratic assembly. No particular class is ever represented there by men commissioned to defend its own interests, so the orator always speaks to the whole nation and in the name of the whole nation. This enlarges his thoughts and heightens his power of language. Precedents have little weight there. No privileges are attached to certain property any longer, and no rights belong to certain bodies or certain individuals. The mind must therefore turn to general truths drawn from human nature to settle the particular question under discussion. Hence the political debates of a democratic people, however small it may be, have a breadth that often makes them attractive to mankind. All men are interested in them, because they deal with man, who is the same everywhere. Among the greatest aristocratic nations, on the contrary, the most general questions are almost always argued on some special grounds drawn from the practice of a particular time or the rights of a particular class. These interest only that class, or at most the people among whom that class happens to exist. This, as much as the greatness of the French people and the favorable disposition of the nations who listen to them, explains the great effect that French political debates sometimes produce in the world. The orators of France often speak to mankind, even when they are addressing only their countrymen.
Section 2: Influence of Democracy on the Feelings of Americans

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Why Democratic Nations Show A More Ardent And Enduring Love Of Equality Than Of Liberty
paragraphs: Of Equality Than of Liberty

The first and most intense passion that the equality of conditions produces is, I hardly need say, the love of that same equality. My readers will therefore not be surprised that I speak of it before all others. Everyone has noticed that in our time, and especially in France, this passion for equality is gaining ground in the human heart every day. People have said a hundred times that our contemporaries are far more ardently and stubbornly attached to equality than to freedom. But since I do not find that the causes of this fact have been analyzed enough, I shall try to point them out.

We can imagine an extreme point at which freedom and equality would meet and merge. Suppose that all the members of the community take part in the government, and that each of them has an equal right to do so. Since no one differs from his fellows, no one can exercise tyrannical power. Men will be perfectly free because they will all be entirely equal, and they will be perfectly equal because they will be entirely free. Democratic nations tend toward this ideal state. It is the most complete form that equality can take on earth, but there are a thousand others that, though not as perfect, are no less dear to those nations.

The principle of equality can be established in civil society without prevailing in the political world. Men may have equal rights to indulge in the same pleasures, to enter the same professions, to frequent the same places — in a word, to live in the same manner and seek wealth by the same means — although they do not all take an equal share in the government. A kind of equality may even be established in the political world where there is no political freedom at all. A man may be the equal of all his countrymen except one, who is the master of all without distinction and who chooses the agents of his power equally from among them all. One could easily imagine several other combinations in which very great equality is joined to institutions that are more or less free, or even to institutions wholly without freedom. Men cannot become absolutely equal unless they are entirely free, and so equality, pushed to its furthest extent, may merge with freedom. Even so, there is good reason to distinguish the one from the other. The taste men have for liberty and the taste they have for equality are in fact two different things, and I am not afraid to add that among democratic nations they are two unequal things.

On close inspection, we see that every age has some particular and dominant fact to which all others are connected. This fact almost always gives birth to some fruitful idea or ruling passion, which draws all the feelings and opinions of the time to itself and carries them along in its course. It is like a great stream toward which each of the surrounding rivulets seems to flow. Freedom has appeared in the world at different times and in various forms. It has not been bound exclusively to any social condition, and it is not confined to democracies. Freedom therefore cannot be the distinguishing characteristic of democratic ages. The particular and dominant fact that marks those ages as its own is the equality of conditions, and the ruling passion of men in those periods is the love of this equality. Do not ask what strange charm the men of democratic ages find in being equal, or what special reasons they may have for clinging so stubbornly to equality rather than to the other advantages that society offers them. Equality is the distinguishing characteristic of the age they live in, and that alone is enough to explain why they prefer it to all the rest.

But apart from this reason, there are several others that will at all times habitually lead men to prefer equality to freedom. If a people could ever succeed in destroying the equality that prevails within it, or even in reducing it, it could do so only through long and laborious effort. Its social condition would have to be changed, its laws abolished, its opinions replaced, its habits altered, its mores corrupted. Political liberty, on the other hand, is more easily lost: to neglect to hold it fast is to let it slip away. Men therefore cling to equality not only because it is dear to them but also because they believe it will last forever.

Even the narrowest and most unthinking minds can see that political freedom, in its excesses, may endanger the peace, the property, and the lives of individuals. But only attentive and clear-sighted men perceive the dangers with which equality threatens us, and they usually avoid pointing them out. They know that the calamities they fear are remote, and they comfort themselves that these will fall only on future generations, about whom the present generation thinks very little. The evils that freedom sometimes brings are immediate. Everyone can see them, and everyone is affected by them more or less. The evils that extreme equality may produce come to light slowly. They creep gradually into the social frame, they are noticed only at intervals, and by the time they become most violent, habit has already stopped people from feeling them. The advantages of freedom show themselves only over time, and it is always easy to mistake the cause from which they come. The advantages of equality are instantaneous, and they can always be traced back to their source. Political liberty bestows exalted pleasures from time to time on a certain number of citizens. Equality confers a number of small enjoyments on every man every day. The charms of equality are felt at every moment and are within everyone’s reach. The noblest hearts are not insensible to them, and the most vulgar souls delight in them. The passion that equality produces must therefore be at once strong and general. Men cannot enjoy political liberty without paying for it with some sacrifices, and they never obtain it without great exertion. But the pleasures of equality offer themselves freely. Each of the small incidents of life seems to bring them about, and to taste them nothing is required but to live.

Democratic nations are fond of equality at all times, but there are certain epochs when their passion for it swells to the height of fury. This happens at the moment when the old social system, long under threat, completes its own destruction after a last internal struggle, and the barriers of rank are finally thrown down. At such times men pounce on equality as their booty, and they cling to it as to a precious treasure they fear to lose. The passion for equality penetrates men’s hearts on every side, spreads there, and fills them entirely. Do not tell them that by surrendering blindly to one exclusive passion they risk their dearest interests: they are deaf. Do not show them freedom slipping from their grasp while they are looking the other way: they are blind — or rather, they can see only one thing in the universe worth desiring.

What I have said applies to all democratic nations. What I am about to say concerns the French alone. Among most modern nations, and especially among all those of the Continent of Europe, the taste for freedom and the idea of it began to exist and to spread only when social conditions were tending toward equality, and as a consequence of that very equality. Absolute kings were the most effective levelers of ranks among their subjects. Among these nations equality came before freedom. Equality was therefore a long-established fact while freedom was still a novelty. Equality had already created customs, opinions, and laws of its own when freedom, alone and for the first time, came into actual existence. So freedom was still only a matter of opinion and taste, while equality had already crept into the habits of the people, taken hold of their mores, and given a particular turn to the smallest actions of their lives. Is it any wonder that the men of our own time prefer the one to the other?

I think that democratic communities have a natural taste for freedom. Left to themselves, they will seek it, cherish it, and regret any loss of it. But their passion for equality is ardent, insatiable, incessant, and invincible. They call for equality in freedom, and if they cannot obtain that, they still call for equality in slavery. They will endure poverty, servitude, and barbarism, but they will not endure aristocracy. This is true at all times, and especially true in our own. Any men or powers who try to fight this irresistible passion will be overthrown and destroyed by it. In our age, freedom cannot be established without it, and despotism itself cannot reign without its support.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Of Individualism In Democratic Countries
paragraphs: I have shown how, in ages of equality, every man looks for his opinions within himself. I am now going to show how, in those same ages, all his feelings are turned toward himself alone. Individualism *a is a new word, born of a new idea. Our forefathers knew only egotism. Egotism is a passionate and exaggerated love of self, which leads a man to relate everything to his own person and to prefer himself to everything in the world. Individualism is a calm and considered feeling that disposes each member of the community to cut himself off from the mass of his fellow creatures and to withdraw with his family and his friends. Once he has formed a little circle of his own in this way, he is willing to leave society at large to itself. Egotism comes from blind instinct. Individualism comes more from mistaken judgment than from corrupt feelings. It arises as much from deficiencies of the mind as from the perversity of the heart. Egotism blights the seed of every virtue. Individualism at first undermines only the virtues of public life, but in the long run it attacks and destroys all the others, and in the end it is absorbed into plain egotism. Egotism is a vice as old as the world, and it belongs to no one form of society more than another. Individualism is of democratic origin, and it threatens to spread in the same proportion as the equality of conditions.

[Footnote a: [I adopt the expression of the original, however strange it may seem to English ears, partly because it illustrates the remark on the introduction of general terms into democratic language that was made in an earlier chapter, and partly because I know of no English word that corresponds to it exactly. The chapter itself defines the meaning the author gives it. — Translator’s Note.]]

Among aristocratic nations, families stay in the same condition for centuries, often on the same spot, so that all generations become, as it were, contemporaries. A man almost always knows his forefathers and respects them. He thinks he can already see his remote descendants, and he loves them. He willingly takes on duties toward both, and he will often sacrifice his personal gratifications for those who went before him and those who will come after him. Aristocratic institutions also have the effect of binding every man closely to several of his fellow citizens. The classes of an aristocratic people are sharply marked and permanent, so each of them is regarded by its own members as a kind of lesser country, more tangible and more cherished than the country at large. In aristocratic communities all citizens occupy fixed positions, one above another. As a result, each of them always sees above him a man whose patronage he needs, and below him another man whose cooperation he may claim. Men living in aristocratic ages are therefore almost always closely attached to something outside their own sphere, and they are often ready to forget themselves. It is true that in those ages the idea of human fellowship is faint, and men seldom think of sacrificing themselves for mankind. But they often sacrifice themselves for other men. In democratic ages, by contrast, each individual’s duties to the human race are much clearer, but devoted service to any one man becomes rarer. The bond of human affection is extended, but it is loosened.

Among democratic nations new families are constantly springing up, others are constantly falling away, and all that remain change their condition. The thread of time is broken at every moment, and the track of the generations is wiped out. Those who went before are soon forgotten, and no one has any idea of those who will come after. A man’s interest is confined to those closest to himself. As each class draws nearer to the other classes and mixes with them, its members become indifferent to one another and like strangers. Aristocracy had made a chain of all the members of the community, from the peasant to the king. Democracy breaks that chain and severs every link of it. As social conditions become more equal, the number grows of people who are neither rich enough nor powerful enough to have any great influence over their fellow creatures, but who have nevertheless acquired or kept enough education and fortune to satisfy their own wants. They owe nothing to any man, and they expect nothing from any man. They form the habit of always considering themselves as standing alone, and they tend to imagine that their whole destiny is in their own hands. Thus democracy not only makes every man forget his ancestors, but also hides his descendants from him and separates him from his contemporaries. It throws him back forever upon himself alone, and threatens in the end to confine him entirely within the solitude of his own heart.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Individualism Stronger At The Close Of A Democratic Revolution Than At Other Periods
paragraphs: Revolution Than at Other Periods

The time when the building of a democratic society on the ruins of an aristocracy has just been completed is the time when this separation of men from one another, and the egotism that results from it, most forcibly strike the observer. Democratic communities contain not only a large number of independent citizens. They are also constantly filled with men who entered their independent condition only yesterday and are intoxicated with their new power. These men have a presumptuous confidence in their strength. They do not suppose that they will ever again need to ask their fellow creatures for help, so they do not hesitate to show that they care for nobody but themselves.

An aristocracy seldom yields without a long struggle, in the course of which implacable hatreds are kindled between the different classes of society. These passions outlast the victory, and traces of them can be seen in the democratic confusion that follows. Those members of the community who were at the top of the old gradations of rank cannot immediately forget their former greatness. For a long time they will regard themselves as strangers in the newly formed society. They look upon all those whom this state of society has made their equals as oppressors, whose fate can arouse no sympathy. They have lost sight of their former equals and no longer feel bound to their fate by any common interest. Each of them, standing apart, thinks he is reduced to caring for himself alone. Those who were formerly at the foot of the social scale, and who have been brought up to the common level by a sudden revolution, cannot enjoy their newly acquired independence without a secret uneasiness. If they meet some of their former superiors on the same footing as themselves, they keep away from them with an air of triumph and of fear. It is therefore usually at the outset of democratic society that citizens are most inclined to live apart. Democracy does not lead men to draw closer to their fellow creatures, but democratic revolutions lead them to avoid one another, and to carry into a state of equality the hatreds that the state of inequality produced. The great advantage of the Americans is that they have arrived at a state of democracy without having to go through a democratic revolution, and that they are born equal instead of becoming so.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — That The Americans Combat The Effects Of Individualism By Free Institutions
paragraphs: Despotism is very timid by nature, and it is never more sure of lasting than when it can keep men apart. All its influence is commonly exerted for that purpose. No vice of the human heart suits it so well as egotism. A despot readily forgives his subjects for not loving him, provided they do not love one another. He does not ask them to help him govern the state. It is enough that they do not aspire to govern it themselves. He brands as turbulent and unruly those who would combine their efforts to promote the prosperity of the community, and, twisting the natural meaning of words, he praises as good citizens those who have no sympathy for anyone but themselves. Thus the vices that despotism produces are precisely those that equality fosters. These two things complete and assist each other, with pernicious results. Equality places men side by side with no common tie between them. Despotism raises barriers to keep them apart. Equality predisposes them not to think of their fellow creatures, and despotism makes general indifference a kind of public virtue.

Despotism, then, which is dangerous at all times, is especially to be feared in democratic ages. It is easy to see that in those same ages men most need freedom. When the members of a community are forced to attend to public affairs, they are necessarily drawn out of the circle of their own interests and pulled, at times, away from self-observation. As soon as a man begins to discuss public affairs in public, he begins to perceive that he is not as independent of his fellow men as he had at first imagined, and that to obtain their support he must often lend them his cooperation.

When the public is supreme, there is no man who does not feel the value of public goodwill or who does not try to win it by gaining the esteem and affection of those among whom he is to live. Many of the passions that chill human hearts and keep them apart are then obliged to withdraw and hide below the surface. Pride must be disguised, disdain dares not break out, and egotism is afraid of itself. Under a free government, most public offices are elective. The men whose lofty minds or ambitious hopes are too narrowly confined in private life therefore feel constantly that they cannot do without the people around them. At such times men learn to think of their fellow men out of ambition, and they often find it, in a way, in their interest to forget themselves.

I may be met here with an objection drawn from electioneering intrigues, the meanness of candidates, and the slanders of their opponents. These are occasions for hostility, and they come more often the more frequent elections become. Such evils are certainly great, but they are temporary, whereas the benefits that go with them remain. The desire to be elected may lead some men to violent hostility for a time. But this same desire leads all men, in the long run, to support one another. And if an election happens to separate two friends, the electoral system brings together permanently a multitude of citizens who would otherwise have remained unknown to each other. Freedom produces private hostilities, but despotism gives birth to general indifference.

The Americans have fought, by means of free institutions, the tendency of equality to keep men apart, and they have overcome it. The legislators of America did not suppose that a general representation of the whole nation would be enough to ward off a disorder at once so natural to the structure of democratic society and so fatal to it. They also thought it would be wise to bring political life into every part of the territory. In this way they would multiply without limit the opportunities for all members of the community to act together, and make them feel constantly their dependence on one another. The plan was a wise one. The general affairs of a country engage only the attention of leading politicians, who gather from time to time in the same places, and since they often lose sight of one another afterward, no lasting ties are formed between them. But if the local affairs of a district are to be conducted by the men who live there, the same persons are always in contact. They are, in a way, forced to become acquainted and to adapt themselves to one another.

It is difficult to draw a man out of his own circle and interest him in the destiny of the state, because he does not clearly understand what influence the destiny of the state can have on his own lot. But if it is proposed to run a road across the end of his estate, he will see at a glance that there is a connection between this small public affair and his greatest private affairs. And he will discover, without anyone showing it to him, the close tie that unites private interest to general interest. So, to interest citizens in the public welfare and to convince them that they constantly need one another in providing for it, far more can be done by entrusting them with the administration of minor affairs than by giving them control of important ones. A brilliant achievement may win you the favor of a people at one stroke. But to earn the love and respect of the people around you, you will need a long succession of small services and obscure good deeds, a constant habit of kindness, and an established reputation for disinterestedness. Local freedom, then, leads a great number of citizens to value the affection of their neighbors and kindred. It perpetually brings men together and forces them to help one another, in spite of the tendencies that divide them.

In the United States the wealthier citizens take great care not to stand aloof from the people. On the contrary, they constantly keep on easy terms with the lower classes: they listen to them and speak to them every day. They know that the rich in democracies always need the poor, and that in democratic ages you attach a poor man to you more by your manner than by the benefits you give him. The size of such benefits brings out the difference of conditions, and this causes a secret irritation in those who profit from them. But the charm of simple manners is almost irresistible. Their friendliness wins men over, and even their lack of polish is not always displeasing. This truth does not take root at once in the minds of the rich. They generally resist it as long as the democratic revolution lasts, and they do not acknowledge it immediately after the revolution is over. They are very ready to do good to the people, but they still choose to keep them at arm’s length. They think that is enough, but they are mistaken. They might spend fortunes this way without warming the hearts of the people around them. These people do not ask them to sacrifice their money, but their pride.

It would seem that every imagination in the United States is strained to invent ways of increasing the wealth and satisfying the wants of the public. The best-informed inhabitants of each district constantly use their knowledge to discover new truths that may increase the general prosperity. If they have made any such discoveries, they eagerly hand them over to the mass of the people.

When we closely examine the vices and weaknesses that those who govern in America frequently display, the prosperity of the people causes surprise, but wrongly so. Elected magistrates do not make American democracy flourish. It flourishes because the magistrates are elective.

It would be unjust to suppose that the patriotism and zeal every American shows for the welfare of his fellow citizens are wholly insincere. Private interest directs the greater part of human actions in the United States as it does elsewhere, but it does not regulate them all. I must say that I have often seen Americans make great and real sacrifices to the public welfare, and I have noted a hundred instances in which they hardly ever failed to give each other faithful support. The free institutions that the inhabitants of the United States possess, and the political rights they use so much, remind every citizen in a thousand ways that he lives in society. At every moment they impress on his mind the idea that it is the duty of men, as well as their interest, to make themselves useful to their fellow creatures. And since he sees no particular ground for hostility toward them, being never either their master or their slave, his heart readily leans toward kindness. Men attend to the interests of the public first out of necessity and afterward by choice. What was deliberate becomes instinct, and by working for the good of one’s fellow citizens one finally acquires the habit and the taste for serving them.

Many people in France consider equality of conditions as one evil and political freedom as a second. When they are forced to yield to the former, they try at least to escape the latter. But I maintain that to combat the evils that equality may produce, there is only one effective remedy, namely political freedom.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Of The Use Which The Americans Make Of Public Associations In Civil Life
paragraphs: I do not intend to speak of those political associations by which men try to defend themselves against the despotic influence of a majority or against the aggressions of royal power. I have already treated that subject. Each citizen becomes more feeble as an individual, and so less able to preserve his freedom single-handed. If he did not learn, as this happens, to combine with his fellow citizens to defend it, it is clear that tyranny would inevitably grow together with equality.

Here I speak only of those associations that are formed in civil life without reference to political objects. The political associations that exist in the United States are only a single feature amid the immense number of associations in that country. Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds: religious, moral, serious, trivial, large or small, enormous or tiny. The Americans form associations to give entertainments, to found educational institutions, to build inns, to construct churches, to spread books, and to send missionaries to the antipodes. In this way they found hospitals, prisons, and schools. If the aim is to promote some truth or to encourage some feeling by the support of a great example, they form a society. Wherever you see the government in France, or a man of rank in England, at the head of some new undertaking, in the United States you will be sure to find an association. I met with several kinds of associations in America of which, I confess, I had no previous idea. I have often admired the extreme skill with which the inhabitants of the United States manage to set a common goal before the efforts of a great many men and to get them to pursue it voluntarily. I have since traveled through England, from which the Americans took some of their laws and many of their customs, and it seemed to me that the principle of association was by no means used so constantly or so skillfully there. The English often accomplish great things alone, whereas the Americans form associations for the smallest undertakings. It is clear that the English consider association a powerful means of action, but the Americans seem to regard it as the only means they have of acting.

Thus the most democratic country on earth is the one where, in our time, men have carried to the highest perfection the art of pursuing in common the object of their common desires, and have applied this new science to the greatest number of purposes. Is this the result of chance? Or is there in reality a necessary connection between the principle of association and the principle of equality? Aristocratic communities always contain, among a multitude of people who are powerless by themselves, a small number of powerful and wealthy citizens, each of whom can carry out great undertakings single-handed. In aristocratic societies men do not need to combine in order to act, because they are strongly held together. Every wealthy and powerful citizen is the head of a permanent and compulsory association, made up of all those who depend on him or whom he makes serve his designs. Among democratic nations, on the contrary, all citizens are independent and feeble. They can do hardly anything by themselves, and none of them can oblige his fellow men to lend him their help. They all therefore fall into a state of incapacity if they do not learn to help each other voluntarily. If men living in democratic countries had no right and no inclination to associate for political purposes, their independence would be in great danger. But they might long preserve their wealth and their cultivation; whereas if they never acquired the habit of forming associations in ordinary life, civilization itself would be endangered. A people in which individuals lost the power to achieve great things single-handed, without gaining the means of producing them by united effort, would soon fall back into barbarism.

Unfortunately, the same social condition that makes associations so necessary to democratic nations also makes them harder to form among those nations than among any others. When several members of an aristocracy agree to combine, they easily succeed. Each of them brings great strength to the partnership, so the number of its members may be very small. And when the members of an association are few, they can easily get to know one another, understand one another, and set fixed rules. The same opportunities do not arise among democratic nations, where the members of an association must always be very numerous for it to have any power.

I am aware that many of my countrymen are not in the least troubled by this difficulty. They argue that the more feeble and incapable the citizens become, the more capable and active the government should be made, so that society at large may do what individuals can no longer do. They believe this answers the whole difficulty, but I think they are mistaken. A government might take the place of some of the largest American companies, and several States of the Union have already attempted it. But what political power could ever carry on the vast multitude of smaller undertakings that American citizens carry out every day with the help of the principle of association? It is easy to foresee that the time is drawing near when man will be less and less able to produce, by himself alone, the commonest necessities of life. The task of the governing power will therefore keep increasing, and its very efforts will extend it every day. The more it takes the place of associations, the more individuals will lose the idea of combining and will need its assistance. These are causes and effects that endlessly produce each other. Will the administration of the country eventually take over the management of all the manufacturing concerns that no single citizen is able to run? And if a time finally comes when, because landed property has been divided up so extremely, the soil is split into an infinite number of parcels and can be cultivated only by companies of farmers, will the head of the government have to leave the helm of state to follow the plow? The morals and the intelligence of a democratic people would be as much endangered as its business and manufactures if the government ever wholly took the place of private companies.

Feelings and opinions are renewed, the heart is enlarged, and the human mind is developed by no other means than the reciprocal influence of men upon each other. I have shown that these influences are almost nonexistent in democratic countries. They must therefore be created artificially, and this can be done only by associations.

When the members of an aristocratic community adopt a new opinion or conceive a new feeling, they give it a place, as it were, beside themselves on the lofty platform where they stand. Opinions or feelings so conspicuous to the eyes of the multitude are easily introduced into the minds or hearts of everyone around. In democratic countries the governing power alone is naturally in a position to act in this way. But it is easy to see that its action is always inadequate and often dangerous. A government is no more able to keep opinions and feelings alive and in circulation among a great people than to manage all the speculations of productive industry. As soon as a government tries to go beyond its political sphere and enter on this new path, it exercises, even unintentionally, an intolerable tyranny. A government can only dictate strict rules, the opinions it favors are rigidly enforced, and it is never easy to tell its advice from its commands. The case will be worse still if the government really believes it has an interest in preventing all circulation of ideas. It will then stand motionless, weighed down by the heaviness of voluntary torpor. Governments therefore should not be the only active powers. In democratic nations, associations ought to take the place of those powerful private individuals whom the equality of conditions has swept away.

As soon as several inhabitants of the United States have taken up an opinion or a feeling that they wish to promote in the world, they look for mutual assistance. As soon as they have found each other, they combine. From that moment they are no longer isolated men but a power seen from afar, whose actions serve as an example and whose words are listened to. The first time I heard in the United States that 100,000 men had publicly bound themselves to abstain from spirituous liquors, it seemed to me more like a joke than a serious commitment. I did not at first see why these temperate citizens could not content themselves with drinking water by their own firesides. At last I understood that 300,000 Americans, alarmed by the spread of drunkenness around them, had made up their minds to support temperance. They acted just like a man of high rank who dresses very plainly in order to inspire the humbler classes with a contempt for luxury. It is probable that if these 100,000 men had lived in France, each of them would have petitioned the government individually to keep watch over the public houses all over the kingdom.

Nothing, in my opinion, deserves our attention more than the intellectual and moral associations of America. The political and industrial associations of that country strike us forcibly. But the others escape our notice, or if we do discover them, we understand them imperfectly, because we have hardly ever seen anything like them. It must be acknowledged, however, that they are as necessary to the American people as the former, and perhaps more so. In democratic countries the science of association is the mother of science. The progress of all the rest depends on the progress it has made. Among the laws that govern human societies, there is one that seems more precise and clear than all the others. If men are to remain civilized, or to become so, the art of associating together must grow and improve in the same proportion as the equality of conditions increases.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Of The Relation Between Public Associations And Newspapers
paragraphs: When people are no longer joined to one another by firm and lasting ties, you cannot win the cooperation of any great number of them unless you can persuade each person whose help you need that his own private interest obliges him to unite his efforts voluntarily with the efforts of all the rest. This can be done regularly and conveniently only through a newspaper. Nothing but a newspaper can drop the same thought into a thousand minds at the same moment. A newspaper is an adviser who does not have to be sought out. It comes of its own accord and talks with you briefly every day about the common good, without drawing you away from your private affairs.

Newspapers therefore become more necessary as people become more equal and individualism becomes more to be feared. To suppose that they serve only to protect freedom would be to underrate them: they sustain civilization. I do not deny that in democratic countries newspapers often lead citizens to launch ill-considered schemes together. But without newspapers there would be no common action at all. The harm they do is therefore much smaller than the harm they cure.

A newspaper does more than suggest the same purpose to a great number of people. It also supplies the means for carrying out together the plans that each of them may have conceived alone. In an aristocratic country, the leading citizens can see one another from far off, and when they want to join forces, they move toward each other and draw a crowd after them. In democratic countries, on the contrary, it often happens that a great number of people who wish or need to combine cannot do so. Each of them is very insignificant and lost in the crowd, so they cannot see one another and do not know where to find one another. A newspaper then takes up the idea or the feeling that had occurred to each of them at the same moment, but separately. All of them are immediately drawn toward this beacon, and these wandering minds, which had long searched for each other in the dark, meet at last and unite.

The newspaper brought them together, and the newspaper is still necessary to keep them united. For an association among a democratic people to have any power, it must be a numerous body. The people who make it up are therefore scattered over a wide area, and each of them is kept in his own home by the narrowness of his income or by the small, unceasing efforts with which he earns it. A way must then be found for them to talk every day without seeing one another, and to take common action without having met. Hardly any democratic association can do without newspapers. There is therefore a necessary connection between public associations and newspapers: newspapers make associations, and associations make newspapers. It has been correctly said that associations will grow in number as the conditions of men become more equal. It is no less certain that the number of newspapers grows in proportion to the number of associations. That is why in America we find at the same time the greatest number of associations and of newspapers.

This connection between the number of newspapers and the number of associations leads us to discover a further connection, between the state of the periodical press and the form of administration in a country. It shows that the number of newspapers must fall or rise among a democratic people according to how centralized or uncentralized its administration is. For among democratic nations, local powers cannot be entrusted to the leading members of the community, as they are in aristocracies. Those powers must either be abolished or placed in the hands of very large numbers of men. These men then form, in effect, an association permanently established by law to administer the affairs of a certain stretch of territory. They need a journal to bring them some news every day, in the midst of their own small concerns, about the state of their public affairs. The more numerous the local powers are, the greater the number of men in whom the law vests them. And since this need is felt every hour, the more abundantly newspapers multiply.

The extraordinary subdivision of administrative power has much more to do with the enormous number of American newspapers than the country’s great political freedom or the absolute liberty of its press. Suppose all the inhabitants of the Union had the vote, but a vote that extended only to choosing their legislators in Congress. They would need few newspapers, because they would have to act together only on a few very important but very rare occasions. But within the broad association of the nation, the law has established lesser associations in every county, every city, and indeed every village, for the purposes of local administration. The laws of the country thus compel every American to cooperate every day of his life with some of his fellow citizens for a common purpose, and each of them needs a newspaper to tell him what all the others are doing.

I am of the opinion that a democratic people *a without any national representative assemblies, but with a great number of small local powers, would in the end have more newspapers than another people governed by a centralized administration and an elected legislature. What best explains to me the enormous circulation of the daily press in the United States is that among the Americans I find the greatest national freedom combined with local freedom of every kind. There is a prevailing opinion in France and England that the circulation of newspapers would increase indefinitely if the taxes laid on the press were removed. This greatly exaggerates the effects of such a reform. Newspapers increase in number not according to how cheap they are, but according to how often a great number of people feel the need to communicate and combine.

[Footnote a: I say a democratic people. The administration of an aristocratic people may be the reverse of centralized, and yet the need for newspapers may be little felt, because local powers are then placed in the hands of a very small number of men. These men either act separately, or they know each other and can easily meet and come to an understanding.]

In the same way, I would attribute the growing influence of the daily press to causes more general than those usually given. A newspaper can survive only on the condition that it publishes feelings or principles shared by a large number of people. A newspaper therefore always represents an association made up of its regular readers. This association may be more or less defined, more or less restricted, more or less numerous. But the very fact that the newspaper stays alive proves that at least the seed of such an association exists in the minds of its readers.

This leads me to one last reflection, with which I shall end this chapter. The more equal the conditions of men become, and the weaker men are as individuals, the more easily they give way to the current of the multitude, and the harder it is for them to hold on alone to an opinion the multitude has abandoned. A newspaper represents an association. It may be said to speak to each of its readers in the name of all the others, and to influence them in proportion to their individual weakness. The power of the newspaper press must therefore increase as the social conditions of men become more equal.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Connection Of Civil And Political Associations
paragraphs: There is only one country on earth where citizens enjoy unlimited freedom of association for political purposes. This same country is the only one in the world where the constant exercise of the right of association has been carried into civil life, and where all the advantages that civilization can offer are obtained through it. In every country where political associations are forbidden, civil associations are rare. It is hardly likely that this is an accident. We should rather infer that there is a natural, and perhaps a necessary, connection between these two kinds of associations. Certain men happen to share an interest in some matter. Either a commercial undertaking is to be managed, or some manufacturing venture is to be tried. They meet and combine, and in this way they gradually become familiar with the principle of association. The more numerous the small affairs are, the more men acquire, without even knowing it, the skill to carry out great undertakings together. Civil associations therefore make political association easier. But political association, on the other hand, remarkably strengthens and improves associations for civil purposes. In civil life every man may, strictly speaking, imagine that he can provide for his own needs. In politics he can imagine nothing of the kind. When a people has any knowledge of public life, then, the idea of association and the wish to unite occur every day to the whole community. Whatever natural reluctance may keep men from acting together, they will always be ready to combine for the sake of a party. Political life thus makes the love and practice of association more general. It gives a desire for union, and teaches the means of combining, to numbers of men who would otherwise have lived apart all their lives.

Politics gives birth not only to numerous associations but to associations on a large scale. In civil life it seldom happens that any single interest draws a very large number of men to act together, and much skill is needed to bring such an interest into being. In politics, however, opportunities arise every day. Now it is only in great associations that the general value of the principle of association shows itself. Citizens who are individually powerless do not clearly foresee the strength they could gain by uniting. It must be shown to them before they can understand it. Hence it is often easier to gather a multitude for a public purpose than a few people. A thousand citizens do not see what interest they have in combining, but ten thousand will see it perfectly well. In politics men combine for great undertakings, and the use they make of the principle of association in important affairs teaches them in practice that it is in their interest to help each other in smaller ones. A political association draws a number of individuals out of their own circle all at once. However much age, mind, and fortune may naturally keep them apart, it brings them closer together and puts them in contact. Once they have met, they can always meet again.

Men can enter few civil partnerships without risking part of their possessions. This is the case with all manufacturing and trading companies. When men are still little practiced in the art of association and do not know its main rules, they are afraid, the first time they combine in this way, of paying dearly for their experience. They therefore prefer to do without a powerful instrument of success rather than run the risks that come with using it. They are less reluctant, however, to join political associations, which seem to them free of danger because they risk no money in them. But they cannot belong to these associations for long without discovering how order is kept among a large number of men, and by what means they are made to advance toward the same object in a harmonious and methodical way. In this way they learn to surrender their own will to the will of all the rest, and to make their own efforts subordinate to the common impulse. These things are just as necessary to know in civil associations as in political ones. Political associations may therefore be seen as large free schools, where all the members of the community go to learn the general theory of association.

But even if political association did not directly contribute to the progress of civil association, destroying the former would still damage the latter. When citizens may meet in public only for certain purposes, they regard such meetings as a strange proceeding that rarely happens, and they hardly think about it at all. When they are allowed to meet freely for every purpose, they come to look on public association as the universal means, and in a way the only means, that men can use to accomplish the various purposes they have in view. Every new need immediately brings the idea back to mind. The art of association then becomes, as I have said before, the mother of action, studied and applied by all.

When some kinds of associations are prohibited and others allowed, it is hard to tell the first from the second in advance. In this state of doubt men avoid associations altogether, and a kind of public opinion takes hold that tends to make any association whatever seem a bold and almost illegal enterprise. *a

[Footnote a: This is especially true when the executive government has discretionary power to allow or prohibit associations. When certain associations are simply prohibited by law, and the courts of justice have to punish violations of that law, the harm is far less considerable. Every citizen then knows fairly well beforehand what to expect. He judges himself before the law judges him, and, avoiding the prohibited associations, he joins those the law permits. It is by such restrictions that all free nations have always admitted that the right of association might be limited. But suppose the legislature were to give a man the power to decide beforehand which associations are dangerous and which are useful, and to authorize him either to destroy all associations in the bud or to allow them to form. Since nobody could foresee in what cases associations might be established and in what cases they would be put down, the spirit of association would be entirely paralyzed. The first of these laws would attack only certain associations; the second would apply to society itself and do it harm. I can conceive that a regular government may resort to the first, but I do not grant that any government has the right to enact the second.]

It is therefore an unrealistic fantasy to suppose that the spirit of association, when it is suppressed on one point, will still show the same vigor on all others. It is just as unrealistic to suppose that if men are allowed to pursue certain undertakings in common, that is enough to make them take them up eagerly. When the members of a community are allowed and accustomed to combine for all purposes, they will combine as readily for the smaller ones as for the more important. But if they are allowed to combine only for small affairs, they will be neither inclined nor able to do it. It is in vain that you leave them entirely free to carry on their business as joint-stock companies. They will hardly care to use the rights you have granted them. And after you have exhausted your strength in vain efforts to put down the prohibited associations, you will be surprised that you cannot persuade men to form the associations you encourage.

I do not say that there can be no civil associations in a country where political association is prohibited, for men can never live in society without engaging in some common undertakings. But I maintain that in such a country civil associations will always be few in number, feebly planned, and unskillfully managed. They will never form any vast designs, or they will fail in carrying them out.

This naturally leads me to think that freedom of association in political matters is not as dangerous to public tranquility as is supposed. It may even be that, after stirring up society for some time, it strengthens the state in the end. In democratic countries, political associations are, so to speak, the only powerful persons who aspire to rule the state. The governments of our time accordingly look on such associations as the sovereigns of the Middle Ages looked on the great vassals of the crown. They feel a kind of instinctive abhorrence of them and combat them on every occasion. They feel, on the contrary, a natural goodwill toward civil associations, because they readily see that these institutions, instead of directing the minds of the community toward public affairs, divert them from such reflections. By engaging men more and more in the pursuit of objects that cannot be attained without public tranquility, civil associations deter them from revolutions. But these governments overlook the fact that political associations tend amazingly to multiply and ease those of a civil character, and that in avoiding a dangerous evil they deprive themselves of an effective remedy.

When you see the Americans freely and constantly forming associations to promote some political principle, to raise one man to the head of affairs, or to take power away from another, you have some difficulty understanding why men so independent do not constantly fall into the abuse of freedom. If, on the other hand, you look at the endless number of trading companies operating in the United States, and see that the Americans are everywhere unceasingly engaged in carrying out important and difficult plans, which the slightest revolution would throw into confusion, you will readily understand why people so well occupied are not at all tempted to disturb the state or to destroy the public tranquility from which they all profit.

Is it enough to observe these things separately? Should we not discover the hidden tie that connects them? In their political associations, Americans of all conditions, minds, and ages acquire every day a general taste for association and grow accustomed to using it. There they meet in large numbers, they talk, they listen to each other, and they spur one another on to all sorts of undertakings. Afterward they carry the ideas they have acquired in this way into civil life and put them to a thousand uses. Thus it is by enjoying a dangerous freedom that the Americans learn the art of making the dangers of freedom less formidable.

If we pick a certain moment in the life of a nation, it is easy to prove that political associations disturb the state and paralyze productive industry. But take the whole life of a people, and it may perhaps be easy to show that freedom of association in political matters is favorable to the prosperity, and even to the tranquility, of the community.

I said in the earlier part of this work, “The unrestrained liberty of political association cannot be entirely assimilated to the liberty of the press. The one is at the same time less necessary and more dangerous than the other. A nation may confine it within certain limits without ceasing to be mistress of itself; and it may sometimes be obliged to do so in order to maintain its own authority.” And further on I added: “It cannot be denied that the unrestrained liberty of association for political purposes is the last degree of liberty which a people is fit for. If it does not throw them into anarchy, it perpetually brings them, as it were, to the verge of it.” So I do not think that a nation is always free to give its citizens an absolute right of association for political purposes. I doubt whether in any country or in any age it would be wise to set no limits to freedom of association. It is said that a certain nation could not keep the community tranquil, make the laws respected, or establish a lasting government unless the right of association were confined within narrow limits.
