These benefits are undoubtedly invaluable. I can imagine that, to gain or keep them, a nation may impose severe temporary restrictions on itself. Still, it is good for the nation to know at what price these benefits are bought. I can understand that it may be advisable to cut off a man’s arm to save his life. But it would be ridiculous to claim that he will be as dexterous as he was before he lost it.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — The Americans Combat Individualism By The Principle Of Interest Rightly Understood
paragraphs: Self-Interest Properly Understood

When the world was managed by a few rich and powerful individuals, these people liked to hold a lofty idea of the duties of man. They were fond of declaring that it is praiseworthy to forget oneself, and that good should be done without hope of reward, as God himself does it. Such were the standard moral opinions of that time. I doubt whether men were more virtuous in aristocratic ages than in others. But they talked ceaselessly about the beauty of virtue, and they studied its usefulness only in private. But now that the imagination takes less lofty flights and every man’s thoughts are centered on himself, moralists are alarmed by this idea of self-sacrifice, and they no longer dare to offer it to the human mind. They therefore content themselves with asking whether the personal advantage of each member of the community does not lie in working for the good of all. When they hit on some point where private interest and public interest meet and merge, they are eager to bring it to notice. Observations of this kind gradually multiply. What was only a single remark becomes a general principle, and it is held to be true that man serves himself in serving his fellow creatures, and that his private interest is to do good.

I have already shown, in several parts of this work, by what means the inhabitants of the United States almost always manage to combine their own advantage with that of their fellow citizens. My purpose now is to point out the general rule that enables them to do so. In the United States hardly anybody talks of the beauty of virtue, but they maintain that virtue is useful, and they prove it every day. American moralists do not claim that men ought to sacrifice themselves for their fellow creatures because it is noble to make such sacrifices. They boldly declare that such sacrifices are as necessary to the person who makes them as to the person for whose sake they are made. They have found that in their country and their age man is driven back upon himself by an irresistible force. They have lost all hope of stopping that force, so they turn all their thought to directing it. They therefore do not deny that every man may follow his own interest, but they try to prove that it is in the interest of every man to be virtuous. I shall not go into the reasons they give here, which would take me away from my subject. It is enough to say that they have convinced their fellow countrymen.

Montaigne said long ago: “Were I not to follow the straight road for its straightness, I should follow it for having found by experience that in the end it is commonly the happiest and most useful track.” The doctrine of self-interest properly understood is therefore not new. But among the Americans of our time it is universally accepted. It has become popular there. You can trace it at the bottom of all their actions, and you will notice it in everything they say. It is as often heard on the lips of the poor man as of the rich. In Europe the principle of interest is much cruder than it is in America, but at the same time it is less common, and above all it is less openly avowed. Among us, men still constantly pretend to a great self-denial that they no longer feel. The Americans, on the contrary, are fond of explaining almost every action of their lives by the principle of self-interest properly understood. They show with satisfaction how an enlightened regard for themselves constantly prompts them to help each other, and inclines them to sacrifice willingly a portion of their time and property to the welfare of the state. In this respect I think they often fail to do themselves justice. In the United States, as elsewhere, people are sometimes seen to yield to the disinterested and spontaneous impulses that are natural to man. But the Americans seldom admit that they give way to emotions of this kind. They are more anxious to do honor to their philosophy than to themselves.

I might stop here, without trying to pass judgment on what I have described. The extreme difficulty of the subject would be my excuse, but I shall not use it. I would rather have my readers, once they see my aim clearly, refuse to follow me than leave them in suspense. The principle of self-interest properly understood is not a lofty one, but it is clear and sure. It does not aim at mighty objects, but it reaches, without excessive effort, all those at which it does aim. Since it lies within the reach of all minds, everyone can grasp and remember it without difficulty. It fits human weaknesses admirably, and so it easily gains great dominion. Nor is that dominion precarious, since the principle checks one personal interest with another and uses, to direct the passions, the very same instrument that excites them. The principle of self-interest properly understood produces no great acts of self-sacrifice, but it suggests small acts of self-denial every day. By itself it cannot make a man virtuous. But it trains a number of citizens in habits of regularity, temperance, moderation, foresight, and self-command. If it does not lead men straight to virtue by the will, it gradually draws them in that direction by their habits. If the principle of self-interest properly understood were to sway the whole moral world, extraordinary virtues would doubtless be rarer. But I think gross depravity would then be less common too. The principle perhaps keeps some men from rising far above the level of mankind. But a great number of other men, who were falling far below it, are caught and held back by it. Look at a few individuals, and they are lowered by it. Look at mankind as a whole, and it is raised. I am not afraid to say that the principle of self-interest properly understood seems to me the best suited of all philosophical theories to the needs of the men of our time, and that I regard it as their chief remaining protection against themselves. The minds of the moralists of our age should therefore turn toward it. Even if they judge it incomplete, they must still adopt it as necessary.

On the whole I do not think there is more egotism among us than in America. The only difference is that there it is enlightened and here it is not. Every American will sacrifice a portion of his private interests to preserve the rest. We would like to preserve the whole, and often the whole is lost. Everybody I see around me seems bent on teaching his contemporaries, by precept and example, that what is useful is never wrong. Will nobody undertake to make them understand how what is right may be useful? No power on earth can prevent the growing equality of conditions from inclining the human mind to seek out what is useful, or from leading every member of the community to be wrapped up in himself. We must therefore expect that personal interest will become more than ever the principal, if not the sole, spring of men’s actions. But it remains to be seen how each man will understand his personal interest. Suppose the members of a community, as they become more equal, also become more ignorant and coarse. Then it is hard to foresee to what pitch of stupid excess their egotism may lead them, and no one can foretell into what disgrace and wretchedness they would plunge themselves rather than sacrifice something of their own well-being to the prosperity of their fellow creatures. I do not think that the system of interest, as it is professed in America, is self-evident in all its parts. But it contains a great number of truths so evident that men, if only they are educated, cannot fail to see them. Educate them, then, at any rate. The age of unquestioning self-sacrifice and instinctive virtues is already drifting far away from us, and the time is fast approaching when freedom, public peace, and social order itself will not be able to exist without education.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — That The Americans Apply The Principle Of Interest Rightly Understood To Religious Matters
paragraphs: Understood to Religious Matters

If the principle of self-interest properly understood had only the present world in view, it would be very inadequate. There are many sacrifices that can find their reward only in another world. And however much ingenuity is spent on demonstrating the usefulness of virtue, it will never be easy to make a man live rightly if he gives no thought to dying. It is therefore necessary to find out whether the principle of self-interest properly understood is easily compatible with religious belief. The philosophers who teach this system of morals tell men that, to be happy in this life, they must watch their own passions and steadily control their excess. They say that lasting happiness can be secured only by giving up a thousand passing pleasures, and that a man must triumph over himself continually in order to secure his own advantage. The founders of almost all religions have said the same. The path they point out to man is the same, except that the goal is more remote. Instead of placing the reward for the sacrifices they impose in this world, they move it to another. Nevertheless, I cannot believe that all who practice virtue from religious motives are driven only by the hope of a reward. I have known zealous Christians who constantly forgot themselves in order to work with greater ardor for the happiness of their fellow men, and I have heard them declare that all they did was only to earn the blessings of a future state. I cannot help thinking that they deceive themselves. I respect them too much to believe them.

Christianity does teach that a man must prefer his neighbor to himself in order to gain eternal life. But Christianity also teaches that men ought to benefit their fellow creatures for the love of God. A sublime expression! Man searches with his intellect into the divine conception and sees that order is the purpose of God. He freely joins in carrying out the great design, and while he sacrifices his personal interests to this consummate order of all created things, he expects no other reward than the pleasure of contemplating it. I do not believe that interest is the sole motive of religious men. But I believe that interest is the principal means that religions themselves use to govern men, and I do not doubt that this is how they reach the multitude and become popular. It is not easy to see clearly why the principle of self-interest properly understood should keep away from religious opinions. It seems to me easier to show why it should draw men to them. Suppose that, in order to gain happiness in this world, a man fights his instincts on every occasion and deliberately calculates every action of his life. Suppose that, instead of yielding blindly to the force of his first desires, he has learned the art of resisting them, and has accustomed himself to sacrifice the pleasure of a moment, without effort, to the lasting interest of his whole life. If such a man believes in the religion he professes, it will cost him little to submit to the restrictions it may impose. Reason itself counsels him to obey, and habit has prepared him to endure them. If he has come to have any doubts about the object of his hopes, he will still not easily let them stop him. He will decide that it is wise to risk some of the advantages of this world in order to keep his claim to the great inheritance promised him in another. “To be mistaken in believing that the Christian religion is true,” says Pascal, “is no great loss to anyone; but how dreadful to be mistaken in believing it to be false!”

The Americans do not affect a brutal indifference to a future state. They affect no childish pride in despising perils that they hope to escape. They therefore profess their religion without shame and without weakness. But there is generally, even in their zeal, something so indescribably calm, methodical, and deliberate that it seems as if the head, far more than the heart, brought them to the foot of the altar. The Americans not only follow their religion from interest, but they often place in this world the interest that makes them follow it. In the Middle Ages the clergy spoke of nothing but a future state. They hardly cared to prove that a sincere Christian may be a happy man here below. American preachers, however, are constantly referring to the earth, and it is only with great difficulty that they can turn their attention away from it. To move their congregations, they always show how favorable religious opinions are to freedom and public tranquility. And it is often difficult to tell from their sermons whether the principal object of religion is to win eternal happiness in the other world or prosperity in this one.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — Of The Taste For Physical Well-Being In America
paragraphs: In America the passion for physical well-being is not always exclusive, but it is general. Not everyone feels it in the same way, yet everyone feels it. Carefully satisfying every need of the body, even the smallest, and providing the little conveniences of life is the first thing on everyone’s mind. Something similar is more and more visible in Europe. Several of the causes that produce these like results in both hemispheres are so closely tied to my subject that they deserve notice.

When wealth is fixed in families by inheritance, a great many people enjoy the comforts of life without developing an exclusive taste for them. The human heart is not so much captured by calmly possessing something valuable as by the desire to have it, while that desire is still only partly satisfied, and by the unceasing fear of losing it. In aristocratic communities the wealthy have never known any condition other than their own, so they have no fear of changing it; the very idea of such a change hardly occurs to them. For them the comforts of life are not the goal of life but simply a way of living. They regard those comforts as existence itself, something enjoyed but scarcely thought about. The natural, instinctive taste that all men feel for being well off is thus satisfied without effort and without worry, and so their faculties turn elsewhere and attach themselves to harder and loftier undertakings, which stir and absorb their minds. That is why the members of an aristocracy, in the midst of physical gratifications, often show a haughty contempt for those very pleasures and an unusual power to endure being deprived of them. Every revolution that has ever shaken or destroyed an aristocracy has shown how easily men used to superfluous luxuries can do without the necessities of life. Men who have labored to earn a modest competence, by contrast, can hardly go on living once they have lost it.

If I turn my attention from the upper to the lower classes, I find similar effects produced by opposite causes. In a nation where aristocracy dominates society and keeps it from changing, the people in the end become as used to poverty as the rich are to their opulence. The rich give no anxious thought to their physical comforts, because they enjoy them without effort. The poor do not think about things they despair of ever getting and know too little about even to desire. In communities of this kind, the imagination of the poor is driven to seek another world. The miseries of real life hem it in, but it slips out of their grip and flies off to find its pleasures far beyond. When, on the contrary, distinctions of rank are blurred and privileges destroyed, when hereditary property is divided up and education and freedom are widely spread, the desire to acquire the comforts of this world haunts the imagination of the poor, and the fear of losing them haunts the imagination of the rich. Many small fortunes spring up. Those who hold them have enough physical gratification to acquire a taste for these pleasures, but not enough to satisfy it. They never get these pleasures without effort, and they never indulge in them without anxiety. They are therefore always straining to pursue or to hold on to gratifications that are so delightful, so imperfect and so fleeting.

Suppose I ask what passion comes most naturally to men who are both spurred on and hemmed in by humble birth or modest fortune. I could find none more peculiarly suited to their condition than this love of physical prosperity. The passion for physical comforts is essentially a passion of the middle classes. With those classes it grows and spreads, and among them it prevails. From there it rises into the higher ranks of society and descends into the mass of the people. In America I never met a citizen so poor that he did not cast a glance of hope and envy at the pleasures of the rich, or whose imagination did not seize in advance on the good things that fate still stubbornly withheld from him. On the other hand, among the wealthier inhabitants of the United States I never noticed that proud contempt for physical gratifications that is sometimes found even in the richest and most dissolute aristocracies. Most of these wealthy men were once poor. They have felt the sting of want, and they were long at the mercy of adverse fortune. Now that the victory is won, the passions that went with the struggle have outlasted it, and their minds are, as it were, intoxicated by the small enjoyments they have pursued for forty years. It is not that in the United States, as elsewhere, there are no wealthy people who inherited their property and possess, without effort, an opulence they have not earned. But even these men are no less devoted to the pleasures of material life. The love of well-being has now become the dominant taste of the nation. The great current of men’s passions runs in that channel and sweeps everything along with it.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Peculiar Effects Of The Love Of Physical Gratifications In Democratic Ages
paragraphs: From what has just been said, one might suppose that the love of physical gratifications must constantly drive the Americans into moral disorder, disturb the peace of families and threaten the security of society as a whole. That is not the case. In democracies the passion for physical gratifications has very different effects from those it has in aristocratic nations. Sometimes an aristocracy grows weary of public affairs and glutted with wealth. Amid the ruin of religious belief and the decline of the state, its heart may be gradually seduced into pursuing nothing but sensual pleasure. At other times the power of the monarch or the weakness of the people forces the nobility to keep away from the administration of affairs, without taking away their fortunes. With the road to great undertakings closed, they are left to the restlessness of their own desires. They then fall heavily back on themselves and look to bodily pleasures to forget their former greatness. When the members of an aristocratic body devote themselves entirely to physical gratifications in this way, they usually pour into that pursuit all the energy they have drawn from their long experience of power. Such men are not satisfied with the pursuit of comfort. They demand sumptuous depravity and splendid corruption. The worship they offer the senses is a gorgeous one, and they seem to compete with one another in the art of degrading their own natures. The stronger, the more famous and the freer an aristocracy has been, the more depraved it will then become. However brilliantly its virtues may once have shone, I dare predict that the splendor of its vices will always outdo them.

The taste for physical gratifications leads a democratic people into no such excesses. There the love of well-being appears as a tenacious, exclusive and universal passion, but its range is narrow. No one thinks of building enormous palaces, of conquering or imitating nature, or of ransacking the world to satisfy one man’s passions. The aim is rather to add a few roods of land to your field, to plant an orchard, to enlarge a house, to keep making life more comfortable and convenient, to avoid trouble, and to meet the smallest needs without effort and almost without cost. These are small objects, but the soul clings to them. It dwells on them closely, day after day, until at last they shut out the rest of the world and sometimes come between the soul and heaven.

It may be said that this applies only to the members of the community who are in humble circumstances, and that wealthier people will show tastes like those they had in aristocratic ages. I deny this. When it comes to physical gratifications, the richest members of a democracy will not show tastes very different from those of the people. Either they rose from the people and truly share those tastes, or they consider it a duty to conform to them. In democratic society the sensuality of the public has taken a moderate and tranquil course, and everyone is bound to follow it. It is as hard to depart from the common rule through one’s vices as through one’s virtues. Rich men who live in democratic nations are therefore more intent on providing for their smallest wants than on extraordinary pleasures. They gratify a host of petty desires without indulging in any great outbursts of passion. They are thus more likely to become enervated than debauched. The particular taste that men of democratic ages have for physical enjoyments is not by nature opposed to the principles of public order. On the contrary, it often needs order in order to be gratified. Nor is it hostile to regularity of morals, for good morals contribute to public tranquillity and favor industry. It may even often be combined with a kind of religious morality. Men want to be as well off as they can in this world without giving up their chance of another. Some physical gratifications cannot be indulged without crime, and from these they strictly abstain. Others are sanctioned by religion and morality, and to these they give up the heart, the imagination and life itself without reserve. In grasping at these lesser gifts, they lose sight of the more precious possessions that make up the glory and greatness of mankind. The reproach I make against the principle of equality is not that it leads men astray in the pursuit of forbidden pleasures, but that it absorbs them entirely in the pursuit of permitted ones. In this way a kind of virtuous materialism may eventually establish itself in the world. It would not corrupt the soul but enervate it, and would silently loosen the springs of its action.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Causes Of Fanatical Enthusiasm In Some Americans
paragraphs: Although the desire to acquire the good things of this world is the dominant passion of the American people, there are certain brief outbreaks when their souls seem to burst the bonds of matter that hold them and soar impetuously toward heaven. In all the States of the Union, but especially in the half-settled country of the Far West, you meet wandering preachers who peddle the word of God from place to place. Whole families, old men, women and children alike, cross rough passes and untrodden wilds, coming from a great distance to join a camp meeting. There, for several days and nights, they forget entirely the cares of business and even the most pressing needs of the body as they listen to these sermons. Here and there in American society you meet men full of a fanatical and almost wild enthusiasm that hardly exists in Europe. From time to time strange sects arise that try to cut out extraordinary paths to eternal happiness. Religious insanity is very common in the United States.

These facts should not surprise us. It was not man who put into himself the taste for the infinite and the love of the immortal. Those lofty instincts are not the product of his whim. Their firm foundation lies in human nature, and they exist in spite of his efforts. He may thwart and distort them, but he cannot destroy them. The soul has needs that must be satisfied. However much trouble is taken to distract it from itself, it soon grows weary, restless and uneasy amid the pleasures of the senses. If the faculties of the great majority of mankind were ever bent exclusively on material objects, we could expect a tremendous reaction in the souls of some men. They would drift far and wide in the world of spirits, for fear of staying shackled by the tight bondage of the body.

It is not surprising, then, that in a community whose thoughts tend toward the earth, a small number of people should turn their eyes to heaven. I would be surprised if mysticism did not soon make some progress among a people wholly occupied with promoting its own worldly welfare. It is said that the deserts of the Thebaid were peopled by the persecutions of the emperors and the massacres of the Circus. I would rather say that they were peopled by the luxuries of Rome and the Epicurean philosophy of Greece. Suppose the social condition, the present circumstances and the laws of the Americans did not confine their minds so tightly to the pursuit of worldly welfare. Then they would probably show more restraint and more experience whenever their attention turns to immaterial things, and they would check themselves without difficulty. But they feel imprisoned within limits that, it seems, they will never be allowed to cross. As soon as they do cross them, their minds do not know where to settle, and they often rush unrestrained beyond the bounds of common sense.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — Causes Of The Restless Spirit Of Americans In The Midst Of Their Prosperity
paragraphs: In certain remote corners of the Old World you may still stumble on a small district that seems to have been forgotten in the general tumult and to have stood still while everything around it was in motion. The inhabitants are for the most part extremely ignorant and poor. They take no part in the affairs of the country, and the government often oppresses them. Yet their faces are generally calm and their spirits light. In America I saw the freest and best-educated men living in the happiest circumstances the world offers, and it seemed to me that a cloud habitually hung over their brows. I thought them serious and almost sad even in their pleasures. The chief reason for this contrast is that the former do not think about the ills they endure, while the latter are forever brooding over the advantages they lack. It is strange to see the feverish ardor with which the Americans pursue their own welfare, and to watch the vague dread that constantly torments them, the fear that they have not chosen the shortest path to it. A native of the United States clings to this world’s goods as if he were certain never to die. He is so hasty to seize everything within his reach that one would think he constantly feared he would not live long enough to enjoy it. He clutches at everything and holds nothing fast, but soon loosens his grasp to chase fresh gratifications.

In the United States a man builds a house to spend his later years in, and sells it before the roof is on. He plants a garden and rents it out just as the trees are beginning to bear fruit. He brings a field into cultivation and leaves others to gather the crops. He takes up a profession and gives it up. He settles in a place and soon leaves it, to carry his changeable longings elsewhere. If his private affairs leave him any free time, he plunges at once into the whirlpool of politics. And if, at the end of a year of unceasing labor, he finds he has a few days’ vacation, his eager curiosity sweeps him across the vast expanse of the United States, and he will travel fifteen hundred miles in a few days to shake off his happiness. Death finally overtakes him, but it comes before he has tired of his fruitless chase after that complete happiness which is forever on the wing.

At first sight there is something surprising in the strange unrest of so many happy men, restless in the midst of abundance. Yet the sight itself is as old as the world. What is new is to see a whole people provide an example of it. Their taste for physical gratifications must be regarded as the original source of the secret uneasiness that the actions of the Americans betray, and of the inconstancy of which they give fresh examples every day. A man who has set his heart exclusively on the pursuit of worldly welfare is always in a hurry, for he has only a limited time to reach it, to grasp it and to enjoy it. The memory of how short life is spurs him on constantly. Besides the good things he has, he imagines at every moment a thousand others that death will prevent him from trying if he does not try them soon. This thought fills him with anxiety, fear and regret, and keeps his mind in ceaseless agitation, which leads him to change his plans and his home again and again. Suppose that, in addition to the taste for physical well-being, there is a social condition in which laws and customs make no condition permanent. That is a powerful further stimulus to this restless temper. Men will then be seen constantly changing their course, for fear of missing the shortest way to happiness. It is easy to see that men passionately bent on physical gratifications desire eagerly, but are also easily discouraged. Their final aim is to enjoy, so the means of reaching it must be quick and easy, or the trouble of getting the gratification would be greater than the gratification itself. Their usual frame of mind is therefore both ardent and slack, violent and enervated. Death is often less dreaded than persevering in continuous effort toward a single end.

Equality of conditions leads by a still more direct road to several of the effects I have described here. When all privileges of birth and fortune are abolished, when all professions are open to everyone, and a man’s own energy can bring him to the top of any of them, an easy and unlimited career seems to lie open to his ambition. He will readily persuade himself that he is born for no ordinary destiny. But this is a mistaken idea, which daily experience corrects. The same equality that allows every citizen to form these lofty hopes makes all citizens less able to realize them. It limits their powers on every side, while giving their desires freer scope. Not only are they themselves powerless, but at every step they meet immense obstacles that they did not see at first. They have swept away the privileges of some of their fellow creatures that stood in their way, but they have opened the door to universal competition. The barrier has changed its shape rather than its place. When men are nearly alike and all follow the same track, it is very difficult for any one of them to walk fast and force a way through the dense crowd that surrounds and presses on him. This constant struggle between the longings that spring from equality of conditions and the means it supplies to satisfy them harasses and wearies the mind.

It is possible to imagine men who have reached a degree of freedom that would content them completely. They would then enjoy their independence without anxiety and without impatience. But men will never establish an equality with which they can be content. However hard a people may try, it will never succeed in reducing all the conditions of society to a perfect level. Even if they unhappily reached that absolute and complete leveling down, the inequality of minds would still remain. That inequality comes directly from the hand of God and will forever escape the laws of man. However democratic the social state and political constitution of a people may be, then, it is certain that every member of the community will always find several points around him that rise above his own position, and we can foresee that he will keep his eyes doggedly fixed in that direction. When inequality of conditions is the common law of society, the most striking inequalities do not catch the eye. When everything is nearly on the same level, the slightest inequality is noticeable enough to hurt. Hence the desire for equality always becomes more insatiable as equality becomes more complete.

Among democratic nations men easily attain a certain equality of conditions, but they can never attain the equality they desire. It is always drawing back from them, yet without hiding from their sight, and as it draws back it draws them on. At every moment they think they are about to seize it, and at every moment it slips from their hold. They are near enough to see its charms but too far away to enjoy them, and they die before they have fully tasted its delights. To these causes we must attribute the strange melancholy that often haunts the inhabitants of democratic countries in the midst of their abundance, and the disgust with life that sometimes seizes them in calm and easy circumstances. In France people complain that the number of suicides is rising. In America suicide is rare, but insanity is said to be more common than anywhere else. These are all different symptoms of the same disease. The Americans, however uneasy they may be, do not end their lives, because their religion forbids it. Among them materialism may be said hardly to exist, despite the general passion for physical gratification. The will resists, but reason often gives way. In democratic ages pleasures are more intense than in aristocratic ages, and above all the number of those who share in them is larger. But on the other hand, it must be admitted that man’s hopes and desires are more often crushed, the soul is more stricken and disturbed, and care itself is sharper.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — Taste For Physical Gratifications United In America To Love Of Freedom And Attention To Public Affairs
paragraphs: Of Freedom and Attention to Public Affairs

When a democratic state turns into an absolute monarchy, the activity that used to be directed at both public and private affairs is suddenly concentrated on private affairs alone. The immediate result, for a time, is great physical prosperity. But this impulse soon slackens, and the amount of productive industry is held back. I do not know whether a single trading or manufacturing people can be named, from the Tyrians down to the Florentines and the English, that was not also a free people. There is therefore a close bond and a necessary relation between these two elements, freedom and productive industry. This proposition is generally true of all nations, but especially of democratic nations. I have already shown that men who live in ages of equality constantly need to form associations in order to obtain the things they want. I have also shown how greatly political freedom improves and spreads the art of association. In these ages, then, freedom is especially favorable to the production of wealth. It is not hard to see that despotism is especially hostile to the same result. The nature of despotic power in democratic ages is not to be fierce or cruel, but petty and meddling. Despotism of this kind, though it does not trample on humanity, is directly opposed to the spirit of commerce and the pursuits of industry.

So men of democratic ages need to be free in order to get more easily the physical enjoyments they are always longing for. It sometimes happens, however, that the excessive taste they acquire for these same enjoyments hands them over to the first master who appears. The passion for worldly welfare then defeats itself and, without their noticing, pushes the object of their desires farther away.

There is, indeed, a most dangerous passage in the history of a democratic people. Among such a people the taste for physical gratifications may grow faster than education and experience of free institutions. Then the time will come when men are carried away and lose all self-restraint at the sight of the new possessions they are about to seize. In their intense and exclusive anxiety to make a fortune, they lose sight of the close connection between each person’s private fortune and the prosperity of all. It is not necessary to use force against such a people in order to strip them of the rights they enjoy. They willingly loosen their own hold. Carrying out political duties seems to them a troublesome annoyance that distracts them from their occupations and business. If they are required to elect representatives, to support the government by personal service, or to meet on public business, they have no time. They cannot waste their precious time on useless engagements. Such idle pastimes, they feel, are unsuited to serious men busy with the more important interests of life. These people think they are following the principle of self-interest, but their idea of that principle is a very crude one. To look after what they call their business, they neglect their chief business, which is to remain their own masters.

The citizens who work do not care to attend to public business, and the class that might have devoted its leisure to these duties has ceased to exist. The place of government is therefore, as it were, left empty. If at that critical moment some able and ambitious man seizes supreme power, he will find the road to every kind of usurpation open before him. If he looks after the material prosperity of the country for some time, nothing more will be asked of him. Above all, he must guarantee public tranquillity. Men possessed by the passion for physical gratification generally discover that the turmoil of freedom disturbs their well-being before they discover how freedom itself helps to promote it. If the slightest rumor of public commotion intrudes on the petty pleasures of private life, they are roused and alarmed by it. The fear of anarchy haunts them constantly, and they are always ready to throw away their freedom at the first disturbance.

I readily admit that public tranquillity is a great good. But at the same time I cannot forget that all nations have been enslaved by being kept in good order. This does not mean, certainly, that nations should despise public tranquillity. But that condition ought not to be enough for them. A nation that asks nothing of its government except the maintenance of order is already a slave at heart, the slave of its own well-being, waiting only for the hand that will bind it. In such a nation the despotism of a faction is no less to be feared than the despotism of an individual. When the bulk of the community is absorbed in private concerns, the smallest parties need not despair of gaining the upper hand in public affairs. At such times it is not rare to see on the great stage of the world, as we see in our theaters, a multitude represented by a few actors. They alone speak in the name of an absent or inattentive crowd. They alone are in action while everyone else stands still. They regulate everything by their own whim. They change the laws and tyrannize at will over the customs of the country. Then men are astonished to see into how few weak and worthless hands a great people can fall.

Up to now the Americans have fortunately escaped all the dangers I have just pointed out, and in this respect they truly deserve admiration. Perhaps there is no country in the world where fewer idle men are to be found than in America, or where all who work are more eager to promote their own welfare. But if the Americans’ passion for physical gratifications is violent, at least it is not indiscriminate. Reason, though unable to restrain it, still directs its course. An American attends to his private concerns as if he were alone in the world, and the next minute he gives himself up to the common good as if he had forgotten them. At one moment he seems driven by the most selfish greed, at another by the most lively patriotism. The human heart cannot be divided in this way. The inhabitants of the United States show, by turns, so strong and so similar a passion for their own welfare and for their freedom that it may be supposed these passions are united and mingled somewhere in their character. And indeed the Americans believe their freedom to be the best instrument and surest safeguard of their welfare. They are attached to the one because of the other. They by no means think that they are not called on to take part in the public good. On the contrary, they believe that their chief business is to secure for themselves a government that will allow them to acquire the things they want, and will not bar them from the peaceful enjoyment of the possessions they have acquired.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — That Religious Belief Sometimes Turns The Thoughts Of The Americans To Immaterial Pleasures
paragraphs: Americans to Immaterial Pleasures

In the United States, on the seventh day of every week, the nation’s commercial and working life seems to stop. All noise ceases. A deep stillness, or rather the solemn calm of meditation, takes the place of the week’s turmoil, and the soul comes back into possession of itself and reflects on itself. On this day the marketplaces stand empty. Every member of the community goes to church with his children, and there he hears language that seems strange and ill suited to his ears. He is told of the countless evils caused by pride and covetousness. He is reminded that he must restrain his desires, that finer pleasures belong to virtue alone, and that true happiness goes with it. When he returns home, he does not reach for the ledgers of his trade; he opens the book of Holy Scripture. There he finds sublime or moving descriptions of the greatness and goodness of the Creator, of the infinite magnificence of God’s handiwork, of the lofty destiny of man, of his duties, and of his immortal privileges. In this way the American at times steals an hour from himself. Setting aside for a while the petty passions that stir his life and the passing interests that absorb it, he wanders at once into an ideal world where everything is great, eternal, and pure.

In another part of this work I tried to point out the causes to which the maintenance of the Americans’ political institutions is owed, and religion appeared to be one of the most prominent of them. Here I am treating the Americans as individuals, and I observe once more that religion is no less useful to each citizen than to the state as a whole. By their practice the Americans show that they feel keenly how necessary it is to give democratic communities their morality by means of religion. What they think of themselves in this respect is a truth of which every democratic nation ought to be thoroughly convinced.

I do not doubt that a people’s social and political constitution inclines them toward a certain belief and certain tastes, which then flourish among them without difficulty. The same causes may turn a people away from certain opinions and propensities, without any deliberate effort on their part and, as it were, without their being clearly aware of it. The whole art of the legislator lies in discerning these natural inclinations of communities of men in advance, so as to know whether they should be helped or whether it may be necessary to check them. For the legislator’s duties differ from one age to another. Only the goal toward which the human race ought always to be moving stays fixed; the means of reaching it must constantly change.

Had I been born in an aristocratic age, in the midst of a nation where the inherited wealth of some and the hopeless poverty of others alike turn men away from the idea of improving their condition, and hold the soul, as it were, in a torpor fixed on the contemplation of another world, I should then wish to rouse that people to a sense of their needs. I should look for quicker and easier means of satisfying the new desires I had awakened. I should direct the most vigorous efforts of the human mind to physical pursuits, and try to spur it on to promote the well-being of man. If some men were excessively stirred up to chase after riches and showed an immoderate liking for physical gratifications, I should not be alarmed; these particular symptoms would soon be lost in the general character of the people.

The legislators of democracies have other concerns to attend to. Give democratic nations education and freedom, and then leave them alone. They will soon learn to draw from this world every benefit it can offer. They will improve each of the useful arts and make life more comfortable, more convenient, and easier day by day. Their social condition pushes them naturally in this direction, and I do not fear that they will slow down.

But while man takes pleasure in this honest and lawful pursuit of his well-being, there is reason to fear that he may in the end lose the use of his noblest faculties, and that while he is busy improving everything around him, he may at length degrade himself. The danger lies here, and only here. The legislators of democracies, and all the virtuous and educated men who live in them, should therefore make it their constant aim to raise the souls of their fellow citizens and keep them lifted toward heaven. All who care about the future of democratic society must unite, and all must make joint and continual efforts to spread the love of the infinite, a sense of greatness, and a love of pleasures that are not of this earth. If, among the opinions of a democratic people, there are any of those pernicious theories that teach that everything perishes with the body, then let the men who profess such theories be marked out as that people’s natural enemies.

The materialists offend me in many respects. I consider their doctrines pernicious, and their arrogance disgusts me. If their system could be of any use to man, it would seem to be by giving him a modest opinion of himself. But these reasoners show that it does not; and when they think they have said enough to prove that they are brutes, they appear as proud as if they had proved that they are gods. Materialism is a dangerous disease of the human mind among all nations, but it is especially to be feared among a democratic people, because it blends easily with the vice that is most familiar to the heart in those circumstances. Democracy encourages a taste for physical gratification. If this taste becomes excessive, it soon leads men to believe that everything is only matter; and materialism, in turn, hurries them back with mad impatience to those same pleasures. Such is the fatal circle in which democratic nations are driven around. It would be well if they saw the danger and held back.

Most religions are simply general, simple, and practical ways of teaching men the doctrine of the immortality of the soul. That is the greatest benefit a democratic people gets from its belief, and so belief is more necessary to such a people than to any other. Therefore, when a religion has sunk its roots deep into a democracy, take care not to disturb them. Watch over it instead, as the most precious legacy of aristocratic ages. Do not try to replace men’s old religious opinions with new ones, for in passing from one faith to another the soul may be left for a while stripped of all belief, and the love of physical gratifications could then grow in it and fill it entirely.

The doctrine of metempsychosis is certainly no more rational than materialism. Nevertheless, if a democracy absolutely had to choose one of the two, I would not hesitate to say that the community would run less risk of being brutalized by believing that the soul of man will pass into the carcass of a hog than by believing that the soul of man is nothing at all. Belief in a supersensual and immortal principle, joined for a time to matter, is so indispensable to man’s greatness that its effects are striking even when it is not joined to the doctrine of future reward and punishment, and when it holds no more than that, after death, the divine principle in man is absorbed into the Deity or passes into the frame of some other creature to animate it. Men with so imperfect a belief will still regard the body as the secondary and inferior part of their nature. They will despise it even while they yield to its influence. Meanwhile they have a natural respect and secret admiration for the immaterial part of man, even though they sometimes refuse to submit to its rule. That is enough to give a lofty cast to their opinions and tastes, and to make them tend, without any self-interested motive and almost by impulse, toward pure feelings and elevated thoughts.

It is not certain that Socrates and his followers held very fixed opinions about what would happen to man in the hereafter. But the one point of belief on which they were resolved — that the soul has nothing in common with the body and outlives it — was enough to give Platonic philosophy the sublime aspiration that distinguishes it. Plato’s works make clear that many philosophical writers, his predecessors or contemporaries, professed materialism. Their writings have not come down to us, or have reached us only in fragments. The same has happened in almost every age: the greater part of the most famous minds in literature adhere to the doctrines of a supersensual philosophy. The instinct and taste of the human race sustain those doctrines. They often save them in spite of men themselves, and raise the names of their defenders above the tide of time. It must not be supposed, then, that at any period or under any political condition, the passion for physical gratifications, and the opinions that this passion brings in its train, can ever satisfy a whole people. The heart of man is cast on a larger mold. It can hold at once a taste for the possessions of earth and a love of those of heaven. At times it may seem to cling devotedly to one, but it will never go long without thinking of the other.

It is easy to see that spiritual opinions are especially important in democratic ages, but it is not easy to say by what means those who govern democratic nations can make them prevail. I do not believe in the prosperity of official philosophies, any more than in their durability. As for state religions, I have always held that, although they may sometimes serve the interests of political power for a moment, they always become fatal to the Church sooner or later. Nor do I agree with those who maintain that, to raise religion in the eyes of the people and make them honor its spiritual doctrines, it is desirable to give her ministers, indirectly, a political influence that the laws deny them. I am so keenly aware of the almost inevitable dangers that threaten religious belief whenever the clergy take part in public affairs, and so convinced that Christianity must be maintained at any cost in the midst of modern democracies, that I would rather confine the priesthood within the sanctuary than let them step beyond it.

What means, then, remain in the hands of the constituted authorities to bring men back to spiritual opinions, or to hold them fast to the religion that suggests those opinions? My answer will damage me in the eyes of politicians. I believe the only effective means that governments can use to have the doctrine of the immortality of the soul properly respected is always to act as if they believed it themselves. And I think that only by strict conformity to religious morality in great affairs can they hope to teach the community at large to know it, to love it, and to observe it in the smaller concerns of life.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — That Excessive Care Of Worldly Welfare May Impair That Welfare
paragraphs: The improvement of the soul and the betterment of what belongs to the body are more closely tied together than people commonly suppose. Man may set the two apart and consider each in turn, but he cannot separate them entirely without finally losing sight of both. The beasts have the same senses we have and very nearly the same appetites. We have no sensual passions that our species does not share with them, or that cannot be found, at least in germ, in a dog as well as in a man. Why is it, then, that animals can provide only for their first and lowest wants, while we can vary our enjoyments without limit and increase them endlessly?

We are superior to the beasts in this: we use our souls to find the material benefits to which they are led only by instinct. In man, the angel teaches the brute the art of satisfying its desires. Because man can rise above the things of the body, and can even hold life in contempt — of which the beasts have not the least notion — he is able to multiply those same bodily things to a degree that lower creatures cannot conceive either. Whatever lifts, enlarges, and expands the soul makes it better able to succeed even in undertakings that do not concern it. Whatever, on the other hand, saps or lowers it weakens it for every purpose, the greatest as well as the least, and threatens to make it almost equally powerless for both. The soul must therefore remain great and strong, if only so that it can devote that strength and greatness from time to time to the service of the body. If men were ever to content themselves with material objects, they would probably lose by degrees the art of producing them, and in the end they would enjoy them like the brutes, without discernment and without improvement.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — That In Times Marked By Equality Of Conditions And Sceptical Opinions, It Is Important To Remove To A Distance The Objects Of Human Actions
paragraphs: Skeptical Opinions, It Is Important to Remove to a Distance the Objects of Human Actions

In ages of faith, the final end of life is placed beyond life. People of those ages therefore naturally, and almost without intending it, grow used to fixing their gaze for many years on some unchanging object toward which they constantly move. They learn, by imperceptible degrees, to suppress a multitude of petty passing desires so as to be better able to satisfy the great and lasting desire that possesses them. When these same men engage in the affairs of this world, the same habits show in their conduct. They tend to set some general and definite aim for their actions here below, and all their efforts are directed toward it. They do not run from day to day after some new object of desire; they have settled designs that they never tire of pursuing. This explains why religious nations have so often achieved such lasting results. While they were thinking only of the other world, they discovered the great secret of success in this one. Religions give men a general habit of conducting themselves with the future in view. In this respect they are no less useful to happiness in this life than to felicity hereafter, and this is one of their chief political characteristics.

But as the light of faith dims, the range of man’s vision shrinks, as though the end and aim of human actions seemed to come within his reach more every day. Once men have allowed themselves to stop thinking about what will happen to them after life, they readily slip into a complete and brutal indifference to the future, which is only too much in keeping with certain propensities of mankind. As soon as they lose the habit of placing their chief hopes on distant events, they naturally seek to gratify their smallest desires without delay. No sooner do they despair of living forever than they are inclined to act as if they would exist for a single day only. In skeptical ages, therefore, there is always reason to fear that men may give way continually to their casual daily desires, and that, renouncing altogether whatever cannot be obtained without prolonged effort, they may establish nothing great, permanent, and calm.

If the social condition of a people in these circumstances becomes democratic, the danger I am pointing out grows greater. Everyone is constantly striving to change his position. An immense field of rivalry is thrown open to all. Wealth is amassed or squandered in the shortest possible time amid the turmoil of democracy. Under these conditions, visions of sudden and easy fortunes, of great possessions easily won and lost, of chance in all its forms, haunt the mind. The instability of society itself feeds the natural instability of man’s desires. Amid these perpetual fluctuations of his lot, the present swells in his mind until it hides the future from his sight, and his looks reach no further than tomorrow.

In countries where, unhappily, irreligion and democracy exist together, the most important duty of philosophers and of those in power is to keep striving to place the objects of human actions far beyond man’s immediate range. Confined by the character of his country and his age, the moralist must learn to defend his principles from that position. He must work constantly to show his contemporaries that, even amid the perpetual commotion around them, it is easier than they think to conceive and carry out long-term undertakings. He must teach them that, although the face of mankind may have changed, the methods by which men can provide for their prosperity in this world are still the same. He must teach them that among democratic nations, as elsewhere, the general and unquenchable passion for happiness can be satisfied only by resisting a thousand petty selfish passions of the moment.

The task of those in power is just as clearly marked out. At all times it is important for those who govern nations to act with the future in view, but it is even more necessary in democratic and skeptical ages than in any others. By doing so, the leading men of democracies not only make public affairs prosper; they also teach private individuals, by their example, the art of managing private concerns. Above all, they must strive as far as possible to banish chance from the sphere of politics. The sudden and undeserved promotion of a courtier makes only a passing impression in an aristocratic country, because the nation’s institutions and opinions taken together habitually force men to advance slowly along tracks they cannot leave. But nothing is more pernicious than similar displays of favor before the eyes of a democratic people. They give the final push to the public mind in a direction where everything is already hurrying it onward. In times of skepticism and equality especially, the favor of the people or of the prince, which chance may bestow or withhold, ought never to take the place of attainments or services. It is desirable that every advancement there should appear to be the result of some effort, so that no greatness comes too easily and ambition has to keep its gaze long fixed on an object before it is gratified. Governments must set themselves to restore to men that love of the future which religion and the state of society no longer inspire in them. Without saying so, they must teach the community in practice, day by day, that wealth, fame, and power are the rewards of labor — that great success lies at the far end of long desires, and that nothing lasting is obtained except by toil. When men have grown used to foreseeing from afar what is likely to happen in the world and to living on hopes, they can hardly keep their minds within the exact circumference of life, and they are ready to break through the boundary and look beyond. I do not doubt that, by training the members of a community to think about their future condition in this world, one would bring them gradually and unconsciously nearer to religious convictions. Thus the means that allow men, up to a certain point, to do without religion are perhaps, after all, the only means we still have of bringing mankind back, by a long and roundabout path, to a state of faith.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — That Amongst The Americans All Honest Callings Are Honorable
paragraphs: Among a democratic people, where there is no hereditary wealth, every man works to earn a living, or has worked, or was born to parents who worked. The idea of labor is therefore presented to the mind on every side as the necessary, natural, and honest condition of human existence. Among such a people labor is not only not dishonorable; it is held in honor. The prejudice is not against it but in its favor. In the United States, a wealthy man thinks he owes it to public opinion to devote his leisure to some industrial or commercial pursuit, or to public business. He would think himself in bad repute if he spent his life merely living. So many rich Americans come to Europe to escape this obligation to work. There they find some scattered remains of aristocratic society, among which idleness is still held in honor.

Equality of conditions not only ennobles the idea of labor in men’s estimation; it also raises the idea of labor as a source of profit. In aristocracies it is not exactly labor that is despised, but labor done for profit. Labor is honorable in itself when it is undertaken solely at the bidding of ambition or virtue. Yet in aristocratic society it constantly happens that a man who works for honor is not insensible to the attractions of profit. But these two desires mingle only in the innermost depths of his soul. He carefully hides from every eye the point where they join, and he would gladly hide it from himself. In aristocratic countries there are few public officials who do not pretend to serve their country without self-interested motives. Their salary is a detail they think little about and always pretend not to think about at all. In this way the idea of profit is kept distinct from that of labor. However closely they may be united in fact, they are not thought of together.

In democratic communities, by contrast, these two ideas are always plainly united. The desire for well-being is universal, fortunes are slender or fluctuating, and everyone wants either to increase his own resources or to provide new ones for his children. Men therefore see clearly that it is profit that leads them to work, if not wholly, at least in part. Even those who are driven chiefly by the love of fame are inevitably made familiar with the thought that fame is not their only motive. They find that the desire to earn a living is mixed in their minds with the desire to make life illustrious.

Once the whole community holds labor to be an honorable necessity of man’s condition, and once labor is always openly performed, wholly or in part, to earn pay, the immense distance that separated different callings in aristocratic societies disappears. If all are not alike, all at least have one feature in common. There is no profession in which men do not work for money, and the pay that is common to all gives them all an air of resemblance. This helps explain the opinions Americans hold about different callings. In America no one is degraded because he works, for everyone around him works too. Nor is anyone humiliated by the idea of receiving pay, for the President of the United States also works for pay. He is paid for giving orders, other men for obeying them. In the United States professions are more or less laborious and more or less profitable, but they are never high or low: every honest calling is honorable.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — That Almost All The Americans Follow Industrial Callings
paragraphs: Agriculture is perhaps, of all the useful arts, the one that improves most slowly among democratic nations. Often it even seems to stand still, because other arts are advancing rapidly toward perfection. On the other hand, almost all the tastes and habits that equality of conditions produces naturally lead men to commercial and industrial occupations.

Suppose an active, educated, and free man who has a comfortable competence but is full of desires. He is too poor to live in idleness, yet rich enough to feel protected from the immediate fear of want, and he wonders how he can better his condition. This man has acquired a taste for physical gratifications, in which thousands of his fellow men indulge around him. He has begun to enjoy these pleasures himself, and he is eager to increase his means of satisfying these tastes more fully. But life is slipping away and time presses. What is he to turn to? Cultivating the ground promises an almost certain result for his efforts, but a slow one; men do not grow rich by it without patience and toil. Agriculture is therefore suited only to those who already have large, superfluous wealth, or to those whose poverty bids them seek only a bare subsistence. The choice of a man such as we have supposed is soon made. He sells his plot of ground, leaves his dwelling, and embarks on some hazardous but lucrative calling. Democratic communities abound in men of this kind, and as equality of conditions grows, their number increases. Thus democracy not only swells the number of working men; it also leads them to prefer one kind of labor to another. While it turns them away from agriculture, it encourages their taste for commerce and manufactures. *a

[Footnote a: People have often remarked that manufacturers and merchants are excessively addicted to physical gratifications, and this has been attributed to commerce and manufactures. But I think that is to mistake the effect for the cause. Commerce and manufactures do not give men the taste for physical gratifications; rather, it is this taste that leads men into commerce and manufactures, as a means by which they hope to satisfy themselves more quickly and more fully. If commerce and manufactures increase the desire for well-being, it is because every passion gathers strength in proportion as it is cultivated, and grows with all the efforts made to satisfy it. All the causes that make the love of worldly welfare predominate in the heart of man are favorable to the growth of commerce and manufactures. Equality of conditions is one of those causes. It encourages trade, not directly by giving men a taste for business, but indirectly by strengthening and expanding in their minds a taste for prosperity.]

Even the wealthiest members of the community show this spirit. In a democratic country a man may be reckoned very rich, yet he is almost always dissatisfied with his fortune, since he sees that he has less than his father had and worries that his sons will have less than he does. So most rich men in democracies are tormented by the wish to gain still more wealth, and they turn naturally to trade and manufactures, which look like the quickest and strongest roads to success. In this they share the instincts of the poor without being under the same pressures. Or rather, they are under the most commanding pressure of all: the need not to slip down in the world.

In aristocracies, the rich are also the men who govern. The attention they ceaselessly give to important public affairs keeps them from the lesser cares that trade and manufactures demand. Suppose, nevertheless, that an individual’s own will turns his attention to business. The will of the body to which he belongs will immediately bar him from pursuing it. For however much men may rail against the rule of numbers, they cannot wholly escape its sway, and even among those aristocratic bodies that most obstinately refuse to acknowledge the rights of the majority of the nation, a private majority forms that governs the rest. *b

[Footnote b: Some aristocracies, however, have plunged eagerly into commerce and have developed manufactures with success. World history offers several striking examples. But in general one can say that the aristocratic principle does not favor the growth of trade and manufactures. Moneyed aristocracies are the only exception to this rule. In them, almost every desire needs wealth to be satisfied. The love of riches becomes, so to speak, the main highway of the human passions, and every lesser path crosses it or joins it. Love of money and thirst for the distinction that comes with power are then so closely mixed in the same souls that it is hard to tell whether men turn greedy out of ambition or ambitious out of greed. This is the case in England, where men try to get rich in order to gain distinction, and seek distinction as a way of displaying their wealth. The mind is then gripped from both ends and hurried into trade and manufactures, which are the shortest roads to opulence.

This, however, strikes me as an exceptional and transitory circumstance. When wealth has become the only symbol of aristocracy, it is very difficult for the wealthy to keep sole possession of political power to the exclusion of all other men. The aristocracy of birth and pure democracy stand at the two extremes of the social and political state of nations, and the moneyed aristocracy finds its place between them. It comes close to the aristocracy of birth by conferring great privileges on a small number of persons. It belongs to the democratic element in that these privileges may be acquired in turn by anyone. It often forms a natural transition between these two conditions of society, and it is hard to say whether it closes the reign of aristocratic institutions or already opens the new era of democracy.]

In democratic countries, money does not lead those who have it to political power, and often removes them from it. There the rich do not know how to spend their leisure. They are driven into active life by the restlessness and greatness of their desires, by the extent of their resources, and by the taste for the extraordinary that is almost always felt by those who rise above the crowd by whatever means. Trade is the only road open to them. In democracies nothing is greater or more brilliant than commerce. It attracts the attention of the public and fills the imagination of the multitude, and all energetic passions are directed toward it. Neither their own prejudices nor anyone else’s can keep the rich from devoting themselves to it. The wealthy members of democracies never form a body with customs and regulations of its own. The opinions peculiar to their class do not restrain them, and the common opinions of their country urge them on. Moreover, since all the large fortunes found in a democratic community have grown out of commerce, many generations must follow one another before their owners can entirely lay aside their habits of business.

Confined within the narrow space that politics leaves them, rich men in democracies throw themselves eagerly into commercial enterprise. There they can extend and use their natural advantages. Indeed, the boldness and scale of their industrial speculations let us measure how slight an esteem they would have had for productive industry if they had been born into an aristocracy.

A similar observation applies to all men living in democracies, whether poor or rich. Those who live amid democratic fluctuations always have the phantom of chance before their eyes, and they end by liking every undertaking in which chance plays a part. All of them are therefore led to engage in commerce, not only for the profit it holds out to them but for love of the constant excitement that this pursuit provides.

The United States of America has been free for only half a century [in 1840] from the colonial dependence in which it stood toward Great Britain. Large fortunes there are few, and capital is still scarce. Yet no people in the world has made such rapid progress in trade and manufactures as the Americans. Today they are the second maritime nation in the world, and although their manufactures must struggle against almost insurmountable natural obstacles, they are not prevented from making great advances every day. In the United States the greatest undertakings and speculations are carried out without difficulty, because the whole population is engaged in productive industry, and because the poorest members of the commonwealth, like the wealthiest, are ready to combine their efforts for such purposes. As a result, a stranger is constantly amazed by the immense public works carried out by a nation that contains, so to speak, no rich men. The Americans arrived on the territory they inhabit only yesterday, and they have already changed the whole order of nature to their own advantage. They have joined the Hudson to the Mississippi and linked the Atlantic Ocean with the Gulf of Mexico across a continent of more than five hundred leagues that separates the two seas. The longest railroads built up to the present time are in America. But what astonishes me most in the United States is not so much the marvelous grandeur of some undertakings as the innumerable multitude of small ones. Almost all the farmers of the United States combine some trade with agriculture, and most of them make agriculture itself a trade. It seldom happens that an American farmer settles for good on the land he occupies. Especially in the districts of the Far West, he brings land into tillage in order to sell it again, not to farm it. He builds a farmhouse on the speculation that, since the condition of the country will soon be changed by the growth of population, a good price will be had for it. Every year a swarm of inhabitants of the North arrives in the Southern States and settles where the cotton plant and the sugar cane grow. These men cultivate the soil to make it yield, in a few years, enough to enrich them, and they already look forward to the time when they can return home to enjoy the competence thus acquired. Thus the Americans carry their business-like qualities into agriculture, and their trading passions show there as in their other pursuits.

The Americans advance enormously in productive industry because every one of them throws himself into it at the same time. For that very reason they face very unexpected and formidable troubles. Everyone is in commerce, so their commercial affairs depend on causes too varied and tangled for anyone to predict what trouble may come. Everyone is more or less in productive industry, so at the slightest jolt to business every private fortune is endangered at once, and the state itself is shaken. I believe that these recurring commercial panics are a disease native to the democratic nations of our age. It can be made less dangerous, but it cannot be cured, since it springs not from accidents but from the temperament of these nations.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 — That Aristocracy May Be Engendered By Manufactures
paragraphs: I have shown that democracy favors the growth of manufactures and swells the ranks of the manufacturing classes without limit. Now we shall see by what indirect route manufacturers may in their turn lead men back to aristocracy. It is generally agreed that when a workman does the same small task every day, the whole product is made more easily, more quickly, and more cheaply. It is equally agreed that the cost of producing manufactured goods falls as the establishment that makes them grows larger, and as the capital or credit it employs grows greater. People had long glimpsed these truths only imperfectly, but in our time they have been proved. They have already been applied to many very important kinds of manufacture, and even the most humble will gradually come under their rule. I know of nothing in politics that deserves the lawmaker’s close attention more than these two new axioms of the science of manufactures.

A workman who spends all his time making one single thing eventually does that work with remarkable skill. At the same time, he loses the general ability to apply his mind to directing the work. Each day he grows more adept and less industrious, so that one may say of him that as the workman improves, the man is degraded. What can be expected of a man who has spent twenty years of his life making heads for pins? And what can that mighty human intelligence, which has so often stirred the world, be used for in him, except to find the best way of making pinheads? When a workman has spent a large part of his life like this, his thoughts are forever fixed on the object of his daily toil. His body has settled into fixed habits that it can never shake off. In a word, he no longer belongs to himself but to the calling he has chosen. It is in vain that laws and customs have taken the trouble to level every barrier around such a man and to open a thousand different roads to fortune before him on every side. A theory of manufactures more powerful than customs and laws ties him to a trade, and often to a place, that he cannot leave. It assigns him a certain position in society, beyond which he cannot go. In the midst of universal movement, it has left him standing still.

The more widely the principle of the division of labor is applied, the weaker, the narrower in mind, and the more dependent the workman becomes. The craft advances; the craftsman falls back. On the other hand, as it becomes more evident that manufactured goods are cheaper and better the larger the manufacture is and the more capital it employs, wealthy and educated men come forward to enter manufactures that used to be left to poor or ignorant craftsmen. The scale of the effort required and the importance of the results to be won attract them. So at the very time that the science of manufactures lowers the class of workmen, it raises the class of masters.

While the workman focuses his faculties more and more on a single detail, the master takes in a broader whole, and his mind expands as the workman’s shrinks. Before long the one will need nothing but physical strength without intelligence, while the other needs knowledge, and almost genius, to succeed. The master comes to resemble more and more the administrator of a vast empire, and the workman a brute. Master and workman thus have nothing in common here, and their differences grow every day. They are linked only like the two rings at either end of a long chain. Each fills the place made for him and cannot get out of it. The one is continually, closely, and necessarily dependent on the other, and seems as much born to obey as the other is born to command. What is this but aristocracy?

As the conditions of the men who make up the nation grow more and more equal, the demand for manufactured goods becomes more general and more extensive. The cheapness that puts these goods within reach of modest fortunes becomes a great element of success. So every day more men of great wealth and education devote their riches and knowledge to manufactures. By opening large establishments and enforcing a strict division of labor, they seek to meet the new demands arising on every side. Thus, as the mass of the nation turns toward democracy, the particular class engaged in manufactures becomes more aristocratic. Men grow more alike in the one and more different in the other, and inequality increases in the smaller class at the same rate at which it decreases in the community. Hence it would appear, if one searches to the bottom, that aristocracy should naturally spring from within democracy itself.

But this kind of aristocracy is in no way like those that came before it. One notices at once that, because it applies only to manufactures and to a few manufacturing callings, it is a monstrous exception in the general character of society. The small aristocratic societies that some manufacturers form amid the immense democracy of our age contain, like the great aristocratic societies of former ages, a few very wealthy men and a multitude of wretchedly poor ones.
