The poor have few ways to escape their condition and become rich. The rich, however, are constantly becoming poor, or they leave business once they have made their fortune. Thus the elements that make up the class of the poor are fixed, but those that make up the class of the rich are not. To tell the truth, though there are rich men, a class of rich men does not exist. These rich individuals have no feelings or aims in common, no shared traditions or hopes. There are therefore members, but no body.

Not only are the rich not closely united among themselves, but there is no real bond between them and the poor. Their relative position is not permanent; their interests constantly draw them together or pull them apart. The workman is generally dependent on the master, but not on any particular master. The two men meet in the factory but do not know each other anywhere else, and while they touch at one point, they stand very far apart on all others. The manufacturer asks nothing of the workman but his labor, and the workman expects nothing from him but his wages. The one takes on no obligation to protect, nor the other to defend, and neither habit nor duty joins them permanently. The aristocracy created by business rarely settles among the manufacturing population it directs. Its aim is not to govern that population but to use it. An aristocracy formed in this way can have no great hold on the people it employs. Even if it manages to keep them at one moment, they slip away the next. It does not know how to will, and it cannot act. The territorial aristocracy of former ages was bound by law, or believed itself bound by custom, to come to the aid of its servants and relieve their distress. But the manufacturing aristocracy of our age first impoverishes and debases the men who serve it, and then abandons them to be supported by public charity. This is a natural consequence of what has been said above. Between workmen and master there are frequent dealings, but no real partnership.

On the whole, I believe that the manufacturing aristocracy growing up before our eyes is one of the harshest that has ever existed in the world, but at the same time one of the most confined and least dangerous. Nevertheless, the friends of democracy should keep their eyes anxiously fixed in this direction. For if a permanent inequality of conditions and aristocracy ever enter the world again, it may be predicted that this is the channel by which they will come in.
Book Three: Influence of Democracy on Manners, Properly So Called

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — That Manners Are Softened As Social Conditions Become More Equal
paragraphs: We observe that for several centuries social conditions have been moving toward equality, and we find that over the same period the manners of society have grown milder. Are these two things merely simultaneous, or is there some hidden link between them, so that one cannot advance without driving the other forward? Several causes may combine to make a people’s manners less rough, but of all of them the most powerful seems to me to be equality of conditions. In my view, then, equality of conditions and increasing civility of manners are not only simultaneous but correlated facts. When fable writers want to interest us in the actions of animals, they give them human ideas and passions. The poets who sing of spirits and angels do the same. No misery is so deep, and no happiness so pure, that it can fill the human mind and touch the heart unless we ourselves are held up before our own eyes in some other form.

This applies exactly to the subject we are now considering. In an aristocratic community, all men are fixed irrevocably in their places by profession, property, and birth. The members of each class regard themselves as children of one family and feel a constant, lively sympathy for one another, which the citizens of a democracy can never feel to the same degree. But the several classes do not feel the same way toward one another. Among an aristocratic people, each caste has its own opinions, feelings, rights, customs, and ways of living. So the men of each caste do not resemble the mass of their fellow citizens. They do not think or feel in the same way, and they hardly believe that they belong to the same human race. They therefore cannot fully understand what others feel, or judge others by themselves. Yet they are sometimes eager to help one another, and this does not contradict my earlier remark. These aristocratic institutions made beings of one and the same race very different, but they nevertheless tied them to one another by close political bonds. The serf had no natural interest in the fate of nobles, yet he still thought himself obliged to devote his person to the service of whichever noble happened to be his lord. And although the noble considered himself of a different nature from his serfs, he nevertheless held that his duty and his honor required him to defend, at the risk of his own life, those who lived on his lands.

Clearly, these mutual obligations did not originate in the law of nature but in the law of society, and the claim of social duty was stronger than that of mere humanity. These services were not thought to be owed from one man to another, but to the vassal or to the lord. Feudal institutions awakened a lively sympathy for the sufferings of certain men, but none at all for the miseries of mankind. They gave the manners of the time generosity rather than gentleness. They prompted men to great acts of self-devotion, but they produced no real sympathies. For real sympathies can exist only between those who are alike, and in aristocratic ages men acknowledge no one but the members of their own caste to be like themselves.

When the chroniclers of the Middle Ages, all of whom belonged to the aristocracy by birth or education, tell of the tragic end of a noble, their grief flows freely. Yet they report in a single breath, and without flinching, the massacres and tortures inflicted on common people. It is not that these writers felt habitual hatred or systematic contempt for the people; war between the classes of the community had not yet been declared. Instinct drove them rather than passion. Since they had formed no clear idea of a poor man’s sufferings, they cared little about his fate. The same feelings moved the lower orders whenever the feudal tie was broken. The very ages that saw so many heroic acts of self-devotion by vassals for their lords were also stained by atrocious cruelties, committed from time to time by the lower classes against the higher. We must not suppose that this mutual insensibility arose solely from the lack of public order and education. Traces of it are found in later centuries, which became peaceful and enlightened while still remaining aristocratic. In 1675 the lower classes in Brittany rose in revolt against a new tax. The disturbances were put down with unparalleled atrocity. Observe the language in which Madame de Sevigne, a witness of these horrors, describes them to her daughter: —
“Aux Rochers, 30 Octobre, 1675.

“Mon Dieu, ma fille, que votre lettre d’Aix est plaisante! Au moins relisez vos lettres avant que de les envoyer; laissez-vous surpendre a leur agrement, et consolez-vous par ce plaisir de la peine que vous avez d’en tant ecrire. Vous avez donc baise toute la Provence? il n’y aurait pas satisfaction a baiser toute la Bretagne, a moins qu’on n’aimat a sentir le vin. . . . Voulez-vous savoir des nouvelles de Rennes? On a fait une taxe de cent mille ecus sur le bourgeois; et si on ne trouve point cette somme dans vingt-quatre heures, elle sera doublee et exigible par les soldats. On a chasse et banni toute une grand rue, et defendu de les recueillir sous peine de la vie; de sorte qu’on voyait tous ces miserables, veillards, femmes accouchees, enfans, errer en pleurs au sortir de cette ville sans savoir ou aller. On roua avant-hier un violon, qui avait commence la danse et la pillerie du papier timbre; il a ete ecartele apres sa mort, et ses quatre quartiers exposes aux quatre coins de la ville. On a pris soixante bourgeois, et on commence demain les punitions. Cette province est un bel exemple pour les autres, et surtout de respecter les gouverneurs et les gouvernantes, et de ne point jeter de pierres dans leur jardin.” *a

[Footnote a: To see the point of this joke, the reader should remember that Madame de Grignan was Gouvernante de Provence.] “Madame de Tarente etait hier dans ces bois par un temps enchante: il n’est question ni de chambre ni de collation; elle entre par la barriere et s’en retourne de meme. . . .”
In another letter she adds: —

“Vous me parlez bien plaisamment de nos miseres; nous ne sommes plus si roues; un en huit jours, pour entretenir la justice. Il est vrai que la penderie me parait maintenant un refraichissement. J’ai une tout autre idee de la justice, depuis que je suis en ce pays. Vos galeriens me paraissent une societe d’honnetes gens qui se sont retires du monde pour mener une vie douce.”

Do not conclude that Madame de Sevigne, the author of these lines, was a selfish or cruel woman. She adored her children and was quick to share her friends’ sorrows. Her letters even show that she was kind and indulgent toward her vassals and servants. Yet she had no clear idea that anyone could suffer who was not a person of quality.

In our time, even the harshest man, writing to the most unfeeling person he knows, would not dare to indulge so wantonly in the cruel joking I have quoted. And even if his own manners permitted it, the manners of society at large would forbid it. Where does this come from? Are we more sensitive than our forefathers? I do not know that we are, but I am sure that our insensibility extends to a far greater range of objects. When all the ranks of a community are nearly equal, all men think and feel in nearly the same way, and each of them can judge in a moment the sensations of all the others. He glances quickly at himself, and that is enough. There is no wretchedness he cannot readily enter into, and a secret instinct tells him how great it is. It does not matter whether the sufferers are strangers or enemies; imagination puts him in their place. Something like a personal feeling mingles with his pity and makes him suffer while his fellow creature’s body is being tortured. In democratic ages men rarely sacrifice themselves for one another, but they show a general compassion for all members of the human race. They inflict no needless harm, and they are glad to relieve the griefs of others when they can do so without hurting themselves much. They are not disinterested, but they are humane.

Although the Americans have in a manner reduced egotism to a social and philosophical theory, they are nonetheless very open to compassion. In no country is criminal justice administered more mildly than in the United States. While the English seem intent on carefully preserving the bloody traces of the dark ages in their penal laws, the Americans have almost erased capital punishment from their codes. North America is, I think, the only country on earth where no citizen’s life has been taken for a political offense in the last fifty years. What conclusively shows that this unusual mildness of the Americans arises chiefly from their social condition is the way they treat their slaves. Perhaps there is not, on the whole, a single European colony in the New World where the physical condition of Black people is less harsh than in the United States. Yet the slaves there still endure horrible sufferings and are constantly exposed to barbarous punishments. It is easy to see that the lot of these unfortunate beings inspires little compassion in their masters, who regard slavery not only as an institution that profits them but as an evil that does not touch them. Thus the same man who is full of humanity toward his fellow creatures when they are also his equals becomes insensible to their afflictions as soon as that equality ends. His mildness should therefore be attributed to equality of conditions rather than to civilization and education.

What I have observed here of individuals applies, to a certain extent, to nations. When each nation has its own distinct opinions, beliefs, laws, and customs, it regards itself as the whole of mankind and is moved by no sorrows but its own. If war breaks out between two nations with this feeling, it is sure to be waged with great cruelty. At the height of their culture, the Romans slaughtered their enemies’ generals after dragging them in triumph behind a chariot, and they threw their prisoners to the beasts of the Circus to amuse the people. Cicero, who spoke so vehemently against the idea of crucifying a Roman citizen, had not a word to say against these horrible abuses of victory. Clearly, in his eyes a barbarian did not belong to the same human race as a Roman. On the contrary, as nations become more like one another, they grow more compassionate toward each other, and the law of nations is softened.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — That Democracy Renders The Habitual Intercourse Of The Americans Simple And Easy
paragraphs: Americans Simple and Easy

Democracy does not attach men strongly to one another, but it puts their everyday dealings on an easier footing. Suppose two Englishmen happen to meet at the Antipodes, surrounded by strangers whose language and customs they hardly know. At first they will stare at each other with great curiosity and a kind of secret uneasiness. Then they will turn away, or, if one speaks to the other, they will take care to talk only about very unimportant subjects, in a constrained and absent manner. Yet there is no enmity between these men; they have never seen each other before, and each believes the other to be respectable. Why, then, do they keep so warily apart? We must go back to England to learn the reason.

When birth alone, regardless of wealth, determines men’s classes in society, everyone knows exactly where he stands on the social scale. He does not try to rise, and he does not fear falling. In a community organized this way, men of different castes have very little contact with one another. But if chance brings them together, they are ready to talk without hoping or fearing to lose their own position. Their relations are not on a footing of equality, but they are not strained. When an aristocracy of money replaces an aristocracy of birth, things change. The privileges of some are still very great, but the chance of acquiring them is open to all. It follows that those who hold privileges are constantly haunted by the fear of losing them or of having others share them. Those who do not yet enjoy them long to possess them at any cost, or, failing that, at least to appear to possess them, which is not impossible. Since men’s social importance is no longer openly and permanently fixed by blood, and varies endlessly with wealth, ranks still exist, but it is not easy to tell at a glance who belongs to which. Secret hostilities then arise in the community. One set of men tries by countless devices to get in among those above them, or to seem to. Another set is constantly up in arms against these usurpers of their rights. Or rather, the same individual does both at once: while he tries to rise into a higher circle, he is always on the defensive against intrusion from those below him.

Such is the condition of England today, and I believe the peculiarity I mentioned above is chiefly due to it. Aristocratic pride is still very great among the English, and the boundaries of the aristocracy are poorly defined. So everyone lives in constant dread that someone will take advantage of his familiarity. Unable to judge at once the social position of the people he meets, an Englishman prudently avoids all contact with them. Men fear that some slight service they render may draw them into an unsuitable acquaintance. They dread civilities, and they avoid a stranger’s intrusive gratitude just as much as his hatred. Many people put these odd anti-social tendencies, and the reserved, taciturn bearing of the English, down to purely physical causes. I may grant that there is something of this in their race, but much more is due to their social condition, as the contrast with the Americans proves.

In America, privileges of birth have never existed, and wealth gives its owners no special rights. There, men who do not know each other readily frequent the same places and find neither danger nor advantage in freely exchanging their thoughts. If they meet by chance, they neither seek nor avoid conversation. Their manner is therefore natural, frank, and open. It is easy to see that they hardly expect or fear anything from each other, and that they care no more to display than to hide their position in the world. If their demeanor is often cold and serious, it is never haughty or constrained. If they do not talk, it is because they are not in the mood, not because they think it in their interest to keep silent. In a foreign country, two Americans are at once friends, simply because they are Americans. No prejudice repels them; their common country draws them together. For two Englishmen, the same blood is not enough; the same rank must bring them together. The Americans notice this unsociable mood of the English as much as the French do, and are no less astonished by it. Yet the Americans are tied to England by their origin, their religion, their language, and partly by their customs; they differ only in social condition. It may therefore be inferred that the reserve of the English comes much more from the constitution of their country than from that of its inhabitants.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Why The Americans Show So Little Sensitiveness In Their Own Country, And Are So Sensitive In Europe
paragraphs: Country, and Are So Sensitive in Europe

The temper of the Americans is vindictive, like that of all serious and reflective nations. They hardly ever forget an offense, but it is not easy to offend them, and their resentment is as slow to kindle as it is to fade. In aristocratic communities, where a small number of people manage everything, the outward dealings of men follow settled conventional rules. Everyone then thinks he knows exactly what marks of respect or condescension he should show, and no one is presumed ignorant of the science of etiquette. The usages of the top class in society then serve as a model for all the others. Each of the others also sets up a code of its own, which all its members must follow. Thus the rules of politeness form a complex system of legislation. It is hard to master perfectly, yet dangerous for anyone to depart from, so that men are constantly exposed to giving or receiving bitter affronts without intending to. But as distinctions of rank are wiped out, and men of different education and birth meet and mingle in the same places, it becomes almost impossible to agree on the rules of good breeding. Since its laws are uncertain, breaking them is no crime, even in the eyes of those who know what they are. Men attach more importance to intentions than to forms. They grow less civil, but also less quarrelsome. There are many little attentions an American does not care about. He thinks they are not due to him, or he presumes they are not known to be due. So he either does not notice a rudeness or forgives it. His manners become less courteous, and his character plainer and more manly.

The mutual indulgence of the Americans, and the manly confidence with which they treat each other, also result from another, deeper and more general cause, which I already mentioned in the preceding chapter. In the United States, distinctions of rank in civil society are slight, and in political society they are nonexistent. An American therefore does not think himself bound to pay particular attentions to any of his fellow citizens, nor does he require them from others toward himself. Since he does not see that it is in his interest to seek the company of any of his countrymen eagerly, he is slow to imagine that his own company is being refused. He despises no one because of his station, so he does not imagine anyone can despise him for that reason. Until he has clearly perceived an insult, he does not suppose that an affront was intended. The social condition of the Americans naturally accustoms them not to take offense over small matters. And in turn, the democratic freedom they enjoy spreads this same mildness of temper through the character of the nation. The political institutions of the United States constantly bring citizens of all ranks into contact and force them to pursue great undertakings together. People so engaged have hardly time to attend to the details of etiquette, and they also have too strong an interest in living harmoniously to stick at such things. They soon acquire the habit of paying more attention to the feelings and opinions of those they meet than to their manners, and they do not let trifles annoy them.

I have often noticed in the United States that it is not easy to make a man understand that his presence can be done without. Hints will not always get rid of him. I contradict an American at every word he says, to show him that his conversation bores me, and he instantly sets to work with fresh stubbornness to convince me. I keep a dogged silence, and he thinks I am deep in thought about the truths he is uttering. At last I rush away from his company, and he supposes that some urgent business is calling me elsewhere. This man will never understand that he is wearing me out unless I tell him so, and the only way to be rid of him is to make him my enemy for life.

At first sight it seems surprising that the same man, once transported to Europe, suddenly becomes so touchy and captious that I often find it as hard to avoid offending him here as it was to put him out of countenance there. These two opposite effects come from the same cause. Democratic institutions generally give men a lofty idea of their country and of themselves. An American leaves home with a heart swollen with pride. On arriving in Europe he discovers at once that we are not as absorbed in the United States and the great people who live there as he had supposed, and this begins to annoy him. He has been told that the conditions of society are not equal in our part of the world, and he sees that among the nations of Europe the traces of rank are not wholly erased. Wealth and birth still keep certain vague privileges, which force themselves on his notice while escaping definition. He is therefore profoundly ignorant of the place he ought to occupy in this half-ruined scale of classes, which are distinct enough to hate and despise each other, yet alike enough that he is always confusing them. He is afraid of placing himself too high, and still more afraid of being placed too low. This twofold danger keeps his mind constantly strained and hampers all he says and does. He learns from tradition that in Europe ceremonial observances varied endlessly according to rank. This memory of former times completes his bewilderment, and he fears the more that he will not get the marks of respect due to him, because he does not know exactly what they consist of. He is like a man surrounded by traps. Society is no recreation for him but serious toil. He weighs your least actions, questions your looks, and scrutinizes everything you say, in case some hidden allusion is meant to insult him. I doubt whether there was ever a provincial man of quality so punctilious in his breeding. He tries to observe the slightest rules of etiquette and does not allow one of them to be waived toward himself. He is full of scruples and, at the same time, of pretensions. He wishes to do enough but fears doing too much, and since he does not know very well where the limits of either lie, he keeps up a haughty and awkward air of reserve.

But this is not all; here is yet another duality of the human heart. An American is forever talking about the admirable equality that prevails in the United States. Aloud he makes it his country’s boast, but in secret he laments it for himself, and he aspires to show that he, for his part, is an exception to the general state of things he vaunts. Hardly any American can be found who does not claim some distant kinship with the first founders of the colonies, and as for scions of the noble families of England, America seemed to me to be covered with them. When a wealthy American arrives in Europe, his first concern is to surround himself with all the luxuries of wealth. He is so afraid of being taken for the plain citizen of a democracy that he adopts a hundred contrived ways of putting some new proof of his wealth before you every day. His house will be in the most fashionable part of town, and he will always be surrounded by a crowd of servants. I have heard an American complain that in the best houses of Paris the company was rather mixed. The prevailing taste there was not pure enough for him, and he ventured to hint that, in his opinion, manners there lacked elegance. He could not get used to seeing wit hidden under such unpretending forms.

These contrasts should not surprise us. If the traces of former aristocratic distinctions were not so completely erased in the United States, the Americans would be less simple and less tolerant at home — they would demand less, and be less fond of borrowed manners, in our country.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — Consequences Of The Three Preceding Chapters
paragraphs: When men feel natural compassion for one another’s sufferings, when easy and frequent contact brings them together, and when no touchy feelings hold them apart, one may readily suppose that they will help one another whenever help is needed. When an American asks his fellow citizens for their cooperation, it is seldom refused, and I have often seen it given spontaneously and with great goodwill. If an accident happens on the highway, everyone hurries to help the victim. If some great and sudden calamity strikes a family, a thousand strangers willingly open their purses, and small but numerous gifts pour in to relieve the family’s distress. Among the most civilized nations of the world, it often happens that a poor wretch is as friendless in the midst of a crowd as the savage in his wilds. This is hardly ever the case in the United States. The Americans, who are always cold and often coarse in their manners, seldom show insensibility. If they do not eagerly offer their services, they do not refuse to give them.

None of this contradicts what I said earlier about individualism. The two things are so far from fighting each other that I can see how they agree. Equality of conditions, while it makes men feel their independence, shows them their own weakness. They are free but exposed to a thousand accidents, and experience soon teaches them that, although they do not habitually need the help of others, a time almost always comes when they cannot do without it. In Europe we constantly see men of the same profession ready to help one another. They are all exposed to the same ills, and that is enough to teach them to seek mutual protection, however hard-hearted and selfish they may otherwise be. When one of them falls into danger, and the others can save him by a slight, passing sacrifice or a sudden effort, they do not fail to try. It is not that they are deeply concerned about his fate. If their efforts happen to fail, they immediately forget what they were for and go back to their own business. But a kind of tacit and almost involuntary agreement has been made among them, by which each owes the others temporary support that he may in turn claim for himself. Extend to a whole people what is said here of a class, and you will understand my meaning. A similar covenant in fact exists among all the citizens of a democracy. They all feel subject to the same weakness and the same dangers, and their interest, as well as their sympathy, makes it a rule with them to lend each other help when it is needed. The more equal social conditions become, the more men show this reciprocal readiness to oblige one another. In democracies no great benefits are conferred, but good turns are constantly done. A man seldom shows self-devotion, but all men are ready to be of service to one another.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — How Democracy Affects the Relation Of Masters And Servants
paragraphs: An American who had spent a long time traveling in Europe once told me, “The English treat their servants with a stiffness and imperiousness of manner which surprise us; but on the other hand the French sometimes treat their attendants with a degree of familiarity or of politeness which we cannot conceive. It looks as if they were afraid to give orders: the posture of the superior and the inferior is ill-maintained.” The remark was just, and I have often made it myself. I have always thought of England as the country in the world where, in our time, the bond of domestic service is drawn tightest, and of France as the country where it is loosest. I have seen masters stand so high, or so low, nowhere else. The Americans fall between these two extremes. That is how the matter looks on the surface. To find the causes behind it, we have to look into it thoroughly.

No society has ever existed in which social conditions were so equal that there were neither rich nor poor, and therefore neither masters nor servants. Democracy does not do away with these two classes, but it alters their dispositions and changes how they relate to each other. Among aristocratic nations, servants form a distinct class, no more varied in makeup than the class of masters. A settled order soon takes shape. In the servants’ class, as in the masters’, a scale develops with many distinctions and clearly marked gradations of rank, and generation follows generation without any change of position. The two communities lie one above the other, always separate, yet governed by similar principles. This aristocratic structure shapes the ideas and customs of servants as powerfully as those of masters; the effects differ, but the same cause is easy to trace. Each class forms a small community within the nation, and in the end fixed ideas of right and wrong arise within it. The various acts of human life are seen in one particular, unchanging light. In the society of servants, as in that of masters, people have great influence over one another: they recognize settled rules, and where there is no law they are guided by a kind of public opinion. Their habits are settled, and their conduct is kept under a certain control.

These men, whose lot is to obey, certainly do not understand fame, virtue, honesty, and honor as their masters do; but they have a pride, a virtue, and an honesty that belong to their condition, and they have an idea, if I may put it so, of a kind of servile honor. *a A class may be mean without all its members being mean-hearted, and to think so would be a great mistake. However lowly the class, the man who stands first in it and has no thought of leaving it holds an aristocratic position, which gives him lofty feelings, pride, and self-respect, and fits him for the higher virtues and for actions above the ordinary. Among aristocratic nations it was by no means rare to find men of noble and vigorous mind in the service of the great, who did not feel the servitude they bore and who submitted to their masters’ will without any fear of displeasing them. But this was hardly ever so among the lower ranks of domestic servants. One may imagine that a man at the bottom of the order of menials stands very low indeed. The French coined a word expressly for the servants of the aristocracy — they called them lackeys. When all other words were used up, “lackey” served as the strongest term for human meanness. Under the old French monarchy, to name a low-spirited, contemptible fellow in a single expression, people would say he had the “soul of a lackey”; the term was enough to convey everything intended. [Footnote a: If one examines closely and in detail the main opinions that guide these men, the analogy appears even more striking, and one is surprised to find among them, just as much as among the haughtiest scions of a feudal line, pride of birth, respect for their ancestors and their descendants, disdain for their inferiors, a dread of contact, and a taste for etiquette, precedents, and antiquity.]

Permanent inequality of conditions not only gives servants certain distinctive virtues and vices; it also puts them in a distinctive relation to their masters. Among aristocratic nations the poor man grows up used to the idea of being commanded: wherever he turns his eyes, he sees the graded structure of society and the look of obedience. In those countries, therefore, the master readily gets prompt, complete, respectful, and easy obedience from his servants, because they revere in him not only their master but the class of masters. He bears down on their will with the entire weight of the aristocracy. He directs their actions — and to some extent even their thoughts. In aristocracies the master often holds an amazing sway, even without realizing it, over the opinions, habits, and customs of those who obey him, and his influence reaches even further than his authority.

In aristocratic communities there are hereditary families of servants as well as of masters, and the same servant families stay attached for several generations to the same master families (like two parallel lines that neither meet nor separate). This considerably changes how the two classes of people relate. So although in aristocratic society master and servant have no natural likeness — although, on the contrary, their fortune, education, and opinions place them at an immense distance on the scale of human beings — time still binds them together in the end. A long chain of shared memories connects them, and however different they are, they come to resemble each other; in democracies, by contrast, where they are naturally almost alike, they always remain strangers. Among an aristocratic people the master comes to regard his servants as an inferior, secondary part of himself, and he often takes an interest in their lot as a last stretch of egotism.

Servants, for their part, are not unwilling to see themselves in the same light, and they sometimes identify with the person of the master, so that they become an appendage of him in their own eyes as well as in his. In aristocracies a servant holds a subordinate position he cannot escape; above him stands another man in a superior rank that he cannot lose. On one side are obscurity, poverty, and lifelong obedience; on the other, equally for life, fame, wealth, and command. The two conditions are always distinct and always close together; the tie between them lasts as long as they do. In this predicament the servant ends by detaching his idea of his interest from his own person. He deserts himself, so to speak, or rather he moves himself into his master’s character and so takes on an imaginary personality. He complacently clothes himself in the wealth of those who command him; he shares their fame, raises himself by their rank, and feeds his mind on borrowed greatness, to which he attaches more importance than those who fully and truly possess it. There is something touching, and at the same time ridiculous, in this strange confusion of two different states of being. When these passions of masters pass into the souls of menials, they take on the natural dimensions of the place they now occupy: they shrink and sink lower. What was pride in the master becomes childish vanity and petty ostentation in the servant. The servants of a great man are usually most punctilious about the marks of respect due to him, and they care more about his slightest privileges than he does himself. In France a few of these old servants of the aristocracy can still be met here and there; they have outlived their race, which will soon vanish altogether with them. In the United States I never saw anyone at all like them. The Americans not only do not know the type; it is hardly possible to make them understand that it ever existed. It is scarcely harder for them to imagine it than for us to form a correct idea of what a slave was among the Romans, or a serf in the Middle Ages. All these men were in fact, though in different degrees, products of the same cause. All of them are withdrawing from our sight and fading into the obscurity of the past, along with the social condition that gave them birth.

Equality of conditions turns servants and masters into new beings and puts them in new positions toward each other. When social conditions are nearly equal, people are constantly changing their situation in life. There is still a class of menials and a class of masters, but these classes are not always made up of the same individuals, still less of the same families, and those who command are no more certain of lasting than those who obey. Because servants do not form a separate people, they have no habits, prejudices, or customs peculiar to themselves; they are not remarkable for any particular turn of mind or mood of feeling. They know no vices or virtues of their condition. They share the education, opinions, feelings, virtues, and vices of their contemporaries, and they are honest men or scoundrels in the same way their masters are. The conditions of servants are no less equal than those of masters. Since no marked ranks or fixed subordination are to be found among them, they will show neither the meanness nor the greatness that marks the aristocracy of menials, as it marks all other aristocracies. I never saw a man in the United States who reminded me of the class of confidential servants of which Europe still keeps a memory, and I never met anything like a lackey: every trace of both has disappeared.

In democracies servants are not only equal among themselves; it may be said that in a certain sense they are the equals of their masters. This needs explaining to be understood correctly. At any moment a servant may become a master, and he aspires to do so; the servant is therefore not a different kind of man from the master. Why, then, does the one have a right to command, and what compels the other to obey? The free and temporary consent of both their wills. Neither is by nature inferior to the other; each becomes so only for a time, by agreement. Within the terms of that agreement, one is a servant and the other a master; beyond it they are two citizens of the commonwealth — two men. I ask the reader particularly to note that servants are not the only ones who see their condition this way; masters regard domestic service in the same light, and the precise limits of authority and obedience are as clearly fixed in the mind of one as in the mind of the other.

When most of the community have long since reached a nearly similar condition, and equality is an old and acknowledged fact, the public mind, which is never swayed by exceptions, sets certain general limits to the value of a man, above or below which no one can long remain. It is in vain that wealth and poverty, authority and obedience, happen to put great distances between two men; public opinion, based on the usual order of things, draws them to a common level and creates a kind of imaginary equality between them, in spite of the real inequality of their conditions. In time this all-powerful opinion penetrates even the hearts of those whose interest might arm them to resist it; it shapes their judgment while it subdues their will. In their inmost convictions the master and the servant no longer see any deep difference between them, and they neither hope nor fear to find one at any time. They are therefore subject neither to disdain nor to anger, and each sees in the other neither humility nor pride. The master holds the contract of service to be the only source of his power, and the servant regards it as the only reason for his obedience. They do not quarrel over their respective positions; each knows his own and keeps to it.

In the French army the common soldier is drawn from nearly the same classes as the officer and may hold the same commissions. Out of the ranks he considers himself entirely equal to his military superiors, and in fact he is; but under arms he does not hesitate to obey, and his obedience is no less prompt, precise, and ready for being voluntary and defined. This example may give an idea of what happens between masters and servants in democratic communities.

It would be absurd to suppose that the warm, deep affections sometimes kindled in the domestic service of an aristocracy will ever spring up between these two men, or that they will show striking instances of self-sacrifice. In aristocracies masters and servants live apart, and often their only dealings are through a third person; yet they commonly stand firmly by one another. In democratic countries master and servant are close together. They are in daily personal contact, but their minds do not mingle; they share occupations, hardly ever interests. Among such a people the servant always thinks of himself as a temporary guest in his masters’ house. He knew nothing of their forefathers, he will see nothing of their descendants, and he has nothing lasting to expect from them. Why then should he entangle his life with theirs, and where would so strange a surrender of himself come from? The relative position of the two men has changed, so their relations must change as well.

I would gladly illustrate all these reflections with the example of the Americans, but for that purpose I must carefully distinguish persons and places. In the South of the Union slavery exists, so everything I have just said is inapplicable there. In the North most servants are either freedmen or the children of freedmen. These people hold a disputed position in public esteem: the laws raise them to the level of their masters, while the customs of the country stubbornly thrust them back down from it. They do not clearly know their own place themselves, and they are almost always either insolent or cowardly. But in the Northern States, especially in New England, there are a certain number of whites who agree, for wages, to yield temporary obedience to the will of their fellow citizens. I have heard that these servants usually carry out the duties of their situation punctually and intelligently, and that without thinking themselves naturally inferior to the person who gives them orders, they submit to obeying him without reluctance. They seem to me to bring into service some of the manly habits that independence and equality produce. Having once chosen a hard way of life, they do not try to escape it by indirect means, and they respect themselves enough not to refuse their master the obedience they freely promised. For their part, masters ask nothing of their servants but faithful and strict performance of the agreement: they do not ask for marks of respect, nor claim their love or devoted attachment; it is enough that, as servants, they are exact and honest. It would not be true, then, to say that in democratic society the relation of servants and masters is disorganized. It is organized on another footing; the rule is different, but there is a rule.

It is not my purpose to ask whether the new state of things I have just described is inferior to the one before it, or simply different. It is enough for me that it is fixed and settled, for what matters most to find among men is not any particular ordering, but order. But what shall I say of those sad and troubled times when equality is established amid the tumult of revolution — when democracy, though already introduced into the state of society, still struggles with difficulty against the prejudices and customs of the country? The laws, and in part public opinion, already declare that there is no natural or permanent inferiority between servant and master. But this new belief has not yet reached the master’s innermost convictions, or rather his heart rejects it. In the secret persuasion of his mind, the master thinks he belongs to a peculiar and superior race. He dares not say so, but he shudders as he lets himself be dragged to the same level. His authority over his servants becomes timid and harsh at once. He has already stopped feeling toward them the patronizing kindness that long uncontested power always produces, and he is surprised that, now that he himself has changed, his servant changes too. He wants his attendants to form regular and lasting habits in a condition of domestic service that is only temporary. He demands that they appear content with, and proud of, a servile condition they will one day shake off; that they sacrifice themselves to a man who can neither protect nor ruin them; and, in short, that they enter an indissoluble engagement to a being like themselves, who will last no longer than they will.

Among aristocratic nations it often happens that domestic service does not degrade the character of those who enter it, because they know and imagine no other life, and the amazing inequality between them and their master seems the necessary and unavoidable result of some hidden law of Providence. In democracies domestic service does not degrade the character of those who enter it, because it is freely chosen and taken up for a time only, because public opinion does not stigmatize it, and because it creates no permanent inequality between servant and master. But while the passage from one social condition to another is under way, there is almost always a period when people’s minds waver between the aristocratic idea of subjection and the democratic idea of obedience. Obedience then loses its moral importance in the eyes of the one who obeys. He no longer regards it as a kind of divine obligation, and he does not yet see it in its purely human aspect; it has for him no character of sanctity or justice, and he submits to it as a degrading but profitable condition. At that moment a confused, imperfect phantom of equality haunts the minds of servants. They do not immediately see whether the equality to which they are entitled is to be found inside or outside the bounds of domestic service, and in their hearts they rebel against a subordination to which they have submitted themselves and from which they draw real profit. They consent to serve, and they blush to obey; they like the advantages of service, but not the master; or rather, they are not sure that they should not be masters themselves, and they are inclined to regard the one who gives them orders as an unjust usurper of their own rights. That is when the home of every citizen presents a spectacle somewhat like the gloomy look of political society. A secret internal war goes on there between powers that are always rivals and always suspicious of one another. The master is ill-natured and weak, the servant ill-natured and intractable; the one constantly tries to evade, by unfair restrictions, his obligation to protect and to pay, the other his obligation to obey. The reins of domestic government dangle between them, to be snatched by one or the other. The lines dividing authority from oppression, liberty from license, and right from might are so jumbled and blurred in their eyes that no one knows exactly what he is, what he may be, or what he ought to be. Such a condition is not democracy, but revolution.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — That Democratic Institutions And Manners Tend To Raise Rents And Shorten The Terms Of Leases
paragraphs: And Shorten the Terms of Leases

What I have said about servants and masters applies, to a certain extent, to landowners and tenant farmers, but this subject deserves to be considered separately. In America there are, properly speaking, no tenant farmers; every man owns the ground he works. It must be admitted that democratic laws greatly tend to increase the number of landowners and to reduce the number of tenants. Yet what happens in the United States owes much less to the country’s institutions than to the country itself. In America land is cheap, so anyone can easily become a landowner; its returns are small, so its produce cannot well be divided between a landowner and a farmer. In this, as in many other respects, America therefore stands alone, and it would be a mistake to take it as an example.

I believe that in democratic countries, as in aristocratic ones, there will be landowners and tenants, but the connection between them will be of a different kind. In aristocracies the hire of a farm is paid to the landlord not only in rent but in respect, regard, and duty; in democracies all of it is paid in cash. When estates are divided and pass from hand to hand, and the lasting connection that once existed between families and the soil is dissolved, landowner and tenant come into contact only by chance. They meet for a moment to settle the terms of the agreement, then lose sight of each other. They are two strangers brought together by a common interest, who bargain keenly over a business matter whose sole object is to make money.

As property is subdivided and wealth spreads across the country, the community fills with people whose former opulence is declining, and with others whose fortunes are of recent growth and whose wants increase faster than their resources. For all of these people the smallest money profit matters, and none of them is inclined to give up any of his claims or to lose any part of his income. As ranks intermingle, and as very large fortunes and very scanty ones both become rarer, every day brings the social condition of the landowner closer to that of the farmer. Neither has any natural, uncontested superiority over the other. Between two equal men, neither of them comfortable in his circumstances, the contract of hire is purely a matter of money. A man whose estate covers a whole district and who owns a hundred farms knows well how important it is to win the affections of several thousand men at once; this goal seems to demand his efforts, and he will readily make considerable sacrifices to reach it. But the man who owns a hundred acres is untouched by such considerations and cares little about winning his tenant’s private regard.

An aristocracy does not die in a single day, as a man does. The aristocratic principle is slowly undermined in people’s opinion before it is attacked in their laws. Long before open war is declared on it, one can see the tie that had held the higher classes to the lower gradually loosen. One class betrays indifference and contempt, the others jealousy and hatred; contact between rich and poor becomes less frequent and less kindly, and rents are raised. This is not the result of a democratic revolution but its sure forerunner; for an aristocracy that has lost the people’s affection, once and for all, is like a tree dead at the root, which the winds tear up the more easily the higher its branches have spread.

Over the last fifty years the rents of farms have risen amazingly, not only in France but across most of Europe. The remarkable improvements in agriculture and manufactures during the same period do not, in my opinion, suffice to explain this; one must look to another cause, more powerful and more hidden. I believe that cause lies in the democratic institutions that several European nations have adopted, and in the democratic passions that more or less stir all the rest. I have often heard great English landowners congratulate themselves that they now draw a much larger income from their estates than their fathers did. They may well have good reason to be pleased, but they certainly do not know what they are pleased about. They think they are making a clear gain, when in reality they are only making an exchange: they are giving up their influence for cash, and what they gain in money they will soon lose in power.

There is another sign by which it is easy to tell that a great democratic revolution is under way or approaching. In the Middle Ages almost all land was leased for lives or for very long terms; the household economy of that period shows that ninety-nine-year leases were then more common than twelve-year leases are now. People believed then that families were immortal. Men’s conditions seemed settled forever, and all of society seemed so fixed that no one imagined anything in its structure would ever be stirred or shaken. In ages of equality the human mind takes a different bent: the prevailing idea is that nothing lasts, and man is haunted by the thought of change. With this feeling, landowner and tenant alike instinctively dislike long terms of obligation. They fear being bound tomorrow by a contract that benefits them today. They have vague expectations of some sudden, unforeseen change in their conditions; they distrust themselves; they fear that their tastes may change, and that they will regret being unable to rid themselves of what they once coveted. Nor are these fears unfounded, for in democratic ages the most changeable thing, amid the changes all around, is the heart of man.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Influence Of Democracy On Wages
paragraphs: Most of the remarks I have already made about servants and masters may be applied to masters and workmen. As the gradations of the social scale are less and less observed, as the great sink while the humble rise, and as poverty, like opulence, ceases to be hereditary, the distance that once separated the workman from the master, in reality and in opinion, shrinks every day. The workman forms a loftier opinion of his rights, his future, and himself; he is filled with new ambition and new desires, and troubled by new wants. At every moment he looks with longing at his employer’s profits, and in order to share in them he tries to sell his labor at a higher rate, and generally succeeds in the end. In democratic countries, as elsewhere, most branches of productive industry are run at small cost by men whose wealth or education raises them little above the level of those they employ. These manufacturing speculators are extremely numerous; their interests differ, so they cannot easily act in concert or combine their efforts. The workmen, on the other hand, almost always have some sure resources that allow them to refuse work when they cannot get what they consider a fair price for their labor. In the constant struggle over wages between these two classes, their strength is divided and success passes back and forth. It is even probable that in the end the interest of the working class must prevail, for the high wages they have already won make them less dependent on their masters every day, and the more independent they grow, the easier it is for them to win a further increase in wages.

I shall take as my example the branch of productive industry that is still, today, the most widely followed in France and in almost every country in the world — I mean the cultivation of the soil. In France most of those who labor for hire in agriculture own small plots of ground themselves, which are just enough to support them without working for anyone else. When these laborers come to offer their services to a neighboring landowner or farmer and he refuses them a certain rate of wages, they withdraw to their own small property and wait for another opportunity.

I think that, on the whole, it may be asserted that a slow and gradual rise of wages is one of the general laws of democratic communities. As social conditions become more equal, wages rise, and as wages become higher, social conditions become more equal. But in our own time a great and gloomy exception occurs. I showed in an earlier chapter that aristocracy, driven out of political society, has taken refuge in certain departments of productive industry and set up its rule there in another form; this has a powerful effect on the rate of wages. A large capital is required to embark on the great manufacturing speculations I have in mind, so the number of people who enter them is extremely small. Because they are few, they can easily act together and fix the rate of wages as they please. Their workmen, by contrast, are extremely numerous, and their number keeps growing; for from time to time an extraordinary rush of business occurs, during which wages are excessively high and draw the surrounding population into the factories. But once people have taken up that way of life, we have already seen that they cannot leave it again, because they soon acquire habits of body and mind that unfit them for any other kind of toil. These men generally have little education and industry, and few resources; they therefore stand almost at the master’s mercy. When competition or other chance circumstances reduce his profits, he can lower his workmen’s wages almost at will and make up from them what he loses to the chances of business. If the workmen strike, the master, being rich, can easily wait, without being ruined, until necessity brings them back to him; but they must work day by day or die, for their only property is in their hands. Oppression has long since impoverished them, and the poorer they become, the more easily they can be oppressed: they can never escape this fatal circle of cause and effect. It is not surprising, then, that wages in this branch of industry, after sometimes rising suddenly, are lowered for good; whereas in other callings the price of labor, which generally rises only a little, nevertheless keeps going up.

This state of dependence and wretchedness, in which part of the manufacturing population of our time lives, is an exception to the general rule and runs contrary to the state of all the rest of the community. For that very reason, no circumstance is more important or more deserving of the lawmaker’s special attention. When the whole of society is in motion, it is hard to keep any one class standing still; and when most people are opening new paths to fortune, it is no less hard to make the few bear their wants and desires in peace.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — Influence Of Democracy On Kindred
paragraphs: I have just examined how the equality of conditions changes the relations among the members of the community in democratic nations, and among the Americans in particular. Now I want to look deeper, at the closer ties of kindred. My purpose here is not to find new truths, but to show how facts already known connect with my subject.

It has been widely remarked that in our time the members of a family stand on an entirely new footing with one another. The distance that once separated a father from his sons has shrunk, and paternal authority, if not destroyed, is at least weakened. Something similar, but even more striking, can be seen in the United States. In America the family, in the Roman and aristocratic sense of the word, does not exist. Only a few traces of it remain in the first years of childhood, when the father exercises, without opposition, the absolute domestic authority that his children’s helplessness makes necessary, and that both their interest and his own undeniable superiority justify. But as soon as the young American nears manhood, the bonds of filial obedience loosen day by day. Master of his thoughts, he soon becomes master of his conduct. Strictly speaking, America has no adolescence: when boyhood ends, the man appears and begins to mark out his own path. It would be a mistake to imagine that a domestic struggle comes first, in which the son wins by a kind of moral violence the liberty his father denied him. The same habits and the same principles that drive the one to assert his independence dispose the other to regard the use of that independence as an undeniable right. The son shows none of the rancorous or unruly passions that trouble men long after they have thrown off an established authority; the father feels none of the bitter, angry regret that tends to outlast a vanished power. The father foresees the limits of his authority long in advance, and when the time comes he gives it up without a fight. The son looks ahead to the exact moment when he will be his own master, and he enters into his freedom without haste and without effort, as a possession that is his own and that no one tries to wrest from him. *a

[Footnote a: The Americans, however, have not yet seen fit to strip the parent of one of the chief elements of parental authority, as has been done in France, by depriving him of the power to dispose of his property at his death. In the United States a testator’s powers have no restrictions. In this respect, as in almost all others, it is easy to see that although the political legislation of the Americans is much more democratic than that of the French, the civil legislation of the French is infinitely more democratic than that of the Americans. There is an easy explanation. The civil legislation of France was the work of a man who saw that it served his interest to satisfy the democratic passions of his contemporaries in everything that was not directly and immediately hostile to his own power. He was willing to let some popular principles govern the distribution of property and the government of families, so long as they were not brought into the administration of public affairs. While the torrent of democracy swept over the civil laws of the country, he hoped to find an easy shelter behind its political institutions. This policy was both adroit and selfish. But a compromise of this kind could not last, because in the end political institutions always become the image and expression of civil society. In this sense it can be said that nothing in a nation is more political than its civil legislation.]

It may be useful to show how these changes in family relations are closely tied to the social and political revolution that is nearing its completion before our eyes. There are certain great social principles that a people either introduces everywhere or tolerates nowhere. In countries organized on aristocratic lines, with all the gradations of rank, the government never appeals directly to the mass of the governed. Because men are bound together, it is enough to lead the foremost, and the rest will follow. The same holds for the family, as for every aristocracy that has a head. Among aristocratic nations, social institutions in truth recognize no one in the family but the father. Society receives the children from his hands; society governs him, and he governs them. So the parent has not only a natural right but also a political right to command them. He is the author and the support of his family, but he is also its appointed ruler. In democracies, the government singles out each individual from the mass to make him subject to the general laws of the community, and no such intermediary is needed. There, in the eyes of the law, a father is only a member of the community, older and richer than his sons.

When most of the conditions of life are extremely unequal, and that inequality is permanent, the idea of a superior takes a growing hold on people’s imaginations. If the law gave him no privileges, custom and public opinion would grant them. When, on the contrary, men differ little from one another and do not always remain in unlike conditions of life, the general idea of a superior grows weaker and less distinct. It is useless for legislation to try to set the one who obeys far beneath the one who commands; the customs of the time bring the two men closer together and draw them daily toward the same level. Suppose the legislation of an aristocratic people granted heads of families no particular privileges. I would be no less convinced that their power is more respected and more extensive than in a democracy, for I know that, whatever the laws may be, superiors always appear higher and inferiors lower in aristocracies than among democratic nations.

When men live more for the memory of what has been than for the care of what is, and when they are more inclined to attend to what their ancestors thought than to think for themselves, the father is the natural and necessary tie between the past and the present — the link joining the ends of these two chains. In aristocracies, then, the father is not only the civil head of the family but also the oracle of its traditions, the interpreter of its customs, and the arbiter of its mores. He is heard with deference and addressed with respect, and the love felt for him is always tempered with fear. When the condition of society becomes democratic, and men adopt as their general principle that it is good and lawful to judge all things for oneself — using earlier beliefs not as a rule of faith but simply as a source of information — the power of a father’s opinions over those of his sons shrinks, as his legal power does.

Perhaps nothing contributes more to changing the relations between a father and his children than the division of estates that democracy brings with it. When the father of a family has little property, he and his son live constantly in the same place and share the same occupations. Habit and necessity bring them together and force them into constant contact. The inevitable result is a kind of familiar intimacy, which makes authority less absolute and can hardly be reconciled with outward forms of respect. Now in democratic countries the class of those who hold small fortunes is precisely the class that gives strength to the ideas, and a particular direction to the mores, of the community. That class makes its opinions prevail as universally as its will, and even those most inclined to resist its commands are carried along in the end by its example. I have known eager opponents of democracy who let their children address them with perfect colloquial equality.

Thus, as the power of aristocracy declines, the austere, conventional and legal part of parental authority disappears, and a kind of equality prevails around the domestic hearth. I do not know whether society, on the whole, loses by the change, but I am inclined to believe that the individual gains by it. I think that as mores and laws become more democratic, the relation between father and son becomes more intimate and more affectionate. People speak less of rules and authority; confidence and tenderness often increase; and it seems that the natural bond tightens as the social bond loosens. In a democratic family the father exercises no power except what people love to give to the affection and experience of age. His orders might perhaps be disobeyed, but his advice is for the most part respected as authoritative. He is not hedged in by ceremonial respect, yet his sons at least approach him with confidence. No set form of speech is reserved for addressing him; they talk to him constantly and are ready to consult him day by day. The master and the appointed ruler have vanished; the father remains. To judge how the two states of society differ in this respect, one needs only to read the family correspondence of aristocratic ages. The style is always correct, ceremonious and stiff, and so cold that the natural warmth of the heart can hardly be felt in the language. The language a son addresses to his father in democratic countries, by contrast, always mixes freedom, familiarity and affection, which shows at once that new relations have sprung up within the family.

A similar revolution takes place in the relations of children to one another. In aristocratic families, as in aristocratic society, every place is marked out in advance. Not only does the father hold a separate rank, with extensive privileges, but even the children are not equal among themselves. Each child’s age and sex fix his rank irrevocably and secure him certain privileges. Democracy abolishes or reduces most of these distinctions. In aristocratic families the eldest son inherits the greater part of the property and almost all the rights of the family, and so becomes the chief, and to some extent the master, of his brothers. Greatness and power are for him; mediocrity and dependence are for them. Nevertheless, it would be wrong to suppose that among aristocratic nations the eldest son’s privileges benefit himself alone, or that they arouse only envy and hatred in those around him. The eldest son usually tries to win wealth and power for his brothers, because the general splendor of the house reflects back on the one who represents it. The younger sons try to support their elder brother in all his undertakings, because the greatness and power of the head of the family put him in a better position to provide for every branch. The members of an aristocratic family are therefore bound very closely together. Their interests are linked and their minds agree, but their hearts are seldom in harmony.

Democracy also binds brothers to one another, but by very different means. Under democratic laws all the children are perfectly equal, and therefore independent. Nothing forcibly brings them together, but nothing keeps them apart. They have the same origin, they are brought up under the same roof, they are treated with the same care, and no particular privilege distinguishes or divides them. So the affectionate, youthful intimacy of the early years easily grows up between them. Hardly any occasion arises to break the tie formed at the start of life, because their brotherhood brings them together every day without embarrassing them. It is not, then, by interest but by shared associations and by the free sympathy of opinion and taste that democracy unites brothers. It divides their inheritance, but it lets their hearts and minds mingle. Such is the charm of these democratic mores that even the partisans of aristocracy are won over by it. After experiencing it for some time, they are not at all tempted to go back to the respectful, frigid observance of aristocratic families. They would gladly keep the domestic habits of democracy if they could cast off its social conditions and its laws. But these elements are inseparably joined, and it is impossible to enjoy the former without putting up with the latter. What I have said about filial love and fraternal affection applies to all the passions that arise spontaneously from human nature itself. If a certain way of thinking or feeling results from some particular condition of life, then when that condition changes, nothing at all remains of the thought or feeling. A law may bind two members of the community very closely to each other, but once that law is abolished, they stand apart. Nothing was stricter than the tie that joined the vassal to the lord under the feudal system. Today the two men do not know each other. The fear, the gratitude and the affection that once connected them have vanished, and not a trace of the tie remains. This is not the case, however, with the feelings that are natural to mankind. Whenever a law tries to direct these feelings in a particular way, it nearly always weakens them. By trying to increase their intensity, it strips them of some of their elements, for they are never stronger than when left to themselves.

Democracy destroys or obscures almost all the old conventional rules of society, and it keeps men from readily accepting new ones. As a result, it entirely wipes out most of the feelings that those conventional rules gave rise to. Others it only modifies, and it often gives them a degree of energy and sweetness unknown before. Perhaps the whole meaning of this chapter, and of several earlier ones, can be condensed into a single proposition. Democracy loosens social ties but draws the ties of nature tighter; it brings kindred closer together while setting the various members of the community farther apart.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — Education Of Young Women In The United States
paragraphs: No free communities have ever existed without morals, and, as I observed in the earlier part of this work, morals are the work of woman. Whatever affects the condition of women, their habits and their opinions, therefore has great political importance in my eyes. Among almost all Protestant nations, young women are far more in charge of their own actions than they are in Catholic countries. This independence is greater still in Protestant countries like England, which have kept or gained the right of self-government; there, political habits and religious opinions bring the spirit of freedom into the domestic circle. In the United States, the doctrines of Protestantism are joined with great political freedom and a most democratic state of society, and nowhere are young women left so early or so completely to their own guidance. Long before an American girl reaches marriageable age, her release from her mother’s control begins. She has hardly stopped being a child when she already thinks for herself, speaks freely and acts on her own impulse. The great scene of the world lies constantly open before her. Far from being hidden from her, it is shown to her more fully every day, and she is taught to look at it with a steady and calm gaze. So the vices and dangers of society are revealed to her early. She sees them clearly, looks at them without illusions and faces them without fear, for she is full of reliance on her own strength, and everyone around her seems to share that reliance. An American girl almost never shows the virginal bloom amid youthful desires, or the innocent, artless grace that usually accompanies the European woman in the passage from girlhood to youth. It is rare for an American woman, at any age, to show childish timidity or ignorance. Like the young women of Europe, she wants to please, but she knows exactly what pleasing costs. If she does not give herself up to evil, at least she knows that it exists, and she is notable more for purity of conduct than for chastity of mind. I have often been surprised, and almost alarmed, by the remarkable skill and happy boldness with which young women in America manage their thoughts and their words through all the difficulties of a stimulating conversation. A philosopher would have stumbled at every step along the narrow path they walked without accident and without effort. It is easy to see that even in the independence of early youth, an American woman is always mistress of herself. She enjoys every permitted pleasure without surrendering to any of them, and her reason never lets the reins of self-guidance fall, though it often seems to hold them loosely.

In France, the opinions and tastes of the people still mix the remnants of every age in strange ways. There, women commonly receive a reserved, secluded and almost cloistered education, as they did in aristocratic times, and then they are suddenly left, without a guide and without help, amid all the irregularities that cannot be separated from democratic society. The Americans are more consistent. They have discovered that in a democracy the independence of individuals cannot fail to be very great, youth premature, tastes poorly restrained, customs fleeting, public opinion often unsettled and powerless, paternal authority weak and marital authority contested. In these circumstances, they believed they had little chance of suppressing the most violent passions of the human heart in woman, and they concluded that the surer way was to teach her the art of fighting those passions herself. Since they could not keep her virtue from being exposed to frequent danger, they resolved that she should know how best to defend it. They placed more trust in the free vigor of her will than in safeguards that have been shaken or overthrown. Instead of teaching her to distrust herself, then, they constantly try to build up her confidence in her own strength of character. Because it is neither possible nor desirable to keep a young woman in perpetual or complete ignorance, they hurry to give her early knowledge on every subject. Far from hiding the corruptions of the world from her, they would rather she saw them at once and trained herself to avoid them, and they think it more important to protect her conduct than to be overly scrupulous about her innocence.

The Americans are a very religious people, yet they do not rely on religion alone to defend a woman’s virtue; they also try to arm her reason. In this they follow the same method as in several other matters. They first make the most vigorous efforts to get individual independence to exercise proper control over itself, and they do not call on the aid of religion until they have reached the utmost limits of human strength. I am aware that an education of this kind is not without danger. I realize that it tends to strengthen the judgment at the expense of the imagination, and to produce cold and virtuous women rather than affectionate wives and agreeable companions for men. Society may be calmer and better regulated, but domestic life often has fewer charms. These, however, are secondary evils, which can be faced for the sake of higher interests. At the stage we have now reached, the time for choosing is no longer in our hands. A democratic education is indispensable to protect women from the dangers that democratic institutions and mores place around them.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — The Young Woman In The Character Of A Wife
paragraphs: In America a woman’s independence is lost for good in the bonds of marriage. An unmarried woman is less restrained there than elsewhere, but a wife is held to stricter obligations. The one makes her father’s house a place of freedom and pleasure; the other lives in her husband’s home as if in a cloister. Yet these two conditions of life are perhaps not as opposed as one might suppose, and it is natural for American women to pass through the one to reach the other.

Religious peoples and trading nations take marriage with particular seriousness. The former consider the regularity of a woman’s life the best pledge and surest sign of the purity of her morals; the latter see it as the strongest guarantee of order and prosperity in the household. The Americans are at once a puritanical people and a commercial nation. Their religious opinions and their trading habits therefore both lead them to demand much self-denial from woman, and a constant sacrifice of her pleasures to her duties that is seldom required of her in Europe. So in the United States public opinion, which allows no exceptions, carefully confines woman within the narrow circle of domestic interests and duties and forbids her to step outside it.

When a young American woman enters the world, she finds these ideas firmly established. She sees the rules that follow from them, and she quickly realizes that she cannot depart for a moment from the established usages of her contemporaries without risking her peace of mind, her honor, even her social existence. She finds the energy for such an act of submission in the firmness of her understanding and in the manly habits her education has given her. It may be said that by using her independence she has learned to give it up, without a struggle and without a murmur, when the time comes for the sacrifice. But no American woman falls into the toils of marriage as into a snare laid for her simplicity and ignorance. She has been taught beforehand what is expected of her, and she enters this engagement voluntarily and freely. She bears her new condition with courage, because she chose it. In America paternal discipline is very relaxed and the marriage tie very strict, so a young woman does not take on the latter without considerable caution and apprehension. Early marriages are rare.
