American women therefore do not marry until their understandings have been exercised and have matured, whereas in other countries most women generally begin to exercise and mature their understandings only after marriage.

I do not at all suppose, however, that the great change in all the habits of women in the United States as soon as they marry should be attributed only to the pressure of public opinion. Often they impose it on themselves, by their own will alone. When the time comes to choose a husband, the cold and stern power of reasoning, educated and strengthened by free observation of the world, teaches an American woman that a spirit of levity and independence within the bonds of marriage is a constant source of annoyance, not of pleasure. It tells her that a girl’s amusements cannot become a wife’s recreations, and that the sources of a married woman’s happiness lie in her husband’s home. She sees clearly beforehand the only road that can lead to domestic happiness, so she enters upon it at once and follows it to the end without trying to turn back.

The same strength of purpose that young wives in America show in bending themselves at once, and without complaint, to the austere duties of their new condition is just as plain in all the great trials of their lives. In no country in the world are private fortunes more precarious than in the United States. It is not unusual for the same man, in the course of his life, to rise and fall again through all the grades that lead from wealth to poverty. American women endure these changes of fortune with calm and unquenchable energy. It seems that their desires shrink as easily as they grow with their fortunes. *a
[Footnote a: See Appendix S.]

Most of the adventurers who migrate every year to settle the western wilds belong, as I noted in the earlier part of this work, to the old Anglo-American race of the Northern States. Many of these men, who rush so boldly forward in pursuit of wealth, already enjoyed a comfortable living in their own part of the country. They take their wives with them and make them share the countless dangers and hardships that always accompany the start of these expeditions. I have often met young women, even on the edge of the wilderness, who had been raised amid all the comforts of the large towns of New England and had gone, almost without any intermediate stage, from their parents’ wealthy home to a comfortless hovel in a forest. Fever, solitude and a tedious life had not broken the springs of their courage. Their features were worn and faded, but their looks were firm; they seemed at once sad and resolute. I do not doubt that these young American women had stored up, in the education of their early years, the inward strength they showed in these circumstances. In the United States, then, the girl’s early training can still be traced in the married woman. Her role has changed and her habits are different, but her character is the same.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — That The Equality Of Conditions Contributes To The Maintenance Of Good Morals In America
paragraphs: Maintenance of Good Morals in America

Some philosophers and historians have claimed, or hinted, that the strictness of women’s morals rises or falls simply with a country’s distance from the equator. That was an easy answer: all it took was a globe and a pair of compasses to settle in an instant one of the hardest problems of human life. But I know of no facts that support this doctrine of the materialists. The same nations have been chaste at one time in their history and dissolute at another. So the strictness or laxity of their morals must have depended on some cause that changes, and not only on the natural features of their country, which never changed. I do not deny that in certain climates the passions arising from the mutual attraction of the sexes are unusually intense. But I believe that this natural intensity can always be stirred up or held in check by the condition of society and by political institutions.

Travelers who have visited North America disagree on a great many points, yet they all remark that morals there are far stricter than anywhere else. On this point the Americans are clearly far superior to their ancestors, the English. A superficial glance at the two nations is enough to establish it. In England, as in every other country of Europe, public malice is forever attacking the frailties of women. Philosophers and statesmen can be heard lamenting that morals are not strict enough, and the country’s literature constantly suggests as much. In America every book, novels included, takes women to be chaste, and no one thinks of telling tales of gallantry. No doubt this great regularity of American morals comes partly from the country, from the race of its people, and from their religion. But these causes, which operate elsewhere too, are not enough to account for it; some special reason must be found. That reason seems to me to be the principle of equality and the institutions that follow from it. Equality of conditions does not by itself produce regularity of morals, but it undoubtedly makes it easier and increases it. *a [Footnote a: See Appendix T.]

Among aristocratic nations, birth and fortune often make man and woman such different beings that they can never be joined to each other. Their passions draw them together, but the condition of society and the ideas it suggests keep them from forming a lasting and public bond. The inevitable result is a great number of brief, secret liaisons. Nature quietly takes revenge for the restraint that human laws place on her. It is much less so when equality of conditions has swept away all the barriers, imaginary or real, that separated man from woman. No girl then believes that she cannot become the wife of the man who loves her, and this makes any breach of morality before marriage very uncommon. For however credulous the passions may be, a woman can hardly persuade herself that she is loved when her lover is perfectly free to marry her and does not.

The same cause works, though more indirectly, on married life. Nothing does more to justify an illicit passion, in the eyes of those who feel it and of the world that watches, than a forced or accidental marriage. *b In a country where a woman is always free to exercise her power of choice, and where her education has prepared her to choose well, public opinion shows her faults no mercy. The strictness of the Americans comes in part from this. They regard marriage as a covenant that is often burdensome, but one whose every condition the parties are strictly bound to fulfill, because they knew all those conditions beforehand and were perfectly free not to enter into it.

[Footnote b: The literature of Europe amply confirms this remark. When a European author wants to portray in a work of imagination one of those great catastrophes of married life that happen so often among us, he takes care to win the reader’s sympathy by showing him ill-matched or forced marriages. Long-standing tolerance has relaxed our morals, yet an author could hardly interest us in the misfortunes of his characters if he did not first excuse their faults. This device seldom fails, because the scenes we see every day have prepared us long in advance to be indulgent. But American writers could never make such excuses believable to their readers. Their customs and laws are against it, and since they despair of making loose conduct appealing, they stop depicting it. This is one of the causes to which the small number of novels published in the United States must be attributed.]

The very circumstances that make marital fidelity more of a duty also make it easier. In aristocratic countries the aim of marriage is to unite properties rather than persons; so the husband is sometimes still at school and the wife still with her nurse when they are betrothed. It is no wonder that the conjugal tie, which holds the couple’s fortunes together, lets their hearts wander. That is the natural result of the nature of the contract. When, on the contrary, a man always chooses his wife for himself, with no outside compulsion or even guidance, it is generally a likeness of tastes and opinions that brings a man and a woman together, and the same likeness keeps them close and settles them in habits of intimacy.

Our forefathers had formed a very strange idea about marriage. They had noticed that the few love matches of their day almost always turned out badly, and they firmly concluded that it was exceedingly dangerous to follow the dictates of the heart in this matter. Chance seemed to them a better guide than choice. Yet it was not hard to see that the examples they witnessed proved nothing at all. In the first place, if democratic nations leave a woman free to choose her husband, they take care to give her mind enough knowledge and her will enough strength to make so important a choice. The young women of aristocratic nations, by contrast, who slip away secretly from their parents’ authority and throw themselves of their own accord into the arms of men they have had neither the time to know nor the ability to judge, are wholly without those safeguards. It is not surprising that they misuse their freedom of action the first time they take it, nor that they fall into such cruel mistakes when, having had no democratic education, they choose to marry according to democratic customs. But that is not all. When a man and a woman are set on marrying despite the differences of an aristocratic state of society, the difficulties to be overcome are enormous. Having broken or loosened the bonds of filial obedience, they must then free themselves by one last effort from the sway of custom and the tyranny of opinion. And when at length they have accomplished this arduous task, they find themselves estranged from their natural friends and kinsmen: the prejudice they have defied separates them from everyone and puts them in a situation that soon breaks their courage and sours their hearts. If a couple married in this way are first unhappy and later guilty, then, this should not be blamed on the freedom of their choice but on their living in a community where that freedom is not admitted.

Moreover, we should not forget that the same effort that makes a man violently throw off a prevailing error usually carries him past the bounds of reason. To dare to declare war, however just the cause, on the opinion of one’s age and country takes a violent and adventurous spirit, and men of that character seldom reach happiness or virtue, whatever path they follow. This, incidentally, is why in the most necessary and righteous revolutions it is so rare to find virtuous or moderate revolutionary figures. There is therefore no good reason for surprise if a man who, in an age of aristocracy, consults nothing but his own opinion and taste in choosing a wife soon finds breaches of morality and domestic misery invading his household. But when this same course of action belongs to the natural and ordinary order of things, when it is sanctioned by parental authority and backed by public opinion, there can be no doubt that it will increase the inner peace of families and make conjugal fidelity more strictly observed.

Almost all men in democracies are engaged in public or professional life; and meanwhile the modest size of ordinary incomes obliges a wife to stay at home and watch over the details of domestic economy in person and very closely. All these separate and compulsory occupations are so many natural barriers. By keeping the two sexes apart, they make the advances of the one less frequent and less ardent, and the resistance of the other easier.

Not that equality of conditions can ever succeed in making men chaste, but it may give their breaches of morality a less dangerous character. Since no one then has enough time or opportunity to assail a virtue that is armed in its own defense, there will be, side by side, a great number of courtesans and a great number of virtuous women. This state of things causes lamentable cases of individual hardship, but it does not keep the body of society from being strong and alert. It does not destroy family ties or weaken the morals of the nation. Society is endangered not by the great profligacy of a few, but by laxity of morals among all. In the eyes of a legislator, prostitution is less to be feared than intrigue.

The restless, ceaselessly harried life that equality makes men lead not only distracts them from the passion of love, by leaving them no time to indulge it, but also turns them away from it by another road, more hidden but more certain. All men who live in democratic ages take on, to some degree, the ways of thinking of the manufacturing and trading classes. Their minds take a serious, deliberate, and practical turn. They tend to give up the ideal in order to pursue some visible, nearby object that seems the natural and necessary aim of their desires. Thus the principle of equality does not destroy the imagination, but it lowers its flight to the level of the earth. No men are less given to reverie than the citizens of a democracy, and few of them are ever known to yield to those idle, solitary musings that usually precede and produce the great emotions of the heart. It is true that they set great store by obtaining for themselves the kind of deep, steady, quiet affection that is the charm and safeguard of life. But they are not inclined to chase after those violent and capricious sources of excitement that disturb it and cut it short.

I am aware that all this applies in its full extent only to America and cannot at present be extended to Europe. Over the last half-century, while laws and customs have driven several European nations toward democracy with unprecedented force, we have had no occasion to observe that the relations between man and woman have become more orderly or more chaste. In some places one may detect the very reverse: some classes are stricter, while the general morality of the people appears laxer. I do not hesitate to say so, for I am as little inclined to flatter my contemporaries as to slander them. This fact must distress us, but it ought not to surprise us. The favorable influence that a democratic state of society may have on orderly habits is one of those tendencies that can only be discovered after some time. If equality of conditions favors purity of morals, the social upheaval by which conditions are made equal works against it. During the last fifty years, in which France has been going through this transformation, that country has rarely had freedom and always had disturbance. Amid this universal confusion of ideas and general stir of opinions, amid this incoherent mixture of the just and the unjust, of truth and falsehood, of right and might, public virtue has become doubtful and private morality unsteady. But all revolutions, whatever their aim or their agents, have at first produced similar consequences; even those that in the end drew the bonds of morality tighter began by loosening them. The violations of morality that the French so often witness do not seem to me permanent, and some curious signs of the times already point that way.

Nothing is more wretchedly corrupt than an aristocracy that keeps its wealth after it has lost its power, and that still has a great deal of leisure after being reduced to ordinary, vulgar pastimes. The energetic passions and great conceptions that once animated it then leave it, and nothing remains but a swarm of petty, consuming vices that cling to it like worms on a carcass. No one denies that the French aristocracy of the last century was extremely dissolute, whereas established habits and ancient belief still preserved some respect for morality among the other classes of society. Nor will anyone dispute that today the remnants of that same aristocracy show a certain severity of morals, while laxity of morals seems to have spread among the middle and lower ranks. So the very families that were most profligate fifty years ago are now the most exemplary, and democracy seems only to have strengthened the morality of the aristocratic classes. The French Revolution divided the fortunes of the nobility, forced them to attend closely to their affairs and their families, made them live under the same roof as their children, and in short gave their minds a more rational and serious turn. In this way it gave them, almost without their realizing it, a reverence for religious belief, a love of order, of quiet pleasures, of domestic affection, and of comfort. The rest of the nation, which naturally had these same tastes, was swept into excesses by the effort needed to overthrow the country’s laws and political habits. The old French aristocracy has undergone the consequences of the Revolution, but it neither felt the revolutionary passions nor shared in the anarchic excitement that produced that crisis. It is easy to see that this aristocracy feels the salutary influence of the Revolution in its customs before those who carried it out. It may therefore be said, however paradoxical it first appears, that today the most anti-democratic classes of the nation are the ones chiefly showing the kind of morality that one may reasonably expect from democracy. I cannot help thinking that when we have obtained all the effects of this democratic Revolution, and have got past the tumult it has caused, the observations that now hold true only of a few will gradually become true of the whole community.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — How The Americans Understand The Equality Of The Sexes
paragraphs: I have shown how democracy destroys or modifies the various inequalities that arise in society. But is that all? Does it not in the end also affect that great inequality of man and woman, which until today has seemed to rest eternally on human nature? I believe that the social changes that bring father and son, master and servant, and superiors and inferiors in general closer to the same level will raise woman as well, and make her more and more the equal of man. But here, more than ever, I feel the need to make myself clearly understood, for there is no subject on which the coarse and lawless fancies of our age have ranged more freely.

There are people in Europe who confuse the distinct characteristics of the sexes and would make man and woman not merely equal but alike. They would give both the same functions, lay on both the same duties, and grant both the same rights; they would mix them together in everything: their occupations, their pleasures, their business. It is easy to see that by trying to make one sex equal to the other in this way, one degrades both; and from so absurd a jumble of nature’s works nothing could ever come but weak men and disorderly women. This is not how the Americans understand the kind of democratic equality that may be established between the sexes. They admit that, since nature has set such wide differences between the physical and moral constitution of man and woman, her evident design was to give their various faculties distinct employments. They hold that improvement does not lie in making beings so unlike do nearly the same things, but in getting each of them to carry out their own tasks as well as possible. The Americans have applied to the sexes the great principle of political economy that governs the manufactures of our age: they carefully divide the duties of man from those of woman, so that the great work of society may be better carried on.

In no country has such constant care been taken as in America to draw two clearly separate lines of action for the two sexes and to have them keep pace with each other, but on paths that are always different. American women never manage the family’s outside affairs, or run a business, or take part in political life. Nor, on the other hand, are they ever forced to do the rough labor of the fields or any of those heavy tasks that demand physical strength. No family is so poor as to be an exception to this rule. If an American woman cannot escape the quiet circle of domestic occupations, neither is she ever forced to go beyond it. So it is that the women of America, who often show a masculine strength of understanding and a manly energy, generally keep great delicacy of personal appearance and always keep the habits of women, although they sometimes prove that they have the hearts and minds of men.

Nor have the Americans ever supposed that one consequence of democratic principles is the overthrow of marital power or the confusion of the natural authorities within the family. They hold that every association must have a head if it is to achieve its purpose, and that the natural head of the conjugal association is the man. They therefore do not deny him the right to direct his partner. They maintain that in the small association of husband and wife, as in the great social community, the object of democracy is to regulate and legalize the powers that are necessary, not to overthrow all power. This opinion is not held by one sex and disputed by the other. I never observed that the women of America regard conjugal authority as a fortunate usurpation of their rights, or that they thought themselves degraded by submitting to it. It seemed to me, on the contrary, that they take a kind of pride in the voluntary surrender of their own will, and make it their boast to bend to the yoke rather than shake it off. Such at least is the feeling expressed by the most virtuous of their sex; the others stay silent; and in the United States it is not the practice for a guilty wife to clamor for the rights of women while she tramples on her holiest duties.

It has often been remarked that in Europe a certain contempt lurks even in the flattery men lavish on women. A European often pretends to be woman’s slave, yet it can be seen that he never sincerely thinks her his equal. In the United States men seldom pay compliments to women, but every day they show how much they esteem them. They constantly display complete confidence in a wife’s understanding and deep respect for her freedom. They have decided that her mind is as fit as a man’s to discover plain truth, and her heart as firm in embracing it; and they have never tried to shelter her virtue, any more than his, behind prejudice, ignorance, and fear. In Europe, where man so easily submits to the despotic sway of women, it seems that women are nonetheless cut off from some of the greatest qualities of the human species and regarded as seductive but imperfect beings. And, what may well provoke astonishment, women in the end see themselves in the same light, and almost regard it as a privilege that they are entitled to show themselves frivolous, feeble, and timid. The women of America claim no such privileges.

Again, it may be said that in our morals we have reserved strange immunities for man, so that there is, as it were, one virtue for his use and another to guide his partner, and that in the view of the public the very same act may be punished at one time as a crime and at another as merely a fault. The Americans do not know this unjust division of duties and rights; among them the seducer is as dishonored as his victim. It is true that the Americans rarely lavish on women the eager attentions commonly paid to them in Europe. But their conduct toward women always implies that they suppose them virtuous and refined. Such is their respect for the moral freedom of the sex that in a woman’s presence the most guarded language is used, lest her ear be offended by some expression. In America a young unmarried woman can undertake a long journey alone and without fear.

The legislators of the United States, who have softened almost all the penalties of criminal law, still make rape a capital offense, and public opinion punishes no crime with more unrelenting severity. This can be explained. The Americans can conceive of nothing more precious than a woman’s honor, and nothing that ought to be more respected than her independence, so they hold that no punishment is too severe for the man who takes them from her against her will. In France, where the same offense is punished with far milder penalties, it is often difficult to get a jury to convict the accused. Does this come from contempt for decency or contempt for women? I cannot help believing that it is contempt for both.

So the Americans do not believe that man and woman have the duty or the right to do the same things. They do, however, hold both of their roles in equal regard, and although the two lots differ, they treat the two as beings of equal worth. They do not give woman’s courage the same form or direction as man’s, but they never doubt that she has it. And if they think a man and his partner should not always use their intellect and understanding in the same way, they at least believe her understanding to be as sound as his, and her intellect as clear. Thus, while leaving woman’s social inferiority in place, they have done everything they could to raise her morally and intellectually to the level of man. In this respect they seem to me to have grasped the true principle of democratic improvement remarkably well. For my part, I do not hesitate to say that, although the women of the United States are confined within the narrow circle of domestic life, and their situation is in some respects one of extreme dependence, I have nowhere seen woman hold a loftier position. And suppose I were asked, now that I am near the end of this work, in which I have described so many important things the Americans have done, what the singular prosperity and growing strength of that people should chiefly be credited to. I would answer: to the superiority of their women.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — That The Principle Of Equality Naturally Divides The Americans Into A Number Of Small Private Circles
paragraphs: Americans into a Number of Small Private Circles

One might suppose that the final consequence and necessary effect of democratic institutions is to throw all members of the community together in private as well as public life, and to force them all to live in common. But that would be to give the equality that arises from democracy a very crude and oppressive form. No state of society and no laws can make men so alike that education, fortune, and tastes will not put some differences between them. And although different men may sometimes find it in their interest to combine for the same purposes, they will never make it their pleasure. They will therefore always tend to evade the provisions of the law, whatever those may be. Departing in some one respect from the circle within which they were meant to be confined, they will set up, close beside the great political community, small private circles united by the similarity of their conditions, habits, and customs.

In the United States the citizens have no kind of superiority over one another; they owe each other neither obedience nor respect. They all meet to administer justice, to govern the State, and in general to treat the affairs that concern their common welfare. But I have never heard that anyone has tried to bring them all to follow the same amusements, or to enjoy themselves indiscriminately in the same places of recreation. The Americans, who mix so readily in their political assemblies and courts of justice, make a habit on the contrary of dividing carefully into small, distinct circles, so as to enjoy the pleasures of private life by themselves. Each of them is willing to acknowledge all his fellow citizens as his equals, but he will receive only a very small number of them as friends or guests. This seems to me quite natural. As the circle of public society widens, one can expect the sphere of private intercourse to narrow. Far from supposing that the members of modern society will end up living in common, I fear they may end by forming nothing but small coteries.

Among aristocratic nations the different classes are like vast chambers: one cannot get out of them or enter them. The classes have no communication with one another, but within each one’s bounds men necessarily live in daily contact. Even if they would not naturally suit, the general conformity of a similar condition brings them closer together. But when neither law nor custom claims to establish frequent and habitual relations between certain men, their dealings arise from a chance likeness of opinions and tastes, and so private society is infinitely varied. In democracies, where the members of the community never differ much from each other and naturally stand so close together that they could at any moment be merged into one general mass, numerous artificial and arbitrary distinctions spring up. Through them each man hopes to keep himself apart, for fear of being carried off in the crowd against his will. This can never fail to happen, for human institutions may be changed, but man cannot. However much a community may try to make its members equal and alike, the personal pride of individuals will always seek to rise above the line and to create somewhere an inequality to their own advantage.

In aristocracies men are separated from one another by lofty, fixed barriers; in democracies they are divided by a multitude of small, almost invisible threads, which are constantly broken or moved from place to place. Thus, whatever the progress of equality, a great number of small private communities will always form within the general bounds of political society in democratic nations. But none of them will resemble in its customs the highest class in aristocracies.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — Some Reflections On American Manners
paragraphs: At first sight nothing seems less important than the outward form of human actions, yet nothing matters more to men: they get used to everything except living in a society whose manners are not their own. The influence of a country’s social and political state on its manners therefore deserves serious examination. Manners are in general the product of the very basis of a people’s character, but they are also sometimes the result of an arbitrary convention among certain men; so they are at once natural and acquired. When certain men see that they are the foremost persons in society, without contest and without effort; when they are constantly occupied with large objects and leave the smaller details to others; and when they live in the enjoyment of wealth they did not amass and do not fear to lose; one may suppose that they feel a kind of haughty disdain for the petty interests and practical cares of life, and that their thoughts take on a natural greatness, which their language and manners show. In democratic countries manners generally lack dignity, because private life there is extremely petty in character; and they are often low, because the mind has few opportunities to rise above the absorbing cares of domestic interests. True dignity in manners consists in always taking one’s proper place, neither too high nor too low; and this is as much within the reach of a peasant as of a prince. In democracies every station appears uncertain. So the manners of democracies, though often full of arrogance, usually lack dignity, and moreover they are never either well disciplined or accomplished.

The men who live in democracies are too unsettled for any number of them ever to succeed in laying down a code of good breeding and forcing people to follow it. Every man therefore behaves in his own way, and there is always a certain incoherence in the manners of such times, because they are shaped by the feelings and ideas of each individual rather than by an ideal model offered for general imitation. This is much more noticeable, however, just after an aristocracy has been overthrown than long after it has been destroyed. New political institutions and new social elements then bring together in the same gathering places, and often force to live in common, men whose education and habits are still amazingly different, and this makes the motley composition of society especially visible. People still remember that a strict code of good breeding once existed, but what it contained or where to find it has already been forgotten. Men have lost the common law of manners, and they have not yet made up their minds to do without it; but everyone tries to build for himself some arbitrary and changeable rule from the remnants of former usages. So manners have neither the regularity and dignity they often show among aristocratic nations, nor the simplicity and freedom they sometimes take on in democracies: they are at once constrained and unconstrained.

This, however, is not the normal state of things. When equality of conditions is long established and complete, all men hold nearly the same ideas and do nearly the same things, so they need not agree or copy one another in order to speak or act in the same way. Their manners are constantly marked by a number of lesser diversities, but not by any great differences. They are never perfectly alike, because they do not copy the same pattern; they are never very unlike, because their social condition is the same. At first sight a traveler would observe that the manners of all Americans are exactly alike; only on close examination can one detect the peculiarities in which they differ.

The English poke fun at the manners of the Americans. It is odd, though, that most of the writers who sketched these ludicrous portraits belonged themselves to the middle classes in England, and the portraits fit those classes perfectly well. These merciless critics thus mostly illustrate the very thing they condemn in the United States. They do not see that they are ridiculing themselves, to the great amusement of the aristocracy of their own country.

Nothing is more harmful to democracy than its outward forms of behavior: many men would willingly put up with its vices who cannot bear its manners. Yet I cannot admit that there is nothing commendable in the manners of a democratic people. Among aristocratic nations, everyone who lives within reach of the first class in society commonly strains to be like it, which gives rise to ridiculous and insipid imitations. A democratic people has no models of high breeding, so at least it is spared the daily sight of wretched copies of them. In democracies manners are never as refined as among aristocratic nations, but on the other hand they are never as coarse. There one hears neither the coarse oaths of the populace nor the elegant and choice expressions of the nobility: the manners of such a people are often vulgar, but they are neither brutal nor mean. I have already observed that in democracies no regular code of good breeding can be laid down; this has some drawbacks and some advantages. In aristocracies the rules of propriety impose the same demeanor on everyone; they make all members of the same class look alike, whatever their private inclinations; they adorn the natural man and they conceal him. Among a democratic people manners are neither so schooled nor so uniform, but they are often more sincere. They form, as it were, a light and loosely woven veil through which the real feelings and private opinions of each individual are easily seen. The form and the substance of human actions therefore often stand in closer relation; and if the great picture of human life is less embellished, it is truer. So it may be said, in one sense, that the effect of democracy is not exactly to give men any particular manners, but to keep them from having manners at all.

The feelings, passions, virtues, and vices of an aristocracy may sometimes reappear in a democracy, but its manners cannot; they are lost, and vanish forever, as soon as the democratic revolution is complete. Nothing seems more lasting than the manners of an aristocratic class, for that class preserves them for some time after it has lost its wealth and power; and nothing seems more fleeting, for no sooner have they disappeared than not a trace of them can be found, and it is scarcely possible to say what they were once they have ceased to be. A change in the state of society works this miracle, and a few generations are enough to complete it. History hands down the principal characteristics of an aristocracy after its destruction, but the light and exquisite touches of its manners are wiped from men’s memories almost as soon as it falls. When men have ceased to see these manners, they can no longer conceive what they were; they are gone, and their departure was unseen and unfelt. For to feel the refined enjoyment that comes from choice and distinguished manners, habit and education must have prepared the heart, and the taste for them is lost almost as easily as the practice of them. Thus a democratic people not only cannot have aristocratic manners, but neither understands nor desires them; and since they have never thought of them, to their minds it is as if such things had never been. Too much importance should not be attached to this loss, but it may well be regretted.

I know that the same men have often joined very refined manners to very base feelings; a look inside the courts shows well enough how imposing an exterior can hide the meanest hearts. Yet even if aristocratic manners were not virtue, they sometimes adorned virtue itself. It was a remarkable sight: a large and powerful class of men whose every outward act seemed guided by a natural loftiness of thought and feeling, by delicate and orderly taste, and by courtesy. Those manners spread a pleasing, illusory charm over human nature. The picture was often false, but no one could look at it without a noble satisfaction.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — Of The Gravity Of The Americans, And Why It Does Not Prevent Them From Often Committing Inconsiderate Actions
paragraphs: Them from Often Committing Inconsiderate Actions

People who live in democratic countries do not care for the simple, rowdy, or coarse amusements that the common people enjoy in aristocratic communities; they find such pastimes childish or dull. Nor are they any more drawn to the intellectual and refined entertainments of the aristocratic classes. They want something productive and substantial in their pleasures; they want to mix real, tangible satisfaction with their enjoyment. In aristocratic communities the people readily surrender to outbursts of noisy, boisterous merriment, which at once drives away the memory of their hardships. The natives of democracies do not like being disturbed so violently, and they never lose sight of themselves without regret. In place of these frivolous delights they prefer quieter, more serious amusements, which resemble business and do not push business entirely out of their minds. An American, instead of going out in a spare hour to dance merrily at some public gathering place, as other men of his occupation still do over most of Europe, shuts himself up at home to drink. He thus enjoys two pleasures: he can keep thinking about his business, and he can get drunk respectably beside his own fireside.

I used to think the English were the most serious nation on earth, but I have since seen the Americans and changed my opinion. I do not mean that temperament has little to do with the character of the people of the United States, but I think their political institutions are a still more influential cause. I believe the seriousness of the Americans comes partly from their pride. In democratic countries even poor men hold a lofty idea of their personal importance. They view themselves with satisfaction and tend to suppose that others are looking at them too. In this frame of mind they guard their words and actions carefully and do not expose themselves in ways that would reveal their shortcomings; to keep their dignity, they think they must keep a grave face.

But I detect another cause, deeper and more powerful, which produces this astonishing gravity among the Americans by instinct. Under a despotism, communities sometimes give way to bursts of vehement joy, but they are generally gloomy and sullen, because they are afraid. Under absolute monarchies that the customs and mores of the country temper, people are often cheerful and even-tempered, because they have some freedom and a good deal of security and so are spared the most important cares of life. But all free peoples are serious, because their minds are habitually absorbed in contemplating some dangerous or difficult purpose. This is especially true of those free nations that form democratic communities. In them, a very large number of men in every class are constantly occupied with the serious affairs of government, and those whose thoughts are not turned to the running of the commonwealth are wholly absorbed in making a private fortune. Among such a people a serious demeanor ceases to be the trait of certain men and becomes a habit of the nation.

We are told of small democracies in antiquity whose citizens met in the public squares wearing garlands of roses and spent nearly all their time in dancing and theatrical entertainments. I no more believe in such republics than in Plato’s; or, if what we read really happened, I do not hesitate to say that these supposed democracies were made up of very different elements from ours and had nothing in common with ours except the name. But we must not suppose that, in the midst of all their toil, the people who live in democracies think themselves pitiable; the opposite is observed. No men are fonder of their own condition. Life would have no savor for them if they were freed from the anxieties that torment them, and they show more attachment to their cares than aristocratic nations show to their pleasures.

Next I am led to ask how these same democratic nations, so serious as they are, sometimes act so thoughtlessly. The Americans, who almost always keep a sober bearing and a cold air, nevertheless often let a sudden passion or a hasty opinion carry them far beyond the bounds of reason, and they sometimes commit strange absurdities with a straight face. This contrast should not surprise us. There is a kind of ignorance that arises from extreme publicity. In despotic States men do not know how to act, because they are told nothing; in democratic nations they often act at random, because nothing is left untold. The former do not know — the latter forget; and the main features of each picture are lost to them in a confusion of details.

It is astonishing what imprudent language a public man can sometimes use in free countries, and especially in democratic States, without being compromised. In absolute monarchies, by contrast, a few words let slip by accident are enough to expose him forever and ruin him beyond hope of recovery. What precedes explains this. When a man speaks in the midst of a great crowd, many of his words are not heard, or are quickly wiped from the memories of those who hear them; but in the silence of a mute and motionless throng the slightest whisper reaches the ear.

In democracies men are never stationary; a thousand chances toss them back and forth, and their lives are always at the mercy of unforeseen or, so to speak, improvised circumstances. So they are often forced to do things they have learned imperfectly, to say things they understand imperfectly, and to take up work for which a long apprenticeship has not prepared them. In aristocracies each man has a single object that he pursues without letting up, but among democratic nations a man’s existence is more complex. The same mind will almost always take in several objects at once, and these objects are often wholly unrelated to each other. Since the mind cannot know them all well, it is easily content with imperfect ideas of each.

When the inhabitant of democracies is not driven by his needs, he is at least driven by his desires, for of all the possessions he sees around him, none is wholly out of his reach. He therefore does everything in a hurry, is always satisfied with “pretty well,” and never stops for more than a moment to consider what he has done. His curiosity is at once insatiable and cheaply satisfied, for he cares more about knowing a great deal quickly than about knowing anything well; he has no time and little taste for getting to the bottom of things. So democratic peoples are grave, because their social and political condition constantly leads them into serious occupations; and they act thoughtlessly, because they give each of these occupations so little time and attention. The habit of inattention must be regarded as the greatest bane of the democratic character.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — Why The National Vanity Of The Americans Is More Restless And Captious Than That Of The English
paragraphs: And Captious Than That of the English

All free nations are vainglorious, but not all show their national pride in the same way. In their dealings with foreigners, the Americans seem unable to bear the smallest criticism and can never get enough praise. The slightest compliment pleases them; the most extravagant rarely satisfies them. They press you incessantly to wring praise out of you, and if you resist their pleading they begin to praise themselves. It seems as if, doubting their own merit, they want it displayed before their eyes at every moment. Their vanity is not only greedy but restless and jealous; it grants nothing while demanding everything, and is ready to beg and to quarrel at the same time. If I tell an American that the country he lives in is a fine one, “Ay,” he replies, “there is not its fellow in the world.” If I applaud the freedom its inhabitants enjoy, he answers, “Freedom is a fine thing, but few nations are worthy to enjoy it.” If I remark on the purity of morals that distinguishes the United States, “I can imagine,” says he, “that a stranger, who has been struck by the corruption of all other nations, is astonished at the difference.” At last I leave him to admire himself; but he comes back to the attack and does not let up until he has made me repeat everything I had just said. It is impossible to imagine a more tiresome or more talkative patriotism; it wearies even those who are inclined to respect it. *a
[Footnote a: See Appendix U.]

The English are not like this. An Englishman calmly enjoys the advantages, real or imagined, that he believes his country has. If he grants nothing to other nations, neither does he ask anything for his own. The criticism of foreigners does not affect him, and their praise hardly flatters him. His attitude toward the rest of the world is one of disdainful, uninformed reserve; his pride needs no feeding, for it nourishes itself. It is remarkable that two nations that sprang so recently from the same stock should be so opposite in their way of feeling and talking.

In aristocratic countries the great hold immense privileges, on which their pride rests, without seeking to rely on the lesser advantages that come to them. Because these privileges reached them by inheritance, they regard them in some sense as part of themselves, or at least as a natural right belonging to their own persons. They therefore have a calm sense of their superiority. They do not dream of boasting about privileges that everyone sees and no one disputes, and these things are not new enough to them to be worth talking about. They stand unmoved in their solitary greatness, confident that all the world sees them without any effort on their part to show themselves off, and that no one will try to dislodge them. When an aristocracy conducts the public affairs, its national pride naturally takes this reserved, indifferent, and haughty form, which all the other classes of the nation imitate.

When, on the contrary, social conditions differ only a little, the slightest privileges matter. Since every man sees around him a million people enjoying exactly the same or similar advantages, his pride becomes greedy and jealous; he clings to mere trifles and defends them stubbornly. In democracies, because the conditions of life fluctuate so much, men have almost always acquired their advantages recently. The result is that they take extreme pleasure in displaying them, to show others and to persuade themselves that they truly enjoy them. Since these same advantages may be lost at any moment, their owners are constantly on the alert and make a point of showing that they still hold them. Men living in democracies love their country just as they love themselves, and they carry over the habits of their private vanity into their vanity as a nation. The restless, insatiable vanity of a democratic people comes so entirely from the equality and precariousness of social conditions that the members of the haughtiest nobility show exactly the same passion in those lesser parts of their existence where anything is fluctuating or contested. An aristocratic class always differs greatly from the other classes of the nation in the extent and permanence of its privileges; but it often happens that the only differences among its own members lie in small, passing advantages that may be lost or gained any day. Members of a powerful aristocracy, gathered in a capital or at a court, have been known to fight bitterly over those frivolous privileges that depend on the whim of fashion or the will of their master. These persons then showed one another exactly the same childish jealousies that move the men of democracies: the same eagerness to snatch the smallest advantages their equals disputed, and the same wish to parade the ones they already held. If national pride ever entered the minds of courtiers, I have no doubt that they would show it in the same way as the members of a democratic community.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — That The Aspect Of Society In The United States Is At Once Excited And Monotonous
paragraphs: Excited and Monotonous

Nothing, it would seem, could be better suited to arouse and feed curiosity than the sight of the United States. Fortunes, opinions, and laws there are in ceaseless variation; it is as if unchanging nature herself had become changeable, so great are the alterations the hand of man works upon her. Yet in the end the sight of this excited community becomes monotonous, and after watching the moving pageant for a time, the spectator grows tired of it. Among aristocratic nations every man stays pretty much in his own sphere, but men are astonishingly unlike one another — their passions, ideas, habits, and tastes are essentially different. Nothing changes, but everything differs. In democracies, on the contrary, all men are alike and do much the same things. It is true that they are subject to great and frequent reversals; but because the same events of good or bad fortune keep recurring, only the names of the actors change, and the play is always the same. The aspect of American society is lively, because men and things are always changing; but it is monotonous, because all these changes are alike.

Men living in democratic ages have many passions, but most of their passions either end in the love of riches or come from it. The reason is not that their souls are narrower but that money truly matters more in such times. When all the members of a community are independent of one another or indifferent to one another, the cooperation of each can be obtained only by paying for it. This multiplies endlessly the uses to which wealth can be put, and raises its value. When the reverence that once belonged to what is old has vanished, birth, condition, and profession no longer distinguish men, or hardly do so at all. Almost nothing but money remains to create strongly marked differences among them and to lift some above the common level. The distinction that springs from wealth grows as every other distinction disappears or shrinks. Among aristocratic nations money reaches only a few points on the vast circle of human desires; in democracies it seems to lead to all of them. The love of wealth can therefore be traced, as a chief or a secondary motive, at the bottom of everything the Americans do. This gives all their passions a kind of family likeness and soon makes the survey of them exceedingly wearisome. This perpetual recurrence of the same passion is monotonous; the particular means by which the passion seeks its own satisfaction are no less so.

In an orderly and established democracy like the United States, where men cannot get rich by war, by public office, or by political confiscation, the love of wealth drives them chiefly into business and manufacturing. Although these pursuits often cause great upheavals and disasters, they cannot prosper without strictly regular habits and a long routine of small, uniform acts. The stronger the passion, the more regular these habits and the more uniform these acts. It may be said that the vehemence of their desires is what makes the Americans so methodical; it disturbs their minds, but it disciplines their lives.

The remark I apply here to America could in fact be made of almost all our contemporaries. Variety is disappearing from the human race; the same ways of acting, thinking, and feeling are found all over the world. This is not only because nations have more influence on one another and imitate one another more faithfully. It is also because the men of each country give up more and more the distinctive opinions and feelings of a caste, a profession, or a family, and so arrive together at something nearer to the nature of man, which is the same everywhere. Thus they grow more alike, even without having imitated one another. They are like travelers scattered through a large forest crossed by paths that all converge on one point. If every one of them keeps his eyes fixed on that point and moves toward it, they draw imperceptibly closer together, though they do not seek one another, do not see one another, and do not know one another; and they will be surprised in the end to find themselves all gathered on the same spot. All the nations that take as the object of their studies and their imitation not any particular man but man himself are tending in the end toward a similar state of society, like these travelers converging on the central clearing of the forest.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — Of Honor In The United States And In Democratic Communities
paragraphs: It seems that people use two quite different standards when they publicly assess *a the actions of others. Sometimes they judge by the simple ideas of right and wrong found everywhere in the world; at other times they defer to a few very particular ideas that belong only to a certain age and country. These two standards often differ, and sometimes they conflict. Yet neither ever fully merges with the other or fully cancels it. At the height of its power, honor governs men’s will more than their belief. Even as they obey its commands without hesitation or complaint, they sense, by a faint but powerful instinct, a more general, more ancient and more sacred law, which they sometimes break but never stop acknowledging. Some actions have been considered virtuous and dishonorable at once; refusing to fight a duel is an example.

[Footnote a: The word “honor” does not always carry the same meaning, in French or in English. I. First, it means the dignity, glory or reverence a man receives from other people; in this sense a man is said to earn honor. 2. It also means the whole set of rules by which that dignity, glory or reverence is gained. So we say that a man has always strictly obeyed the laws of honor, or that a man has violated his honor. In this chapter the word is always used in the second sense.]

I think these peculiarities can be explained otherwise than by the mere whims of particular individuals and nations, which until now has been the usual way of reasoning on the subject. Humanity has general and lasting needs, and these have given rise to moral laws. Everywhere and always, people have attached blame and shame to neglecting those laws: breaking them was “to do ill,” and “to do well” was to follow them. Within this vast association of the human race, smaller associations have formed, which are called nations; and within those nations, further divisions have taken the names of classes or castes. Each of these associations is, so to speak, a separate kind of human being. It differs in no essential way from the mass of humanity, yet to some extent it stands apart and has needs of its own. These special needs account for the changes, varying in degree from country to country, in how human actions are viewed and in the judgment that ought to be passed on them. It is the general and permanent interest of mankind that people should not kill one another; but it may happen to be the particular and temporary interest of a people or a class to justify homicide, or even to honor it.

Honor is simply the particular rule, grounded in a particular state of society, by which a people or a class hands out praise or blame. Nothing is less fruitful to the mind than an abstract idea, so I hurry to bring in facts and examples to show what I mean.

For my illustration I choose the most extraordinary kind of honor the world has ever known, and the one we know best: aristocratic honor, which grew out of feudal society. I shall explain it through the principle I have laid down, and I shall explain the principle through this illustration. I will not ask here when and how the aristocracy of the Middle Ages arose, why it was so sharply cut off from the rest of the nation, or what founded and strengthened its power. I take its existence as established, and I am trying to account for the peculiar view it took of most human actions. What strikes me first is that in the feudal world actions were not always praised or blamed according to their intrinsic worth. Sometimes they were valued solely by reference to the person who did them or to whom they were done, which offends the general conscience of mankind. Thus certain actions that meant nothing coming from a man of humble station dishonored a noble, and others changed their whole character depending on whether the person wronged belonged to the aristocracy. When these distinctions first arose, the nobility was a separate body among the people, ruling them from the unreachable heights where it had entrenched itself. To keep this distinct position, which was the source of its strength, it needed not only political privileges but also a standard of right and wrong made for its own use. That a particular virtue or vice should belong to the nobility rather than to the humble classes, and that certain actions should be harmless when they touched a villein but criminal when they touched a noble, were often arbitrary matters. But that honor or shame should attach to a man’s actions according to his condition was a result of the inner structure of an aristocratic community. This has indeed been the case in every country that has had an aristocracy; as long as any trace of the principle survives, these peculiarities will persist. To debauch a woman of color hardly harms an American’s reputation; to marry her dishonors him.

In some cases feudal honor demanded revenge and branded forgiveness of insults as shameful; in others it sternly ordered men to master their own passions and to forget themselves. It did not make humanity or kindness its law, but it praised generosity; it valued open-handedness above benevolence; it allowed men to get rich by gambling or war, but not by work; it preferred great crimes to small earnings; it was less repelled by covetousness than by miserliness; it often sanctioned violence, but always condemned cunning and treachery as contemptible. These fantastic ideas did not come solely from the whims of those who held them. A class that has placed itself at the head of all others and above them, and that constantly strains to keep that high position, must honor above all the virtues that stand out for dignity and splendor and that combine easily with pride and love of power. Such men would not hesitate to turn the natural order of conscience upside down in order to put those virtues ahead of all others. One can even imagine that some of the bolder and more brilliant vices would readily be ranked above the quiet, unassuming virtues. The mere existence of such a class in society makes these things unavoidable.

The nobles of the Middle Ages ranked military courage first among the virtues, and made it stand in place of many of them. This too was a peculiar opinion, and it arose necessarily from the peculiar state of society. Feudal aristocracy lived by war and for war. Arms had founded its power, and arms maintained it. It therefore needed nothing beyond military courage, and that quality was naturally raised above all others. Whatever showed it, even at the expense of reason and humanity, was approved and often required by the customs of the time. That was the main principle; human whim can be traced only in the smaller details. That a man should take a tap on the cheek as an unbearable insult, and be obliged to kill in single combat the person who struck him so lightly, is an arbitrary rule. But that a noble could not calmly accept an insult, and was dishonored if he took a blow without fighting, were direct consequences of the basic principles and needs of a military aristocracy.

So it was true, to a certain extent, to say that the laws of honor were capricious; but those caprices always stayed within certain necessary limits. What our forefathers called honor is so far from being an arbitrary law in my eyes that I would readily undertake to trace its most incoherent and fantastic demands to a small number of fixed, unchanging needs inherent in feudal society.

If I followed the idea of feudal honor into politics, I should find its dictates no harder to explain. The social state and political institutions of the Middle Ages were such that the nation’s supreme power never governed the community directly. In the people’s eyes that power did not exist. Each man looked up to a particular individual whom he was bound to obey, and through that intermediary he was connected to everyone else. So in feudal society the whole system of the commonwealth rested on the feeling of fidelity to the person of the lord, and to destroy that feeling was to open the floodgates of anarchy. Moreover, all members of the aristocracy had constant occasion to appreciate how important fidelity to a political superior was, since each of them was a vassal as well as a lord and had to command as well as obey. To stay faithful to the lord, to sacrifice oneself for him if called upon, to share his good or bad fortune, to stand by him in his undertakings whatever they were: these were the first demands of feudal honor in relation to the political institutions of those times. Public opinion branded a vassal’s treachery with extraordinary severity, and a name of particular infamy, “felony,” was coined for the offense.

By contrast, one finds few traces in the Middle Ages of the passion that gave life to the nations of antiquity, I mean patriotism; the word itself is not very old in the language. *b Feudal institutions hid the country as a whole from men’s sight and made love of it less necessary. The nation was forgotten in the passions that bound men to persons. So remaining faithful to one’s country was no part of the strict law of feudal honor. This is not to say that love of country did not exist in our forefathers’ hearts; but it was a dim, feeble instinct, which has grown clearer and stronger as aristocratic classes have been abolished and the nation’s supreme power centralized. One can see this plainly in the opposite judgments that European nations have passed on events in their histories, depending on the generation making them. What most dishonored the Constable de Bourbon in his contemporaries’ eyes was that he took up arms against his king; what most dishonors him in ours is that he made war on his country. We condemn him as harshly as our forefathers did, but for different reasons.
[Footnote b: French writers did not use even the word “patrie” until the sixteenth century.]

I have taken the honor of feudal times to illustrate my point because its features are more sharply marked, and more familiar to us, than those of any other period. But I could have chosen an example elsewhere and reached the same conclusion by another road. We know the Romans less well than our own ancestors, yet we know that they had certain peculiar ideas of glory and disgrace, which did not derive solely from the general principles of right and wrong. Many human actions were judged differently depending on whether they affected a Roman citizen or a stranger, a freeman or a slave; certain vices were publicly proclaimed, and certain virtues were praised above all others. “In that age,” says Plutarch in the life of Coriolanus, “martial prowess was more honored and prized in Rome than all the other virtues, insomuch that it was called virtus, the name of virtue itself, by applying the name of the kind to this particular species; so that virtue in Latin was as much as to say valor.” Can anyone fail to recognize the particular need of that singular community, which was formed to conquer the world?

Any nation would give us similar grounds for observation. As I have already remarked, whenever men gather as a distinct community, the notion of honor immediately grows up among them, that is, a system of opinions of their own about what deserves blame or praise; and these special rules always originate in the community’s special habits and interests. To a certain extent this applies to democratic communities as well as to others, as we shall now prove by the example of the Americans. *c Some vague ideas of the old aristocratic honor of Europe can still be found scattered among Americans’ opinions. But these inherited opinions are few, they have little root in the country, and little power. They are like a religion that still has some temples standing, though men have stopped believing in it. Yet amid these half-erased notions of foreign honor, some new opinions have sprung up, which make up what may be called, in our day, American honor. I have shown how the Americans are constantly driven into commerce and industry. Their origin, their social condition, their political institutions, and even the place they live all push them irresistibly in this direction. Their present condition, then, is that of an almost exclusively manufacturing and commercial association, set in the midst of a new and boundless country, which their chief aim is to explore for profit. This is the trait that most distinguishes the American people from all others at present. All the quiet virtues that give the community a regular movement and encourage business will therefore be held in particular honor by that people, and neglecting them will bring public contempt. All the more turbulent virtues, which often dazzle but more often disturb society, will on the contrary rank lower in this same people’s estimation. They may be neglected without losing the community’s esteem; acquiring them would perhaps risk losing it.
[Footnote c: By “the Americans” I mean here those who live in the States without slavery; they alone can be said to offer a complete picture of democratic society.]

The Americans classify men’s vices in a way that is just as arbitrary. There are certain propensities that seem blameworthy to universal reason and to the conscience of all mankind, but that happen to suit the particular and temporary needs of the American community. These are only lightly reproved, and sometimes even encouraged. The love of wealth and the lesser propensities connected with it are the clearest example. To clear, to farm and to transform the vast uninhabited continent that is his domain, the American needs the daily support of an energetic passion, and that passion can only be the love of wealth. So the passion for wealth is not condemned in America, and as long as it does not go beyond the limits set for public safety, it is held in honor. The American praises as a noble and praiseworthy ambition what our own forefathers in the Middle Ages branded as servile greed, just as he treats the ardor for conquest and the martial temper that drove them to battle as a blind and barbarous frenzy. In the United States fortunes are lost and regained without difficulty; the country is boundless and its resources inexhaustible. The people have all the needs and cravings of a growing creature, and whatever their efforts, they are always surrounded by more than they can take. What would be fatal to such a people is not the ruin of a few individuals, which can soon be repaired, but the inactivity and sloth of the community at large. Boldness in enterprise is the chief cause of its rapid progress, its strength and its greatness. Commercial business there is like a vast lottery, in which a small number of men constantly lose, but the state always gains; such a people ought therefore to encourage and honor boldness in commercial speculation. But any bold speculation risks the fortune of the speculator and of all who trust him. The Americans, who make a virtue of commercial recklessness, have no right in any case to brand with disgrace those who practice it. Hence the strange indulgence shown to bankrupts in the United States; their honor does not suffer from such a misfortune. In this respect the Americans differ not only from the nations of Europe but from all the commercial nations of our time, and accordingly they resemble none of them in their position or their needs.

In America, all the vices that tend to impair purity of morals and destroy the marriage bond are treated with a severity unknown in the rest of the world. At first sight this seems strangely at odds with the tolerance shown there on other subjects, and one is surprised to find such relaxed and such strict morality in the same people. But these things are less incoherent than they seem. Public opinion in the United States represses very gently the love of wealth that promotes the nation’s commercial greatness and prosperity, and it especially condemns the looseness of morals that turns the human mind from the pursuit of well-being and disrupts the internal order of home life, which is so necessary to business success. To win the esteem of their fellow citizens, Americans are therefore forced to adopt orderly habits, and in this sense it may be said that they make it a point of honor to live chastely.

On one point American honor agrees with the ideas of honor recognized in Europe: it ranks courage as the highest virtue and treats it as the greatest of man’s moral necessities. But the idea of courage itself takes on a different look. In the United States military valor is little prized. The courage best known and most esteemed is the kind that makes men brave the dangers of the ocean to reach port sooner, endure the hardships of the wilderness without complaint, and bear a solitude more cruel than hardship. It is the courage that leaves them almost unmoved by the loss of a fortune laboriously acquired, and instantly drives them to fresh efforts to make another. This kind of courage is particularly necessary to the maintenance and prosperity of the American communities, and they hold it in particular honor and esteem; to show a lack of it is to incur certain disgrace.

I have one more characteristic point that may bring out the idea of this chapter more strongly. In a democratic society like that of the United States, where fortunes are small and insecure, everybody works, and work opens the way to everything. This has turned the point of honor completely around and set it against idleness. In America I have sometimes met wealthy young men who personally disliked any laborious effort but had been forced to take up a profession. Their disposition and their fortune would have allowed them to stay without employment, but public opinion forbade it, too imperiously to be disobeyed. In the European countries, by contrast, where aristocracy is still struggling against the flood that is overwhelming it, I have often seen men, constantly spurred by their needs and desires, remain idle so as not to lose the esteem of their equals; and I have known them to put up with boredom and hardship rather than work. No one can fail to see that these opposite obligations are two different rules of conduct, both nevertheless originating in the notion of honor.

What our forefathers called honor without qualification was really only one of its forms; they gave a general name to what was only one kind. Honor is therefore found in democratic ages as well as aristocratic ones, but it will not be hard to show that it looks different in the former. Not only are its injunctions different; as we shall shortly see, they are fewer and less precise, and its dictates are obeyed less strictly. The position of a caste is always much more peculiar than that of a people. Nothing is so far from the ordinary world as a small community always made up of the same families (as the aristocracy of the Middle Ages was, for example), whose aim is to concentrate and keep education, wealth and power exclusively and hereditarily among its own members. But the further a community’s position departs from the ordinary, the more numerous its special needs are, and the more extensive its notions of honor corresponding to those needs. The rules of honor will therefore always be fewer among a people not divided into castes than among any other. If nations ever come into being in which it is even hard to find any distinct classes of society, the notion of honor will be limited to a small number of precepts, more and more in accord with the moral laws adopted by the mass of mankind. Thus the laws of honor will be less peculiar and less varied among a democratic people than in an aristocracy. They will also be more obscure, which follows necessarily from what precedes; for if the distinguishing marks of honor are fewer and less peculiar, they must often be hard to tell apart. Other reasons can be added. Among the aristocratic nations of the Middle Ages, generation followed generation in vain; each family was like a man who never dies and never moves, and opinions changed hardly more than conditions did. Everyone then had the same objects always before his eyes, viewed from the same point; his eyes gradually picked out the smallest details, and his discernment could not fail in the end to become clear and accurate. So the men of feudal times not only held very extraordinary opinions on matters of honor, but each of those opinions was present to their minds in a clear and precise form.

This can never happen in America, where all men are in constant motion, and where society, transformed daily by its own workings, changes its opinions along with its needs. In such a country people catch glimpses of the rules of honor, but they rarely have time to fix their attention on them.

But even if society stood still, it would still be hard to settle what the word “honor” ought to mean. In the Middle Ages each class had its own honor, so the same opinion was never held at the same time by a large number of men. This made it possible to give honor a fixed and exact form, all the more easily because everyone who held it, being in a perfectly identical and highly particular position, was naturally inclined to agree on the points of a law made for themselves alone. Thus the code of honor became a complete and detailed system in which everything was anticipated and provided for in advance, and a fixed and always visible standard was applied to human actions. Among a democratic nation like the Americans, where ranks are merged and the whole of society forms one single mass, made of elements that are all alike though not entirely identical, it is impossible ever to agree beforehand on what the laws of honor will or will not allow. Among that people, indeed, some national needs do exist that give rise to opinions on points of honor shared by the whole nation; but these opinions never occur at the same time, in the same way, or with the same intensity to the minds of the whole community. The law of honor exists, but it has no organs to proclaim it.

The confusion is greater still in a democratic country like France. There the different classes that made up the former fabric of society have been brought together but not yet blended, and day by day they bring into one another’s circles various and sometimes conflicting notions of honor. Every man, at his own will and pleasure, abandons one part of his forefathers’ creed and keeps another. Amid so many arbitrary choices no common rule can ever be established, and it is almost impossible to predict which actions will be held in honor and which will be thought disgraceful. Such times are wretched, but they do not last long.

Because honor among democratic nations is imperfectly defined, its influence is naturally weaker; it is hard to apply with certainty and firmness a law that is not distinctly known. Public opinion, the natural and supreme interpreter of the laws of honor, cannot clearly see which way blame or approval should lean, and so can only pass a hesitant judgment. Sometimes public opinion may contradict itself; more often it does not act and lets things pass.

The weakness of the sense of honor in democracies also arises from several other causes. In aristocratic countries the same notions of honor are always held by only a few people, always limited in number, and often set apart from their fellow citizens. In their minds honor is easily mingled and identified with everything that distinguishes their own position; it appears to them as the chief characteristic of their own rank. They apply its various rules with all the warmth of personal interest, and they feel (if I may use the expression) a passion for complying with its dictates. This truth is plain in the old black-letter lawbooks on “trial by battel.” The nobles in their disputes were bound to use the lance and sword, whereas the villeins used only sticks among themselves, “inasmuch as,” in the words of the old books, “villains have no honor.” This did not mean, as one might imagine today, that these people were contemptible, but simply that their actions were not to be judged by the same rules as the actions of the aristocracy.

At first sight it is surprising that when the sense of honor is at its strongest, its injunctions are usually at their strangest, so that the further honor is from common reason, the better it is obeyed. From this some have inferred that the laws of honor gained strength from their own extravagance. The two things do spring from the same source, but one is not derived from the other. Honor becomes fantastic in proportion to the peculiarity of the needs it expresses and the smallness of the number of men who feel them; and it is because it expresses needs of this kind that its influence is great. So the notion of honor is not stronger for being fantastic; it is fantastic and strong from one and the same cause.

Furthermore, among aristocratic nations each rank is different but all ranks are fixed. Every man occupies a place in his own sphere that he cannot leave, and he lives there among other men bound by the same ties. Among these nations no man can hope or fear to escape notice. No one is placed so low that he lacks a stage of his own, and no one can avoid blame or applause through obscurity.
