In democratic states, by contrast, where all members of the community are mixed together in the same crowd and in constant agitation, public opinion has no hold on men; they vanish at every moment and slip out of its power. Consequently the dictates of honor will be less imperious and less stringent there, for honor acts solely for the public eye, differing in this from mere virtue, which lives on itself, content with its own approval.

If the reader has clearly grasped all that precedes, he will understand that there is a close and necessary relation between inequality of social conditions and what has here been called honor, a relation that, if I am not mistaken, had not been clearly pointed out before. I shall therefore make one more attempt to illustrate it satisfactorily. Suppose a nation stands apart from the rest of mankind. Besides certain general needs inherent in the human race, it will have needs and interests peculiar to itself. At once certain opinions of blame or approval arise in the community that are its own, and that the members of the community call honor. Now suppose that in this same nation a caste arises that in its turn stands apart from all the other classes and acquires certain peculiar needs, which in turn give rise to special opinions. The honor of this caste, made up of a mixture of the nation’s peculiar notions and the caste’s still more peculiar ones, will be as far removed as can be imagined from the simple and general opinions of men.

Having reached this extreme point of the argument, I now turn back. When ranks are mingled and privileges abolished, the men who make up a nation become equal and alike once more. Their interests and needs become identical, and all the peculiar notions that each caste called honor gradually disappear. The notion of honor then comes from no source other than the needs peculiar to the nation at large, and it shows the world that nation’s individual character. Finally, if one may suppose that all the races of mankind were mingled, and that all the peoples of the earth came in the end to have the same interests and the same needs, with no characteristic peculiarities to tell them apart, then no conventional value at all would be attached to men’s actions. All would be viewed by all in the same light; the general necessities of mankind, revealed by conscience to every man, would become the common standard. Only the simple and general notions of right and wrong would then be recognized in the world, and by a natural and necessary tie the idea of blame or approval would be attached to them. Thus, to sum up my whole meaning in a single proposition: the dissimilarities and inequalities among men gave rise to the notion of honor; that notion weakens as those differences are wiped out, and with them it would disappear.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — Why So Many Ambitious Men And So Little Lofty Ambition Are To Be Found In The United States
paragraphs: To Be Found in the United States

The first thing that strikes a traveler in the United States is the huge number of people trying to rise out of the condition they were born into. The second is how seldom one sees lofty ambition amid this restless, universal striving. Every American longs to get ahead, yet hardly any seem to cherish great hopes or to aim very high. All are constantly trying to gain property, power, and reputation, but few think of these things on a grand scale. This is all the more surprising because nothing in the customs or laws of America appears to hold desire back or to keep it from pressing outward in every direction. It seems hard to attribute this odd state of affairs to the equality of social conditions, since at the moment that same equality was established in France, ambition took flight without limit. Even so, I believe the chief cause that can be given for this fact lies in the social condition and the democratic customs of the Americans.

Every revolution enlarges men’s ambition, and this is especially true of revolutions that overthrow an aristocracy. When the old barriers that kept the multitude away from fame and power are suddenly torn down, everyone surges upward toward the heights they have coveted for so long and can at last enjoy. In this first rush of triumph nothing seems impossible to anyone. Desires are boundless, and the power to satisfy them seems almost boundless too. Laws and customs are renewed all at once, and all men and all institutions are thrown into vast confusion. Amid it, the members of the community rise and fall again with extreme speed, and power passes so quickly from hand to hand that no one need despair of seizing it in turn. We must also remember that the people who destroy an aristocracy have lived under its laws. They have seen its splendor, and without noticing it they have absorbed the feelings and ideas it held. So at the moment an aristocracy breaks up, its spirit still pervades the mass of the community, and its tendencies linger long after its defeat. Ambition therefore stays extremely great for as long as a democratic revolution lasts, and it remains so for some time after the revolution is over. Men do not forget the extraordinary events they have witnessed in a single day. The passions a revolution has stirred up do not vanish when it ends. A sense of instability lingers even in restored order. The notion that success comes easily outlives the strange reversals that produced it. Desires stay greatly inflated while the means of satisfying them shrink day by day. The taste for large fortunes persists, though large fortunes have become rare. On every side we see the ravages of excessive and unhappy ambition, kindled in hearts that it consumes in secret and to no purpose.

In the end, however, the last traces of the struggle fade away. The remnants of the aristocracy vanish completely, and people forget the great events that accompanied its fall. Peace follows war, and order rules again in the new realm. Desires are once more fitted to the means of fulfilling them. The needs, opinions, and feelings of men fall into agreement again. The level of the community is fixed for good, and democratic society is established. A democratic nation that has reached this settled and regular state of things will offer a very different sight from the one we have just described. We may readily conclude that if ambition grows great while the conditions of society are becoming equal, it loses that quality once they have become so. Wealth is divided into smaller shares and knowledge is spread widely, so no one is wholly without education or property. The privileges and disqualifications of caste are abolished, and men have broken the bonds that held them in place. The idea of advancement then occurs to every mind, the wish to rise swells in every heart, and everyone wants to climb above his station. Ambition becomes the universal feeling.

But if the equality of conditions gives every member of the community some resources, it also keeps any of them from having resources on a large scale. That necessarily confines their desires within rather narrow limits. So among democratic nations ambition is ardent and unceasing, but it does not usually aim high. Life is mostly spent in eagerly pursuing small goals that lie within reach. What chiefly turns the men of democracies away from lofty ambition is not the smallness of their fortunes but the fierceness of the efforts they make every day to improve them. They strain their faculties to the utmost to achieve paltry results, and this cannot fail to narrow their vision and limit their powers before long. They could be much poorer and still be greater. The small number of wealthy citizens found in a democracy are no exception to this rule. A man who rises gradually to wealth and power picks up, during this long labor, habits of prudence and restraint that he can never afterward shake off. A man cannot enlarge his mind the way he enlarges his house. The same applies to the sons of such a man. They are born, it is true, into a high position, but their parents were humble. They have grown up among feelings and ideas that they cannot easily get rid of later, and we may presume that they will inherit their father’s inclinations along with his wealth. The opposite may happen: the poorest descendant of a powerful aristocracy may show vast ambition, because the traditional opinions of his family and the general spirit of his order still carry him, for a time, above his means. Something else also keeps the men of democratic periods from readily pursuing lofty goals: they foresee how much time must pass before they are ready to approach them. “It is a great advantage,” says Pascal, “to be a man of quality, since it brings one man as forward at eighteen or twenty as another man would be at fifty, which is a clear gain of thirty years.” Those thirty years are usually missing for the ambitious men of democracies. The principle of equality, which lets every man arrive at everything, prevents all men from advancing quickly.

In a democratic society, as anywhere else, only a certain number of great fortunes can be made. And because the paths leading to them are open to all without distinction, everyone’s progress must be slowed. The candidates look nearly alike, and it is hard to choose among them without violating the principle of equality, which is the supreme law of democratic societies. So the first idea that occurs is to make them all advance at the same pace and go through the same trial. Thus, the more alike men become, and the more peacefully and deeply the principle of equality enters the institutions and customs of the country, the stiffer the rules of advancement grow. Advancement itself becomes slower, and it becomes far harder to reach a certain height quickly. Out of hatred of privilege, and out of the difficulty of choosing, all men are finally compelled, whatever their abilities, to pass the same ordeal. All are subjected without distinction to a host of petty preliminary exercises, in which their youth is wasted and their imagination is snuffed out. They despair of ever fully attaining what is held out to them, and by the time they are at last able to do something extraordinary, they have lost the taste for it.

In China, where equality of conditions is extreme and very ancient, no man moves from one public office to another without going through a probationary trial. This trial begins again at every stage of his career. The idea is by now so rooted in the customs of the people that I remember reading a Chinese novel in which the hero, after countless setbacks, finally wins his beloved’s heart by earning honors. Lofty ambition can hardly breathe in such an atmosphere.

What I say of politics applies to everything. Equality produces the same effects everywhere. Where a country’s laws do not regulate and slow men’s advancement by explicit enactment, competition accomplishes the same thing. In a well-established democratic community, then, great and rapid elevation is rare. It is an exception to the common rule, and the very strangeness of such cases makes men forget how seldom they occur. People living in democracies come to see this in the end. They find out that the laws of their country open a boundless field of action before them, but that no one can hope to hurry across it. Between themselves and the final object of their desires they see a multitude of small intermediate obstacles, which must be overcome slowly. This prospect wearies their ambition and discourages it at once. They therefore give up hopes so doubtful and distant, and look closer to hand for pleasures that are less lofty and easier to obtain. Their horizon is not limited by the laws; they narrow it themselves.

I have observed that lofty ambitions are rarer in ages of democracy than in aristocratic times. I may add that when they do arise in spite of these natural obstacles, their character is different. In aristocracies the career of ambition is often broad, but its boundaries are fixed. In democracies ambition usually moves within a narrower field, but once it gets beyond that field, hardly any limits can be set on it. Men are individually weak. They live apart from one another and in constant motion. Precedents carry little authority and laws last only a short time. So resistance to novelty is feeble, and the structure of society never looks fully upright or firmly consolidated. As a result, once an ambitious man has power in his grasp, there is nothing he will not dare. When power slips from him, he plots the overthrow of the state to win it back. This gives great political ambition a character of revolutionary violence that it seldom shows to the same degree in aristocratic communities. The usual picture in democratic nations is a great number of small and very reasonable objects of ambition. From among them, at intervals, a few ill-controlled desires of larger growth break out. But ambition conceived and carried out on a vast scale is not to be found there.

I have shown elsewhere by what hidden influence the principle of equality makes the passion for physical gratifications and the exclusive love of the present dominate the human heart. These propensities mix with the feeling of ambition and tinge it, so to speak, with their colors. I believe that ambitious men in democracies are less concerned than any others with the interests and the judgment of posterity. The present moment alone engages and absorbs them. They are more inclined to complete a number of undertakings quickly than to raise lasting monuments to their achievements, and they care far more for success than for fame. What they most demand from men is obedience, and what they most covet is empire. Their manners have almost always stayed below the height of their station. The result is that they often bring very low tastes into their extraordinary fortunes, and they seem to have acquired supreme power only to serve their coarse or petty pleasures.

I think that in our time it is very necessary to purify, regulate, and adapt the feeling of ambition, but that it would be extremely dangerous to try to impoverish it or suppress it too much. We should try to set certain outer limits that it must never be allowed to cross, but within those limits its range should not be restricted too far. I admit that what I fear for democratic society is not so much the boldness of desires as their mediocrity. What seems to me most to be dreaded is that, amid the small and ceaseless occupations of private life, ambition may lose its vigor and its greatness. I fear that the passions of man may subside and at the same time be lowered, so that the march of society becomes every day calmer and less aspiring. I think, then, that the leaders of modern society would be wrong to try to lull the community with a state of happiness that is too uniform and too peaceful. It is good to expose the community from time to time to difficulty and danger, in order to raise ambition and give it a field of action. Moralists constantly complain that the ruling vice of the present time is pride. This is true in one sense, for no one thinks he is not better than his neighbor, or agrees to obey his superior. But it is extremely false in another sense, for the same man who cannot bear subordination or equality has so contemptible an opinion of himself that he thinks he was born only for vulgar pleasures. He readily settles for low desires, without daring to embark on lofty enterprises, of which he hardly dreams. So, far from thinking that humility ought to be preached to our contemporaries, I would have efforts made to give them a larger idea of themselves and of their kind. Humility is unhealthy for them. What they most lack, in my opinion, is pride. I would gladly trade several of our small virtues for this one vice.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 — The Trade Of Place-Hunting In Certain Democratic Countries
paragraphs: In the United States, as soon as a man has gained some education and some money, he either tries to get rich through commerce or industry, or he buys land in the backwoods and becomes a pioneer. All he asks of the state is that it not disturb his labor and that it keep his earnings safe. Among most European nations, when a man begins to feel his strength and his desires widen, the first thing he thinks of is getting a public job. These opposite effects, which spring from the same cause, deserve a brief look.

When public employments are few, poorly paid, and insecure, while the various lines of business are numerous and profitable, the new and eager desires that the principle of equality produces turn from every side toward business, not toward official duties. But if, while the ranks of society are growing more equal, the education of the people stays incomplete, or their spirit is anything but bold, and if commerce and industry, held back in their growth, offer only slow and difficult ways of making a fortune, then the members of the community, despairing of improving their own condition, rush to the head of the state and demand its help. To relieve their own needs at the expense of the public treasury seems to them the easiest and most open way, if not the only one, to rise above a condition that no longer satisfies them. Place-hunting becomes the most widely followed of all trades. This must be especially so in those great centralized monarchies where paid offices are immensely numerous and the tenure of them fairly secure, so that no one despairs of getting a place and enjoying it as undisturbedly as an inherited fortune.

I will not point out that the universal and excessive desire for office is a great social evil, that it destroys the citizen’s spirit of independence and spreads a venal and servile temper through the whole body of society, and that it stifles the manlier virtues. Nor will I take the trouble to show that this kind of traffic creates only unproductive activity, which stirs up the country without adding to its resources. All of this is obvious. But I would point out that a government that encourages this tendency endangers its own tranquillity and puts its very existence at great risk. I know that in a time like ours, when the love and respect that once attached to authority are seen slowly to fade, it may seem necessary to those in power to hold every man more tightly through his own interest. It may seem convenient to use his own passions to keep him orderly and quiet. But this cannot last. What may look like a source of strength for a time will surely become, in the end, a great cause of embarrassment and weakness.

Among democratic nations, as elsewhere, the number of official appointments has limits in the end, but among those nations the number of aspirants has none. It rises continually, gradually and irresistibly, as social conditions become more equal, and it is checked only by the size of the population. So when public employments offer the only outlet for ambition, the government eventually meets with permanent opposition, because it is charged with satisfying unlimited desires with limited means. It is quite certain that, of all the peoples in the world, the hardest to restrain and to manage is a people of petitioners. Whatever rulers may do, such a people can never be satisfied, and there is always reason to fear that in the end they will overturn the constitution of the country and change the face of the state, for the sole purpose of clearing out places. The sovereigns of the present age try to take upon themselves alone all the new desires that equality arouses, and to satisfy them. Unless I am mistaken, they will come to regret ever embarking on this policy. One day they will find that they have put their own power at risk by making it so necessary, and that the safer and more honest course would have been to teach their subjects the art of providing for themselves. *a

[Footnote a: In fact, more recent experience has shown that place-hunting is just as intense in the United States as in any country in Europe. The Americans themselves regard it as one of the great evils of their social condition, and it strongly affects their political institutions. But the American who seeks a place seeks not so much a means of livelihood as the distinction that office and public employment confer. Where there is no true aristocracy, the public service creates a false one, which is as much an object of ambition as the distinctions of rank in aristocratic countries. — Translator’s Note.]

chapters.title: Chapter 21 — Why Great Revolutions Will Become More Rare
paragraphs: A people that has lived for centuries under a system of castes and classes can reach a democratic state of society only by passing through a long series of transformations, more or less critical. These are brought about by violent efforts and after many reversals of fortune, during which property, opinions, and power pass rapidly from one set of hands to another. Even after this great revolution is complete, the revolutionary habits it created can be traced for a long time, and deep turmoil will follow it. All of this happens at the very time when social conditions are becoming more equal. People therefore infer that some hidden relation and secret tie links the principle of equality itself to revolution, so that the one cannot exist without producing the other.

On this point, reasoning may seem to lead to the same conclusion as experience. Among a people whose ranks are nearly equal, no visible bond connects men to one another or keeps them fixed in their station. None of them has a permanent right or power to command, and none is forced by his condition to obey. Instead, each man, finding himself with some education and some resources, may choose his own path and go off apart from all his fellow men. The same causes that make the members of the community independent of one another keep driving them toward new and restless desires and constantly spur them on. It therefore seems natural that in a democratic community men, things, and opinions should be forever changing their form and place, and that democratic ages should be times of rapid and incessant transformation.

But is this really so? Does equality of conditions habitually and permanently lead men to revolution? Does that state of society contain some disturbing principle that keeps the community from ever settling into calm, and inclines the citizens to keep altering their laws, their principles, and their customs? I do not believe it. Because the subject is important, I ask the reader to give it close attention. Almost all the revolutions that have changed the face of nations were made either to consolidate social inequality or to destroy it. Remove the secondary causes behind the great convulsions of the world, and you will almost always find the principle of inequality at the bottom. Either the poor tried to plunder the rich, or the rich tried to enslave the poor. If, then, a state of society can ever be founded in which every man has something to keep and little to gain by taking from others, much will have been done for the peace of the world. I know that in a great democratic people there will always be some members of the community in great poverty and others in great wealth. But the poor, instead of forming the immense majority of the nation, as they always do in aristocratic communities, are comparatively few, and the laws do not bind them together in a hopeless, hereditary poverty. The wealthy, for their part, are few and powerless. They have no privileges that draw public attention; even their wealth, no longer tied to the soil and incorporated in it, is intangible and, as it were, invisible. Just as there is no longer a race of poor men, there is no longer a race of rich men; the rich spring up daily from the multitude and sink back into it. Hence they do not form a distinct class that could easily be singled out and plundered. Moreover, since they are connected with the mass of their fellow citizens by a thousand hidden ties, the people cannot attack them without injuring itself. Between these two extremes of democratic communities stands an innumerable multitude of men who are almost alike. Without being exactly rich or poor, they have enough property to want order maintained, yet not enough to arouse envy. Such men are the natural enemies of violent upheavals: their stillness keeps everyone beneath them and above them still, and secures the balance of the whole fabric of society. This is not to say that even these men are content with what they have, or that they feel a natural horror of a revolution in which they might share the spoils without sharing the disaster. On the contrary, they desire to get rich with unparalleled ardor; but the difficulty is to know from whom wealth can be taken. The same state of society that constantly stirs up desires keeps those desires within necessary limits. It gives men more liberty to change and less interest in changing.

Men in democracies are not only without a natural desire for revolutions; they are afraid of them. Every revolution threatens the tenure of property to some degree. But most people in democratic countries own property, and they are not merely owners: they live as men who set the greatest store by what they own. If we look closely at each of the classes that make up society, it is easy to see that the passions property creates are keenest and most tenacious among the middle classes. The poor often care little about what they possess, because they suffer far more from lacking what they do not have than they enjoy the little they have. The rich have many other passions to satisfy besides the passion for riches; and besides, long and arduous enjoyment of a great fortune sometimes leaves them in the end insensible to its charms. But men with a competence, equally far from opulence and from penury, attach an enormous value to their possessions. Since they are still almost within reach of poverty, they see its hardships close at hand and dread them. Between poverty and themselves there is nothing but a scanty fortune, and on it they at once fix their fears and their hopes. Every day the constant cares it causes increase the interest they take in it, and their continual exertions to enlarge it attach them to it all the more. The idea of giving up even the smallest part of it is unbearable to them, and they regard losing all of it as the worst of misfortunes. Now these eager and apprehensive men of small property make up the class that equality of conditions constantly enlarges. Hence in democratic communities the majority of the people do not clearly see what they have to gain from a revolution, but they feel continually, and in a thousand ways, that they might lose by one.

I have shown in another part of this work that equality of conditions naturally pushes men into commercial and industrial pursuits and tends to increase and spread the ownership of real property. I have also pointed out how it inspires every man with an eager and constant desire to improve his welfare. Nothing is more opposed to revolutionary passions than these things. The final result of a revolution may be favorable to commerce and manufactures, but its first consequence will almost always be the ruin of manufacturers and merchants, because a revolution must always change the general patterns of consumption at once and temporarily upset the existing balance between supply and demand. I know of nothing more opposed to revolutionary customs than commercial customs. Commerce is naturally hostile to all violent passions. It likes to temporize, delights in compromise, and carefully avoids irritation. It is patient, insinuating, and flexible, and it never resorts to extreme measures unless absolute necessity forces it. Commerce makes men independent of one another, gives them a lofty sense of their personal importance, leads them to want to manage their own affairs, and teaches them to manage them well. It therefore prepares men for freedom but keeps them from revolutions. In a revolution, owners of personal property have more to fear than anyone else. On the one hand, their property is often easy to seize; on the other, it can vanish entirely at any moment. Owners of real property are less exposed to this alarm, since even if they lose the income from their estates, they may hope to keep the land itself through the greatest upheavals. Hence the former are far more alarmed than the latter at signs of revolutionary commotion. Thus nations become less inclined to make revolutions as personal property grows and spreads among them and as the number of its owners increases. Moreover, whatever profession men may take up and whatever kind of property they may own, one trait is common to them all: no one is fully content with his present fortune, and all are perpetually striving in a thousand ways to improve it. Take any one of them at any point in his life, and you will find him busy with some new project to increase what he has. Do not talk to him of the interests and rights of mankind: this small domestic concern absorbs all his thoughts for the time and inclines him to put off political excitement to some other season. This not only keeps men from making revolutions; it keeps them from wanting them. Violent political passions have little hold on those who have devoted all their faculties to pursuing their well-being. The ardor they show in small matters cools their zeal for momentous undertakings.

From time to time, it is true, enterprising and ambitious men will arise in democratic communities whose boundless aspirations cannot be satisfied by following the beaten track. Such men like revolutions and welcome their approach, but they have great difficulty bringing them about unless unusual events come to their aid. No man can struggle successfully against the spirit of his age and country. However powerful he may be supposed to be, he will find it hard to make his contemporaries share feelings and opinions that run against all their own feelings and desires.

It is a mistake to believe that, once equality of conditions has become the old and unquestioned state of society and has stamped its characteristics on the customs of a nation, men will easily let themselves be pushed into perilous risks by a reckless leader or a bold innovator. This is not to say that they will resist him openly, by well-laid schemes or even by a deliberate plan of resistance. They will not struggle energetically against him, and sometimes they will even applaud him, but they do not follow him. To his vehemence they secretly oppose their inertia; to his revolutionary tendencies, their conservative interests; to his adventurous passions, their homely tastes; to the flights of his genius, their good sense; to his poetry, their prose. With immense effort he lifts them up for an instant, but they soon slip away from him and fall back, as it were, under their own weight. He strains to rouse the indifferent and distracted multitude, and he finds in the end that he is reduced to impotence, not because he has been defeated, but because he is alone.

I do not claim that men living in democratic communities are naturally stationary. On the contrary, I think a perpetual stir prevails in the heart of those societies and that rest is unknown there. But I think men stir themselves within certain limits that they hardly ever go beyond. They are forever varying, altering, and restoring secondary matters, but they carefully abstain from touching what is fundamental. They love change, but they dread revolutions. Although the Americans are constantly modifying or repealing some of their laws, they show no revolutionary passions at all. One can easily see, from the promptness with which they check and calm themselves when public excitement begins to grow alarming, and at the very moment when passions seem most aroused, that they dread revolution as the worst of misfortunes and that every one of them is inwardly resolved to make great sacrifices to avoid such a catastrophe. In no country in the world is the love of property more active and more anxious than in the United States, and nowhere does the majority show less inclination toward principles that threaten to alter the laws of property in any way. I have often remarked that theories of a revolutionary nature are viewed much less favorably in the United States than in the great monarchical countries of Europe, because they cannot be put into practice without a complete and sometimes sudden change in the state of property and persons. If some men profess them, the bulk of the people reject them with instinctive abhorrence. I do not hesitate to say that most of the maxims commonly called democratic in France would be outlawed by the democracy of the United States. This is easily understood: in America men have the opinions and passions of democracy, whereas in Europe we still have the passions and opinions of revolution. If America ever undergoes great revolutions, they will be brought about by the presence of the Black population on the soil of the United States. That is to say, they will owe their origin not to equality of conditions but to inequality of conditions.

When social conditions are equal, every man tends to live apart, centered in himself and forgetful of the public. Suppose the rulers of democratic nations either neglected to correct this fatal tendency or encouraged it, believing that it weans men from political passions and so wards off revolutions. They might in the end produce the very evil they want to avoid, and a time might come when the inordinate passions of a few men, aided by the unintelligent selfishness or the cowardice of the greater number, would finally force society through strange upheavals. In democratic communities revolutions are seldom desired except by a minority, but a minority may sometimes bring them about. I do not claim that democratic nations are safe from revolutions. I say only that the state of society in those nations does not lead to revolutions but rather wards them off. A democratic people left to itself will not easily embark on great hazards; it is led into revolutions only unawares. It may sometimes undergo them, but it does not make them. I will add that when such a people has been allowed to acquire enough knowledge and experience, it will not permit them to be made. I am well aware that in this respect public institutions can themselves do much; they may encourage or repress the tendencies that originate in the state of society. I therefore do not maintain, I repeat, that a people is safe from revolutions merely because conditions are equal in the community. But I think that, whatever such a people’s institutions may be, great revolutions will always be far less violent and less frequent than is supposed. And I can easily picture a form of polity which, combined with the principle of equality, would make society more stationary than it has ever been in our western part of the world.

What I have said here about events may also be applied, in part, to opinions. Two things are surprising in the United States: the changeability of most human actions and the remarkable stability of certain principles. Men are in constant motion, yet the human mind appears almost unmoved. Once an opinion has spread across the country and taken root there, it would seem that no power on earth is strong enough to eradicate it. In the United States, general principles in religion, philosophy, morality, and even politics do not vary, or are at most modified by a hidden and often imperceptible process. Even the grossest prejudices are erased with incredible slowness amid the continual friction of men and things. I hear it said that it is in the nature and habits of democracies to be constantly changing their opinions and feelings. This may be true of small democratic nations like those of the ancient world, where the whole community could be assembled in a public place and then stirred up at will by an orator. But I saw nothing of the kind among the great democratic people living on the opposite shore of the Atlantic Ocean. What struck me in the United States was how hard it is to shake the majority from an opinion once formed, or to draw it away from a leader once adopted. Neither speaking nor writing can do it; nothing but experience will, and even experience must be repeated. This is surprising at first sight, but closer investigation explains it. I do not think it is as easy as people suppose to uproot the prejudices of a democratic people, to change its beliefs, to replace established principles with new ones in religion, politics, and morals — in a word, to make great and frequent changes in men’s minds. Not that the human mind is at rest there: it is in constant agitation. But it is occupied with endlessly varying the consequences of known principles and with looking for new consequences, rather than with looking for new principles. Its motion is a rapid circling rather than a straightforward thrust made by swift, direct effort. It widens its orbit by small, continual, hasty movements, but it does not suddenly change its position.

Men who are equal in rights, education, and fortune — or, to sum it all up in one word, in social condition — necessarily have wants, habits, and tastes that are hardly different. Since they view things from the same standpoint, their minds naturally tend toward similar conclusions. Though each of them may depart from his contemporaries and form opinions of his own, they will involuntarily and unconsciously agree on a certain number of received opinions. The more closely I consider the effects of equality on the mind, the more I am persuaded that the intellectual anarchy we see around us is not, as many suppose, the natural state of democratic nations. I think it should rather be regarded as an accident peculiar to their youth. It breaks out only in that period of transition when men have already snapped the old ties that bound them together but are still amazingly different in origin, education, and customs. Having kept opinions, propensities, and tastes of great diversity, they find that nothing any longer prevents them from avowing these openly. The leading opinions of men become alike in proportion as their conditions become alike. This seems to me the general and permanent law; the rest is casual and transient.

I believe it will rarely happen that a man in a democratic community suddenly frames a system of ideas very far from the one his contemporaries have adopted. If some such innovator did appear, I think he would have great difficulty finding listeners, and still more finding believers. When the conditions of men are almost equal, they do not easily let themselves be persuaded by one another. Because they all live in close contact, have learned the same things together, and lead the same life, they are not naturally disposed to take one of themselves as a guide and follow him implicitly. Men seldom accept on trust the opinion of their equal, or of a man like themselves. In democratic nations, as I have remarked elsewhere, confidence in the superior attainments of particular individuals is weakened. But more than that, the general idea of intellectual superiority that any man might gain over the rest of the community is soon overshadowed. As men grow more like each other, the doctrine of the equality of the intellect gradually works its way into their opinions, and it becomes harder for any innovator to gain or exercise much influence over the minds of a people. Sudden intellectual revolutions will therefore be rare in such communities. If we read the history of the world rightly, we will find that great and rapid changes in human opinions have been produced far less by the force of reasoning than by the authority of a name. Observe, too, that since the men who live in democratic societies are not connected with each other by any tie, each of them must be convinced individually, whereas in an aristocratic society it is enough to convince a few, and the rest follow. If Luther had lived in an age of equality and had not had princes and potentates for his audience, he would perhaps have found it harder to change the face of Europe. This is not to say that the men of democracies are naturally very sure of the correctness of their opinions or unwavering in belief. They often entertain doubts that, in their eyes, no one can remove. At such times the human mind would sometimes gladly change its position; but since nothing urges or guides it forward, it swings back and forth without making progress. *a

[Footnote a: If I ask which state of society is most favorable to the great revolutions of the mind, I find that it lies somewhere between the complete equality of the whole community and the absolute separation of ranks. Under a system of castes, generations succeed one another without altering men’s positions; some have nothing more, others nothing better, to hope for. The imagination slumbers in this universal silence and stillness, and the very idea of change fades from the human mind. When ranks have been abolished and social conditions are almost equalized, all men are in ceaseless excitement, but each stands alone, independent and weak. This latter state of things is extremely different from the former, yet it has one point in common: great revolutions of the human mind seldom occur in it. But between these two extremes in the history of nations there is an intermediate period, as glorious as it is turbulent. In it the conditions of men are not settled enough for the mind to be lulled into torpor, yet they are unequal enough for men to exercise a vast power over one another’s minds, and a few may modify the convictions of all. It is at such times that great reformers start up and new opinions suddenly change the face of the world.]

Even when a democratic people’s trust has been won, it is still no easy matter to gain their attention. It is extremely hard to get a hearing from men living in democracies unless one is speaking to them about themselves. They pay no attention to what is said to them, because they are always wholly taken up with what they are doing. Indeed, few men are idle in democratic nations; life is passed amid noise and excitement, and men are so busy acting that they have little left for thinking. I would especially point out that they are not merely employed; they are passionately devoted to their employments. They are always in action, and each action absorbs their faculties. The zeal they show in business extinguishes the enthusiasm they might otherwise feel for ideas. I think it is extremely difficult to arouse the enthusiasm of a democratic people for any theory that has no palpable, direct, and immediate connection with the daily occupations of life. Therefore they will not readily give up their old opinions. For it is enthusiasm that flings men’s minds out of the beaten track and brings about the great revolutions of the intellect as well as the great revolutions of the political world. Thus democratic nations have neither the time nor the taste to go looking for new opinions. Even when the opinions they hold become doubtful, they keep them anyway, because changing them would take too much time and inquiry. They keep them not as certain but as established.

There are other and more compelling reasons why no great change can easily be made in the principles of a democratic people. I touched on them at the beginning of this part of my work. If the influence of individuals among such a people is weak and hardly noticeable, the power the mass exercises over the mind of each individual is extremely great; I have already shown why. I would now add that it is wrong to suppose this depends solely on the form of government, and that the majority would lose its intellectual supremacy if it lost its political power. In aristocracies men often have much greatness and strength of their own. When they find themselves at odds with most of their fellow countrymen, they withdraw into their own circle, where they support and console themselves. That is not the case in a democratic country. There public favor seems as necessary as the air we breathe, and to live at odds with the multitude is, as it were, not to live. The multitude needs no laws to coerce those who do not think as it does: public disapproval is enough. A sense of their loneliness and impotence overtakes them and drives them to despair.

Whenever social conditions are equal, public opinion presses with enormous weight on the mind of each individual. It surrounds, directs, and oppresses him, and this comes from the very constitution of society much more than from its political laws. As men grow more alike, each man feels weaker in relation to all the rest. He sees nothing that raises him far above them or sets him apart from them, so he mistrusts himself as soon as they attack him. Not only does he mistrust his strength; he even doubts his right, and he comes very near acknowledging that he is in the wrong when the greater number of his countrymen say that he is. The majority do not need to constrain him; they convince him. However the powers of a democratic community may be organized and balanced, it will therefore always be extremely difficult to believe what the bulk of the people reject, or to profess what they condemn.

This circumstance is extraordinarily favorable to the stability of opinions. When an opinion has taken root among a democratic people and established itself in the minds of the bulk of the community, it afterward survives by itself and is maintained without effort, because no one attacks it. Those who at first rejected it as false end by accepting it as the general impression, and those who still dispute it in their hearts conceal their dissent. They take care not to engage in a dangerous and useless conflict. It is true that when the majority of a democratic people change their opinions, they may suddenly and arbitrarily bring about strange revolutions in men’s minds. But their opinions do not change without much difficulty, and it is almost as difficult to show that they have changed.

Time, events, or the mind’s own unaided individual action will sometimes undermine or destroy an opinion without any outward sign of the change. It has not been openly attacked, and no conspiracy has been formed to make war on it, but its followers quietly withdraw one by one. Day by day a few of them abandon it, until at last only a minority professes it. In this state it will still continue to prevail. Because its enemies remain silent, or exchange their thoughts only by stealth, they are themselves unaware for a long time that a great revolution has actually taken place. In this uncertainty they take no steps; they watch each other and keep silent. The majority have ceased to believe what they believed before, but they still pretend to believe it, and this empty phantom of public opinion is strong enough to chill innovators and to keep them silent and at a respectful distance. We live at a time that has seen the most rapid changes of opinion in men’s minds. Nevertheless, it may be that the leading opinions of society will before long be more settled than they have been for several centuries of our history. That time has not yet come, but perhaps it is approaching. The more closely I examine the natural wants and tendencies of democratic nations, the more I am persuaded that if social equality is ever generally and permanently established in the world, great intellectual and political revolutions will become more difficult and less frequent than is supposed. The men of democracies appear always excited, uncertain, eager, and changeable in their wills and in their positions, and so it is imagined that they are about to abolish their laws suddenly, adopt new opinions, and take on new customs. But if the principle of equality predisposes men to change, it also suggests to them certain interests and tastes that cannot be satisfied without a settled order of things. Equality urges them on, but at the same time it holds them back; it spurs them, but fastens them to earth; it kindles their desires, but limits their powers. This is not perceived at first. The passions that tend to separate the citizens of a democracy are obvious enough, but the hidden force that restrains and unites them cannot be seen at a glance.

Amid the ruins that surround me, shall I dare to say that revolutions are not what I most fear for coming generations? If men continue to shut themselves up more closely in the narrow circle of domestic interests and to live on that kind of excitement, it is to be feared that they may ultimately become closed to those great and powerful public emotions that disturb nations but also enlarge them and renew them. When property becomes so unstable and the love of property so restless and so ardent, I cannot help fearing that men may reach a state in which they regard every new theory as a peril, every innovation as a wearisome toil, and every social improvement as a stepping-stone to revolution, and so refuse to move at all for fear of being moved too far. I dread, and I confess it, that they may in the end give way so completely to a cowardly love of present enjoyment that they lose sight of the interests of their future selves and of their descendants, and prefer to glide along the easy current of life rather than make, when necessary, a strong and sudden effort toward a higher purpose. Some believe that modern society will keep changing its aspect forever. For my part, I fear that it will ultimately be too unchangingly fixed in the same institutions, the same prejudices, the same customs, so that mankind will be halted and hemmed in; that the mind will swing back and forth forever without producing fresh ideas; that man will waste his strength in futile and solitary trifling; and that, though in continual motion, humanity will cease to advance.

chapters.title: Chapter 22 — Why Democratic Nations Are Naturally Desirous Of Peace, And Democratic Armies Of War
paragraphs: And Democratic Armies of War

The same interests, fears and passions that keep democratic nations from revolution also keep them from war. The love of military glory and the revolutionary spirit are weakened together, and by the same causes. Property owners, who love peace, grow ever more numerous. Personal wealth, which war consumes so quickly, keeps increasing. Customs have become milder and hearts gentler, with that inclination to pity which equality of conditions produces, and a coolness of understanding that leaves men relatively untouched by the violent, poetic excitement of arms. All these causes work together to extinguish the military spirit. I think it can be accepted as a general and constant rule that, among civilized nations, warlike passions become rarer and weaker the more equal social conditions are. Yet war is something every nation is exposed to, democratic nations like any other. However much they prefer peace, they must be prepared to repel an attack; in other words, they must have an army.

Fortune, which has granted the inhabitants of the United States so many special advantages, has set them in the middle of a wilderness, where they have, one might say, no neighbors. A few thousand soldiers meet their needs. But this is a peculiarity of America, not of democracy. Equality of conditions, together with the customs and institutions that follow from it, does not free a democratic people from the need for standing armies, and those armies always have a powerful effect on its fate. It is therefore especially important to ask what the natural tendencies are of the men who make up these armies.

Among aristocratic nations, especially those where birth is the only source of rank, the army has the same inequality as the nation. The officer is a noble and the soldier a serf; the first is naturally called to command and the second to obey. In aristocratic armies, then, the ordinary soldier’s ambition is held within very narrow limits. The officer’s ambition has no unlimited range either. An aristocratic body is not only one step on the nation’s ladder of ranks; it also holds a ladder of ranks within itself, and its members stand one above another in a fixed and unchanging order. So one man is born to command a regiment and another a company. Once they reach the farthest goal of their hopes, they stop of their own accord and are content with their lot. In aristocracies there is, besides, a strong reason why the officer’s desire for promotion is weak. Among aristocratic nations an officer, apart from his army rank, also holds a high rank in society, and in his eyes the first is almost always just an addition to the second. A nobleman who takes up the profession of arms follows it less out of ambition than out of a sense of the duties his birth imposes on him. He joins the army to find honorable occupation for the idle years of his youth, and to bring back to his home and his peers some honorable memories of military life. But his main aim is not to gain property, distinction or power through that profession, since he already holds these advantages by right and enjoys them without leaving home.

In democratic armies every soldier may become an officer. That makes the desire for promotion universal and extends the range of military ambition without measure. The officer, for his part, sees nothing that would naturally and necessarily stop him at one grade rather than another, and each grade matters enormously to him, because his standing in society almost always depends on his rank in the army. Among democratic nations an officer often has no property except his pay and no distinction except military honors. So whenever his duties change, his fortune changes, and he becomes, in a sense, a new man. What was merely an accessory to his position in aristocratic armies has become the main thing, the foundation of his whole condition. Under the old French monarchy officers were always addressed by their titles of nobility; now they are always addressed by their military rank. This small change in the forms of speech is enough to show that a great revolution has occurred in the structure of society and of the army. In democratic armies the desire for advancement is nearly universal. It is ardent, stubborn and unending; every other desire reinforces it, and only death puts it out. Yet it is easy to see that, of all the armies in the world, those where promotion must come slowest in peacetime are the armies of democratic countries. The number of commissions is naturally limited, while the number of competitors is almost unlimited, and the strict law of equality bears on everyone alike. No one can advance quickly, and many cannot advance at all. So the desire for advancement is stronger there, and the chances of advancement fewer, than anywhere else. Every ambitious spirit in a democratic army therefore longs ardently for war, because war creates vacancies and justifies breaking the rule of seniority, which is the one privilege natural to democracy.

We thus reach a curious result: of all armies, democratic armies are the most eager for war, and of all nations, democratic nations are the fondest of peace. What makes these facts more remarkable still is that the principle of equality produces both these opposite effects at the same time.

All the members of the community are alike, and they constantly harbor the wish, and see the possibility, of changing their condition and improving their well-being. This makes them fond of peace, which favors industry and lets each man carry his own small undertakings through to completion. This same equality, on the other hand, makes soldiers dream of battlefields. It raises the value of military honors in the eyes of those who follow the profession of arms, and it puts those honors within everyone’s reach. In both cases the heart’s restlessness is the same, the appetite for enjoyment is just as insatiable and the ambition to succeed just as great; only the means of satisfying it differ.

These opposite tendencies in the nation and the army expose democratic communities to great dangers. When the military spirit leaves a people, the profession of arms at once ceases to be honored, and military men drop to the lowest rank among public servants. They are little respected and no longer understood. The opposite of what happens in aristocratic ages then takes place: the men who enter the army are no longer of the highest rank but of the lowest. Military ambition is indulged only when no other kind is possible. This creates a circle of cause and effect that is hard to escape. The best part of the nation avoids the military profession because it is not honored, and the profession is not honored because the best part of the nation has stopped following it. It is then no surprise that democratic armies are often restless, bad-tempered and dissatisfied with their lot, although their material condition is usually much better and their discipline less strict than in other countries. The soldier feels he holds an inferior position. His wounded pride either stirs his appetite for hostilities, which would make his services necessary, or inclines him toward revolutions, in which he may hope to win by force of arms the political influence and personal importance that are now denied him. The makeup of democratic armies makes this last danger very much to be feared. In democratic communities almost every man has some property to protect, but democratic armies are generally led by men with none, most of whom have little to lose in civil strife. The bulk of the nation is naturally far more afraid of revolutions than in aristocratic ages, but the army’s leaders are far less afraid of them.

Moreover, as I have just observed, the wealthiest, best educated and ablest men in democratic nations seldom take up the military profession. So the army, taken as a whole, eventually forms a small nation of its own, where minds are less broadened and habits coarser than in the nation at large. Now this small uncivilized nation holds the weapons and alone knows how to use them. Indeed, the peaceful temper of the community increases the danger a democratic people runs from the military and turbulent spirit of its army. Nothing is so dangerous as an army in the midst of an unwarlike nation. The whole community’s excessive love of quiet continually places its constitution at the mercy of the soldiery. It may therefore be said, speaking generally, that if democratic nations are naturally inclined to peace by their interests and tendencies, their armies constantly pull them toward war and revolution. Military revolutions, which are hardly ever to be feared in aristocracies, are always to be dreaded among democratic nations. These perils must be counted among the most formidable that threaten their future, and statesmen should give careful and constant attention to finding a remedy.

When a nation sees that it is troubled from within by its army’s restless ambition, the first idea that comes to mind is to give this awkward ambition something to aim at by going to war. I do not speak ill of war. War almost always broadens a people’s mind and raises its character. In some cases it is the only check on the excessive growth of certain tendencies that arise naturally from equality of conditions, and it must be regarded as a necessary cure for certain deep-rooted diseases to which democratic communities are prone. War has great advantages, but we must not flatter ourselves that it can reduce the danger I have just pointed out. It only suspends that peril, which comes back more fiercely when the war is over, because armies that have tasted military exploits are far more impatient with peace. War could be a remedy only for a people that always thirsted for military glory. I foresee that any military rulers who may rise in great democratic nations will find it easier to conquer with their armies than to make their armies live at peace after the conquest. There are two things a democratic people will always find very hard: to begin a war and to end one.

Again, if war has certain special advantages for democratic nations, it also exposes them to certain dangers that aristocracies need not fear to the same degree. I shall point out only two. War gratifies the army, but it hampers, and often infuriates, the countless multitude of men whose lesser passions need peace every day to be satisfied. So there is some risk that it will cause, in another form, the very disturbance it was meant to prevent. No long war can fail to endanger the freedom of a democratic country. This is not to say that after every victory one need fear that the victorious generals will seize supreme power by force, as Sylla and Caesar did; the danger is of a different kind. War does not always hand democratic communities over to military government, but it must always, and immeasurably, increase the powers of civil government. It must almost inevitably gather the direction of all men and the management of all things into the hands of the administration. If it does not lead to despotism by sudden violence, it prepares men for it more gently, through their habits. Anyone who wants to destroy the liberties of a democratic nation should know that war is the surest and shortest way to do it. This is the first axiom of the science.

One remedy that seems obvious, when the ambition of soldiers and officers becomes alarming, is to increase the number of commissions available by enlarging the army. This gives temporary relief but plunges the country into deeper trouble at some later time. Enlarging the army may have a lasting effect in an aristocratic community, because military ambition there is confined to one class of men and each individual’s ambition stops, so to speak, at a set limit, so that it may be possible to satisfy everyone who feels it. But enlarging the army gains nothing among a democratic people, because the number of aspirants rises in exactly the same proportion as the army itself. Those whose claims were met by the new commissions are immediately followed by a fresh multitude that no one could satisfy. Even those who were satisfied a moment ago soon begin to want further advancement. The same excitement reigns in the ranks of the army as among the civilian classes of democratic society, and what men want is not to reach a certain grade but to keep being promoted. These wants may not be very large, but they come back without end. So a democratic nation that enlarges its army only calms, for a time, the ambition of the military profession, which soon becomes even more formidable because more people feel it. I am of the opinion that a restless and turbulent spirit is an evil inherent in the very constitution of democratic armies and beyond hope of cure. The lawmakers of democracies must not expect to devise any military organization whose influence could calm and restrain the military profession. Their efforts would use up their strength before the goal was reached.

The remedy for the vices of the army is to be found not in the army itself but in the country. Democratic nations naturally fear disorder and despotism; the aim is to turn these natural instincts into well-considered, deliberate and lasting tastes. When men have at last learned to use freedom peacefully and profitably, and have felt its blessings; when they have developed a manly love of order and freely submitted themselves to discipline; then these same men, if they take up the profession of arms, carry these same habits and customs into it, without realizing it and almost against their will. The general spirit of the nation, infused into the spirit particular to the army, tempers the opinions and desires that military life produces, or suppresses them through the mighty force of public opinion. Teach the citizens to be educated, orderly, firm and free, and the soldiers will be disciplined and obedient. Any law that, in suppressing the turbulent spirit of the army, tended to weaken the spirit of freedom in the nation and to cast a shadow over the idea of law and right, would defeat its own purpose. It would do far more to help than to hinder the establishment of military tyranny.

After all, and despite every precaution, a large army in the midst of a democratic people will always be a source of great danger. The most effective way to reduce that danger would be to reduce the army, but that is a remedy not every nation has the power to use.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 — Which Is The Most Warlike And Most Revolutionary Class In Democratic Armies?
paragraphs: It is part of the essence of a democratic army, as I shall show later, to be very large in proportion to the population it belongs to. On the other hand, people who live in democratic times seldom choose a military life. Democratic nations are therefore soon led to abandon voluntary recruiting in favor of compulsory enlistment. Their social condition forces them to the latter, and it is easy to foresee that all of them will eventually adopt it. When military service is compulsory, the burden falls equally and without exception on the whole community. This too is a necessary result of the social condition of these nations and of their ideas. The government can do almost anything it likes, provided it addresses the whole community at once. It is the unequal distribution of the weight, not the weight itself, that usually provokes resistance. But since military service is shared by all citizens, the plain consequence is that each of them stays on active duty only a few years. So it is in the nature of things that the soldier in democracies merely passes through the army, whereas among most aristocratic nations the military is a profession that the soldier chooses, or has forced upon him, for life.

This has important consequences. Among the soldiers of a democratic army, some develop a taste for military life. But the majority were enlisted against their will and are always ready to go back home. They do not regard themselves as seriously committed to the military profession, and they are always thinking of leaving it. Such men do not take on the needs, and share only half the passions, that this way of life breeds. They adapt to their military duties, but their minds remain attached to the interests and duties that occupied them in civilian life. So they do not absorb the spirit of the army; rather, they bring the spirit of the community at large into the army and keep it there. In democratic nations the private soldiers stay most like civilians. The habits of the nation have the firmest hold on them, and public opinion has the most influence. It is chiefly through the private soldiers that a democratic army may be filled with the love of freedom and respect for rights, once these principles have been successfully instilled in the people at large. The opposite happens among aristocratic nations, where the soldiery eventually have nothing in common with their fellow citizens and live among them as strangers, often as enemies. In aristocratic armies the officers are the conservative element, because the officers alone have kept a close tie with civil society and never give up their intention of returning to it sooner or later. In democratic armies the private soldiers are in that position, for the same reason.

In these same democratic armies, by contrast, it often happens that the officers acquire tastes and needs wholly different from those of the nation. The explanation is this. Among democratic nations, the man who becomes an officer cuts every tie that bound him to civilian life. He leaves it for good and has no interest in returning. His true country is the army, since he owes everything he has to the rank he has reached in it. So he follows the army’s fortunes, rises or falls with it, and from then on directs all his hopes to that quarter alone. Because an officer’s needs differ from the country’s, he may passionately desire war, or work to bring about a revolution, at the very moment when the nation most wants stability and peace. There are nevertheless some causes that soothe this restless and warlike spirit. Ambition is universal and continual among democratic nations, but we have seen that it is seldom great. A man born into the lower classes of the community who has risen from the ranks to become an officer has already taken an enormous step. He has gained a foothold in a sphere above the one he occupied in civilian life, and he has acquired rights that most democratic nations will always regard as inalienable. *a He is willing to pause after such a great effort and enjoy what he has won. The fear of risking what he already has dampens his desire to gain what he does not yet have. Having overcome the first and greatest obstacle to his advancement, he accepts the slowness of his progress with less impatience. His ambition will cool more and more as the growing distinction of his rank teaches him that he has more to put at risk. If I am not mistaken, the least warlike part of a democratic army, and also the least revolutionary, will always be its senior commanders. [Footnote a: The position of officers is in fact much more secure among democratic nations than elsewhere. The lower a man’s personal standing, the greater the relative importance of his military grade, and the more just and necessary it is that the laws secure his enjoyment of that rank.]

But what I have just said about officers and soldiers does not apply to a numerous class that, in every army, fills the space between them. I mean the non-commissioned officers. This class, which played no part in history until the present century, is destined from now on, I think, to play a fairly important one. Like the officers, non-commissioned officers have broken, in their minds, every tie that bound them to civilian life. Like them, they give themselves to the service permanently, and perhaps make it even more exclusively the object of all their desires. But non-commissioned officers have not yet reached a firm and lofty post where they can pause and breathe more freely before going on to further promotion. By the very nature of his duties, which never change, a non-commissioned officer is condemned to an obscure, cramped, comfortless and precarious existence. So far he sees nothing of military life but its dangers. He knows nothing of it but its privations and its discipline, which are harder to bear than dangers. He suffers more from his present miseries because he knows that the structure of society and of the army allows him to rise above them. He may in fact obtain his commission at any time and step at once into command, honors, independence, rights and enjoyments. Not only does this object of his hopes seem immensely important to him, but he is never sure of reaching it until it is actually his. The grade he holds is by no means permanent. He is always entirely at the arbitrary pleasure of his commanding officer, since the needs of discipline imperiously require this. A slight fault or a whim can strip him in an instant of the fruits of many years of toil and effort. Until he reaches the grade he aspires to, he has accomplished nothing; only when he reaches it does his career seem to begin. A desperate ambition cannot fail to be kindled in a man who is goaded on without pause by his youth, his wants, his passions, the spirit of his age, his hopes and his fears. Non-commissioned officers are therefore set on war, on war always and at any cost. If war is denied them, they want revolutions that suspend the authority of established regulations, so that, helped by the general confusion and the political passions of the time, they can get rid of their superior officers and take their places. Nor is it impossible for them to bring about such a crisis, because their common origin and habits give them great influence over the soldiers, however different the soldiers’ passions and desires may be.

It would be a mistake to suppose that these various characteristics of officers, non-commissioned officers and men belong to a particular time or country. They will always appear, in every period and among all democratic nations. In every democratic army the non-commissioned officers will be the worst representatives of the country’s peaceful and orderly spirit, and the private soldiers the best. The private soldiers will carry into military life the strength or weakness of the national customs and will faithfully mirror the community. If the community is ignorant and weak, they will let their leaders draw them into disorder, either unwittingly or against their will. If it is educated and energetic, the community itself will keep them within the bounds of order.

chapters.title: Chapter 24 — Causes Which Render Democratic Armies Weaker Than Other Armies At The Outset Of A Campaign, And More Formidable In Protracted Warfare
paragraphs: Armies at the Outset of a Campaign, and More Formidable in Protracted Warfare

After a long peace, any army is in danger of being beaten at the start of a campaign, and any army that has been at war for a long time has a strong chance of victory. This truth applies with particular force to democratic armies. In aristocracies the military is a privileged career and is honored even in peacetime. Men of great talent, great accomplishments and great ambition enter it, and the army is in every respect level with the nation and often above it. We have seen, by contrast, that among a democratic people the better minds of the nation are gradually drawn away from the military profession to seek distinction, power and especially wealth by other paths. After a long peace (and in democratic ages periods of peace are long), the army is always inferior to the country itself. In this state it is called into active service, and until war has changed it, the country is in danger as well as the army.

I have shown that in democratic armies in peacetime, seniority is the supreme and inflexible rule of advancement. As I noted earlier, this follows not only from the structure of these armies but from the nature of the people, and it will always be so. Also, because an officer in these nations gets his standing in the country entirely from his standing in the army, and draws from the same source all the distinction and comfortable means he enjoys, he does not leave his profession, or get retired for age, until very near the end of his life. The result of these two causes is that when a democratic people goes to war after a long stretch of peace, all the leading officers of the army are old men. I speak not only of the generals but of the non-commissioned officers, most of whom have stood still or advanced only step by step. One may notice with surprise that in a democratic army after a long peace all the soldiers are mere boys and all the senior officers are in their declining years, so that the former lack experience and the latter lack vigor. This is a strong element of defeat, for the first condition of successful generalship is youth. I would not have ventured to say so if the greatest captain of modern times had not made the observation. These two causes do not act in the same way on aristocratic armies. Men there are promoted by right of birth far more than by seniority, so at every rank there are a certain number of young men who bring to their profession the full early vigor of body and mind. Also, since the men who seek military honors among an aristocratic people hold a settled position in civil society, they seldom stay in the army until old age overtakes them. After giving the most vigorous years of their youth to the career of arms, they retire of their own accord and spend the rest of their mature years at home.

A long peace not only fills democratic armies with elderly officers; it also gives all the officers habits of body and mind that make them unfit for real service. A man who has lived long in the calm, lukewarm atmosphere of democratic customs adapts poorly, at first, to the harder labors and sterner duties of war. If he has not entirely lost his taste for arms, he has at least taken up a way of life that unfits him for conquest.

Among aristocratic nations the comforts of civil life have less influence on the customs of the army, because there the aristocracy commands the army. An aristocracy, however deeply sunk in luxurious pleasures, always has many other passions besides its own well-being, and it will readily sacrifice that well-being to satisfy those passions more fully. *a
[Footnote a: See Appendix V.]

I have shown that in democratic armies in peacetime promotion is extremely slow. At first the officers bear this state of affairs impatiently. They grow excited, restless and exasperated, but in the end most of them resign themselves to it. Those with the most ambition and the most resources leave the army. The others adjust their tastes and desires to their small fortunes and eventually come to view the military profession from a civilian standpoint. The quality they value most in it is the comfortable means and security that go with it. Their whole idea of the future rests on the certainty of this modest provision, and all they ask is to enjoy it in peace. So a long peace not only fills an army with old men; it often gives the outlook of old men to those who are still in their prime.

I have also shown that among democratic nations in peacetime the military profession is held in little honor and followed without much zeal. This lack of public favor is a heavy discouragement to the army. It weighs on the spirits of the troops, and when war finally breaks out, they cannot at once recover their spring and vigor. Aristocratic armies have no comparable cause of moral weakness. Their officers are never lowered in their own eyes or in their countrymen’s, because, apart from their military greatness, they are personally great. But even if peace affected the two kinds of armies in the same way, the results would still differ. When the officers of an aristocratic army have lost their warlike spirit and their desire to rise through service, they still keep a certain respect for the honor of their class and an old habit of being the first to set an example. But when the officers of a democratic army no longer have the love of war and the ambition of arms, nothing at all is left to them.

I am therefore of the opinion that when a democratic people goes to war after a long peace, it runs a much greater risk of defeat than any other nation. But it should not be easily discouraged by its reverses, because the chances of success for such an army increase as the war goes on. When a war has at last, by its long duration, roused the whole community from its peaceful occupations and ruined its small undertakings, the same passions that made the people attach so much importance to keeping the peace will turn to arms. After war has destroyed every other kind of speculation, it becomes itself the great and only speculation, and all the ardent and ambitious desires that equality produces are directed to it alone. This is why the very same democratic nations that are so reluctant to go to war sometimes accomplish prodigious feats once they have taken the field. As the war draws more and more of the public’s attention, and is seen to make great reputations and great fortunes in a short time, the best spirits of the nation enter the military profession.
