All the enterprising, proud and martial minds, no longer of the aristocracy alone but of the whole country, are drawn in this direction. The number of competitors for military honors is huge, and war sends every man to his proper level, so great generals are sure to emerge. A long war has the same effect on a democratic army that a revolution has on a people: it breaks through regulations and lets extraordinary men rise above the common level. The officers whose bodies and minds have aged in peace are removed, or retired for age, or die. In their place a host of young men press forward, whose frames are already hardened and whose desires have been widened and inflamed by active service. They are set on advancement at any cost, and on constant advancement. Behind them come others with the same passions and desires, and behind these still others, limited by nothing but the size of the army. The principle of equality opens the door of ambition to everyone, and death supplies the openings for ambition. Death constantly thins the ranks, creating vacancies, closing and opening the career of arms.

There is, moreover, a secret connection between the military character and the character of democracies, which war brings to light. The men of democracies are naturally passionate in their eagerness to get what they covet and to enjoy it on easy terms. For the most part they worship chance, and they fear death much less than they fear difficulty. This is the spirit they bring to commerce and manufacturing, and the same spirit, carried onto the battlefield, leads them to risk their lives willingly in order to win the rewards of victory in a moment. No kind of greatness appeals more to the imagination of a democratic people than military greatness, a greatness of vivid and sudden brilliance, won without toil by nothing but the risk of life. So while the interests and tastes of the members of a democratic community turn them away from war, their habits of mind fit them to wage it well. Once roused from their business and their pleasures, they soon make good soldiers. If peace is especially harmful to democratic armies, war gives them advantages that no other armies ever have, and these advantages, however little felt at first, cannot fail in the end to give them victory. An aristocratic nation that, in a contest with a democratic people, fails to ruin the latter at the outset of the war always runs a great risk of being conquered by it.

chapters.title: Chapter 25 — Of Discipline In Democratic Armies
paragraphs: It is a very common opinion, especially in aristocratic countries, that the great social equality prevailing in democracies eventually makes the private soldier independent of the officer and so destroys the bond of discipline. This is a mistake, for there are two kinds of discipline, and it is important not to confuse them. When the officer is a noble and the soldier a serf, one rich and the other poor, the first educated and strong and the second ignorant and weak, the strictest bond of obedience can easily be established between them. The soldier is, so to speak, broken in to military discipline before he enters the army; or rather, military discipline is nothing but a heightening of social servitude. In aristocratic armies the soldier soon becomes deaf to everything but the orders of his superiors. He acts without reflection, triumphs without enthusiasm and dies without complaint. In this state he is no longer a man, but he is still a most formidable animal trained for war.

A democratic people must give up hope of ever getting from soldiers the blind, minute, submissive and unvarying obedience that an aristocratic people can impose on them without difficulty. The state of society does not prepare them for it, and the nation might risk losing its natural advantages if it tried to acquire advantages of this particular kind by artificial means. Among democratic communities, military discipline should not try to destroy the free play of the faculties. All discipline can do is direct it. The obedience it instills is less exact, but it is more eager and more intelligent. It is rooted in the will of the one who obeys; it rests not only on his instinct but on his reason. As a result, it will often tighten of its own accord when danger demands it. The discipline of an aristocratic army tends to slacken in war, because that discipline rests on habit, and war disrupts habit. The discipline of a democratic army, by contrast, grows stronger within sight of the enemy, because every soldier then sees clearly that he must be silent and obedient in order to win.

The nations that have achieved the greatest feats of war knew no other discipline than the kind I am speaking of. Among the ancients, only freemen and citizens were admitted into the armies. They differed little from one another and were used to treating each other as equals. In this respect the armies of antiquity may be called democratic, though they came out of the bosom of aristocracy. As a result, a kind of brotherly familiarity prevailed in those armies between officers and men. Plutarch’s lives of great commanders offer convincing examples. The soldiers were in the constant habit of speaking freely to their general, and the general listened to whatever the soldiers had to say and answered it. They were kept in order by words and example far more than by compulsion or punishment. The general was as much their companion as their chief. I do not know whether the soldiers of Greece and Rome ever carried the fine points of military discipline to the same degree of perfection as the Russians have. But this did not prevent Alexander from conquering Asia, or Rome from conquering the world.

chapters.title: Chapter 26 — Some Considerations On War In Democratic Communities
paragraphs: When the principle of equality is growing not only within a single nation but across several neighboring nations at the same time, as is now the case in Europe, the inhabitants of these countries come to resemble one another in their shared dread of war and their common love of peace, however different their languages, customs and laws. *a Ambition or anger may put weapons in the hands of princes, but to no purpose: a general apathy and goodwill calms them in spite of themselves, the sword drops from their grasp, and wars become rarer. The spread of equality in several countries at once also impels their various inhabitants alike toward manufacturing and commerce. Their tastes then grow alike, and their interests become so mixed and entangled that no nation can do harm to others without the harm coming back on itself. In the end all nations see war as a calamity, almost as severe for the conqueror as for the conquered. So in democratic ages it is extremely difficult, on the one hand, to draw nations into hostilities; on the other hand, it is almost impossible for any two of them to go to war without involving the rest. The interests of all are so interlaced, and their opinions and needs so much alike, that none can stay quiet when the others are stirring. Wars therefore become rarer, but when they do break out they spread over a wider field. Neighboring democratic nations not only become alike in some respects; they end up resembling each other in almost all. *b This likeness between nations has very important consequences for war.

[Footnote a: I hardly need point out that the dread of war shown by the nations of Europe cannot be put down solely to the progress of the principle of equality among them. Besides this permanent cause, several accidental causes of great weight could be named, and above all of them I would place the extreme exhaustion left behind by the wars of the Revolution and the Empire.]

[Footnote b: This is not only because these nations share the same social condition; it comes from the very nature of that social condition, which leads men to imitate one another and identify with one another. When the members of a community are divided into castes and classes, they not only differ from one another but have no taste or desire to be alike. On the contrary, each person tries harder and harder to keep his own opinions undisturbed, to hold on to his own distinctive habits, and to remain himself. The characteristics of individuals are very strongly marked. When the state of society among a people is democratic — that is, when there are no longer any castes or classes in the community and all its members are nearly equal in education and in property — the human mind moves in the opposite direction. Men are much alike, and any departure from that likeness annoys them, as it were. Far from trying to preserve what is singular in themselves, they try to shake it off, so as to merge with the general mass of the people, which in their eyes is the sole representative of right and of might. The characteristics of individuals are nearly obliterated. In the ages of aristocracy, even people who are naturally alike strive to invent imaginary differences between themselves. In the ages of democracy, even people who are not alike seek only to become so and to copy each other, so strongly is every man’s mind swept along by the general impulse of mankind. Something of the same kind can be observed between nations. Two nations with the same aristocratic social condition might remain thoroughly distinct and very different, because the spirit of aristocracy is to keep strong individual characteristics. But if two neighboring nations have the same democratic social condition, they cannot fail to adopt similar opinions and customs, because the spirit of democracy tends to make men alike.]

Suppose I ask why the Helvetic Confederacy made the greatest and most powerful nations of Europe tremble in the fifteenth century, while today that country’s power is exactly proportioned to its population. I see that the Swiss have become like all the surrounding communities, and those surrounding communities like the Swiss. Since numerical strength is now the only difference between them, victory necessarily goes to the largest army. One consequence of the democratic revolution going on in Europe, then, is to make numerical strength prevail on every battlefield and to force all small nations either to merge with large States or at least to adopt their policy. Because numbers decide victory, every people ought of course to strive by every means in its power to put the greatest possible number of men in the field. When it was possible to recruit a kind of troops superior to all others, such as the Swiss infantry or the French cavalry of the sixteenth century, it was not thought necessary to raise very large armies. But matters change when one soldier is as good as another.

The same cause that creates this new need also supplies the means of meeting it. As I have already observed, when men are all alike they are all weak, and the supreme power of the state is naturally much stronger among democratic nations than elsewhere. So while these nations want to enroll the whole male population in the ranks of the army, they also have the power to do it. The result is that in democratic ages armies seem to grow larger as the love of war declines. In the same ages, the same causes also change the way war is waged. Machiavelli observes in “The Prince” “that it is much more difficult to subdue a people which has a prince and his barons for its leaders, than a nation which is commanded by a prince and his slaves.” To avoid giving offense, let us read “public officials” for “slaves,” and this important truth applies strictly to our own time.

A great aristocratic people can neither conquer its neighbors nor be conquered by them without great difficulty. It cannot conquer them, because it can never gather all its forces and hold them together for any considerable time. It cannot be conquered, because an enemy meets small centers of resistance at every step, and these stop the invasion. War against an aristocracy is like war in a mountainous country: the defeated side keeps finding chances to rally its forces and make a stand in a new position. Among democratic nations exactly the opposite occurs. They easily bring their whole available force into the field, and when the nation is wealthy and populous it soon wins. But if it is ever conquered and its territory invaded, it has few resources left to call on, and if the enemy takes the capital, the nation is lost. The reason is easy to see. Each member of the community is isolated and extremely powerless, so no one in the whole body can either defend himself or give others a point to rally around. Nothing in a democratic country is strong except the state. Once the destruction of the army has broken the state’s military strength and the capture of the chief city has paralyzed its civil power, all that remains is a multitude without strength or government, unable to resist the organized power attacking it. I am aware that the creation of provincial liberties, and with them provincial powers, can lessen this danger, but that remedy will always be insufficient. After such a catastrophe, not only is the population unable to continue the fighting, but one may fear that it will not even be inclined to try. Under the law of nations accepted in civilized countries, the object of wars is not to seize the property of private individuals but simply to take possession of political power. The destruction of private property is resorted to only occasionally, as a means to that end. When an aristocratic country is invaded after its army has been defeated, the nobles will go on defending themselves individually rather than submit, even though they are also the wealthiest members of the community. For if the conqueror remained master of the country, he would strip them of their political power, to which they cling even more closely than to their property. They therefore prefer fighting to subjection, which to them is the greatest of all misfortunes, and they readily carry the people along with them, because the people have long been used to following and obeying them and, besides, have little to risk in the war. Among a nation where equality of conditions prevails, by contrast, each citizen has only a slender share of political power, and often none at all. On the other hand, all are independent and all have something to lose. They are therefore much less afraid of being conquered, and much more afraid of war, than an aristocratic people. It will always be extremely difficult to persuade a democratic population to take up arms once hostilities have reached its own territory. Hence the necessity of giving such a people the rights and the political character that can give every citizen some of those interests which make the nobles act for the public welfare in aristocratic countries.

The princes and other leaders of democratic nations should never forget that only the passion and the habit of freedom can hold up successfully against the passion and the habit of physical well-being. I can imagine nothing better prepared for subjection, in the event of defeat, than a democratic people without free institutions.

In the past it was usual to take the field with a small body of troops, fight small engagements, and carry out long, regular sieges. Modern tactics consist in fighting decisive battles and, as soon as a line of march opens before the army, rushing on the capital city to end the war with a single blow. Napoleon, it is said, invented this new system. But its invention did not depend on any one man, whoever he might be. The state of society in his time suggested to Napoleon his way of making war. That way succeeded because it was admirably suited to that state of society, and because he was the first to use it. Napoleon was the first commander to march at the head of an army from capital to capital, but the ruin of feudal society had opened the road for him. It is fair to believe that if that extraordinary man had been born three hundred years ago, he would not have got the same results from his method of warfare — or rather, that he would have had a different method.

I will add only a few words on civil wars, for fear of exhausting the reader’s patience. Most of what I have said about foreign wars applies a fortiori to civil wars. Men who live in democracies are not naturally inclined to the military character. They sometimes take it on when they have been dragged into the field by compulsion. But rising in a body and voluntarily exposing themselves to the horrors of war, and especially civil war, is a course that the men of democracies are not apt to take. Only the most adventurous members of the community agree to run such risks; the bulk of the population stays motionless. Even if the population were inclined to act, considerable obstacles would stand in its way. It has no old, well-established influence that it is willing to obey, no well-known leaders to rally the discontented as well as to discipline and lead them, and no political powers subordinate to the supreme power of the nation that could give effective support to resistance directed against the government. In democratic countries the moral power of the majority is immense, and the physical resources at its command are out of all proportion to those that could be combined against it. Therefore the party that occupies the seat of the majority, speaks in its name and wields its power, triumphs instantly and irresistibly over all private resistance. It does not even give such opposition time to exist but nips it in the bud. Those who seek to bring about a revolution by force of arms in such nations have no other resource than suddenly to seize the whole machinery of government as it stands, and a single blow can do that better than a war. For as soon as a regular war begins, the party that represents the state is always certain to win. The only case in which a civil war could arise is if the army split into two factions, one raising the standard of rebellion and the other remaining loyal. An army is a small community, very closely united, endowed with great vitality, and able to supply its own needs for some time. Such a war might be bloody, but it could not be long. Either the rebellious army would win over the government by the mere display of its resources, or by its first victory, and then the war would be over; or the struggle would take place, and then the part of the army not supported by the organized powers of the state would quickly either disband or be destroyed. It may therefore be accepted as a general truth that in ages of equality civil wars will become much less frequent and shorter. *c

[Footnote c: Remember that I am speaking here of sovereign and independent democratic nations, not of confederate democracies. In confederacies the preponderant power always resides, in spite of all political fictions, in the state governments and not in the federal government, so civil wars are in fact nothing but foreign wars in disguise.]
Book Four: Influence of Democratic Opinions on Political Society

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — That Equality Naturally Gives Men A Taste For Free Institutions
paragraphs: I would fulfill the purpose of this book only imperfectly if I showed which opinions and feelings the principle of equality suggests, and then closed without pointing out their general influence on how human societies are governed. To do this I will often have to go back over ground already covered. I trust the reader will still follow me down paths he already knows, since they may lead to some new truth.

The principle of equality makes men independent of one another. It gives them the habit and the taste of following only their own will in their private actions. They enjoy this complete independence all the time, toward their equals and in the dealings of private life. It inclines them to regard every authority with jealousy, and it soon puts the idea and love of political freedom into their heads. Men who live in such times lean naturally toward free institutions. Pick any one of them at random and search, if you can, his most deeply rooted instincts. Of all governments, you will find, the one he will most quickly imagine and most highly prize is the one whose head he has elected himself and whose administration he can control. Of all the political effects of equality of conditions, this love of independence is the first to strike the observer and to alarm the timid. Their alarm is not wholly misplaced, either, because anarchy looks more formidable in democratic countries than elsewhere. Citizens have no direct influence on one another. If the supreme power of the nation fails, the power that kept each of them in his place, disorder would seem bound to reach its peak at once. Every man would go off in a different direction, and the fabric of society would immediately fall to pieces.

Nonetheless I am convinced that anarchy is the least of the evils democratic ages have to fear, not the chief one. The principle of equality produces two tendencies. One carries men straight to independence and can drive them suddenly into anarchy. The other takes them to servitude along a longer, more hidden, but surer road. Nations easily notice the first tendency and are ready to resist it. The second sweeps them along without their seeing where it ends, and that is why it matters so much to point it out. As for me, I do not blame the principle of equality for making men hard to govern. That very quality is what I mainly approve of in it. I admire how it plants in the mind and heart of man a dim notion and an instinctive love of political independence, and so prepares the cure for the evil it causes. For this reason I am attached to it.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — That The Notions Of Democratic Nations On Government Are Naturally Favorable To The Concentration Of Power
paragraphs: Naturally Favorable to the Concentration of Power

Aristocratic nations came naturally to imagine secondary powers standing between the sovereign and his subjects. Their communities held individuals or families set above the common level, who seemed destined to command through birth, education and wealth. Men in democratic ages lack this idea naturally, for the opposite reasons. It can be brought in only artificially and kept only with effort. What they do grasp, almost without reflecting on it, is the idea of one central power governing the whole community by direct influence. In politics, as in philosophy and religion, the intellect of democratic nations is also especially receptive to simple, general ideas. Complicated systems repel it. Its favorite picture is a great nation of citizens who all fit the same pattern and are all governed by a single power.

Next to the idea of one central power, the notion that occurs most readily to men in ages of equality is uniform legislation. Each man sees that he is not very different from those around him. He cannot see why a rule that suits one person should not suit everyone else. Even the slightest privilege therefore offends his reason, and the faintest variation in a single people’s political institutions irritates him. To him, uniform legislation is the first condition of good government. In aristocratic ages, I find, the human mind knew almost nothing of a uniform rule binding equally on every member of the community; people either never thought of it or rejected it. On each side, these opposing tendencies of opinion end up as blind instincts and uncontrollable habits, so that they still guide men’s actions despite individual exceptions. The Middle Ages had an immense variety of conditions, and a certain number of people were then in exactly similar circumstances. Even so, the laws of the time gave each of them different duties and different rights. Today, by contrast, every power of government is being used to impose the same customs and laws on populations that so far have few points in common. When the conditions of men become equal within a people, individuals appear less important and society looms larger. Or, more exactly, each citizen is made like all the others and gets lost in the crowd, and nothing stands out except the great and imposing image of the people as a whole. The men of democratic periods are naturally led to think very highly of society’s privileges and very modestly of individuals’ rights. They are ready to grant that the interests of the first are everything and those of the second nothing. They will accept that the power representing the community has much more information and wisdom than any of its members, and that it has both the duty and the right to guide each private citizen as well as to govern him.

Look closely at our contemporaries and dig down to the roots of their political opinions, and you will meet some of the ideas I have just described. The agreement may perhaps come as a surprise, among men who so often disagree. Americans hold that in every State the supreme power ought to come from the people. Once that power exists, however, they can imagine hardly any limit to it, and they are ready to concede that it has the right to do whatever it likes. They have not the faintest notion of special privileges for cities, families or persons. It seems never to have occurred to them that the same laws might fail to be applied, with strict uniformity, to every part and every inhabitant. These same opinions are spreading further in Europe. They are even working their way into the nations that most vehemently reject the sovereignty of the people. Those nations trace the supreme power to a different source but attribute the same characteristics to it. In all of them the idea of intermediate powers is growing faint and being erased. The idea of rights belonging inherently to certain individuals is fast vanishing from men’s minds, and the idea that society at large is omnipotent and sole authority is rising to fill the space. As social conditions grow more equal and men more alike, these ideas take root and spread. Equality produces them, and they in turn speed equality along.

In France, the revolution I am discussing has gone further than anywhere else in Europe, and these opinions there have taken full possession of the public mind. Listen carefully to what the various French parties say, and you will find that every one has adopted them. Most of the parties condemn the government’s conduct, but all of them believe it should act without pause and meddle in everything that is done. Even the parties most opposed to each other agree on this. The unity, ubiquity and omnipotence of the supreme power, together with the uniformity of its rules, are the principal characteristics of all the political systems put forward in our age. They turn up even in the wildest visions of political regeneration, and the human mind chases them in its dreams. If private individuals come to these ideas spontaneously, princes feel their pull still more strongly. The ancient fabric of European society is being altered and dissolved. Sovereigns are forming new conceptions of what they can do and what they owe. They are learning, for the first time, that the central power they stand for may and should administer all the affairs of the whole community through its own agents, on a single plan. I will venture to say that no monarch in Europe had conceived this opinion before our time. It now sinks deep into the minds of kings and remains there amid every stirring of more restless thought.

Our contemporaries are therefore far less divided than people usually suppose. They argue endlessly about whose hands should hold supremacy, yet they readily agree about what that supremacy should do and what rights it has. All of them picture government as a single, simple, providential and creative power. Every other political opinion is unsettled, but this one stays fixed, unvarying and consistent. Statesmen and political philosophers embrace it, and the multitude seizes on it eagerly. Rulers and ruled alike pursue it with equal ardor. It is the first idea in their minds, and it seems inborn. It does not, then, spring from any whim of the human intellect. It is a necessary condition of mankind’s present state.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — That The Sentiments Of Democratic Nations Accord With Their Opinions In Leading Them To Concentrate Political Power
paragraphs: Opinions in Leading Them to Concentrate Political Power

If it is true that men in ages of equality readily take up the idea of a great central power, it cannot be doubted, on the other hand, that their habits and feelings dispose them to accept such a power and back it. A few words will show this, since I have already given most of the reasons. *a People in democratic countries have no superiors, no inferiors and no habitual or necessary partners in what they undertake. They easily turn in on themselves and think of themselves as separate beings. I made this point at some length when I dealt with individualism. As a result, it always takes an effort for such men to pull themselves away from their private affairs and attend to public business. Their natural leaning is to hand that business over to the one visible, lasting representative of the community’s interests, namely the state. They do not merely lack a taste for public business; they frequently lack the time. Private life in democratic periods is so busy, so feverish, so crowded with desires and labors, that each individual has almost no energy or leisure left for public life. I would be the last to claim that these inclinations cannot be overcome, since my main purpose in writing this book has been to fight them. My claim is only that today a hidden force is nourishing them in the human heart, and that unless they are checked they will smother it completely.
[Footnote a: See Appendix W.]

I have also had occasion to show that two things make democratic nations dread any violent disturbance: the growing love of well-being and the shifting nature of property. Often the love of public tranquility is the only passion such nations still have, and it grows more active and powerful in them in proportion as every other passion droops and dies. This naturally leads the members of the community to keep handing over further rights to the central power, or giving them up. That power alone seems to have a stake in defending those rights, and to use the same means for them that it uses for itself. In ages of equality, nobody is obliged to help his fellow men, and nobody has any right to expect much support from them. Everyone is therefore independent and powerless at once. These two conditions must never be looked at separately or run together, for they give the citizen of a democratic country quite opposite inclinations. His independence fills him with self-reliance and pride among his equals. His weakness makes him feel, now and then, that he needs help from outside. He cannot hope for it from any of them, since they are all powerless and unsympathetic. In this plight he naturally looks to the imposing power that alone stands above the general level of depression. His needs, and above all his desires, keep calling that power to his mind, until in the end he sees it as the only support his weakness can have, and a necessary one. *b This may go further toward explaining a common sight in democratic countries. The very men who cannot bear superiors will put up patiently with a master, and so show their pride and their servility together.

[Footnote b: In democratic communities only the central power has a stable position or lasting undertakings. Every other member of society is in ceaseless stir and change. Now, all governments by nature seek constantly to widen the range of their action. Such a government can hardly fail to succeed in the end, because it acts on a fixed principle and with a constant will, upon men whose position, ideas and desires keep shifting. Members of the community often strengthen the influence of the central power without meaning to. Democratic ages are periods of experiment, innovation and adventure. At such times a multitude of men are always engaged in difficult or novel enterprises, which they pursue alone, with no concern for their fellow men. They may be willing to grant, as a general principle, that the public authority should not interfere in private concerns. Yet each of them makes an exception for the particular concern he is working on. He asks for the authority’s help there and tries to use the government’s influence for his own advantage, while wanting to restrict it everywhere else. Suppose a large number of men make this same exception for a great variety of different purposes. The sphere of the central power then grows imperceptibly in every direction, although each of them wishes it to stay limited. A democratic government thus increases its power merely by lasting. Time is on its side, every incident helps it, and the passions of individuals unconsciously advance it. It may be asserted that the older a democratic community is, the more centralized its government will become.]

The more privileges dwindle and shrink, the more men hate them. Democratic passions would therefore seem to burn hottest just when they have the least fuel. I have already explained why. Where all conditions are unequal, no inequality is large enough to offend the eye. In the midst of general uniformity, though, the slightest difference is hateful, and the more complete the uniformity, the harder that difference is to bear. It is natural, then, that the love of equality should keep growing along with equality itself, and should swell on what it feeds on. This undying hatred, forever kindled anew, sets a democratic people against even the smallest privilege. It is especially favorable to a gradual concentration of all political rights in the hands of the state’s representative alone. The sovereign stands necessarily and unquestionably above every citizen, so he arouses no envy. Each citizen imagines that he is taking from his equals the prerogative he grants to the crown. A man of a democratic age very much dislikes obeying a neighbor who is his equal. He will not admit that such a person has greater ability than he does. He distrusts his fairness and resents his power; he fears him and holds him in contempt; and he loves to remind him, again and again, that both of them depend on the same master. Any central power that follows its natural tendencies courts and encourages the principle of equality, because equality remarkably eases, widens and secures the influence of a central power.

The same can be said of uniformity: every central government worships it. Uniformity spares the government an investigation into an endless number of small details. Those details would demand attention if rules had to be fitted to men, and men were not simply made subject to rules without distinction. So the government likes what the citizens like and naturally hates what they hate. In democratic nations, these shared feelings keep joining the sovereign and every member of the community in a single conviction, and they create a secret and lasting sympathy between them. The government’s faults are forgiven for the sake of its tastes. Public confidence is withdrawn only reluctantly, even amid its excesses and mistakes, and it comes back at the first call. Democratic nations often hate the people who hold the central power, but they always love the power itself.

I have thus arrived at one conclusion by two separate paths. I showed that the principle of equality puts into men’s heads the idea of a single, uniform and strong government. I have now shown that the same principle gives them a taste for it. The nations of our age are therefore moving toward governments of this kind. Their natural bent of mind and heart pulls them that way, and all they need to do to get there is not to restrain themselves along the road. In the democratic ages now opening before us, I believe that individual independence and local liberties will always be products of artificial contrivance, while centralization will be the natural form of government. *c
[Footnote c: See Appendix X.]

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — Of Certain Peculiar And Accidental Causes Which Either Lead A People To Complete Centralization Of Government, Or Which Divert Them From It
paragraphs: A People to Complete Centralization of Government, or Which Divert Them from It

All democratic nations are led by instinct toward the centralization of government, but they do not move toward it to the same degree. That depends on particular circumstances, which can either help or hinder the natural results of this social condition. These circumstances are very numerous, and I shall mention only a few. Where men enjoyed liberty long before they became equal, the tendencies that free institutions gave them resist, up to a point, the inclinations that equality produces. The central power may add to its privileges among such a people, yet the private citizens of that community will never lose their independence entirely. But suppose equality of conditions arises among a people that has never known freedom, or that stopped knowing it long ago. This is the situation on the Continent of Europe. Then the nation’s old habits suddenly join, as if by a natural attraction, with the new habits and principles that its social condition has produced. All powers seem to rush of their own accord toward the center. They pile up there with astonishing speed, and the state at once reaches the outer limit of its strength, while private persons sink just as suddenly into the deepest weakness.

The English who emigrated three hundred years ago to found a democratic commonwealth on the shores of the New World had all learned, in their mother country, to take part in public affairs. They knew trial by jury. They were used to freedom of speech and of the press, to personal freedom, to the idea of rights and the practice of asserting them. They brought these free institutions and manly customs with them to America, and the institutions protected them from the encroachments of the state. So among the Americans it is freedom that is old, and equality that is comparatively recent. In Europe the reverse is happening. There equality was introduced by absolute power, under the rule of kings, and had already soaked into the habits of nations long before freedom had entered their thinking.

I have said that among democratic nations the idea of government comes naturally to the mind as a single, central power, and that the idea of intermediate powers is unfamiliar to them. This applies above all to democratic nations in which equality has triumphed through a violent revolution. The classes that managed local affairs have been swept away suddenly by the storm. The confused mass that remains has neither the organization nor the habits needed to take over that administration. So the state alone appears able to take on every detail of government, and centralization becomes, so to speak, the unavoidable condition of the country. Napoleon deserves neither praise nor blame for gathering almost all the administrative power of France into his own hands. After the nobility and the upper ranks of the middle classes vanished so abruptly, these powers passed to him as a matter of course, and it would have been nearly as hard for him to refuse them as to take them. The Americans have never felt any such necessity. They went through no revolution and have governed themselves from the beginning, so they never had to ask the state to act as their guardian for a time. Thus the progress of centralization among a democratic people depends not only on the progress of equality but also on the way equality was established.

At the start of a great democratic revolution, when hostilities have only just broken out between the different classes of society, the people try to centralize the public administration in the hands of the government, so as to tear the management of local affairs away from the aristocracy. Toward the end of such a revolution, by contrast, it is usually the defeated aristocracy that tries to hand the management of every affair over to the state. It dreads the tyranny of a people that has become its equal and, not infrequently, its master. So it is not always the same class that works to enlarge the prerogative of the government. But as long as the democratic revolution lasts, there is always some class in the nation, strong in numbers or in wealth, that its own particular passions or interests push toward centralizing the public administration. This comes in addition to the hatred of being governed by one’s neighbor, a feeling that is general and permanent among democratic nations. We may note that today the lower orders in England are straining with all their might to destroy local independence and to move the administration from every point on the circumference to the center, while the higher classes are working to keep it within its ancient bounds. I venture to predict that a time will come when exactly the opposite will happen.

These observations explain why the supreme power is always stronger, and private individuals weaker, among a democratic people that has gone through a long and difficult struggle to reach equality than in a democratic community whose citizens were equal from the start. The Americans prove the point conclusively. The inhabitants of the United States were never divided by privileges. They have never known the relation of master and inferior. Since they neither fear nor hate one another, they have never felt any need to call in the supreme power to manage their affairs. The Americans’ lot is unusual. From the aristocracy of England they took the idea of private rights and a taste for local freedom, and they have kept both, because they had no aristocracy to fight.

At all times education enables men to defend their independence, and this is especially true in democratic ages. When all men are alike, it is easy to establish a single, all-powerful government, and instinct alone is enough to do it. But under the same conditions, men need a great deal of intelligence, knowledge, and skill to organize and sustain secondary powers. They need the same qualities to create, amid the citizens’ independence and individual weakness, free associations that are able to resist tyranny without destroying public order.

So among democratic nations the concentration of power and the subjection of individuals will grow in proportion to their ignorance as well as to their equality. It is true that in ages of imperfect civilization a government is often as short of the knowledge needed to impose despotism on a people as the people are short of the knowledge needed to throw it off. But the effect is not the same on both sides. However rude a democratic people may be, the central power that rules it is never entirely without cultivation. It readily draws to its own use whatever little cultivation the country has, and if necessary it can look for help elsewhere. So in a nation that is ignorant as well as democratic, a striking difference cannot fail to open up soon between the intellectual capacity of the ruler and that of each of his subjects. That completes the easy concentration of all power in his hands. The administrative function of the state keeps expanding, because the state alone is competent to administer the country’s affairs. Aristocratic nations, however unenlightened, never present the same spectacle, because among them instruction is spread almost equally between the monarch and the leading members of the community.

The pasha who now rules Egypt found a population of exceedingly ignorant and equal men, and he has borrowed the science and skill of Europe to govern them. The sovereign’s personal accomplishments are thus joined to the ignorance and democratic weakness of his subjects. Complete centralization has been established without any obstacle, and the pasha has made the country his factory and its inhabitants his workmen.

I think extreme centralization of government eventually saps society, and so, after some time, weakens the government itself. But I do not deny that a centralized social power can carry out great undertakings with ease, within a given time and at a particular point. This is most true in war, where success depends far more on the ability to move all of a nation’s resources to one place than on how large those resources are. Hence it is chiefly in war that nations want, and often need, to increase the powers of the central government. All men of military genius like centralization, because it adds to their strength. All men with a genius for centralizing like war, because it forces nations to combine all their powers in the hands of the government. Thus the democratic tendency that leads men without pause to multiply the privileges of the state and to narrow the rights of private persons is much faster and steadier among those democratic nations whose position exposes them to great and frequent wars than among all the others.

I have shown how the fear of disorder and the love of well-being lead democratic nations, without their noticing it, to enlarge the functions of the central government. It seems to them the only power that is, in itself, strong, enlightened, and secure enough to protect them from anarchy. I would now add that every particular circumstance that makes the condition of a democratic community unsettled and precarious strengthens this general propensity and leads private persons more and more to sacrifice their rights to their tranquility. A people is therefore never so ready to enlarge the functions of central government as at the end of a long and bloody revolution. Such a revolution has torn property from its former owners, shaken every belief, and filled the nation with fierce hatreds, clashing interests, and warring factions. At such times the love of public tranquility becomes an indiscriminate passion, and the members of the community tend to form an immoderate devotion to order.

I have already examined several of the incidents that can help promote the centralization of power, but the chief cause remains to be noticed. The foremost of the accidental causes that can draw the management of all affairs into the ruler’s hands in democratic countries is the ruler’s own origin and his own inclinations. Men who live in ages of equality are naturally fond of central power and willing to extend its privileges. But suppose this same power faithfully represents their own interests and exactly mirrors their own inclinations. Then the confidence they place in it knows no bounds, and they think that whatever they give to it they are giving to themselves.

Administrative powers will always be drawn toward the center less easily and less quickly under kings who are still connected in some way with the old aristocratic order than under new princes. These are the children of their own achievements, and their birth, prejudices, inclinations, and habits seem to bind them inseparably to the cause of equality. I do not mean that princes of aristocratic origin who live in democratic ages make no attempt to centralize. I believe they pursue that goal as diligently as any others. For them the only advantages of equality lie in that direction. But their opportunities are fewer, because the community, instead of readily complying with their wishes, often obeys them reluctantly. In democratic communities the rule is that centralization must increase to the degree that the sovereign is less aristocratic. When an ancient line of kings stands at the head of an aristocracy, the sovereign’s natural prejudices agree perfectly with those of the nobility. The vices inherent in aristocratic communities then run freely and meet no corrective. The opposite is true when the offspring of a feudal stock is placed at the head of a democratic people. His education, habits, and associations constantly lead the sovereign to adopt the feelings that inequality of conditions suggests, while the people, by their social condition, tend just as constantly toward the customs that equality produces. At such times it often happens that the citizens seek to restrain the central power far less as a tyrannical power than as an aristocratic one. They stand firm in defending their independence, not only because they want to stay free, but above all because they are determined to stay equal. A revolution that overthrows an ancient royal family in order to put men of more recent growth at the head of a democratic people may weaken the central power for a time. But however anarchic such a revolution may look at first, we need not hesitate to predict that its final and certain consequence will be to extend and secure that power’s prerogatives. The first condition for success in centralizing the supreme power in a democratic community, indeed the only one, is to love equality, or to make men believe that you love it. Thus the science of despotism, once so complicated, is simplified and reduced, as it were, to a single principle.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — That Amongst The European Nations Of Our Time The Power Of Governments Is Increasing, Although The Persons Who Govern Are Less Stable
paragraphs: Governments Is Increasing, Although the Persons Who Govern Are Less Stable

Looking back over what has been said so far, the reader will be startled and alarmed to find that in Europe everything seems to work toward an unlimited extension of the government’s prerogatives. It seems also to make everyone who enjoyed the rights of private independence weaker, more dependent, and more insecure. The democratic nations of Europe have all the general and lasting tendencies that push the Americans toward the centralization of government. On top of that, they are exposed to a number of secondary and accidental causes that the Americans do not know. It seems as though every step they take toward equality brings them closer to despotism. And in fact, if we simply look around us, we shall be convinced that this is so. In the aristocratic ages before our own, the sovereigns of Europe had been stripped of many of the rights that belong to their power, or had given them up. Less than a hundred years ago, in most European nations, numerous private persons and corporations were independent enough to administer justice, to raise and maintain troops, to levy taxes, and often even to make or interpret the law. The state has taken back for itself alone these natural attributes of sovereign power everywhere. In every matter of government it tolerates no intermediary between itself and the people, and in general business it directs the people by its own direct influence. I am far from blaming this concentration of power. I only point it out.

In the same period Europe had a great number of secondary powers, which represented local interests and administered local affairs. Most of these local authorities have already disappeared, and all are rapidly tending either to disappear or to fall into complete dependence. From one end of Europe to the other, the privileges of the nobility, the liberties of cities, and the powers of provincial bodies are either destroyed or close to destruction. In the last half-century Europe has lived through many revolutions and counter-revolutions, which have driven it in opposite directions. But all these upheavals resemble one another in one respect: they have all shaken or destroyed the secondary powers of government. The local privileges that the French did not abolish in the countries they conquered have finally given way to the policy of the princes who conquered the French. Those princes rejected every innovation of the French Revolution except centralization. That is the only principle they agreed to accept from such a source. My point is that all these various rights, wrested in our time one after another from classes, corporations, and individuals, have not been used to build new secondary powers on a more democratic basis. They have uniformly been concentrated in the sovereign’s hands. Everywhere the state gains more and more direct control over the humblest members of the community, and a more exclusive power to govern each of them in his smallest concerns. *a Almost all the charitable establishments of Europe used to be in the hands of private persons or corporations. Now they depend almost entirely on the supreme government, and in many countries that power actually runs them. The state takes on almost exclusively the task of giving bread to the hungry, help and shelter to the sick, and work to the idle, and it acts as the sole reliever of every kind of misery. Education, like charity, has become in most countries today a national concern. The state receives the child from its mother’s arms, and often takes it, in order to hand it over to official agents. The state undertakes to train the heart and instruct the mind of each generation. Public instruction follows a uniform course, as everything else does, and diversity, like freedom, is vanishing day by day. Nor do I hesitate to affirm that among almost all the Christian nations of our day, Catholic as well as Protestant, religion is in danger of falling into the hands of the government. It is not that rulers are overly jealous of the right to settle points of doctrine. But they take a firmer and firmer hold on the will of those who expound doctrine. They deprive the clergy of their property and pay them salaries. They divert the influence of the priesthood to their own use and make priests their own ministers, often their own servants. Through this alliance with religion they reach the inner depths of the human soul. *b

[Footnote a: This gradual weakening of individuals in relation to society as a whole can be traced in a thousand ways. From among these examples I shall choose one drawn from the law of wills. In aristocracies it is common to profess the deepest reverence for a man’s last testamentary wishes. Among the older nations of Europe this feeling sometimes even became superstitious. The power of the state, far from interfering with the whims of a dying man, gave full force to the smallest of them and secured for him a perpetual power. When all living men are enfeebled, the will of the dead gets less respect. It is confined within a narrow range, and beyond that range the supreme power of the laws annuls or checks it. In the Middle Ages, testamentary power had, so to speak, no limits. Among the French today, a man cannot divide his fortune among his children without the state’s interference. Having domineered over a whole life, the law insists on regulating the very last act of it.]

[Footnote b: As the duties of the central power grow, the number of public officials who represent that power must grow too. They form a nation within each nation, and since they share the government’s stability, they increasingly fill the place of an aristocracy.
In almost every part of Europe the government rules in two ways. It rules one part of the community through their fear of its agents, and the other part through their hope of becoming its agents.]

But this is still only one side of the picture. As we have just seen, the authority of government has spread throughout the sphere of all existing powers until that sphere can no longer hold it. It goes further and invades the domain that used to be reserved to private independence. In our time a multitude of actions that were formerly entirely beyond the control of the public administration have been placed under it, and their number keeps growing. Among aristocratic nations the supreme government usually contented itself with managing and supervising the community in whatever directly and visibly touched the national honor. In all other respects the people were left to follow their own free will. Among these nations the government often seemed to forget that there is a point at which the faults and sufferings of private persons affect the general prosperity, and that preventing the ruin of a private individual must sometimes be a matter of public importance. The democratic nations of our time lean toward the opposite extreme. It is evident that most of our rulers will not be content with governing the people collectively. They seem to think themselves responsible for the actions and private condition of their subjects. They seem to have undertaken to guide and instruct each of them through the various events of life, and to secure their happiness quite apart from their own consent. Private individuals, for their part, are more and more inclined to see the supreme power in the same light. They call on its help in all their needs, and they look to the administration as their mentor and guide.

I assert that in no country of Europe has the public administration failed to become not only more centralized but also more inquisitive and more minute. Everywhere it meddles in private concerns more than it did. It regulates more undertakings, and smaller ones, and every day it gains a firmer footing around, above, and about all private persons, to assist, advise, and coerce them. A sovereign used to live on the income of his lands or the revenue from his taxes. That is no longer so, now that his wants have grown along with his power. In circumstances that once forced a prince to impose a new tax, he now turns to a loan. Thus the state gradually becomes the debtor of most of the wealthier members of the community and centralizes the largest amounts of capital in its own hands. It draws small capital into its keeping by another method. As men mingle and conditions become more equal, the poor have more resources, more education, and more desires. They form the idea of improving their condition, and this teaches them to save. Their savings are daily producing an endless number of small capitals, the slow and gradual yield of labor, and these keep growing. But most of this money would be unproductive if it stayed scattered in its owners’ hands. This fact has given rise to a philanthropic institution that, unless I am mistaken, will soon become one of our most important political institutions. Some charitable persons conceived the idea of collecting the savings of the poor and putting them out at interest. In some countries these benevolent associations are still entirely separate from the state. But in almost all of them they clearly tend to merge with the government, and in some the government has replaced them. It has taken on the enormous task of gathering in one place, and lending out at interest on its own responsibility, the daily savings of many millions of working people. Thus the state draws the wealth of the rich to itself by loans, and it has the poor man’s mite at its disposal in the savings banks. The wealth of the country is perpetually flowing around the government and passing through its hands. The accumulation grows in step with the equality of conditions, because in a democratic country the state alone inspires confidence in private individuals, since it alone seems to have strength and permanence. *c So the sovereign does not limit himself to managing the public treasury. He interferes in private money matters. He is the superior, and often the master, of all the members of the community, and on top of that he takes the role of their steward and paymaster.

[Footnote c: On the one hand the taste for worldly well-being is perpetually increasing, and on the other the government gets more and more complete possession of the sources of that well-being. So men are following two separate roads to servitude. Their taste for their own well-being keeps them from taking part in government, and their love of that well-being makes them ever more dependent on those who govern.]

The central power not only performs by itself all the duties once discharged by various authorities, extending those duties and surpassing those authorities. It also performs them with more alertness, strength, and independence than it showed before. In our time all the governments of Europe have remarkably improved the science of administration. They do more things, and they do everything with more order, more speed, and less expense. They seem to be constantly enriched by all the experience they have taken from private persons. From day to day the princes of Europe hold their subordinate officers under stricter control, and they invent new methods for guiding them more closely and inspecting them with less trouble. They are not content to manage everything through their agents. They undertake to manage their agents’ conduct in everything. So the public administration not only depends on one and the same power, but is also more and more confined to one spot and concentrated in the same hands. The government centralizes its agency while it increases its prerogative, and the result is a twofold increase of strength.

When we examine the ancient constitution of the judicial power among most European nations, two things strike us: the independence of that power and the extent of its functions. Not only did the courts of justice decide almost all disputes between private persons, but in very many cases they acted as arbiters between private persons and the state. I am not speaking here of the political and administrative offices that courts had seized in some countries, but of the judicial office that all of them shared. In most countries of Europe there were, and there still are, many private rights, linked for the most part to the general right of property, that stood under the protection of the courts of justice. The state could not violate them without the courts’ sanction. This semi-political power was what chiefly distinguished the European courts from all others. All nations have had judges, but not all have given their judges the same privileges. Look at what is happening now among the democratic nations of Europe that are called free, and among the others as well. New and more dependent courts are springing up everywhere beside the old ones, for the express purpose of deciding, by an extraordinary jurisdiction, any disputed matters that may arise between the government and private persons. The older judicial power keeps its independence, but its jurisdiction is narrowed, and there is a growing tendency to reduce it to serving only as the arbiter between private interests. The number of these special courts keeps increasing, and so do their functions. Thus the government is more and more freed from the need to submit its policy and its rights to the sanction of another power. Judges cannot be done without, but at least the state chooses them and always holds them under its control. So between the government and private individuals they put the image of justice rather than justice itself. The state is not satisfied with drawing all affairs to itself. It acquires an ever-growing power to decide on all of them without restriction and without appeal. *d

[Footnote d: A strange sophism has been advanced on this subject in France. When a suit arises between the government and a private person, it is not to be tried before an ordinary judge, in order, they say, not to mix the administrative and judicial powers. As if giving the government the office of judging and administering at the same time were not mixing those powers, and mixing them in the most dangerous and oppressive way.]

Among the modern nations of Europe there is one great cause, separate from all those already pointed out, that perpetually helps to extend the agency of the supreme power or to strengthen its prerogative, though it has not received enough attention. I mean the growth of manufactures, which the progress of social equality fosters. Manufactures generally gather a multitude of men in one place, and new and complicated relations spring up among them. By their trade these men are exposed to sharp and sudden swings between plenty and want, and public tranquility is endangered during them. It may also happen that these occupations sacrifice the health, and even the life, of those who profit from them or who live by them. So the manufacturing classes need more regulation, supervision, and restraint than the other classes of society, and it is natural that the powers of government should grow in the same proportion as those classes.

This is a truth of general application. What follows concerns the nations of Europe in particular. In the centuries before our own, the aristocracy owned the soil and was able to defend it. Landed property was therefore surrounded by ample safeguards, and its owners enjoyed great independence. This gave rise to laws and customs that have lasted despite the division of land and the ruin of the nobility. Even now, landowners and farmers are still the members of the community who most easily escape the control of the supreme power. In those same aristocratic ages, to which all the sources of our history go back, personal property was of small importance, and those who held it were despised and weak. The manufacturing class was an exception within those aristocratic communities. It had no sure patronage, it was not protected from outside, and it was often unable to protect itself.

Hence a habit grew up of regarding manufacturing property as something of a particular nature. It was not owed the same deference or worth the same safeguards as property in general, and manufacturers were seen as a small class within the mass of the people, whose independence mattered little and who could properly be abandoned to the disciplinary passions of princes. When we glance through the codes of the Middle Ages, we are surprised to see how many royal regulations hampered manufactures, down to their smallest details, in those periods of personal independence. On this point centralization was as active and as minute as it can ever be. Since then a great revolution has taken place in the world. Manufacturing property, then only in embryo, has spread until it covers Europe. The manufacturing class has grown in numbers and wealth from the remnants of all other ranks. It has kept growing, and it is still growing in number, in importance, and in wealth. Almost everyone who does not belong to it is tied to it at some point at least. After having been an exception in society, it threatens to become the chief class, if not the only one. Nevertheless, the ideas and political precedents it produced long ago still cling to it. These ideas and precedents stay unchanged, because they are old, and also because they happen to fit perfectly with the new ideas and general habits of our contemporaries. Manufacturing property, then, does not extend its rights in proportion to its importance. The manufacturing classes do not become less dependent as they become more numerous. On the contrary, it seems as though despotism lurked within them and naturally grew with their growth. *e As a nation becomes more engaged in manufactures, it feels more strongly the lack of roads, canals, harbors, and other works of a semi-public nature that make it easier to acquire wealth. And as a nation becomes more democratic, private individuals become less able, and the state more able, to carry out works on such a scale. I do not hesitate to assert that the clear tendency of all governments at present is to take on the execution of these undertakings entirely by themselves, and by doing so they hold the population they govern in closer dependence every day.

[Footnote e: I shall cite a few facts in support of this remark. Mines are the natural sources of manufacturing wealth. As manufactures have grown up in Europe, the output of mines has become of more general importance, and good mining has become harder because of the division of property, which is a consequence of the equality of conditions. Most governments have claimed a right to own the soil in which the mines lie and to inspect the workings, which has never been done with any other kind of property. Thus mines, which were private property, subject to the same obligations and sheltered by the same guarantees as all other landed property, have fallen under the control of the state. The state either works them or leases them. Their owners are mere tenants, deriving their rights from the state. Moreover, the state almost everywhere claims the power to direct their operations. It lays down rules, requires particular methods to be adopted, and subjects the mining adventurers to constant supervision. If they resist, a government court of justice removes them, and the government transfers their contract to other hands. So the government not only owns the mines but has all the adventurers in its power. Nevertheless, as manufactures increase, the working of old mines increases too. New ones are opened, and the mining population spreads and grows. Day by day governments enlarge their underground dominions and populate them with their agents.]

On the other hand, as the power of a state grows and its needs increase, the state’s own consumption of manufactured goods keeps growing larger, and these goods are generally made in the arsenals or establishments of the government. Thus in every kingdom the ruler becomes the principal manufacturer. He gathers and keeps in his service a vast number of engineers, architects, mechanics, and craftsmen. Not only is he the principal manufacturer, but he tends more and more to become the chief of all the other manufacturers, or rather their master. Private persons grow more powerless as they grow more equal, so they can accomplish nothing in manufactures without combination. The government, naturally, seeks to bring these combinations under its own control.

It must be admitted that these collective beings, called combinations, are stronger and more formidable than a private individual can ever be, and that they bear less responsibility for their own actions. From this it seems reasonable that they should not be allowed to keep so much independence from the supreme government as might be granted to a private individual.

Rulers are all the more inclined to follow this policy because their own inclinations invite them to it. Among democratic nations the people’s resistance to the government can show itself only through association. So the government always looks with disfavor on associations that are not in its own power. It is also well worth noticing that among democratic nations the people themselves often feel a secret fear and jealousy toward these very associations, which keeps the citizens from defending institutions they need so much. The power and the longevity of these small private bodies, amid the weakness and instability of the whole community, astonish and alarm the people. The free use that each association makes of its natural powers is almost regarded as a dangerous privilege. Moreover, all the associations that spring up in our age are new corporate powers whose rights time has not sanctioned. They come into existence when the idea of private rights is weak and the power of government is unbounded, so it is no wonder that they lose their freedom at birth. Among all European nations there are some kinds of associations that cannot be formed until the state has examined their bylaws and authorized their existence. In several others, attempts are made to extend this rule to all associations. The consequences of such a policy, if it succeeded, are easy to foresee. Once the sovereign had a general right to authorize associations of every kind on certain conditions, he would soon claim the right to supervise and manage them, so as to keep them from departing from the rules he had laid down. In this way the state, having made all who wish to form associations dependent on it, would go on to reduce to the same condition everyone who belongs to associations already formed, that is to say, almost all the men now living. Governments thus take over, and turn to their own purposes, most of the new power that manufacturing interests have brought into the world in our time. Manufacturers govern us; they govern manufactures.

I attach so much importance to all that I have just said that I am tormented by the fear of having weakened my meaning in trying to make it clearer. Suppose the reader thinks the examples I have offered to support my observations are insufficient or badly chosen. Suppose he imagines that I have somewhere exaggerated the encroachments of the supreme power, and on the other hand that I have underestimated the sphere still open to the exertions of individual independence. I beg him to put the book down for a moment and to think for himself about the subjects I have tried to explain. Let him look closely at what is happening in France and in other countries. Let him ask those around him. Let him search himself. I am much mistaken if he does not arrive, without my guidance and by other paths, at the point to which I have tried to lead him. He will see that for the last half-century centralization has been growing everywhere in a thousand different ways. Wars, revolutions, and conquests have promoted it, and all men have worked to increase it. During the same period men have followed one another at the head of affairs with remarkable speed, and their ideas, interests, and passions have been endlessly varied. Yet all of them have, by one means or another, sought to centralize. This instinctive centralization has been the one fixed point amid the extreme changeability of their lives and thoughts.

Suppose the reader, having studied these details of human affairs, tries to take in the whole broad prospect. He will be struck by the result. On one side he will see the most settled dynasties shaken or overthrown. Peoples everywhere are violently escaping the rule of their laws and abolishing or limiting the authority of their rulers or princes. The nations that are not in open revolution are at least restless and excited, and all of them are animated by the same spirit of revolt. On the other side, in this very period of anarchy and among these unruly nations, the prerogative of the supreme government is growing without pause. It becomes more centralized, more adventurous, more absolute, and more extensive. The people fall continually under the control of the public administration. They are led, without noticing it, to give up to it some further portion of their individual independence, until the very men who from time to time overturn a throne and trample on a line of kings bow more and more servilely to the slightest dictate of a clerk. Thus two contrary revolutions seem to be under way in our day. One continually weakens the supreme power, and the other continually strengthens it. At no other time in our history has that power seemed so weak or so strong. But if we look more attentively at the state of the world, it appears that these two revolutions are closely connected, that they spring from the same source, and that after following separate courses they lead men at last to the same result. I may venture to repeat once more what I have already said or implied in several parts of this book. We must take great care not to confuse the principle of equality itself with the revolution that finally establishes that principle in a nation’s social condition and laws. Here lies the reason for almost all the phenomena that astonish us. All the old political powers of Europe, the greatest as well as the least, were founded in ages of aristocracy, and they more or less represented or defended the principles of inequality and privilege. To make the new wants and interests that the growing principle of equality brought in prevail in government, our contemporaries had to overturn or coerce the established powers. This led them to make revolutions, and it breathed into many of them that fierce love of disturbance and independence which all revolutions, whatever their object, always produce. I do not believe there is a single country in Europe where the progress of equality has not been preceded or followed by some violent changes in the state of property and persons. Almost all these changes have come with much anarchy and license, because they were made by the least civilized part of the nation against the most civilized. From this came the two contrary tendencies I have just pointed out. While the democratic revolution was glowing with heat, the men bent on destroying the old aristocratic powers that opposed it showed a strong spirit of independence. But as the victory of the principle of equality became more complete, they gradually surrendered to the propensities natural to that condition of equality, and they strengthened and centralized their governments. They had sought to be free in order to make themselves equal. But the more equality was established with the help of freedom, the harder freedom itself became to attain.

These two conditions of a nation have sometimes existed together. The last generation in France showed how a people could build an enormous tyranny within the community at the very time they were thwarting the authority of the nobility and defying the power of all kings. They taught the world at once how to win freedom and how to lose it. In our day men see established powers falling apart on every side. They see all ancient authority gasping its last and all ancient barriers tottering toward their fall, and the judgment of the wisest is troubled by the sight. They attend only to the astonishing revolution taking place before their eyes, and they imagine that mankind is about to fall into perpetual anarchy. If they looked to the final consequences of this revolution, their fears might perhaps take a different shape. For my part, I confess that I put no trust in the spirit of freedom that seems to animate my contemporaries. I can see well enough that the nations of this age are turbulent, but I do not clearly see that they are liberal. And I fear that, when the disturbances that rock the foundations of thrones have ended, the domination of sovereigns may prove more powerful than it ever was before.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — What Sort Of Despotism Democratic Nations Have To Fear
paragraphs: While I was in the United States, I noticed that a democratic state of society like the Americans’ might offer unusual openings for establishing despotism. After I returned to Europe, I saw how much most of our rulers had already exploited the ideas, feelings, and needs that this same social condition produces, in order to widen the reach of their power. This made me think that the nations of Christendom might in time suffer some kind of oppression like the one that once weighed on several nations of the ancient world. I have examined the subject more closely and thought about it for five more years. My fears have not lessened, but they now point at a different object. In earlier ages, no sovereign was ever so absolute or so powerful that he tried to administer every part of a great empire by his own agency, without intermediate powers to help him. None ever tried to bind all his subjects, without distinction, to a strict uniformity of regulation, or to tutor and direct each member of the community in person. Such an undertaking never occurred to the human mind. And had anyone conceived it, the lack of information, the flaws of the administrative system, and above all the natural obstacles that the inequality of conditions created would soon have stopped so vast a design from being carried out.
