When the Roman emperors were at the height of their power, the different nations of the empire kept very diverse customs and ways of life. Though all were subject to the same monarch, most of the provinces were administered separately, and they were full of strong and active municipalities. And although the whole government of the empire was concentrated in the emperor’s hands, and he remained, on occasion, the final arbiter in every matter, the details of social life and of private occupations were for the most part beyond his control. It is true that the emperors held an immense and unchecked power, which let them indulge every whim and use the whole strength of the state for that purpose. They often abused this power arbitrarily, taking away their subjects’ property or lives. Their tyranny weighed very heavily on a few people, but it did not reach the majority. It fixed on a handful of main objects and ignored the rest; it was violent, but its range was limited.

But it seems that if despotism were ever established among the democratic nations of our day, it would have a different character. It would be wider in extent and milder in manner; it would degrade men without tormenting them. I do not doubt that in an age of education and equality like ours, sovereigns could more easily gather all political power into their own hands, and could intrude more regularly and more forcefully into the sphere of private interests, than any sovereign of antiquity ever could. Yet the very principle of equality that makes despotism easier also softens its harshness. We have seen that the customs of a society grow more humane and gentle as men become more equal and more alike. When no member of the community has great power or great wealth, tyranny has, so to speak, no openings and no ground to work on. Since every fortune is modest, people’s passions are naturally confined, their imaginations are limited, and their pleasures are simple. This universal moderation moderates the sovereign too, and holds the excessive reach of his desires within certain bounds.

Apart from these reasons, which come from the nature of the social state itself, I could add many others that arise from causes outside my subject, but I will stay within the limits I have set for myself. Democratic governments may turn violent and even cruel in times of extreme agitation or great danger, but such crises will be rare and short. When I consider the petty passions of our contemporaries, the mildness of their customs, the breadth of their education, the purity of their religion, the gentleness of their morality, their orderly and hardworking habits, and the restraint that almost all of them show in their vices as well as in their virtues, I have no fear that they will find tyrants in their rulers, but rather guardians. *a I think, then, that the kind of oppression threatening democratic nations is unlike anything that has existed in the world before; our contemporaries will find no precedent for it in their memories. I am trying to find a word that would convey the whole idea I have formed of it, but I try in vain. The old words “despotism” and “tyranny” do not fit; the thing itself is new, and since I cannot name it, I must try to define it.
[Footnote a: See Appendix Y.]

I want to trace the new features under which despotism might appear in the world. The first thing that strikes the observer is an innumerable crowd of men, all equal and alike, constantly striving to win the small and trivial pleasures that fill their lives. Each of them, living apart, is like a stranger to the fate of all the others. His children and his close friends make up the whole of mankind for him. As for his other fellow citizens, he stands beside them but does not see them; he touches them but does not feel them. He exists only in himself and for himself alone; and if he still has his family, he can at least be said to have lost his country. Above this crowd stands an immense and protective power, which takes on the sole task of securing their enjoyments and watching over their fate. That power is absolute, detailed, regular, farsighted, and mild. It would resemble parental authority if, like that authority, its aim were to prepare men for adulthood. But it seeks instead to keep them in permanent childhood. It is quite content for the people to enjoy themselves, so long as they think of nothing but enjoyment. Such a government works willingly for their happiness, but it insists on being the only agent and sole judge of that happiness. It provides for their security, foresees and supplies their needs, makes their pleasures easier, manages their main concerns, directs their industry, regulates the passing down of property, and divides up their inheritances. What is left, except to spare them the effort of thinking and the trouble of living? In this way it makes the use of free will less useful and less frequent every day. It confines the will within a narrower range and gradually strips each man of the use of himself. The principle of equality has readied men for all this: it has inclined them to put up with it, and often even to see it as a benefit.

Once the supreme power has taken each member of the community in its strong grip in turn and shaped each one as it pleases, it stretches its arm over the whole community. It covers the surface of society with a web of small, intricate rules, detailed and uniform, which even the most original minds and the most energetic characters cannot break through to rise above the crowd. The will of man is not shattered but softened, bent, and guided. Men are seldom forced to act, but they are constantly held back from acting. Such a power does not destroy; it prevents things from coming into being. It does not tyrannize; it compresses, weakens, extinguishes, and dulls a people, until each nation is reduced to nothing better than a flock of timid, hardworking animals with the government as its shepherd. I have always believed that servitude of the regular, quiet, and gentle kind I have just described could be combined more easily than people commonly think with some of the outward forms of freedom, and that it could even take root under the wing of the sovereignty of the people. Our contemporaries are constantly pulled by two conflicting passions: they want to be led, and they want to remain free. Since they cannot destroy either of these opposing inclinations, they try to satisfy both at once. They imagine a single, protective, all-powerful government, but one chosen by the people. They combine centralization with the sovereignty of the people. This gives them some relief. They console themselves for being under guardianship by reflecting that they chose their own guardians. Each man lets himself be put in leading-strings because he sees that it is not a person or a class but the people as a whole who hold the end of his chain. Under this system the people throw off their dependence just long enough to choose a master, and then fall back into it. A great many people today are quite content with this sort of compromise between administrative despotism and the sovereignty of the people, and they think they have done enough to protect individual freedom once they have handed it over to the power of the nation at large. That does not satisfy me. It matters less to me who the master is that I must obey than that obedience is being extorted from me.

I do not deny, however, that a constitution of this kind seems to me infinitely better than one that would concentrate all the powers of government and then place them in the hands of an irresponsible person or body. Of all the forms democratic despotism could take, the latter would certainly be the worst. When the sovereign is elected, or is closely watched by a legislature that is truly elected and independent, the oppression he exerts over individuals is sometimes heavier, but it is always less degrading. For each man, even while oppressed and disarmed, can still imagine that in obeying he is obeying himself, and that all his other wishes are yielding to one of his own inclinations. In the same way, I can see that when the sovereign represents the nation and depends on the people, the rights and power taken from every citizen serve not only the head of state but the state itself, and individuals get something back in return for the independence they have given up to the public. So to create a representation of the people in every centralized country is to reduce the evil that extreme centralization can produce, but not to be rid of it. I grant that this leaves room for individuals to take part in the more important affairs, but their intervention is no less suppressed in the smaller and more private ones. We must not forget that it is especially dangerous to enslave men in the small details of life. For my part, I would be inclined to think that freedom matters less in great things than in small ones, if one could be sure of having the former without the latter. Subjection in small matters shows itself every day and is felt by the whole community without distinction. It does not drive men to resist, but it thwarts them at every turn, until they give up using their will at all. In this way their spirit is gradually broken and their character weakened. Obedience demanded only on a few important but rare occasions, by contrast, shows servitude only at intervals and puts its burden on a small number of men. It is pointless to call on a people made so dependent on the central power to choose that power’s representatives from time to time. This rare and brief use of their free choice, however important, will not stop them from gradually losing the ability to think, feel, and act for themselves, and so from sinking gradually below the level of humanity. *b I add that they will soon be unable to use the great and only privilege that remains to them. The democratic nations that introduced freedom into their political constitution at the very moment they were increasing the despotism of their administrative constitution have been led into strange contradictions. For managing small affairs, where plain good sense is all that is needed, the people are judged unequal to the task. Yet when the government of the country is at stake, the people are given immense powers. They are made, by turns, the playthings of their ruler and his masters — more than kings, and less than men. After trying every method of election without finding one that suits them, they are still astonished and still determined to look further, as if the evil they notice came far more from the constitution of the country than from that of the electoral body. It is indeed hard to see how men who have entirely given up the habit of governing themselves could succeed in choosing well those who are to govern them. And no one will ever believe that a liberal, wise, and energetic government can come from the votes of a subservient people. A constitution that was republican at its head and ultra-monarchical in all its other parts has always seemed to me a short-lived monster. The vices of the rulers and the ineptitude of the people would soon bring about its ruin. The nation, tired of its representatives and of itself, would then create freer institutions, or before long return to stretch itself out at the feet of a single master.
[Footnote b: See Appendix Z.]

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Continuation Of The Preceding Chapters
paragraphs: I believe it is easier to set up an absolute, despotic government among a people whose conditions are equal than among any other. And I think that once such a government was established among such a people, it would not only oppress men; in time it would strip each of them of several of the highest qualities of humanity. Despotism therefore seems to me especially to be feared in democratic ages. I believe I would have loved freedom in any age, but in the age we live in I am ready to worship it. On the other hand, I am convinced that everyone who tries, in the ages we are entering, to base freedom on aristocratic privilege will fail, and so will everyone who tries to gather and hold authority within a single class. Today no ruler is skillful or strong enough to found a despotism by restoring permanent distinctions of rank among his subjects. No legislator is wise or powerful enough to preserve free institutions unless he makes equality his first principle and his watchword. All of our contemporaries who want to establish or protect the independence and dignity of their fellow men must show themselves friends of equality, and the only worthy way to show it is to be so. The success of their sacred enterprise depends on this. So the question is not how to rebuild aristocratic society, but how to bring liberty out of the democratic state of society in which God has placed us.

These two truths seem to me simple, clear, and rich in consequences, and they lead me naturally to ask what kind of free government can be established among a people whose conditions are equal. The very constitution of democratic nations and their needs have this result: the power of government among them must be more uniform, more centralized, more extensive, more probing, and more effective than in other countries. Society as a whole is naturally stronger and more active, and individuals are more dependent and weak. Society does more and individuals do less, and this cannot be otherwise. So we should not expect private independence ever to reach as far in democratic countries as in aristocratic ones, nor is that to be wished. Among aristocratic nations the many are often sacrificed to the individual, and the prosperity of the greater number to the greatness of a few. The government of a democratic people needs to be active and powerful, and it is desirable that it should be. Our aim should not be to make it weak or sluggish, but only to keep it from abusing its capacity and its strength.

What did most to protect the independence of private persons in aristocratic ages was that the supreme power did not claim to take the government and administration of the community wholly on itself. Those functions were necessarily left in part to the members of the aristocracy. Since the supreme power was always divided, it never pressed with its whole weight, or in the same way, on each individual. Not only did the government not do everything through its own direct agency. Most of the agents who carried out its duties drew their power not from the state but from their birth, and so they were not under its constant control. The government could not make or unmake them in an instant at its pleasure, or bend them into strict uniformity to its slightest whim. This was a further guarantee of private independence. I readily admit that we cannot turn to the same means today, but I find certain democratic expedients that may take their place. Instead of placing in the government alone all the administrative powers taken from corporations and nobles, some of them can be entrusted to secondary public bodies, made up temporarily of private citizens. In this way the liberty of individuals will be more secure, and their equality will not be reduced.

The Americans, who care less about words than the French do, still call their largest administrative districts “counties.” But a provincial assembly performs part of the duties of the count or lord-lieutenant. In an age of equality like ours, it would be unjust and unreasonable to create hereditary officers, but nothing prevents us from substituting elected public officials to a certain extent. Election is a democratic expedient. It secures the independence of the public official from the government as well as, and even better than, hereditary rank can in aristocratic nations. Aristocratic countries are full of wealthy and influential people who can look after themselves and cannot easily or secretly be oppressed. Such people keep a government within general habits of moderation and restraint. I am well aware that democratic countries contain no such people by nature, but something comparable can be created by artificial means. I firmly believe that an aristocracy cannot be founded in the world again. But I think that private citizens, by joining together, can form bodies of great wealth, influence, and strength, matching the individuals of an aristocracy. In this way, many of the greatest political advantages of aristocracy would be gained without its injustice or its dangers. An association formed for political, commercial, or manufacturing purposes, or even for science and literature, is a powerful and well-informed member of the community. It cannot be disposed of at will, or oppressed without protest, and by defending its own rights against the government’s encroachments it saves the common liberties of the country.

In periods of aristocracy, each man is always so closely tied to many of his fellow citizens that he cannot be attacked without their coming to his aid. In ages of equality, each man naturally stands alone. He has no hereditary friends whose cooperation he can demand, and no class whose sympathy he can count on. He is easily got rid of, and he is trampled on with impunity. So today an oppressed member of the community has only one means of defending himself: he can appeal to the whole nation, and if the whole nation is deaf to his complaint, he can appeal to mankind. The only way he can make that appeal is through the press. Thus the liberty of the press is infinitely more valuable among democratic nations than among any others; it is the only cure for the evils that equality may produce. Equality isolates men and weakens them, but the press puts a powerful weapon within every man’s reach, one that the weakest and loneliest of them can use. Equality takes away a man’s support from his connections, but the press lets him call all his countrymen and all his fellow men to his aid. Printing has hastened the progress of equality, and it is also one of the best correctives to it.

I think that people living in aristocracies can, strictly speaking, do without the liberty of the press, but this is not true of those who live in democratic countries. To protect their personal independence, I do not rely on great political assemblies, on parliamentary privilege, or on declarations of the sovereignty of the people. All of these can, to some extent, be reconciled with personal servitude, but that servitude cannot be complete if the press is free. The press is the foremost democratic instrument of freedom.

Something similar can be said of the judicial power. It belongs to the essence of judicial power to attend to private interests and to fasten with a special liking on the small matters brought before it. Another essential quality of the judicial power is that it never volunteers its help to the oppressed, but is always available to the humblest person who asks for it. However weak the complainants may be, their complaint will force itself on the ear of justice and demand redress, for this is inherent in the very constitution of the courts. A power of this kind is therefore especially suited to the needs of freedom at a time when the government’s eye and hand are constantly reaching into the smallest details of human actions, and when private persons are too weak to protect themselves and too isolated to count on the help of others. The strength of the courts has always been the greatest security that can be offered to personal independence, and this is especially true in democratic ages. Private rights and interests are in constant danger unless the judicial power grows more extensive and stronger to keep pace with the growing equality of conditions.

Equality awakens in men several inclinations that are extremely dangerous to freedom, and the legislator should keep his attention constantly fixed on them. I will only remind the reader of the most important. Men living in democratic ages do not readily grasp the usefulness of forms; they feel an instinctive contempt for them, and I have shown elsewhere why. Forms arouse their contempt and often their hatred. Since they generally aim only at easy and immediate satisfactions, they rush toward what they desire, and the slightest delay exasperates them. This same temper, carried into political life, makes them hostile to forms, which constantly slow or halt them in some of their projects. Yet the very objection that men in democracies make to forms is what makes forms so useful to freedom. Their chief merit is to serve as a barrier between the strong and the weak, between ruler and people, to hold back the one and give the other time to look around. Forms become more necessary as the government grows more active and more powerful, while private persons grow more idle and more feeble. So democratic nations naturally need forms more than other nations do, and naturally respect them less. This deserves the most serious attention. Nothing is more pitiful than the arrogant disdain most of our contemporaries show for questions of form, since even the smallest of them have gained in our time an importance they never had before, and many of mankind’s greatest interests depend on them. I think that if the statesmen of aristocratic ages could sometimes scorn forms with impunity, and often rise above them, then the statesmen to whom the government of nations is now entrusted should treat even the least of them with respect, and should not neglect them unless necessity compels. In aristocracies, forms were observed superstitiously; among us they should be kept with a deliberate and informed deference.

Another tendency, which is entirely natural to democratic nations and extremely dangerous, leads them to despise and undervalue the rights of private persons. The attachment men feel to a right, and the respect they show it, is generally proportional to its importance or to how long they have enjoyed it. Among democratic nations, the rights of private persons are usually of little importance, recent in origin, and extremely precarious. The result is that they are often sacrificed without regret and almost always violated without remorse. But it happens that in the same period, and among the same nations, in which men naturally come to despise the rights of private persons, the rights of society at large are naturally extended and consolidated. In other words, men become less attached to private rights at exactly the time when it would be most necessary to keep and defend what little remains of them. It is therefore above all in the democratic ages we live in that the true friends of human liberty and greatness should constantly be on guard, to prevent the power of government from lightly sacrificing the private rights of individuals to the general carrying out of its plans. In such times no citizen is so obscure that it is not very dangerous to let him be oppressed, and no private right is so unimportant that it can be given up with impunity to a government’s whims. The reason is clear. If an individual’s private right is violated at a time when the human mind is fully impressed with the importance and sanctity of such rights, the harm is confined to the individual whose right is infringed. But to violate such a right today is to corrupt the customs of the nation deeply and to endanger the whole community, because the very idea of this kind of right keeps tending, among us, to be weakened and lost.

Certain habits, certain ideas, and certain vices are peculiar to a state of revolution, and a long revolution cannot fail to produce and spread them, whatever its character, its purpose, or the place where it occurs. When a nation has repeatedly changed its rulers, its opinions, and its laws within a short time, the men who make it up eventually acquire a taste for change and grow used to seeing every change brought about by sudden violence. So they naturally come to despise forms that prove ineffective day after day, and they do not bear patiently the rule of regulations they have so often seen broken. The ordinary ideas of fairness and morality no longer suffice to explain and justify all the innovations a revolution gives birth to every day. So the principle of public utility is summoned, the doctrine of political necessity is conjured up, and men grow used to sacrificing private interests without scruple and to trampling on the rights of individuals in order to accomplish any public purpose more quickly.

These habits and ideas, which I will call revolutionary because every revolution produces them, appear in aristocracies just as much as among democratic nations. But in the former they are often less powerful and always shorter-lived, because there they meet habits, ideas, defects, and obstacles that work against them. Consequently they vanish as soon as the revolution is over, and the nation goes back to its former political ways. This is not always so in democratic countries, where it is always to be feared that revolutionary tendencies, becoming gentler and more regular without disappearing entirely from society, will gradually turn into habits of submission to the administrative authority of the government. I know of no countries in which revolutions are more dangerous than democratic ones. Apart from the accidental and passing evils that always go with them, they may always create some evils that are permanent and endless. I believe there is such a thing as justifiable resistance and legitimate rebellion. So I do not assert, as an absolute rule, that men in democratic ages should never make revolutions. But I think they have particular reason to hesitate before embarking on one, and that it is far better to put up with many grievances in their present condition than to turn to so dangerous a remedy.

I will conclude with one general idea, which contains not only all the particular ideas expressed in this chapter but also most of those this book sets out to treat. In the aristocratic ages before our own, there were private persons of great power, and a social authority of extreme weakness. The outline of society itself was hard to make out and was constantly confused with the various powers that ruled the community. The main efforts of the men of those times had to go into strengthening, enlarging, and securing the supreme power, and, on the other side, into confining individual independence within narrower limits and subordinating private interests to the public interest. Other dangers and other cares await the men of our age. Among most modern nations, the government, whatever its origin, its constitution, or its name, has become almost all-powerful, and private persons are sinking more and more into the lowest stage of weakness and dependence. In the older society, everything was different: unity and uniformity were found nowhere. In modern society, everything threatens to become so alike that the distinctive traits of each individual will soon be lost entirely in the general appearance of the world. Our forefathers were always inclined to misuse the idea that private rights ought to be respected. We, for our part, are naturally inclined to exaggerate the idea that the interest of a private individual ought always to give way to the interest of the many. The political world has been transformed, and new remedies must now be sought for new disorders. These seem to me the main objects for legislators in the ages we are now entering: to set wide but clear and settled limits on the action of the government; to give private persons certain rights and secure their undisputed enjoyment of them; to enable the individual to keep whatever independence, strength, and original power he still has; and to raise him up beside society at large and sustain him in that position. It would seem that the rulers of our time want only to use men in order to make things great. I wish they would try a little more to make men great. I wish they would value the work less and the worker more, and never forget that a nation cannot long remain strong when each of its members is weak, and that no form or combination of social order has yet been devised that can make an energetic people out of a community of timid and enfeebled citizens.

I see two opposite ideas among our contemporaries, and both are equally harmful. One group of men can see nothing in the principle of equality except the anarchic tendencies it produces. They dread their own free will; they fear themselves. Other thinkers, fewer in number but better informed, take a different view. Besides the path that runs from the principle of equality to anarchy, they have at last found the road that seems to lead men to inevitable servitude. They shape their souls in advance to this necessary condition, and, despairing of staying free, they already bow in their hearts to the master who will soon appear. The first group give up freedom because they think it dangerous, the second because they think it impossible. Had I held the second conviction, I would not have written this book; I would have limited myself to grieving in secret over the fate of mankind. I have tried to point out the dangers that the principle of equality poses to human independence because I firmly believe these dangers are the most formidable, and the least foreseen, of all those the future holds in store. But I do not think they are insurmountable. Men living in the democratic ages we are entering naturally have a taste for independence. They are naturally impatient of regulation, and they tire even of the permanence of the condition they themselves prefer. They are fond of power, but they tend to despise and hate those who wield it, and by their own mobility and insignificance they easily slip out of its grasp. These inclinations will always show themselves, because they originate in the foundations of society, which will not change. For a long time they will prevent any despotism from being established, and they will supply new weapons to each generation that struggles on behalf of human liberty. Let us then look to the future with that healthy fear which makes men stand watch and guard for freedom, and not with that faint and idle terror which depresses and weakens the heart.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — General Survey Of The Subject
paragraphs: Before I close forever the subject that has held me so long, I would gladly take a last look over all the different features of modern society and finally weigh the general influence that the principle of equality will have on the fate of mankind. But the difficulty of the task stops me. Faced with so great an object, my sight is clouded and my reason fails. The society of the modern world, which I have tried to describe and now try to judge, has only just come into existence. Time has not yet given it its final shape. The great revolution that created it is not yet over, and amid the events of our day it is almost impossible to tell what will pass away with the revolution itself and what will outlast it. The world that is rising is still half burdened with the remains of the world that is sinking into decay. Amid the vast confusion of human affairs, no one can say how much of the old institutions and former customs will survive, or how much will disappear entirely. The revolution now under way in the social condition, the laws, the opinions, and the feelings of men is still very far from over. Even so, its results already cannot be compared with anything the world has seen before. I go back age by age to the most distant antiquity and find nothing like what is happening before my eyes. Since the past no longer lights the way into the future, the human mind wanders in the dark. Still, in the midst of a prospect so wide, so new, and so confused, some of the more prominent features can already be made out and pointed to. The good things and the evils of life are more evenly spread across the world. Great wealth tends to vanish and small fortunes to multiply. Desires and satisfactions increase, but extraordinary prosperity and hopeless poverty are equally unknown. The feeling of ambition is universal, but its scope is seldom large. Each individual stands apart in lonely weakness, while society as a whole is active, farsighted, and powerful. What private persons accomplish is insignificant; what the state accomplishes is immense. There is little energy of character, but customs are mild and laws are humane. There are few examples of lofty heroism or of the highest, brightest, and purest virtues, but men’s habits are orderly, violence is rare, and cruelty is almost unknown. Human life grows longer and property more secure. Life is not adorned with brilliant trophies, but it is very easy and peaceful. Few pleasures are either very refined or very coarse, and highly polished manners are as uncommon as great brutality of taste. One finds neither men of great learning nor communities of extreme ignorance. Genius grows rarer and information more widespread. The human mind is moved forward by the small efforts of all mankind combined, not by the strenuous activity of certain men. There is less perfection but more abundance in everything the arts produce. The ties of race, rank, and country are loosened, and the great bond of humanity is strengthened. If I try to find the most general and most prominent of all these features, I will see that what is happening to men’s fortunes appears in a thousand other forms. Almost all extremes are softened or blunted. Everything that stood out most is replaced by some middle term, at once less lofty and less low, less brilliant and less obscure, than what the world had known before.

When I look over this countless multitude of beings, formed in one another’s likeness, among whom nothing rises and nothing falls, the sight of such universal uniformity saddens and chills me, and I am tempted to regret the state of society that has ceased to exist. When the world was full of men of great importance and extreme insignificance, of great wealth and extreme poverty, of great learning and extreme ignorance, I turned away from the latter and fixed my attention on the former alone, who pleased my sympathies. But I admit that this pleasure came from my own weakness. Because I cannot see everything around me at once, I am able to pick out and set apart the objects of my preference from among so many others. It is not so with that almighty and eternal Being whose gaze necessarily takes in all created things, and who sees mankind and man distinctly, though at the same moment. We may naturally believe that what most pleases the Creator and Preserver of men is not the singular prosperity of the few but the greater well-being of all. What seems to me a decline in man is, in His eyes, an advance; what grieves me is acceptable to Him. A state of equality is perhaps less lofty, but it is more just, and its justice makes up its greatness and its beauty. I would try, then, to raise myself to this standpoint of divine contemplation, and from there to view and judge the concerns of men.

No one on earth can yet say, absolutely and in general, that the new state of the world is better than the old one. But it is already easy to see that it is different. Some vices and some virtues were so bound up with the constitution of an aristocratic nation, and are so contrary to the character of a modern people, that they can never be instilled into it. Some good tendencies and some bad inclinations that the former never knew are natural to the latter. Some ideas come spontaneously to the imagination of one that are wholly repugnant to the mind of the other. They are like two distinct orders of human beings, each with its own merits and defects, its own advantages and its own evils. So we must take care not to judge the state of society now coming into existence by ideas drawn from a state of society that no longer exists. These two states are so different in structure that they cannot be compared justly or fairly. It would hardly be more reasonable to demand of our contemporaries the particular virtues that arose from the social condition of their forefathers, since that social condition has itself fallen and has dragged down, in one indiscriminate ruin, the good and the evil that belonged to it.

But so far these things are only imperfectly understood. I find that a great number of my contemporaries set out to make a selection from among the institutions, opinions, and ideas that arose from the aristocratic constitution of society as it was. They would gladly give up some of these elements, but they would keep the rest and transplant them into their new world. I fear that such men are wasting their time and strength in efforts that are virtuous but unprofitable. The goal is not to keep the particular advantages that inequality of conditions gave to mankind, but to secure the new benefits that equality can offer. We should not try to make ourselves like our ancestors, but strive to work out the kind of greatness and happiness that is our own. As for me, I now look back from the far end of my task and see from a distance, but all at once, the various objects that drew my closer attention along the way. I am full of fears and of hopes. I see great dangers that can be warded off, and great evils that can be avoided or lessened. And I hold more firmly to the belief that democratic nations need only will it in order to be virtuous and prosperous. I know that many of my contemporaries maintain that nations are never their own masters here below, and that they necessarily obey some unyielding and unthinking power that arises from earlier events, from their race, or from the soil and climate of their country. Such doctrines are false and cowardly, and they can never produce anything but feeble men and timid nations. Providence has not made mankind wholly independent or wholly free. It is true that a fatal circle is drawn around every man, which he cannot cross. But within the wide bounds of that circle he is powerful and free, and what is true of man is true of communities. The nations of our time cannot prevent conditions from becoming equal. But it depends on themselves whether the principle of equality leads them to servitude or to freedom, to knowledge or to barbarism, to prosperity or to wretchedness.
